No. 1. 
Vir. Hudson to the Karl of Clarendon.—(Recetved December 18.) 


(No, 119. Confidential.) 
My Lord, . Turin, December 15, 1854, 530 A.M. 


| HAD the honour to receive yesterday, at a_quarter past 2 P.M, your 
Lordship’s despatch marked Seeret and Confidential, No. 76, of the Bth instant, 
instructing me to ascertain confidentially the views of the Piedmontese Govern- 
ment as to their disposition to accede to the Treaty of Alliance between Great 
Britain and France of the Oth Apu, 1854; and, should they be favourable, to 
propose (in conjunction with my French colleague) to the Minister for Foreign 
‘Affairs to sign the declaration which your Lordship transmitted to me. 

Yesterday | was in conference with the Charge d’Affaires of France upon 
your Lordshi its instructions, when the Minister for Foreign Affairs entered my 
room, and 1 then read to him your Lordship’s: despatch (marked No. 76); and 
the Charge d'Afiaires of France then communicated to him the contents of a 
despatch from M. Drouyn de Lhuys, whieh, m substance, is identical with that 
addressed to me by your Lordship. 

The Minister for Foreign Afiuirs caid that at 6 o'clock in the afternoon he 
would take the King’s pleasure: upon the subject, and would receive us at 
) o'clock at night. 

‘At that hour 1 proceeded with the Count de Guitout to the Department of 
Foreign Affairs, and there found the President of the Council, and the Ministers 
for Foreign Affairs, of War, and of the Interior, waiting to receive Us. 

The Minister for Foreign Affairs said that the King was disposed to accede 
to the ‘Treaty of Alliance of the 10th April on certain conditions; but that there 
were two proposals to consider : 

The first, the accession to the Treaty of the 10th April; 

The second, the dispateh of a corps of 10,000 men to the Crimea. 

That it was the opinion of the King’s Government that it would greatly 
simplify matters ‘¢ two Conventions were drawn Up on those two separate 
proposils, and that both Conventions should be signed simultancously. 

The first Convention wis political ; the second military. 

With regard to the first, whieh naturally entailed the second, they desired 
to point out that the feeling of the King was against subsidizing his troops, 85 
was also that of the Government and of the country. But they considered they 
could arrive at the point desired by the Government of Great Britam in another 
and : beeen manner to it; that ns (the Sardinian Government) could

increase by one-half the number of men desired by Great Britain, and would be 
prepared to send 15,000 instead of 10,000 men; and would dispatch to the 
Crimea the entire force within less than one month from the present date, on a 
condition which I shall state in its proper place in this despatch. 

Politically speaking, they renounced all intention of putting forward any 
pretension or claim to territorial aggrandizement; that they accepted the war 
on the same grounds as Great Britain and France: but entering into that war on 
those grounds, they naturally expected to take such a stand in the general 
questions which would arise after the conclusion of the war, as would be due to 
parties who had borne their share in the struggle. 

That one of the main difficulties they would have to contend with at home 
would be the feeling of discontent which would be engendered by placing them- 
selves in the same line as Austria, from whom Sardinia had recently suffered a 
series of unmerited and unjustifiable insults, breach of treaty stipulations and 
of international law, and with whom they barely maintain diplomatic relations. 

That nevertheless they were quite prepared to stand whatever odium might 
arise from that source of public discontent, were prepared to use their best efforts to 
repel all attempts to revolutionize Italy on the part of demagogues or of foreign 
States, and were determined to do their duty to the great principles which had 
moved the allied Governments to take up arms against Russia. 

They therefore entertained the just expectation that if they accepted the 
Treaty of the 10th April, and if they sent 15,000 of their best troops to fight 
alongside of the allied armies, they would be entitled to some political conside- 
ration, and, considering the financial condition of Sardinia, to some assistance. 

They proposed, then, to accede to the Treaty of the 10th April, with the 
andeatiudine that Great Britain and France should use their best efforts to 
itiduce the Government of Austria to undo the injustice of the Act of Seques- 
tration ; because the moment that they (the Sardinian Government) acceded 
to the Treaty of the 10th April, they guve the strongest possible guarantee 
with regard to their future political conduct: for Austria had declared that she 
used the measure of sequestration as a measure of protection, prevention, and 
surely against revolutionary attempts on the ie of Piedmont. 

This pretext, therefore, fell to the ground, and was no longer tenable the 
instant that Piedmont joined her powers to the allies, and sent nearly half her 
army to fight in the same cause in which Austria is embarked, 

They thought that Great Britain and France would feel no difficulty in 
urging Austria to be just, nor in accepting another proposition, namely, to adopt 
an Article which should merely stipulate that the condition of Italy should be 
taken into consideration at the conclusion of this war. 

Their object in desiring this stipulation is to be able to assure the Italians 
that they are not forgotten, and that the Sardmian Government go into this 
war from no selfish motive; and a knowledge of this at the proper time would 
tend greatly to disarm revolutionary attempts in Italy. 

Militarily speaking, the Sardinian Government could not accept subsidies ; 
the point of honour of the King and of his subjects is so utterly against: it. 

They therefore propose to send 15,000 men at their own expense (transport 
in part not leing included) to the Crimea, in such proportion of the three arms 
as Her Majesty’s Government deem best suited to carry on the war with the 
ereatest efficiency. 

They propose to borrow 2,000,0001. sterling of Great Britain, at 3 per cent. 
per annum, to be drawn and repaid in such manner as may be agreed upon. That 
this loan, if granted, saves the point of honour to the Sovereign and to the 
people of Sardinia, on the score of subsidies, and will subject the British 

overnment to no absolute loss, as would be the case with subsidies. 

They desire to stipulate for the free transport of part of the.15,000 men ; 
they on their part using the means at their disposal, which are scanty and 
almost confined tothe two stenm-frigates, the * Carlo Alberto” and “ Governolo,” 
capable of carrying about 1,800 men. 

They desire that the British Commissariat shall supply rations to the 
Sardinian contingent, they (the Sardinian Government) paying for the same 
at a rate to be agreed upon, all other expenses in the field being defrayed by 
the Sardinian Treasury. 

These proposals having been discussed, were then reduced to writing, and I 
have the honour to imelose— 


a 


1. A memorandum upon the points which relate to the political part of this 
question ; and, 

2. The observations of the Sardinian Government to the proposal of Her 
Majesty’s Government to send a contingent of Piedmontese troops to the 
Crimea, to be there placed under the ordera of Her Majesty’s Commander-in- 
chief. 

These two papers, if their tenour is accepted, will serve as the bases of the 
Conventions with Great Britain and France, which the Sardiman Government 
are ready to accept. 

The Chargé d’ Affaires of France will communicate copies of these papers 
to the Imperial Government by this oceasion. 

I have, &c., 
(Signed) JAMES HUDSON.

The Earl of Clarendon to Mr. Hudson. 


(No. 86. Secret and Confidential.) 
Sir, Foreign Office, December 28, 1854. 

YOUR despatch No. 119, marked Seeret and Confidential, has been 
reecived and laid before the Queen. Stal) i 

Her Majesty's Government learn with sincere satisfaction that the Pied- 
montese Government have cordially responded to the mvitation fo accede to 
the ‘Treaty of April 10, between England and Franee, and have announced 
their readiness to send an army of 15,000 men to the Crimea, 

The conditions upon which the Piedmontese Government prapose to accede 
to the Treaty have been anxiously considered by Ter Majesty s Government, 
and | shall now state to you the result of their deliberations. ; ae 

As rezards the transport of the Piedimontese troops and the Commissariat 
arrangements for supplying them at the seat of war, Her Majesty s Government 
anticipate no material difficulty; but with respect to a loan of 2,000,000 at 
3 per cent. | have to observe that it would entail considerable expense on this 
~quntry, us, at the present value of money a loan could not he raised here by 
Her Majesty's Government at a rate of interest so low a8 3 per cent., and I 
have further to remark that a loan of 2 000,001 appears to be greatly in excess 
of the requirements of the Picdmontese Government for the object proposed. 
The pay of a British soldier, and the general seale of expenditure in the British 
army, are higher than the Picdmontese, but the annual cost of 15,000 British 
troops would be less than G00,0008, “ind a loan ol 1,000,000! . therefore would 
appear to be sufficient ut present, with, the understanding that a like sum should 
he advanced on the demand of the Picdmontese Government at the expiration 
of a twelvemonth. : 

Hier Majesty's Government attach great importance to the necession ol 
Piedmont to the Treaty, not alone on account of the military support they will 
derive in the war heats Russia from the Picdmontese army, hut because they are 
convineed that it will be attended with signal advantage (4 Piedmont, by enabling 
her to take an active part inthe great question which now agitates Europe. 

It is therefore wot without some regret that Her Majesty’s Government 
have had to consider the political conditions which the Piedmontese Govern- 
ment desire to athich to then accession. 

Picdmiont, in consideration of the sacrifices she may make, desires to have 
a voice in the deliherations for peace, and upon that | have to observe that the 
Piedmontese Government may rest assured that no peace will be made im which 
Piedmont is not included, and her interests duly consulted; but Her Majesty's 
Government apprehend that Piedmont cannot seck to be consulted on the 
various questions that may cone under discussion when negotiations for peace 
are undertaken. oA 

Sooret, Articles to ‘Treaties are genorally speaking abjectionable; their 
existence is always known, their purport is always exagaerated, they lead to 
Hnisapprelerstont, vnd unless the necessity for them is absolute they should Ie 
avoided; but the Secret Articles proposed by the Picdinontese Government are 
peculiarly lintle to objection. ‘Phe first provides that England and France shill 
use all their efforts to induce Austria to remove the sequestration upon the 
properties of Sardinian subjects. Her Majesty's Goverment have often, but 


5 


in vain, endeavoured to induce the Austrian Government to perform this act at 
justice, but have always been answered that it was a matter of internal 
administration, in which the intervention of foreign Governments could not be 
admitted; but if England and France were now to enter into a Treaty engage- 
ment, whether patent or secret, with Piedmont on the subject, it would become 
a point of national honour with Austria to maintain the sequestration, and the 
proposed Article would be found to mar the object which the Predmontese 
Government has at heart. 

If Piedmont aceedes to the Convention and is found engaged in the same 
ange with Austria, the Governments of England and France would consider 
that an opportunity most favourable for the renewal of ther efforts had arisen, 
and they would use it to the best advantage; and with such an assurance it 1s 
hoped that the Piedmontese Government will be satistied. 

The second Seeret Article provides that on the restoration of peace the 
High Contracting Parties shall take into consideration the state of Italy. 

~The intention of this Article is not manifest, but Her Majesty’s Govern- 
ment must decline to enter into a vague engagement which might hereafter be 
the cause of misunderstanding. ‘ 

Her Majesty’s Government are informed that the object is to satisfy pubhe 
opinion in Piedmont that the interests of Italy have not been forgotten ; but as 
the proposed Article is to be secret, no such use could be made of it. On the 
other hand, however, it might be adverted to, and expectations of great and 
fundamental changes might be raised, to which Her Majesty's Government are 
not prepared to commit themselves. 

Her Majesty's Government take a deep interest in the welfare of Italy, and 
they will miss no Sponeualhy of affording their aid towards the improvement 
that the state of Italy imperatively demands; but Her Majesty's Government 
inust reserve to themselves the unfettered right of acting at the time and in the 
manner that they think most expedient, and most likely to be attended with 
success, ‘hey are disposed to think that this object will be obtained more 
surely, because more amicably, by improving the relations between Austria and 
Piedmont, and by bringing the two Powers to cooperate cordially together in a 
reat European cause, than if Austria were alarmed by a Treaty between England, 
France and Piedmont respecting Italy, to which she was no party, and the 
project of which, being concealed from her, she would naturally infer was hostile 
to her interests in that country, 

Tam, &e, 
(Signed) CLARENDON,

Colonel Williams to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recetwed December 30.) 
{ Private.) 


My Lord, Erseroom, December 9, 1854. 
THE communication which I made to Mr, Hammond on the 28th of 
November, will show your Lordship with what ratification [ received your 
private letter of the 23rd of October, which records your Lordship’s approbation 
of my conduct out here, ji | 
To save repetitions, and your Lordship needless trouble, [refer you to my 
despatch to Lord Stratford® which accompanies this private communication ; 
fucts will there speak for themselves. at your Lordship's remarks, with 
respect to the conduct of Lord Stratford, are couched in these terms, ‘There ts 
a mystery about it all that I shall be glad if you ean unravel.” [ will not flinch 
from doing so. | 
That “mystery” is of 4 double nature; one portion relates to the war, and 
another to myself, 
With regard to the first. part, | must inform your Lorilship that even before 
landing at Constantinople from England, I sent # copy of my Foreign Office 
instructions to the Ambassador, and immediately waited on him at ‘Therapia. 
J ut once saw that a storm was raging in his breast, and, after a cool reception 
he invited me into the garden; scarcely five minutes had been occupied in mM

conversation upon the war, when his Excellency brake out into a violent passion, 
and said, 1 ought to have had a political direction of the naval and miltary 
operations of this war;” in saying so, he stamped on the garden walk, and I 
remained silent, | told lis Exceileney of the great importance attached to my 
mission by your Lordship and the Duke of Neweastle, and then conversed with 
lim on the chances of my suceess, but he gave me no promise of assistance, nor 
let fall any expressions of sympathy, 1 dined with his Excelleney, and started 
next day for Varna. ' 

On my return, 1 sent Lord Stratford a copy of my tnstructhons from Lord 
Ravlan, where the former was praised for “ his unrivalled disernnmation of the 
character of Turkish public men; and hopes recorded for Ins assistance, I saw 
Lord Stratford three times, and dined with him on all those occasions (after my 
return from Varnal; the last time [asked him for lis commands, as [ was to 
embark the following morning, Tis Excellency first replied, “ Anything T have 
to send wauld reach vou on the road;"? but he turned suddenly towards me and 
(with an eye which thirteen years have enabled me to read) added, I have 
nothing for you.’ ‘Thus his desperate determination was taken, although I did 
not comprehend its nature; indeed, when 1 was saluted by cannon at Trebizond 
and Erzeroom, I fully believed that the Turkish Government had been made 
acquainted with my mission; these honours were however due to Messrs, Stevens 
and Brant. who had announced my coming under the title of Commissioner and 
Brigadier-General, which they had heard Twas. ; 

“On the receipt of Lord Stratford's only letter, which [ have this day 
‘nelosed to Lord Wodehouse, | again fancied that all was right ; and cOnse= 
quently considered the assertions of the Governor-General of Erzeroom and Zarit 
Mustapha Pasha (as to their ignorance of my mission and title) as mere 
specimens of Turkish cunning ; so did Mv, Brant. although he informed me of 
their denials. Le a are 

My Lord, I must conclude this too long recital by intimating that the 
solution of the first part of the mystery’ Is contained in those tew words which

Colonel Williams to Lord Stratford de Redelijfe. 


My Lord, Erzeroom, December 8, 1354. 

SINCE I fulfilled the duties confided to me, as Her Majesty’s Commis- 
sioner to the head-quarters of the army of Kars, I have had the honour ol 
addressing to your Excellency fifty-four despatches, identic with those forward atl 
simultaneously to the Earl of Clarendon and General Lord Raglan. Kael 
packet has been accompanied by a private letter containing details and sugges 
tions, which, had they found place in my public communications, would have 
inconveniently lengthened those documents. 

On the 23rd of September | was honoured by a private letter from your 
Lordship, appealing to my “spirit and humanity '’ relative to the ora of 
those unfortunate Russian ladies who had then recently been seized and carried 
into the mountains by Sheik Schamy!], the Circassian Chieftain. Since the above 
date, | have not been favoured with a line by your Excellency, even with an 
acknowledgment of the reception of my public or private communications. To 
one who has served your Lordship for so many years, such an avowal, on ny 
part, cun only be recorded with feelings of deep disappointment and mortitica- 
tion—teelings which I have studiously endeavoured to conceal, even from my 
aide-de-eamp and secretaries, because cach successive post was anxtously looked 
for, in the hope of receiving answers from your Lordship on the pressing and 
important atfuirs connected with my mission ta the head-quirters of the army 
al Kars, 

Nor have lL cither, for the above reasons, directly or indirectly, to Lords 
Clarendon or Raglan, hinted at the silence which your Lordship has been pleased 
to preserve towards me, until the 28th of November, when IT aequainted the 
authorities of the Foreign Office with my intention to make my representations 
on this, to me, distressing subject. 

I need not trouble your Lordship with a recapitulation of the contents of 
my various identic despatches ; but as the Earl of Clarendon and General Lord 
Raglan will be furnished with a copy of this communication, Lowe it to Her 
Majesty’s Government and to myself ta remind your Lordship of communications, 
public—and private especially—addressed to you. 

First. Independent of my various conversations with your Lordship, before 
and after my visit to Lord Raglan at Varna, Linvoked, in a public despatch 
dated 20th September, your Excellency’s “countenance and support’ in my 
endeavours to save the remnant of the Kars army from the horrors of last year. 

Secondly, I forwarded, with my first packet from Kars, for your [Excel- 
lency’s inspection, a Russian and a Turkish cavalry sabre; and having thins 
shown one of the principal causes of the want of efliciency of the Turkish Horse 
at the battle of Injéderé, I stated the necessity of having 5,000 English Light 
Cavalry sabres, as the only hope of rendering that important arm efficient for 
next spring. On this point Tat the same time addressed 1 private memorandum 
on the necessity of allowing Baron de Schwartzenburg to reorganize and drill 
this wretched arm of the service. 

‘Thirdly. In consequenee of the great scarcity of a certain kind of ball- 
cartridge in the magazines of Kars, and applicable to the arms in use by the 
only really efficient troops in that intrenched camp, | hoped that your Lordship 
would excuse the great liberty [ was taking, and respond to my urgent prayer 
for asupply to be sent me, when I inclosed two cartridges in a despatch, telling 


i 
+ 


RN PeSTINTE TS 


UE 


8 


vour Excellency, at the same time, that it was only through you, and you alone, 
that I could hope for sucha boon. T need not add that, in the event of an 
attack during the winter, this ‘ntrenched camp may owe its capture to the want 
of this ammunition; for none other, as I at the time explained to your Lordship, 
will fit the muskets and rifles of these corps of élite, which were the only regi- 
monts which behaved well at the battle of Injédere. . 

Fourthly, [ had the honour of offering to your Lordship my reasons for 
thinking that Arslan and Shahin Pashas (the two Poles) were Russian spies ; 
but they are still at Constantinople, intriguiue against the very existence of this 
army by corresponding with its Pashas, and sowing the seeds of dissension, and 
falsely accusing General Guyon of every species of nubtary dereliction, who, 
whatever may be his faults—especially those arising from in unhappy mlirmity 
of temper—is a brave man, and, as an Englishman, worthy of the protection of 
Hor Majesty's Government, 

Fitthly. When, at Kars, L first heard of the intention on the part of Shaker 
Pasha to treat me with contempt, [| adtled to my public despatch on that subject 
a private note, assuring your Excellency that your promptly-exerted influence 
could alone stop this dangerous conspiracy, or effectually sound the real inten- 
tions, as regarded myself, of the newly-named Mushir; and | have faithfully 
detailed in subsequent despatches und private letters the insolence of Shukri and 
and Hussein Pashas since my arrival here. 

The last report of Lieutenant Tocsdale, which your Lordship will receive 
hy this messenger, proves what results the fear of that retribution which T know 
they hourly expect, is working upen the minds of the Pashas ant! Colonels. For 
the safety of this army, I trust twill not be long: ere 1 fall upon all those 
officers whose names stand forth in infamous notoriety in my desputehes, either 
for theft, cowardice, or drunkenness: but, unhappily, the result [allude to by 
my quotation of Lieutenant ‘Teesdale’s report is merely temporary 5 for the 
consciousness of worthlessness on the part of those Pashas and Colonels will not 
vender them either more brave or less thievish, and the danger to that earrison 
is consequently imminent. 

Under these eircumstanees, | most respectfully, but as firmly. instat, through 
the influence and interference of your Lordship, that my reports be promptly 
attended to by the ‘Turkish Government ; ‘hat those oflicers, Pashas and 
Colonels, who have been convieted of robbery by false muster, direct thefts, 
and drunkenness, be dismissed, and others named in their places. 

With regard to the principal criminal, Zarit Musab Pasha, who, as 1 
have stated in my despatches from Kars, might have, by iis fulse muster-rolls 
and other dangerous deceptions, caused the discomfiture and disgrace of any 
British foree sent to his assistance, | leave him in the hands of the allied 
Governments; lor, happily, he can do no more harm here, 

With regard to Shukri and Hussein Pashas, if they are not instantly 
recalled to Constantinople, there will be very little, if any, use in my attempting 
to execute the difficult and onerous duties imposed upon me, And, having 
made this appeal to your Lordship, in the name of Ter Majesty's Government, 
itis my duty to state distinctly that I shall not he able to give such intelligence 
to my superiors as 1s absolutely necessary for them to be masters of; that 1 shall 
fail to preserve the power which | have, unaided, seized; and that I shall, 
consequently, not succeed in shielding the troops from starvation, without my 
demands be vomplied with, If they be not, the dissolution of this army and 
the fate of Asia Minor will inevitably follow, and a olden opportunity Lost. 

| have, &e.

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Recetved January 1, 1855.) 


(No. 530. Confidential.) , 
My Lord, Berlin, December 29, 1854. 

BARON MANTEUFFEL having obtained permission to go to the country 
for a few days, is absent from Berlin and returns to-morrow. 

Before his departure Count Esterhazy communicated to his Excellency a 
despatch from Count Buol on the subject of mobilising the Prussian army, and 
preparing to meet the arrangements stipulated by the Treaty of the 20th of 
April; and urged the placing 100,000 men without loss of time on the eastern 
frontier, for the purpose of covering the Austrian territory from any attack on 
the part of Russia. Baron Manteuifel appears to lieve replied that he would 
tuke the King’s orders, observing that it was scarcely necessary to remind the 
Prussian Government of the obligations of the Treaty; and that he could inform 
him that the army would probably be placed on the war-footing by the Ist ot 
Mavel, and that Prussia would then be in a position to support whatever policy 
the King might think fit to adopt, and take up his attitude accontingly. 

Count Ksterhazy, in mentioning the foregoing to me, said Baron Man- 
teuffel’s tone led him to believe that there was no longer any question of the 
adhesion of Prussia to the Treaty of the 2nd of December, and that lis language 
almost implied that it was doubtful if Prussia would keep the engagements 
which she had contracted with Austria in April last. 

He added that after making some observations on the four points as bases 
for negotiations with Hussia, and of the ignorance in which the Prussian 
Government had been kept as to the interpretation which had been put upon 
them by the allies, Baron Manteuffel said that it was impossible that Prussia 
could become a party to engagements of which she did not know the bearing 
and extent; he then hinted that Austria had been carried away from her German 
interests hy England, and that he felt satisfied when England lad obtained all 
she wanted in the Blick Sea, she would cease to carry on the war with the 
yigour which was now displayed, and that Austria would then be left to seek 
support elsewhere. oa Ot, 

Count Esterhavy is naturally extremely dissatistied with the appearance of 
affairs here, and told me that Count Arnim, the Prussiin Minister at Vienna, 
had lately read to Count Buol a despatch containing observations on the change 
which hid come over the relations of Austrian and Prussia, nnd throwing out a 
hint as to the Treaty of the 20th of April becoming a dead letter, Count Buok 
appears to have made no remark whatever to Count Arnim on this communica- 
tion, and informed Count Esterhazy that as no copy of the despatch was left, he 
should take no notice of it, ) 

In forwarding this intelligence to your Lordship, I cannot omit observing 
that we have now before us a further proof of the false and double policy of the 
Prussian Government, Taron Manteuffel has attempted to throw discredit. on 
the intentions of Her Majesty!s Goverument to carry on the war in good faith 
with our ally; whereas a few days ago he told me thut the King of Prussia was 
desirous to effect a rapprochement’ with Englimd, and for this purpose had 
sent a special Envoy to London; and to the French Minister he holds language 
which is more friendly ta that country even than to England, 

The drift of all this is clear enough. Prussia is becoming every day more 
resolved to remain neutral; Baron Manteuffel’s language to Count Esterhazy is 
intended to intimidate Austria by hinting at the possibility of Prussin’s with- 
drawing from her treaty engagéments with her, whilst she makes vain attempts 
to cajole England and France by a special mission, and a proposal to make a 
‘reaty with them separate from Austria; her own intention being to support 
the objects and favour the plans of the common enemy, cate 

The opinion is gaining ground here that Prussia is preparing to maintain an 
urmed neutrality, and Tam assured on good authonty that orders have already been 
issuect to the Generals of Division to make arrangements to call out the reserves 
at the shortest notice; that orders for a considerable purchase of horses have 
be n given; and that an additional battery of Artillery is to be immediately

made to each corps d'armée, which will give 96 guns for each, or 3 guns to every 
1,000 men. 

An article appeared two days ago in the “Kreuz Zeitung,’ which is 
remarkable as showing the feeling of the Court party on the subject of the 
pence which they wish Prussia to occupy in the present crisis in Europe, and | 

ave the honour to forward it in original and translation. 1 bee to draw your

Inclosure in No. 12, 


Extract from the “ Kreuz Zeitung.” 

(Translation.) Berlin, December 28, 1854. 
'P is demanded of Prussia for the maintenance of her dignity and inde- 
pendence asa ¢reat European Power to join in a “concert,” with the fandamental 
principles of which she does not harmonise, and never can harmonise. Prussia 
cannot and does not desire that Russia should be weakened and humiliated, and 
for the reason, independently of all motives of fidelity and honour, that Prussia 
in her position can gain nothing of what Russia may lose, and would consequently 
be a loser in comparison to the other gainers. Moreover, it is apparent that 

Russia, on the first occurrence of dissension in the European concert after the 
reestablishment of peace (as has already been hinted at in this paper, and which 
cannot be too often brought to notice), will try to repair her losses, and Prussia 
is the nearest neighbour against whom, no longer fettered by old obligations, 
she might be inclined to turn, That however the acquisition of the new 
friendship would counterbalance the loss of the old one, and that the Huropean 
coneert would again vise in favour of Prussia, is still less to be expected than 
that in such ease a totally new and not very favourable coalition would be 
formed. The European concert accordingly appears to Prussia as a true 
*“societas leonina,’’ from which she has to expect no advantages, but rather 
disadvantages. To all this it must be added that Prussia, if she follows the 
counsels of liberalism in her foreign policy, will infullibly raise it to power at 
liome. 

“But,” they say, “Prussia enters into the European concert for the 
purpose of consolidating her influence in it.” 

___ Independently of the consideration that he who enters into an alliance against 
his will cannot expect a very influential position in the same, Prussia bas been 
already from the beginning out-voted inthe present European concert, and it isas 
little to be expected that the majority will be drawn ane hy Prussia, as that 
Prussia will be drawn along by the majority. Inany ense Prussia will be enabled 
to cast her weight into the balanee with more certainty by a position free on all 
sides, than if she stood on the inclined plane of an alliance which has been half: 
and-half forced on her, and the bases of which are nat clear, ‘To maintain such 
an independent position is now the most important duty of Prussia, and if it is 
her serious will, nobody is able to dispute it with her. Neutral Prussia might 
also, if altacked from without, have the same and even ereater claims on the 
aid of the Diet than Austria has for her position in the Danubian Principulities,

No. 20. 


Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received 
January 5, 1855.) 


(No. 778.) 


My Lord, Constantinople, December 24, 1854. 

AT the suggestion of the Ottoman Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, 
a meeting took place at this Embassy the day before yesterday, between Aali 
Pasha, M. Benedetti, and myself. The subject matter of our conference was a 
letter from Omer Pasha to the Grand Vizier, making difficultiesas to his proposed 
expedition to the Crimea, and an application from the Generalissimo to be 
allowed to visit Constantinople for two or three days, 

The Ottoman Minister had previously put us in possession of Omer Pasha's 
objections, and he now informed me thut the Porte apprehended inconventence 
from the proposed visit, On loth points he expressed his wish to know my 
opinion, and also that of the French Chargé d’Aflaires. 

The conversation which ensued brought out the opinions of all parties, and 
we agreed that it would be better for Omer Pasha to relinquish his idea of 
visiting Constantinople at the present moment ; that more advantage might result 
from his taking a different direction, and putting himeelf in personal communi. 
eation with the Commanders-in-chief of the allied forces before Sebastopol; that 


| 
| 
| 
| 


_—_ 


= Ts S Oey 


24 


the execution of this idea ought, however, to depend upon its capability of being 
carried into effect, without retarding the preparations for embarking the expedi- 
tionary troops, and that, in order to prevent a signal failure, perhaps even a fatal 
calamity, it was essential to calculate beforehand the amount of steam transport 
required for conveying provisions, ammunition, and clothing, to the Crimea, for 
the use of the Ottoman forees there, and even to attach at once to that service 
the requisite number of vessels by specific appropriation. 

‘The Porte has since caused an instruction to be drawn up in this sense to 
Omer Pasha; but the transmission of it is delayed by forms of office, and the 
necessity of taking the Sovereign’s commanils. 

Omer Pasha’s despatches to the Grand Vizier were forwarded to your 
Lordship in translation with my No. 770 of the 19th instant. 

M. Benedetti, in the course of our conference, expressed surprise, not 
unmingled with intimations of censure, that the report of a British officer sent 
to prepare for the Ottoman expedition to Mupatoria, should have been so drawn 
up as to afford ground for the objections urged by Omer Pasha, and, although 
[ endeavoured to soften his impressions; I could not in justice take upon myself 
to vindicate the circumstances of which he found reason to complain. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLITTE,

No, 22. 


Brigadier-General Williams to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Reveiued 
January 5, 1855.) 
(No. 58.) 
My Lord, Erseroom, December 12, 1854, 

I WAS informed by Her Majesty’s Ambassador, in his private letter dated 
26th September, that Ismail Pasha, the then newly appointed Mushir of this 
army, had been attacked by inflammation in the eyes, which threatened his 
Bight. 

~ On the arrival of Hussein Pasha (whose reprehensible conduct I have been 
obliged to bring before your Lordship on more than one occasion), | was 
informed by him that this inflammation was of a chronic natare, and that it 
never had threatened his sight. ‘This was asserted in presence of NKerim 
Pasha. Be this os it may, it is my duty to inform your Lordship, that four 
orders, for its re-orgunization, have reached this army, addressed to it by Lsmail 
Pasha, ‘They have been read to the troops and stand as follows :— 

1. The edging of the clothing of the army of Anatolia will in future be red 
instead of yellow, ; 

2, Officers will wear black cravats, 

§. The tassel of the fex will in future be worn on the left side over 
the car. 

4. Officers are not to frequent the baths where the men assemble to bathe. 

Ismail Pasha has a high reputation, but I suggest for the consideration of 
your Lordship, whether this be not the place for that General to show that his 
renown is based on solid grounds, 


on 


Frost and snow have now given to this shattered army breathing time to 
reform and organize its ranks; and supposing that we begin to-day, we shall not 
have an hour to spare to prepare it for action in the spring. But if Ismail 
Pasha, under the pretext of wringing from the Porte all the stipulations he 
requires, should wish to eseape the rigours of an Armenian climate, and pass the 
winter at Constantinople (which I shrewdly suspect he intends doing), he will 
find on his arrival here in April, strangers to command, instead of familiar faces 
to encourage ; no magazines here to enable him to take the field; mo entrench- 
ments and redoubts to defend this, the heart of Armenia and the base of his 
operations. . 

| repeat it, my Lord, that not a day is to be lost; and I urgently impress 
upon your Lordship the necessity of prone active, and ample support in the 
execution of my duties, We are defending Turkey, and assuredly we have a 
right to insist on these things. 
Il have, &c. 
(Signed) W. F. WILLIAMS. 


No. 23. 


Mr. Buchanan to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received January 6, 1855.) 


(No. 367. Confidential.) 


My Lord, Copenhagen, December 30, 1854. 

I HAVE been informed by the Swedish Minister that M. Stirkey, the 
Vice-Consul of Sweden at St. Petersburgh, has arrived here, having lett that 
capital on the L4th instant. 

M. Stirkey reports the Emperor to he living at Gatehina, and to be in a 
state of great excitement respecting the events of the war, He also states that 
all couriers coming from the Crimea are sent direct to His Imperial Majesty, at 
whatever hour of the night they may arrive, without being allowed to communi- 
cate with any of his civil or military officers. 

M. Stirkey describes the language of persons holding military and civil 
appointments, and particularly those about the Court, as being warlike, these 
gentlemen declaring that the most disastrous war would be preferable to the 
acceptance of conditions of peace humiliating to Russia. He believes, however, 
that the Emperor himself is anxious to bring the war to an immediate termina- 
tion, and he entirely confirms the report which | had the honour of transmitting 
to your Lordship in my despatch No. 318 of the 4th ultimo, as to the general 
distress existing among the landed proprictors throughout the country. 

| have, &e. 
(Signed) ANDREW BUCHANAN, 


No. 24. 


Mr. Buchanan to the Earl of Clarenilon.—{ Received January 6.) 
(No. 3.) 
My Lord, Copenhagen, January 2, 1855. 
_ THE King held a Court yesterday, on the first day of the year, ut 
Priedericksborg Palace. 
} ry? yee ‘ k er Tee ‘ a ; a ‘ 

The different forcign Missions were received in turn by the King in the 
morning, and adinner took place in the alternoon, to which the foreign Ministers 
had the honour of being invited, 

Eis Majesty received me most graciously, and after expressing his sympathy 
with me on a severe domestic affliction which | had suflercd in the death of my 
wile, made some general observations on the events of the day, which enabled 
me to refer to the communications which have lately taken place between the

Conference of Vienna and the Russian Minister at that Court, and to the proba- 
bility that the war would soon assume a more general character, if the Emperor 
of Russia was not disposed to make peace on the only terms on which the 
allies could treat with him, 

The King replied, that these Governments, however, which were neutral, 
would naturally endeavour to remain so, and that he would be very unwilling to 
change his present policy. 

i said I could quite understand such a wish on the part of His Majesty, but 
that the time had now arrived when it might be expected that Austria would 
beeome the ally of England and France if the war was prolonged, and that it 
appeared to me, under such circumstances, all Governments would do well to 
consider whether neutrality might not prove eventually prejudicial to their 
interests; as if any modification of the present general arrangements of Europe 
were to be nade at the end of a great war, the interests of neutral States were 
not likely to meet with the same consideration as those of belligerents, who 
would have powerful friends to support them. 

His Majesty admitted that this might be the ease, and said that the next 
campaign would either find him the ally of the Western Powers, or still 
maintaining his neutrality, but as this must depend upon circumstances, he 
would not say at present which of these contingencies was most probable, but 
resumed the state of the ease by using the words of a Danish proverb, which 
says, * Deu tid deu sag,” namely, “ to every day its own afta.” 

I replied that J did not expect to ask His Majesty to state what course he 
would pursue in the event of a continuation of the war, but I thought His 
Majesty would do well to consider the observations which I had ventured to 
make to him. 

J have, &c. 
(Signed) ANDREW BUCHANAN.

My Lord, Foreign Office, January 6, 1855, 

BRIGADIER-GENERAL WILLIAMS has transmitted to ie @ copy or 
the despatch which he addressed to your Excellency on the 8th of December, 
recapitulating the various communications which he has at different times made 
to vou on the state of the Turkish army in Asia, and of which it would seem 
that your Excellency has not taken any notice to Brigadier-General Williams. 

Her Majesty's Government desire to receive your I’xcelleney's observations 
upon the despatch of General Williams, which | need hardly say has been read 
by them with great regret after the anxiety they have felt, and the remonstrances 
which they have in vain addressed through your Excellency to the Porte, 
respecting the unfortunate army at Kurs. fae ee ie | 

Asan instance of the disrespect shown to Brigadier-General Williams by 
the Turkish military authorities, 1 transmit to your Excellency the cover of a 
letter addressed to him, which he has sent to this otlice, 

Such is the conduct of Shukri Pasha, the man just sent from, Constantinople 
to take the command at Kars, and who, if he had not positive instructions to 
treat General Williams with contempt, can have had none to show him respect, 
although your Excellency announced on the Lith of November last that he was 
to have the rank of Ferik in the ‘Turkish service, 

ut Her Majesty's Government will no longer endure to be trifled with, and 
they are determined that if the Turkish Government still persist in treacheroualy 
disregarding the Sultan's interests, the ‘Turkish officers shall at all events not 
‘asult the Queen’s Commissioner ; and your Excellency 1s instructed to demand 
the immediate dismissal of the person who give orders that General Williams 
shall be thus unbecomingly addressed. ie 

Your Excellency will also transmit to me a copy of your application to the 


rai 


Turkish Government for the official recognition of General Williams when he 
went to Kars, and of the answer which you received, and you will also demand, 
if you have not got it, a copy of the instruction that was sent by the Porte. 

Your Excellency will understand that Her Majesty's Government require to 
be furnished with a full and detailed report of everything which has passed 
between Her Majesty's Embassy and the Porte respecting the army at Kars, in 
compliance with the instructions that so frequently, but in vain, have been 
addressed to your Excellency. 

Tam, &e.

No. 28. 


Mr. Hudson to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recetved January 6.) 


(No.1. Secret and Confidential.) 
My Lord, Turin, January |, 1855, 

THE messenger Negrini, with your Lordship's despatch marked Secret and 
Confidential, No. 86 of the 28th of December, arrived here at 7 p.m. on the 
Stst ultima. 

The Court. ceremonial consequent upon New Year's day, prevented my 
secing the Minister for Foreign Affairs until 9 o’elock in the evening of 
this day. 

General Dabormida read your Lordship’s despatch, and asked me to leave 
it with him, in order that he might communicate its substance to his collearues. 
I told the General that | was not authorized to give him a copy, consequently I 
could not leave the despatch with him. 

He asked me, How do you propose to carry on negotiations ? 

I said, if he was disposed to accede to the Treaty of Alliance of the 10th of 
April last, | would then state, in a note, the interpretation which your Lordship 
rave to the propositions contained in my despatch No. 119; and I gave him the 
heads of that interpretation, together with the outline of 4 Military Convention, 
in order to serve as bases for the negotiation of the Treaties, 

M. Dabormida then said that he regretted to find that Her Majesty's 
Government had misinterpreted the intentions of the Sardinian Government, lor 
by the Sceret Articles they desired to guarantee the interests of Sardinia, and 
not to raisc difficulty, ‘That so long as the Austrian sequestrations existed, it 
was impossible for the Sardinian Government to hope to be able to carry public 
opinion with them, or to procure the necessary authorisation for sending an army 
into the Crimea, or for maintaining that army during the war. That the 
Sardinian Government, however, did not insist upon the form of the stipulation 
for raising those sequestrations: they were ready to abandon the form of a 
Secret Article, provided by some means or other, which they left to the decision 
of the Governments of Great Britain and France, those sequestrations were 
raised. 

In short, unless the sequestrations were taken off, the Sardinian Govern- 
ment cannot send an arnty to the East, 

The General then said, “The Due de Guiche will return to his post at 
Turin trom leave of absence, probably to-morrow; 1 have reason to believe that 
he is instructed by his Government to demand such an alteration in our laws 
rewarding the press, as will completely destroy the freedom of the press in this 
country. My colleagues and myself will retire from office rather than consent 
toany such alteration ; consequently you perceive that when the British Govern- 
ment declare, and when the French Government. reiterate, that the war with 
Russia is a war for the liberties of Europe, we must consider it a war for such 
liberties in Hurope as satisfy and are agreeable to France and Austria, for 1 will 
not do your Government the injustice of supposing that it would countenance 
the destruction of the liberties of Piedmont; which has endeavoured to act up to 
it British model, 

“You, therefore, sec our position; our turn has come first, We are likely 
to be crushed (broyé) between those two Powers. Your Government probably 
never suspeeted that one of the first fruits of the war with Russia for * the 
liberties of Kurope,’ was to be the downtall of the ‘liberties of Piedmont.’ 
However such appears to be the case, and if you, as British Minister, are not 
prepared to sign with me a declaration guaranteeing the constitutional liberties 
of Piedmont, | see no use in our discussing the bases of a Treaty which will 
probably ever be signed by myself, We must wait tll the French Minister 
arrives, and till we learn officially whether his: instructions correspond with the 
declarations which he himself has communicated to me privately, and by which 
he meant to rehare us for the official demand. I now ask whether you will 
insert such a declaration as | have pointed out, in the interpretation to be given 
to the Treaty.’ 

| said | was not prepared to sign anything of the kind, and I stated my 
reasons, with which it is unnecessary to trouble your Lordship, T added that

But the well-known proverb, which contrasts the facility of binging a 
horse to water, with the impossibility of forcing him to drink, is no less true at 
Constantinople than in London or Paris. Unfortunately, too, the horses whose 
reluctance J have to overcome are not without circumstances to excuse, though 
hot entirely to justify, the slowness of their pace. 

Winter, distance, roads scareely passable, want of funds, the extent of evil 
to be cured, the scarcity of trustworthy officers, the greater interest of operations 
elsewhere, the illness of Ismail Pasha, all these eanses of difficulty, and others 
which might be enumerated, have concurred to produce hesitation and delay. | 
reeret the existence of such obstacles, and blame the Turkish Ministers for not 
surmounting them with more activity. But can | wonder? No! Corruption, 
ignorance, prejudice, want of public spirit, and the instincts of sclitshness, engen- 
der the sume consequences wherever they prevail in long habitual exuberance. 
Such cankers, wide-spreading and deep-rooted, have ever been the harbingers 
and instruments of ruin, except in those few and favoured States where public 
opinion proclaims the danger and suggests the remedy in time. ' 

Has England itself been always without a taint?) Have we never heard of 
Bacon or of Marlborough? Have we forgotten the Memoirs of Pepys, the 
profligacies of his day, and the one claim of an exiled Sovereign to the gratitude 
of his country? Are not the denunciations of Burke still ringing in our ears; 
Place, time, and circumstances vary altogether, but the disease differs only in 
degree. In Turkey it has reached the stage of extreme virulence ; in Christendom, 
generally, it is in abeyance, or shows itself only under mild forms; in Russia it 
mingles with the system of administration, and would, no doubt, fulfil its mission 
there, as elsewhere, if the power and energy of government did not maintain a 
counteracting vitality, 

Within the last few days | have learnt from one of the Turkish Ministers, 
on whom I can rely in this instance, that the real cause of the culpable inatten- 
tion shown last year by the Turkish authorities to the wants of the army in Asia 
was the jealousy entertained by Mehemet Ali Pasha, first Grand Vizier and 
subsequently Seraskier, of Mehemet Houzdi Pasha, at one time is colleague, 
and at another threatening to become his successor. 

Unhappily this is by no means a solitary instance. The present Seraskier 
and Omer Pasha have long been at variance with cach other. Mutual 
accusations take place, and while the Seraskicr asserts that he has sent ample 
supplies ta the army in Roumelia, the Generalissime complains of being 
neglected, und all is contradiction and uncertainty, except one painful fact, the 
suffering of the soldiers. 

It remains for me to say a wonl respecting my silence towards Colonel 
Williams ; it has, in truth, continued longer than 1 intended. It originated in 
my anxicty not to occasion disappointment by announcing measures which might. 
or might not be carried into eflect. I knew that during the winter season little, 
comparatively, could be done, and I preferred, under the pressure of business 
flowing in abundantly from other sources, to give my correspondent an answer 
in full, rather than keep up a succession of partial communications. ‘To this 

may be added the total want of punctuality with which of late the packets for 
Trebizond have left Constantinople. It has happened more than once that the 
opportunity was not brought to my knowledge till within an hour or two of 
the vessel's departure; thus to the motive for not making preparation, was 
added the difficulty of writing at the moment, from want of time. 
L have, &e. 


(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE,

My Lord, Constantinople, December 28, 1854. 

I AM informed by M. Benedetti that he has receryed instructions from 
Paris to engage the Porte to authorize its Ambassador at Vienna to take part in 
conferences expected to be held there between Prince Gortchakoff and Count 
Buol, in concert with the British and French Representatives, on the subject of 
Russia’s acceptance of the four points as a basis of negotiation. 

[ told the French Chargé d’Affaires that I was not only without instructions, 
but even destitute of information on the subject to which he alluded.

HER Majesty the Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and 
(reland, with a view to the more effectual prosecution of the war in which Her 
Majesty, the Emperor of the French, and His [lighness the Sultan are engaged, 
having proposed to His Highness the Sultan to take into the British service for 
a time, and in all respects to provide for, such a proportion of Turkish troops as 
might be agreed upon between [Her Majesty and the Sultan; anid His Highness 
the Sultan having signified his concurrence in that proposal of his ally ; their said 
Majesties have seen fit to conclude a Convention for the purpose of determinin 
the conditions on which such ‘Turkish troops shall be employed, and have name 
as their Plenipotentiaries, that is to Say :-— 

Her Majesty the Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and 
Ireland, &e,, &e ; 


And His Majesty the Sultan, &e., Se.5 


Who, after having communicated to each other their respective full powers, 
found in good and due form, have agreed upon and concluded the following 
articles : 


ARTICLE I. ‘ 

Her Britannic Majesty engages to take ‘nto her service a body of Turkish 
regular troops, to consist at thousand men of all arms. 

‘The above-mentioned troops shall be detached from the regular troops now 
serving with the armies of the Sultan, and in addition thereto, the Sublime 
Porte engages to assign for the same purpose thousand of the 
Redif. | 

The troops thus engaged in Her Britannic Mujesty’a service may be 
employed in any manner whieh may be deemed advisuble for the purposes af 
the present war by his Excelleney the Commander of the British forees in the 
bast. 


ARTICLE II. 
The Turkish troops mentioned in the preceding Article, whether composed 


of Regulars or Redif, shall be placed under the command of one or more general 
uificers, to be named by Her Britunmc Majesty, who shall severally receive from the

Porte the rank and precedence of a general officer in the Turkish service ; and Her 
Britannic Majesty will further appoint such a number of superior British officers 
as she may deem sufficient for the maintenance of the troops ina proper state of 
discipline and efficiency. 

His Highness the Sultan engages to confer upon the officers thus selected 
by Her Britannic Majesty, euch yank in the Turkish service as Her Majesty may 
recommend, and as mity be sufficient to ensure the necessary subordination of the 
Ottoman officers and men employed in Her Majesty's service, 

The ‘Turkish troops in question shall im every respect be subject to the disci- 
pline and regulations of the British service. ‘The colour of their uniform shall 
be left to the diseretion of the Commander-in-chief of the British army, but its 
reneral style and appearance shall be similar to those of the regular Turkish 
army. 


ARTICLE Ill. 


The Turkish troops on being made over to the British service shall bring 
with them in the first instance their arms and accoutrements, but Her Britannic 
Majesty engages thenceforward to provide for the pay, arming, clothing, equipment, 
and maintenance of the whole of the troops thus placed at her disposal, and: to 
furnish everything that may be necessary to enable them to take the field, as well 
as to provide the means of conveyance of the same from point to point by sea, 
whenever necessary. 

The pay of the Turkish officers and men shall correspond with the rate to 
which they would be entitled in the Sultan's service, |* 


ARTICLE IV. 


Her Britannic Majesty further engages that the Turkish officers and men 
so to be employed in her service, shall in no way be interfered with as regards 
the observance of the rites and ceremonies of their religion. 


ARTICLE ¥, 


_ The date at» hich the Turkish troops shall begin to be at the charge of Her

the object of the present Convention, shall be settled by oflicers to be 


nA for that purpose by the Governments of the two High Contracting 
arties. 


ARTICLE VI. 


When the present war shall ke terminated by the conclusion of a ‘Treaty of 
Peace, the whole of the soldiers forming the body of troops to which this Conven: 
tion relates, together with all the Turkish officers, shall be placed at the disposal 
of the ‘Turkish Government, which shall be at liberty either to incorporate them 
with the Turkish army, or to disband them either wholly or in part. 


ARTICLE VII. 


The present Convention shall be ratified, and the ratifications shall be 
exchanged at assoon as possible.

He stated his objections us he had done at our last meeting to the designation of

enter inte negotiations upon the principle which was put forward. 

The other Representatives stated, that on reading the interpretation of that 
basis, it would be seen that it had for its object, to attach more completely the 
Ottoman Empire tothe European equilibrium, and for that purpose to put an end 
tothe preponderance of Russia inthe Black Sea; and that the arrangements to he 
made for this purpose depended too direetly upon the events of the war to allow 
of their being at once laid dawn, Prince Gortchakoif replied, that he acknow- 
lodged the principle so announced, and accepted) it as a basis for negotiation, 

As to the fourth basts, Prince Gortehakoff said, that he felt, not as a 
politician, but as a Christin, that it was necessary that the protection aut 
present existing for the Christians of different denominations in Turkey shoul 
not cease until it was replaced by sufficient securities, and with this expectation

Baron Bourqueney then read out the identic interpretation given by the 
three Powers to the four bases, and pointed out to the Hussian Representative, 
that the first Article implied the abolition of Russia's protectorate over the Princi- 
palities, the future orginazution of which would be based on the general interests 
of Europe; and that it stipulated for the maintenance of the privileges of the 
Principulities, whose future organization should find no obstacle in the provisions 
of former Treaties. The second Article had for its object, to put an end to the 
jurisdiction of Russia on the Danube, and to establish pericct freedom of nivi- 
gution on that river, The third Article stipulated for the revision of the Treaty

Extract from the Oest, Deutsche Post Gacelte”’ of January 9, 1859. 


(Translation. ) Vienna, January 8, 1859, 

_ THE news of the Conference which took place in Vienna on the 28th 
ultimo, has-searcely yet spread over Hurope, when it has already been followed 
hy the far more important Conference held on the 7th January, which presents 
a complete contrast to the meeting at Lord Westinorland’s. house ten days 
earlier, On that occasion Prince Gortchakoff declared the interpreted proposi- 
tions of the allied Powers exorbitant, exaggerated, almost ‘nadmissible; in the 
Conference of yesterday the Russian Minister, 10 consequence af instructions 
received the day before from Si, Petersburgh, displayed great willingness 
to adopt the bases of the future peace m the manner in which they were 
again more precisely interpreted by the Representatives of the three Powers. 

Phe courier, who is bringing Prince Gortchakofl new instructions and new 
powers, has of course not yet had time to accomplish his journey from 
St. Petersburgh to Vienna; but the preliminary instructions transmitted by 
telegraph suffice to chow that the importance of this critical moment 18 fully 
appreciated in St, Petersburgh, and that, there, everything will be done, every 
effort made, to prevent the defensive alliance of the 2nd December being con- 
verted into-an offensive one. 

Russia hay introduced, within the last few weeks, an entirely new system 
into the treatment of the great Vuropean question. Whilst lier language hitherto 
had always borne the character of pride, overbearing importance, and pertect 
inflexibility, and was always seeking to bully or threaten, she has now, since 
November, assumed in all her public acts a spirit of mildness and of concession ; 
she seeks to soften, to gain, we had almost suid to touch (sie). 

This character ie aiso borne out by the last manifesto, whose whole spirit 
is very different from what the first telegraphic extract had led us to believe. 

_. The general direction of this manifesto will probably be found to coincide 
with the new instructions sent to Pance Gortchakoff, whose willingness anid 
conciliatory tone int the Conference of yesterday was is unexpected as surprising. 
The chief condition made by Russia was siid to be: that there should be 
nothing in the conditions of peace restricting the sovereignty of the Czar in: his 
own Empire, 

There is much to be understood by this sentence, Sebastopol, before all, 
which is said, from a natural delicacy, not ta have been aMtaded to in either 
Conference, ‘The destruction of Srastopol: the anmbilation of the Russian 


naval establishments in the Black Sea, the reduction of the maritime power of 
Russia in her ports in that sea, this would all be a restriction of sovereignty Mm 
her own Empire. ; 

Here lies the chief difficulty of the negotiations. 

For hesides the four points there is the great question; how 18 the Crimea 
expedition to be honourably terminated ? Each of the contending parties must 


= ——— 


a2 


seck to save their honour, and that can only be decided on the field of battle, 
not at the writing-table. 

The prelude to the commencement of negotiations for pence took place 
yesterday at Count Buol's, The prelude to a decisive contest in the Crimea ts 
nt hand. All we hear confirms us in our opinion that the fight round Sebastopol 
will be immediately recommenced, That negotiations for peace need not 
impede the prosecution of hostilities has often been prove! by examples from 
history. In the thirty years’ war, Plenipotentiaries met to treat for peace in 
l6d4, and in 1648 fighting had not ecased. 

Heaven preserve us from a thirty years’ war! But let the sword take what 
is the sword’s ; the pen what is the pen’s. A great step in the road to peace has 
been gained by diplomacy; but the Generals alone can fully mature aiid bring it 
to u decision,

hut that Russia, nevertheless, might aceuse us of something like bad faith, and 
she might, not unsuccessfully, appeal to the public opinion of Europe against 
our determination not to make peace nor to adhere to the conditions of peace 
that we had-alrendy annowneed. Supposing, lowever, that Russia consented, 
what, | asked, was proposed with respect to Sebastopol? Was the garrison to 
he withdrawn in order that the allies might take the place, or was the garrison 
to be left when the main body of Prince Menchikoff’s army quitted the Crimea? 
In the latter ease the siege could not be continued, and the proposal would then, 
ii fuet, be one for un armistice on the part of England and branee. 

Count Walewski yesterday read to me another despatch from M. Drouyn 
de Lhuys, stating that the evacuation of the Crimean should not be proposed as 
a preliminury step, but should be made if the negotiations wens protracted and 
there appeared no prospect of Russia agreeing to our terms. I told Count 
Walewrst that when it became clear that Russia would not agres to our terms, 
there could be no difficulty about breaking off the negotiations, and stating the 
true reason for it, ‘There might, however, then be grounds for making the 
proposal suggested by M. Drouyu de Lhuvs, but [ ventured to recommend that 
no engagement to that effect should now be taken, as the two Governments 
could always consult together as to the course to be pursued with reference to

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received January LA.) 


(No, 14.) 
My Lord, Paris, January 14, 1800. 
THE correspondence from Vely and Omer Pashas, relative to the future 
destiny of the Crimea, forwarded to your Lordship by Viscount Stratford de 
Redcliffe, and inclosed in copy in your Lordship’s despatch No. 2 of the 
10th instant, to myself, accorded so little with what I had the honour to state te 
you on this subject in my despatch No. 1,557 of the #2nd ultimo, that [ have 
taken an opportunity of inquiring of M. Drouyn de Lhuys whether he ever 
authorized Vely Pasha to make any proposals to Omer Pasha, on the part of 
the French Government. His Excellency assured me in the most positive 
manner that although he had spoken to Vely Pasha of the chances which an 
enterprizing man like Omer Pasha might have if he aided in freeing the Crimea 
from the sovereignty of Russia, he had been so careful not to engage his 
responsibility in conveying such sentiments himself to Omer Pasha, that he 
had cannes stated to Vely Pasha that if he (Vely) wrote on the subject to 
Omer, He must do it as if the ideas put forward in his letter origmated with 
himself. 
I have also had an opportunity of hearing the statement of Vely Pasha 
relative to this transaction, and so soon after my interview with M. Drouyn de 
Lhuys, that it is impossible they could have seen cach other in the interval. 
He confirmed M. Drouyn de Lhuys’ statement word for word, and affirmed 
moreover that in hinting to Omer Pasha the possibility of his becoming 
Viceroy or Governor of the Crimea, he had expressly stated that it was an ides 
of his own, and he added that he had written in the same sense to the Grand 
Vizier at Constantinople. 
What therefore I presume to be the case is this: M. Drouyn de Lhuys 
wishing Omer Pasha to go to the Crimea, very unguardedly throws out hints 
to Vely Pasha that by doing so he might possibly become Viceroy of that 
Province; Vely Pasha also, with the desire of overcoming Omer Pasha’s 
indecision, turns these hints into a direct proposition coming from the French 
Government. Omer Pasha seeing the little suecess likely to attend any such 
scheme, shows up Vely Pasha to the Porte, and thus the matter has acquired 
an importance which never really belonged to it. 


I have, &c. 
(Signed) COWLEY.

My Lord, Berlin, January 9, 1855. 

| HAVE just returned from an interview with Baron Manteuffel, at which 
[read to his Excellency your Loriship's despatch No. 6 of the 4th instant, 
which was delivered to me yesterday by Mr. Carruthers, ae : 

Baron Manteuffel had been fully prepared for this communication by Count 
Bernstorff’s despatch, and seemed gratified to receive the assurances which I 
gave him of the readiness of Her Majesty’s Government to meet the desire 
expressed in his despatch of the 19th ultimo, that the question which agitated 
the whole of Europe should be treated between the two Governments ima spirit 
of frankness and cordiality. His Excellency made but few observations as I 
proceeded to translate your Lordship's despatch. When | came to that passage 
which related to the interpretation of the four bases, upon which the Prussian 
Government was probably as well informed as Her Majesty's Government, he said 
that he certainly possessed, he believed, tolerablyaccurate intelligence on the subject, 
but still no official or confidential communication had been made respecting it, 
I then remarked that it was not to he expected that we could make confidential 
communications until we felt more satisfied that our confidences would be in safe 
keeping, for we felt that if sceresy were to be observed in the matter, that it 
would stand a good chance of being betrayed by some of the persons about the 
King, who are one and all devoted to the interests of Russia, and who would 
luke pleasure in conveying our confidences into the hands of our enemy, It 
became therefore, | said, a question forthe King to decide in what manner he 
would be disposed to meet the difficulties le had placed himself in, by the 
political course which His Majesty had thought fit to follow during the last nine 
months. . 

Baron Manteutlel expressed great readiness to submit to the King the 
proposal that a ‘Treaty should be signed between Englind, Austria, Prance, and 
Prussia, based on the principles of that of December 2, but omitting Articles II 
and V1, and he promised to take His Majesty's orders on the subject. 1 then 
proposed that this Treaty, which could soon be negotiated i the King were 
favourably disposed, night be signed at Berlin, in preference to any other place, 
Vo this his Excelleney said that he believed the King would prefer Vienna, as 
being the seat of the negotiations. IT replied that the place to be selected for 
this purpose muttered little, but that whilst Austria signed her Treaty at Vienna, 
Prussia might perhaps desire to have her Treaty with the allies dated from her 
own capital, ; 

Upon that part of your Lordship's despatch referring to the interpretation 
al the four bases, in which you state that Baron Manteullel required more than 
Count Buol had done, for that your Lordship bad come to no understanding 
with the Austrian Government before the signature of the Treaty beyond some 
veneral issuranees, Baron Manteuffel said that the King considered the 
Austrian Government had committed an error in. signing this Treaty as long as 
it was in imneraunce of the Intentions of the maritime Powers, 1 rejomed that if 
the King now agreed to the ‘Treaty proposed, His Majesty would not at all 
events have any reproach of the kind ta: make to himself, as. the interpretation 
put upon the four points was almost a matter of public notoriety, =a 

[ must not close this despatch without observing that the communication 
with which | had been charged appears to be satishietory to Baron Munteutfel; 
he evidently considers it to: be indicative of a friendly disposition on the part of 
England, and he certainly appears to hope that the result may be that the 
relations of Prussia and Englund will be placed on a better footing,

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received January 15.) 


(No. 10. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, January 9, 1855. 

WITH reference to my preceding despatch, [ have the honour to inform 
your Lordship that in the course of my conversation with Baron Manteuftel, [ 
told his Excellency that as the King had chosen from his own free will to leave 
the Conference in July last, and had since that time given many proofs of his 
desire to favour Russia, he would not be surprised if I ventured to observe that 
in the event of Prussia’s not entering into a Treaty with us, the Conferences 
might continue without the participation of the Prussian Plenipotentiary, anid it 
was desirable that we should hold some guarantee as to the future policy to be 
pursued by the King, [ said it was essential that we should appear in the Con- 
ference as all holding the same opinions opposed to the pretensions of Russia ; 
this T said would soon lower the demands of our enemy, and show that afhe did 
not wish sincerely for peace, and make offers that would be accepted, he would, 
if the negotiations were broken off, have no longer to deal with the Western 
Powers alone, but with Germany also. 

Baron Manteuffel seemed to agree that I advanced nothing that was 
unreasonable under the circumstances. I said, of course a change of the King’s 
paliey must naturally involve a change of persons about the Court; for once a 
Treaty signed with us, it must be properly carried out, and that it became 
natural for us to expect that all those persons now devoted to Russian interests 
about the Bing, would consider it Impossible to remain, and I might add if they 
did not retire, we should have no confidence that the King was in earnest, and 
would not desert to the enemy on the first occasion. 

Baron Manteutlel endeavours to persuade me that if the Treaty were made, 
the King would keep to its stipulations whether the party were in power or not. 
I replied that the King might possibly not listen to them as much as heretofore, 
but their presence at Court would expose the King to continued suspicions on 
the part of the allics, whilst they must always be considered a rallying point for 
the Russian faction throughout Germany, 

[ have, &e. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD,

points, although that basis of pence still goes beyond what, at the conclusion of 
the Treaty of the 20th April, both the Contracting Powers had in view as the 
object which they were to attain together by means of the allianee. A confiden- 
tial discussion has already taken place for the purpose of determining the four 
points more precisely. We do not know its result; but exactly because we do 
not know it, and as long as we do not know it, we consider it an imperative duty 
to adopt as our undeviating line of conduct, the simple and in themselves indubi- 
table conditions of the Treaty ; to keep the circle of our obligations free from every 
extension which cannot be distinctly foreseen, and especially as regards military 
assistance, inasmuch as it is pourtrayed to us. as an obligation, strictly to adhere to 
the leading idea of the Treaty of April, which also is expressed in the end of the 
Military Convention, and designates as the object of mutual aid the defence against 
an attack, Even the obligations undertaken by Prussia in the Additional Article 
of the 26th of November last, although clearly extending much beyond the leading 
idea of the Treaty of April, preserve this defensive character, They are further- 
more indissolubly connected with the supposition of common effurts to give cflect 
to the four points. That such common action does not take place as long as 
Prussia does not take part in the definition of these points, nor exerts her influcnce 
on them, is clear. ‘The title however to this participation, as far as it regards 
decisions which, though the intention is continuously pronounced to maintain 
the balance of power in Europe, appear to have the object of changing the 
whole of the international stale of Europe, and of modifying Treaties which 
Prussia also has signed. ‘This title Prussia does not derive from her participation 
in this or that stipulation referring to the present Oriental complications; she 
derives it from her quality of a Great European Power which has taken part in 
the conclusion of the Treaties reculating the state of public law in Europe by 
virtue of its own well acquired rizht. It hardly requires to be affirmed that His 
Majesty the King will steadfastly adhere to this view, and for the purpose of 
giving effect to it, if it should be menaced by any encroachment, will not be 
deterred by suerilices and dangers, which his faithful people will share with 
wonted devotion, and with the whole foree and endurance of true patriotism. It 
is least of all necessary to do so towards the august relation and ally of the King 
His Majesty the Emperor Frincis Joseph. It ts likewise not necessary with the 
Sovereigns and leading statesmen of other Powers. [i spite of certain differences 
of opinion and interests, Prussia calculates with confidence in their just appre- 
ciation of her claims, and she is ready to bring them to be acknowledged by the 
way of an agreement and an arrangement, 

Your Excellency will easily conceive from the above remarks on. the 
principles which guide His Majesty the King with regard to his own military 
attitude, that he dees not also at present consider it imperative to take the 
initiative in the Diet in fayour of an immediate mobilisation of the several con- 
tingents, The mention of the project which was recommended to the Diet by 
ourselves and Austria as a basis has been particularly omitted in the proposition 
of the Committee, as well as in the Federal Decree identic with it, and Prussia 
considers it duc to her other German allies not to recur formally to this proposi- 
tion, and thus to anticipate the labours of the Military Committee. On the 
other hand, it follows of itself that the Prussian Military Plenipotentiary will 
always find himself provided with the necessary instructions to promote the 
activity of the Military Committee on the basis of the Federal War Constitution, 
and to assist in bringing it to a conclusion in a suitable manner. Thus the 
doubts which urge themselves upon us, as we do not conceal, with regard to the 
propositions of the Austrian Cabinet, mentioned in the despatch of the 24th 
ultimo, will be solved in the most appropriate manner in the way ordained by 
the Federal Constitution, 

Your Excellency will communicate a copy of this despatch to Count Buol.
