Lord Bloomfield to the Eurl of Clarendon.—( Received January 15.) 


(No, 14. Confidential.) . 
My Lord, Berlin, January 12, 1855. 

| CALLED this morning on Baron Manteuffel, aud my first inquiry was, 
whether he had received any instructions from the King on the subject of the 
communication which I had made to him on the 9th instant, and whether 
anything had been settled about the proposed Treaty, THis Excelleney said that 
His Majesty was not indisposed to enter on the negotiation, but that before 
iloing so, he wished to await some further letters from M. de Usedom from 
London. 

I then asked if he had made any observations to the King as to the altered 
position Eis Majesty would occupy if he consented to this alliance. Baron 
Manteuftel said that he had done so, but that the King does not admit that this 
‘Treaty would imply a change in his policy. I rejoined that 1 could not under- 
stand how the Kang interpreted the object of the Treaty ; he was at present in & 
position of neutrality, whereas the Treaty would bind him, under certam contini- 
-encies, to enter hereafter into certain chgagements of an offensive and defensive 
character, Baron Manteuffel made no reply to this remark, merely saying that 
the above was the King’s impression. 

Your Lordship will thus perceive that no progress im this affair has been 
made since my first communication on the subject; on the contrary, 1 should 
say that Baron Manteuffel’s tone was less satisfactory than on ‘Tuesday last, and 
that some unfortunate influences appear to have already been at work, which 
have rendered the King less inclined to adopt the Treaty than Baron Manteuilel 
supposed at our first interview. This, perhaps, may be the result of the sudden 
and unexpected arrival of M. de Bismarck from Frankfort, who has seen the 
King several times within the last few days. 

The language of that Minister is, that the true policy for Prussia ts 
seutvality, and to avoid entering mto alliances that will bind her to Austria at 
this moment. I cannot, however, aver that M.de Bismarck’s opinions have 
made this impression on the King, but he may have brought assurances to His 
Majesty, which have not been without effect, that the South German States are 
ready to support Prussia in the present crisis, and are most of them bent on 
maintaining a neutral position that will enable them to leave their armies 
inactive, and give full scope to the mtrigues of Russian diplomacy. 1 asked 
Baron Munteuflel whether there was any truth in a rumour which had reached 
me, that Bavaria, Saxony, and Wurtemburg had announced their adhesion to 
the policy of the King; and he replied that he had received no official intelli- 
gence from any of them, but that the Kings of Bavaria, Saxony, and Wurtemburg 
had written to the King of Prussia within the last few days, expressing their 
hope that he would maintain his neutrality. Having inquired if this announce- 
ment had produced any effect on the King, Baron Manteuffel answered that His 
Majesty's opinions were, thit though Prussia, as a great Power, might take up 
arins for European purposes, the interest of the smaller States should be 
respected ; that their positions were essentially defensive ; and that they ought 
to be allowed to maintain their neutrality and independence. 

This, L said to his Excellency, was & position which did not, as far as | was 
informed, at all agree with the views of Austria; and the information whieh he 
had just given me showed that the two Great Powers differed on an essential 
point, whieh I thought greatly to be deplored, as it might lead to serious disunion 
in Germany if the war assumed a more extensive character. 

Your Lordship will judge from the foregoing how far we may count on the 
King's sincerity to enter into an alliance with us; and TL would venture to 
suggest that, as We have not yet obtained from His Majesty any assurance of 
his desive to pursue a policy different from that which he has followed for many 
months past, but that we have a proof of the contrary in his despatch of the 
Ath instint to Count Arnim, whether we should not resist the readmission of 
Prosi to the Conference about to be held at Vienna, to consider the four 
bases accepted by Russia, until such time as the King has given some guarantee 
that his policy Is modified, If Prussia is allowed to assist at the Conference 


G5 


without some such guarantee, we may be assured that her Representative will 
come in under doubtful colours, and would be more likely to favour the cause 
of Russia, particularly when the discussion is brought forward on the interpreta- 
tion of the third basis. At present we know that we are, at all events, three 
to one in the Conference; and the admission of Prussia, who has, up to the 
present moment, refused to give any solid assurances of a willingness to act 
with us, and who, perhaps, only comes forward with unacceptable propositions 
to Her Majesty's Government, in the hope of regaining her European position, 
may advance the pretensions of Russia, create embarrassment to Austria, and 
thereby tend to weaken the influence of England and France in the seale. 
I have, &c. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD,

Mr. Hudson to the Bart of Clarendon.—(Received January 19.) 


(No. ey 
My Lord, Turin, January 10, 1859, 

1 HAVE the honour to report to your Lordship, that with my French 
colleague, | assisted last night at a conference with the Sardinian Government 
upon the subject of the accession of Eis Sardinian Majesty to the Treaty between 
France and England of the oth of April, 1854, 

General Dabormida repeated the objections which in previous conferences 
he had stated that he entertained to the accession of his Sovereign to that Treaty 
without some formal engagement on the part of the Ministers of England and 
France to induce the Austrian Government to remove the sequestrations Upon 
the property in Lombardy of Saydinian subjects, and to make some mention of 
the present condition of Italy, and of its amelioration, 

Mvself and my French colleague repeated the objections which we were 
inatyucted to make known to the Sardinian Cabinet; and we declared with regard 
to the sequestration question, Not only that we would sign no such engagement, 
whether patent or seeret, but that we strongly recommended the sarclinian 
Cabinet not to insist. upon & measure which must inevitably produce a persis- 
tanee on the part af Austria in that state of things which the Government of the 
King was desirous to remove; and with regard to the imei of Italy, that 
whilst the Governments of Great Britain and of France take a lively interest in 
the well-being of that Peninsula, and are disposed to afford their nil towards its 
improvement, they must reserve to themselves the unfettered right of acting wt 
the time and in the manner they think most expedient and the most likely to 
be attended with sucecss. 

The President of the Council then said. that as it would be necessary to 
conclude certain details of the Military Convent on, which would be the comple- 
ment of the Treaty of Accession, he thought it would be advisable to send the 
Minister of War to Paris and London, where he might state the situation in 
which Piedmont found herself politically, as regards the sequestrations, and 
conclude at the same time the neecssary arrangements respecting, the Sardinian 
army corps of 15,000 men which will proceed to the Crimea, 

To this iden my French colleague expressed himself entirely adverse; he 
said, that both on public and personal grounds he was bound to oppose the most 


i) 


strenuous resistance to any such scheme, which he must consider as a slight 
upon his position and powers, and called in question the verbal and written 
instructions of the Governments of France and England to their Representatives 
at Turin: consequently, he protested against it, and declared that he would 
suggest to his Government not to receive the Sardinian Envoy. 

On my part I restated the question at issue between England, France, and 
Sardinia. | pointed out that the Governments of Great Britain and of 
France, animated by the most friendly sentiments towards Sardinia, declined to 
concur in the desire of the Sardinian Government, from a conviction that it would 
mar the object which they had most at heart; consequently, the Sardinian 
Government would not do wisely im exposing its Envoy to receive, at Paris and at 
London, the same reply as that which the Representatives at Turin of England 
and of Franee had on more than one occasion returned to the demand in 
question. 

The Sardinian Cabinet appeared particularly struck by the arguments of my 
French colleague. and took time to consider, They retired from the Conference 
whilst my F rench colleague und myself undertook, upon the demand of the 
President of the Council, to draw up a Protocol which should detail the proceed- 
ings of the Conference, and should contam the reasons for the rejection of the 
terms upon which General Dabormida so strongly insisted. 

[his Protocol (a copy of which 1 have the honour to annex), being then 
drawn up, the Conference re-assembled, and the President of the Council, and 
the Ministers of War and of the Interior, evidently approved it. ‘The Minister 
af Foreign Affairs preserved a moody silence, and offered no observation 
upon it, 

Tt was then agreed that a copy of the Protocol should be transmitted to 
the Sardinian Government at 7 o'clock A.M., on the morrow (it was then mic: 
night), and that myself and my colleague ahould be invited to attend a further 
eonference in order to hear the opinion of the Sardinian Cabinet upon the terms 
of that Protocol. 

‘This morning we were invited to call at the Ministry of Finance, when the 
President of the Council, Count Cavour, informed us that the King had been 
graciously pleased to necept the resignation of General Dabormida, and that he 
(Count Cuvour), had veeeived from his Majesty the Portfolio of Voreign 
Affairs; that the Sardinian Government accepted the Protocol of Conference of 
the Sth instant (yesterday), acceded to the Treaty of the 10th of April between 
Great Brita and France, and would be prepared to settle the terms of the 
Military Convention between England, France, and Sardinia, tor the despatch of 
15,000 Sardinian troops to the seat of war in the East, and would be prepared 
to sign that Military Convention as soon as miyself and my French colleague 
received our full powers to accept the accession of Sardinia to the ‘Treaty of the 
Loth of April. a eles 

My French colleague and myself stated in reply that we would announce by 
telegraph to our respective Governments, the declaration now made to us: by 
the President of the Council of the accession of Sardinia to the Treaty of the 
Oth of April; and that we had every reason to believe that the necessary full 
powers to accept that Treaty of Acecesion, and to conclude also the Military 
Convention, would be immediately forwarded to” us. j 

__ Asi am desirous to submit the Protocol of Conference te your Lordship 
with the least possible delay, I have now the honour to forward it with this 
despatch. |

Mr. Hudson to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recetved January 15.) 


(No. 4.) 


My Lord, Turin, January 11, 1855. 

| HAVE the honour to report to your Lordship that the President of the 
Council of Ministers notified to the Chamber of Deputies this day, that His 
Sardinian Majesty had been pleased to accept the resignation by General 
Dabormida of the Portfolio of Foreign Affairs, and had confided the minagement 
of that department to him, Count Cavour. 

M. Valerio having inquired the reasons of this change in the Cabinet, 
Count Cavour replied that the circumstances which had led to the resignation 
of General Dabormida would very shortly be communicated to the Chamber, and 
that le should on that occasion make known the foreign policy of the Sardinian 
Government. 

__M. Valerio again rose to urge upon Count Cavour the expediency of tran- 
quillizing the public mind by an early explanation of what had occurred, as the 
rumours in circulation had Batirally produced eonsiderable excitement; to 
which Count Cavour returned no reply. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) JAMES HUDSON.

The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Bloomsield. 
(No. Ts.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, January 16, 1855. 

COUNT BERNSTORFF has read to me & despateh: from Baron Manteuffel 
to Count Arnim in reply to the demand of Austria that the Prussian army should 
be mobilized und placed on the eastern frontier. 

[ expressed to Count Bernstorif much regret at the terms in which this 
despatch was written, 08 well as at the manner in which Prussia seemed to 
regard her treaty engagements with Austria, which afforded little prospect of that 
harmonious action between the two Powers which at this moment was 50 much 
to be desired. 

Count Bernstorff replied in a tone of irritation and bitterness that the 
conduct of Austria had been perfidious to Prussia, who would not allow herself 
to be dictated to; that Prussia would not forego her rights nor permit any 
important European question to be settled, nor any Treaty to which she had 
been a party to be annulled or reviged, without her concurrence. He declared 
that a great Power like Prussia could not remain isolated ; that she would have 
to determine which side to select, and he thought if her overtures were still 
rejected by the Western Powers, there would be great danger of her joining 
Russia. 

I told Count Bernstorif | was at a loss to understand what he meant by the 
rejection of overtures, 1s None that could be considered serious had been made ; 
that Prussia had voluntarily retired from the Conference some months ago, since 
which time her hostility to Austria had imerensed, her Russian predilections hac 
been undisguised, and her demand for peace “A tout prix’’ had been incessant. 
Count Bernstorif, | added, knew well how much the estrangement from Prussia 
was regretted by Her Majesty's Government, who were TOW a5 anxious as ¢ver 
for her cooperation, provided it wus sincere; because upon the firmness and 
anion of the Great Powers depended the restoration of peace, which the 
Government of Her Majesty desired as heartily as the King of Prussia himself. 

Without disputing the right of Prussia to interpret her own obligations, | 
atthe same time requested Count Bernstortf to bear in mind that the Power 
which voluntarily abdicated its position and shrank from incurring the risks and 
dangers of war, forfeited all right to take part in negotiations for peace, 

Count Bernstorft said he did not doubt the goodwill and friendly feeling, 


73 


of Her Majesty's Government, but he did not feel ag certain with respect to 
France and Austria; but I assured him that there existed no grounds for such 
doubts, and that those two Powers were as desirous as England to arrive ata 
real and bond fide understanding with Prassia. 


lam, &c. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

No. 61. 


Sir J. Milbanke to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received January 16.) 
(No. 1.) 
My Lord, Munich, January, 1899. 


THE hopes of a pacific solution of the present European crisis which were 
raised here by the news of the acceptance of the four points by the Russian 
Envoy at Vienna, have, upon calmer reflection, undergone a sensible modifi- 
eation; and, although there are still many who cling to ideas of peace, 
Baron von der Pfordten, who was among the most sanguine at first, is no longer 
of the number. He is, | understand, of opinion that the negotiations towards 
which a first step has been taken by the Russian Cabinet, do not offer any 
reasonable prospect of a satisfactory settlement of the question at issue, and he 
consequently declares it to be his ‘ntention to advise the King to proceed at 
once to make the military preparations called for by the actual state o affairs in 
Europe, and the interest of this country in particular. He considers, T am told, 
the mere fact of war breaking out between Austria and Russia under existing 
circumstances, in the light of a complete liberation of Bavaria from all her 
federal obligations, or, in other words, he looks upon such an event as necessarily 
leading to an immediate dissolution of the Germanic Confederation, and in that 
case he deems it to be the duty of the Sovereign alone to consult the interests of 
himself and his people; he acknowledges that the traditionary policy of this 
country ought rather to incline her to side with Austria; but he says that the 
conduct of the Imperial Cabinet towards the Bavarian Government has of late 
assumed a character so much the reverse of friendly or confidential, that Bavaria 
would not be justified in placing unlimited reliance upon its assurances, and 
that accordingly she must secure herself beforehand by putting a price upon her 
aid, and insisting upon Austria's subseribing to her conditions. In what the 
latter consist, | ean do no more than conjecture, though [ believe one of them 
to be the admission of a Bavarian Plenipotentiary to tale part in the negotiations 
for peace which may ultimately be entered upon. This concession, however, it 
would not be in the power of Austria to make, unless with the consent af the 
other two Powers, and I do not think it would be possible for Franee and 
England to commit a greater mistake than to afford to any one of the minor 
States of Germany an opportunity of embarrassing the Conferences by a renewal 
of the Bamberg propositions, upon which, if there be a shadow of consistency in 
the policy of this Government, 4 Bavarian Plenipotentiary must, as a matter of 
course, take his stand. I need not call to ane the declared hostility towards 
the two Western Powers which was set forth in Baron von der Plordten’s cele- 
brated memorandum, as well as in the despatch subsequently written for 
eommunication to Her Majesty's Government to the Saxon Minister in London 
by Baron de Beust, to show what sort of coadjutors in the work of establishing 
peace in the East we should be likely to find in the Representatives of either of 
these States, or, indeed, of many others. 

But the eagerness with which this Government has, from the commencement 
of these Eastern complications, pressed for the varticipation of the smaller 
States of Germany in the negotiations for their final settlement, must not be 
misunderstood. It may certainly in part arise from the sympathy between the 
Courts of Greece and Bavaria, which is but natural, and it may also proceed 
from a certain amount of compassion felt by the German public for the hard and 
cruel lot of the Christian subjects of the Porte, which the Court and * Phil- 
hellenic” party have made repeated efforts to excite to a higher point of enthusiasm 
with a view to the advantage of the King of Greece; but the real object which 
none of the middle-sized States of the Confederation ever for a moment lose

If | am correctly informed, we are about to witness a new application of the 
balancing system in the matter of the federal contingents, for it is said that 
unless the demand of Austria for putting them on a war footing be supported in 
the Diet by Prussia, this Government will give what it denominates a reserved

| have reason to believe that the proposals on military affairs made by my 
Austrian colleague to this Government within the last few days, have been well 
reecived, and that no difficulty will be made to placing the Bavarian contingent, 
should it eventually be called upon to take the field, under the orders of an

No. 83. 
The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received January 17.) 


(No, 23.) 
My Lord, Vienna, January 13, 1855. 
IMMEDIATELY upon my receiving the first intelligence, through a tele- 
eraphic despatch which had been received by Count Buol from Bucharest, of the 
movement of a corps of Russian troops into Toultcha, amounting to six battalions 
and some Cavalry and Artillery, I wrote to Count Buol the note a copy ol which 
T have the honour to inclose, stating the alarm with which this news would be 
received in England, and asking if he did not think a demonstration on the part 
of the Austrian troops in Moldavia near the Danube, might prevent this Russian 
operation from extending itself, Count Buol replied that in his despatch it was 
stated that this news required conlirmation ; that consequently lefore he gave an 
answer to the question put to him, he must ascertain what was the real state 
of the ease, and yesterday when I waited upon him, he told me he was still 
without information on the subject, but that he could not but consiuler it a great 
neglect on the part of the Turkish Government, that upon the only fronticr on 
which they were exposed to be attacked, and extending but from opposite Reni 
ta the mouths of the Danube, they should have had but a small force of Light 
Cavalry which, upon the first advance of the Russians, left the whole defensive 


76 


osition and retired to Ibraila. Count Buol said the whole frontier of Moldavia 

is defended by the Austrian troops ; Omer Pasha had 80,000 men, of whom 
30,000 are destined for the Crimea, and the rest ought certainly to have been 
destined to defend the only vulnerable point of the Turkish frontier which I 
have above alluded to. Count Buol, however, observed that if the Russian 
operation should turn out to be anything serious, he should be ready to 
deliberate upon it, 

Since writing the above, I have received your Lordship’s telesraphic despatch, 
dated yesterday 9 p.m, desiring me to express to Count Buol your feelings, upon 
your having received the inteliigence above relerred to, and | immediately wrote 
to Count Buol the note I have now the honour of inclosing, in which I transmitted 
your telegraphic message, and in which T expressed my anxious desire to receive 
a favourable reply from him, as he would himself be aware of the importance 
attached to it by your Lordship and by Her Majesty's Government. 

Count Buel has just sent me word that he has received no further 
intelligence whatever from the Dobrudscha, so that he can at present form 
no judgment upon what is the real import af the operation which has been 
reported, 

I write in great laste to make your Lordship this communication as it 
is post hour, and [ have not a moment to spare. 

[ have, &e. 
(Signed) WESTMORLAND.

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.— (Received January 17.) 


(Telegraphic.) Berlin, January 17, 1655. 

I HAVE presented Her Britannic Majesty's letter to the King of Prussia 
this day, at a special audience, in the presence of Baron Manteuttel. 

His Majesty, gratified at the improved relations between the two Courts, 
seems disposed to enter into further engagements with us. Violent against 
Austria, and at his exclusion from the Conference, stating that his future policy 
might depend on his readmission, and that in default of this, his attitude might 
become detrimental to us. He declared that Russia had been throughout 
wrong (or wrong-headed), but that he believed the Emperor of Russia was now 
sincere in his desire of peace.

No. 5.) . 
My Lord, Frankfort, January 18, 1899. 


] HAVE just learnt from good authority that a circular has been sent by 
the Austrian Cabinet to the several Governments of the Confederation, announe= 
ing the intention ofthe Imperial Government, in consequence of Prussia’s refusal 
to place the force stipulated by the Berlin Treaty of April 20 in activity, to appeal 
bute Dict, and to give that body the opportunity of pronouncing on the point 
in dispute. 

+ seems that in one of the notes recently elaborated by the Berlin Cabinet 
(I believe it to be in one bearing date the Sth of January), an assertion is made 
that the Military Convention appended to the Treaty of April 20 is invalid, as 
being in contradiction with the Terms of the Federal Act, in as far as it stipulated 
conditions which might bring a portion of the military force of the contingents 
ito the field without the sanction of the Diet, and solely by the independent 
action of the several Governments, 

Without openly admitting this ground of invalidity of that Convention, the 
Government of Austria will, it seems, do so indirectly by the form of its intended 
motion in the Diet, which will be to the effect, that a portion of the Federal 
contingents shall be put on the war footing, and that the Military Commission 
shall be enjoined to settle the distribution of the corps so put in activity, and 
with the choice of the Generals who are to be placed in command. 

| understand that Austria counts on a majority of votes; but it is not yet 
clear whether a matter of this importance will have to be decided in the Plenary 
Assembly, or in the restricted and more usual form of voting. In either case a 
simple majority is reckoned upon; but as Prussia, Bavaria, Saxony, and 
Wurtemburg will, from all the information 1 can obtain, he in the minority, the 
actual value of the vote seems to be at least nicely balanced, and the erisia is one 
of very great ane 

No sitting of the Diet takes place on this the ordinary day of assembly. 

It is expected that this weighty question will be discussed in the sitting of 
Thursday next, the 25th instant, before which period M. ile Bismarck is expected 
to return from Berlin. 

I have, &e.

Lieutenant-Colonel Simmons to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Varna, December 30, 1854. 


| HAVE to acknowledge the receipt of your Lordship’s letter marked 
Confidential, of the 7th December, which I received at Bucharest on the 15th 
instant, 

Having rejoined his Highness Omer Pasha at Rustchuk on the 7th instant, 
Tgave him the letter of which your Lordship inclosed me a copy. He hus 
desired me to thank you for that communication, and to state that it is with 
much pleasure that he has entrusted to General Cannon the command of one of 
the brigades of the troops which were selected in the first instance to go to the 
Crimea, as he has a high opinion of that officer’s merits, and has already expe- 
rienced the benetit of his services, as also of the officers who, by the liberality of 
Her Majesty's Government, are attached to him in the command of troops of 
the Ottoman army. 

The Pasha has desired me to inform your Lordship that he is so penctrated 
with the justice of your Lordship's observations, that on the qualities of the 
officer depends the conduct of the soldier, as well as with a knowledge of the 
inferiovity which unfortunately exists in the Turkish army generally, that he is 
quite decided, if ever he was entrusted with the control and organization of the 
army, to apply for officers from foreign Governments, for the purposes of forming 
an Etat-Major, and of taking a great part of the superior commands in the 
()ttoman army. 

The Pasha is of opinion that this step should be taken by an official demand 
to foreign Governments, who would thus be responsible for selecting capable and 
eflicient officers, who, by having Turkish officers judiciously associated with 
them, might he the means of eventually forming a superior class of officers to 
those which exist ut present in the Ottoman army, 

LHe desires me to state that he esteems the services of thase officers who are 
now with his army so highly, that he has reeammended some of them for promo- 
tion, and to be regularly enrolled in the Ottoman army. 

The Seraskier has replied by asking if they were willing to be enrolled for 
permanent service; to which the Pasha replied by begging that the promotion 
micht be made, when he would endeavour to get them to take permanent service 
in the army, 

The Pasha has since received a letter from the Seraskier approving of sonie 
of these appointments being made temporarily, 

On ths subject I would remind your Lordship that it is only since the 
commencement of the war that the Turkish soldiers huve been under the imme- 
diate command of Christians, and of the few who now have commands by fir 
the larger portion are Englishmen. Your Lordship will also remember that wt 
Silistria Omer Pasha gave the temporary rank of Mirali (Colonel) to three 
British officers, Captain Butler, Lieutenant Nasmyth, and Lieutenant Ballard, 
whose services he afterwards acknowledged by decorations which he presented 
to Lord Raglan with a request thet his Lordship would take the neces- 
sury measures for obtaining Her Majesty's permission for them to reeeive 
them. : 
‘The Pasha desires me to render his best thanks to your Lordship for the 
ausistance whieh you rendered him in seconding the demand whieh he has made 
to his Government to supply the necessities of his troops. Some of the articles 
which he has demanded have arrived at Varna, and hive tended much to the 
elliciency and comfort of the division now going to the Crimea, He trusts that 
the Government will use their utmost endeavours to send such other things as 
he fas demanded, and to place at his disposal the steamers and other transports 
demanded by him. 

With regard to the investiture of the Order of the Bath, the Pasha desires 
im ta express to your Lordship how highly sensible heis of the honour which 
Ler Majesty hus been pleased to conteron him, as wellas of the gratifying manner 
in whieh your Lordship has expressed yourself on this subject. Asevents, how- 
ever, have oveurred which have prevented him from receiving the investment in 
the manner he had desired from the hands of your Lordship and Lord Raglan, 


83 


he hopes, by deferring the ceremony, to add during the ensuing campaign in the 
Crimea some new claims to those humble services which Her Majesty has 
deemed worthy of this very distinguished honour. 

The Pasha desires me to express his regret that he is not able to answer 
your Lordship’s letter personally, and to add the assurance of his high respect and 
esteem for your Lordship.

(Signed) J, L. A. SIMMONS,

My Lord, Foreign Office, January 20, 1855. 


YOUR Lordship's despatch No. 10 of the 8th instant® was received on the 
Hifi instant and has been laid before the Queen, 

Your Lordship states in that despateh. that Prince Gortchakoff having 
received instructions from his Court requested through Count Buol, on the 
sth instant, a Conference with the Representatives of Great Britain, France, and 
Austria, and that his request haying been complied with, the Russian Envoy 
announced that he had received instructions from his Government, which he 
had embodied in an unofticial document, which he read, and which enabled lim 
to enter into explanations upon the subjects which had been brought before 
him on the 2sth of December. Your Lordship proceeds to state that thereupon 
Baron Bourqueney read out the identic interpretation given by the three Powers 
to the four bases, and pointed out to the Russian Representative that tlie first 
Article implied the abolition of the Protectorate of Russia over the Principalities, 
the future organization of which would be based on the general interests of 
Burope, and that it stipulated for the maintenance of the privileges: of the 
Prineipalities, whose future organization ehould find no obstacle in the provisions 
of former Treaties, That the second Article had for its object to put an end 
to the jurisdiction of Russia on the Danube and to establish perfect freedom 
of navigation on that river. ‘That the third Article stipulated for the revision of 
the Treaty of 1841, and for the cessation of Russiv’s preponderance in the Black 
Seas and that the fourth Article provided for the abolition of the official Pro- 
tectorate of Russia over the Cliristian subjects of the Sultan belonging to the 
Greek Church, and for the non-renewnl of the Articles of her former ‘Treaties, 
Prince Gortchakoif then withdrew the unofficial document he had read, as merely 
a memorandum for his own guidance, and adinitied that le accepted the inter- 
pretation of the four Articles, us they had again been rend to him, as a basis upon 
which he agreed that a negotiation with the three Powers whose Representatives 
were present, and with the Turkish Representative, could be established, 

It does not appear, however, that a proces-verbal was taken of this Conter- 
ence, or that Prince Gortchakolls acceptance of the buses was certified by hts 
signature to any written document. ‘This omission, which may: be the cause 
of embarrassment hereafter, is a matter of much regret to Her Majesty’s 
Government. 

lt is my duty to inform your Lordship that the sincerity of this acceptance 
«; doubted, and that the proceedings of the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh are 
regarded with suspicion by Her Majesty s Government. 

In August last, when the Austrian Government, upon its own responsibility, 
and without the participation of England and France, urved upon Russia the 
acceptance of the bases that had been agreed upon between the three Powers 
us the indispensable “point de départ" for negotiations for peace, they were 
peremptorily rejected by Count Nesselrode, who, in his despatch of August 26th 
to Prince Gortehakoff, declared that the form of those bases was ill calculated to 
permit of their being honourably accepted by Russia, and that with regard to 
their object there could be no mistake, as by the “interest of European eqquilt 
brium” was meant the abrogation of all the former Treaties of Russia, the rain” 
of her maritime establishinents, which were said to be a perpetual menace to the 
Ottoman Empire, and the limitation of Russian power i the Black Sea. 

Count Nesselrode further stated, that it would be superfluous to enter into 
any exumination of conditions which implied that the Russian Empire was 
already reduced to extremity by the exhuustion of a long struggle, and to whieh, 
if Russia could ever by the momentary force of circumstances be compelled to 
eubmit, so far from securing to Europe a solid and, above all, a durable peace, 
would only render that peace Hable to eternal complicutions. 

Count Nesselrade concluded by saying, that Russia having evacuuted the 
Prineipalities, and withdrawn withinher own frontier, would hence forward act on 
the defensive, and in that position wait until equitable overtures should enable 
her to reconcile her desire for peace with her dignity and politicul interests,

It thus appears that the true interpretation of the bases, and the intenti 
of the allies, were fully understood by “the Russian Government iT AGeee: aes 
since which time, although the arms of Russia have met with severe reverses yet 
she is neither reduced to extremity, nor are her resources exhausted, nor has she 
received the fresh overtures for which she was waiting. But towards the 
close of last autumn, she became aware that. Austria was on the point of 
signing a Treaty of Offensive and Defensive Alliance with England and France 
and the Russian Minister at Vienna then suddenly announeed to Count Buol 
the pure and simple acceptance of the four bases by his Government. 

To the great surprise and unconcealed mortification of Prince Gortchakoff 
the Treaty was nevertheless signed, and on the 28th of December, in consequence

Representatives of England, France, and Austria, who, in order to prevent

from Hie Eten! Present pened by the three Powers,

the following day he accepted, without reserve, the bases which, in August last, 
were designated as humiliating and dishonourable by Count Nesselrode, 

Now, taking all these cireumstances together, and calmly considering the 
course that Russia has hitherto pursued, and the Tinmistakieable objects of her 
policy, Her Majesty’s Government cannot but distrust the sincerity of the 
Cabinet of St. Petersburgh. They fear that the bases have been accepted for 
the purpose of detaching Austria from her alliance with England and France, and 
in order, by a hollow and protracted negotiation, to gain time until the season 
shall arrive for pouring fresh troops into the Crimea ; that the interpretation of 
the bases will then be disputed, and the aid of Prussia and the German Courts 
will be invoked to impress upon Austria, that if she insists upon conditions that 
Russia cannot accept with honour she must be prepared for the neutrality, if not 
for the hostility, of Germany in a war against Russia. 

Notwithstanding the reasons | have assigned for entertaining strong doubts 
of the sincerity of the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh in its acceptance of the four 
bases, as interpreted by the allies, and the little hope with which Her Majesty's 
Government look to the success of any negotiation at this moment, they are 
prepared to act in conformity with the pledges they have given. 

Prince Gortchakoff having announced that Russia had aecepted the 
conditions laid down by the three Powers, Her Majesty’s Government will be 
ready, according to the declarations contained in my despatch to your Lordship 
No. 422 of the 18th ultimo, to enter into negotiations for the restoration of 
peace; and they will do so with a sincere desire to remove, as far as it may 
be practicable, any obstacles in the way of a Treaty that will, by its provisions, 
afford security for its observance. 

In order to obtain this end it is necessary that England and France should 
come to.an understanding with Austria as to the meaning of the third Article, This 
is tore espeeiilly necessary, as Prince Gortchakotf, before entering into nego- 
tiation, has-attempted to secure to himself a retreat, by assuming that any 
destruction of the maritime arsenals of Russia, or any diminution of the torces 
which the Emperor may choose to maintain in and near those arsenals, would 
be considered as an interference with Russia's rights of sovereignty and 
derogatory to her dignity. Thus, were the belligerent Powers now to enter into 
negotiations, they might be oceupied for weeks with details respecting the 
Treaties concerning the Principalities, and stipulations concerning the appli- 
cation of the ‘Treaty of Vienna to the navigation of the Danube, and when fee 
nmitters: had been elaborately discussed, be stopped at the third Article bya decla- 
ration that Prince Gortchakoff had, from the outset, protested against any 
interpretation of that Article which compelled Russia to reduce her forces or 
abate her menacing attitude in the Black Sea. 

The gain of Russia by such a proceeding would be obvious; she would for 
the next three months, or perhaps six, direct all her troops to the Crimea 
without having any interruption from Austria to dread, 

Tt is, therefore, absolutely necessary that the three Powers should agree 
together upon the sense to be affixed to the third Article. 

It would appear that there are but two modes of putting an end to the 
preponderance of Russia in the Black Sea, Either a power, as strong as Russia 
now is, must be introduecd into the Black Sea, or the foree of Russia in that sea 
must be reduced. 

The demolition of her arsenals and fortresses, antl the limitation of the 
number of her vesecls of war, are the most effectual means of securing that 
object, 

The first of these methods, viz., introducing into the Black Sean power as 
alrong as Russia, scoms to be impossible. ‘Turkey cannot be raised to an 
equality with Russia as she now is. England and France could not engage to 
keep up cighteen sail of the line in the Black Sea, and if they did the Treaty 
containing that engagement would be an armed truce and not a peace. 

It is obvious that the second method is the only one practicable, and Her 
Majesty's Government cannot doubt that the Austdan Government will look at 
this question in the same light, and concur in the necessity of an agreement being 
established between the three Powers before entering into negotiation, 

In the meantime they gladly assent to the proposal of the Austrian Govern- 
ment to give effect to the Vth and the Secret Article of the Treaty of the 2nd of 


S7 


December, with the conviction that upon the firmness and decision of the three 
Powers at this moment may depend the success of negotiation and the prospects 
of peace, 

: Your Lordship is instructed to read this despatch to Count Buol.

The Earl of Clarendon to Mr. Hudson. 


(No, 6.) 
Sir, Foreign Office, January 20, 1855. 


HER Majesty's Government have attentively considered the important 
documents forwarded by you in your despatches Nos. 3 and 6 of the 10th and 
2th instant, and consisting, lst, of the Protocol of a Conference held between 
the French Minister at Turin, the Sardinian Minister for Foreign Affairs, and 
yourself, on the 10th instant, recording the previous communications which had 
taken place between the respective Governments with a view to the accession of 
Sardinia to the Treaty between England and France of the 10th April, 1854, and 
announcing that accession, and the readiness of the Sardinian Government to 
conclude with the two Powers a Military Convention providing for the active 
co-operation of Sardinia in the existitg war; 2ndly, of the form of the 
Sardinian Act of Accession; Srdly, of the draft of a Military Convention. 

I have in the first place to state to you that Her Majesty's Government 
sntirely approve of your proceedings in this negotiation, and of the Protocol 
nelosed in your despatch No. 3; and I send you herewith the draft of the 
British acceptance of the Sardinian accession, which you are authorized to sign 
ind exchange against the Act of Accession of the Sardinian Government. 

As regards the draft of Military Convention, circumstances which Twill 
proceed to explain, prevent Her Majesty's Government agreemg to it in its 
present form, though you will see that they fully concur in. its substance. Phe 
amendment which is required, applies to the Vth Article of the Sardinian draft, 
which would stipulate for a loan to be guaranteed hy england and France to 
Sardinia, to enable her to provide the military contingent specified in the 
Convention. : 

Her Majesty's Government are agreed with that of Franee, that the duty of 
providing for this loan shall be undertaken by England alone ; and it would 
therefore seem to be unnecessary, and might lead to inconvenience, that France 
should engage to beara part in the loan, which, in point of fact, it is not intended 
that she should do, 

Her Majesty's Government therefore propose to strike out altogether the 
Vih Article of the proposed tripartite ‘Treaty, and to record in a separate Treaty 
between England and Sarcinia the terms in which the loan in question shall be 
advanced. Her Majesty's Government do not apprehend any objection on the 
vart of Sardinia to so reasonable a proposal, but before | proceed to explain the 
intentions of Her Majesty's Government in regard to the loan, T will add, as 
regards the original Conveution, that they think it desirable to insert in it twa 
Articles; one providing that the military contingent to be furnished by Sardinia 
shall be composed of a due proportion of all arms; the other that the Sarclininn 
Goverument shall keep up the contingent to the amount specified in the Con. 
vention. You will find drafts of the proposed Articles inserted as Articles ILL 
and IV in the draft of tripartite Convention which | inclose. ‘ 

I also inclose the draft of Convention respecting the loan between England 
and Sardinia, which you will subimit to the Sardinian Government, It differs 
from the original stipulation in Article V of the Sardinian draft, Tst, in con. 
taining no reference to France; 2ndly, in the tering on which the loun is to 
be made; drdly, in the arrangement for its repayment. . ’ 

I have already explained why France should be no party to any stipulation 
touching the loan, eoneee 

As regards the terms on which the loan is to be made, the Sardinian 
Government proposed that it should be lent at an annual rate of interest calcu. 


a8 


lated on the average price of English consols during the last three months ; and 
as regards the repayment, that the condition should be settled at the peace. 

Now if the loan were to be made in the manner stated above, the interest 
payable upon it by Sardinia, would probably be found to be about 34 per cent, ; 
and no part of that interest would be applicable in diminution of the capital, 
which would have to be repaid by the appropriation hereafter of a large sum in 
one or at all events in a few payments. 

Her Majesty's Government, moreover, apprehend that some objection might 
be raised in the British Parliament to the indefinite nature of the proposed stipu- 
lation regarding the repayment of the loan. To obviate this last difficulty, Her 
Majesty's Government propose an arrangement which will be much more for 
the advantage of Sardinia, while it will enable them to satisfy Parliament that a 
substantial provision has been made for the repayment of the advance, The 
arrangement is, that the loan should be taken by Sardinia at + per cent., of 
which | per cent. shall be set apart by Great Britain as a sinking fund. Sardinia 
would thus have, in point of fact, only 3 per cent. to pay as interest on the 
loan, instead of 84, as she is now prepared to pay; and the amount to be 
provided by Sardinia for the periodical discharge of the interest of the loan will 
be progressively diminished in proportion as the capital is reduced by the 
application for that purpose of the | per cent. sinking fund, 

This mode of providing for the loan is so clearly for the interest of Sardinia, 
that Her Majesty's Government cannot doubt that the Sardinian Government 
will readily concur in it, 

Tt only remains for me to notice the clause of the Article which makes the 
advance of the loan subject to the consent of Parliament. You will have no 
difficulty in explaining to the Sardinian Government the impossibility of the 
Queen contracting an engagement of this nature without such a reservation ; 
but you may assure them that, immediately on the exchange of the ratifications 
of the Treaty, Her Majesty will seck the concurrence of her Parhament for the 
proposed loan: and Her Majesty does not doubt that such concurrence will be 
wiven so promptly as to ensure her being able to advance the money to Sardinia 
in ample time to enable that Power to prepare to take part in the war at the 
earliest period at which arrangements can be made for the transport of her 
troops to the scene of action. 

If, indeed, the Sardinian Government should consent to sign the Treaties 
as they are now sent to you in draft, it might save time if the Sardinian ratifica- 
tions were sent at once to Paris and London to be exchanged against those of 
Her Majesty and the Emperor of the French in the case of one Convention, and 
against that of Her Majesty alone in the case of the other.

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received January 22.) 


(No, 17. Confidential.) 


My Lord, Berlin, January 17, (855. 

THE King of Prussia granted me a private audience this day at Charlotten- 
burg, for the purpose of receiving from my hands the letter from Her Majesty 
the Queen, which your Lordship forwarded to me by the messenger Grattan. 

The audience lasted one hour and a quarter. Baron Manteutlel was 
present. 

To describe with accuracy the desultory, rambling conversation of the King 
is impossible, but lshall endeavour to repeat to your Lordship the leading 
points of it, and Lvegret to say that it has left me with the impression that 
there 1s very little prospect at the present moment of bringing the King round 
10 our poliey on the Eastern question; and that if we do sueceed in effecting so 
desirable a change, the progress towards i will be attended with difliculty, 
and much provoking delay at every stage of the neratition. 

The King commenced the conversation by saying that he was glad to have 
an opportunity of secing me, and spoke in the most kind and gracious manner. 
I delivered to His Majesty the Queen's letter, observing that the mission of 
M. d'Usedom had given sincere pleasure to Her Majesty, and that Her Majesty's 
Government hoped it was a prelude toa better and iinpreved understanding 
between the two countries on the great political question of the day, 

The King replied that he desired this most ardently, and that the reports 
which he had alreudy received from M.d’Usedom had been highly satisfactor 
and useful to lim, and that he was thankful to the Queen and to Her Majesty's 
Government for: the kindness and frankness with which his propositions had 
heen received, 

observed that we were desirous to meet the King’s wishes as to the Treaty, 
and that Her Mijesiy’s Government would consent to make any alteration that 
might be suggested in the form and words of it, provided the sense of the trans- 
actions of the 2nd of December were carried out, omitting those Articles which 
more particularly related to Austria, 

On the word “Austria” falling from my lips, the King spoke of the conduct 
of Count Buol towards him in the most violent terms, His Majesty suid. that 
that Minister had taken an unjustifiable advantage of Prussia last July, and put 
a forced interpretation on the proecedings of Count Alvensleben at Vienna, 
which had led to his present difheulties, ‘That he lad always been ready to act 
up to the envagements of April 9th; that he had supported the notes of the 
Sith af August at St. Petersburgh, and that in reality he had never retired from 
the Conference; that he had been cheated by Austria out of his place; and 
thik it was now attempted to treat him like a miinehty child. "That, however, 
he knew the strength of his position and the weakness of that of Austria ; that 
he was portestly aware that Austria couldd not move without him; and that if 
he was ta be excluded from the Conterence about to be held at Vienna, at which 
he considers that Prussia had a right as agrealt Power to assist, he should 
apypeil to his people to stand by him, and felt assured that he should not do so 
in vali when the dignity of his Crown and the honour of the nation were so

The above remarks appeared to make an impression on the King, for His 
Majesty immediately observed that the advantages of Austria were much greater 
than those of Prussia in the question, and he again inveighed in almost unmea- 
gured terms, amounting to a tone of exasperation, against Austria, as having 
been deceived by her; but he eaidl that, if attacked by Russia, he should be 
ready always to advance with his whole force to her defence. 

His Majesty, however, said nothing that might lead to the belief that he 
would make a Treaty for offensive purposes, though he stated that if Austria 
were attacked, he should consider it his duty to adopt that policy towards 
Russia that would be most conducive to the interests of his German ally. 

‘The King made repeated allusions to the manner in which he considered 
that he had been tricked out of the Conference, and to the resistance to his 
re-admission on the part of the allies; he contrasted the tone of the communi- 
cations which were addressed to him from Russia, and those from London, Paris, 
and Vienna: and al one moment His Majesty even said that menacing language 
had been used to him, 

| replied, that, certainly, I had never been instructed to speak in such 
terms, and His Majesty then appealed to Baron Manteufiel, who denied that 
the Marquis de Moustier had ever done so, and this matter was not further 
discussed. 

Twice the King spoke, and with much warmth, of proceedings which had 
been reported to him of the Jesuits of a conspiracy against Protestantism, which 
His Majesty believes to have been set on foot by the Court of Rome, and to be 
fostered by Austria and France, and His Majesty said that he had directed 
M. d’Usedom to communicate with Her Majesty’s Government on the subject, 
but that he had not yet heard from him on this matter. 

[ availed myself of an allusion being made by the King to his desire that 
the relutions of the two Governments should be placed on a better footing, to say 
that this feeling was fully reciprocated in enna but that we despaired of 
seeing confidence re-established as long as His Majesty's Court was composed of 
persons whose sympathies were completely Russian, That this: was at the 
present moment a serious obstacle to a renewal of confidence. 

| waited anxiously for an answer from the King, but His Majesty was 
silent + his countenance betrayed, however, that T had touched a painful chord. 
He took what I said in good part, and after a considerable pause turned the 
conversation to another subject. 

I am sorry to give your Lordship so imperfect an account of my audience, 
++ is with difficulty that one can follow the King from one subject to another ; but 
I think that I have not omitted mentioning the important parts, and those which 
may have been of real interest to Her Majesty's Government, His Majesty 
made several attempts to defend himself from the imputation of having acted 
unfairly in the late diplomatic transactions ; but his arguments were really incom- 
prehensible, and related to trifling incidents connected with the negotiations 
rather than to the real question under debate. 

I think | have said enouzh to your Lordship to show that although the 
King may desire to be on better terms with the Western Powers, His Majesty is 
completely in the hands of the Russian party; he is, indeed, so surrounded by 
them that | doubt his having the courage to disperse the phalanx around hin— 
indeed, | fear that he will never dare to break up this party, and that nothing 
will now change him but the force of circumstances. 

He allows that the Emperor of Russia was in the wrong ; he states that His 
limperial Majesty has now made every possible concession to bring about the 
approaching Conlerenee, tht he is sincere in his desire for peace, and that peace 

will result from the negotiations if we do not demand things incompatible with 
the honour of Russia. 

At the same time, however, that the King allows that Russia was the 
original cause of the present complications in Europe, he will not bind himself 
to act offensively either with Austria or with the Western Powers; he has 
declared that the time has not arrived for fulfilling the engagements contracted 
onthe 20th of April; he declines to mobilise at the invitation of Austria; and 
at the same moment he proposes to us to place 100,000, nay 200,000 men on the 
Vistula, but will not bind himself to act azainst Our OneMy. 

Such, indeed, are the continued inconsistencies of the King's policy that he 
would seem to he powerless, and the mere tool of the Russian party, whose 


05 


object would appear to be to ‘solate Prussia, and to establish an armed neutrality 
fxvourable to Russia: at the same time the King declares he will not support 
Russia, that he disapproves of her conduct; but he refuses to take an active 
part with us, and if not admitted to the Conference at Vienna, threatens to 
appeal to his people. 

This is the present state of things at the Prussian Court, and I fear they are 
not likely to become improved after the arrival of Duke George of Mecklenburg 
Strelitz, the Emperor of Russia’s nephew, who is shortly to arrive here from 
St. Petersburgh. 

This Prince did much injury to our cause last year, when, as your Lordship 
will recollect, he came on a visit to the King, and a more critical moment could 
not have been selected, or one more favourable to make an impression on the 
mind of a weak and vacillating monarch. 

The time is come when it might be expected that His Majesty should take 
a decision that would bind him to us or Russia, or place him in complete 
isolation in Europe and in Germany, but I doubt that His Majesty will do 
anything to fix his policy : he ts certainly unwilling to join the Western Powers; 
he is equally unwilliug to ally himself openly with Russia, and which ever way 
he looks he sees war in the distance. ‘To avoid this the King appears to con- 
sider that his best chance is for the present not to interfere actively one way OF 
the other, to take no decision, but to place his army on the war footing, perhaps 
to declare his neutrality, and at all events to he prepared to repel an attack from 
either side, and hereafter to throw his weight into which ever scale may be most 
to the advantage of Prussia, 

I have, &c. 


(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received January 22.) 


(No. 18. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, January 18, 1855. 
BARON MANTEUFFEL begged me to call upon him this morning, when 
he told me that he had had some conversation with the King yesterday, alter my 
departure from Charlottenburg, relative to what passed at my audience. 
He asked what | thought of all that had been stated by the King. 1

Inclosure | in No. 101. 
Circular to Austrian Representatives at the German Courts. 


(Translation.) Vienna, January 10, 1855. 

MY last cominunication has informed you that the Representatives of the 
three Powers, allied by the Treaty of December 2 at the meeting which took 
place on the 25th ultimo, entered into explanations to the Russian Minieter 
as to the sense and meaning which their Courts assign to the four points lad 
down as the bases of peace, and that as Prince Gortchakoff did not consider 
his instructions sufficient to express himself on the explanations offered to him, 
but declared himself ready to procure the necessary orders from his Court, 
the Plenipotentiaries agreed after a delay of fourteen days to meet in a second 
Conference. 

The result of Prince Gortchakoff’s report to his Court has been that that 
Minister informed me on the Gth instant that he was now enabled, in the name 
of his Government, to declare himself on the subject of the communication 
made to him by the Representatives of Austria, France, and Great Britain, 
‘Thereupon a second Conference between the four Plenipotentiaries took place 
on the 7th instant. 

On the basis of the discussions held, and the explanations exchanged im 
this new Conference, it was unanimously acknowledged by them, under reser- 
vation of the approval of the Cabinets of Pais and London, that no essential 
difference existed between the Courts of Austria, France, and Great Britain, 
aud Russia, as to the understanding of the sense and general range of the four 
preliminary points, and that accordingly a common basis had now been attamed 
on which regular negotiations of peace could be opened. 

The Imperial Cabinet has forthwith conveyed this to its Ministers in Paris 
aid London, as alsa to the Internuncto at Constantinople, with directions to 
urge the quickest possible transmission here of the full powers and instructions 
necessary for the commencement of the negotiations of peace. 

You are requested to communicate this important fact to 
We are convinced beforehand that you will varticipate in the high satisfaction 
with whieh the Imperial Cabinet has hniled the hopes of a speedy return of 
general peace, arising from the preliminary results already attained, 

Moreover it searcely requires to be specially remarked, that the real 
attainment of peace depends on the course of the negotiutions which are to. be 
opened, and that well-founded hopes may be placed on their suceessiul result, 
although it cannot be calculated upon with any degree of certainty, The 
impending attempt at peace cannot therefore exercise any influence on our 
military measures, so long as its result ts not assured, and we cannot doubt but 
that the Governments of Germany will approve of our solicitude and our 
attention continuing to be directed to the fullest extent towards the military 
preparations not only of Austria, but also of our German allies. 

In conclusion, we observe that we shall soon have occasion to make a 
further communication on this subject on the receipt of the answer of the 
Prussian Cabinet to our despatch of December ®4, addressed to Berlin. 

_ Reetive, &e.

Ineclosure 2 in No. 101. 


Circular to Austrian Representatives at the German Courts. 


( Translation.) Vienna, January 14, 1855. 

AFTER the decision taken by the Assembly of the Germanic Diet by their 
resolution of December 9, we believed it to be a duty incumbent on us to confer 
confidentially without delay with the Prussian Court, as to the practical cffect to 
be given to the resolution of the Diet, 

The instructions which we gave to our Minister at Berlin for this end, have 
been made known to by my communication of December 26. 
\t appears from the reply which we have now received, and of which I have the 
honour to annex a copy, that the views of the Cabinets of Vienna and of Berlin 
are nob agreed in essential points. 

Prussia denies the menacing character of the relations recoznized by the 
totality of the Dict, on the ground of the assurance of Russia, unconfirmed by 
any species of guarantees, that she was desirous of confining herself to the 
defence of her own territory, We do not undervalue the worth which such an 
assurance may have to a Power involved in war for the circumseription of the 
complication, but the German Governments, 28 well as Austria, can never 
attribute to this promise, accepted by no one, # binding and a secure character 
which could act restrictively on the carrying out of the resolutions adopted by 
the Dict, Was a confirmation only required that Russia herself did not 
conceive herself able to subordinate the claims of her military position to. this 
circumstance, it may be proved precisely at this moment by the advance of 
Russia against the Turks on the right bank of the Danube. 

If we do not also relinquish the hopes which Europe associates with. the 
late promises given by Russia at the Conference of the 7th instant, the definitive 
aim jé nevertheless too far removed, the opinions concerning the practical 
accomplishment and application of the four preliminary points miry be too 
ranifatdly divided, and the dilemmas of the war may operate too variously, as 
that the Jmperinl Court can resign themselves to the belief that they already 
hold in thar hands a sure pledge, in the already attained preliminary result, 
that peace will be really assured. 

We appeal to the upright sense of the German Governments, whether 
they can deceive themselves that the state of the world has lost us yet anything 
of that threatening gravity which the Dict itself has ucknowledged as existing. 
His Majesty the Emperor, our august Ruler, considers it mecessary to remain 
in the fullest preparation for all eventualities, and the impending negotiations 
for peace will consequently, so long as the certainty af success is wanting, 
neither influence the military measures of Austria herself, nor, in the opinion of 
Fis Majesty, ought they ta cheek the obligations taken by his German allies 
for the attainment of a common purpose. 

Such un attitude can ulone promote the interests of peace, and enhance 
the probabilities of a suceessful issue of the negotiations. According to our 
deep conviction, therefore, our German confederates should also now come to a 
resalution to give to the totality of Germany a position commanding respect. 
The highest interest of the German nation and of their Princes appears to us to 
require that Gormany should be sufficiently prepared for all possible events. 
Whatever expression also may be given shortly to the resolution of the Diet in 
its capacity as a political Power, at all events we must now again especially 
address our proposal to the eflvet that the necessary development of the military 
forces of the Diet should be provided for without delay, 

You will easily judge that, guided by these views, we could not reply to the 
expression of the Prussian Cabinet with respect to the armament of Prussia and 
of the German Dict, otherwise than has been done in the accompanying despateh 
to Count Usterhazy. 

The [imperial President of the Diet will consequently now move, in the 
appointed Committee, that the mobilisation of at least the half of the contingents 
shall be proposed in the assembly of the Diet, in case the opinion should not 
prevail, that it was preferable to render at once the whole Federal army dispos- 
able for operations, ‘The question whether in the first ease two combined Sart 
W'armces, or whether four independent corps, should be formed, which would be 


99 


followed in the case of necessity by the other half of the contingents, as well as 
all other questions of detail, will have to form the subject of deliberation as 
expeditiously as possible, and of the resolutions of the Diet. The selection of a 
Federal Commander-in-chief will likewise be necessary, in order that the union 
of the different corps of the Federal army under one common supreme command 
may take place according to the constitution; and we are consequently of 
opinion that the Dict should occupy themselves immediately with this point, and 
take the proper steps for the election of the Commander-in-chiet of the forees 
of the Diet; whilst in the separate States measures should be taken in order 
that the Federal corps may be ready equipped to be placed at the disposal of the 
Commander-in-chief to be elected, 

You will communicate this despatch to with 
the request that they will be pleased to inform us of the determination to which 
this communication will give rise, as also of the instructions which they may be 
induced to send to their Representative at Frankfort, in order that we may 
cooperate towards the fulfilment of the important task which is submitted to the 
organ of the will of entire Germany, | 

Receive, &c. 
(Signed) BUOL, 


Inclosure 3 in No. 101, 
Count Buol to Count Esterhazy. 


(Translation, ) Viewna, January 14, 1855. 


COUNT ARNIM has communicated to us the despatch, copy of which is 
inclosed, in which the Cabinet of Berlin replies to our overtures of the 24th 
ultimo, respecting the military preparation of Prussia and the Germanic 
Confederation, 

The Additional Article of November 28, and the Federal Deerees of 
December 9, were necessarily the cause and motive of our bringing forward this 

uvestion. Our demand, therefore, could surely not be unexpected to the Royal 
‘abinet. Baron Manteuffel even appeals to Prussia having, in maintenance of 
the point of view of the military obligations contracted by her, with a continual 
regard to the gravity of the situation, already made proper arrangements to 
secure to her army an increased readiness for war, and to render it possible te 
place in position greater bodies of troops ready for action, in shorter periods 
than those of the Military Convention of April 20. We can only rejoice at this 
declaration, but must abstain from all judgment of the measures alluded to, as 
they have not been communicated to us more particularly, nor pointed out as 
the subject of an agreement with us. 

The Prussian Government, further, does not enter into our proposal, on the 
grounds that they cannot share the opinion that an aggressive advance is 
intended on the part of Russia. 

In their eyes this apprehension is contradicted by the repeated declarations 
of the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh, and by its conduct with respect to the nego- 
tiations of peace, and is also not justified by the nature of the movements of the 
Russian troops. We, on the other side, can on no point and in no respect 
consider the danger of the situation to be diminished, as long as peace is not 
really secured, Russia is continually making greater exertions to concentrate 
the forces of her yast Empire, of which the newly-ordered levy also furnishes a 
proof,and no other limits are assigned to the way and manner ofapplying her means, 
thun those which she deems advisable to observe in her own momentary interest, 
At this moment the Russian troops are again advancing into the Dobrudscha, to 
cut off the communications of the Turkish commander, ‘The military caleula- 
tions of Russia can menace any other point in the same way as they now do the 
right bank of the Danube, if the resolutions of the Court of St. Petersburgh do 
not incline towards the conclusion of peace, 

The war can penetrate into our own provinces, into the Danubian Princ 
palities, into the passes of the Balkan; and, according to the march of events, 
the armies of Russia can necessitate not only the realisation of the defensive 


100 


obligations of Prussia, but also the cases of an active advance of both the German 
Powers already provided in the Treaty of April. We regret that the Cabinet of 
Berlin attaches a weight to the views and measures of Russia alluded to, im 
whieb we cannot participate in such a state of things. 

The communication of Baron Manteuffel touches further on the political 
position of his Court. We have anticipated the Prussian Gabinet in not acknow- 
ledwing that, under present circumstances, the obligations of Prussia are litnited 
to the conditions of the Treaty of April, to the Additional Article of November 
98, and to the Federal Decrees following it. We cannot accept the remark of 
Baron Manteuffel that those obligations were indissolubly connected with the sup- 
joxition of the common efforts to give effect to the four poirits, ina sense is if 

‘russia considered the force of the contracted obligations to be dissolved by the 
difference at present existing in the position of the two Powers. Morcover, as 
we can deduce nothing positive as to the further intentions of Prussia from that 
remark, we confine ourselves to assuring her that we will inno respeet place our- 
selves in contradiction with the rights which Prussia derives from her quality of 
a Great European Power, and to manifesting on this fresh occasion our sincerc 
desire of seeing the action of the two German Powers in one way or other soon 
reunited on a perfectly equal basis. 

The German Diet has acknowledged by its decrees that the menacing 
attitude of European affairs rendered military arrangements on the part of the 
Germanic Confederation necessary. It has directed the Military Committee to 
make suitable proposals, and with this view the separate Governments have now 
freely to declare their views as to the mode of carrymg out the resolutions 
passed by their ‘netructions to the members of the Committee, and then by their 
vote. We for our part thonght we only need abide by the agreements already 
made between Austria and Prussia on the 20th of April last, for the purpose of 
eventually regulating the military action of the two Powers, as well as the 
prep whieh they were to address in common to the Germanic Confederation. 
Jrussin does now not desire to take such an initiative with the Diet, but ehe 
informa ws that the Royal Military Plenipotentiary will find himself provided 
with the necessary instructions to promote the task of the Military Committee 


‘according to the Federal War Constitution, and to help to bring it toa conclu. 


sion in a suitable manner. It can only be a matter of rejoicing for us to be able 
to derive the hope from this, that on ihe whole the influence of Prussia, as well 
as our own, will be directed to the object of the sufficient readiness lor war on 
the part of the Germanic Confederation. 

Accordingly the Imperial Government will, in. the Committee of the Diet, 
declare itself in favour of a mobilisation of half of the Federal contingents. At 
the same time, in consideration of the fact that after the rules of the War 
Constitution, when the formation of a Federal army ‘a decreed, the nomination 
of a Federal Commander-in-clief must take place, and that this election forms t 
preliminary condition for the union of the Federal corps under one cCOMMOT 
command, the Federal Government will add a proposition that the Diet shall 

seupy itself with the necessary preliminaries for the election of a Commander- 
in-chief, We do not delay to communicate our opinions to the separate 
Governments of the ‘onfederution, and inclose in this despatch a copy of a 
crenlar which we have addressed to the Imperial Missions at the German States 
for that purpose. 

You are requested to communicate the above remarks to the Minister 
President, and to inform him of the step we have taken towards our confederates 
in expressing « wish that we may be assured by the answer of the Royal 
Government that Prussia appreciates our proceedings in the apie of an ully. 

Keceive, &e. 
(Signed) BUOL,

The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon —(Received January 22:) 


(No. 4.) 
My Lord, Vienna, January 17, 1855 


1 HAVE the honour of inclosing copies of the telecraphic despatches | 
forwarded to your Lordship on the Lith and 15th instant, by the latter of which 
the Russian Commander-in-chief, Prince Gortehakoff, announces the return of 
the Russian troops which had attacked the body of ‘Turkish furces stationed on 
the right bank of the Danube, in and about Toultcha, to their original position 
near Ismail, In referring to my despatch to your Lordship No, 23 of the 13th 
instant, in which | inclosed the notes | had addressed to Count Buol wpon the 
subject of these movements on the part of the Russian forces, and in which | 
staie the answers | had received to the communications I had made to him of 
your Lordship’s telegraphic despatch of the [dth, T have now to add that 
on the day after the date of my despatch No. 28, Count Buol announced that 
he had reecived a telegraphic message from Bucharest, stating that the Russian 
troops had not advanced further than Babadagh, and reporting that two Turkish 
corps, under the orders of Sadik and Achmet Pashas, had passed the Danube at 
Surdavei and. Yara Jalunizza, with the view of offering an effectual check to any 
further advance of the Russians towards the south, and he therefore believed 
that the movement made by the Russian troops had for its object only to attack 
the small body of Turkish forces which were immediately opposite to them. 

On the same evening (the 4th instant) Baron Bourjueney reecived from 
his Consul at Bucharest, M. de Poujade, a most alarming telegraphic despatch, 
stating that the Russian corps of eighteen battalions of Infantry and a lange body 
of Cavalry, and seventy-six guns, was marching with the greatest rapidity upon 
Baltehik, near Varna, 1 went early next morning to Count Buol to represent 
to him the gravity of this’ intelligence, of which, however, U had received no 
report from Her Majesty's Consul at Bucharest, when, to my surprise, he placed 
in my hands the telegraphic despatel of the 12th instant from Prince Gortchakoff, 
which put an end to all the reports of the advance of the Russians towards 
Baltchik and Varna, which had previously been announced with so much 
nesurance, 

Count Buol expressed his great satisfaction at the contents of this despatch, 
as it confirmed the belief that he had always entertained, that no serious 
operation by the Russians on the right bank of the Danube could be attempted, 
as he felt, in common with General Hess, that it was much too dangerous an 
operation for the Russians to undertake from their present positions, and in the 
actual state of the relations of Austria towards the Nisin Government. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) WESTMORLAND.

My Lord, Paris, January 21, 1855. 
‘THE messenger who was the bearer of your Lordships despatch No. 44 
of the 19th instant, inclosing the drafts of two despatches which you proposed 
to address to the Earl of Westmorland, and which you desired should be com- 
municated to M. Drouyn de Lhuys, was-delayed on his journey by the weather, 
and it became impossible for ine to carry out your Lordship’s farther instructions 
to make you acquainted by the telegraph with the opinion of the Frenct 
Government, so as to enable you to dispatch a messenger to Vienna yesterday 
evening. 

1 have now the honour to report that I read to M. Drouyn de Lhuys the 
two drafts in question. His Excellency, after listening to them with attention, said 
that it was impossible to restime more impartially, or with greater force, the 
incidents which had preceded and accompanied Prince Gortehn offs demand to 
treat for peace. He should have sreferred however, his Excellency added, that 
the longer despatch of the two 5 iould have been written rather as a guide to 
Her Majesty's Minister at Vienna, as to the language which he should hold in 
his conversation with Count Buol, than as a direct communication to be made to 
the Austrian Minister for Foreign Afftirs. He quite agreed that the time was 
come when the Western Powers should not allow the Austrian Government, to 
remain in ignorance of their firm determination to carry on the war until the 
preponderance of Russia in the Black Sea was put an end to in the manner 
insisted on by your Lordship; but he asked himeelt, and he ventured to ask your 
Lordship, whether some inconvenience might not arise from demanding an 
immediate expression of opinion from Austria, whether in effect it was nut 
hazarding an unswer from ine which might become a source of embarrassment 
for the future. Suppose an official demand to be made to Count Buol to assent 
to the interpretation given by your Lordship of the only practical mode of 
destroying the preponderance of Russia in the Black Sea, and the Count to 
refuse his assent to that interpretation, would it not be placing an obstacle in the 
way of a future understanding with Austria, which might be aveided by con- 
fining the communication to be made to Count uol to a simple announcement 
of the intentions of the Western Powers? It was with this view, lis Excellency 
observed, that he had written the despatch to M. de Bourqueney of which I 
made mention in my despatch No. 44 of the LOth instant, and of which Count 
Walewski has received a copy for communication to your Lordship. 

Before adverting to M. Drouyn de Lhuys’ remarks upon your Lordship's 
second despatch, | must state that im a conversation which | had with his Exeel- 
lency the day before yesterday, | had suggested that in consequence of the can- 
ficting accounts given of what occurred at the Conference of the 8th, and of the 
reports prevalent in Germany that Prince Gortehakoff's interpretation of the 
four points had been accepted by the allies, it might be advisable that Her 
Majesty's and the Emperor's Representatives at Vienna, should be instructed to 
call Count Buol’s attention to these circumstances, and to request him to call 
a Conterence at which a Protocol should be signed by the four Plenipotentiaries 
who had attended the former, attesting Prince Gorte hakotl’s acceptance of the 
interpretation given by the allies to the four points. lt appeared to me that if
