(No. 26.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, January 11, 1895. 

HE Grand Vizier has expressed disappointment at the silence maintained 
with respect to Turkey in Her Majesty's speech, and more particularly in that of 
the French /mperor, 

In reply to what his Highness remarked to me upon the subject, I said, 
that in ignores of the real cause, if eause there was, | could only hazard a 
conjecture, which it gave me pain to enuneciate, namely, that the two allied Courts 
having no new circumstance to announce in favour of ‘Turkey, had exercised a 
friendly discretion im reserving the mention of its name. 1 ventured to add 
that the same friendly sentiment would doubtless inspire a more gratifying 
procedure as offen as the ‘Turkish Government or its arinies gave proof of that 
progress in military and administrative improvement, ou which so much 
depended for the success ani ultimate benefit of the common cause, 

I have since learnt that the Turkish Ambassador at Paris on observing the 
omission to which I have referred, applied to M. Dronyn de Lhuys in search of 
an explanation, and was assured by that Minister that the Emperor's silence, 
grounded upon nothing bit a similar silence preserved by Her Majesty the 
Queen, would be forthwith ctified by the insertion of a suitable paragraph in 
the ‘' Moniteur.” 

I have, &e.

No. 119. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received January 24.) 


(No. 28, Confidential.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, January 11, 1855. 

1 WAS visited the day before yesterday by Vassif Pasha, who, as your 
Lordship is aware, has undertaken the charge of commanding the army at Kare 
during Ismail Pasha’s gbeence in Bulgaria, Lavailed myself of the opportunity 
to recommend Ganorit Williams to bis confidence and attention in the most 
unreserved terms, aud | endeavoured to impress upon his mind the importance 
of his acting in cordial concert with that officer, if he wished to render the army 
efficient and to meet the views of Her Majesty’s Government, identified as they 
were with those of the Sultan and the Porte, 

The assurances with which he replied to my injunctions were quite satis- 
factory, and L hope that his conduet will be such us to redeem the pledge which 
they conveyed. 

[cannot affirm that I was equally satisfied with the indications which he 
gave of being put in possession by the War Department of all that was necessary 
to mect the demands of General Williams, or to fulfil the expectations which I 
have been authorized to entertain. 

The Pasha is military by profession, and his language is that of a sincere and 
well-intentioned man. He spoke unspatingly—though, of course, in confidence 
—of the deficiencies existing in the War Department; and foam under an 
impression that further exertions will be necessary to have him properly 
instructed, and promptly sent forward to his destination. | have already expressed, 
myself with earnestness to Reshid Pasha on this subject, and | hope Uiat my 
words have not fallen on a barren soil. 

His Highness aseured me that Shukri Pasha shall be recalled, that proper 
deference shall be paid to General Willams, as Her Majesty's Commissioner, 
and that a Council shall be formed at the War Department to assist the Seraskier, 
and to give a more steady and efficient direction to his operations. 

L have, &c. 


(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

I have thought it my duty to report these remarks to your Lordship, not 
that they were said as if the Emperor himself believed in the truth of the latter 
of them, Indeed, on my observing that Great Hritain had never made such 
efforts as in the commencement of this war, and that there were circumstances 
attending it which could attend no other, but which told particularly on the 
efficiency of the British forces, His Majesty coincided in the justice of the 
observation. An 

Another matter which was disonssed with His Majesty, but which is not 
alluded to in-his letter, was the establishment of a Military Board or Council at 
Paris, I am persuaded that Her Majesty's Government would derive great 
advantage from associating in such a plan. The reports reecived by the French 
Government from the East are very detailed; they would, I am sure, he laid 
before any officers whom Her Majesty might please to send over, and future 
operations might be discussed with advantage. As it is, there is, I think your 
Lordship will admit, a want of unity between the two countries, not of purpose, 
but of plan; and I see no way of remedying this great evil but by the creation 
of a permanent council of war, That this Council should meet at Paris seems 
but revsonable, and I venture to urge the matter upon the consideration of Her 
Majesty’s Government. The plan proposed is, that a general officer, an officer 
of Engineers, and a superior naval officer, should be sent over, and accredited for 
this purpose ; and ifthe Austrian Government decides eventually on a military 
cooperation with the Western Powers, the general officer whom the Emperor 
Francis Joseph is about to send to Paris, might be added with advantage to the 
Council,

THE “ Hamburgh Correspondent” a few day ursori :

of the Austrian note of December 24, requiring Prussia to mobilise Pan 000 Pen 
and the Prussian answer of the Sth instant, declining this request. 
The Austrian note founds its demand on the Military Convention of the

Treaty of April, according to which the necessity of Prussia’s placing 100,000 
or 200,000 men in position is to be determined by mutual agreement. The 
existence of this necessity is deduced from the circumstance that Russia stands 
“ready for battle” on the eastern frontiers of Austria; and therefore Prussia 
is by the Military Convention obliged to mobilize. It is added, that in the 
opinion of General Hess, Austria would only be strong enough to accept the 
combat with certainty of sueeess if supported by 100,000 Prussians. 

We have already stated that Prussia refused this demand of Austria, because 
the intention of Russia to attack Austria was in no way confirmed, aud because 
according to all that we know of the intentions of Russia, an offensive war with 
Austria on her part was not to be feared. The Prussian note of January 
says in this respect: “ Austria and Prussia are bound to common efforts to give 
effect to the four points ; such common aetion docs not tuke place if Prussia 
has no part in their de inition of the four points, Prussia derives her title to this 
participation regarding decisions which relate to the maintenance of peace, whilst 
they invalve a change of the international state of Europe and a modification of 
those “Treaties to which Prussia was a party, from her position as agreat Muropean 
Power, in virtue of which she signed those ‘Treaties, and not from any recent 
stipulations. ‘The King will steadfastly adhere to this view, and will fear neither 
dangers nor sacrifices if menaced hy encroachments. Prussia is ready to enter 
into further agreements, but ut the Diet she will designate the immediate 
preparation for warns not demanded by circumstances.” 

This passage fully bears out what we pomted out as the line of Prussian 
policy in our last article, The common action of Austria and Prussia cannot 
consist in Austria, France, and Great Britain defining the four points, and 
afterwards inviting Prussia to join, but must be shown in common consultations 
as well as action. Prussia cannot act where she lias not taken part in the 
deliberations. ‘This is so natural that one cannot conceive how it was overluoked 
at Vienna, 

‘That the King will adhere to the views taken in the note of January 5, 
must give satisfiction throughout Prussia, and the nation will faithfully support 
him mm this policy. 

In the meantime we do not fear a continuous conflict. If a mistake has 
heen made at Vienna as to considerations due to Prussia, if it even waa 
expected to surprise us with an accomplished fact, the note of January 5 will, 
it is to be hoped, have had the effect of removing this error. From the first 
mecting of the Conference ta the separate alliance of December 2, Prussia has 
not undertaken the least thing without the concurrence of Austria; Prussia 
may forget that the same was not done by her, but the first condition of an 
harmonious action in the spirit of the Confederation will and must be the 
reestublishment of deliberations incommon. If this be not the case, well, then, 
Prussia will remain Prussia. 

Whether after having deviated from the open and straight course by the 
Treaty of December 2, by the negotiations of December 28 and January 7, 
Austria may think fit to return amicably to it, will soon be shown. The 
Cabinet of Vienna knows by the Prussian note of January 5, that Prassia will 
oppose herself to a proposal for mobilisation to be made at Frankfort, os not 
necessitated by circumstances. Austrian has announced that she is: resolved to 
propose in the Diet that the Federal contingent, of which for the present only 
oneshalf is to be mobilized, be made realy for war, and at the same time the 
election of a Federal Commander-in-chief, We can only sincerely hope that 
Austria wi!l desist from this attempt, in order that the unity and concord of 
Germany may be maintained,

No. 130. 
Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received January 25.) 
(No. 28.) 
My Lord, Berlin, January 23, 1855. 


M. DE BISMARCK-SCHONHAUSEN, who had been summoned here 
to confer with the King of Prussia on the policy to be pursued by the Germanic 
Diet with reference to the Eastern question, returned to his post at Frankfort on 
Saturday last. 

I am informed that M. de Bismarck will meet the Austrian proposal for a 
mobilisation of half the contingent of the Confederation, by submitting a 
counter-proposal requiring the Diet provisionally to decide whether they judge 
that the moment has arrived for carrying into execution the engagements to 
which they are bound in the Additional Article. He hopes to obtain a majority 
in favour of this proposal, counting largely on the great desire of the smaller 
States to avoid to the latest moment the expenses of mobilising their con- 
tingents, 

Intelligence has this day arrived from Frankfort that the Austrian proposal 
was submitted to the Diet yesterday by Baron Prokesch, and that as the several 
Ministers declared themselves without instructions, its discussion was deferred, 
1am informed that Saxony has declared her intention of supporting Prussia, 
and that Bavaria, Wurtemburg, and Baden have agreed to act together, although 
it ismot yet known in what sense their votes will be given. 

Lam told that M. von der Pfordten has written to this Government in the 
strongest manner, pourtraying the dangers to Germany which are imminent 
from a division between the two leading German Powers, and foreseeing with 
alarm the dissolution of the Confederation as a necessary consequence of their 
disunion, The object of this Minister has doubtless been to induce this 
Government to make such concession as will bring about an harmonious under- 
standing between the two States, and prevent an open breach from taking place 
at the Dict. 

I have, Xe. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD,

Inclosure in No. 135. 
M. E, Pisani to Lord Stratford de Redeliffe, 


My Lord, Pera, January 12, 1865, 

IN Elrenence of your Excellency’s instruction of yesterday's date, waited 
on Aah Pasha, to whom I read word for word, and explained the contents-of the 
said instruction, and haye now the honour to report that his Highness gave me 
the most unequivocal and official assurances that the Ottoman Ministers engage 
to fulfil punctually the promises which the Ficld-Marshul and the Admiral 
equally require of them, 

‘Two steam-frigates, said he, and a steamer of a smaller size, are itlready 
appropriated to the service of conveying exclusively provisions to the Crimea. 
Their respective names are * Muhbir Sourur,”’ “ Saik Shaadi,” and “ Chahper.”' 
The first is actually plying between Bourgas and Eupatoria, the second lett this 
a week ago for Varna, with provisions for the troops to be embarked for the 
Crimea, and the third sailed three days since with provisions for the Ottoman 
troops stationed near Sebastopol. 

With reference to a month's provisions being embarked together with the 
troops punctually in Bulgaria, the bulk, nature, and weight of provisions, and 
places whence they are to come, the Seraskier Pasha, and the head of the 
department which supplies the troops with provisions, assured me that arrange. 
ments have been made by the Generalissimo to send a month's supplies with the 
troops embarking at Varna, Baltchik, and Bourgas, As regards the provisions to 
be forwarded from Constantinople, and ready to be shipped immediately, they 
consist of 720 casks of cavourma, or preserved meat, 40 okes each; 1,300 bags 
of biseuit, containing each 35 okes ; 140 hogsheads of grease, of 150 okes each ; 
5,000 chekis or loads of firewood, 20,000 okes of candles, 10,000 okes of oil, 
10,000 okes of soap, 20,000 okes of beans, 15,000 okes of rice, 2,000 chekis or 
loads of firewood ta be transported from Sinope, and 200,000 okes of beans to 
be shipped at Trebizond, Besides there are here ready to be towed four sailing 
vessels, charged with planking for making huts, and two vessels loaded with 
charcoal. These ure the provisions to be sent this week. A similar quantity 
will be forwarded every week,

consequence of Lord Westmorland’s transmission of Count Buol's communica 
tion, had passed between himself and M, de Poujade, on the one side, and the 
Wallachian Secretary of State, on the other. From this correspondence it 
appears that, according to the information conveyed to Count Buol, the Sultan 
was accused of having issued firmans against twenty-three Boyards, expelling 
these individuals, and confiscating their respective properties. It appears at the 
same time that the information thus filed against His Majesty, was altogether 
groundless and without a shadow of foundation. Had it been otherwise, my 
Lord, I think it highly improbable that any such measure would have been 
taken by the Turkish Government without its being known by Her Majesty's 
Embassy. It is all but certain, indeed, that the Porte would not have resorted, 
under present circumstances, to so violent an extreme without ascertaining 
beforehand the opinion of the British and French Representatives. 

Mr, Gardner informs me that several Ionian subjects have been arbitrarily 
arrested in Moldavia by the Turkish military authorities, on a suspicion of bein 
employed as spies by Russia. This I have no doubt is a local act ARanthoniaen 
by any specific warrant from here. It appears that General Coronini reversed 
the irregularity by a proceeding equally inconsistent with the regular forms of 
justice. He caused the persons who had been arrested to be set at liberty 
without trial, ; 

The arrest of these Ioniauns may probably have given rise to the story of the 
exiled Boyards. If so, it was for Her Majesty's Consul at Jassy to interfere on 
their behalf. Atall events it does not appear that there was any case either 
against the Wallachian Government or against the Ministers of the Porte,

ALTHOUGH you are to consider the Pirmus as your rendezvous, [ wish 
you to take frequent opportunities of visiting the various islands in the 
Archipelago. 

It will not be necessary for you to remain at any place more than 4 day or

You will on all occasions place yourself i communication with our Consuls

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received January 27.) 


(No. 80.) 
My Lord, Paris, January 26, 1855. 

1 HAVE inquired of M. Drouyn de Lhuys whether the reports to which 
Mr. Wyse alludes in his despatch No. 7 of the 17th instant, of Austrian troops 
heing about to replace the British and French troops of occupation in Greeee, 
had reached his Excellency. He replied tn the negative, and on my pressing 
him for an opinion as to the utility of such a measure, he said that he was 
decidedly opposed to it, There might have been a moment, he observed, when, 
in order to compromise Austria, the presence of her uniform in Greeee might 
have been desirable, but that motive existed no longer, or at all events not with 
the same force, and he was quite against her military interference in Greece.

_ THE substance of a despatch written by M. de Werther, the Prussian 
Minister at St. Petersburgh, to iis Court, on the 26th ultimo, has been commiu- 
nicated to me confidentially, and 2s there is some interest attaching to his 
statements, | do myself the honour of repeating them to your Lordship on 
the chance of your having no knowledge of the despatel in question. x 

_ M. de Werther states it to be the apinion of Count Nesselrode, of Count 
Orloff, of Count Kisscleff, and of Count Pahlen (the General), who are all at 
heart partisans of peace, that it will be impossible for the Emperor to necept 
conditions dishonourable to Russia, and that.it would he far less dangerous to 
the Emperor to permit the temporary occupation of some of his provinces than 
to make concessions that would be a triumph to the Western Powers. The 
Prussian Minister states further that, although the mass of the Russian peo ale 
does not know of the true state of things, the more enlightened part are better 
informed, and are in favour of resistance ; and if the attempts at negotiations lead 
i a jean and a coalition is formed against the Emperor, His Majesty will 
; an opera, and then will be seen what the enthusiasm of the 

It is evidently M, de Werther’s opinion, that Russia nay make a successful 
defence even against an European coalition. He observes that she wants 
nothing from other countries to enable her to carry on the war; that she can 
get as many soldiers as she wants, whom she can supply from her own resources 
with every necessary requisite, whether of arms, food, or clothing; that so lon 
as the war is confined to Russia, the want of a metallic currency will not be 
felt, though he admits that the depreciation of money involved in a long paper 
currency may lead to financial difficulties later. Vig

No. 143. 


The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Bloomfield. 
(No. 28.) 


My Lord, Foreign Office, January 27, 1855, 

COUNT BERNSTORFF has this day read to me a despatch from Baron 
Manteuffel, of which he afterwards placed the copy in my hands; a copy of the 
despatch is herewith inclosed for the information of your Lordship. 

1 told Count Bernstorif that the position and attributes of Prussia, as one 
of the Great Powers of Europe, were fully recognized by Her Majesty's 
Government, . 

I again expressed fo him the regret of Her Majesty's Government at the 
estrangement that had occurred between England and paint and [ renewed 
to him the assurance, that no effort on our part had been, or should be, wanting 
in order to secure unity of action between the two Governments; but that with 
every wish to arrive at this desirable result in the manner most conformable to 
the honour and dignity of Prussia, I did not see how England, France, and 
Austria, could admit the ¢laim of Prussia unconditionally and without any 
previous engagement to take part in the negotiations for peace that might 
shortly be commenced at Vienna. 

OF the Five Parties to those negotiations, four, I said, were actually belli- 
gerents, and the fifth was not only fully prepared for war, but bad actually 
engaged to make war if the negotiations for peace should fail. The belligerents 
would not discontinue hostilities during the negotiations, and the non-belligerent 
was bound to commence them ina certain contingeucy. The position of all 
these parties was clear and intelligible ; but what, | begged to ask, would be the 
position of Prussia at these Conferences, and upon what did she found her 
Tight to take part in them with Powers situated so differently to herself? 
Prussia had incurred no expense, had made no preparution, had entered into 
m0) ten oe anid had announced she would contract none. She had declared 
that the Eastern question did not affect her as it did other Powers. She 
had proclaimed her neutrality, and had rendered eminent service to Russin by 
unremitting efforts to thwart the policy of Austria, In no one respect then dil 
the position of Prussia resemble that of the Powers with respect to whose 

differences she would take no part, and incur no risk + but who, she now declared, 
had no right except in her presence to deliberate upon the conditions on which 
they would make peace. “The claim of Prussia, in short, was to enjoy the 
privileges, and to evade the obligations of a Great European Power; but 
supposing, IT said, that Prussia was admitted to the Conference unfettered by 
habla chgagements, as Baron Manteuffel proposed, What, Dasked, would be 
er course if Russia refused the terms of peace offered to her, and Austria, in 
fulfilment of the Treaty of the 2nd of December, declared war against Russia: 
would Prussia declare war also, or HoH she then abdicate her position as

Great European Power, and assume that ofa member of the Confederation, and 
again reverting to neutrality wait till the events of war once more led tu 
negotiations for peace, and then again claim a right to take part in them ? 

These questions, I said, required definite answers, and a clear understand- 
ing must be come to upon them ; for great Powers engaged in war could not 
lightly admit another into theit deliberations without knowing whether that 
Power was a friend, a foe, or a neutral. ; 

Count Bernstorffsaid he had no instructions as to the part that Prassia would 
take in the contingency to which I had adverted; but he reminded me that 
Prussia had entered into engagements, and had concluded a Treaty on the 20th 
April, and subsequently an ‘Additional Article to it, with Austria. 

answered that that was an engagement taken by two non-belligerent German 
Powers exclusively for the protection of German interests, without reference to 
England and France, or to the war which they were carrying on against Russia ; 
and although England and France wished well to Germany, and heartily desired 
that it should be protected from Russian aggression and relieved from Russian 
influence, yet their objects in the war with Russia were European and not 
German, and that until Prussia entered into engagements with England and 
France, | must persist in saying that as an European Power she had contracted 
Tone, 

Count Bernstorif said, that Prussia having been a party to the Treaty of 1841, 
denied the right of the other Contracting Powers to modify that Treaty without 
her concurrence, and on that ground she insisted upon taking part at the 
Conference. 

i answered that it was doubtful whether the Treaty of 1841 was not 
abrogated ly the war, and at all events it would require to be renewed, and 
whenever its revival or modification came under discussion, a communication 
might be made to Prussia upon the subject, but that question was only one of 
the four bases, and upon that Prussia could not sustain a claim to take part in 
discussing the other Hes. 

Count Bernstorff then again denied that Prussia had ever withdrawn from 
the Conferences, and said, that as the present Conferences were a continuation of 
the former ones in which Prussia had taken part, she must now insist on not 
being excluded from them. 

T assured Count Bernstorff that he was in error, and that the present 
Conferences were not a continuation of the original ones in which Prussia had 
taken part; Austria, it was true, had proposed to resume the Conferences, 
in order to consider the Sul ane of the four bases, but the answer 
of England and France was that the time for Conferences was gone by, 
ant that they could not be renewed except as a consequence of some 
definite engagement between the three Powers, and this eventually led to the 
Treaty of December 2. But Prussia, I said, was now in the same position 
towards England and France as Austria when she proposed to renew the 
Conferences, and England and Frince might make to her the same answer 
as to Austria—enter with us into a contingent engagement for war, and we 
will then enter with you into immediate negotiations for peace. Prussia, 
however, complained of the [nd Article of the Treaty of December 2, as 
not affecting her interests, and of the Vith Article as contrary to her 
dignity ;_ and 1 would therefore propose that those Articles should be omitted. 
Prussia had complained of the manner in which she had been called upon 
by Austria to mobilize her army, in fulfilment of the Treaty of April 20, 
and appeared disinclined to enter into any fresh engagement with that Power, 
and 1 accordingly suggested that the Treaty should be made with England and 
France alone, and that the same interpretation of the bases should be given to 
Prussia as to Austria, and a similar Protocol should be signed. ‘The three 
Powers being then ugreed among themselves, should announce the fact of that 
agreement to Austria, and Prussia would thus establish her claim to take part 
in the negotiations for peace upon a footing of perfect equality. 

In offering this suggestion to the consideration of Count Bornstorff 1 begged 
to assure him that [ had not even submitted it to my colleagues, nor had T any 
authority to speak in the name of the French and Austrian Governments ; but 
the desire of all waa so sincere to re-establish cordial relations with Prussia, and 
to secure her active groper in the present crisis, that I felt sure they would 
readily concur in any plan for that object, and the more so because it would be

The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl! of Clarendon.—(Keceived January 29.) 
No. 45, Confidential.) 


My Lord, Vienna, January + 

: , January 24, 0859. 

. coum BUOL spoke to me to-day of the importance he could not but 
attac a ee at communication he had received from the Prussian Govern- 
Sree fae ich they appeared to have determined to separate themselves 
as 1e policy adopted by Austria, as well as by the Governments of England 
Lae ne Count Buol remarked that the announcement which had now been 
mils a russia, that she would not support the proposition of Austria, that a 
B 0 Be war Sonne RE of the German States should be assembled, and that 
ae wou pat mobilize any part of her own army, had placed her in an attitude 
“ so much estrangement from Austria, whose measures with respect to 

ermany were regulated by the strictest adherence to the engagements she had 
contracted, that he felt it was of the Poe consequence that both France and 


8 ee 


138 


England should make the most pressing repiteséntations to the Cabinet of Berlin, 
in order to ascertain what line they would take, and the extent to which they 
would go in giving their assistance to the policy which they had hitherto 
supported. Count Buol stated that he made this appeal at the present moment, 
because on entering upon the discussion of the military plans to be adopted in 
ease the state of things contemplated in the Vth Article of the Treaty of the 
2nd December should arise, it was absolutely necessary to know the attitude 
which Prussia was determined to assume. 

Count Buol said, that as far as Austria was concerned, he should be 
perfectly content to treat with Prussia, simply in her attitude as a German 
Power, leaving it to England and France to enter into engagements with her as 
un European Power. All, therefore, that he should desire of Prussia was, that 
she should recognize and become a party to the “ Protocole Réserve ” of the 25th 
ultimo, and that she should engage to act in support of its stipulations, and 
then that she would support the Austrian proposttion to the Diet of Frankfort 
that a ba of the war contingent of the Confederation should be mobilized and 
assembled, and that Prussia should consent to join her contingent to that of the 
rest of Germany. Count Buol begged that | would inform your Lordship that 
with such conditions from Prussia he would now be satisfied, but if they were 
refused, it would alter yery much the position of things as they had hitherto 
existed in Germany, and that Austria, instead of being able to count upon the 
cooperation of a Prussian army, in conjunction with her own, might feel it 
necessury to keep an army of observation upon her frontier, which might 
heeome to her and to the allies a source of considerable anxiety and weakness. 

I have, &e. 


(Signed) WESTMORLAND.

The Earl of Westmorland to Count Buol. 


Vienna, January 22, 1855. 

THE Undersigned has the honour to notify to his Excellency Count Buol, 
&e., that Her Majesty has been pleased to appoint Brigadier-General Crawfurd 
to be her Commissioner at the head-quarters of His Imperial Majesty's army in 
the room of the late lamented Brigadier-General Du Plat, oe 

The officer in question, who is of high standing in the British army, and 
has for a long while held a command in the Grenadier Guards, the regiment of 
His Royal Highness Prince Albert, would liave already proceeded to his post, 
had he not been prevented doing so by the sudden death of a near relation, He 
llopes, however, to arrive at Vienna on Thursday evening next. 

The Undersigned, &e. (Signed) WESTMORLAND.

14& 


“Let us," T observed, “try and forget the Conference, for the King's entrance 
into it will follow as a matter of course.” 

His Excellency rejoined that he would apply to the King again, and would 
tell me the result; and he then spoke in a tone which led me to believe that 
His Majesty was becoming alarmed at the state of confusion in Germany and in 
Europe, and at the determined language which was held in London and Paris as 
tothe war, He spoke of the Prussian army, and said that the Government 
had not funds to commence active operations ; that it was true they could bring 
150,000 men into the field at a short notice, but that the military organization 
of this country rendered it extremely difficult to do more; and that the prepa- 
ration for so large a foree as this almost paralyzed further arrangements, 

I rejoined that evervbody was aware that war could not be carried on 
without great sacrifices, but that an appeal to the country in the sense of an 
alliance with the Western Powers would be successful, when in any other case it 
would assuredly fail, 

Our conversation then reverted to the subject of the Treaty. I told his 
Excellency that up to the present moment Prussian was not bound to us in any 
way; that in fact she was fullowing the policy of a neutral State, without 
having made any declaration on the subject, and that until her position was 
defined our present relations would remain as they were. 

Baron Manteuffel said that Prussia was, however, bound te Austria, and 
would keep her engagements. 

Yes, | replied, for defensive purposes, but not for offensive operations ; and it 
was on this account that we were anxious to see a different state of things esta- 
blished that would pave the way for Prussia joining the general allianee. As to 
the Treaty of 1841, upon which the King Glaimed to enter the Conference, | 
observed that ail ‘Treaties were annalled by the war which had broken out, and 
that after all it was only on the third point that Prussia had any claims to enter 
into the discussion, and that if she did not agree to the Treaty which had been 
proposed, we could only look upon such refusal asa desire to see the war 
extended and prolonged. 

Baron Manteuffel remarked that the Protocel of the 28th of Decomber had 
never been communicated to the Prussian Government, and that if it. were 
proposed to the King, it would surely not be expected that His Majesty should 
adopt it until it had been fully eoueiiered in-all its bearings; and he added that 
at all events His Majesty took a most lively interest in the question of the 
Principalities, and especially in the state of the Protestant churches there 
established, which His Majesty is informed are exposed to great annoyances 
since the Austrian occupation. 

I replied that the interest taken in this question ought to be a further 
inducement to the King to join our cause, which would entitle him to see justice 
done to his co-religionists, 

Here the conversation came to a close, and [ saw it was useless attempting 
to prolong it with such slender hopes of coming to any result, notwithstanding 
the expectation which Baron Munteuffel held out of a more favourable disposition 
on the part of the King, . 

1 learned from his Excellency that an impression had been made on His 
Majesty by a despatch which he tead to me from Baron Brockhausen, the 
Prussian Minister at Brussels, announcing that some modifications were 
expeeted in Her Majesty's Government, but that no abatement in the determi- 
nation to carry on the war was likely to result from such changes in London or 
Paris. His Excellency added also that the King had been much struck by a 
rumour which had arrived from Paris that a French army of 100,000 men was 
being prepared to support Austria, ) 

Allintelligence or decided military cooperation of the allies is more likely to 
influence the King’s resolution than anything else, und the policy of Prussia 
niny become more identified with ours, When all doubts are removed as to any 
present chainees of the restoration of peace, and when the action of the. allies 
Is Hinbued with still greater firmness and mutual confidence, 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD,

My Lord, Paris, January 26, 1255, 

M. DROUYN DE LHUYS has informed me that he is about to send a 
circular despatch to the French Diplomatic Agents in Germany expressive of 
the regret of the French Government at the want of union which appears to 
exist in the Confederation on the Bastern question—union which the French 
Government had always, without interfering unduly with the prerogatives of the 
Confederation, assisted to maintain; and declaring that it was the fault of 
Prussia alone if she was not represented in the Conference at Vienna, she having 
retired from it at her own free will and choice. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys added that his despatch would be worded so as not to 
give offence, and to let the smaller States see that they had no reason to be 
apprehensive of France.

My Lord, Turin, January 26, 1855. 

TI HAD the honour to receive yesterday at 2 o'clock p.m., by the 
messenger Gasparini, your Lordship’s despatch No. 6 of the 20th instant, 
transmitting to me thedraft of the British Acceptance of the Sardiniun Accession 
to the ‘Treaty of Alliance between Great Britain and Franee of April 10, 1854; 
the amended draft of the Military Convention between Great Britain, France, 
and Sardinia; and the draft of a Separate und Supplementary Treaty for a lean 
by Great Britain to Sardinia, 

And 1 have the honour to report to your Lordship, that 1 met the Due de 
Guiche and Comte de Cavour in conference at 11 o'clock last night, when 
we discussed those several Acts and Conventions; and I have the satisfaction 
of informing your Lordship, that M. de Cavour, on the part of His Sardinian 
Majesty, accepted the modilications (with one exception), both of form and 
substanee, as proposed by the orders contained in your Lordship’s above- 
mentioned despateli; and that at 3 o'clock this day [ again met my French 
colleague and Count de Cayour, when we exchanged the several Acts of Accession 
and Acceptance, and signed the Tripartite Military Convention, and the 
Convention for a loan between Great Britain and Sardinia, 

‘The exception to whieh I have alluded is contamed in the Vth Article of 
the Tripartite Military Convention, which in the British dratt runs as follows : 


 Tlis Majesty the King of Surdinia engages that the said body of troops 
shall be supplied every three months, or at shorter intervals if Necessary, with 
regiments or drafts to keep it up to the full stipulated number of 14,000 men.”

For this draft M. de Cavour, after conference with his colleague the Minister of 
War, desired to propose the following reading : 


“Sa Majesté le Rot de Sardaigne ‘His Majesty the King of Sardinia 
s'engage i maintenir le corps expédi- engages to tnaintain the expeditionary 
tionnaire au chiffre de 15,000 hommes, corps at the number of 15,000 men, 
par Venvoi successif et régulier des by the successive and regular trans- 
renforts néecssnires.” mission of such reinforcements a3 miy 

be necessary.” 


This alteration my French colleague and myself determined, after due 
consultation, to accept, The alteration 1s, as your Lordship will perceive, in 
the form and not in the Substance. ‘Chere is the same engagement to niaintain 
the Sardinian force at the number of 15,000 men; but the Minister of War 
remarked, that if the British draft of the Article were accepted, it would entail 
the necessity of having transports constantly ready in the port of Genoa, in 
order to be able to act up to the letter of the stipulation as to time, whereas, 
whenever the corps in campaign fell short of its complement he could, on the 
spot, communicate with Her Majesty's Admiral, or other authority commanding 
the transports, and could with him concert measures more eflicaciously, more 
surely, and more promptly, than by the method which he presumed was 
proposed in the British draft of Article 1V. | 

The substance of the Article being preserved, my French colleague and 
myself did not hesitate to accept the Article as it now appears. 

With the exception of this alteration, which I have now the hononr to 
submit to your Lordship, the Acts of Accession and of Acceptance, the Military 
Convention, and the Supplementary Convention for the loan by Great Britain 
to Sardinia, are returned duly signed, and in the same shape as when transmitted 
to me by your Lordship. 

I have only further to add, that at 4 o'clock this afternoon M. de Cavour 
made an official statement to the Sardinian Chamber of Deputies of the tenour 
of the several above-mentioned Acts and Conventions, with a view to the 
presentation to that House of so much of them as concerns the terms of the 
loan: a matter which the constitutional forms of the Sardinian States. requires 
should be presented to them for their leislative action, 

The House received the announcement with calmness and dignity, but with 
evident satisfaction, The only member who offered an observation upon it in 
a hostile spirit was the Deputy Valerio of the extreme left, who reserved his 
final opinion until he had had an opportunity of studying the doctiments in 
committee.

Inclosure in No. 160. 
Instruction to the Ottoman Embassy at Vienna, 


(‘Translation.) December 15, 1854. 


1 HAVE received your Exeellency’s despatch, together with the other 
a atating that the three Powers, having entered into communication on the 
subject, had deemed fitting that on the occurrence of any difficulty on current 
affairs between the Agents of the Porte and the Austrian Generals in the Prinei- 
palities, it should be referred by those Agents to the Ottoman Embassy at 
Vienna, in the event of its being impossible to settle it on the spot, and that 
the matter was to be then discussed between your Excellency, Count Buol, and 
the Ambassadors of England and France, and the decision come to communi- 
cattd to the Agents in question; and that it was required that the Sublime 
Porte should come into this arrangement, and issue the necessary instructions 
on the subject. Your Excellency's despatch has been laid before His Imperial 
Majesty the Sultan, 

This decision on the part of the Powers has proceeded from facilities which 
they foresee in the settlement at Vienna with your Excelleney’s concurrence of 
any difficulties which may arise between the Agents of the two parties. The 
arrangement is limited to the misunderstandings taking place between the 
Ottoman and Austrian Agents, and the Austrian Government has naturally her 
share in this; there is, therefore, no objection on the score of right te the 
settlement of such matters in the way decided upon at Vienna by the Repre- 
sentatives of the four Powers, more particularly as at the present time there 15 
not much cause for such disagreements, 

As, however, misunderstanding on some subjects may take place with the 
Austrian Agents, His Imperial Majesty's sanction was asked, and has been 
vranted, to the purport that mstruchons should be sent to the Ottoman 
Commanders, who are to remainat Gucharest, to communicate, in that event, with 
the Embassy at Vienna and with the Sublime Porte; and that your Excellency 
should be likewise instructed to discuss the matter in question with Count Buol 
and the French and English Ambassadors, and report the decision come to to 
Constantinople as well as to the aforesaid Commanders, 

On the oceurrence, however, of anything affecting the internal adminis- 
tration of the Principalities, ov the sovereign rights or the dignity of the Sublime 
Porte, any discussion or decision thereon must naturally be at Constantinople. 
In such a ease, therefore, your Excellency 1s instructed not to apply the present 
arrangement, and to come to no decision without a reference to the Sublime 
Porte. 

The necessary instructions have heen, in consequence, sent to the Com- 
mianders in question, and your Exeellency ts recommended to observe the closest 
and most serupulous attention with reference to the measures and proceedings 
hail in the discussion and settlement of the disagreements in question.

“ Informeés que des envois considérables de munition et de contrebande ale

My Lord, Constantinople, January 17, 1855. 
__1 HAVE the honour to reply to your Lordship’s despatch No. 3 of the 
Ist instant. | 
‘There are two points requiring “notice; the one is the efficiency of Vassif 
Pasha, the other regards Colone) Williams’ Turkish rank. 
; On this point I have to state that the firman constituting that officer a 

erik, or General of Division, under the denomination of “ Williams Pasha,” 
was addressed to him by me on the 20th ultime. 
_ With respect to the qualifications of Vassif Pasha, the result of my 
inquiries, antecedent to the receipt of any instructions, was, that he is a min 
of military education ; that he was engaged in active service against the Russians 
i 1829; that he possesses an independent fortune, and that no one suspects 
tim of corruption. His language to me was that of an honest and conscientious 
public servant. On the other hand he is no longer young, and his appearance 
denotes but little energy of mind or body. re ; 
__ Your Lordship can hardly mean to hold me responsible for bis success 
incommand. The object of change in office or command throughout Turkey 
when taken at the best, is not. the promotion of known desert but the removal 
of tried demerit. On such occasions the chanees are quite as much in favour 
of change for the worse as of change for the better. As to the command of an 
army, | know but one man in the Sultan’s service who enjoys the reputation 
of decided fitness for it, and that is Omer Pasha, In the present instanee there 
is much to presume in favour of the new Commander; he shows public spirit 
in undertaking an irksome task, and a difficult Journey in the dead of minter 
Besides, he is not the Commander-in-chief destined for operations in the field, 
but an acting Commander appointed to keep the army together, and if possible 
to aN : ons the season of retreat. j ee 

iope he will act cordially in concert with Ge illiams. No efforts 
have been wanting on my part te make him do ean ea ieee

No. 166. 
Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Reeetved January 31 } 


(No. 95. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, January 29, 1855. 

M. DROUYN DE LHUYS informed me this afternoon that he had 
received a despatch from Count Walewski, stating the result of a conversation 
which he had had with your Lordship respecting the course which should be 
pursued at Vienna. Your Lordship’s opinion was described by M, Walewski 
to be— 

lst. That every means should be taken of informing Count Buol of the 
views of the allies in regard to Sebastopol and the Russian fleet, but without 
pressing him for a categorical answer as to whether he approved those views. 

Yndly, That all questions which were likely to give rise to controversy 

should be discussed between the three Powers before negotiations were resumed, 
it being of the highest importance that Prince Gortchakoff should not be a 
witness of, or derive benetit from, any difference of opinion manifested in Is 
presence, 
' ‘To these views M. Drouyn de Lhuys said that he heartily subscribed. 
He had every desire that the fullest information should be given to Austria as ta 
the wishes, plans, and intentions of the Western Powers, and he only deprecated 
the demand of a categorical answer from Count Buol, That answer would, he 
was convinced, be unfavourable at the present moment, and no advantage was 
to be gained by pressing Austria to give a decision to which she might think it 
right or expedient to adhere pertinaciously hereafter. He agreed, however, that 
hefore negotiations were resumed, all the questions of detail respecting the four 
points must be discussed between the three Powers. 

He then adverted to the question of the immediate signature of a Protocol, 
which, to judge, he said, from your Lordship’s observations to Count Walewski, 
he did not think had ever been properly placed before you. He still adhered to 
the opinion that it was the safest and casicst, aswell a5 the most straightforward, 
manner of putting the sincerity of both Austria and Russia to the test, but it 
had never crossed his imagination to unite the four Representatives in Conference 
for the signature of a Protocol without some previous knowledge of the 
sentiments of Austria, His idea had been that M. de Bourqueney and Lord 
Westmorland should have treated the signature of a Protocol as a matter of 
eourse to which Count Buol could raise no objection, and should have asked 
him to procure the signature of Count Gortchakoff, If Count Buol had raised 
objections there would, of course, have been an end of the matter; but he 
thought, with all deference to your Lordship'’s opinion, that it would have been 
preferable that the French and English Governments should not of their own 
account have expressed a doubt as to Count uol’s viewing Prince Gortchakotl’s 
aeceptance of the four points in the same light as themmelves. And he wis 
afvaid that by calling Count Buot’s attention to the differences whieh existed 
hetween his version of the Conference of the Sth instant and that of Lore 
Westmorland, this doubt would be admitted,

Consul-General Colguhoun to the Earl of Westmorland. 
My Lord, Bucharest, January 16, 1855. 
| HAVE the honour to acknowledge receipt of your Exeellency’s despatch 
by telegraph of the th instant. . 

[tis of course quite impossible to procure an assurance from Prince Stirbey, 
that the money now collecting, produce of the two-tenths, is specially raised for 
Russia: the Hospadar could never so commit himself, 

The order for levying that tax was published in the Bulletin, The doen- 
ments | have already forwarded in my despatch to Lord Clarendon No. 112, 
establish beyond a doubt that the said tax was specially established to pay 
Russia. No doubt can exist as to its being actually levied in spite of the 
number of years since it was first imposed, and of the numerous charges weighing 
upon the country, in consequence of the late occupation, which not only must 
have extinguished or cancelled the debt (a debt, | may here recall to your 
Exeellency's mind, illegally established, which the Porte has never recognized), 
but must have given to Wallachia a balance in her favour. 

[tis now a question whether this tax ts destined to pay off the old debt of 
the provinee to Russia, 1 confess | do not see how we are to arrive at a proof, 
other than those already given, which are strongly presumptive. 

Tn fuet a decliration was made to the Ottoman Commissioner by the Prince 
himself to this effect. 

Dervish Pasha, when M. Poujade read to him, in my presence, M. de 
Bourqueney’s letter on this subject, about the beginning of December, made use 
af the follawing words: “T asked the Prince for explanations on the subject of 
this tax of the two-tenths; he replied that the tax had been levied or ereated to 
pay olf a debt of Wallachia to Russia, and that now the amount collected was 
deposited in a special chest, beeause the Wallachian Government had ‘des comptes 
iLrtgler? with Russia, arising from the recent occupation, which would be settled 
at a fitting moment.” 

Dervish Pasha subsequently applied to the Finance Minister, who gave the 
same account of the origin.of the debt, but he said that the sums already 
receiverl had been expended on various objects, and the sums figured merely 
nominally in the chest. 

In conclusion, the tax was, without any doubt, levied for Kussia; its levying 
still continues in spite of the cancelling of that illegal debt, whether by the state 
of war or by the fact of the late charges imposed by Russia on the province 
having exceeded the amount of the debt, while azain a tax established merely 
temporarily, “pour cette seule fois,” is being illegally perpetuated, and is illegally 
employed, and turned into a channel different from its first destination. 

annex herewith a memorandum on this tax, with three official documents 

appended, 
I have, &e. 


(Signed) ROBERT G. COLQUHOUN,

Memorandum on the Russian Debt, 


RUSSIA, under the pretence of having been called in to pacity the country 
after the movement of 1848, demanded the “ frats a ees 
To this end, a tax of two-tenths was levied on landed property; this tax 
was to yield annually 2,120,001) piastres (82.G001,). 
In May 1852, M. de Nessclrode, in a despatch to the Russian Consul- 
General, establishes as the full amount claimed by Russia, 27,018,000 piastres 
(415,661/); this sum was received without any opposition on the part of Prince 
Stirbey, but without any authority on the part of the Sublime Porte. 

: ‘The tax, voted in the first instance for only one year, was continued, m 
virtue of an Ordonnance of the General Divan, for four years, confirmed by the 
Hospodar, with a clause appended, that its amount sliould be set apart ina 
special chest, and dedicated solely to the extinction of the Russian debt; and 
has subsequently been implicitly authorized for a further indefinite term, by the 
Minister's letter above-mentioned, which fixes for the liquidation of the debt a 
period of six years 

Since the lute invasion, this tax on property has continued to be levied, 
and agit has been specially assigned for payment of the Russian debt, and does 
not figure, nor can figure, among the ordinary receipts of the budget, at is 
clearly evident, heyond doubt, that the Hospodar, even alter declaration of war, 
and up to the present moment, continues ta recognize the obligations: he had 
contracted towards Tussin before the war, even when he must have known 
that, ah initia, he himself had no right to sanction the demands of Russia, on 
principle, neither to fix ther amount, nor to continue to levy for an indefinite 
period, this special tax which was to serve ta pay off the debt, nor, in fact, to 
decide upon the application of money se collected. 

Moreover, even supposing the balance duc of this debt, which should now 

: amount to merely some 14,000,000 pustres (207,0001)—sinee the tax must have 

| produced, since 1844, above 12,000,000 piastres——to be still due, surely this 

halanee must have been mere than compensated by the expenses of the late

No. 173. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received Febrnery 2.) 


(No. 52.) 
My Lord, Conslantinople, January 22, 1855. 

THE Sultan on being reminded privately by me of his promise that the 
‘haratch’’ should beabolished, admitted the pledge, which he had so graciously 
given, and ordered my interpreter to see the Grand Vizier upon the subject, in 
order that his Highness might communicate with the Sheik-ul-Islam and settle 
the most advisable mode of proceeding. His Majesty, in explination of the 
delay which had oceurred, remarked that an imposition which had been enforced 
it Constantinople during four centuries, required some little time and some 
lithe consideration for its removal. 

I have frequently pressed this important measure on Reshid Pasha, who is 
well disposed in principle, laut apprehensive of producing discontent, 1 have 
told him repeatedly that if the Porte will secure a better administration of justice 
to the Sultan's Mussulman subjects, by means of suitable enacttnents properly 
guranteed, they will not object to any reasonable relief acceded to the Rayalis. 
My firm conviction is that the “ haratch” might in that case be frankly abolished 
without more ado. [lis Highness assures me that important measures of 
reform, which have been long in preparation, will be shortly promulgated ; but 
in spite of the best intentions, | fear that several weeks may yet clapet before 
lis assurances are realized. 

[ have, &e, 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE,

My Lord, Varna, January 14, 1855. 

WITH respect to the general subject of the supply of provisions for the 
Turkish army, 1 have the satisfaction to acquaint your Excellency, that great 
progress his already been made at Varna and at Bourgas in the purchase of 
a considerable quantity. } 

When I had last the honour to address your Excellency upon this subject, 
and when also Mashar Pasha proceeded to Constantinople regarding it, the 
authorities at Varna had declared the impossibility of procuring the quantity of 
stores of every kind which had been required of them, nor indeed would it have 
been practicable to have done so, if the usual system had been adopted, of 
making requisitions on the villages. But in my interview with the Mustechar 
Mahmoud Bey, and subsequently with his Highness Omer Pasha, I repeatedly 
and foreibly laid before them the practicability of purchasing a not inconsiderable 
quantity of provisions at Varna which were on the spot, and pointed out the 
merchants in whose hands they weve. Tis Highness Omer Pasha and Mahmoud 
Boy, upon this, having overruled the usual seruples and difficulties made by the 
local authorities to deal with Europetn merchants, or offerthem terms which they 
would accept, the whole of the provisions | have referred to have been bought, 
and in great part already shipped; they consisted of 65,000 okes of rice, 
2,500 kilos of barley, 1,000 kantars of biscuit: other purchises have also been 
made from other merchants. But I more especially Inid great stress on the fact 
that there was actuilly in, the Government stores at Varna nearly 100,000 kilos 
of wheat, which had hitherto been represented to be wnavailable for the troops, 
heeause it could not, without great delay and ifticulties, be reduced inte flour: 
but T acquainted Omer Pasha and Mahmoud Bey that I lad ascertained from 
the principal French Commissarint Officer in Varna, the Buron de Durand, that 
he would not objecet to allow the Turkish authorities in Varna to avail themselves 
for a fortnight of the steam flour-mill of Messrs. Charnand, which had been 
engaged for six ionths by the French authorities: and this most important 
advantage has been taken advantage of by the positive orders of his Highness 
Omer Pusha and of the Mustechar, althouch this, the sole means of obtaining a 
large supply of flour at Varna, itself the port of shipment, had been rejected by 
Osman Bey and the ordinary local authorities, upon the plea that the merchants 
(Messrs. Charnaud) had demanded too much for the use of their mill, while, in 
fact, they had only sought to obtain equal profits to those which they derived 
from the Mrenech Commissariat, : 

The general vesult of the adoption of all these’ practical measures on the 
part of his Highness Omer Pasha und the Musteehar, is, that in reward to the 
chief essentials of bisenit of flour, a sufficient supply may now be assured for an 
army of 40,000 men for three months, and rice, if issued three times a-week, for 
six weeks. Turther supplies will be purchased at Varna whenever they can be 
found. 

At Dourgus, Mashar Pasha (Sir stephen Lakeman’, who is likely to 
remain there, | understand, for some time, has made considerable purchases of 
supplies, of the precise nature or quantities of whieh | am not acquainted; but 
[am informed that among these there are $0,000 Constantinople kilos of barley 
equal to one month’s supply for 1,000 horses. %

SINCE I had the honour of addressing your Excellency this morning by 
ny despatch No, 7, 1 have again waited upon his Highness Omer Pasha, who

numbers also had been exaggerated in the previous reports from Poultcha. 
However, his Highness informs me that they carried off with them about 100 of 
the Turkish inhabitants, some cattle, and such provisions as they found in the 
netzhbourhood, ‘ | 
sit apprehend, however, that the fact of the Russians having crossed the 
Danube, and of their having committed these ravages, with the possibility of 
their doing so again at any moment, renders all communication between. the 
Vanube and the sea coast across the Dobrudscha, impracticable.

Inclosure 5 in No, 174, 
Consul Neale to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Varna, Junuary 17, 1855. 


I YESTERDAY received a letter from Mr. Cunningham, dated Galatz the 
L1th instant, He writes: ‘The Austrians have about 5,000 or 6,000 men in 
Jassy, 3,500 in Galatz, and altogether in Moldavia not over 11,000 or 12,000 
men, Without artillery. In Wallachia perhaps 20,000 men; so that they have 
not in all more than 32,000 men. I believe that should war be declared, the 
Austrians will retire from Galata and Jassy, in order to concentrate ; and I am 
told the Moldavian Government has already taken measures to transfer itself to 
Romano. Whether the Russians will enter remains to be seen.” 

With respect to the number of Austrian troops in the two provinces, your 
Lordship will have been more exactly informed by Mr. Colquhoun, The French 
Military Commissioner, Colonel Dieu, however, informs me that they amount 
to 45,000, Mr. Cunningham adds, “ It is generally estimated that the Russians 
have 30,000 men in Bessarabia,”

Inclosure 3 in Ne, 175. 
Consul Brant to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


(Extract.) Erzeroom, April 10, 1854. 

THE General tells me that Zarif Mustapha and the Musteshar Riza Bey 
were tallting of resigning, so much were they discouraged by the want of almost 
everything, particularly of money, of which the military chest had been entirely 
emptied, there being debts to the extent of 40,000 purses, and monthly out- 
goings of about 12,000 purses. He tried to encourage them with the hape that 
money would come. In the latter part. of the letter, which extended over five 
days, he says it was reported that the Mushir and Musteshar were to be recalled, 
On this he remarks that the Mushir is a good man, but not being brought up 
a soldier does not undersiand what he should do; when he sees some things in 
order he thinks all are right, but does not know that a link in the chain is 
wanting, and destrovs its elficacy : but still, he is the best Mushir they have had, 
and would do well could the General be always at his elbow, but he has so 
many duties to perform which he cannot trust to others that that is quite 
impossible. 

I find the Musteshar Riza Bey a perfect gentleman, and were I Mushir 
Ido not know a man I should so much wish to haye at my side as Riza Bey, 
[ hope both will remain while the war lasts, as I should not find two others who 
like Europeans as they do; besides, the Mushir is a patriot and an honest mtn, 
who acts up to his duty. Do write to Lord Stratford to use his influence to 
prevent his recall.

My Lord, Copenhagen, January 26, 1855. 
IN the course of the conversation with M. de Scheel, reported ta your 
Lordship in my preceding number, his Excellency having endeavoured to dispose 
of the question under discussion by expressing i ae that peace was about to he 
re-established, T said to him that whatever his hopes might be [was convinced 
he did not believe that there was any probability of their being realized, and 


2X 


< 


170 


that in my opinion he would do well to look the future in the face, and think 
seriously on the line of policy which he ought to follow as most conducive to 
the interests of his country in the event of a general war, | repeated to lim 
much of what | said on previous occasions to his predecessor on this subject, 
spoke of the disadvantuzeous position which Denmark would oceupy by remain- 
ing neutral if Sweden should become a belligerent, and reminded him that the 
‘nterests of Denmark would not be taken into consideration at a general peace if 
she selfishly withheld the trifling sacrifices which she might be expected to 
make for the common cause, and declined affording any assistance to the Powers 
who were fichting for the independence of Europe. 

M. de Scheel replied that Sweden might certainly eventually consider it 
her interest to become a belligerent, and that Denmark might also consider it 
advisable to do the same, but that he could not understand why the Western 
Powers should think it of any importance whether Denmark renounced her 
neutrality or retained it, as they already derived from her harbours almost all 
the advantages which she could offer them as an ally. Hesaid that he therefore 
trusted she would at all events not be forced to lay aside her neutrality. 

Lsaid there was at present no question of forcing her to act otherwise than 
as she might think best for herself, and that Her Majesty's Government had 
given her ample assurances as to lier neutrality being respected ; but, though | 
had no instructions to say so to him, T knew that her cooperation would be 
thankfully accepted, and were zhe to offer it she would obtain all the advantages 
of a belligerent, without being called upon ta make any sacrifices of importance, 
whereas under her present cireunistinces she would have to furnish a contingent 
to the German Confederation, without gaining the goodwill of any one. 

M. de Seheel said J must, however, remember that Denmark had great 
difficulties to contend with; that in the tirst place her financial resources) were 
limited’: and in the seeond her geographical position exposed her to many 
dangers. [He said that he had entire contidenee in England; that he trusted 
fully in the justice of Her Majesty's Government, and telt assured that as long 
as Denmark aeted an honest and a friendly port towards England, which she 
would always do, she would have nothing to fear from her, * But,” sad he, 
“are we equally safe with respect to France?” Tis Excellency then, after 
observing that the French Government had been endeavouring to induce 
Denmark to renounce her neutrality, went on to say, “Let us suppose that a 
Power had given us to understand thit Pruksia wished a part of our territory a8 
an inducement to go to war, and that we should afterwards learn that the Power 
in question had actually offered our territory to Prussia, what would you think 
of our position towards that Power oil 

L replied that if le meant that France had offered Holstein to Prussia, 1 did 
not believe it, I suid that your Lordship had once remarked to me ina 
private letter that if Her Majesty's Government were dishonest cnough to hold 
out a hope that the Sehloswig- Holstein question should be re-opened, there wis 
little doubt that they might have thus obtained much support in Germiny; that 
something of the same kind may have been said by the Emperor of the French 
or by the French Minister for Foreign Affairs, and that the expression of such an 
opinion may have been perverted by others in order to excite distrust against the 
Western Powers, but that I felt assured no overture of the kind had ever been 
mide to Prossta. 

M. de Scheel finding me hold this language, replied he had not stated that 
such an offer had been made, nor did he believe it, and that lie had merely 
spoken to me of a supposition, 

[have thought it right, however, to mention this part of our conversation 
to your Lordship, though from not being yet much acquainted with M, de 
Scheel, | do not know what value | ought to attuch to his observations, and 
though it appeared from some other remarks which he made to me that he is 
apt to hazard assertions with a view to gain information. 

I touched upon the subject slightly in a conversation this morming with my 
French colleague, but he either attached no importance to what | said, or wished 
ine to believe so. | have hitherto always found him to net towards ine with the 
confidence which 1 have a right to expect; but if he has had any instructions to 
press the Danish Government to dechire itself, he has not mentioned the cireum- 
atance to me. L lve, &e,

Mo Lord, Berlin, February 2, 1855. 

. HAVE the honour to inclose, in translation, an article from the 
newspaper “ Zeit,’ which is considered to be the organ of Baron Manteuflel, 
upon the subject of the secret circular despateh of Count Buol of the [4th 
ultimo. 

It has caused some sensation at Berlin, and was considered so offensive by 
the Austrian Minister at this Court, that he has thought it his duty to call 
Count Buol’s attention to it. The latter part is indeed written in such an 
acrimonious spirit, that if the paper had a wide circulation in Germany, it might 
be supposed that the Prussian Government had determined on the adoption of 
a policy directly hostile to Austria, but this can searcely yet be the case, 
However Count Esterhazy felt his position to be one of so much delicacy here, 
that he has thought it advisable to hold a personal conversation with Count Buol, 
and has gone to Vienna for a few days. — 

I likewise annex herewith a copy in French translation of the Austrian 
secret circular of the 14th of January, to which the aceompanving article refers.

(Signed) BLOOMFIELD,

Eatract from the “ Zeit” of January 30, 1855. 
(Translation.) Berlin, January 29, 1855. 
WE do not positively know whether the text given of the seeret circular 
despatch of Count Buol of the 14th instant, which we gave in our yesterday's 
number from the Dusseldorlf paper, is authentic. We will wait to see whether 
they are enabled at Vienna to disavow this document. It cannot indeed be 
doubted from intelligence which has lately appeared in the press that there exists 
a despateh of the Austrian Cabinet of some such a nature, We again find that 
the document in question contains everything which has been notified from the 
most opposite quarters—ofiers of guarantee for the possession and the terri- 
torial position of the German States, a promise of participation in the advantages 
to be attained by the war, and finally the command-in-chief of the Emperor of 
Austria over the contingents to be furnished by the German States, We may 
therefore be permitted, until proof of the contrary, to consider the secret despatch 
of the 14th instant as genuine, 

The Imperial Cabinet in Vienna is apprehensive that ‘ Prussia may altempt 
still ta persevere for some time longer in her undecided policy.” They (the 
Imperial Cabinet) will indeed first strive for the attainment of constitutional 
decrees of the Diet, and will take upon themselves the consequences of such 
decrees ; but they are not certain themselves whether the attainment of such a 
deerce of the Dict as Austria is desirous of can really be expected. Now in 
such event, that is if the proposition submitted to the Diet by Baron Prokesch 
on the 22nd instant should be constitutionally rejected, Austria wishes to learn 
the intentions of those German Governments which are disposed, independently 
of the decree of the Diet to unite with Austria, or in other words to contract 
separate Treaty with her, 

Such an accession to Austria taking place beyond the Federal Constitution 
could not certainly be ealled an alliance for those States who might agree to it, 
Austria only wishes for the contingents of ber German Confederates who may 
desert from the Federal Constitution, and join her. She harters for this the 
formal promise that their possessions and territorial position shall be guaranteed ; 
indeed what is inare, that they shall even have a share in the advantages of the 
war in proportion to the forees employed. It remains naturally reserved to 
Austria how these promises shall be afterwards fulfilled. ‘The union with

Austrian would signify nothing else than passing from a constitutional bs 
position to an Austrian vassalage, We are eager to know, if only any single one 
of the German Federal States will feel itself called upon to tend an ear to the 
Vienna siren-cong. At all events the history of the present time pall nate e 
record this attempt of Austrian diplomacy against the political union of . any 
for the maintenance and protection of which, at a time when it ae y ue 
really questionable, Austria once exhibited such zealous efforts. I ae Bren 
Cabinet of Vienna exerted itself confidentially with the Somat ores? 8 
for votes in support of their proposal to mobilise, this might ve blameab! S. ee 
such contluet is always manceuvre, But af the German Governments shoule 
be reduced to a desertion from the federal unity by a promise of advantages 
certainly of quite an indefinite character, we forbear to say how this action is to 
be denominated, ‘This, however, is certain, that if is not honourably Geraint: 
Advantages! or the first time since the “ great question” is pending, were 
this word used in an official document by the Austrian Government. Does 
then Austria seek “advantages”? This is quite new, What she secks oo net 
been thoroughly known up to the present hour, for the objects at mu ut e 
Austrian policy aims are so continually concealed, that they may 1 ine i 

ressed, but by no means known with certainty. Now it is known Austria

udvantage, not for an European, not for a German tmterest, Thereby much ts 
See aeeret despatch has no breath of a conservative policy. tt 15 entirely 
revolutionary, The result which it has in view is a splittmg of Germany into 
hostile camps, possibly a war of Germans against Germans. May Heaven 
prevent the attainment of such a result!

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon —(Received February 5.) 
(No. 34,) 


My Lord, Berlin, February 2, 1855, 
IN obedience to your Lordship's instructions, 1 have this evening read to 
Baron Manteutiel your Lordship's despatch No. 26 of the 27th ultimo, upon the 
subject of a communication which has been lately made by Count Hernstorf, 
respecting the Pree position of Prussia with regard to the Eastern question. 
His Excellency seemed well pleased with those passages which relate to the 
desire of Her Majesty's Government that the relations of the two countries 
should be placed on a better footing, and the disposition which exists to arrive 
at this result ina maoner which would be conformable to the honour ind dignity 
of Prussian; but notwithstanding all the arguments contained in your Lordship’s 
despateh, Baron Manteuttel would not admit that Prussia could be excluded 
from the approaching Conference at Vienna, without entering into some previous 
engagement that would secure unity of action between the two Governments: 
on the contrary, his Excellency seemed to think that Prussia, asa Great Power, 
was mot to be fettered by Treaty, and had a right to her position as an 
independent Power, 3 
His Excellency said that it was not true that Prussia had not made military 
preparations, for they were busily engaged in them; and he added that she had 
never declared her neutrality. To this I said that she might not have issued 
any formal declaration on the subject, but that her policy was even more than 
neutral as far as Russia was concerned, because ercat favour had been shown to 
herin the transport of arms, This he did not deny; but he added that these 
favours were not exclusively shown to Russian: and he might mention that he 
had just received a communication from Baron Budberg on the subject of a 
quantity of lead which had been lately sold in Prussia to the Mrench Govern- 
ment, "Woll) Tosaid, “this fet only shows that your policy is justly styled 
neutral, as you furnish munitions of war to the belligerents; aod itis with a 
view to consider the best means of arriving at a change of system that 1 was 
charged with the present communication, and that we wished to have some 
definite answer to the proposals I had made, that Pruesin should enter into an 
alliance by Treaty whieh would regulate her position towards us, ns it was 
impossible for great Powers engaged in war to admit lightly into their delibera- 
tions another Power without possessing some knowledve us to tts real intentions,’

its Federal contingent in readiness to mect any demand for its services which

Chambers to a loan of 15,000,000 florins, which it ts proposed to. raise for

before the Lower Chumber, consists of five Articles, under the first of which 
1,800,000 florins of the new loan would be devoted to the repayment of various 
sums appropriated to the requirements of the miliary establishments of the 
country out of funds destined to other purposes, which require to be made good,

Mr. Jerningham to the Earl of Clarendon.—CRecewed February 5.) 


(No, 6.) 
My Lord, Stuttgardl, January 30, 1855. 

[ NEED hardly mention that sinee the departure of my despatch No, 2 of 
the 17th instant, stating that no proposition had been made to this Government 
far mobilizing their contingent, the Austrian circular of the 14th instant, 
recommending such mobilization, has been received here, as well as another 
circular of the same date, signifying the disposition of Austria to avail herself, 
should it appear advisable, of her right to form a separate alliance in Germany. 

The language held to me yesterday by Baron de Linden respecting those 
despatches was, that this Government objected to immediate mobilization because 
they considered it unnecessary, but that they were taking all the measures 
requisite for mobilizing their contingent in & week's time, should it be called for 
hy the Diet; and that he should much regret to see Austria making use of a 
separate right, which might serve to create discord and disunion in Germany, of 
which even Russia might possibly take advantage. 

Lobserved that nothing could of course be less desirable than to create discord 
in Germany, but that 1 considered the best kind of German Union to be such as 
would present a formidable front to Russia, and thereby favour the conclusion of 
peace ; that any other attitude might have just the contrary effect, in the same 
way as last. spring, when, had Prussia agreed to Austria's proposal to adhere 
to the Convention of England and Franee, the war might very possibly have 
been strangled in its birth ; and that, whereas Prussia had apparently held aloof 
out of consideration for Russia, she had perhaps been the eause of her having to 
undergo the four points instead of reverting to the status quo ante bellum—au 
alternative which Russia could hardly consider but as a great calamity, since it 
was not to be supposed that she could bring herself to look upon the defeat ol 
her Turkish policy, however dangerous, as a benefit rather than an injury, 

I further observed that Turkey and the Danube, as regarded Russia, 
appeared to me open to con raet with Belgium and the Rhine, as regarded 

rance, since the wishes of both on those points were opposed by the convemlence 
of Europe, and since what wis calculated to promote a general coalition could 
never be permanently accomplished; that this fact had been proved on the 
vreatest scale by the Emperor Napoleon, who had shown that a country might 
be too powerful to be strong, by becoming the common enemy; that Count 
Nesselrade had appeared to me in error when he stated that a forced peace, on 
the principle of the four points, would exhibit anything but durability, since it 
must be recollected that the long peace which ended last year had been a forced 
peace as regarded France, and maintained principally, if not solely, by the 
vermanent readiness of a general coalition; and that, consequently, even had 
Raul been allowed to make peace on ante bellum terms, her position would 
have undergone the great change of the discovery that any further aggression 
upon Turkey would raise Kurope against her—a possibility of which the Emperor 
Nicholas, to judge by the despotic haughtiness of his language previously to the 
war, seemed not to have entertained the faintest idea. ; 

Baron de Linden admitted that the Emperor had deceived himself, or rather 
that he had been deceived by the flatterers who surrounded him; but he 
proceeded to argue in the sense that the Eastern question could not be really 
settled, except by partitioning ‘Turkey, and by relegating the Mahometans: ta 
Asia. 

I replied that the partition of Turkey was considered in England to be the 
most difficult and perilous of all questions, and, consequently, to be avoided as 
long as possible; while we could not see the slightest reason tor considering the 
question more urgent now than in past times, but on the contrary, since “Turkey 
was making progress and improving the condition of Her Christian subjects ; 
that I nevertheless believed the destiny of Turkey in Europe to be the gradual 
out-breeding of the Mahometans by the Christians, since the former diminished, 
while the latter increased, and that perhaps some future Sultan might preserve 
his throne by changing his religion; but, at the same time, that | could sce no

Bosphorus and the Dardanelles. 

I cannot say that my reasoning seemed to convinee his Excellency; and

In illustration of a part of the foregoms, { told Baron de Linden that, when

never possess Turkey, because | was convinced that Europe would always oppose

have been going on now for nearly a year, since, although England and France 
alone had actually made war on Russia, the whole of Germany had told her they 
would do the same if she persisted to encroach on Turkey. 

It may be worth mentioning that one of Baron de Linden’s observations 
was that, were Russia to acquire Turkey, her preponderance might be prevented 
hy the impossibility of so large an Empire's hanging toecther.

funds to the Chambers, which are to reassemble on the 14th of next month.

[ replied in the sense that no ‘atention could exist of wounding Prussia ;
