amicable relations with Prussia, and that it indicated a measure of the kind 
proposed by M, Drouyn de Lhuys as caleulated to put an end to the estrange- 
ment, which Her Majesty’s Government lamented should exist between Prussia 
and the three Powers. i 

Count Hatzfeldt said that he was certain that the tone of your Lordship’s 
despatch would give the King sincere pleasure. If it made no concession to 
Prussia, it evinced at all events a very friendly spirit. | 

With respect to General Wedel’s conversation with M. Drouyn de Lhuys, 
Count Hatateldt observed that too much stress should not be laid on the 
General's opinious. The General was not a diplomatist, and would hardly 
understand the bearing of such a proposition as had been made to him by 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys, . 

The Count, however, went on to say that he had reason to know that the 
King of Prussia was really desirous of escaping from the isolated position in 
which he had placed himself He desorbed the King’s feelings as follows ;— 
Above all, a great horror of drawing the sword; fear of, but no real sympathy 
for Russia; great irritation agaist Austria; a natural antipathy to France ; and 
a liking as natural for England, which had not been destroyed by late events, 
or by all the oblaquy thrown upon him by the English press. The King more- 
aver felt the danger of his present position. THe saw that that the war might 
become general: that in that case Germany would beeome the battle-field; that 
he could not ally himself to Russia without secking the disaffection of lis 
people, nor could war take place without rousing the dormant passions of the 
German nation, He wished, therefore, to draw nearer to the Western Powers, 
but without wounding his own pride, or having the appearance of ceding to 
Austria. It would not be difficult, Count Hutefeldt thought, to bring His 
Majesty to the signature of a Treaty, if the King was previously readmitted to 
the Conference. 

I replicd that unfortunately the whole question was invelved in that point, 
Count Hatzfeldt asked what hope there would be of placing matters on a better 
footing if both parties maimtamed their present ground, Something should be 
ceded on both sides, If the King agreed to sign a Treaty, the terms of which 
might be arranged confidentially beforehand, why should he mot be adinitted to 
the Conference previous to the actual signature?’ I sugeested that it might be 
posstble to make ita simultaneous transaction, that is, a Conlerence—signature 
of the Treaty during the Conference—information given by the belligerent 
Powers on the one side of the Austrian Treaty to Prussia, on the other side of 
the Prussian Treaty to Austria. Thus: all parties might again be brought 
together. 

Count Ilatefeldt seemed to think that the suceess of that or any other 
scheme would depend on the nature of the proposition made to the Prussian 
Government. Lf the King was at once presented with an ultimatum which 
he was to accept without discussion, His Majesty would not be in the condition 
of a free Sovereign; his pride would again be alarmed, or at least others (the 
Russian party) would alarm it for him, and no good result could be anticipated, 
Lasked Count Hatefeldt why then did not the Prussian Government take the 
initiative, and itsel) make propositions. There was nothing undignified in that, 
But he met me with the King’s objection to take any steps until he was 
readmitted into the Conference, ; 

Count Hatateldt added that he did not think that many weeks wonld 
elapse before Prussia would, for her own satety, place her armies on the war 
footing. Everything was already prepared. The smaller States of Germany 
were, he said, urging his Government to take this step for their protection. 
And then, he asked, what would be the infallible consequence? Austria would be 
unable to assist the allies with a Prussian army assembled on her flank, and 
France could not leave her north-eastern frontier uncovered, which would 
seriously interfere with her silitary streneth elsewhere, T replied that this 
might be very true, but what did it prove: that instead of confining the ticld of 
battle to the East, which a determined attitude on the part of Europe would 
ensure, the whole of Europe would be gradually involved in war, the end of 
which no one could foresee, Large armed bodies could not remain long in each 
others’ vicinity without hostilities being the consequence, Let not the King of 
Prussia think that he could arm and long remain neutral, ; 

I have been more particular in giving your Lordship some of the details of

Lord Cowley to the Earl af Clarendon. —( Received February 7.) 


(No. 188. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, February 6, 1855. 

THE perusal of Mr. Buchanan’s confidential despatch No, 16 of the 26th 
ultimo, inelosed in your Lordship’s despateh, No. 111 of the 3rd instant to me, 
‘duces me to trouble you with the following remarks. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys, in his conversation with me respecting the position 
of Prassia, and the possibility of inducing her to pronounce herself in favour of 
the Western Powers, has often remarked that nothing would be more likely to 
enlist the sympathies of Prussia and Germany than holding out the prospect of 
the annexation of Schleswig to the German Confederation, or of Holstem to 
Peussit, with a fresh arrangement of the Sound dues. He has as often, when 
speaking of the advantage whieh the allies would derive if the smaller Northern 
States were to declare for them, saul that a hint to Denmark that Holstein 
might, whenever peace was signed, be more closely ineprporated with Denmark, 
ar an intimation to Sweden that Finland might again come under the Swedish 
seeptre, might convert the neutrality of those two States into an alliance. 

1 have in general treated these observations with very little attention, os 
they did not appear to be made seriously. It was not until two days ago that, 
finding that M. Drouyn de Lhuys had, as | had the honour to inform your 
Lordship in my confidential despatch No. 128, actually introduced into a Treaty 
which he wanted to conclude with Prussia, a clause relative to the navigation af 
the Baltic, that | observed on the consequences which such a proposition "ie 
likely to entail. 

T had hoped that the ideas which M. Drouyn de Lhuys had, at various 
times, let fall in his conversations with me, and which, as I said before, seemed 
rather to rise up in the warmth of discourse than to he seriously entertained, 
had not been imparted to others. Unfortunately this does not appear to have 
hoon the ease, and although I feel certain that his Excellency has never gone so 
far as to make any distinct proposition m regal to Holstein, as the Danish 
Minister for Foreign Affairs seems to suspect, I cannot doubt that he has been 
co far indisereet, both with his tongue and with his pen, as to throw out hints 
both in speaking and writing, of possible contingencies which he has no more 
idea of secing realized than haye Her Majesty's Government, 

It is in vain (I grieve to say it) to hope that a French Minister may be 
made to understand that such proceedings not only are not honest in themselves, 
but lead generally to the very reverse of whit ts antivipated fram them, 1 shall 
he more careful in future, when I see any indications of such exuberant fancies 
on the part of M, Drouyn de Lhuys, to combat them at once, 

In the meantime, | beg to acquaint your Lordship that his Execlleney 
informed me yesterday that, in consequence af my observations the day before 
he had retrenched from the Prussian “ Projet de ‘Traité” the clause relating to 
the navigation of the Baltic. I believe that the projet was sent last night to 
Count Walewski for the consideration of Her Mujesty’s Government, 2 

1 have, &e. 
(Signed) COWLEY.

Inclosure in No. 107. 
Colonel Williams to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe, 


My Lord, Erzeroom, January 16, 1855, 

YOUR Lordship may be aware that'a certain chief of the Bashi-Bozouks, 
Injeh Arap by name, had, during the latter part of 1844, been convicted of many 
crimes of eruelty and peculation, and imprisoned in chains in this city, where, in 
apite of his well-known delinquencies, also resides Hasson Yaziji, the late Com- 
mander of the [reegular Cavalry of the Kars army, whose character, in conjune- 
tion with that of Zari Mustapha Pasha, his coadjutor in dishonesty, I have had 
the honour to bring before your Lordship. Tt involved, as your Excellency 
knows, the most glaring cases of false musters and dangerous deeeptions— 
doubly dangerous because they might have compromised the safety of any allied 
force sent to the aid of this ‘army on papere’ 

[ have now to acquaint your Excellency that intrigue has at Inst succeeded, 
and that this notorious culprit, Injeh Amp, is at lirge on the bail of Hassan 
Yaviji, who, instead of finding himself a prisoner at Constantinople in the same 
strong-room with Zarif Mustapha Pasha, walks these streets and pliys the part 
of protector to a culprit perhaps of not so dark a die ns himself. ; ' 

Thia scandal eries aloud for vindication ; and 1 trust, hy the return of post, 
that, throuzh your Lordship’s insistance, an order will arrive liere to seize this 
man as well as his protégé, put seals on their effects, and send them under escort 
to Constantinople. They scem to laugh at the idea of retribution coming on 
them, and talk of their return to Damascus in the spring, there to enjoy the 
fruits of their iniquitics. 

L hope that all who have the success of this war-at heart, may be spared this 
mortification, and, in consequence, L- strongly insist on the prompt punishment 
of these men through your Excelleney’s influence. We are now thinking of the 
organization of an irregular foree, to keep the enemy from our communications 
during the next campaign, and without the signal disgrace of Hassan Yaziji and 
Injeh Arup, it will be futile to attempt that organization. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) W. F, WILLIAMS.

No, 199. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon. — (Received February 7.) 


No. 69.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, January 29, 1859. 

1 HAVE communicated to Reshid Pasha the draft of Convention trans- 
mitted to me with yout Lordship’s instruction No, 26 of the | lth instant. 

1 adopted this course in order that his Highness might take the Sultan's 
pleasure at onee, and settle the matter at a single mecting. He has proposed an 
amendment affecting Articles IL and IIL, with a view principally to stipulating 
that the rations to be given to the Turkish troops in Her Majesty's service shall 
be of the kind to which they are accustomed, and that any punishments inflicted 
for the support of discipline among them, shall take place according to the 
established practice of the Turkish army. 

It appears to me that these modifications of the draft are reasonable, and 
that they are by no means at variance with the spirit and general character of 
the intended Convention, But the wording proposed by Reshid Pasha being 
more vague and comprehensive than the proposed objects require, | have offered 
a version of my own, which I hope will be accepted, 

It is not impossible that 1 may be able to send your Lordship the Convention 
signed and concluded by the next messenger. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

Sitting of February 1, 1855. 
Gentlemen, 


IN the struggle now pending between the allied Powers and Russia, in the 
Fast, are involved the future destinies of Asia and Europe. Desirous to avoul 
exaggeration we will not designate this a war of civilization against barbarism ; 
that is to say, in the sense of fearing that the triumph of Russia would replunge 
civilized Europe into all the obscurity of the middle ages. 

Civilization, which was then confined to a few nations, has since become an 
European inheritance: it has taken root even in another hemisphere; it has 
penctrated into every nation, and many of those savage and barbarous hordes 
who trampled under foot the civilization of Rome, have since been illumined by 
the very light which they had attempted to extinguish, But if the fear of again 
sinking into barbarism is uncalled for, no one will deny that were Russia to 
succeed in possessing herself of Constantinople, the fate of all the other States 
of Europe would become most lamentable, 

Picture to yourself a power of 80,000,000 of souls, obeying blindly the 
nod of a despot and Pontiff, absolute master of the Baltic and the Black Sea, 
of which he would then hold the keys; and you will easily understand, were 
that event to come to pass, what would be the condition of Europe? ‘The trade 
between Europe and Asia would depend on his will; no political act of moment 
could be consummated in Europe without his sanction, 

The liberty of peoples and the independence of nations would be dependent 
upon the will of an autocrat ruling on the throne of Constantine. 

The dangers were present to the vast mind of Napoleon the Great, when, 
fram the rock of St. Helena he gave the counsel to Europe: “It will be time 
when Russia threatens the existence of Constantinople, for every village in 
Lurape to ring its alarm bell,” 

he danger foreseen by all civilized nations will account for the universal 
applause which greeted the declaration of war against Russia on the part of the 
allied Powers, 

_ We will not, a8 an impartial observer of events, deny that certain inauspi- 
cious political and military Set have subsequently taken place which

For the last eight centuries the cross of Savoy has shone on almost every

Victory # wreath of laurel, which increased the glory and power of its States, 

It took part, directly or indirectly, in all the great European Congresses, 
when it profited sagaciously from its blood and valour. 

It is certainly not alter the events of L843, which Inaugurated a more 
enlightened and thorouzly national policy, that Sardinia should recede from the 
path of glory trodden till that time, and adopt a timid, egotistical policy, as if it 
had already fulfilled its destiny. 

That policy would suit only a State which had nothing further to hope— 
nothing further to fear; a nation ready to declare itself’ satisfied with the status 
e such certainly is not the condition of Constitutional Piedmont Of 
tedmont, no contemptible portion of that ltaly which is entitled to look forward 
to better destinies, which places its fondest hopes in this happy corner of the 
classic land, 

Let us repeat, to the credit of our country and of this Parliament, that not 
i single voice was raised in favour of an absolute isolation in the serious Crisis 
in which Europe is now involved, 

There are, however, several deputies who are of opinion that we should 
await more favourable circumstanees before pronouncing ourselves, 

They observe that the policy followed by Government is too hazardous in 
sending the bulk of its forces to regions so distant, whilst none of the Powers of 
our standing has yet made up its mind to take part in the conflict = whilst two 
Powers of the first rank are still wavering, and one of these is watching 
our every movement with no friendly eye. That prudence would sugeest, 
therefore, our awaiting the further development of events, and the decision 
of these Powers: which policy would be the more advisable because our 
linances are exhausted, and can hope for relief only from peace and internal 
prosperity, 

In addition to these objections, others are brought forward of o different 
order, but no less grave, : 

Some say—From this war Italy can expect no good, and none therefore ean 
accrue to Piedmont, which after all is an essential part thereof, and whose 
general policy must necessarily be identified with the general good of the nation. 
Let us reserve our forees—our means—our last resuurces—for the supreme 
hioment in which interests more near and more vital to our country's fate shall 
be brought inte play, 

The war, a8 at present directed, is a diplomatic war; that isto say, a war, 
the object of which is to decide whether this or that great European Power shall 
preserve or lose more or less influence, Civilization, liberty, the independence 
of nations have nothing to giin in thisstrugele, Why, therefore, should a State 
like ours, of the second order, make sacrifices which incur risks far a cause fron 
whieh it can hope for no idvantages, from which no one of the greqt sociak 
principles cin Expect a solution?

The finances not having yet recovered from the wounds inflicted by the War

As regards the loan to be contracted for the expenses of the war, we are ol 
opinion that we could not with dignity desire more advantageous terms ; and 
thor ean be no doubt that by longer delay we should have had greater difficulty 
in obtaining capital, ‘he finance of the State will certainly be more encum- 
bered hy the participation of Piedmont in the present war, but such a war is like 
the spear of Achilles that wounds and heals. ‘To those who seem to think that 
the Eastern war is solely carried on by the ambition of predominance on the part 
of England and France, on the one hand, and Russia, on the other; who declare 
that neither good nor harm can arise from the triumph of either party to the 
smaller States of Europe: that in this struggle the great social principles of 
civilization, liberty, and independence have nothing to gain or lose ; we declare 
that we have not strength to combat such assertions, on reflecting that not even 
the opinion of the greatest statesmen, or the unanimous assent of civilized 
peaple, or the evidence of the disasters which befel the nations of Southern and 
Western Europe, when the monstrous design of Peter the Great was crowned 
with suecess, do not suffice to convince them. And without hesitation we assert 
that not less than France and England, Italy would haye to deplore this unhappy 
event, | 

Italy, by her position in the Mediterranean, will always find the Mastern 
road most convenient for her traffic. ‘This same road will soon, by a rapid snc 
cusy communication, lead to the Bast Indies, emporium of universal commerce. 
Suppose, now, the Czar master of the keys of the Black Sea, the liberty of this 
‘mmense trate will fall into his hands. But the injuty which will threaten Italy 
will not stop here: a colossal Power such as Russia would be, mistress of the 
storehouses und moritime arsenals of the Euxine, would soon become so great a 
muritime Power as to dominate imperiously both sides of the Dardanelles; her war- 
fleet would plough menacingly the Mediterranean, and we eannotsee what security 
there would be for free nations—what hope for those who pant for liberty, 
Lastly, we ask our antagonists what would have been the condition and the 
power of the Czar in 1848, if the nations of the various parts of Italy had tasted 
for a little time the delights of liberty; if the War of Independence could have 
commenced with so much hope of success? ‘The triumph of Russia, there 15 no 
concealing it, would inflict a severe wound on European civilization; and sup- 
posing it admitted that the triumph of the allies would not profit: the political 
liberty of the people and their nationalities, it is certain that the suecess of 
Russia would be very prejudicial to them, 

Neither must we ignore the afliliation which connects the great social prin- 
ciples. The civilization of Europe must necessarily lead to political liberty, and 
at the same time to the nationalities of the people. He who is convinced of the 
‘ndissoluble conmexions, let him procure the triumph of the first by niding 
civilization, now in danger, according to his means, and await confidently the 
result, [fcivilization triumph in this conflict, it will receive such an impulse in 
Europe that it would soon bring forth all the other benefits with which it is 
laden, 

These are the considerations and the motives which have chiefly induced 
the great majority of your Bureaus, and of the Commission, to believe that the 
accession of the Government to the Treaty of the 10th April, 1854, is necessary,

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon —( Received February 8.) 


(No. 143. Confidential.) 


My Lord, Paris, February 7, 1895. 

M. DROUYN DE LHUYS renewed with me yesterday the conversation 
which had been commenced between us on the previous day, relative to the 
course to be pursued in respect to the Vienna negotiations, and reported in my 
despatch No, 1387. Ue said that he had been turning the matter anxiously in his 
mind; that he thought there were two ways in which negotiations might vet be 
avoided : the first, by requesting the Austrian Government to insert im the full 
powers to be given to their Plenipotentiary, the text of the memorandum 
accepted by Prince Gortchakoff. This had been done in the French and in the 
Turkish full powers. He hoped that Her Majesty’s Government would adopt 
the same plan; and a request might then be made to Count Buol to conform to 
the course followed by the allies of Austria. If he refused, it might be a 
question whether such refusal would not justify France and England in demurring 
to commence negotiations. But supposing him to accede, and the Conference 
to meet, the first demand made by the French and English Plenipotentinries 
should he the signature of a Protocol, or procés-verbal, recording in unequivocal 
terms the acceptance of the four points as interpreted by the allied Cabinets. 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys observed that he felt certain that Prince Gortchakoff 
would not coneede this demand, 

His Exeelleney had, he said, been informed upon authority which carried 
conviction to his mind, that it was understood at St. Petersburgh that Prince 
Gortchakolfs interpretation of the four points had been adinitted by the 
allied Representatives. He had learnt further, that Prince Gortchakoff’s 
proceedings, although supposed to have been so far successful, had not been 
approved ; that he was considered to have gone too far; and that he had only 
not been disavowed, because it was thought undesirable to weaken his position 
at Vienna at the present moment, But the Prince had, M. Drouyn de Lhuys 
continued to say, received the most positive instructions to confine himself 
etrictly within the limits of his own interpretation; and it might therefore be 
presumed that he would not sign such a Protocol as that which would be 
proposed to him. In this case there could be no doubt France and England 
would be justified in refusing to enter into further negotiation, 

I replied to M. Drouyn de Lhuys that 1 sincerely hoped that his anticipa- 
tions would prove true, but that it behoved the two Governments to be prepared 
for every eventuality. Prince Gortchakoff might, notwithstanding the infor 
mation which had reached M. Drouyn de Lhuys, sign the Protoeal, What 
course would his Exeelleney then propose to take ? 

M, Drouyn de Lhuys admitted the embarrassment in which the allied 
Governments would then be placed, Decline further negotiation they could 
not in honour, and yet to proceed invelved a choice of difficulties. He alluded, 
but not in very distinct terms, to demanding an armistice and the evacuation of 
the Crimea—an idea, as your Lordship knows already, put forward by the French 
as an expedient-to break off negotiations, 

Lobserved that if an armistice: was proposed by Russia, such a condition, 
however unlikely to be accepted, might perhaps be put forward. But what 
would be the effect of tts coming trom two Governments who had declared 
that they would not suspend their military operations before preliminaries of 
peace liad been signed ? ; 

M, Drouyn de Lhuys did not press this point farther. 

___He then said that one of two courses was still left open —to begin the 
discussion of the points in the order in which they stood, or to require that the 
third should be first tuken into consideration. ‘The objection to taking them 
iti the order in which they stood arose from the two first being those whieh 
admitted of the easiest arrangement, and which interested Austria and Germany 
the most, and that consequently it might be apprehended that the questions of 
the future relations of the Principulitics towards ‘Turkey and of the navigation of 
the Danube being settled, Austria would be legs disposed to support our demands 
in respect to the Black Sea, |

On the other hand, we must consider the position in which we should stand, 

‘ewe insisted on commencing negotiations by an examination: ol the I{rd 
Article. We must not forget that Austria, previous to signing the ‘Treaty of the 
ond of December, had asked two questions of the belligerent: Powers: first, 

whether they contemplated any considerable territorial alteration ; secondly, 

whether they intended to require conditions whieh tt could not fairly be expected 
would Le accepted by Russia, Having received satisfactory assurances On these 
two points, Austria signed the Treaty, Now, in putting forward the third basis 
first, how would the two Powers stand in regard to these assurances ? Could a 
demand for dismantling Sebastopol be considered as-an infringement of the 
territorial sovercignty of Russia ! Could it, in the second place, be looked 
upon as exorbitant and such as would prevent all chance of the restora ion of 
peace? ‘The first of these pretensions, M. Drouyn de Lhuys was inclined we 
think, might be successfully resisted: but, conscientiously speaking, he coule 

not say as much in regard to the second; nor, whatever might be the confi- 
dential. communieations exchanged between (he two Governments as to their 
intentions, did he think that they were in a position to demand of Russie, in the 
face of all Europe, the surrender of 1 strongheld on which their arnnes hac, 
after four months’ trial, been able to eke no impression. He knew, moreover, 
positively that the Austrian Plenipotentiary would not support such 4 pretension. 
[His opinion therefore was, saving the sovereign decision of the Emperor, that, i 
negotiations could not be avoided altogether, the bases must be taken in the 
order in which they had been offered to Russia. Supposing the discussion on 
the two first to terminate ina manner favourable to Austria, und to be broken 
olf altogether on the third, Austria would not-stand in a mueh better position, 
heenuse no‘l'reaty would have heen concluded. . 

I observed to M. Drouyn de Lhuys, in reply, that 1 inferred from his 
remarks that he had abandoned all hape of the active cooperation of Austria, 
since it was cortain that, so long as we were in negotiation with Russia, Austria 
would not resort to hostilities; and it appeared equally cortain, from information 
received by him, that Austria would not support us, either morally or materially, 
in any demands we might make in regard to the Black Sea. Whether, therefore, 
these demands were made sooner or later, did not seem to me to Lie of much 
consequence. But owned that | could not conceive a more untoward position 
than for the two Governments to find themselves inthe midst of a negotiation, 
with several points satisfactorily settled, and the negotiation to he broken olf, in 
consequence of France nnd England insisting on conditions which Europe would 
in general pronounce they were ot Mo situation te demon, Let us suppose 
the question of the (uture: protectorate of the Principalities settled, and the mavi- 
gation of the Danube satishictovly pr ovided for, would if not be said that France 
and England were pursuing their own miterests alone, 1 demanding more, anid 
should we not risk having an European coalition against ourselves? Neither let 
it he forgotten that Austria would haye no great desire to see the fourth basis 
settled: for, if she joined in denouncing the Russian protection of the Greek 
subjects of the Sultan, she would herself be obliged to renounee the protection 
which she exercised over a large portion of the Homan C utholic subjects of the 
Porte in Bosnia and Herzewovine,—a protection to which she had always held 
with extreme tenacity. 

With respect to the assurances given to Austria before the signature of the

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received February 9.) 
(No, 145.) 
My Lord, Paris, February 8, 1856, 

AFTER writing my despateh No. 143 of yesterday’s date to your Lordship: 
1 saw M. Drouyn de Lhuys again, when he told me that the Emperor’s sanction 
had been given to the course which his Excellency proposed to follow at Vienna, 
and your Lordship may, therefore, eonsider that despatch, which was marked 
« Confidential,’ to be an official record of the wishes of the French Govern- 
THent. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys went again through all the arguments which he had 
employed on the previous day. 1 abstained from any expression of opinion, but 
I asked him to tell me frankly whether I was still to understand that the 
Emperor and his Government felt that these negotiations could lead to no imme- 
diate result, and whether their object was to break them off without entangling 
the belligerent Powers in fresh engagements. M. Drouyn de Lhuys replied that 
my understanding of the views of the French Government was correct. 1 then 
asked him whether he had made any communication to the Austrian Govern- 
ment on the subject, observing that until the opinions of Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment were known, I trusted that the action of the French Government would 
continue suspended. M. Drouyn de Lhuys assured me that he had not as yet 
made, and would make, no communication to Vienna until your Lordship's 
answer was received, 

Knowing your Lordship's great desire to prevent discussions in Conference, 
which might have the effect of showing Prince Gortchakoff that a difference of 
opinion existed between the Plenipotentiaries of England and France, and the 
Plenipotentiary of Austria, I asked M. Drouyn de Lhuys whether he would 
object, should Her Majesty's Government desire it, to authorise M. de Bour- 
quency, on the receipt of his full powers, to go with the Earl of Westmorland 
to Count Buol, when the two Ministers, after showing their full powers, and 
inviting Count Buol, as proposed by M. Drouyn de Lhuys, to assimilate his to 
theirs, might proceed to declare that they were instructed by their respective 
Governments, before proceeding further with the negotiations (their intentions to 
enter into which were proved by the transmission of their full powers), to 
explain themselves frankly with Count Buol in regard to the third point; and if 
they found a great divergence of opinion between themselyes and Count Buol, 
and an unwillingness on his part to support the demands they were instructed 
to make, to ask him of what advantage it could be proeceding in the nego- 
tiations, which could only serve to show that the parties to the Treaty of the 
28nd December were not agreed im their views. ; 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys replied that, not only he should have no objection to 
such a proceeding, but he thought that advantage might be derived from tt. lf 
Austria found that the allies were reluctant to enter into Conference unless she 
engaged herself more positively on the third point, she might be induced to take 
that course rather than see the negotiations on which she founded so much hope 
nipped in the bud,

Mu Lee, Berlin, February 9, 1855. 

. BARON MANTEUFEL has just informed me, in the strictest confidence, 
that the Russian Minister has for some time past been pressing him to declare 
thot Prussin aceepted, in the broadest sense, the Interpretation put on the four 
points by the Imperial Government, and promised, in consideration of the 


& 


concessions made by Russia, to disengage herself from her alliance with Austria. 


213 


His Excellency stated further, that Baron Budberg had presented several 
memorandums on the subject, but that he had always refused to recommend 
the matter in any way, and had been exposed to some altercations with certain 

srsons at Court who took a different view of the question; but that he had 
been pressed so hard, and assured that the King was disposed to yield the point, 
that he had seen the King this evening, who, on learning what had been told to 
Baron Manteuffel, assumed an air of great surprise that his opinions should 
have been represented as changed, and, instead of showing a disposition to adopt 
the suggested policy, has declared to Baron Manteuffel that he will not bind 
himself to Russia in the sense proposed by Baron Budberg. 

I told Baron Manteuttel that 1 was glad to hear that he had so successfully 
ecombated the intrigues of the Court party, and that I hoped advantage would 
be taken of the King’s present disposition to advance the object of M. d'Usedom's 
and General Wedel’s missions, and that no more time would be lost in 
negotiating the Treaty which was under discussion. His Exeelleney replied 
that no progress had been made in this matter, and that Mis Majesty still 
insisted that he must be admitted into the Conference before signing the Treaty. 
I then observed to his Excellency that I did not see how we could well do more 
for Prussia that we had done for Austria in this respect; for if | was well 
informed, we had declined the proposal of Austria to enter into conference with 
her until she made engagements which would bind her future conduct, and the 
Treaty of the 2nd December had been the result of our refusal; and I added, 
will you answer for the King making a Treaty that will identify his policy with 
ours if he is admitted to the Conference? Baron Manteuffel replied, that he 
could not do so; and he gave me further to understand, that the King’s mind 
appeared to be made up on the point; that his amour propre was concerned in 
it; and that if we did not choose to make this concession, we might find him 
disinclined to go on with the negotiations. 

Having reported this conversation to your Lordslip,it is my duty to add, 
that I by no means pretend to suggest that the course proposed by the King 
should be adopted, and that His Majesty should be readmitted to the Conference 
unconditionally ; for, to judge trom the little disposition which has hitherio been 
shown by this Court to join the alliance, it may be fairly doubted whether we 
should gain anything by acceding to the King’s wishes, and whether it would 
be of advantage to our ulterior objects to permit [is Majesty to have a 
Plenipotentiary at the consultations about to take place at Vienna, until he is 
hound to take part with us hereafter, in the event of the Conference not leadng 
to the result which is so much desired by His Majesty,

Brigadier-General Craufurd to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received February 11.) 
(No. 3.) 
My Lord, Vienna, February 7, 1855, 


1 HAVE the honour to inclose the document spoken of in my last despatch, 
viz., the most recent state of the Russian forces furnished by the Austrian 
staif. 

These forces are divided into six armies. The tabular form in which 
the details are conveyed will, I think, carry to the minda more clear and com- 
prehensive idea of the nature and distribution of them, than if the various details 
were brought successively to the eye, and I therefore forward to your Lordship, 
a translation and copy of the Austrian paper, 

The total number stated exceeds that given in a despatch addressed to your 
Lordship by Her Britannic Majesty's Minister, in the month of November fast, 
No. 317. The disposition of the troops also varies, but the sum total would be 
in accordance with the calculation made by Mr. Buchanan in November 1854, 
together with his observation that it was stated in St. Petersburgh at that time, 
that the force indicated would be very considerably augmented before the 
spring.

In this immense number of soldiers, it must of course be recollected that 
great bodies of Irregular troops are comprised, and also that the army of the 
Caucasus must be in a great part absorbed by furnishing an army to oppose the 
Turks in Asia Minor, and by supplying garrisons for the various Russian stations 

forts in that country. : 
a Thad the honour ‘of a long conversation with Baron Hess to-day. With 
regard to the military Conferences, of which mention has often been made in 
public prints, he expressed his surprise at the report having got abroad that such 
Conferences had taken place. His Excellency said that he had received no 
intimation from His Imperial Majesty of the project of opening at present such 
Conferences, nor did Baron Hess appear to think that the moment had arrived 
when they could be held with advantage. ‘The first necessity was considered by 
him to be, that of securing a sufficient force to cope with armies of the numerical 
strength presented by the inclosed document ; secondly, that of securing Prussian 
cooperation, and also the support of the army of the German Empire in an 
offensive operation, and thus, as well as by the aid of the allies in other quarters, 
being able to count upon a mass of armed men, of numbers equal to those 
ascertained to be collected upon the side of Russia. | 

In speaking of the Russian army General Hess assumed a lower total 
(by about 100,000 men) than that indicated in the “ general view inclosed, 
and spoke of the number of 850,000 men as the foree eventually to be opposed 

Lhies. ' 
n eWithont numbers approaching the above upon the side of the allies, the 
Haron considered that a war, surpassing, as he anticipates, all modern wars in 
magnitude, could not be undertaken with rational hope of success, 

The collection therefore of a power from different quarters with which to 
act offensively against the Russian army in Poland, must, he conceived, occupy 
two months at the least, and the concentration of them for the purpose of 
warlike operations would, he estimated, require a month in addition ; added to 
which, the state of the roads in Galicia made an carlier commencement of 
warlike movements nearly impossible, under any circumstances. 

With all these considerations he considered the present moment too early 
for the opening of Conferences. The object of them must principally be the 
discussion of a plan of military operations, and since, if formed, it could only 
be executed after the expiration of three months, such a discussion would at 
present be useless, The greatest changes might possibly take place in the state 
of Europe before that period has elapsed, anil should the war continue, the 
result of the siege of Sebastopol must influence incalculably its whole progress, 
und especially the disposition of the Russian armies. 

Haron Hess's couversation lasted for a considerable time, and appeared 
characterized by great frankness. I will take more time than 1s af i 
hefore the departure of the messenger, to reflect upon the tenour of his obser- 
vations, and will write to your Lordship any conclusions 1 may be led to, As 
I hope to have the good fortune to mect Baron Hess soon again, he will no 
doubt make some observations in reference to what passed to-day, and 1 will 
merely remark, that with some qualifications of his Excellency’s views, they are 
what 1 had anticipated from an exacngtion of siting circumstances, 

ive, ke.

The Earl! of Clarendon to Lord Stratford de Redelijfe. 
(No. 124:) 


My Lord, Foreign Office, February 12, 1859, 

IN reply to your Excelleney’s despatelh No. 71 of the 29th ultimo, IT have 
to inform you that Her Majesty's Government approve of the communication 
which you directed M. Pisani on the 29th of January to make to the Porte 
relative to the instructions to be given to the Ottoman Ambassador at Vienna, 
and which Her Majesty's Government hope will be received by the Porte as a 
judicious and friendly warning with respect to the course that the Turkish 
Plenipotentiary should pursue in the negotiations there. 

A. peace that enpuld be inglorious and unsafe for Turkey would be equally 
s0 for Mngland and France, and it is not to be supposed that those two Powers 
would submit to sucha result of the struggle in which they are engaged for 
maintaining the independence of the Ottoman Empire, and guarding Murope 
against the ageressions of Russia. 

Her Majesty’s Government pronounce no opinion upon the sincerity of 
Russia in accepting the four bases, The negotiations which are about to 
commence may lead to a satisfactory arrangement, or they may at onee be 
broken off, but Her Majesty's Government trust that no unnecessary obstacles 
or delays will be created by the Porte, and that the Turkish Plenipotentiary 
will be instructed to place confidence in the Representatives of Mngland and 
France, and to. act cordially in coneert with them for the common object. 

Her Majesty's Government have given so many proofs of their desire to 
uphold the sovereign rights of the Sultan, that any fresh professions on that 
subject would be superfluous; but at the same time they have a duty to perform 
from which they cannot shrink, and they desire the Porte distinctly to under- 
stand, that in return for the enormous sacrifices of every kind made by this 
country and by France, they have a right to exer not only that religious 
immunitics, buta perfect equality of civil rights shall be effectually secured ta 
the Christian subjects of the Sultan. 

Her Majesty's Government do not doubt the intention of His Highness: to 
promote the welture and happiness of all classes of his subjects, but assurances 
of this description, however sincere and well intended, afford no guarantee 
aguinst the oppression to which the Christian subjects of the Porte are at this 
moment exposed, and although the question is surrounded by difficulties, yet a 
solution must be arrived at and cannot longer be postponed, 

Your Excelleney will accordingly make known to Aali Pasha the views of 
Her Majesty's Government, and their desire that you should consult the Turkish 
Government upon: this important subject ina frank and friendly spirit, with the 
hope that a mode may be devised of reconciling the just expectations of Christian 
Powers with the independence and sovercign rights of the Sultan. 


Tam, &e. 
(Signed) CLARENDON,

Foreign Office, February 13, 1655. 

COUNT COLLOREDO. has communicated to me a despatch from Count 
Buol stating that the French Government had considered it necessary, In conse- 
quence of the difference which, according to the public newspapers, exists 
between the interpretation put by the allies upon the acceptance of the four 
bases by Prince Gortchakof! at the meeting of the 7th of January, and that 
which is assigned to it by the Russian Cabinet, that the doubts which have 
arisen upon this point should be cleared up: and with the view of ascertaining 
whether tliat aeee ance refers solely to the statement of the four points which 
Prince Gortchakoll read to the Conference, or whether it refers to the extent of 

uK 


a3 


the Protocol of December 28th, which was communicated to that Minister, 
M. Drouvn de Lhuys proposes that another Conference should be held at which 
Prince Gortehakoff should he asked to sign a Protocol, declaring that he is, or 
is not, authorized to accept without reserve the interpretation which was com- 
municated to him on December 28th. 

Count Buol then, after adverting to my despatch No, 24 of the 23rd 
ultimo, communicated to him by your Lordship, in which Tpomted out the 
discrepancies between the account given in your despatch No. 10 of the 8th 
ultimo, of what passed at the Conference of the 7th January, and that which he 
had himself given in his despatch to Count Colloredo, and also to my despatch 
No. 21 of the 20th ultimo, explaining the views of Her Majesty's Government 
as to the third basis, proceeds to state the explanations which he had furnished 
on this subject to M.'de Bourqueney and yourself. 

The Austr Government entertains no doubt as to the full and entire 
naeceptanee of the four bases by Prince Gortchakoff at the Conference of the 7th 
of January, and the fulfilment thereby of the condition laid down by the 
matilime Powers as indispensable to the opening of negotiations. They regard 
the different versions of what passed at the Conference, proceeding from non- 
official sourees, and put about by the newspapers, as not being of sufficient 
weight to render advisable further explanations with Prince Gortchakof? on this 
point. ; a 

The fact then of the acceptance being in their onan completely esta- 
blished, the only doubt that can be entertained is a5 to the intention with which 
that acceptance wis given; but this intention, Count Buol argues, can only be 
aseertamed by entering upon negotiations, All other attempts must necessarily 
fail, and will only cause delays, whieh will be ‘assuredly turned to account, as 
they have already been but too suecessfully, by the partisans of Russia, to: set 
on foot new intrigues, and to increase the existing elements of discord. in the 
7eruninic Confederation. 

‘To obtain the complete certainty beforehand of the favourable issue of the 
negotiations is an impossibility ; the essential thing is to lose no time in entering 
upon them, ‘There is reason to believe that the Emperor of Russia hus had 
great difficulty in resigning hinisell’ to the sacrifices imposed upon him by the 
acecptance of the four bases. Would it be prudent to give him a specious 
pretext for retracting a resolution which, if the Austrian Government is correctly 
informed, has met with a very doubtful reception from the Russian people? 
Would it not be a serious mistake to afford ground for the opinion that 
te Western Powers threw obstacles in the way of negotiations for peace, 
whilst the Emperor of Russia, alter accepting the bases dictated by those 
Powers ilicmselves: has, without delay, furnished his Plenipotentiary with the 
necessary full powers; when, moreover, this example has been followed by 
the principal belligerent, the Sublime Porte having sent full powers to Arf 
Eifendi authorizing him to assist at the Conferences ? 

Under these cireumstances the Austrian Government again urges the 
Cabinets of Paris and London to send full powers to the Representatives of 
France and England to treat for peace. 

With respect to the meaning attached to the third guarantee, Count Buol 
says: that the profession of faith of the Austrian Government on this subject 15 
contained in the formula inserted in the reserved Protocol of the 28th December; 
revision of the Treaty of the 1th July, 1841, with the double object of attaching 
more completely the existence of the Ottoman Empire to the European equili- 
brium, and of patting an end to the preponderanee of Russia in the Black Sea, 

The Austrian Government continues to believe that various modes present 
themselves of attaining this object, and consequently they reserve to themselves 
the liberty of appreciating them eventually, at the proper time and place, without 
wishing thereby to prejudge either the rights of the belligcrents or the events of 
the war, Lassured Count Colloredo that no intentional delay had taken place, 
as ib was useless to send full powers to Her Majesty's Representative until a 
Turkish Plenipotentiary was appointed, and impossible to do so during the late 
Ministerial crisis in this country, but that there could exist no intention of 
avoiding the negotiations, and for the simple reason that the honour of Her 
Majesty's Government was pledged to enter upon them when certain conditions 
had beon fulfilled by Russia, The tall powers should, however, now, be inne 
diately prepared ; but Her Majesty's Government, I said, were far from anticl-

by Russia would be found to differ widely from that of the Western Powers, and 
that Austria might be unwilling to support the terms which the Governmeuts of 
Encland and France thought essential to a safe and bo peace.

The Earl af Clarendon to Lord Bloomfield. 


(No, 45,) 
My Lort, Foreiyn Office, February 13, 1855. 

COUNT BERNSTORFF yesterday read to me a despateh from Baron 
Manteuftel, declining the Treaty that your Lordship was instructed by my 
despatch No. 28 of the 27th ultimo to propose for the acceptance of the Prussian 
Government, and renewing, on the part of the King, his demand that Prussia 
should take part in the Conferences at Vienna. 

L asked Count Bernstorff if he had any counter-proposition to make. 

He said he had not. 

I asked him if, under any circumstances, the King would enter into any 
engagement, 

Count Bernstorff said that he had no instructions to that effect; nor could 
he tell me what course His Majesty would take if he was readmitted to the 
Conferences, and, the negotiations being broken off, Austria declared war, and 
took part with England and France in active hostilities against Russia. 

1 inquired if, in that case, it was not the purpose of the King that his 
Representative should return to Berlin, and that the claim of His Majcsty as a 
Great European Power to take part in the affairs of Europe should be suspended 
as long us the war lasted, and that it would again become active when negotia- 
tions for peace were resumed, 

Count Bernstorff could give no assurance of any kind, and I remarked 
that, creat as our desire was to plaice our relations with Prussia on a footing of 
cordiility, I feared it would be impossible until we got some clue to her policy or 
intentions. She would aeeept no propositions, and would make none; she 
would enter into no engagement, cither immediate or eventual, ‘There were at 
this moment two special Envoys in London and Paris who belonged to the 
Liberal party; and an active member of the Kreuz Zeitung party had just been 
sent to the Hague, Brussels, and Copenhagen, with objects altogether distinct 
from those of the two Envoys; in short, I said, we could not arrive at a convic- 
tion, or even an opinion, as to whether Prussia was a friend or foe, or whether 
she would persevere in that nondescript neutrality which in'so many ways had 
served the Emperor of Russia, and was now rendering more distant the prospects 
of peace, 

lam, &c. 


(Signed) CLARENDON,

(lxtract.) Munich, February 10, 1855. 
WITHIN the last few days instructions have been sent from hence to the 
Bavarian Minister at St. Petersburgh to enlighten the Imperial Cabinet os to 
the possible eventual attitude of Germany on the Oriental question, Count 
Bray is directed to notice the distrust which its policy has inspired in many 
quarters, mune the anxious suspense which this state of things creates in others 
and which is so detrimental to the common interests of Kurope, and to Germany

especially. He is told to exhort the Russian Government to relieve all parties 
from the doubt which prevails as to its sincerity by immediately giving the most 
positive and solemn assurances that no attempt is to be made to retract in the 
slightest degree the engagements it has recently taken at Vienna by the accepl- 
ance of the four points; and, above all, to promise on no account to proceed 
aggressively against Austria, Should it, however, neglect or decline to subseribe 
to these conditions in such a form as shall offer a satisfactory security for their 
fulfilment, Count Bray is authorized to let Count Nesselrode clearly comprehend 
that the Emperor must not be surprised to see the whole of Germany arrayed 
acninst him. 

This language, which conveys to the Russian Cabinet what nearly approaches 
to an indirect menace, and which is quite new, may, | hope, be accepted as the 
commencement of a change of system on the part of the Bavarian Government, 
and as the first step towards a reconciliation with Austria, to be followed, ere 
long, by the complete adliesion of this country to her policy. Other symptoms 
begin to indicate that, at all events, the extreme bitterness felt at what was 
regarded inthe light of studied neglect on the part of Austria towards the minor 
States of Germany ison the wane; and in proof of this Tmay mention that, in a 
recent conversation (the substance of which lias been repeated to me) with my 
Austrian colleague, Duron von der Pfordten went so far as to say that, if the 
Austrian Cabinet was in a position to demonstrate to the Bavarian Government 
that a menacing attitude towards Russia was in accordance with the interests of 
Germany, this country would not be backward in throwing its weight into the 
scale on the side of Austria. 

This I believe to be the sense of Garon von cer Viordten’s language, but | 
eannot vouch for the precise terms, for the information reached me (as did also 
that relative to the despatch to Count Bray) through the medium of a third person. 
However, from all | hear, very little eoaxing just now on the part of Austria-would 
secure to her the support of Bavaria, whose opposition hitherto, it must not be 
forgotten, has proceeded entirely from a very small but influential circle in the 
capital, and not in the least from the nation, as is 1 think sufliciently manifested 
by the result of the discussions on the demand for an extraordinary credit for 
military preparations in the Lower Chamber, on which occasion net a single 
voice, with the slightest claim te independence, was raised imupproval of the policy 
of the Government, In point of fact, instead of its hbousted victory it only 
narrowly eseaped a vote of want of confidence, and itis by no means unlikely that 
the danger it then incurred may in reality have exereised a monitory intlucnee toa 
greater extent, perhaps, than the Ministers themselves may be willing to admit. 
still such is the variable and uneertain course of German politics that many 
different pliases may yet be traversed before the final, and as | conecive inevitable, 
adhesion to Austria is declared. Jam not exactly aware how matters stand in 
this respect with the other small States of the Coufederation; but | have reason 
to believe that Saxony is the least manageable of all, 

In all his recent conversations with my French colleague, Baron von der 
Pfordten has pleaded, in the strongest manner, the cause of Prussia, and has 
urged her readmission to a participation in the Conferences which are expected 
to be held at Vienna, on the ground of expediency and policy, arguing, as | 
understand, that the assertion that the Cabinet of Berlin is placed in its present 
isolated position by its own act 1s founded on an erroneous appreciation of the 
motives which dictated the withdrawal of Prussia from the path pursued by the 
other three Powers. In fiet upon this point his Excellency seems to hold nearly 
the same language as the Prussian Government itself, 

In the meantime the signs of military preparation are becoming more 
apparent as the moment for the solution of the actual crisis approaches. Orders 
have been issued for the immediate purchase of 4,000 horses, and a fresh con- 
scription of 16,009 men, in addition to the 13,000 who have already joined their 
respective corps within the last fortnight, is te be carried out without loss of 
time. Indeed, I am told, that it is the intention of the Government to place, as 
soon as possible, an army of between 60,000 and 70,000 men on the war 
footing. 

I hiave, &e. 
(Signed) J. R. MILBANKE.

Mr. Buchanan to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recewed February 9.) 


(No. 21.) 
My Lord, Copenhagen, January 30, 1850, 

WITH reference to my despateh No. 14 of the 26th instant, 1 have the 
honour to inform your Lordship that instructions were sent yesterday to 
M. de Bulow, the Danish Representative in the Diet at Frankfort, to vote against 
the proposal of Austria, that the contingent of the Confederation should be 
immediately organized for active service. | | 

Being confined to the house by indisposition | have not seen M. de Scheel 
for the last three days, but my French colleague informs me that his Excellency 
says the King considers the measure proposed by Austria to be mopportune, 
and is of opinion that Denmark cannot vote for it consistently with her declara- 
tion of neutrality. 

She will, however, conform herself to whatever resolution may be adopted 
by the majority of the Diet.

(Signed) ANDREW BUCHANAN,

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Keceived February 11.) 


(No. 75.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, January 24, 1855. 


|] HAVE the honour to forward herewith three documents: calculated to 
throw light upon the conduct of the Ottoman War Department with respect to 
the army of Kars and the points recommended by me for immediate adoption on 
the suggestion of General Williams. One of them is a report from the Council 
of the Seraskier’s Office to the head of that department. The second is un 
instruction addressed by the Seraskier, Riza Pasha, to the new Commander-in- 
Chief, ad interim, who embarked for Trebizond a few days age, The third is an 
instruction addressed by the Grand Vizier to the same Commander with the 
intention of supplying deficiencies in the former. 

I have no choice but to reserve for another opportunity the comments which 
[ have to make on these papers.

Inclosure 1 in No. 224. 


Copy of a Paper of Suggestions to be delivered to his Excellency Vassif Pasha, 
Commander-in-chief of the Imperial Army of Anatolia, dated January 28, 
1855. 


Translation. } 


AS the numerous things written on the article of war, and of their being 
hrought under a systematic and technical application, are subjects of delicate 
importance, it is impossible to enter here upon this great and weighty subject. 
His Excellency the Commander-in-chief is versed in the art of war and in 
military matters, and as, more especially, the manner in which the circumstances 
below related, and the necessary measures to be scientifically and wisely applied 
with respect to them, are not known, it is decided that it is not requisite to 
furnish him with full instructions on the subject; anda few needful suggestions 
are, therefore, only made to him. 

A temporary Board has been instituted for looking to the administration of 
the army in question, and for attending to its affairs conformably with the 
military system and regulations, The settlement and execution of all military 
matters in conformity with the instructions and system, and with the orders to 
be issued by his Exeellency the Seraskier, by the Board in question as. now 
established in its complete state, and in other ways, and the necessary supplies 
of grain, &e., for the rations of the Iinperial troops, have been already provided 
for by the Government, from the necessary quarters, and up to this time a con- 
siderable quantity has been sent to Erzeroom. If there be any defietency in the 
provisions allotted, the Commander-in-chief will enter into communication with 
the authorities of those places, and see that proper measures are taken for feeding 
the troops, and providing for their comfort, as far as that is possible with refer- 
ence to place. 

Winter is not the season for military operations, and it is His Imperial 
Majesty's orders that the army in question should not act uggressively, but 
remain on the defensive. As the enemy, however, may attack the fortifications 
raised, and invade the Ottoman territory, in that case the Ottoman authorities 
will consult with the Ferik Williams Pasha, who is at the Imperial camp, and 
with the chief commanders, officers, and others, and see to ranelling the enemy 
by adapting those measures and movements whieh may be approved of aecording 
to the proper application of military science, 

This is not the weather for dulling; but the Commander-in-chief will, 
when the weather permits, see that the troops should load and fire off their guns, 
and practice ball-firing—n most essential thing. 

There may be a deficiency in the army of gunners and cavalry horses ; and 
the Commander-in-chief will on lis arrival supply the deficiency of horses, and 
report upon the provisions of war and other things necessary to be sent from 
this, in order that they may be promptly forwarded. 

It is highly requisite and important that precise information should be 
obtained with respect to the actual foree of the enemy, to his operations and 
actual circumstances, and to be always well informed and on the alert; and in urder 
that the enemy may not learn what is going on in the Imperial camp, it will be 
the constant duty of the Commander-in-chief to see that those individuals 
coming over to the camp, and the traders and merchants thereat, should not 
enter the camp and separate military detachments, and take information thereon, 

It has been alleged, as an excuse, that the army being in the field, the 
reports drawn up have not been hitherto duly forwarded. The object of requiring 
those reports was to know the wetual returns of the Regiments aud Battalions in 
the Imperial camp; their position; und to acquire information concerning the 
the army, the importance of which itis needless to state. As it will be easier 
to dispateh a succinct monthly report, the Commander-in-chief will see that 
this is done. 

The Commander-in-chief will, on his arrival, report accurately to the 
Seraskierat on the officers to be dismissed or changed. 

lt is superfluous to repeat how desirable it is that the commanders and 
officers of the army, should be on terms of perfect submission, concord and 


225 


unity. A want of concord, that is, dislike of one officer towards another, is 
productive of all manner of disorder. ‘The Commander-in-chief will, therefore. 
look to the establishment of concord, &c., among all the officers. 


Inclosure @ in No. 224. 


The Grand Visier's Addition to the Suggestions furnished by the Seraskier to the 
Commander-in-chief of the Army of Anatolia, Vassif Pasha, 


Translation.) 


WHILST the force that ought really to have made an impression upon the 
Russians in this war was the army of Anatolia, the irregular proceedings of some 
functionaries, owing simply to their ignorance and carelessness, and the various 
misdeeds of others amounting to nothing less than robbery and corruption, have 
brought that army to its present state of disorganization; namely, they acted 
ignorantly and madly in the untimely offensive operations of last year. After 
going beyond the Russian frontier, it was necessary to reassure and protect in 
every way the inhabitants who came to make their submission and offer their 
services ; but they frightened them by leaving the Bashi-Bozouks without any 
rule, and allowing them to commit all sorts of disorders, and even in the Imperial 
dominions themselves they exposed numberless helpless people to the acts of 
those vagabonds. Above all things, the disgusting practice of peculation is at 
all times an odious action; but more especially ata time when the Sublime Porte 
is Cnguged in a great question of vital importance to her, it is the bounden duty 
of persons who profess the least part of zeal, honesty, or patriotism, to abstain 
altogether from such matters, and never to leave the path of integrity. Some 
contemptible persons, utterly unmindful of such matters, have thought these 
troubled times an excellent opportunity for pursuing their own interested ends 
by buying up corn and provisions at a low rate, and then selling to the Govern- 
ment at double price, Others have had the audacity to defaleate from the 
established rations of the Imperial army, of which we take more care than of 
ourselves, and which we are bound to content more than our ownselves. “These 
reprehensible acts, which have brought the Imperial army to such a state of 
disorganization, have left His Majesty's soldiers in a helpless state, and filled 
with dismay and with despair the inhabitants who were desirous of serving the 
Imperial Ottoman anny with their heart and soul. 

The Sublime Porte, however, considering it a matter of the highest import- 
ance to ameliorate the existing state of the army, and, by correcting all its deti- 
clencies, to procure a real force to oppose the enemy; and, knowing from 
experience the fidelity and honesty of Vassif Pasha, has selected him for the 
command of the above army, and the execution of the following matter will 
form part of his duties. 

Massif Pasha, immediately upon bis arrival at the army, will first make 
inquiries from persons conversant with the subject us to the proceedings and 
doings of the officers, high and low. As soon as he shall have, by putting upon 
their trial whosoever among them may have committed acts of corruption, proved 
their guilt, he shall cashier them, and send them here, along with the judicial 
proceedings, to be punished according to law; and since the Sublime Porte has 
come to the firm resolution not to grant impunity to such persons in future, but 
to be severe against them, such as-shall have, by the commission of nets of 
corruption and robbery, degraded themselves below the scale of humanity, no 
matter how high their rank or connection, such reasons or considerations shall 
not procure them any indulgence, or screen them from punishment. In short, 
the Sublime Porte will not, for the sake of a few thieves, consent to tread under 
loot 80 many sacred imperial and national interests. Tt is, therefore, the decided 
wish of the Imperial Government that Vassit’ Pasha, free from any sort of 
anxiety, should exert himself effectually to purge the army of the band of pecu- 
lators. Aiter having done so, should the same inefficient mode of action be 
pursued, there is no doubt that the former state of things will return. Besides, 
tis not enough that the General himself’ be honest; he must also net allow

heretofore sent hither have been taken into due consideration, and proper

ypon Williams Pasha as a stranger, but will consult.with him frankly on subjects

Art. 31.—Harvest. 


The harvest has been injured by hail and severe cold. lt has been neces- 
sary to bring provisions from distant places, and the Governor of Erzeroom 
has been upplied to on the subject. 


Note.—The question of provisions was fully discussed in the note on the 4th

Art. 32.—-Arrears of Pay. 


A portion of the army las not received its pay for twenty-two months, 
another for eighteen, and another for fifteen. The privates cannot purchase 
articles of the first necessity, even tobacco. The Redifg have been prevented 
from remitting anything to their families ; many soldiers have deserted on this 
account, Privates maimed and wounded in action are obliged to beg their bread 
‘athe strect, [t does not require a strong feeling of humanity to point out the 
necessity of assisting these individuals, ‘There is not the least doubt that the 
well known kindly feelings of the Sultan will be moved at the state of these 
men, and that a firman on the subject will be issued for the next campaign. 
‘The soldiers pull down the roofs of their houses im order to find wood to burn. 
The Pashas allow this to be done, whilst there is no lack of forests in the neigh- 
hourhood, ‘The villages are thus exposed to damage in this and other ways, and 
ane, therefore, entitled to commiseration. Very little money lias been sent to 
the army, and what was sent consisted of paper, which 1s a dire calamity to the 
coldier, who loses considerably by it, Shopkeepers also are ruined by taking it, 
and some are shutting up their shops. It ts very profitable to civil functionaries 
to take up out of circulation hard eash, and sive out paper in lien of it, but it is 
pure loss to the soldiers. Caimes are exchanged for cash at a discount of 
20 per cent. 

Twelve thousand cloaks, the property of deceased soldiers, have disappeared, 
and the Mushir and other general officers deal in the clothes of the dead 
Wen, 


What is required -— 


1, ‘To pay the arrears of pay, 

®. ‘To pay the soldiers’ wages in current com, : 

3. ‘I'o exercise a stricter supervision over the persons who furnish bread, 
heeause the bread is had and not properly baked, and gives rise to divers 
Hiseuses. 

4. Colonels have dealt in caimes; this must be looked to. 


Note.—As money has been appropriated and sent to this army for payment 
of arrears, the General in command will receive orders to investigate, on his 
arrival, the other pots contained in this Article. 


Art. 33,— Officers, : 


Officers have made drunkenness a habit; and this is even seen among the 
afficers of the highest rank, This must be puta stop to, because it endangers 
the safety of the army. Several of the officers showed cowantice on the field of 
battle, Nadir Bey (of the 6th Arabistan) and Khoorshid Bey (of the 5th) took 
to flight along with their subalterns at Koorookdéré as soon as the fight had 
commenced, and consequently were taken prisoners by the Russians along with 
the third part oftheir respective regiments.

No, 227, 
Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon, —( Received February 11.) 


(No. 40. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Aerlin, February 9, (855. 

M. NIEBUHR, the King of Prussia’s private secretary, and one of 
the most influential and active agents of the Kreuz Zeitung party, and an 
avowed partisan of Russia, has left Berlin for Brussels and the Hague. It was 
originally intended that this gentleman should proceed to Paris, and it was 
supposed that his journey was connected with the mission of General Wedel, 
and had for its object the neutralizing any attempt to bring about an under- 
standing with the French Government. ‘The project was objected to by Baron 
Manteuffel, and the journey to Paris has, at his suggestion, been abandoned for 
the moment, but, it is my duty to inform your Lordship that it 1s generally 
believed here that the mission of M. Niebuhr, if it can be so called, to Brussels 
and the Hague, is to discover the feelings of these Courts as to the advantage 
of entering into m general league of neutrality. 

This intelligence having reached me from quarters deserving of credence, 
Ihave spoken to Buron Mantenflel on the subject, observing that it seemed 
strange that at the very time the Prussian Government was discussing the ques- 
tion of a ‘Treaty with England and France, persons about the Court should 
report that it was desirous to learn the opinions of the Governments of Belgium 
and Holland on a matter whieh implied the intention to adopt a policy of a 
totally different character from that which we were desirous to see established, 
His Excellency said that M. Niebuhr had received no instructions from him ; 


that this journey had no official character; and that he had no knowledge of 


his being charged with any communication such as | suspected. His Excellency, 
in fact, denied that he was sent on a political mission; but from the intimate 
vonnection of M. Niebuhr with General Gerlach, and his. confidential post- 
tion about the King, it can seareely be supposed that he has proceeded on 
this journey at this time of the year for recreation or repose from his arduous 
duties, and Lam strongly impressed with the idea that he must be charged with 
some scerel and important business, 

‘The opinion, indeed, is general here, since the late differences with the 


aod 


Austrian Government, that the King is intent on carrying out a policy of 
neutrality; and that, in addition to the States of the Germanic Confederation, 
he is in hopes of being able to bring into his views, not only the Courts of 
Brussels and the Hague, but also that of Copenhagen and even the Govern- 
ment of the United States. How far these supposed opinions of the Prussian 
Government will be listened to [am unable to judge, but the idea is not a new 
one. and if Prussia is not readmitted into the Conference ab Vienna it 18 not 
impossible that she may have resolved to adopt this course, and | would venture 
to suggest the expediency, without loss of time, of endeavouring to counteract 
any attempts of tle kind which may be made. 
I have, &c, 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

The Earl of Westmorland to the Karl of Clarendon.—( Received February 11.) 


(No. 57.) 
My Lord, Vienna, February 7, 1855. 

WITH reference to your Lordship’s despatch No. 33 of the 29th ultimo, 
desiring to be made acquainted with the source from which Count Buol derived 
the report mentioned in my despatch No, 469 of the 13th of December, 1854, 
as to the intention of the Ottoman authorities to expel a number of Boyards 
from the Danubian Principalities, the property of some of whom was to be con- 
fiscated, I have to state that this subject was brought before the Commission 
which was assembled in Vienna for the affairs of the Princtpalities, and that this 
information (which has since proved to be entirely erroneous) was contained in 
a confidential correspondence from the Moldavian authorities to General 
Coronini, and by him transmitted to his Government ; and that the originals of 
these documents were the grounds upon which the Commissioners (as stated in 
my above-named despatch), came to the determination of sending the confiden- 
tial letters to the Consular Agents, Messrs. Colquhoun and Gardner, which are 
inclosed in that despatch, 

As the directions given in that memorandum were only to act by way of 
advice, if the contemplated case arose, and as I stated in my letter to Mr. 
Colquhoun ‘that I was not inclined to believe the report,” 1 did not think 
it necessary, when that belief was proved to be correct, to transmit any account 
of it to Mr, Colquhoun, 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) WESTMORLAND,

No, 232. ‘ 
Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received Vebruary 15.) 


(No. 160.) ' 
My Lord, Paris, February 12, 1855. 

THE Sardinian Minister has been desired to communicate to me an 
instruction, dated the Ist instant, addressed by Count Cavour to the Sardinian 
Chargé d’ Affaires at Vienna, ; 

As M. Villa-Marina could not tell me positively whether a copy of this 
instruction had been transmitted to M. d’Azeglio, for communication to your 
Lordship, | think it better to state, as shortly as I can, its substance. | 

It appears that, when M. de Bourqueney infornied Count Buol of the 
intention of the Western Powers to accept the adhesion of Sardinia to the 
Treaty of the 10th of April last, Count Buol expressed a wish to see the diplo- 
matic relations between Austria and Sardinia placed ona better footing. M, de 
Bourqueney repeated this fact to M, Vronyn de Lhuys, who in his turn 
instructed the Duc de Guiche to speak to M, de Cavour on the subject, The 
result is, the despatch to which | am calling your Lordship’s attention, 

M. de Cavour states that the Sardinian Government is ready and anxious 
to renew its-former amicable relations with the Cabinet of Vienna; but he 
pots out that it is only possible, when the Decree of Sequestration, which 
weighs so heavily on certain Sardinian subjects, shall have been repealed. He 
ubserves that Count Buol himself admits that he has no ground of complaint 
agaist the Sardinian Government, though he thinks that the license of the 
Sardinian press ought to be repressed, ‘To this M. de Cayour replies, that the 
liberty of the press, being essential to liberal institutions, must naturally Gxist in 
Sardinia: that he does not suppose that Count Buol's remurks apply to the 


Mt it in ie SOs ee eee PEF 
a ae ee ee Bia kai: O° 
+. - Tei HL. Cv el A: © 


241 


freedom with which the press examines affairs affecting the internal government 
of the country, but that they are directed against the attacks made against the 
Emperor of Austria and his Government; that an effectual remedy had been 
found for all such abuses—a remedy which has completely put a stop to attacks 
of a similar nature made against the Emperor of the French and the Queen of 
Spain, and whieh, if resorted to by Austria, would as cflectually secure her 
Government from all further aggressions on the part of the Sardinian press, 1 
do not enter more at large on this part of the despatch, as it is irrelevant to the 
main object at issue. 

On the subject of the repeal of the Sequestration Decree, M. de Cavour 
observes that he is fur from giving that extended sense to the rights of naturali- 
gation which is contended for by the United States, but that he must say that 
Lombardian subjects who have become suljects of the King of Sardinia with 
the full permission of the Emperor of Austria, acquire all the rights of Sardinian- 
born subjects, and that the Sardinian Government ts justified in tmsisting on the 
repeal of the Decree of Sequestration so far as it affects such persons, It 
would only be worthy the generosity and magnaniunity of a great Sovercign, 
Count Cavour remarks, if this repeal was mate at onee, and without reserve: 
but should this proceeding be declined by Count Buol, he suggests that the 
Austrian Government should carry the repeal out by degrees, and in selecting 
the persons to whom the cxemption is from time to time to apply. The 
Austrian Government had already taken the initiative in such a.course by raising 
the sequestration which had been placed on the properties of the Princess 
Belgoioso and the Duke of Litta, 

In general, the Sardinian Chargé d’Affaires at Vienna is charged to receive 
with urbanity and frankness any overture that may be made to him by Count 
Buol, vither directly or through M. de Bourquency, and to keep M, de Bour- 
queney and Lord Westmorland informed of what may pass between him and 
the Austrian Cabinet, 

I said that I was sure that Her Majesty's Governinent would learn with 
sincere pleasure the amicable sentiments which seemed to prevail in the 
Cabinets of Vienna and ‘Turin, and that your Lordship would aid in amy way 
you could to the conversion of those sentiments into more stable relations. 

1 observed, however, to M. Villa-Marina, that although the Austrian 
Decree of Sequestration might have fallen npon many innocent persons, there 
might be a lew of whose dispositions the Austrian Government had real grounds 
for apprehension, and I suggested that some arrangement might perhaps be
