Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received February 13.) 


(No. 163. Confidential.) 


My Lord, Paris, February 12, 1855. 

DURING a conversation which I had with M. Drouyn de Lhuys a few 
days ago, his Execlleney reverted to the project of a ‘Treaty with Prussia, 
and he expressed the hope that Her Majesty's Government would not consent 
to the re-admission of a Prussian Plenipotentiary to the Conferences at Vienna, 
unless the Prussian Government entered previously into some cugagement with 
the Western Powers in the sense of the engagement which already existed 
between them and Austria. . 

L replied to M. Dronyn de Lhuys that | believed that the opinions of Her 
Majesty's Government on this matter coincided with his. | remarked at the 
samme time that it might be worthy of the consideration of the two Governments 
whether some middle course might not be found by which the wounded dignity 


242 


af the King of Prussia and the interests of the allied Powers might be conciliated 
in a way satisfactory to both. His Excellency acquiesced in this remark, | 

This morning Count Hatzfeldt called upon me. He said that he regretted 
to see by his last despatches from Berlin that the hing continued to insist on his 
readmission to the Conference as a right emanating from the Protocol of the oth 
of April,and that His Majesty was resolved to consider a further refusal of the 
allied Powers to admit this right as absolving him from all other engagements 
contracted by the said Protocol. ‘This, Count Hatefeldt said, was the official 
lanwuase which he was desired to hold, but he would at the same time tell me 
confidentially that the letters received by General Wedel and by M. Usedom, who 
was now at Paris, showed a great desire on the part of the King to draw nearer 
to the Western Powers, and he again put it to me whether some scheme might 
not be devised for saving the King’s amour propre, and yet restoring the united 
action of the Four Powers. é; 

[ told Count Hatzfeldt | could only refer him to the conversation which | 
had with him on the Sth instant, and which was reported in my despatch 
“io. 134, of that date, to your Lordship. 

The Count then inquired whether it might not be possible to place the 
interpretation given by the three Powers to the four points before his Sovereign, 
without referring to the Protocol to which that interpretation had been consigned, 
and whether, if the King signified his agreement in that interpretation, the 
signature ofa Treaty, offensive and defensive, might not be postponed. — [ replied 
ta Count Hatzieldt that although | thought some plan might be devised to 
extricate the King from the untenable position which His Majesty liad taken in 
assuming a right to be consulted on all matters regarding the settlement of the 
Eastern question, it could, in my opinion, only be done upon the understanding 
that His Majesty would frankly join the allies afterwards, for otherwise no 
advantage would aeerue to the latter. | at 

Count Hatefeldt inquired further whether I thought that Her Majesty's 
Government would be satistied with a declaration of striet neutrality on the part 
of Prussia, [ replied that he must forgive me if T said that Ler Majesty's 
Governinent could have no confidence that any such declaration would be fairly 
curried out. | 

In the course of this conversation Count Hatzfeldt said that there was one 
thing which might have a great effect with the King, if made use of at the right 
moment, namely, intimidation ; but he did not think, be uddedd, that either 
Austria or France were at this moment in such a state of mnilitary preparation 
as would enable them to make a demonstration that would alarm the Prussian 
Govermment. Austria was obliged to keep a large army to watch the forces ol 
Russia; the flower of the French troops was in the Crimea. He hinted that 
what would be most feared would bea blockade; though hé remarked that too 
much reliance must not be placed on such a measure of coercion, as the Prussian 
ports had been blockiwled by Denmark in 1848, without creating much pressure 
on Prussian commerce. f 

Your Lordship will of course understand that this conversation was entirely 
of a private nature, both Count Hatafeldt and myself having agreed that it was a 
mere exchange of personal opinions, | need not, therefore, request you not to 
mention Connt Hatafeldt’s name in any communication which you may have 
either with Count Bernstortf or M.dUsedom. At the same time | must again 
express my conviction of the sincerity of Count Hatzfeldt's wishes to lead his 
Covernment to a better understanding with the Western Powers. 

[ have, ke. 
(Signed) COWLEY.

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon —( Received February 16.) 
(No, 86.) 


My Lord, Constantinople, February 3, 1856, 

IN pursuance of your Lordship’s instructions, have this day concluded 
and signed with Reshil Pasha, Grand Vizier, and Auli Pasha, Minister for 
Foreign Affairs, a Convention in wine Articles, by which if is agreed on the part 
of their Majesties the Queen and the Sultan respectively, that a body of 20,000 
Ottoman troops of all arms, commanded by British officers, shall be taken into 
the pay and service of the British Government during the present war, 

Originals of this instrument in English and Turkish, signed and sealed by 
the respective Plenipotentiarics, are lerewith inclosed. 

A duplicate original in each language, signed and sealed in the same 
manner, remains in the hands of the ‘Turkish Ministers, . | 

Your Lordship will observe that the ratilications are to be exchanged at 
Constantinople within six weeks at the latest. 

It has not been necessary for me to avail myself of the latitude afforded by 
your Lordship's instructions with respect to the amount ef pay, which 15 
limited to the rate established in the Turkish arm’‘es. 

The two Articles Vil and VILL, which I have ventured to add to the original 
draft, require a few words of explanation. 

The Grand Viaier proposed wo alterations in Article IL; first, by omitting 
eertain words from the text of the draft, and substituting certain others; secondly, 
by the insertion of afresh clause: the former amendment being ostensibly intended 
to provide that the Turkish troops should receive rations according to their 
customary practice; the latter, that any punishments inflicted upon the soldicrs 
shall also be in aceordance with the Turkish regulations, 

The terms of the proposed amendments we submitted to your Lordship 
herewith in a separate inclosure, 

Not secing any material objection to the Grand Vigier'’s suggestions, but 


249 


desirous not to weaken or disturb unnecessarily the wording of the draft trans- 
mitted from your Lordship’s office, | proposed embodying them in an explanatory 
Article (VITth of the Convention now concluded), and I took advantage of the 
aceasion to add another (the VIIM[th), declaring in our favour the construction to 
be put upon the opening clause of Article IIT. 

I venture to hope that these modifications will meet with the approval of 
Her Majesty's Government. 

The accompanying certificate delivered to me by Mr. Alison, the Oriental 
Secretary, will serve to show that the original versions of the Convention in 
English and Turkish may be relied upon as substantially identical in meaning. 

Unnecessary though it be, your Lordship will excuse my observing how 
greatly the future efficiency of the Ottoman troops in Her Majesty's service will 
depend upon the selection of their officers, not only in respect to military 
knowledge and ability, but in point of qualifications adapted to the management 
and addressed to the confidence of soldiers differing so widely from the Hritish 
in language, customs, and religion. Were greater difficulties likely to arise out 
this difference, they might be cheerfully encountered for the sake of a measure 
which tends to results beyond those of a military character, and which, if 
properly directed, may conduce more than any other to the extension of our 
influence, and the promotion of salutary improvements in this Empire. 

I] have, &e. 


(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE. 


Inclosure in No. 299. 


Proposed Amendments to the Convention of February 3, 1854. 


(Translation.) 


THE following passage is proposed to be substituted for the words under- 
lined in Article 11," 

All the soldiers and officers of the Imperial troops shall, in all matters 
respecting war and military movements, be under the orders and command of 
the chic! Commanders to be placed over them by the British Government, just 
as if they were appointed by the Sublime Porte; and their internal affairs, their 
discipline, their punishments, shall be as before according to the system pursued 
in the ‘Turkish army. Their rations, pay, and clothes, shall, as stated in Article 
IIT, be of the description to which they are accustomed, and be distributed to 
them by the English authorities according to the established system of the 
British Government.” 


[t is proposed to add the following passage at the end of Article IIL: 
“ And their rations shall be issued to them according to their custom.”

imposible, and provides for its occurrence ina manner which, in the supposed

Inclosure in No. 240. 


Memorandum. 


THE present memorandum 15 intended to declare that the British Govern- 
ment, in leaving to the Turkish authorities the appointment of subultern officers 
in the body of troops to be tuken into its service according to the Convention 
signed to-day, reserves only the nomination among them of a few British drill- 
serjeants, and that in ease of difficulty or delay in making up the complete 
number of privates agreed upon by the terms of the Convention, the British 
communding officers shall he ut liberty to recruit and make up the deficiency 
from the subjects of the Sublime Porte indiscriminately, without reference to 
their being already either Regulars or Rediffs.

ALTHOUGH the afternoon is considerably advanced, and the weather fine, 
| have not yet received any advices from the Crimea. If the mail is arrived, it

it has passed on straight to England. My own state of ignorance, as to official 
‘nformation, is the more vexatious, us rumours of deep interest, not unattended 
with anxiety, have been afloat since yesterday, According to these reports a 
violent sortie has been made from Sebastopol against the Freneh lines, and one 
of less force against the British, It is said that the Russians were repulsed in 
both eases, in the former with heavy loss, and not without inflicting considerable 
injury on the allies, “The French are described as having lost 800 men, and the 
British 40. When the vessel which brought this intelligence left the const, a 
large Russian foree—so runs the statement—vwas seen to march in heavy masses 
towurds Balaklava. 

{ grieve to add that the sick continue to come down in considerable 
numbers.

M. Benedetti, returned with a general corrobation of the preceding intelligence

No. 245. 
Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.— Received February 1G.) 


(No. 176. Most Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, February 15, 1895, 

COUNT HATZFELDT came to me this morning, and informed me that 
the Emperor had sent for General Wedel yesterday, and had placed in his hands 
the “ Projet de Traité’’ which His Majesty proposed the Prussian Governinent 
should sign, in order that Prussia might resume her place in the Conferences at 
Vienna. Count Hatzfeldt added that he had learnt the fact through a contiden- 
tial source: that the “ projet” had not been communicated to him, though he 
believed that it had been sent for the approbation of the Cabinets of London 
and Vienna, Further, he had reason to know that General Wedel had not 
transmitted it to Berlin, nor as yet communicated the fact af its existence to his 
Government. Count Hatzteldt attributed this seeming negligence to the existence 
of another “ projet,” coneacted by M. d'Usedom and General Wedel, which had 
already been forwarded to Berlin for the King of Prussia’s approval. } 

Count Hatafeldt went on to say that he regretted that this overture had 
been made. In the first place, its originating in France was sufficient to set his 
Government against ity in the next, it was too crude, and would commit his 
Government too immediately to have a chance of obtaining the King’s approval. 
ven that which was a Seeret Article with Austria had been made patent in the 
“projet” destined for Prussia. All that could be hoped for at this moment (to 
ase the Count’s own words) was, to tarn the horse's head in the right direction, 
in the hope that he might be coaxed or forced to go on hereafter. 

There was, however, the Count continued to say, i change for the better 
at Berlin. His last despatches showed this, The King was not ayerse to 
some sort of transaction, such as my late despatches: on this subject have given 
an outline of; but there were two points to which [ts Majesty would hold : 
the prevention of the march of French troops into Germany, und a guaranter 
that Poland should not be revolutionized. If these points were settled to the 
King’s satisfaction, he (Count Llutzieldt) thought that Ths Majesty would enter 
into further engagements to succour Austria, if she attacked Russia und met 
with reverses, and even, under certain eventualities, which must, however, be 
lett for the King’s appreciation, to assume the offensive igainst Russia. 

With recard to the prevention of the entry of Ivench troops into Germany, 
Count Hatafeldt remarked that it was the King’s apprehension of this—an appre- 
hension which applied equally to their presence on German soil as friends or as 
enemies—which had created this sudden change in the King’s feclings, 

With regard to Poland, T said to Count Hatefeldt that 1 would speak os 
frankly to him as he had to me. 1 could assure him with all honesty and 
sincerity, and so, | was sure, would Her Majesty's Government assure the King, 
that they had no thoughts of exciting or aiding, cither openly or covertly, a 


258 


revolution in Poland; but I was equally certain that neither Her Majesty's nor 
the French Government would bind themselves by any engagements respecting 
the future lot of that country. If the war was to be prolonged with Russia, it 
was impossible to foresee to what further complications that war would give 
rise; and, independent of the sympathy which the cause of Poland had ever 
excited in the minds of the British nation, it would be impossible for any 
Government so to tie their hands as not to take advantage of any internal 
movement in Poland against Russia, which the prolongation of hostilities might 
accidentally produce. If the King of Prussia feared this contingency, the best 
plan to prevent it was to aid us in putting an end to the war, 

Count Hatefeldt hag too much good sense not to comprehend and appreciate 
fully the position of Her Majesty's Government in regard to this question, Still 
he appears to apprehend that the King of Prussia will require explicit decla- 
rations regarding it, before he binds himself more closely to the policy of the 
allies.

(Signed) COWLEY.

No. 247,

(No. 181. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, February 16, 1855. 

{ HAVE not alluded to the reports prevalent of a body of French troops 
being about to be sent to assist those of Austria, referred tom your Lordship’s 
despatch No. 147 of the 18th instant, because I was convinced that at the 
present moment there was no foundation for such reports, and that they had 
been put in circulation by these who thought that an apprehension of their 
proving true would indispose the smaller States of Germany towards the alliance 
between Austria and the Western Powers. 

Nevertheless, | mentioned the subject yesterday to M. Drouyn de Lhuys. 
He assured me immediately that had any such project been in contemplation, 
Her Majesty’s Government would at once have been informed of it. The 
reports had arisen, he supposed, in consequence of the double mission of 
Generals Crenneville and Wedel to Paris ; bat although these officers, somewhat 
irregularly he admitted, had been charged with letters direct ta the Emperor, he 
(M. Drouyn de Liuys) was well informed of what passed at the interviews with 
which they had been honoured by His Majesty, und he cauld state with certainty 
that the question of sending French troops to any part of Europe, except the 
East, had not been mooted, 

There was nothing whatever military, M. Drouya de Lhuys continued, in 
General Wedel's mission, nor did General Crenneville appear to be the bearer of 
any distinet propositions on the part of his Government. His object appearcd to 
be to prove that the Emperor of Russia could bring 1,200,000 into the field; that 
to cope: with them, Europe must have, at least, 1,400,000, and that the allies 
could not bring that number together, ‘The Emperor, in admitting the truth of 
the lutter assertion, had shown that so large a foree wis by no means necessary, 
even if Russia were as strong as Austria represented her to be; and that Austria,

dislike are so strong, that sooner or later they must, one would apprehend, find 
vent in open quarrel, 

In this state of things, my Lord, I have carefully avoided lauguage that 
could irritate the too great susceptibilities already existing on both sides. I 
have never failed to point out the advantages of union, or the fatal consequences 
likely to ensue from a breach between these two States, not to themselves alone, 
but to the whole Confederation, I have, indeed, so far deprecated the policy of 
Prussia, that [ have never shrunk from qualifying it as, in my opinion, the least 
calculated for obtaining her professed object of obtaining peace, and have said 
that her attitude was such as must continue to encourage the resistance of 
Russia, while there would be every prospect of the common object being attained 
by a frank adhesion to the side of the Western Powers, 

There have recently occurred such sudden changes in the views of some of 
the minor Governments, that it is extremely difficult to pronounce on which 
side lies the majority of votes in the Dict on any question decisive of the attitude 
to be taken by the Confederation ; and, us generally happens, Bavaria thinking 
land, perhaps, not erroneously) that the decision lies with her, is making her 
importance felt on both sides, and helping Prussia to delay decision, 

The Secret Circular of the Vienna Cabinet of the 14th of last month has 
been adroitly turned to her own purpose by Prussia, and that Government, whose 
views as far as regards territorial arrangements and encroachments on her neigh- 
bours are notorious, has made use of that document to impute all sorts of projects 
of that kind to the Government of Vienna, and, as is said, with considerable 
success in detaching from the Imperial Government certain not very fast adherents. 

The reported intended movement of French troops in support of Austria 
is now attempted to be turned to similar account, but J apprehend with less 
success, for itis not ditheult to see that such assistance to Austria need give 
little umbrage, and would hold out but slight menace to Prussia if she honestly 
fulfils her professed wish of remaining immoveable, and that, if really contem- 
plated, it is only provoked and rendered necessary by the doubtiulness of the 
attitude now taken by the Cabinet of Berlin. ! 

I have, &c, 
(Signed) A, MALET.

Sir R. Abercromby to the Karl of Clarendon.— (Received February 17.) 
(No. 13.) 


My Lord, The Hague, february 12, 1855. 

AN incident has recently occurred here which, although purporting to refer 
simply to a question of ceremony, has nevertheless, when taken in connection 
with other circumstances, some political colour, and | therefore think it my duty 
to report the affair to your Lordship ts succinctly as possible, | 

On the arrival of the Ottoman Envoy at this Court, he addressed, after 
he had been received by His Netherland Majesty, the usual letters requesting 
presentation audiences of the other members of the Royal family of this country, 
and amongst others, to Her Majesty the Queen-Mother, and he reeeived from 
Her Majesty’s Grand Muster, a perfectly civil and satisfactory answer, stating 
that Her Majesty having declined to grant any audiences this winter, Her 
Majesty must defer to some other occasion the reception of the Ottaman Envoy 
and of his son, first Secretary of the Ottoman Legation at this Court. 

As this placed the Ottoman Envoy, Prince Caradja, exactly on the same 
footing as the rest of his colleagues with regard to their reception this year by 
Her Majesty the Queen-Mother, every form of attention and respect had been 
complied with on either side, 

Subsequently, however, to the above exchange of communications between 
Her Majesty the Queen-Mother and Prince Caradja, my Prussian colleague, 
Count Konigsmark, availed himself of an accidental meeting with Prince 
Caradja at the house of the French Minister, ta state to him, in his capacity of 
“ Doyen” of the Diplomatic body, that Her Majesty the Queen-Mother hod 
informed him of her intention of not granting audiences this winter, and

Sir R. Abercromby to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recetved February 17.) 


(No. 20.) 
My Lord, The Hague, February 14, 1855. 


M. DE NIEBUHR leaves the Hague on bis return to Berlin to-day. 

In a former despatch I reported to your Lordship that the Prussian 
Minister at this Court officially announced that M.de Niebuhr had come here on 
a party of pleasure only, and for the purpose of seeing a country he did not know : 
this explanation of the journey of the Secretary of His Prussian Majesty's 
Cabinet in the depth of winter, continues to be persevered in; but with what 
degree of belief on the part of the political public of this residence, | leave your 
Lordship to judge. . por 

M. de Niebuhr, although applying through Count Konigsmark for 
M. Van Hall’s assistance to have an exception in point of etiquette made in his 
favour, by expressing a wish that His Netherland Majesty would be pleased to 
receive him at the Court ball of last night, though not previously presented to 
His Majesty, has not, so far as Lam at present informed, had the civility to call 
upon M. Van Hall, or to be introduced to him; thus pointedly marking his 
want of courtesy towards the Government of His Netherland Majesty. 

His Netherland Majesty is not a person to allow such a want of respect 
towards himself to pass unheeded ; and | have good reason for believing that it 
hus made due impression on His Netherland Majesty’s mind, This belief has 
been strengthened by learning this instant that the King’s reception of M, de 
Niebuhr at the ball last night was pointedly cold, the only words which His 
Majesty addressed to him, being to inquire whether he intended to remain long 
in this country; and on learning from M, Niebuhr that he proposed to quit the 
Hague to-day, His Netherland Majesty lett him without speaking another word ; 
and turning to my French colleague, who was. standing at a short distance, His 
Majesty gave him the most marked and flattering reception. It was only at an 
advanced period of the evening that M. de Niebuhr thought proper to hove 
himself introduced to his Excellency M. Van Hall. 

I believe that I shall not be misleading your Lordship when I state, that 
my impression is, that the object of M. de Niebuhr’s journey to this country 
has been to inquire into the state of public opinion here with regard to Prussia 
and Prussian policy; to judge how far it might be prudent for the Prussian 
Kreuz faction at Berlin to reckon on Netherland support and sympathy ; to 
ealeulate pon what amount of opposition to the policy of the Western Powers, 
and to that of Austria in particular, might be expected from public opinion in 
the Netherlands ; and lastly, to discover what chance existed of undermining the 
present Cabinet of the Hague, and of substituting in its place an Administration 
that should be more favourable to Prussia and to Prussian policy than the 
Cabinets of M, Van Hall, 

Whatever foundation there may be for the first suppositions which I have 
ventured to suggest, there is abundant evidence to prove that the Inst is at lenst 
correct, and both His Netherland Majesty and his Ministers are profoundly 
irritated by the course of proceeding whieh the Court of Berlin has followed, and 
which is marked by such a want of the ordinary forms of decorum, and which is 
wlike offensive to the dignity of His Netherland Majesty, and to the proper 
respect which the Government of one country owes to that of another with 
whom they profess to be on terms of amity. 

I think the reception which M. de Niebuhr met with from His Netherland 
Majesty last night will be sufficient to prove to him that in that quarter he is 
not likely to tind an ally in his wish to overthrow M, Van Hall and his Cabinet ; 
and if lie has really taken bot ordinary pains to sift the opinion of political men 
here with regard to the expediency of an unrestricted adoption of Prussian policy, 
he will also have discovered that, with the exception of some individuals See 
for their extreme admiration and devation to the Kussian Court, he could count 
upon none who would be willing to embark their country and their own 
pecuniary interests in a course of policy that would probably be fatal ta both. 

I must also add my conviction that the more the public becomes acquainted

My Lord, Vienna, February 14, 1850. 
THE ‘Turkish Ambassador called upon me to report his having reeeived 
instructions from his Government relating to the negotiations which, in conse- 
quence of the acceptation by the Emperor of Russia of the interpretation of 
the four bases which had been submitted to Prince Gortchakoll by the allied 
Representatives, it was expected would be commenced at Vienna. ‘The Ambas- 
sadur stated that, according to these instructions, he wis to attend at the 
Conferences which would be opened for the purposes of this negotiation, if he 
wis invited to do so; but in case any resolution was arrived at, or any project 
of Treaty which it was intended to transmit to St, Petersburgh for the approval 


261 


of the Russian Government, the Ambassador was to require that it should first 
be submitted to the Government of the Sultan at Constantinople. 

IT asked the Ambassador if he had no other instruction by which lias 
conduct would be regulated in the discussions which might arise during the 
negotiation, but he stated that he had not, but that he was informed that his 
full powers would be sent to him by Riza Bey, who was appointed Conseiller 
d’Ambassade, and who was to assist at the Conferences, I told the Ambassador 
that it appeared that his present: instructions were very incomplete; that there 
was no probability that any preliminary arrangement which might be agreed to 
by the Plenipotentiaries would be transmitted for approval to St. Petersburgh, 
but that all questions of such a nature would naturally be referred hy the 
Russian Representative to his Government; but the important question would 
be to know, if the Representatives of the other Powers, parties to the 
negotiations, agreed to any preliminary arrangement or Treaty, whether he 
would be authorised to take part in it; and upon his saying that he was not, 
and that both Count Buol and M. de Bourqueney had poimted out to him the 
difficulties which might arise from the nature of his instructions, and had 
recommended him to apply to his Government, in order that they might be 
rectified, I told him that I could not but concur in the same recommendation.

Inclosure in No, 260, 
Consul-General Colquioun to Lord Stratford de Redeliffe. 


My Lord, Bucharest, February 4, 1855. 


FOR some days past it has been bruited that the Prince was to send a 
sveret. Agent to Constantinople, to advance his interests, wud my special attention 
his been directed to the circumstances. 

Yesterday a mecting took place at the palace, when three persons were put 
forward as fit Agents; 

M. Jean Mano, some time Secretary of State; M, Plagino, at present 
filling that post (le is the Prince's son-in-law); and listly, M. Rossetti, now 
Agu of the Police, some time Governor of [braila. 

After some discussion the two first of these were rejected as being too well 
known as creatures of the Hospodar, and, by a strange resolution, the mission 
has been confided to the last-named, M. Rodolphe Rossetti, who is to be sent, 
varly next week, to Constantinople, 

One of liis principal instructions is, to endeavour to invratiate himself in the 
favour of the new Austrian Internuncio, Baron Koller, so as to secure his Excel 
leney’s sympathy in favour of Prince Stirbey. To cnable him to effect this, he 
will be furnished with very strong letters of recommendation from certain 
Austrians here, staunch partisans of the Prince, 

Of course no means are to be spared with the Turks. 

L consider it my duty to warn your Excellency of this move, and to give 
you some account of this emissary (whose name tus already figured, not aver 
creditably, in several of my preceding despatches), that your Excellency may be 
able to take measures, i you think fit, to counteract so iniquitous a plan. 

M. Rossetti is a bankrupt Boyard who has dissipated a large fortune, and, 
since Prince Stirbey’s Hospodariut, has been an active tool of his. 

When Governor of Tbraila he is known to have abstracted a sum of 120,000 
piastres (2,0000) from the Municipal Chest, of which he was the guardian, This 
sum has not been to this-day replaced. Heis reported to have paid a large sum 
for his post as Aga. 


We now come to his aets since he bas held this office, in which he was 


maintained by the Russian authorities as being an unscrupulous agent, 

He it was whe organised the band of Greek Volunteers ; who drew up their 
rules and regulations, administered the oaths to the affiliated, &e. 

He distinguished himself by the unrelenting severity with which he perse- 
cuted every Wallachian of known liberal opinions, as well as all deserters from 
the Russians about the period of their retreat from Wallachia in July last; and 


within the first four days of the advent of the Turks to the capital, he sent off 
seven deserters after the rear of the Russians. 

All these circumstances were made known to Omer Pasha, but his Highness 
was captivated by the apparent earnestness with which Rossetti offered his 
serviecs to the Turk. He avowed his many obligations to Russia, which he told 
the Pasha he had served faithfully; but that from that day, if Omer accepted 
his services, he would as devotedly serve Turkey. Omer continued him in his 
post in despite of my remonstrances. 

During his service with the Turk he repeatedly presented himself at my 
door, and, wearied at my refusal to receive him, he asked through Mazhar Pasha 
for an audience. 

I received him, and frankly let him know that I had advised Ins bemg 
removed by the Pasha. He repeated all his confessions of error, saying he had 
served the Prince faithfully; a4 well as Russia, to whom he owed all. So had 
he served Turkey; and now—being, above all, more than cither Russian or 
Turk, a sincere Wallachian, and seeing Wallachia's only hope lay in France and 
England—he offered me those services, This was atter the Prince's return ; 
and he finished by hoping | would hold out a friendly hand to the Prince, who 
was now a devoted patriot and friend to his country, 

[ told him 1 was no cnemy to the Peimee, but as he was under the weight of 
an official inquiry, 1 should be the first to congratulate him on the favourable 
issue of such inquiry; but, in the meantime, T must observe a distant attitude of 
simple observation. 

Sinee that period I have kept my eye on M. Rossetti, and have no hesita- 
tion in saying that a more unprincipled and unserupulous agent does not 
exist, 

With these details, your Excellency will be the best judge of what should 
be done when M, Rossetti makes his appearance at Constantinople, 1 have 
reason to believe the French Embassy will be equally forewarned ; and I learnt 
this evening that Baron Meusebach, the Prussian Consul-General, has, besides 
most of the above details, informed M. de Wildenbruch of certain acts in which 
M. Rossetti figured after my departure. 

Your Exeellency will observe that the principal grounds on which the 
Turkish Government may legitimately lay hold of M. Rosetti are, his having 
taken so open and notorious a part in the formation of the Greek Volunteers — 
a fact of public notoriety. This may offer fair reasons for taking measures to 
sccure his papers before he be allowed to land in Constantinople. In ease hy 
any chance any stray document should be found to convict him, the Porte may 
act as it thinks consistent with its own dignity. He bears with him a very large 
sum, in specie or in letters of credit, whieh he should be asked to account for ; 
and if he be permitted to land, he should be carefully looked after. 

Ll have reason to believe he will be especially recommended to Fuad 

‘fendi, 

There was arrested, when | was at Constantinople, a certain person calling” 
himself Baron Elloner. THe had contrived to get into the Turkish police service, 
but was convicted of being a Tussian spy, ‘Uhis man was employed also by 
M. Rossetti at Bucharest, and was sent from this place by the Russians to act in 
their interest. 

If I learn anything further on the subject, I will write by a return French 
Tatar on the Gth. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) ROBERT G, COLQUTOUN,

IN obedience to the instructions contained in your Lordship’s despatch

several letters which | have received from Her Majesty's Consular Agents on 
the subject. 

Consul-General Plaw writes from Dantzie that the principal shipments of 
contraband of war for that port were made from London, Hull, and Newcastle, 
on Prussian account, in Prussian or foreign bottoms, sometimes in British, He 
states that 250 tons of lead appear to have been sent into Poland from Dantzic. 

The report from Konigsberg is, that though the importations of lead from 
England have not much exceeded the average, about 7,000 ewt, of lead and 
alee had arrived by railway, and had, it was believed, been forwarded to 

UUssii. 

From Pillau the Vice-Consul writes that, in December last, 1,200 pigs of 
lead had been imported from Hull, and 1,000 pigs from Newenstle. It may be 
supposed that this lead was also on its way to Russia. :

T have the honour to inelose to your Lordship a précis of M. Wagner's

the Viceroy for carrying into effect the decree of expulsion, together with a short

large congregation resident there have been deprived of the means of public

do so. j

Inclosure 3 in No, 267. 
Account of the Mission established in Poland for the Conversion of Jews. 


THE London Society for promoting Christianity among the Jews had an 
established Mission in the Kingdom of Poland for thirty-three years, by special 
permission of the late and present Emperors. ‘The missionaries are seven in 
number, with their families. Their principal station was Warsaw, where four of the 
seven resided, and where they maintained an institution for inquivers and converts, 
with a considerable printing and bookbinding establishment. 

During the thirty-three years of this Mission, none of its members were ever 
charged with any political offence, nor have they ever at any time taken a prt, 
directly or indirectly, in any political movement whatsoever, so that the order for 
expulsion came upon them unexpectedly and took them much by surprise, since 
several of them were Russian subjects, two by birth and one from long residence. 
One of them has three sons married there and in the Russian Government 
employ, A fourth son, likewise a Russian subject, was expelled with bis father 
(the translator), because it was known that he had assisted his father in his 
labours, 

They had the first indication of the pending storm on the 22nd of December, 
1854, when they were cited to appear at the Consistory before its President (und 
Chief of the Secret Police and Spies)«Krusenstern, where the annexed Protocol 
was read to them and finully signed by them, and of which as a personal favour, 
a copy (in Polish) was handed over to them at their special request. 

fiesides Warsaw, they had also stations at Lublin, Suwalki, and Petrikan, 
where the other three missionaries were employed, 

The date originally fixed for their expulsion, January 14, 1855, wos i se 
far not strietly adhered to, us, when it was found impossible to wind up the 
business in so short a time, another week was granted them on their petitioning, 
for which they had to thank General Riidiger, . 

And not only had they to suffer severe losses on the sudden disposal of their 
woods, but they were not even allowed to tuke the proceeds of it out of the 
country in hard cash, but in the deteriorated paper of the country, 

Though the Government had granted them another week, yet they neglected 
to publish that favour in this country, so that the three missionaries in the pro- 
vinices relying on that favour, were actually driven out by gendarmes,

No. 270. 
Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received February 19.) 


(No. 54.) 
My Lord, Berlin, February 17, 1895. 

THE French Minister has addressed a note to the Prussian Government, 
enumerating the quantities of arms and munitions of war which, according ta 
reports that he has received from credible sources, have passed through this 
country into Russia. M. de Moustier has had the goodness to let me take a 
copy of this paper, which I have the honour to forward herewith. 

Your Lordship will perceive that the quantities of contraband of war which 
have thus found their way to our enemy are very considerable; and it 1s probable 
that they are even greater than is stated in the inclosed paper, for many articles 
may have got into Russia without any knowledge of their passage through 
Germany having been obtained. 

The greater quantities have apparently come from Belgium; but lead, salt- 
petre, and sulphur, have been imported into Prussia from England to so large 
an amount, that if Her Majesty's Government desires. to place a more effectual 
impediment to this trafic, 1 would suggest the propriety of prohibiting the 
shipment of contraband of war in English ports for the Baltic, except under 
certain conditions. 

I have, &e: 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

No. 273. 
Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recemed Bebruary 19.) 


(No. 198, Contidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, February 18, 1855, 

I PROMISED, at the end of my despatch No. 192 of the 16th instant, 
to explain how it is that, while the French Government desires to be released 
from the Vienna Conterences, they yet have the appearance of wishing to pursue 
negotiations for peace with Russia. 

These facts may be reconciled in the following way; The French Govern- 
nent has no expectation that the Conterences about to be resumed at Vienna 
can lead, at the present moment, to such a peace as will justify the allied 
Governments in recalling their troops from the East; and they would be glad 
if nerotiations could be broken off in a preliminary stage without calling in 
question the good fiith of the two Governments. But if this cannot be done, 
they are then anxious to delay the discussion of those points on which they 
know beforehand they should not have the support of the Austrian Govern- 
ment. What, therefore, they would desire is, that Prince Gortchakoff should 
refuse to ratify by his signature a simple aceeptation of the interpretation given 
by the three Powers to the four points, because they conceive that under such 
circumstanees France and England would be freed from their engagements 
towards Russia, and could quit the Conferences without engaging in any disens- 
sion which would show them to be at variance with Austria. while the latter 
could not, if the Conferences were broken olf through a refusal of the Russian 
Plenipotentiary to give a solemn ratification to lis former declarations, escape 
from the engacements which she had contracted with the Western Powers. On 
the other hand, if those Powers put forward demands which appeared exorbitant 
and untenable to Austria, Austria might say that she was not bound to counte- 
nanee such demands, and that if they were persisted in, she should consider 
lierself free to net as she judged best for her own interests. 

To my observation that, this moment must arrive sooner or later, and that 
in the meantime, by continuing useless negotiations, we furnished Austria with 
an excuse for her coutinued inidetivity, M. Drouyn de Lhuys has constantly 
replied that he prefers that, to hier having an cxeuse to quit the alliance 
altogether. If the evil day must come, it is as well to put it off as long as 
possible, and to avoid, until the last practical moment, making demands to 
which it is known beforchand Austria will not give her support, In the mean- 
time events may take a more favourable turn in the Crimea; the period which 
Austria had always tixed as the moment for active operations, if she was to 
engage in them, namely, the spring, was drawing gradually nearer; the attitude 
of Germany will be better defined, and the military power of France will be 
improved, Letit not be forgotten, says M. Drouyn de Lhuys, that a rupture 
with Austria may lead to her placing herself at the head of that armed German 
neutrality at which Prussia is supposed to be ating, and that the country 
which that armed neutrality will threaten will be France. 

This short explanation will, I trust, enable Her Majesty's Government: to 
comprehend the otherwise somewhat inexplicable position assumed ut this 
moment by the French Government. 

1 have, &c. 
(Signed) COW LEY.

Much speculation is afloat in regard to the rumoured desire of Prussia to

Austrian Treaty of the 2nd of December; and the missions of General de Wedel 
and of M. Niebuhr, the King’s Cabinct Secretary, to Paris, are believed to have 
had this end in view. The jealous rivalry with which Prussia watches every 
step of the Vienna Cabinet would, of course, make a Separate Treaty more 
palateable in Berlin than that Prussia should be dragged in the train of Austria 
into the Treaty of the 2nd of December. But the Liberal party here do not 
believe it possible that the Western Powers could gain anything by such a 
Separate Treaty, They remark that Prussia will naturally not concede more 
than Austria has done by the Treaty of the 2nd of December, and that if she 
concedes as much, she will be sure to evade her engagements by differences of 
interpretation, in the same way as she has evaded her obligations to Austria 
under the Treaty of the 20th of April. The common opinion seems to be, that 
the object of the Prussian Government is rather to delude the Western Powers 
with the name of an alliance, than to do anything to assist their cause in the 
contest with Russia. The bad faith of Prussia is, unfortunately, so notorious, 
that the greatest suspicion cannot but attach to any overtures of an alliance 
with England proceeding from her. By the state of isolation in which Prussia 
hus placed herself,she docs Russia all the good, and the allies all the harm that 
she can. She cannot ally herself with Russia, for she knows that such a course

use every means of pressing Prussia forward: and if she cannot do sa with 
effect, there is very little chance of England or France being able to accomplish 
the object by the contingent stipulations of a Separate Treaty.

On the other hand, Prossia feels keenly the insulated position in which she

withdrawn from the exclusive Protectorate of Russia, or that the mayigation at 
the Danube shall be set free from the obstructions which impede it, unless effec-

European system, and sufficient restraint be imposed upon the military and

the Porte, 

But, although much may be urged in favour of making the thied basis the

hasis. Nevertheless it will be for your Lordship to judve whether, before entering 
into negotiation with the Russian Plenipotentiary, or before the third basts 
eomes into discussion in the Conference, it would be expedient for the three 
Powers to come among themselves to some general understanding, subject, 
indeed, to be modified by future circumstances as to the form which that hasis 
should ultimately assume. ‘The end in view is the formal recognition of the 
‘Turkish Empire in its character as an independent and self-existent State, us a 
member of the great European family, and as an essential clement of the balance 
of power in Europe, One of the means by which that end is to he accom- 
plished is the abrogation of Russian supremacy in the Black Sea. How this is 
to be effected with the least inconvenience to the Powers of Europe, is: the 
problem to be solved, 

[t might be brought about, by a common agreement that the maritime 
Powers should maintain in the Black Sea a force adequate to counterbalance the 
naval forees which Russia has heretofore maintained, and, if uncontrolled, may 
again hereafter maintain, in that sea. But this would be nothing more than an 
armed truce, liable to be interrupted at every moment by chance collisions, and 
entailing on the maritime Powers a perpetual expenditure to keep up, at a 
distance from their ursennis, an eflicient foree in the Black Sea, while Mussia, 
having her arsenals at hand, and her harbours of refuge always open, would be 
relieved in a great measure from the costs to which the other Powers would be 
exposed. It may well be doubted whether, after a few years, Great Britain 
would continue such an expenditure, 

This object might be etlected by a twofold process; by reducing the mari- 
tiine force of Russia in the Black Sea within reasonable compass, and by opening 
that sen, with the consent of Turkey, to the maritime forces of other nations. 
Her Majesty’s Government would much regret that the Porte should he so 
impressed with a sense of its own comparative weakness as to be prepared to 
abdicate its power to defend the Turkish Mimpire against even a limited display 
of hostile force. It would be better for the nations of Europe that the Porte 
should be encouraged to rely on its own resources, though left at liberty to call 
in the aid of friendly Powers to counteract the menaces of its powerlul neigh- 
bour; but the reduction of the Russian naval force in the Black Sea within such 
hounds as might, in cooperation with an equal Turkish force, suffice to provide 
ndequate protection for peaceful conumerce, would have the further indirect 
advantage of preventing, at any future period, the march of Russian armies on 
Constantinople, or at all events of rendering any such operation one of extrenie 
hazard; for, as far as present experience extends, the support of w powerful 
flect, capable of cooperating with the advance of armies and affording the means 
of providing them with requisite supplies, is essential to the success of any 
movement on the Turkish capital. ; 

The imposition therefore, of adequate restrictions on the naval power of 
Russia in the Black Sea, would give to Turkey the material protection of which 
she stands in need, while her recognition as an essential clement in the balance 
of power in Europe, would afford her a moral guarantee under the safeguard of 
which she might fearlessly carry out those plans of internal reform and social 
reorganization which have been so carnestly pressed pon the Porte for many 
ears, But in proportion to the importance of the sacrifice to be required of 
Rissa, would in all probability be ‘is reluctance of the Russian Plenipotentiary 
to enter into discussion of this vital question, on the sutisfictory solution of 
which the continuance or premature interruption of the negotiations woul 
depend; and Austria and France might on their part urge, with no small appear 
ance of reason, that it would better to take up the points in the order in which 
they have hitherto stood, and tuke the chance of the events which might happen 
in the discussion of the previous points, or in the prosecution of the war, for 
detining the precise manner in which the prepomlerance of Russia in the Black 
Sea should be put an end to.

It may be proper to mention that he lately passed some days at Munich, 
though not for any evident political object. a 

Having met M. de Titoff last night at the Queen’s ball, he entered very 
freely into conversation with me regarding his mission to Vienna, saying, in 
substance, that he had but little hope of any useful issue to the Conterences, 
since the question appeared to him at present to be in military and not in 
diplomatic hands; that he did not consider the proposed hasis of peace caleulated 
to bring about a state of things materially different from the former arrangement, 
that perhaps a few decisive inquiries between the members of the Conference 
woul soon test the possibility of their coming to an understanding; and that 
he was glad of the appointment of Lord John Russell, who, he trusted, would 
do his lest to instil perceful sentiments mto Baron de Bourqueney, whom he 
had known at Constantinople. 

L observed to M. de ‘Titoif that it was useless to deny the existence of a 
erent obstacle to iminediate peace in the siege of Sebastopol, but that some 
simplifying event might possibly take place before long, and that, at all events, 
the Conferences would serve the purpose of throwing light on many points of 
importance ; in which last observation he concurred, | 

M, de Titoff subsequently touched upon the origin of the war; and he 
tried to prove that greater moral courage on the part of Lord Aberdeen mrvigelit 
have rendered triumphant his evident bias in favour of peace, 1 replied, that 
Lord Aberdeen had been the last to cleave to the hope of peace, but that his 
Lordship had never shown any symptom of beleving that war could be avoided 
were Russia not to recede. 

The general tone of M, de Titoff seemed to me that of a person mode- 
rately disposed, and anxiously desiring, though far from expecting, an early 
peuce.

The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Bloomfteld. 


(No. 61. 
My Lord, Foreign Office, February 24, 1855. 

HER Majesty's Government have learned with deep dissatisfaction from 
your Lordships despatch No, 50.of the 17th instant, the unjust and arbitrary 
course pursued by the Russian Government towards English missionaries, whose 
residence in Poland was specially sanctioned by the late and present Emperors of 
Russia, Some of those missionaries have rested there for upwards of thirty 
years in pursuit of their pious labours without accusation of any kind being 
brought against them, and all of them have now been treated os criminals antl 
with extreme cruelty. 

The dissatisfaction of Her Majesty’s Government is morcover increased by 
the fact that on the same day that your Lordship’s despatch arrived, a despatch, 
of which a copy is herewith inclosed, was received from Her Majesty's Minister 
at Copenhagen reporting, on the authority of Baron Plessen, the Danish 
Minister at St. Petersburgh, that “the Russian Government does not consider 
the situation of British subjects residing in Russia as being changed in con- 
sequence of the war, and that M. de Seniavine regards the regulation according 
to whieh British subjects leaving the country are not permitted to return during 
the war, as the only exceptional measure which has been adopted with respect 
to them.” The measure adopted towards the missionaries shows how little 
reliunce can be placed on the assurance of the Russian Minister; but the expul- 
sion of these worthy men has deprived the British residents in Warsaw of the 
celebration of divine service, and Her Majesty's Government being most anxious 
that they should still enjoy this all-important comfort, will be grateful to the 
King of Prussia for any measures which His Majesty may take to procure the 
restoration of the privilege. ae 

It is hardly necessary to add that Her Majesty's Government ask no more 
than they have granted. At the commencement of the war they engaged that 
the persons and properties of Russian subjects should be safe in this country, 
and accordingly no Russian has been sent out of the country, or has been im 
any way wolested, 

Her Majesty's Government readily assented to the request of the Russian 
Government that the Chaplain of the Russian Mission should continue to reside 
in London, and perform Divine service as usual at the chapel of the Mission, 
That reverend gentleman has continued freely to exercise his functions, and 
even when detected in a correspondence with some Russian prisoners he was 
merely warned that if he persisted in it he could not be allowed to communicate 
with them. Promises of a similar kind were made by the Russian Government, 
but the treatment of the missionaries in Poland shows how those promises have 
heen observed. 

Your Lordship will read this despatch to Baron Manteuffel, and express 
to his Excellency the thanks of Her Majesty's Government for the friendly 
intervention of the Prussian Consul-General at Warsaw in behalf of the unfortu- 
nate missionaries, 

Tam, &e. 


(Signed) CLARENDON,

My Lord, Bagdad, January 10, 1855, 

HIS Excellency Reshid Pasha has within these few days returned ta Bagdad, 
and is now actively Gmployed in preparing a respectable foree of Regular Infantry 
and Artillery for service to the northward, if the course of events should render 
its employment necessary, 

As dissensions, however, are said to have already broken out between the 
rival Koordish Chiefs, and Yezdasheer Bey is believed to have met with a reverse 
in Khirzan, his Excellency seems to anticipate that the insurrection in Dohtan 
will dic a natural death, without requiring any further interference on the part 
of the troops or officers of the Porte. 

In the meantime, although the Shanmar and Anczeh have retired to the 
Desert, the general state of the Bagdad Pushalic is not such as to admit, without 
risk, of the einployment at a distance of any considerable portion of the military 
force of the province. 

The navigation of the Lower Tigris is still at the merey of the Albee 
Mahomed Arabs, and the communication between Bagdad and Bassorah thos 
continues to be suspended, to the very serious injury of trade; while the Tat anid 
the Obeid having also resumed their depredations on the Upper Tigris, the 
Moossul merchants areafraid to permit their rafts to deseend the river to Bagdad 
That the commerce of the country, indeed, has not been entirely paralyzed by the 
stoppage of the communications both to the north and south, is merely owing to 
the cnormous influx of Persian pilgrims, and their consumption both of goods 
and of supplics. Tt 1s calculated that above 40,000. of these. stringers hive 
poured into Bagdad during the last three months, and the numbers, of lite, have 
been rather increasing than diminishing, notwithstanding that the country about 
Kerbeluh and Nejif is still infested with Arab marauders, who are continually 
attacking the caravans, and notwithstanding that the quarantine subjects all 
arrivals from Persian to a detention af five days upon ie froutier, where no 
accommodation is provided for them, and where, accordingly, at this inclement 
season they kre exposed to much suffering,

My Lord, Moossul, January 15, 1855, 

| HAVE the honour to inform your Excellency that since the date of my 
lust despatch, Naniet Agu, the chiel of Zibur, was summoned to Moossul by his 
Exeelleney Helmy Pasha, to consult with him upon the best mode of defending 
the mountain distriets from the invasion of the Koords under Miausoor Bey, who 
were preparing to make asudiden descent upon this Pashalic also, 

Nimet Aga arrived here on the Srd instant, and imuaediately handed over 
to the Pasha two letters which he had réeeived from Veulial ost Hey and 
Mausoor Bey, copies of which, with their translations, | have the honour to 
inclose, 

Helmy Pasha at first irged tpon Namet Aga to return and collect upon 
the mountains about 4,000 Koordish troops, and by the time he had done so, he, 
the Pusha, would have also raised a body af Irregulars, and carly in the spring 


rt) 


the whole troop would march upon Zakho, to wrest that town from the rebels. 
Namet Aga, however, considered it advisable to wait until they could have the

Dear Sir, Therapia, October 31, 1854, 

I SEND you herewith a work which has given me much trouble and taken 
up a large portion of time wanted for other affairs. It is a précis of Colonel 
Williams’ despatches from Kars, after inspecting the different military establish- 
ments and troops of various descriptions, and after communicating with Mustapha 
Zarit Pusha nad others incommand andemployment. ‘The correspondence may 
be considered a complement to what Colonel Williams’ reported from Erzeroom, 
and which | desired you to recommend to the Soraskier s attention, nit.as | have 
since learnt from you, without a eertam degree of beneficial result, 

[ have endeavoured to present the later reports in such manner as to make 
it easy for you to explain their substance to the Turkish Ministers, particularly 
to the Seraskier. : 

The various departments of inquiry are distributed over severl separate 
sheets, cach exhibiting marginal heads, and the names and quantities of the 
several articles of supply which are most needed for the maintenance and 
vflicieney of the troops. 

These are to be found in the left-hand columns. ‘The explanations—in 
summary—are consigned to the right-hand columns. 

‘There are, moreover, two lists of names, explained by the titles, ane relerred 
to in sheet No. 7, together with a medical report, worthy of serious and practical 
attention (rom Dr. Sancdwith, 

The object of the whole communication is threefold; Ist, to state the imme- 
diate wants of the army; 2nd, to give an idea of its true condition ; sre, to 
bring the shameful conduet of the principal officers, and the merits of a few, 
to the Knowledge of the Seraskior aud his colleagues. 

I venture to hope that the result will be a thorough amendment, both 
materially and personally. 

In bringing the whole ease before the Grind Vizier, Reshid Pasha, and the 
Seraskier, preparatory to a more farmal communication, if necessary, to the 
Council and Sultan, you will remind their [ighnesses and Exeellencies, that Mer 
Majesty the Queen has sent out an officer of weight and experience to the army 
of Kars, for the express purpose of inquiring into the causes of the late deplor- 
able disasters and pointing out the means of preventing thelr recurrence, 

That officer has now done his duty, and it is for them to do theirs. 

1 cannot conceal from them that Colonel Williams has little reason to be 
satisfied with the attention paid to his suggestions by the Mushit Zarit Mustapha 
Pasha. In one of his latest despatches he states that he had twice endeavoured 
with all seriousness and the necessary explanations, to persuade the Pusha te 
aiopt certain measures of the most abyiouws prudence; that he could at first 
mike 10 impression on his Exeelleney, who treated him with disrespect ; and 
that lic only succeeded later in obtaining some assurances of compliance, by

ALREADY, after our former conversation, you will not have doubted that 
the Deore of the Diet of the 8th instant, according to which the whole principal 
contingent of the Federal army is to be held ready for marching, and in fighting 
order, within a period of fourteen days alter the summons is given, has been 
received hy the Tenoeral Government with gratification. 

In fact, we perceive in this Deeree of the Diet an event of great importance, 
were it only for the reason that thereby the schism which the question of the 
military preparations af the Germanic Confederation threatened to produce has 
heen th reby happily avoided, But also viewed by itself the Decree which was 
passed appears to us to be the logical consequence of the considerations which 
the present state of things calls forth; and to satisly the necessary demand that 
the Federalarmy should be perfectly prepared to take up a stratesical position 
without lass of time: 

We have certainly not been able to appropriate to ourselves the motives on 
which the United Committees of the Diet founded their proposition which lias 
now beeome i Decree, 

ft will be understood that we, for our part, could not permit our adherence 
toappea te the Western Powers in the light of a demonstration directed against 
beth sides, but also the whole Confederation, which in this matter no longer rests 
solely on the basis of the Federal Act, but also on that of the Offensive and 
Defensive Allwnee of April 20th, and of the subsequent Decrees connected with 
it, has already, in our opinion, assumed far too decided an attitude to be able to 
derive the motive for the measure now resolved on solely in general from the 
menacing position of European affairs, 

Novertheless we believe we ean be assured that those considerations which 
are unsatistuctory in our eves, will find a corrective to the legal and matter-of 
fact state of the aflair, aud more especially in the nature of our relations with 
the Powers with wham we are allied by formal Treaty. . 

You will generally udapt your langudge respecting the present Decree of the 
Diet to these reniarks. 

The immediate und most energetic exeention of this Decree now certainly 
appears asa matter in whieh the honour of Germany is sl gai > and we do 
not entertain the slightest doubt that all the Governments af the Confederation wall 
strive with the same zeal to give foree on their part to the measure resalved on, 
and to contribute by their actions that the military constitution of Germany on 
this oceasion may prove itself as practicably commensurate with the duty of the 
Confederation usa great combined Power.

My Lari, Leipzig, Iebruary oe [854, 

I HAVE the honour to report that a considerable sensation appears to 
have been produced in Germany ly the news of the Caar’s ukase and manilesto 
of the 29th of January ithe 10th of this month’, which order the calling out and 
arming of all the men inthe Russian Empire capable of bearing arms. This 
proceeding, not atlopted since the memorable year 1S12, ts universally thought 
to be of serious importance to Austria and the Western Powers, and to denote 
that the Cvar has littl confidence in the Vienna Conferences leadine to a pacific 
result. The stvong professions of a desire for peace with whieh the i serial 
nunitvsto is necompanied, are considered as intended to fortity Prussia in her 
Hately ; whilst the levy en masse itself is to intimidate Austria, and to inspire 
Het ily he fear that Russia may decide upon taking the offensive against her 

The Prussian, liberal pesaba ners praise. the high state of equipment and 
preparation ot their army, which they declare to he tlie most effective in Europe 
and the best armed, since the Minié guns have long been in reneral use iy it. 
The German Federal army (according to the tables made up for 1853 and laid 
before the Dict) consists of 525,037 men, distributed into ten army corps and a 
reserve, of which the Austrian contingent amounts to 143,293, and the! Pragsial 
to 170,500 men, besides the forees of those States not comprised in their Federal 
contingents, ‘This lirge army is now so fur prepared as to be able to put itself 
into marching order upon fourteen days’ notice; and people ask with whit 
object? Against whom is the army to act? ‘The Confederation is up to this 
time pledged to nothing more than to defend Austria in case of kok bein 
attacked, and the Prussian Government seems determined to persist inh nak 
making common cause with the Western Powers; still a general impression 
sevens to prevail, that it is the destiny of Germany to Lecome involved in the 


307 


war, and that the course of events will accomplish that, eventually, which the 
egatism of the Governments is working so hard to prevent. 

The Saxon Cabinet, whose policy was openly avowed in its despatch of 
instruction to its Envoy at Vienna of the 19th of January last, has been publish- 
ing a series of articles in its organ, the “ Leipzig Gazette,” for the purpose of 
showing that neutrality is still the wisest course for Germany to pursue ; that 
Avstria, having got possession of the Danubian Principalities, has no further 
nterest in the wat ; that the designs attributed to Russia have never heen proved ; 
and that the best plan is to let the Western Powers and Russia exhaust their 
strength on both sides by the war, for, when they are exhausted, then will be the 
right time for Germany to appear with her million of fresh soldiers, and to 
mediate, or rather dictate the conditions of peace. Such are the sentiments of 
the Saxon Minister, M. de Beust, and they seem to agree essentially with those 
entertained in the Cabinets of Berlin and of Munich. ‘These arguments, however, 
have been so repeatedly and so well refuted by the liberal press (such as the 
‘« National Gazette,” “ Voss's Gazette,” the © Prussian Weekly Journal,” the 
‘German Universal Gazette of Leipzig,” the “ Cologne Gazette,” &c) that I 
cannot believe M. de Beust’s organ will produce much effect upon the public 
mind, or convert many to the opinion that Germany has no interest at stake in 
the war.

My Lord, Rustchuk, October 18, 1855. 


IN execution of the mission intrusted to me by your Lordship to proceed 
to Bulgaria, and there to observe the effects of the measures to be tuken by the 
Turkish Commissioner, Medhet Effendi, to put an end to the murders practised 
on the ‘Turkish Rayah subjects, and also to observe the general state of the 
country, | left Constantinople on the 30th ultimo, and arrived at Varna on the 
following day. 

Having fully explained to Mr, Consul Neale the object of my mission, he 
informed me that Medhet Elfendi had arrived sone days previously at Varna; 
that he had made a short excursion in the neighbourhood, and returned; that 
he had lett Varna the day before, for Buzarjik, and would retarn to Varna in 
five days. Colonel Neale therefore recommended that | should remain at 
Varna not only until Medhet Effendi returned, but further for several days atter 
Medhet Effendi had commenced his tour. Although I agreed with Colonel 
Neale aa to the propriety of allowing Medhet Eifendi to have a sufficient start 
of me, yet 1 preferred making some oxcursion in the neighbourhood, to remaining 
idle in Varna: f therefore lett Varna on the 4th instant, for shaman and 
Rustchuk. 

On leaving Varna 1 was not aware that the route | was about to take was 
infested with robbers, but such proved to be the case. ‘Two hours out of Varna, 
we met with two Armenians, who complained of having been robbed near

Devina. J passed the night at Devina, and was informed by the villagers that 
robberies were committed almest daily, at about an hour's distance between 
that place and Varna. I had a Turk with me, conducting the oraba with my 
luggage, and also a gabtiyie or guard; the arabygee declared he would not 
proceed with me unless 1 took two more guards at the village of Yasitepe, as 
between that villace and the next there was a regular band of robbers, aid that 
four days previously he himself had seen them attack a party of travellers and 
murder one of them, Wherefore, when we arrived at the village of Yasitepe, 
our zabtivie went to look for guards to accompany us, but he could not find 
any, and after considerable delay 1 prevailed on our arabagee to proceed, We 
passed the haunt of the robbers without any interruption, having found a convoy 
of buffalo carts resting at the place. In half-an- hour we arrived at the Turkish 
village of Uniseui, and passed the night at the khan. 

The Aga happened to come to the khan, and I asked him concerning the 
robberies, and why he tolerated them so near his residence. He did not deny 
that a band of robbers frequented the vicinity of the village, but he said the 
place was out of his district, and that he was about to leave his situation, and 
was expecting his successor to arrive in the course of four or five days. 

At the khan there was a party of ten or twelve Bulgarian travellers; on 
entering into conversation with them, they informed me that they came from 
the town of Kasan, and were going to Varna; that the roads were very unsafe, 
and that they did not venture to travel in smaller parties than twelve, and that 
consequently they were sometimes very much inconvenienced in their affairs,

Your Lordship will be able, from what 1 have stated, to form a pretty

robberies, abductions, and murders, Your Lordship will observe that nearly all

country is fearful—nnsupportable—tor Christians. 

The arrival of Medhet Effendi seems certainly to have put the suthorities 
on the alert, and they are pursuing rolibers and making prisoners; whether they 
are capturing the proper persons may be a matter of doubt. 1 much fear, 
however, that they are seizing insignificant persons, and leaving the great and 
formidable robbers at liberty; at least, no robber of note is yet reported to bave 
been taken.

My Lord, Shumla, November 18, 1855. 

HAVING arrived here on the 14th instant, | inquired after Medhet 
Effendi, and was sorry to learn that he had left this place sone days previously 
for Varna, He is to return here, and has left a portion of his luggage ; and on 
leaving, he-said he expected to be buck in ten or twelve days; but 1 now learn 
that he goes round by Carnabat on his return, and that the time of his arrival 
here is quite uncertain, so thitt L must leave this place without seeing him, 


1 was not anxious to sce Medhet Etfendi before | was well informed of the 


etate of the country; but, as [consider Lam now sufficiently informed as regards 
robberies to have been able to judge of the efficiency of any measures he was 
taking to render the roads safe, | would have been well pleased to have met 
him here. 


ali 


I have taken information of what Medhet Effendi had done since his arrival 
here to put down the robberies now so prevalent in this provinee, and the result 
is that thirty or forty persons, said to be robbers, have been broucht here from 
different parts of the country, and put into prison; he has caused fifteen or 
twenty of these robbers to be sent to Varna, to be from thence sent to Constan- 
tinople, and he has caused a gipsy to be hanged. | 

Those who had expectations that the mission of Medhet Effendi would 
have tended to put down the robbers and murderers, have been disappointed 
anid dispirited ; they say that, when so many murders have been committed here 
lately, the authorities must have more than one murderer in prison whose 
execution, by way of example, is urgent. Then they interpretate the fact of the 
authorities having chosen a gipsy for eapital punishment as a manifesto that 
they will on no account put a ‘Turk to death for the murder of a Christian ; and 
they fear that the visit of Medhet Etfendi, far from preventing or causing a dimi- 
nution in the number of murders, will, on the contrary, cause an increase, as 
the 'Turks will now consider themselves exempt from capital punishment for the 
murder of a Christian, as they lave been heretofore. As to sending guilty 
persons to Constantinople, that can have little or no effect on the robbers, as 
every one, robbers and others, expect to see them back here shortly ; and, even if 
some of those sent to Constantinople be capitally punished, that could not serve 
as a warning to robbers here. 

The gipsies no doubt profess the Mahometan religion, but they are a 
degraded race in Turkey, as they are in other countries. 
‘The ¢rime for which this gipsy suffered was, that he, another gipsy and a 
lurk, seized a hoy of twelve years of age, near a village called Smedova, and 
carried him to the mountains. They then sent to the father of the boy to sily

aman of that great age would be respected, but the robbers took the ransom 
and murdered both the old man and the boy. 1am told that both the Turk and 
the gipsy remain here in prison, the gipsy ready to be hanged should another 
execution he necessary, and the Turk to be hanged also in an extreme case. 

Your Lordship, having taken a first step to put a stop to these murders, will

its officer; therefore [ doubt not that your Lordship will insist that the mission
