Inclosure 15 in No. 313, 
Vice-Consul Cunningham to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Giurgevo, December 11, 1854. 


I TAKE the earliest opportunity of making a report on the causes of the 
frequency of robberies and murders of Christians int Bulgaria, and the WHS of 
putting an end to them. j 

The causes of these robberies and murders, and of their frequency, 
are : 


1. The desire of plunder. 

| ‘The small esteem in which the lives and property of Christians are held 
by the Turks, and that no infamy attaches to a Turk for the murder of a 
Christian. 

3. The very great chance of not being arrested, through a defective 
police and good protection, and, when arrested, of not being punished, through 
the same protection. 


As the first cause requires no remark, I may at once proceed to the 
second. 

My belief, founded on a long residence in Turkey, is that a Turk does not 
value the life of a Christian at all, not so much as he values the life of a dog; 
nav, I believe, that by many ‘Turks it is considered meritorious, not infamous, to 
take the life of a Christian, Persons who have resided in Turkey may sy that 
the foregoing is too severe; that they are acquainted with many Turks who, far 
from killing a Christian, would not intentionally do him harm. This 1 freely 
adinit: still that same Turk looks on the taking of the lite of a Christian as a 
very different niatter from taking the lite of a Mussulman. It is only justice to 
the Turks to add, that the Christians of Turkey, generally, do not consider it a 
very heinuus erime to take the lite of a Turk. Christians seldom take the lives 
of Turks, because punishment is almost certain; Turks. often take the lives of 
Christians, because impunity is almost certain. 

When public opinion among Turks does not place the murder of a Christian 
in the rank of crime, and the law seldom punishes the offence, it is evident that 
no infamy can, in the opinion of the Turks, can attach to the murderer of a 
Christian. . 

‘The Turks have somehow or other got a great name for honesty, and so far 
they deserve it, thut they seldom or never steal clandestinely ,; but they will take 
anything openly from a Christian : without foree, if yielded freely, and by force, 
if opposition 18 offered ; and sometimes they murder the person on taking his 
property. ‘The Turks will also deprive a Christian of his: property by false 
witriesses, or through any other injustice or chieane of the law. ‘Therefore 
the ‘Turks are honest in a very limited sense of the word, 

On the third point, with regard to a defective police, I will state some of 
those defects in the words of a person in authority in this neighbourhood : 

« All the Zabtivies belong to the district in whieh they act, and, consequently, 
have friends and relations all around, and are frequently connected in friendship 
or interest with the robbers, and therefore will not seize them, When it 1s 
attvmpled to appoint strangers as Zabtiyies, the members of the Medjlis are 
opposed, saying, that natives of the district should be provided for, 

“The Zabtivies have no uniform, and, therefore, on the road cannot be known 
for good or for evil, The Zabtiyie not unfrequently acts the part of the robber, 
stopping passengers, and robbing and murdering them; while the robber agin 
often assumes the part of the Zabtiyie, stopping passengers on the road under 
pretext of examining their tescarets, and then falling on them unawares, The 
robbers also enter the villages under the assumed character of Zabtiyies, and 
obtain lodgings and food for themselves and horses without payment ; and happy 
for the villugers if the robbers content themselves with this. . 

« Jusufficient Pay—The pay of a mounted Zabtivie is one hundred and forty 
viastres per month (or twenty-two shillings), for which he must provide his 
eee and arms, and feed himself and horse,” 


On this present journey | have paid as much as 8 piastres per month for 


324 


barley for the feed of one horse, morning and evening, and no where have I pa il 
less than 34 piastres. ‘Dherelore, supposing the Zabtiyie only to pay the lowest 


rate, 84, plastres, 105 pinstres is required monthly for his horse's barley, leaving 
35 piastres on which to support himself and family fora month. Now this low 
pay does not permit a Zabtiyic to perform his duty faithfully; he cannot live on 
his pay, and must seek illegitimate means of supporting himself, among which 
tribute from robbers, and robbery itself, may be reckoned. It 1s true that in 
Christian villages, the Zabtiyie never pays for his own or his horse's food; the 
law says he should pay for both, but le has not the means were he willing. 

But besides these defects pointed out of the Zabtiyies, it is generally 
believed that higher officers, even to the chiefs of districts, prevent robbers from 
heing arrested, either direetly by not taking the needful measures, or indivectly 
by them known indifference, 

Another great obstacle to the apprehension of robbers is the number of 
districts into which the country is divided; each with its separate police and 
authorities, and the officers of one district not being allowed to act in another 
district. ‘The Zabtivies of a Pasha ean no doubt act all over the Pashalic, but 
the Zabtiyie of a sub-Governor can only act in a sub-district. A robber there- 
fora hus only to retire into another district, after having committed a erime, and 
he js secure from immediate arrest. ‘The Governor of the district wherein the 
crime was committed, must write ta the Governor of the district into which the 
cviminal has retived, to have him arrested. ‘The Governor written to seldom 
takes any trouble in the matter, because the crime not having been committed 
in his district his reputation dees not suffer. And perhaps he is pleased that an 
offence has been committed in the district of a neighbour, 


Good protection from arrest dnd punishment—All persons with whom I have 
had an opportunity of conversing, Christians and ‘Turks, agree that everywhere 
hereabouts the robbers have protectors in powerful Turks, both in and out of 
office, and down to the common people. The motives for giving protection 
differ in degrees; from a partnership with the robbers and sharing the plunder, 
to a mere desire of protecting the Turk from beg punished foran offence iguinst 
a Christian, and to hinder the late reforms, which give protection to Chiistians 
from being carried into effect. 

In every Medjlis (Municipal Councils), and in every district, the person is 
openly named who is the chiet protector of the robbers. But even when the 
protectors of robbers are known, it must still be difheult to ascertain the motives 
of cach person, and in what degree he is induenced by interest, relationship, and 
friendship, or the hutred of Christians and opposition to reforms for their pro- 
iwetion, TL eonsider, however, that ull Turks of the old school, that is, those 
opposed to refornis for the benefit of the Christians, see these robberies and 
muriers of Christians with no unfavourable eye; and if they do not instigate to 
the committal of these crimes, they at least do all in their power to sereen the 
criniinals (rom arrest and punishment, This I believe to be the great difficulty 
uf putting down these robberies and murders now so frequent. But besides the 
mere hatred of Christians there isa powerlul class of Turks in’ Bulgaria (and 
probably all over Turkey), who have interested motives for preventing the 
reforms for the protection of Christians coming into force, These are the great 
landed proprictors, who even now in some instances oblige the Christians to cul- 
tivate their land, secure their erops, &e.. without payment. Then there are all the 
Turks, and some Christians also, who are in the habit of taking the “ietishims ” 
or tithes; who wt present profit hy the unprotected state of the Christians to 
take more from thei thin they are entitled ta take, and which they will not be 
able to do ence the reforms are real, 

How it comes about it is diffigult to explain, but certain it is that the 
Christians have got the idea that the ‘Tansimat is the cause of the great increase 
of murders and robberies: whenever | have asked the Christians to whut they 
attribute the great increase of robbery of late, they have always answered, “to the 
Tanzimat.” ‘They say that since it was put in force the Paushas and Turks in 
office have no longer the power to punish robbers and inurderers, and thence 
the greit inertane, | 

With regard to the means of putting an end to the robberies, I will 
commence by the most inportant point, although the last in order; that 
is, the punishment of the criminals. In order that there may be a chance af 


a25 


justice being done, the trial must be taken entirely out of the hands of the local 
tribunals or Medjlis: on the members of which local influence, old prejudices 
and interest are so strong, and a Commission or Commissioners should be sent 
from Constantinople to judge the criminals. ‘The sentence of death should be 
passed in every case of murder where clearly proved, and in some cases of abduc- 
tion, and inexorably carried into execution. The manner of execution should 
be by hanging; and, if possible, in. some cases the body should be ordered to be 
hung in chains, to render the crime infamous, and to be a memorial to the living. 
As to leaving the body of the criminal exposed, this would not be a novelty but 
a revival: twenty years ago, on the borders of Servia, [ saw exposed on wazgon 
wheels on the point of stakes, three several skeletons. No person should be 
condemned to death who had not committed murder or been guilty of cruelty, 
however large the ammount he might have robbed. 

But besides the actual robbers it would be neeessary to inquire for and 
bring to punishment all their aiders, abettors, and protectors, Turks and Chris- 
tians, and the Commission sent should have special instructions to attend to this, 
All such as eame within the scope of the criminal law should be proceeded 
against criminully ; and some who liad not brought themselves within the scope 
of the criminal law, should still be removed from the district (for a time at least) 
as perturbators of the peace. 

As to the means of taking the robbers, | consider that it would be necessary 
to send a person of standing, with authority both in Balvaria and Roumelia, and 
that he should have a special corps of Zabtiyies with him; the authorities of 
the different districts to have to assist him in every way,and with the Aubtiyies 
of the district, But as it is important that the chief robbers should be taken, 
their names shonld be obtained and a liberal reward should be offered for their 
apprehension, and be paid to Zabtiyies or others who took them dead or alive. 
As an encouragement to the Zabtiyies, a certain reward should be given for any 
robber they seized, payable on conviction of the robber. 

No doubt it would be well to reform the local Zabtivies by giving them an 
adequate pay, a uniform, and by employing persons who have no local ties, 

The Pashas and other local Governors should have more security of office, 
and be more protected than they seein to be against the Medjlis or local Councils, 
in order to be able to do their duty faithfully, "There is always some person in 
the Medjlis of greater influence than the others, he therefore generally commands 
a majority in the Medjlis; the Pasha or Governor must then either put himself 
under the protection of this person, and do his bidding, or the Medjlis opposes 
the Governor in everything he wishes to do. The consequence then is that 
the atairs of the sistrict are badly managed and get into confusion ; and on this, 
although caused by itself, the Medjlis sends complaints againsts the Governor 
to Constantinople. At Constantinople there are always many waiting for a 
vacancy, who eagerly support the complaint, and the Goyernor fills a victim to 
the influential man of the Medjlis, ‘The succeeding Governor enters on office, 
and holds it on condition of conforming to the will of the great man of the 
Medjlis, who thus governs the district to his own profit, and without responsibility, 

In order to put down the robberies in these parts, the persons having the 
charze must have no expectation or desire of making friends in the locality ; 
they must not be afratd of the enemies they may make; they must be firmly 
supported at Constantinople ; they must have the will und the nerve to do 
their duty. On these terms robberies will soon be put down; otherwise, little 
or nothing can he done, 

But in order to insure that the persons charged do their duty, they must 
know that full and correct accounts of their proceedings will reach Constan- 
tinople. ‘This can ouly be insured ly your Lordship keeping agents where 
necessary, tO give information. . 

There can be litthe doubt that Christians are sometimes concerned in 
committing robberies ind murders on trivellers. but they never do so clone; 
they only assist the Turks, aud then they also disguise themselves as Turks: 
they iso shelter and feed the Turkish robbers, but thisthey no doubt do more 
offen from fear than from love, or even interest. 

] have, &e. 
(Signed) CHARLES CUNNINGHAM,

THE following instance of the Guards or Aabtiyies commntine: Eases ae 
and robbery was related to me in Turnova. tis true that, in this tance, t

About two months ago a merchant, the nephew of the Archbishop of 
Turnova, was travelling between Plevna and Rahova; he had four persons with 
him as euards. When about the hours distant from Rahova, the partly met 
seven Turks en horseback, who first allowed them to pass, and then turned 
round on them and ordered them to show their “tescarets,”” dechiing they, the 
Turks, were a Balouk-bashi, and his party. To this the party of the merchant 
replied, that there on the road they would not show their “ tescarets;” that they 
did not know that the other party were really of the police; thatif they were 
a0 they had only to follow them to a villaze which was near, anid there they 
hight examine their papers. 

The party of the Balouk-bashi, however, mesisted on sceing their ‘ tescarets” 
at once, and was about to attack the other party, when one of the guards 
of the merchant, an Albanian, dismounted from his horse, and placing himself 
behind it, threatened to shoot any of the other party who advanced. ‘This kept 
in check the party of the Balouk-bashi for some time, by which the merchant 
and his three remaining guards profiting, they set spurs to their horses and fled, 
abandoning the Albanian to his fate. “hey were soon pursued, however, by a 
vortion of the party of the Balouk-basii, wha got so near to the fugitives as to 

e able to shoot one of them dead; he was a Mussulman gipsy. The other three 
made good their escape, The Albanian after a time yielded himself prisoner. 

The Turkish party was really a Balouk-bashi, with six Zabtivies. My 
informant told me that some of them had the indiserction to avow that they 
intended to have murdered the whole of the merchant's party, for the sake of 
robbing them ; had they succeeded, the crime would no doubt have been laid to 
the charge of robbers unknown.

Inclosure 19 in No. 314. 
Fice-Consul Cunningham to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Giurgero, December 12, 1854. 

IN Bulgaria there is no relaxation of the old restraints to the celebration of 
the rites of the Christian religion. 

In a large village in the district of Turnova, composed partly of Christians 
and partly of Turks, there is no church. ‘The Christians of the village applied 
to the Pasha for permission to build a church, which the Pasha granted, The 
Turks of the village, however, prevent the ehureh from being commenced, and 
remonstrated with the Pasha for having granted the permis-ion, As the Pasha 
would not recall the permission, the Turks hive sent a complaint against him to 
Constantinople, and in this state the affair is al present, 

I was well aware that the use of bells was prohibited, but | thought that 
the use of the sounding-hoard was permitted to Christian churches all over 
Turkey, the same as in Constantinople; such is not the case, however, and the 
use of the board is not permitted in Bulgaria. 

Some time back the Archbishop of Turnova obtained a firman permitting 


the use of the board in the Greek churches of that town: but when the Turks 


learnt this, they signified to the Archbishop that they would oppose the execution 
of the tirman; therefore the Christians did not attempt to intreduee the use of 
the board. The Pasha encouraged the Archbishop to carry out the firman, but 
the Archbishop refused to dose at tle risk of causing a demonstration of the 
Turks against the churehes and Christians. 

[was informed that the Greeks of a neighbouring town (Plevna, T believe) 
had got a similar firman some time back, and were determined to vive force to 
it notwithstanding the menaces of the Turks; the board was accordingly fixed 
ina sinall wooden tower. When, however, the person commenced to sound the 
board at the dawn of day, he was fired on by several Turks lying in wait for 
him, ind shot; since then, the attempt to sound the board has not been renewed. 

I have, Ac. fi 
(Signed) CHARLES CUNNINGHAM.

My Lord, Paris, February 27, 1855. 

COUNT HATZFELDT called yesterday morning upon M. Drouyn de 
Lhuys, and informed him that he was commissioned, in conjunction with General 
Wedel, to enter into communication with the French Government respecting 
the project of ‘Treaty which had been placed in the latter's hands by the 
Smperor, as [ had the honour to state to your Lordship in. my despatch

by the extraordinary addition, that the King of Prussia had been much gratified 
by the invitation of the Emperor, conveyed through General Wedel, to resume 
his place in the Conferences at Vienna; an invitation which the Prussian 
Government hoped that M. Drouyn de Lhuys would have no objection to 
repeat in writing to Count Hatafeldt, 

It is almost needless, alter the communications which have passed between 
Her Majesty's and the French Governments, that I should state to your Lordship 
how greatly General Wedel, probably from being an imperfect French scholar, 
has exaggerated what passed between the Emperor and himself. 1 believe the 
facts to be, that General Wedel, on rceeiving the draft of “Treaty from the

bility. about the Vienna Conferences, of His Majesty’s entering into further 
engagements before receiving an invitation to take part in those Conlerences, 
from which His Majesty considered himself to have been excluded, and that 
the Emperor, pointing to the draft which he had given the General, rejoined, 
“There is my invitation,” or words to that effeet. 

However this may be, M. Drouyn de Lhuys stated to Count Hatafaldt 
that the Emperor's words had been misinterpreted, and that His Majesty 
intended to say no more than that, if the Treaty was accepted by Prussia, u

Inclosure 1 in No, 317. 


Lord Stratford de Redeliffe io M. E. Pisani; 
Sir, Eritish Embassy. February 17, 1855. 
YOU informed me some little time ago, that the Grand Vizier had expressed 
his intention to send a detachment from the army at Kars against the Koordish 
rebel chief, Yeazdashver Bey, I desired you to request that his Highness would 
give up that intention, which could not be carried into effect without weakening 
the frontier army, and exposing it hereafter to an attack from the enemy, Tf 
ailvised, ut the same time, that troops should be sent with all practicable dispatch 
from Constantinople, and that joined by others from Syria, they should march 
by way of Aleppo against the Koords, You assured me afterwards that my 
proposal had been accepted, and that.a detachment from the Sultan’s forces. in 
the province of Bagdad would also be sent to the same destination. 

Notwithstanding these communications and assuranees, 1 learn from 
Brigadier-General Williams that a regiment of Infantry, a regiment of Cavalry, 
and i battery of six guns, had been ordercd to leave Toprak-Kalé, and to 
advance upon Sert and Jexirah, 

Besides the contradiction which is thus shown to exist between fact and 
assurance, it appears that Toprak-Kalé is the most important outpost of the 
Kars army; that the detachment could never reach its destination, owing to the 
deep snow and intense cold; and finally, that so hazardous a measure as the 
one in question was adopted without reference to the opinion of the British 
Commissioner, and by orders transmitted from Constantinople, 

You will read what precedes to Reshid Pasha, and you will express the 
deep concern with which | contemplate this inconsistency of conduct on the part 
of Government over which he presides. You will prepare him for the impres- 
sion Which will be made in England by a knowledge of the circumstances, and 
you will observe how impossible it is for the allies to act with any confidence of 
success, or to pronide for their own responsibility, if the principal functionaries of 
the Porte exhibit so lamentable a want of fair dealing and common prudence, 

You will draw up an official report of his Highness’ reply, and you will 
ascertain its correctness, by reading it over to him before you send it to me for 
transmission to the Earl of Clarendon. 2 

Your, &c. 
(Signed) SERATFORD DE REDCLIIFE,

Inclosure 2 in No. 317. 
M. E. Pisani to Lovd Stratford de Redeliffe, 


My Lord, Pera, February 28, 1855. 
HAVE the honour to report that I have, in pursuance of your Excel- 

lency's directions, read and explained, word for word, to Reshid Pasha, your 

Instructions to me of yesterday's date. 


4Q 


doe 


His Highness, far from denying your Excellency’s statement, has fully 
confirmed it; but he does not accept the charge of having dealt inconsistently 
and unfairly with Her Majesty's Embassy. He said, that the order to Shukri 
Pasha to detach a brigade from the frontier, and send it against the Koordish 
rebel chief, was forwarded long betore your Excellency had made any represen- 
tation to the Porte on the subject ; that subsequently, on your sugeestions, the 
Council having decided upon adopting them, the Scraskier sent a counter-order 
to Shukri Pasha, to abstain from disposing of any of the troops under his 
command, and informing him that the Porte had adopted other measures to 
quell the disturbances i question. Resides, the Grand Vizier himself gave 
verbal instructions to the new Commander-in-chief, two days previous to his 
departure, to prevent any ofthe troaps of the army at Kars or Erzeroom leaving 
their posts. 

As to the non-reference to the opinion of the British Commissioner, his 
Highness observed that Shukri Pasha was not bound to do so, because the orders 
he received from his superiors were peremptory, and consequently could on no 
account disregard them without swerving from his duty. The British Com- 
missioner, added he, his a right to be consulted on matters immediately 
connected with the army in general, but not to interfere with orders issued direct 
from the Porte to its own officers on internal questions. 

I have, &c. 
(Sicned) ET, PISANI. 


P.S.—Having read the whole of this report to Reshid Pasha, he found it 
to be in perfect accordance with what he sail ta me.

No. 318. 
Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Receited March 1.) 


(No. £34. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, February 28, 1859. 

THE meeting of which 1 had the honour to speak to your Lordship in my 
despatch No. 229 of the 27th instant, took pluce yesterday between M. Drouyn 
de Lhuys, Count Haltafeldt, and, General Wedel. 

Before entering on the general discussion of the Treaty propbsed by France 
for the acceptance of the Prussian Government, Count Hataleldt asked whether 
M, Drouvu de Lhuys would object to an alteration of the terms of the Protocol 
af the 28th December, to which reference is made in the [st Article. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys replied at once that he could not consent to any pro- 
weition of the kind. Tt contained an interpretation of the four Articles, which 
mid since been accented by Russia, and any alteration proposed by Prussia must 
have the effect of strengthening or of weakening that interpretation, But the 
allies could not, with loyalty, add to the stringency of an interpretation on which 
they had consented 16 treat with Russia, and if, as was more probable, the 
Prussian Government were desirous of weakening iis sense, they were, in fact, 
showing themselves to be more Russian than the Russians themselves. His 

‘cellency considered this objection alone to be fatal to the proposal ; but if that 

waa not sufficient, what chance, he asked, could there be of any successful issuc 
to negotiations, the bases of which were comprehended by five out of the Bix 
parties concerned, in one sense, and by the sixth inanother, 

Count Hatzteldt replied that it would be useless to open any diseussion on 
the Treaty, if this was the decision of the Freneh Government, as his instructions 
obliged him to insist on & modification of the Protocol in question. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys rejoined that he considered his reasoning to be so 
conelusive that it could not fail of obtaining the concurrence of the King of 
Prussia when laid before His Majesty. He, therefore, engaged M. de Hutateldt 
to refer to Berlin, and in the meantinie to begin contidential discussion of the 
terms of the Treaty itself, 

Count Haltzteldt having agreed to this course asked for. an alteration in the 
wording of the preamble. On referring to it your Lordship will find that it is 


ohh 


proposed to conclude “un Traité d’Alliance.” The Prussian Government 
objects to the word “alliance,” and demands its omission, and suggests other 
changes in the wording which weaken essentially the object for which the Treaty 
is to be concluded. 

In the Ist Article the Prussian Government requires that all reference to 
the right which the allies have reserved to themselves of p.tting forward in the 
interests of Europe other conditions than those contained in the four Articles 
should be omitted, and they propose such an alteration in the wording of the 
second ag would render it impossible to ask for the active military cooperation of 
Prussia, unless she consented to breaking off negotiations. 

M, Drouyn de Lhuys of course combatted the whole of these pretensions, 
and here the conversation (for it was not to be considered in any other light) 
terminated, the Prussian Representatives saying that they would renew it on 
the remaining Articles another day. The impression left upon M, Drouyn de 
Lhuys’ mind is, that these discussions will lead to no result, because he has 
reason to believe that even if these points, and others which will probably be 
raised in the remaining Articles, should be settled, the King of Prussia 1s ‘still 
determined to insist on some engagements being taken with respect to Poland, 
and to the passage of French troops through Germany, as a sine qud non to the 
signature of any ‘Treaty. ; 

I asked M. Drouyn de Lhuys whether M. de Hatafeldt had informed him 
more particularly of the modifications which the Prussian Government desired to 
introduce into the Protocol of the 28th of December. He replied that the Count 
did not offer to read them to him, until after he (M. Drouyn de Lhuys) had 
refused to admit of any, and that he had thought it would weaken his position if 
he had then consented to listen ta them.

for communication to your Lordship.

(Secret and Confidential.) = 
My Lord, The Haque, February 26, 1855. 

MY despatch marked Sceret and Confidential, dated yesterday, will have 
yut your Lordship in possession of the details connected with the incident that 
has recently occurred here, with peterence to the eonduct pursued by Count 
Kénigsmark relative to the alfuirs aud position of the Grand Duchy of Luxem- 
burg. 

I therein stated to your Lordship that a conference had been held upon 
this subject between His Netherlands Majesty, his Excellency M. Van Hall, and 
M. Simons, and that I hoped to be able to inform you inn subsequent despatch 
of the determination come to in that conference. . 

T am now happy to be able to report to your Lordship that T have learnt, 
on confidential authority, on which T can rely, that this affair has followed 
exactly the course which T had previously indicated it would take, with reference 
to the preliminary steps required to bring it officially before His Netherlands 
Majesty’s Government at the Hague. 

The King’s Government have not filed to appreciate the gravity of this 
affair,—to perceive the importance of the language employed by Count Konigs- 
mark on this occasion, if authorized by his Government, and: the character of 
menace which under such circumstances it would yinqnestionably bear, 

His Netherlands Majesty and his Government determined in the conference 
above alluded to, that an official eommunication upon this subject shall be 
addressed by the Cabinet of the Hague ta that of Berlio, detailing all the 
circumstances of this case, and communicating the language employed by Count 
Konigsmark in his letter to M. Simons, 

The Government of His Netherlands Majesty will state, while they make 
their communication and seek for satisfiictory explanations with regard to it at 
the hands of the Prussian Cabinet, their readiness to believe that in the affair 
in question Count Kénigsmark has been led to give utterance to his own personal 
and private opinions, not to the avowed and official instructions of his Govern- 
ment. 

Your Lordship will, TP think, approve of this course, which I have reason 
to believe it is the intention of the Netherlands Government to pursuc in the 
management of this affair: it is calm and firm, and leaves the King’s Govern- 
ment at liberty to adopt such further mensures in vindication of the dignity and 
independence of the Netherlands as may be considered nceessary utter the reply 
of the Prussian Government to the representations of the Cabinet of the Hague 
ahall have been received, shoul! such a course be deemed expedient, ‘This 
matter, therefore, remains for the moment on the above footing, 

Before closing however my present despatch, your Lordship will perhaps 
allow me to adda few observations with resurd to the particular position of this 
Government in this business, and to state what, from my own knowledge of 
their feelings with regard to it, would, Lam contident, be agreeable to them as 
regards any immediate support which friendly Governments might be disposed 
to afford them at Berlin, 

As 1 have already reported to your Lordship, Dam satisfied that both on 
the part of His Netherlands Majesty himsel!, and on that of his Government, 


359 


every disposition exists to do all that is necessary to uphold alike the dignity 
and the independence of this country in its relations with neighbouring States. 
and particularly with Prussia, whose long: practised system of attempts to exercise 
a aa oe influence here, is keenly felt and openly uvowed. 

| cannot, therefore, doubt that under the able management of M. Van Fall, 
whose personal position is also somewhat attacked by the recent proceedings 
of Count Kinigsmark, this affair will receive all the attention, and be met with 
all the firmness, which it so clearly deserves. 

Such being the case, it would be for the honour and for the proper respect 
due to an independent Government, that their representations af Berlin should, 
for the present at all events, bear all the character of being uninfluenced by the 
advice or assistance of other Governments, and the Netherlands Government 
are, | am confident, extremely anxious to avoid all appearance of allowing 
whatever causes of complaint may exist between them and the Government of 
Prussia to become, in the present state of Eurapean politics, a souree of 
increased difficulty or discussion between the Cabinet of Berlin and those of 
other States, 

Such feeling, on the part of the Netherlands Government, Lam certain your 
Lordship will not only approve of, but respect ; and in expressing them, | have 
only to add that which 1 am satistied would also be the wish af the Netherlands 
Government, though they are at the same time fully sensible of the uctive 
interest which Her Majesty’s Government would be disposed to exert for the 
peebely and independence of this country, if thought advisuble, namely, that 
for the moment at least, Her Majesty's Government should, out of consideration 
for this Government, abstain from adding at Berlin any representations of their 
own upon this subject, to those which the Government of His Netherlands 
M..esty have deemed it to be their duty to make on their own behalf,

My Lord, The Hague, Mareh 1, 1859, 


M. ELOUT, a member of the Second Chamber of the States General of 
the Netherlands, belonging to the Grén von Prinsterer or ultra-Protestant party, 
which holds, with regard to palitics, much the same opinions as those which are 
advocated by the Kreuz party in Prussia, addressed, in yesterday s sitting of the 
Chamber, some questions to the Government with respect to their intention of 
maintaining their policy of neutrality for this country in the contest now 
carrying on by the Western Powers of Burope and their-allies against Russia, 

M. Elout founded the expediency of addressing his questions to the Govern- 
ment on the repeated assertions contained in various public journals, that the 
Netherlands were about to enter into an alliance with the Western Powers, arid 
thus abundon the neutral position which they had hitherto held; and that, in 
order that the public mind wight be set at rest with respect to a subject so mate- 
rially aflecting the interests of this country, it was highly desirable that the 
Government of His Netherlands Majesty should have an opportunity afforded to 
them of explaining their views and intentions. 

The Chamber having consented to allow these questions to he put, and 
having decided that the Government should be permitted to accomplish their 
wish of replying to them immediately, his Excellency M. Van Hall rose, and 
in distinet terms declared that the Government of His Netherlands Majesty had 
no intention whatever of altering the course of poliey they had hitherto pursued 
with regard to the war now in course of progress hetween certain European 
States ; that there was no truth in the various reports which had been cireulated 
by the public press, of the intention of the Netherlands Government to relinquish 
the system of neutrality which they hud hitherto adopted, and which would be 
persevered in; and his Excellency concluded lis reply by oliserving that he could 
give the Chamber the most positive assurances that no influence (‘ pression ”)

(No. 4. Confidential) 
My Lord, Bertin, March 1, L855. 
ALTHOUGH. your Lordship is fully aware of the present position of 
Prussia, | cannot forbear making some remarks on the anxious aspects which 
that position has assumed during the last few weeks. 
fhe King holds in his hands the direction of the whole of the foreign policy 
of his kingdow. Baron Manteuffel, and various other instruments, otticial and 
non-oflicial, are taken up and laid aside, supported or disavowed, exactly us the 
King pleases. Nor is there any man in Prussia who seems to have sutherent 
independence of mind ty resent the manner in which he ts Hatly contradicted or 
quictly dismissed, . 
It seems to be the King’s settled object to refrain from tuking any part in 
the present war, He has no partiality for Russia as a Power: he has no 
sympathy with the cause which the allies have undertaken to uphold. The 
decision perhaps is not surprising, but the mode af adhering to it is singular, 
Instead of standing still and refusing to move, the King agitates and bustes 


himself in every direction: an agent is sent to London, whose liberal views 
might induce Hor Majesty's Government to suppose the King was about to 
chunge his Ministers and his policy; another special agent in Paris i8 80 ignorant 
of diplomacy that his negotiations are sure to produce misunderstandings and 
delay: a third ugent, with no ostensible mission, is sent to Holland to create a 
Prussian interest, and disturb, if not insult, the Ministers of the Crown. All 
these special Envoys are employed in erossing and in thwarting the ostensible 
fureign missions of the Court ‘The object seems to be to five mse Lo hopes; 


345 


afterwards to be dashed to the ground, and to gain time till fresh pretexts for 
delay can be invented. | 

The period is come, however, when the Conferences at Vienna will be 
opened. ‘The position of Prussia, it must be confessed, may seriously affect the 
conduct and materially disturb the action of Austria. But it appears to me to 
be better to accept and count upon these consequences, than to give a feather’s 
weight to the consideration that by further delay, by protracted efforts or fresh 
compliances, we shall obtain the cooperation of Prussia. 

A very grave question remains for the decision of Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment. 

Supposing Prussia to refuse all uid to Austria, and Austria on that account 
to hesitate committing herself against Russia, what are the terms of peace, 
within the meaning of the memento, which the allies will think absolutely 
necessary for their own honour and the security of Europe? Upon this 
important subject I shall have the honour of addressing your Lordship soon after 
my arrival at Vienna. 

I have, &c.

THE transit of rifles for the use of the Russian army has been fately 
earried on in the following manner: 

The manufacturer or purchaser at Liege exports the arms to a fresh firm at 
Aix-la-Chapelle, which pays the duty, and then exports them to Russia, The

however, anxious to maintain the freedom of export from his ports. of Russian

My Lord, Berlin, March 2, 1855. 

I HAD this morning the honour of an interview with the Prince of 
Prussia, 

The death of the Emperor of Russia was not known at that time. Indeed 
it took place at the very hour when | was proceeding ta the Prince's residence. 

As, however, the intelligence of this important event was expected every 
moment, His Royal Highness alluded to it very carly in our conversstion. The 
Prince said that the Hereditary Grand Duke had always given advice in oppo- 
sition to the policy which had been pursued, and that if that advice had been 
followed, there would have been no war. But when [ asked whether the 
necession of the Grand Duke might not be the cause of tuniults, Mis Royal 
Mighness answered that unless the Grand Duke declared lis intention of follow- 
ing the poliey of his father, there might be discontent, and even tumults, Many 
would be disposed to adopt the Grand Duke Constantine as their leader. 

Tremarked that His tmperial Highness might be sent to Sweaborg to inspect 
the fleet. 

Tt will not be difficult, however, for the young Emperor, if he 1s disposed to 
peace, to change gradually the direction of his policy, and under the able 
guidance of Cotnt Nesselrode to consent to guarantees that might satisfy the 
Jealousies anid fears of Murope. 

The Prince of Prussia, as your Lordship is aware, is entirely apposed to 
the policy of the King: and he had no difficulty in stating in the strongest 
terms his belief that if Prussia were at any time to join the Western Powers, 
peace would he made in a fortnight. 

This opinion often expressed has led to a complete estrangement from the 
King, and the Prince of Prussia seemed to be very incompletely informed of the 
btate of the negotiations between France and Prussia, [lis Royal Highness, 
however, was fully aware of the two conditions respecting Poland and. the 
passage of foreign troops through Germany, upon which the King lays so great 
astress; and the Prince thought very justly that neither condition could be 
maintained, 

With regard to Poland he said no insurrection existed, and therefore 
nothing had arisen to justify such a demand; while if a resolution should here- 
after take place, no one could prescribe beforehand what course would be 
justifiable on the part oftthe allies, 

With respect to foreign troops, he said, “They will either be our allies, and 
then we shall be glad te see them aid us, or they will not be our allies, and then 
they have no claim to usk us fora passage.” 

In short the ingenious speculations of the King find no reeeptacle in the 
plain and honest mind of the Prince. 

His Royal Highness still entertains some hopes of the success of the 
negotiations fora Treaty of Alliance with the Western Powers. Ile disapproves, 
however, of the demand fora limitation of the naval power of Russiw in the 
Black Sea, and thinks it would be more efficacious for the allies, and less 
humiliating for the Russian Government, to provide hy Treaty arsenals and fleets 
of Great Britain and France an the coast af the Black Sea, 

T combatted this opinion, but it was unnecessary to argue the question with 
the Prince of Prussia, : 

It may, however, be useful to mention to your Lordship, that it is the only 
one of the four bases apon which | have heard any discussion upon the Con- 
tinent, une the only one to which the advocates of Russia seem to have any 
strong abjeetion, : 

The Prince of Prussia spoke in the highest terms of admiration of the 
English arniy.

My Lord, Foreign Office, March 5, 1855, 

HAVING learnt from Vice-Consul Cunningham that he was waiting for 
instructions from your Exeellency as to whether he was to forward to this office 
copies of his correspondence with the Embassy, regarding his recent mission to 
Bulgaria, | desired him to transmit them without further delay ; and 1 have in 
consequence received his report, contained in his despatches Nos. | to 20 to 
your Excellency. 

i presume your Excellency supposed that Mr, Cunningham would have 
transmitted his report to the Foreign Otfice, or you would not have failed to 
eonvey to Her Majesty's Government information whieh throws such a terrible 
light upon the internal administration of one of the largest and most important 
provinces of the Turkish Empire. 

Her Majesty's Government have taken this correspondence into their seriour 
consideration, and I have to express their deep concern at finding, that in 
Bulgaria, people say no Turk is put to death for the murder of a Christian ; that 
every means is used by persecution and annoyance to compel the relations of 
murdered Cliristians to accept the “price of blood ;” that in the case of a Turk 
accused of a murder committed near Rasgrad last August, the evidence of fifteen 
most respectable Bulgarians was rejected, and there being no ‘Turkish witnesses, 
the murderer was allowed to depart unquestioned; that a practice pretails 
among the Turks of robbing Christians oftheir property by neans of false witnesses, 
and so common is this practice as regards cattle, that a Christian can hardly 
consider his horse, or his cow, his own, that at Shumla and at Sistova, 
Mr. Cunningham met with cases of this kind, where the testimony of Christians 
was deliberately rejected by the Cadis, and, i spite of the tender of such evidence, 
the stolen property was adjudged to the Mussulman claimant; that the police 
openly rob travellers; that there is no relaxation of the old restraints anes 
Christian rites; that a Cliristian on liorseback meeting a Turk is obliged to 
dismount and stand until the Turk has passed; that, according to the statement 
ofthe Austrian Viee-Consul at Soffia, the suflerings of the Christians in the 
Pashalic of Nissa, from the cruelty and oppression of the Turks, are indescribable ; 
that, in short, as Mr. Cunningham expresses it in one of his letters, the state of 
the country is fearful and insupportable for Christians. 

Her Majesty's Government are bound to believe that the Porte was in dis- 
graceful ignorance of this state of things in Uulgavia, although its at — von 
should have been awakened to it by the indignant remonstrances of Lord 
Raglan and the Duke of Cambridge, against the iniquities committed almost 
within the pale of the British camp, and which were made known by your 
Excelleney to the Turkish Government. 

Her Majesty's Government do not, however, doubt that upon the receipt 
of Mr, Cunningham's despatches, your Excellency commonicated their contents 
to the Porte, and demanded that measures for the punishment of offenders, and 
for giving some security to life and property ii Bulgaria, should forthwith be 
adopted, and | have to instruct your Execllency to report what was the nature 
of your communications, and with what results they were attended; for the 
Porte must not suppose that at the conelusion of the war, a state of things so 
revolting to humanity, and so degrading to the Chvistian religion, will be tole- 
tated by the Christian Powers of Europe. % 

The Porte in its instructions to the Turkish Plenipotentiary at Vienna, 
states: “Le Gouvernement Impérial fait tous ses efforts pour que les sujets 
Chrétions de Sa Majesté Imperiale jouissent du bien-ttre et de la prospérité 
nécessaires ; lit Sublime Porte voue sa sollicitude réelle d cet objet important, 
car elle n'ignore pas que e'est dans son propre intérét, Aussi n’li¢site-t-clle pus

Brigadier-General Craufurd to the Karl of Clarendon.— (Received March 5.) 


(No. 6.3 
My Lord, Vienna, February 28, 1855, 


| WENT to Feldzengmeister Hess on Friday 23rd instant, according to 
his wish, and met him already leaving his office to go to the Emperor. He 
returned with me, and put into my hand a state of the armies under his com- 
mand, viz, Srd and 4th armies, with every detail bearing upon their strength, 
composition and station at the present time, Upon doing so, Baron Hess 
added, that the Emperor desired this document should be used or shown with 
reserve: and he requested me not to forward the paper itself ina despatch, but 
to reserve it for use and reference here, and to content myself with a summary of 
the details contained in it, for conveying the information I might wish to send 
to Eneland. | 

The 8rd and 4th armies are under the command of Baron Hess, and com- 
prehend all the troops to be employed in the first line, in case of hostilities either 
in Poland or the Danubian Principalities, These two armies are stationed near 
the frontiers, both to the north and south-east; and their united numbers 
amount to 244,978 men, with 720 pieces of Artillery. The proportion of Cavalry 
is 39,404 men. 

Each army contains three Infantry armée corps. Each Ss consists of 
five brigades, and each brigade of a regiment, which lust, if complete, has four 
battalions containing 1,080 privates ench ; besides this one battalion of Jiigers ot 
nearly the same strensth, completes the brigade. ‘The six corps of Infantry, 
composing the 8rd and 4th armies, are numbered as follows: (Srd Army), 
Oth, 11th, 12th army corps; (4th Army), 2nd, 4th, 10th army corps; one 
regiment of Cavalry, numbering 1,460 men, divided into eight squadrons, is

A report has been eurrent here that great sickness prevails amongst the 
Austrian troops in Poland. I have authority for saying that this sickness is 
very partial, having attacked especially three Cavalry regiments, and one Infantry 
reciment, 11 Poland, 

It appears to have excited more attention than would otherwise have been 
given to it, fram its being of an unusual character in those provinces ; the 
complaint being an agueish fever, which has not been considered a characteristic 
malady of those districts. As it has prevailed principally in the Cavalry, the 
sickness of one man obliges a second, who is charaed with the care of his horse, 
to be also absent from parades, and some other duties; and it has given the 
appearance of the illness being more extensive than is really the case, The 
average throughout the two armies under the command of Baron Hess, does 
not exceed by the last report 7 per cent., which is below the usual sick state of 
Austrian troops when concentrated in readiness for war.

WHEN I was with Baron Manteuffel this evening, his [xcellency read 
to me a despatch just received from Count Arnim, from Vienna. 

The Prussian Minister states that he has nothing new to report, except that 
in consequence of the nominition of Count Rechberg to Frankfort, Count Than 
had been appointed to succeed him as an adjoint to Field-Marshal Radetzky, 
in the Lomburdian Kingdom, and that Count Thun would shortly repair to 
Berlin to deliver to the King his letters recalling him from the post of Envoy 
at this Court. 

Count Arnim states that the desire for a pacific settlement of the Eastern 
question, is daily increasing at Vienna; that money is searce, and provisions 
dear; and that he believes the Austrian Government are most anxious fo Come 
to an arrangement which would enable them to reduce their inilitary expenses. 
He adds, that questions are frequently put to him as to General Wedel’s mission 
to Paris: that he is happy in being unable to give any information on the 
subject, and hopes for the interest of his country that no change in the present 


political relations of Prussia will take place, for a Treaty with France and 
England would assuredly not have the effect of improving the prospect of peace, 
but, on the contrary, of increasing the pretensions of the Western Powers. 

Baron Mantentfel after reading this despatch, suid, that he begged me not 
to imagine that he participated in these sentiments, for he regretted that Count 
Arnim should write in the above sense.

My Lord, Berlin, March 2, 1855. 

THLE impression produced here by the late manifesto of the Emperor of 
Russin, and the simultaneous appeal to the Russian nation, ordaining the 
formation of a general militia for the defence of the Empire, has been af a varied 
and opposite nature, according to the political opmions of the judging partics. 
To the friends and devotees of Russia, it has been viewed as a proof ot Itussian 
omnipotence, tempered with that spirit of conciliation and love of pedee which 
in their blind fanaticism they are still willing to adjudge the Czar; nor do they 
appear to attribute any undue importance to the cliims of Russia put forth in 
that document to protect the rights of her co-religionists im the Bust, and to 


dal 


raise her arm in defence of the orthadox Church, as this language is evidently 
addressed to the Slavonic races in Russia, and is equally applicable to those of 
Galicia, Bohemia, and Servia, On the other hand, those who are opposed to 
the Russian policy, view in this manifesto a threat of defiance to Europe, and 
a wish thereby to deter the minor European States from entering into the 
Western coalition. 

Taken generally, it would seem to offer some proof of weakness, an apparent 
sign that the ordinary means of conscription in Russia have reached their utmost 
limit, and that it has been found necessary to give the wara fresh churacter of 
religious zeal, in order to stimulate the popular and national enthusiasm. It 
may be however further affirmed, that a feeling of indifference has of late sprung 
up here in the public mind, which may be traced to two causes, nided by the 
constant endeavours of Baron Manteuffel’s Cabinet. The first cause to which 
L allude, is a general fecling that Prussia has allowed the favourable moment to 
vo by when she might have taken the lead of Germany, and have pliyed a 
conspicuous part in Europe; it is felt that she has been forestalled, if not put 
aside by Austria, and that inactivity is now preferable to playing a secondary 
part under the control and at the bidding ol Austria, The second cause is a 
very general feeling of want of confidenee in the Sovercign, a fecling that it were 
perhaps better for Prussin to bide her time, and to husband her strength and 
resources for some future occasion, rather than to incur saerifices, and possibly 
to risk disasters, without sufficient hopes of corresponding gain, 

With respect to the general levy ordered in Russia tor the defence of the 
Empire, it may be calculated to amount to about twenty-five per mille of the 
male population, which would for the whole Empire amount to 500,000 tn 
round nimbers, 

Hitherto only eighteen Governments have been ordered to furnish their 
quota, but as they are the most populous parts of the Empire as regards serts, 
the levy may be caleulated to produce about 300,000 men. These levies, 
although nominally forming a sert of local militia, are at the complete disposal 
of the Emperor, and as was the case in 1812 and 1513, would be incerporated 
into line regiments, in case of need, to fill up vacances. 

Poland, Lithuanix, Podolia, and other Polish and Russian provinces and 
Governments, are not as yet included, but on the other hand, the landed 
proprietors are to pay [S.cilver roubles per hooft (about 60 Prussian uveres) of 
land, in money, as an indemnity, and | believe without any regard as to their 
being arable, pasture, woodlands, or steppe. 

Qwners of serfs are to provide the entire equipment (except arms and 
ammunition) for all men supplied by them, and a sum of money, or in nadurd, 
equivilent to ning months’ consumption of food, They are likewise to contribute 
ta their pay, at the rate of less than ane firthing per day whilst the men ure 
under arms, that is, during the war, and are to provide for the wounded and 
invalids afterwards. I! men die, the owners are to receive a ecrtificate, which 
will entitle the latter to proportionate exemption at future ardinary levies, ‘This 
fresh exaction will prove a heavy burthen on the landed proprietors, for inde. 
pendently of the costs, they will he deprived of a large population for tilling the 
estates, and of the means of obtaining thereby some remuneration for the losses 
they incur. 

itis very difficult to form any just appreciation with respect to the state of the 
finances of the Russian Empire, but the foregoing would seem to indicate that 
the Government is reduced to the necessity of increasing their armaments at the 
expense of the landed proprietors, and a question of economy may I SOE Wihy 
explain their not again recurring to the usual mode of conseription. 

I am informed by a person who served with the Russian army i TS12 and 
[818, that the body of men raised by a similar process, then proved to be totally 
uselvss and inefficient, so much so, that they could not even be employed on 
services of the most trivial nature. ; } 

With respect to the large emission of paper-money which his taken place 
since the commencement of the war, it may be observed that as long as Russia 
carries on war Within her own territory, and the popular feeling ts in favour of 
the war, the paper currency will maintain ita eredit. As fir us Lam enabled to 
learn, and judging from the large armaments which have been litely going on 
along the Baltic coast, no symptoms have yet been manitested that funds are 
winting to the State.

In conversing with Baron Manteuffel on this subject, his Excellency 
‘formed me that he was not aware that the Russian Government were mn any 
financial embarrassment, and his Excellency further assured me that the amount 
cf reserve bullion kept at the fortress at St. Petersburgh was still intact.

Inclosure in No. 340. 
/ice-Coneul Hertslet to Lord Bloomfield. 
( Extract.) Memel, February 27, 1855, 


| HAVE the honour to bring to your Lordship’s notice, that | have observed 
from the debates in the House of Commons that Mr. Mitchell, M.P., of the 
large mercantile firm of same name in London, has always been most prominent 
m pressing the stoppage of the overland Russian trade through Prussia. This 
appears the more extraordinary as Mr. Armisstead, the chief of the house Mitchell 
and Co. in Riga, has been all along, and stillis, the largest exporter of flax and 
hemp brought in this manner to Memel, and has created depdts for these articles 
through persons in his employment, at the Russian border villages of Garsden 
and Plungahn, and is at the present moment almost the sole purchaser 
here. 

The objection to stopping this trade for fear of German manufacturers 
buying up all Russian produce at a cheap rate, and competing with British 
manufacturers, appears to be too far extended. As long as the Russian ports are 
blockaded, the land carriage to any part of Germany will always prove an effectual 
barrier against cheapness, and it would require years to set up sufficient machi- 
hery in Germany to manufacture a fraction of the usual export of Russia, and an 
enormous outlay of capital to build them; to which must be added the want of 
customers When the goods are finished, and the general dulness of trade in wavlike 
times, 

It would require a lengthened period of years of similar cireumstances to 
enable German manufacturers to grow to a formidable rivalry. The instantaneous 
effect of the stoppage of the trade would in England be a reaction both in the 
price of raw material and manufactured goods in Great Britain, by whieh the 
heavy losses which have so paralyzed trade in England might be made good 
again, whilst from the heavy stock said to be accumulated there, and the slack 
demand, no actual want of the raw materials is likely to take place in [859. 

The instantaneous effect of the same cause to Russia would be incalculable, 
The nobles and producers of the raw article in Russia may have obtained a less 
price for their goods in 1854; but it has been fully made good to them by 
the employment of their horses, sledges, and labourers, in transporting the 
foods. 

I have myself heard Courland noblemen state, that their farmers and serts 
(Bauern) never had so much money in 1854; that they never before lived so 
well, and never paid the head and other taxes more easily than in that year: and 
indeed it is obvious than aton of flax or hemp at 42L.,at Memel, for which about 
201. has been expended on land carriage, must leave more money in the country 
than the same flax or hemp shipped at St, Petersburgh at or under 34/, per ton, 
although the money flows back to the producer in a different or unusual 
manner, 

The effect of such a stoppage would be the immediate cessation of all the 
present bustle on the Russian goods, and vender useless all the plans which have 
been executed by that Government for carrying on this trade, and paralyze the 
country, 

Having opportunity daily of seeing Russian, English, Prussian, and Jewisli 


Polish merchants, | have endeavoured to convey to your Lordship the result of 


tiny private reflections on the subject, and the interesting debates in the House 
of Commons lead me to believe that any remarks frona purty on this side might 
not be looked upon as over officious,

appeared to me merely another way of saying that Russia would like to save 
Sebastopol, and to which accordingly | made no reply. 

It struck me at the same time that this point might very possibly be urged 
by the Russian Plenipotentiaries at Vienna, more particularly as it had always 
seemed to me that the Emperor Nicholas had signified his acceptance of the four 
points: for the double purpose of saving Sebastopol and of preventing the 
hostility of Austria.

Sir A. Malet to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recetwed March 5.) 


(No. 36. Confidential.) 


My Lord, Frankfort, March 2, 1865, 

YOUR Lordship’s despatch No. 16 of the 27th ultimo reached me last 
night. With reference thereto, and to my despatch No. 26 of February 23rd, 
to which it relates, | think it right to put your Lordship in possession of the 
exact circumstances under which M. de Prokesch told me that his Prussian 
colleague had affirmed that the Cabinet of Berlin had received from M, d’Usedom 
the assurance, that in no case whatever would Great Britain participate in 
hostilities against Prussia, which assertion was the tenour of what I thought it 
my duty to write to your Lordship in my despatch above referred to. 

I have already more than once touched on the animosity evinced by M. de 


Prokesch towards Prussia. Late events have not tended to modify that feeling ; 


and the occasion on which he gave me the information above referred to, was in 
a conversation which | had with his Excellency immediately after the sitting of 
the Diet of February 22nd, in which he had had what he himself styled “a 
inost disagreeable discussion” with M. de Bismark; the main points of which 
diseussion, and the check which M, de Prokeseli met with, were detailed in my 
despateh No. 27 of February 23rd. 

M. de Prokesch was therefore not unnaturally in a state of considerable 
irritation, Speaking with reference to the intended Prussian proposition of 
urming the Federal fortresses, reported in my despatch No. 28 of February 23rd, 
und the general adhesion whieh her policy met with among the minor States, he 
declaimed with much vehemence against the continual thwarting which his own 
national policy met with from that quarter. 

England and France had, in his opinion, treated Prussia with far too much 
indulgence: “ Vous ne leur avez donne que de bonnes paroles: tandis qu'il 
fallait leur faire peur.” 

“ Prussia,” he said, ' wholly relies on your forbearance, and that whatever 
she docs will be indulgently viewed and interpreted by you.” 

It was not my place to make any observation which should add to the 
irritation under which M, de Prokesch was speaking; but | thought it not 
amiss to observe, that if such opinions prevailed in Prussia, they might lead to 
very mistaken conclusions. In my own judgment, much, if not all of the 
friendly feeling hitherto existing in England towards that country, had been 
seriously weakened, if not obliterated, by the couduct of the Berlin Government, 
anid had given place to feelings of an opposite nature. I did not think, | said, 
if Prussia provoked France to hostility, which was what le seemed to believe 
was her project, that she could in any way reckon on our neutrality, or even on 
or not acting against lier; that in many of the transactions which had taken 
place since the earlier Conferences of Vienna, Prussian had, in my judgment, 
played the part of “ faux frére,” and indignation at being deceived was usually 
proportionate to confidence previously reposed. 

Here it was that Baron de Prokescli said what [ reported to your Lordship 
of the nature of M. d'Usedom’s assurances; but whether he meant me to

understand that M. de Bismark had spoken to him on the subject as of an

Bismark himself on the subject, after your Lordship’s despatch, which says that 
M. d’Usedom could have had no authority for such a communication, had 
reached me. 43 

I put the question to him very directly; firstly, whether he hada knowledge 
of M. d'Usedom’s having given an assurance of the kind to his Cabinet; but 
did not sneceed in eliciting a direct reply. His Excellency went off upon the 
subject of the intended or alleged intended obstacles to be placed on Russian 
commerce through Prussian ports; and when | brought him back to the point, 
and told him distinctly | had learnt le had said that M. d‘Usedom had reported

his answer was sull indirect, and 1 thought embarrassed ; so that the impression 
T received is, that he has used language of that import, but is indisposed to avow 
having done so to me. 

The object of spreading such a report might either be to produce its effect 
on the minor German States, in leading them to think Prussia risks a danger 
the less in her present course, or upon Austria, though in the latter case the 
effect would not be durable, as the Imperial Cabinet must be well aware what 
the state of the case really ts. 

That there is a party, however, in Prussia, actually calculating the chances 
of a war with Lrance at this moment, there can be no sort of doubt; and the 
sume amount of political sagacity which would plunge the country into such a 
struggle, may very likely also calculate on the neutrality, or even on the support 
of Great Britain.

My Lord, Paris, March 5, 1894, 


M. DROUYN DE LHUYS mentioned to me this afternoon that Count 
Buol had expressed to M. de Bourqueney desire that the Moldavian and 
Wallachian Governments should be requested to send each an Agent to Vienna 
during the Conferences, to rive any information that might be required as to 
the wants and resources of those two Provinces, His Excellency observed that

entrusted with this selection. though he admitted that the measure might be a 
good one; nor would it be proper, he aided, to take such a step without the 
consent of the Porte. He Feared, moreover, that a Servian Agent should like- 
wise be required to attend, as it appeared to him that the Austrian Government 
always aimed at excluding Servia from any participation in the affairs of Turkey, 
which were now, if possible, to be regulated.

Inclosure in No. 374. 
Colonel Simmons to Field-Marshal Lord Raglan. 


My Lord, Eupatoria, February 11, 1855. 

| HAVE to inform your Lordship that Omer Pasha called off Kamiesch on 
the 7th instant, and saw Sir Edmund Lyons, when hie explained to him his 
wishes with respect to the embarkation of the remainder of his troops, pro- 
visions, &e. 

At present there are about 96,000 men here, with two batteries of artillery 
horsed. 

A third battery has arrived this morning, but is not yet disembarked. 

‘The Russians surround this place at a distance of about 3000 yards, by a 
cordon of videttes, supported by a line of picquets, which are again supported by 
a line of strong guards, 

There may be about four squadrons constantly on this duty, with Bix pleces 
of Artillery. 

Aceording to the best information we have, there are about four regiments 
of Cavalry in this neighbourhood. 

About a week ago the Turks made a reconnaissance up to within a mile of 
the village of Sak, supported by Her Majesty's steam gun-boat © Viper.” 

In driving in the Russian picquets, they killed five men and four horses, and 
afterwards destroyed the guard-houses, and captured some hay, “There were no 
casualties on the side of the Turks. 

It is reported by deserters, of whom three or four have lately come in, that 
since the reconnaissance, a regiment of Dragoons has arrived from Simpheropol 
to reinforce the Cavalry at Sak, and that a regiment of Infantry has come to the 
neighbourliood af Tip Mamat; also that the Russians are on hall rations of 
bread, and there is much sickness among them. 

In coming from Kamiesch, we passed close along the coast, but saw nothing 
of the enemy. 

In rear of Cape Ulukul there appeared, at some distance inland (three or 
four miles), a good deal of smoke, as it rising from what might be the fires of a 
camp or large occupied village; otherwise there was no trice of the enemy visible. 

The troops here appear to be in good health; there are about 650 in 
hospital, amongst which several cnses of typhus, 

The small-pox, which hud broken out on board the “ Curacoa,” does not 
appear to spread, l | 

There is a plentiful supply of bread and vegetable food, peas, rice, &e,, for 
the men here, but little meat. 

Foruze also and firewood are not in abundance, but the stores appear to 
improve daily, by the arrivals from Turkey, | 

| shall, however, in afew days be able, | hope, to give your Lordship a 
more particular account of the position of affairs here. hh 

At present T am much occupied in laying out for the Generalissimo a chain 
of works to surround the town at a distance of about 1,000 yards, thus to obtain 
space for a camp and for HMANCoUVTINE.

This measure is the more necessary as the town is very full, and, owing to 


the defective police, very filthy; and if the troops are more crowded in it, disease 
may Cnsuc.

(No: 10.) 


My Lord, Vienna, Mareh 4, 1855. 

COUNT BUOL, having fixed | o'clock this day to receive me, | was intro- 
duced to him by Lord Westmorland at that hour, 

Count Buol received me with great cordiality. Our conversation naturally 
turned, in the first instance, upon the sudden death of the Emperor Nicholas. 

Count Buol said that this event would make no change in the policy of 
Austria; what they thought necessary before they thought necessary now, 
neither more nor less. The only change would be in the weight and authority 
of the Emperor of Russia; the present Sovereign could not have the authority 
which, from the length of his reign and the foree of his chnracter, attached to 
the late Emperor. | | 

lL remarked that, however true that observation might be, the policy of 
Russia was not a thing of yesterday ; that, in 1875, it might be what it was in 
1775, and that at behoved the Powers of Europe to take guarantees against the 
progress of her ambition. 

After a time Lord Westmorland left us, and 1 had a conversation of great 
interest with Count Buol. 

He told me that he thought Austria had more interest than any other Power 
in checking the advances of Russia, and that he was prepared to act with us. in 
conformity to that view. 

I suid I thought there was an obvious difference in our positions: that 
England had made great sacrifices in fitting out fleets and incurring great 
expenses ; that she had felt deeply the sufferings of herarmy; that any peace 
which did not provide solid guarantees for the future would be i severe disap- 
pointment; that Austria, not having shed her blood in the cause, might more 
easily content herself with less efficient securities ; that I believed, though I did 
not pretend to-answer for it, that the feeling in France was: similar to that in 
England, 

Count Buol said that Powers already at war felt less difficulty in continuing 
hostilities thin a Power at peace felt in commencing war; that cach Power must 
make allowances for the different situation of the other, and that the object ought 
to be to bring Austria, France, and England, to agree on the terms they would 
think necessary to ask of Russia, 

Adverting then to the mode of proceeding, he proposed ,that Lord Weat- 
morland and | should meet Baron Bourquency at his house previously to the 
opening of the Conference.

They left, however, 453 dead on the field, and five prisoners were taken 
(four of whom wounded), and nearly 300 horses were also left dead on the field. 

That the attack was intended to be seriously pushed, is evident from the 
fact that the enemy left a great many planks and scaling ladders on the field, 
and that each Infantry soldier was provided with a small fageot about 18 inches 
long by $ inches in diameter; but whether these latter were intended for incen- 
diary purposes or to fill up the ditches has not been ascertained, 

The attacking foree consisted, so far as I can ascertain, of the 8th Division 
(16 Battalions), of the Grd Corps of a Division, formed of 16 Reserve Battalions 
of different Regiments, which all came from Perekop ; and of the Azowski, 23rd 
Regiment, belonging to the 12th (Liprandi’s) Division, which came frem ecan- 
tonments five versts from Sievernaya, and 1500 Greek volunteers, who wear 
the cross on their appointments, 

Besides this force there must have been 100 picees of Artillery in the field, 
of which about 80 were brought into position, and 6 Regiments of Cavalry, 
besides Cossacks, or altogether a foree of near 40,000 men, 

Their loss must have been heavy, probably in killed and wounded not less 
than 2,000. | 

The Turkish foree engaged might have been about 27,000 men with guns. 

They turned out with great alacrity, and behaved with perfect steadiness. 

Several battalions who were disembarked during the cannonade, showed the 
greatest energy in getting to the front. 

The Turks’ loss amounts to 87 killed and 277 wounded, of all ranks. 
The au naval detachment behaved most admirably ; they lost 4 killed and 
7 woutided, 


Among the population 13 were killed and 11 wounded, and the Turks lost 
79 horses killed and 18 wounded, 

I regret to add, that among the killed was Selim Pasha, whe commanded 
the Eeyptian Division with his Highness Omer Pasha'’s army. He was a General 
of much courage, and at all times a most zealous, hard-working officer. 

Suliman Pasha, the Eeyptian General of Brigade, who has succeeded in 
the command, was wounded in the head, but did not retire from the field. 

Aniong the officers there are ineluded in the numbers above, 7 killed and 
17 wounded, 

His Highness Omer Pasha has requested me to inform your Lordship, that 
Kutchinsky, who is attached to the Eeyptian Brigade, having been recom. 
mended some years ago by your Lordship for the military service of Eeypt. 
distinguished himself in the most marked manner, 

In the battery, when all the 6 guns were disabled, the Captain of Artillery 
having been killed, Major Kutehinsky took charge, and under a very heavy 
eross fire of artillery, continued to direct the guns until the last. 

His Highness is much satisfied with the conduct of the whole of his troops, 
and has expressed himself in the most flattering manner as to the able 
cooperation of that portion of Her Majesty's fleet which was in the bay under 
the command of the Honourable Captain Hastings, of the ‘ Curaeou."

Buol, suge¢sting that Agents should be sent from Wallachia, Moldavia, and 
Servia, to Vienna, for the purpose of furnishing information upon loeal 
questions, and aiding the Conference in their decision with respect to the fature 
administration of the Principilitics. 

I told Count Colloredo that this measure appeared to be of a doubtful 
usefulness and ¢xpediency, and | asked how and by whom the agents were to 
he selected; if by the Hospodars, they would be the advocates of misgovernment 
and abuse, and if by the foreign Agents in the Principalities, there would be little 
chance of agreement with the Austrian authorities, who unfortunately had 
shown no fayour to persons desirous and capable of introducing reforms. — 

Moreover, [thought that the presence of such Agents at Vienna might be 
a cause of embarrassment, as they might in various wavs use their loeal 
knowledge to obstruct the general and comprehensive views whieh, it was to be 
hoped, the Conterence would take of the svstém of government to be established 
in the Principalities, | | 

Atvall events, Tadded, Ter Majesty's Government could not assent to the 
proposal of Count Buol, without previous communication with the Parte, as it 
was alike the duty and the interest of the Sultan's allies to uphold his authority 
throughout the Ottoman Empire. :

My Lord, Berlin, March Gb, 85h. 

| HAVE the honour to inform vour Lordship that the Emperor Nicholas 
had scarecly ceased to breathe, when the Empress directed a messaze to the 
following effect to be sent by televraph to the Kine of Prussia:—" A midi dix 
minutes, PEmpercur a extialé sa noble fime, Avant de mouriv i n'a prié 
demander son cher Fritz ie rester lami de la Russie ct fidéle aux dernitres 
paroles de Papa.” 
om The last words of the late King of Prussia above alluded to, were an 
junction to maintain under all contingencies the principles of the Moly 
Alliance; and your Lordship can easily understand that this luperial mUssuce 


* No. a4. 
aya 


a he Lo 1 1 #4, . ~_ 2) rae 5 = 7 de 
re i eee pee epee er ee ee ee a ee Cary 2

was well calculated to produce an important effect on the King at such a 
moment, and to shake any inclination he might have of drawing his policy 
nearer to the Western Powers. 

It has succeeded in’so far that all public business is suspended. The King 
has seareely seen his Ministers since the 2nd instant, and his mind is over- 
whelmed by thoughts of this unexpected event. 

Lutterly, lithe cordiality of feeling existed between the brothers-in-law ; 
the Emperor despised the King, and the King dreaded the Emperor. However, 
notwithstanding the dissimilarity of character of the two Sovereigns, and an 
oecasional difference in their opinions, the tendency of their foreign policy has 
cenerally been the same. This last message will undoubtedly serve to Keep the 
King away from the Western Powers, but still it cannot be expected that the 
Emperor Alexander of Russia will ever exercise such an ascendency over the 
King as that which has lasted so many years; and though at first His Majesty 
may be carried away by sentiment, and may allow nothing to interfere with his 
present train of melancholy feelings, they will gradually subside; and it is not 
improbable that in time he may rejoice to have got rid of a weight which 
pressed heavily on him, and may not object to give a new direction to the 
political affairs of his country. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received March 8.) 


(No. 83.) 


My Lord, Berlin, Mareh 6, 1855. 

NO written despatches having reached the Prussian Government since the 
death of the Emperor Nicholas, we are indebted to the telegraph for the few 
details whieh have arrived connected with this event, and which [ have al-eady 
forwarded to your Lordship, The effect of the intelligence on the King of 
Prussia, the Royal Family, and the Court, is desponding; they feel that they 
have lost a friend who possessed the means of assisting them in case of need: a 
portion of the public partake also of this feeling, but it is only partial, for many 
rejoice that Germany has been relieved from the oppressive influence which has 
been exercised over the country for so many years past, 

To mark the event to the Prussian army, with whom the Emperor was 
very popular, a mourning of four weeks has been ordered, and this is the more 
remarkable as it is not usual for so long a mourning to be worn except fora King 
of Prussia, tiree days being the period for which it is worn for one of the 
Princes of the blood, ora Picld-Marshal. 

Asatoken of reminiscence to the Prussian regiment of which he was 
Colonel, the Emperor Nicholas has directed in his will that his Prussian wniform 
should he deposited with his regiment, and I believe that this intention has been 
well received, 

[have thought it might to mention the foregoing in order that Her Majesty's 
Government may be aware of the influences which are now at work at Berlin to 
keep alive the spirit which has directed the policy of this country for so many 
years piist. 

Te great theatres at Berlin have been closed for three nights, but all other 
places of amusement have been more than usually crowded, which shows the 
little feeling really entertamed by the public on the occasion. 

‘ 1 have, &c.
