My Lord, Berlin, March 6, 1855. 

I HAVE had the honour to inform your Lordship by telegraph that Prince 
Menchikof had been recalled from his command inthe Crimea, This. intelli- 
gence reached me last night in the form in which I reported it to your Lordship: 
but | have since heard that it was the act of the late Emperor, and the result of 
the Prince’s request to be relieved from his duties on account of the state of his 
health. LI understand that Baron Osten-Sacken is to command the Russian 
troops in the Crimea, General Liders on the Pruth, and General Prinee Gortcha- 
koff to be invested with the supreme command over the whole. 

Count Miinster reports from St. Petersburgh that the Russian army in the 
Crimea is inatolerable condition at this moment; but that they have lost 
46,000 men since the commencement of the campaign. 

He alludes, I hear, to the fear of plague and pestilence as likely to arise on 
the approach of warm weather from the numbers of interments, and from the 
putridity of the soil around Sebastopol, and expresses this opinion of the 
Russian Generals in such strong terms that 1 am induced to mention the 
subject. 

[ atn informed that General Riidiger is to command the corps of Russian 
Guards. 

General Griimwald is shortly expected here with the notification of the 
accession of the Emperor AlexanderlI, and General Baron Lieven 1s to proceed to 
Vienna on a like mission, 

Everything, as far as it is known, has proceeded at St. Petersburgh 
according to the forms observed on the accessions of former Sovereigns, and the 
succession has apparently passed off without the occurrence of any incident 
deserving of notice. 

The Emperor Alexander is said to have ratified all his father's acts, and to have 
directed that Prince Gortchakoff shall be immediately empowered to attend the 
Tonferenees at Vienna.

(Translation.) 


IN the constant aggrandizement of Russia in the Bast, Europe has long 
acen with great and jealous distrust the progressive application of the system 
innugurated by Peter the Great, and naturalized inthe Museovite nition, more 
even thiamin its Sovercigns, tending with its whole occult and avowed foree 
towards the conquest of Constantinople, not as to a tinal object, but as to the 
first step om the ladder of great anil unmeasured ambition, 

These projects on the part of Russia, subversive af the balunce of power in 
Envope, menace to the hiberty of peoples and to the independence of nations, 
were perhaps never revealed with the same evidenee as in the unjust invasion of 
the Danubian Principalities, and in the diplomatic acts by whieh it was preceded 
and followed, 

Wherefore France and England very properly, after a long and useless trial 
of conciliatory meusures, hil recourse to arms, und proceeded to support the 
Ottommn Empire against the aggression of its overbearing neighbour. 


387 


Upon the solution of the Eastern question depend the destinies, if not 
immediate, at least to be foreseen, of Europe and Asia, and more directly and 
proximately those of the States bordering on the Mediterranean Sea, which 
Stites, therefore, cannot remain indifierent spectators of a conflict in which their 
most vital interests are at stuke, in which the result of the contest will decide 
whither they are to remain free and independent, or vassals in fact, if not in 
uame, of the colossal Russian Minpire. 

The justice of the cause espoused by the generous defenders of the Sublime 
Porte, the consideration of the national dignity and independence, always of 
such weight on the King's heart, have determined His Majesty the King of 
Sardinia, in consequence of a formal invitation which he has received from the 
two great Western Powers, by an Act dated the 12th of January last, to accede 
to the Treaty of Alliance, offensive and defensive, concluded on the 10th of 
April, 1854, between their Majesties the pepeyor of the French and the Queen 
of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. But some time before 
that Act could receive its legal fulfilment by the exchange of the ratifications, 
before, therefore, it could have even a commencement of execution, the 
Emperor Nicholas, complaining ef us in linguage not exempt from bitterness, 
that we had committed o breach of public law, in having (as he assumes) 
without o previous dechiration of war, sent an expedition to the Crimea, and, 
moreover, accusing the King of ingratitude, for having overlooked the ancient 
proofs of friendship and sympathy given by Russia to Sardinia, hastened on his 
part to declare war against us. 

Without stopping to comment on the supposed violation of the Law of 
Nations, which can only be an error of officials, we will observe, that to the 
ancient recollections of friendly correspondence between the predecessors of 
His Imperial Majesty and those of His Sardinian Majesty, the Emperor might 
have contrasted more recent ones, and personal ones, on the conduct which he 
has pursued tor the last eight years towards the Kings Carlo Alberto and Victor 
Ernanuel LH. 

But, first of all, he ought to have convinced himself that His Majesty took 
purtin this allianee, not from forgetfulness of old friendships, nor from a sense 
of recent injuries, but from the firm conviction of being urgently impelled to it 
by the general interests of Europe, and by the particular ones of that nation 
whose welfare Providence has committed to lis ahatee 

It is on that account that the King, in taking part inan arduous war, does 
not in the least doubt that his beloved people and brave soldiers: respond to his 
call with their old fidelity, trosting, 18 he also trusts, in the protection of that 
Gad, who, in the course af more than eight centuries, his so often sustained 
them in great dangers, and guided the House of Savey to glorious successes, 

His Majesty is tranquil in the convielion of having fulfilled a duty, Nor, 
though overwhelmed by so great domestic afhtictions, will he be less resolute 
and firm in defending with all his power, against every aggression, the sacred 
interests of his people and the impreseriptible rights of the Crown, 

While the King offers up prayers to God for the success of the negotiations 
for pence, already begun at Vienna, fulfilling the obligutions contracted by him 
towards: France, England and Turkey, he has ordered the undersigned Minister 
to decline, that by virtue of the Act of Accession previously mentioned, his land 
and marine forces are at war with Russia. 

The Undersigned declares, besides, by order of His Majesty, that the 
“exequatur’ accorded to the Russian Consuls in the Sardinian States ts 


revoked; that the property and persons of Russian subjects will be nevertheless 


scrupulously respected, and that a sutlicient interval of time will be conceded to 
Russian vessels to allow of their leaving the Sardinian States. 
Turin, March 4, 1856, 
(Signed) C. CAVOUR, 
President of the Council.

[said that L thought the objection of Russia to any interference with her

at hand, was a perpetual menace to Turkey. lie 

Baron Bourqueney observed, we hada right to say to Russia, “Explain

Count Buol differed from this view. He thought other securities might 
be more eHective.. He thought we might provide that if Mussia increased 
her force in the Black Sea, say beyond fifteen ships, the Sultan might call 
his allies to the Bosphorus to bis assistance; that we might have ports 
in the Black Sea, and a brig or two of war at the mouth of the Danube, 
which might watch the proceedings of Russia, hove all he relied on 
a proposal he should make that the integrity of Turkey should be guaranteed by 
the four Powers. Ile thought such a guarantee would be more valuable to 
Turkey than a Treaty suggested by me, by which the three Powers, Austria, 
France, and Great vitain, ‘should promise Turkey to come to lier assistance 
with stipulated forces in case of her being attacked by Russia. 

suid that when we were establishing peace we should take care that what 
we establish was really a state of peace; that the presence of forces counter 
balancing each other in the Black Sea would look too like an armed truce. 
That with respect to the proposed guarantee unless we were all bound to act on 
a given occasion, the three Powers might differ widely as to the moment of 
interference. ‘That with regard to the aggression of Russia, which had brought 
us together, France had sent her fleet from Toulon to the waters of Greece at 
an early period, England somewhat later; nd Austria, although she had made 
great preparations, was not yet in the lield as a belligerent. It was therefore 
essential, in my opinion, that we should be hound together by positive stipula- 
tions 40 resist an overession of Russia upon Turkey; that, however, the best 
secarity would be the limitation of the Russian naval forces in the Black Sea, 
and I asked Count Buol whether he had a convietion that Russia would not

Black Sea. Baron Prokesch appeared to approve of this suggestion, but some 
discussion arose as to the reciprocity which Russia might claim for the purpose 
of sending her ships of war from the Black Sea into the Mediterranean, or from 
the Baltic to the Black Sea. In conclusion, Count Buol said that he was ready 
to propose the limitation of the naval power of Russia in the Black Sea, as the 
best and most simple arrangement, but that if the Russian Ministers positively 
declined to accede to sucha condition, he should be ready to discuss other means 
of carrying the third point into effect, It might be, he continued, that those 
other means would be so distasteful to Russia that she would prefer the limita- 
tion of her ships as the least onerous obligation. 

I expressed myself ready to concur in the proposed course, but thought it 
necessary to reserve for my Government the power of declaring that on exami- 
nation they found the proposed alternatives would not attain the proposed end, 
Baron Bourqueney made a similar reserve ; and Count Buol readily agreed that 
in this respect we should all be free. 

A considerable time having been employed in this discussion, we scarcely 
entered upon the fourth point, which, however, we considered to be one of the 
highest importance as well as considerable difficulty. Baron Prokesch considered 
it as the germ of a complete change in the state of the Turkish Empire; and as 
opening to the Christian subjects of the Porte a greater freedom from oppression 
and vexation than they had ever obtained from Russian protection. 

In concluding this report I cannot omit to state the impression I have 
received af the earnest desire of Count Buol and his colleague to ward off the 
dangers which hang over Europe from Russian preponderance. Indeed it is not 
to be wondered at that Austrian statesmen should feel peculiar anxiety on this 
head; the cloud that would burst over Turkey would involve Austria in the 
ravages of the storm. It might happen, as I hinted to Count Buol, that on the 
next occasion, while Austrian was directing her army to impede the Russian 
march to the Balkan, France and England might for various reasons, unless 
bound by positive Treaty, be slow to come to her assistance. Two years ago 
indeed, Austria might have abandoned the cause of Europe, and have contented 
herself with such share of the spoils of Turkey as the Russian Emperor might 
have youchsafed to her: but that moment is past—the relations of Austria 
and Russia have passed from intimacy and confidence to estrangement and 
SUSPICION, 

Every day adds to the proofs of the deep-laid designs of Russia; the sub- 
serviency of German Courts; the Russian interest pervading and corrupting the 
officers of German armies as well ns the Cabinets ef German Sovereigns; the 
pains taken by the late Emperor Nicholas to undermine all wational feeling in 
Germany; the intrigues in Bulgaria, and the meditated fortifications at Bomar- 
sund, all tend to show that Austria, having disdained the part of a vassal and an 
accomplice, must be prepared to beamong the foremost in defence of the barriers 
of European independence, If she can secure these barriers by military pre- 
paration and successtul diplomacy alone, she will greatly prefer the construction 
ofa Treaty to the hazard ofa war, But she cannot retire from the position she 
his assumed without suffering from the vengeance, the insolence, and the 
devouring ambition of Russia, 

[t will be for Her Majestyand Her Majesty’s Ministers to consider how far 
they will abandon or modily preconceived opinions to mect the views of Austria. 
The question is a very serious one, and the time is not yetarrived for its positive 
solution; bot T shall be glad to learn fur my guidanee the general views of Her 
Majesty’s Government upon a subject so importunt to the future safety of 
Europe. I have, &e.

No, 410. 
Lord John Russell to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received March 13.) 


(No. 13.) 
My Lord, Vienna, March 10, 1855. 

I AM sorry to be obliged to state to your Lordship that considerable 
difficulties have arisen in the preliminary discussions relative to the insertion m 
the Protocol of the interpretation of the four ponits. 

Finding from Baron Bourqueney that Count Buol felt great repugnance to 
asking the consent of Prince Gortchakoll to the insertion of the memorandum 
containing the interpretation of the four pomts in the Protocol, I met Baron 
Bourqueney yesterday morning at Lord Westmorlind’s. 

We endeavoured at first to see whether any abstract of the memorandum 
could be given, containing the substance of that document. But we soon found 
that it waa impossible to omit certain parts of the document, without at onee 
departing from the instructions of our respective Governments, and weakening 
our position during the negotiations. 

It was agreed that I should go to Count Buol, and state: to him our 
difficulty. He informed me that it was his wish to state briefly to the Confer- 
ence the situation in which we assembled, to refer to the bases as known, and 
to leave to the Plenipotentiaries of France and Great Britain any further 
preliminary, 

Impressed with the importance of this first step; the danger of showing, 
on the one side, any disagreement with Austria in the commencement of nego- 
tations, or on the other, of giving up the advantage already gained, T went to 
Count Buol at Lo'clock this day with Lord Westmorland, having: previously 
settled with Baron Bourqueney that he should be there at the same hour. 

Count Buol was fully prepared to argue’ the question with us. He told us 
he had received an intimation from Prince Gortehakotf that he expected his full 
powers this evening, so that the Conferences: may be opened immediately. 

He proposed to open the Conference very briefly, stating either that the 
Powers had already agreed to negot inte, or giving, in very few words, un abstract 
of the four points agreed upon as buses of negotiation, A et 

He proposed. in the nest place, to take the first Article of the interpretation, 
and so continue, Article by Article, till the four were discussed. 

Lord Westmorland and 1 observed that if Count Buol was prepared to state 
the four points singly, us they had been agreed upon between us, he could 
hardly object to state the four together as the foundation of a Protocol. 

Count Buol took exception to this reasoning. He thought the proposal to 
record int Protocol the four bases might naturally be objected to by the Russian 
Plenipotentiaries. Prince Gortchakolf had already, in a former meeting, agreed 
to accept those buses, and to eo back on that former meeting would be in some 
kort ta call in doubt his word, [le (Prince Gortchakolf) would say that the 
preliminary stage was passed ; that he was there ready to negotiate, and would 
vither break off, oy refer to his Court for instructions. 

Count Buol thought cither a rupture or a delay of negotiations would be 
very unfortunate: that the demur being on a point of form, those who raised 
the point of form would be accounted responsille by the opinion of Europe; 
that, on the part of Austria, he was not ready to accept such responsibility ; 
that, after be had made: his statement, ib wits open to us to say that we wished 
the four points more extensively developed, and to ask for the insertion in the 

Protocol of the memorandam, 

Count Buol declared he did not know the course which Prince Gortchakolf 
would pursue in that case; but he might absolutely refuse to go back on the 
past, or he might again refer to his own reserves. 8: 

We discussed the matter at considerable length, I stated the impression 


307 


which Baron Manteuffel told me was prevalent in Germany, that Prince Gort- 
chakoff had not accepted the interpretation of the three Powers, 

Count Buol replied that Lerd Westmorland, Baron Bourqueney, and he, 
were all witnesses of the acceptance by Prince Gortehakoff. He had not thought 
it advisable to have a procés-verbai, but he should be ready, if any doubt should 
arise in the course of the negotiation, to maintain the fact of the acceptance, 

There cannot be any doubt that Count Buol’s fears are founded, not so 
much on the point of formas on the presumed repngnance of Russia to give a 
more formal and definite adherence to the interpretation of the three Courts, 

The declarations of Count Buol have entirely altered the position of the 
belligerent Powers. When I left London it was supposed that the Austrian 
Minister would give his willing assent to the insertion of the memorandum in 
the first Protocol. It was imagined, therefore, that if we should break upon this 
question, we should break off in union with Austria. 

‘It now appears that the Austrian Government will refuse to concur with us, 
and will throw upon us the responsibility of breaking off upon what she will 
allege is a point of form, 

There are evidently only two courses to pursue. 

The one is to rest satislied with the abstract of the four points, to be stated 
by Count Buol, and the assurance of Prince Gortchakoif that he abides by his 
declarations of the 7th of January 

If we take this course we may possibly induce Count Buol to make his 
statement somewhat fuller than he had intended. At all events this will be 
desirable. 

‘The other course is to insist on the acceptance of the memorandum as the 
basis of negotiation, and to require its insertion in the Protocol, 

This last course is most in accordance with your Lordship’s instructions 
which were communicated to me before [left London, and with the intentions 
of the French Government. 

At the same time, the positive divergence of Austria from this line of con- 
duct seetus to me to mike such a course of doubtful expediency, 

We might, indeed, throw upon Russia the reproach of insincerity and 
bad faith. But the language of the Austrian Minister would weaken, very 
materially, the impressions against Russia, which would otherwise be produced. 

The real question is, whether there is ainy hope of peace from these negotiu- 
tions. I believe there issuch hope. Sach being my belief, fam inclined to 
think that, although the thread may snap hereafter, at some part of the line, it 
would be right to proceed so long as no essential security to ‘Turkey and Europe 
is refused by Russia. 

Having seen Lord Westmorland since the foregoing parts of this despatch 
were written, | find he concurs both in the correctness of the relation which | 
have given, and the conclusion at which | have arrived. 

IL shall, however, be better able to form a judgment after the meeting of 
ta-Miorraw, 

I have, &e. 


(Signed) J. RUSSELL.

that upon their accepted interpretation he considered the negotiation might be 
commenced, 

Count Buol’s speech would be embodied in the Protocol of the Conference, 
which would be signed by all the Representatives. 

Baron Bourqueney and Lord John proposed that the whole document 
containing the interpretation, should be laid before the Representatives, as the 
one to which adhesion had been given on the 7th January. 

Count Buol did not contest the right of each Plenipotentiary to propose 
what he chose, but he did not see the advantage of this proceeding : if Pringe 
Gortchakoff did not object to Count Buol's statement, “ that he (Prince 
Gortchakoff) had consented to the interpretation of the bases,” it would be 
asking him for another acceptation of the interpretation, by requiring his signa- 
ture to the Protocol in whieh these four conditions were textually ta be recorded ; 
and as one reason against it, he stated that both in Articles [Land LV there 
were passages to which both Lord John and Baron Bourqueney acknowledged 
that Prince Gortchakoff could not give the sanction of his approval. Tt would 
be difficult to get rid of these passages, or to explain their erasure ; and it 
would certainly bring on a dissussion, which would probably end by Prince 
Gortchakoff making objections to one alteration unless all the points to which 
he night demur were made subject to revision, 

Count Buol also thought that it was not fitting, when three Ministers, 
invested with the character of Representatives of their respective Governments, 
asserted that the interpretation had been accepted, and when that nesertion was 
not disputed by the other party, to require him, for the satislaction of the Govern- 
ments represented by those Plenipotentiaries, to have their report confirmed by 
asking him fora second acceptation of the same interpretation, ) 

Under these explanations, it was agreed that Count Buol, Lord John, 
Baron Bourqueney, and myself, should meet to-morrow to examine the draft of 
the speech with which Count Buol would open the negotiation, and he (Count 
Buol) stated, that if any additional specitication of the four points than that 
which he proposed to introduce into his speech, was required, he would readily 
take it into consideration, and (subject to lis own opinion as to what he thought 
would conduce to the progress of the negotiations) he would give it his most 
favourable attention. 

As up to the present time I have reecived no instructions from your Lordship 
as to the line | am to pursue in the course of the negotiation, | stated to Lord 
John Russell, that considering him as entirely informed of the views of Her 
Majesty's Government, | should give my best support to the decisions he might 
think it advisable to adopt, 

T have, &e.

erroneous, I endeavoured to correct in my despatch to your Lordship No. 53 of

The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland. 


(No, 93.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, March 18, 18.5. 

COUNT COLLOREDO has communicated to me a circular despatch 
from Count Buol to the Austrian Ministers at the German Courts, on the recent 
proceedings in the Diet. | . 

Count Buol commences by stating that Baron Prokesch had laid before the 
Diet a report of the Austrian army under the command of General Hess, in 
fulflment of the resolution of the Diet of the 8th of February, The Prussian 
Plenipotentiary had proposed in the Military Commission that the preparation 
of the Federal contingents should take place within the territary of the Confede- 
ration. 

This proposal was not adopted, but the Austrian Government points out 
that the present question cannot be considered merely as a Federal question ; 
the Confederation is called upon in pursuance of the Treaty of the 20th of 
April, and of the resolution of the 9th of December, not only to defend the 
Federal territory, but to uphold the four points as buses of peace, and to repel 
every attack upon the Austrian territory aud algo upon the Austrian troops itt 
the Principalities. 

When, however, Baron Prokesch submitted the report of the Austrian army 
to the Diet, the Prussian Plenipotentiary distinctly dented that the resolution of 
the Sth of February was founded on those of the 24th of July and 9th of 
December. 

M. de Bismark maintained that united resistance to an attack on the 
Austrian Empire, or the Principalities, was altogether out of the question, and 
that the SanlitOn of the &th of February was based on entirely new grounds, 
namely, on the necessity, in the present state of Europe, of maintaining an armed 

force ready to be employed in any direction. 

In a conversation with Baron Prokesch, M. de Bismark had mentioned the 
intention of the Prussian Government to propose that the garrisons of the 
Federal fortresses of Rastadt, Mayence, Landau, and Luxemburgh, should be 
placed on the war footing. 

lt is difticult, Count Buol observes, to reconcile these views, which imply 
an armed neutrality, with the missions of Baron Usedom and General Wedel 
to Landon and Paris. 

The Austrian Government thinks it right to call the serious attention of 
the Confederates. to the danger of giving any other meaning to their present 
attitude than that of preparation to carry out the resolution of the Diet last 
rear. 

: Hitherto Austria had not considered it necessary to make any specific 


401 


declaration respecting the purpose of the military measures of the Diet; the 
engagements entered into by the Confederation, the policy of Austria, and of 
those German States who agree with her, rendered such a declaration super- 
fluous : but it would be otherwise if at the moment when Germany is arming, 
and when it must shortly be decided whether or not peace is to be restored to 
Europe, the Confederation should by its declarations and measures follow that 
tendency towards an expectant neutrality, free from all specific obligations, which 
has already been but too plainly indicated. Against such measures and decla- 
rations the Austrian Government would regard it as an imperative duty empha- 
tically to protest, and to decline all responsibility as to the consequences which 
might ensue: they would especially consider a demand for the withdrawal of the 
Austrian Contingent to German territory as an indirect abandonment of the 
engagements entered into by the Dict in the true interest of Germany, and they 
would denounce as an uncalled-for provocation the proposal to place on the 
wie (OO nOe the aoe on the frontier of France. 
i¢ Imperial Plenipotentiary has been instruct hese consi 
ith cotta ue iP ce ' structed to urge these considerations 
_ ‘The Austrian Government trust that they will meet with the same convic- 
tions among the Representatives of their Federal allies ; and that the Germanic 
Confederation, while, in conjunction with Austria, it develops its power, will 
not, in case the nezotiations for peace should fail, give any of its members, or 
any of the European Cabinets, any reason to doubt the object of its armament. 
I thanked Count Colloredo for this communication, which was sutisfactory 
and said that the tone of Count Buol’s despatch seemed well adapted to the 
occasion, as it would have been impossible to have met in a less decided manner 
the proposal of M. de Bismark, which was a fresh proof of the determination of

o share the suspicious and unfriendly feclings with which England and France

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon—(Recetved March 13.) 


(No, 94.) 
My lord, Berlin, March 10, 1855, 

UPON the receipt of your Lordship’s despatch No. 84 of the &th instant, 
| immediately called upon Baron Manteuffel, and informed him that intelligence 
had reached Her Majesty’s Government that 40,000 muskets from the Prussian 
stores at Cologne had been lately sold to the Russian Government, and that | 
was directed to request an explanation of a proceeding which amounted to an 
act of hostility against England and France. 

His lxcelleney replied that it was impossible that this could have taken 
place, and that he believed the amount of arms | had stated would not be found 
in any of the stores on the Rhine. 1 rejoined that it was not probable that this. 
story could be altogether without foundation, though there might be an error in 
the quantity of arms stated, He replied that he should make inquines of the

I have since had some conversation with Baron Manteuffel respecting this 
document, and endeavoured to discover the interpretation which the King of 
Prussia and his Government were disposed to put on the passage which states 
that the views and intentions of Peter, Catherine, Alexander, and Nicholas, will 
be carried into execution, 

Baron Manteuffel said that the King spoke of the manifesto last night as 
being moderate in its tone, and that it was not intended for foreign countries, 
but for Tussia. 

L answered that I could by no means view it in this light, and that the 
allusions to the policy of his predecessors and to his intention to place Russia in 
the highest pinnacle of glory, was not calculated to satisfy England and France 
that the Enpeter of Russia was disposed to desist from attempts at future 
spoliation of Turkey, and was much to be regretted, particularly at a moment 
when Conferences for peace were about to be opened at Vienna; and further 
ie these allusions were likely to be considered as throwing down the gauntlet 
to Europe. 

Baron Manteuffel replied that the King had observed to him on this passage 
of the manifesto that something of the same kind would be found in that 
ublished by the Emperor Nicholas on his accession; and that His Majesty 
ne desired a copy of this document to be brought, to him that he might compare 

em. 

I rejoined that I begged him toa speak to the King on the objectionable 
passages, and urge His Majesty to lose no time in requiring an explanation of 
them from St. Petersburgh, for it appeared to me impossible that an impartial

_ I LEARN, from a private and confidential source, that, in lis reports 
from St. Petersburgh, Count Miinster states that, in the opinion of the highest 
military authorities, entire confidence may be placed in the sufficiency of the 
defensive measures adopted by Russia on her line of frontier from the northern 
part of Finland to the extreme limit of her Asiatic provinees, with the exception 
of the line extending from Riga to the Vistula and the Pruth, for the defence of 
which she has less reason to care, so long as Prussia (on whom she counts with 
perfect reliance) maintains her present system. 

In stating that this quarter is regarded by the Russian Government as the 
most vulneruble for attack, and the least euarded, Count Minster expresses his 
opinion that, in the event of any attack on the part of Austria, a sufficient force 
could he concentrated to act on the defensive, but le does not seem to consider 
any offensive operations os in any way premeditated on the part of Russia. 

Previous to his death, the late limperor had concerted a new defensive 
organisation, by which fresh corps of the reserves would be formed into divi- 
sions, anid Placed in support of the first line of the army. ‘These would be again 
supported by a third line composed of the militia lately called into vigour, to 
which i Cavalry force of Cossacks and Irregulars would be attached, Thus 
three lines of military defence would be established in like manner with the 
three lines of fortresses which now form the bulwark of the Russian Empire on 
the Polish frontier.

helmet used by the army (in imitation ot those worn by the Prussian army), and 
to substitute for them the fur cap now worn by the Caucasian treops, which is

Inclosure in No. 425. 
Extract from the Un-afficial part of the “ Staats Anzeiger.” 


f Translation.} 


Berlin, March 9.—WE hive received details from St. Petersburgh, dated 
Marcel 3, respecting the illness and death of His Majesty the Emperor Nicholas, 

For some time back [is Majesty, as now appears, suffered very severely 
from grippe. About the 16th February, the physician in ordinary, Dr. Mandt, 
requested permission to consult other medical men, ‘The Einperor received 
this lightly, and allowed the physician in. ordinary, Dr. Karell, to be called in. 
The state of the Emperor became gradually worse in consequence of sleeplessiiess 
anil increased cough, with great secretion, so much so, that the physicians on the 
Oth Vebruary, requested His Majesty not to leave his apartment. “i 

The Emperor would not hear of it, upon which one of the physicians said : 
“ No surgeon in the whole army would permit a soldier who was as ill as your 
Majesty, to loave the hospital, because the patient would be certain to return 
to it in a worse state.” The Emperor replied: ‘Gentlemen, you lave now 
done your duty; 1 thank you: 1 will do mine.” In rather-a cold day he got 
into his sledge and drove to the manéye, for the purpose of inspecting some men 
of the Infantry of the Guard, who were under orders for Lithuania, to fill up the 
regiments, 

During this inspection, which was his lust; appearance in public, the 
Emperor was very fatigued, coughed much, spat a creat deal, and said, in going 
away, “Tamas if 1 came out of a bath," though it was anything but warm in 
the manége. In this state the Emperor went to the Minister of War (Prince 
Dolzorucki), who was unwell, told him not to go out too soon, and returned to 
the Winter Paluee. In the evening he attended the pravers for the first week in 
Lent, then remained with the Empress, but complained of cold, and kept his 
cloak on in the room. 

From that evening the Eniperor left his small study no more. He there 
received the Colonel and Aide-de-camp vou ‘Tettenborn on the 44 of February, 
lying on his sofa, covered with a cloak, and dispatched him to Sebastopol. His 
Majesty afterwards gave up the management of business to the Grand Duke 
Hereditary, 

From the 24th-27th of February, nothing further was answered to ques- 
tions, than the Emperor keeps his bed because he is “ieverish; the cough is 
becoming loose, kc." 

During the whole illness, the Emperor lay on his camp-bed, that is, a leather 
sack filled with hay, and a pillow ofthe same sort, covered with a blanket and a 
cloak, 

It was only on the 28th of February that his state was considered as 
decidedly serious. During the night of the Ist of March he beeame rapidly 
worse. ‘The physicians feared a paralysis of the lings. On the evening of the 
Ist of March, all hopes for the Emperor were given up. ‘The Empress and the 
Grand Duke Hereditary, at the desire of the physicians, requested him to receive 
the sacrament. 

On this occasion the Emperor appears for the first time to have perceived 
the danger of his state. But hardly any impression appears to have been 
perceptible, ; 

During the night (from Ist-2nd of March), De. Mandt told the Emperor 
that he was dangerously ill, and that his lunes were dangerously affected. The 
Emperor said very quietly, “Then, perhaps, Lam in danger of a paralysis of the 
lungs.” Dr. Mandt replied, ‘It is very possible.” 

The Emperor thereupon received the sacrament very calmly and collectedly, 
took leave of the Empress, the linperial children and grand-children, blessed and 
embraced each of them, giving the blessing with a firm voice, and kept only the 
Empress and the Grind Duke Hereditary with him, 

This took place about 4 o'clock in the morning, 

Later the Emperor said to the Empress, Now go and repose yourself a 
little, T pray you.” She replied, Let me stay with you; 1 should like to 
depart with you, if it were possible.’ Upon whieh he said, “No, you must 
still remain here below; take care of your health, that you may become the 


411 


centre of the whole family; go, I will have you called when the moment 
approaches.” The Empress obeyed this wish so decidedly pronounced, and 
went. 

Then the Emperor caused Count Orloff, Count Adlerberg, and Prince 
Dolgorucki to enter; thanked them for their fidelity, and took leave of them. 
Later he called in his own servants, thanked them for their services, blessed 
them, and took leave of them, during which the Emperor himself is said to have 
been much affected, At last the woman of the bedehamber, Von Rohrbeck, was 
for. The Emperor thanked her also for the fidelity she had always shown 
towards the Empress, for the care with which she had always tended her during 
her illnesses, and even lately ; requested her not to forsake the Empress, and 
finally added: “ And salute my dear Peterhof for me.” ‘The Emperor also took 
the hand of Dr. Karell, and said, “Itis not your fault.” 

When the confessor, Bajanoff, spoke to the Emperor, he took the Empress’ 
hand and placed it in that of the priest, as if confiding the Empress to the 
clergyman. 

After this the Emperor for a time lost the power of speech, during which he 
erossed himself often, and prayed silently. Later the Emperor regained his 
speech, and spoke occasionally till his death, which took place in presence of 
the whole family on the 2nd March, at 10 minutes past 12 o'clock at noon. 

Almost the last distinct words the Emperor uttered were: “ Dites 4 Fritz 
~ rester toujours le méme pour la Russie, et de ne pas oublier les paroles de 

apa. 

The Emperor suffered the agonies of death with a calmness of soul, a 
Christian resignation and a manly fortitude, which was truly sublime. Only a 
man of a pure conscience, and with the firm conviction of having always desired 
what was right, and having acted accordingly, could die thus. God will be 
merciful to the Emperor! [tis truly superhuinan what that Sovereign person- 
ally in the course of the last years has morally suffered and struggled with ; 
how every wounded soldier was a pang to his heart, 

The corpse at first became much altered. ‘Towards the evening the fine 
features had become more imposing than ever in their calmness and regularity, 

Until now Her Majesty the Empress has withstood this unexpected and 
terrible blow with a wonderful fortitude. Yesterday evening she passed a whole 
hour alone with the body. 

The state of stupefaction into which the suddenness of this terrible blow 
had placed everybody, is gradually giving way to the feeling of grief,

receipt of them, | proceeded to the residence of M, Drouyn de Lhuys to inquire

and, if so, what impression they had made upon him, 

His Excellency stated that he had no very late news from M. de Bourqueney; 
but a telegraphic epee of yesterday's date from that Minister was brought to 
him while Lwas with him, It contained the substance of the speceh which Count 
Buol proposed making on opening the Couferences, the text of the four points 
being word for word the sane as that contained in the despatch addressed by the 
British Plenipotentiaries to your Lordship. It stated somewhat more distinctly the 
proceedings which Count Buol proposed should be followed at the first meeting, 
as also the engagement of Austria to persist in obtaining of Russia the develop-

No. 441. 
The Earl of Clarendon to Lord John Russell, 
(No. 14.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, March 15, 1855. 


YOUR Lordship’s despatches Nos. 11 and 12 have been received, and laid 
before the Queen. 

Her Majesty's Government have read with particular interest your Lord- 
ship’s able and important despatch No, 12 of the 7th instant, and | shall now 
briefly state to your Lordship their opinion upon the different subjects to which 
that despatch relates. ae. 

Her Majesty's Government entirely approve of the determination of your 
Lordship and of Lord Westmorland, not to meet the Russian Plenipotentianies 
until their full powers were received, 

They approve of your intention to record in a Protocol, at the first Confer- 
ence, the bases of negotiation that were agreed to on January 7th; and they 
had every reason to believe that Count Buol was virtually pledged to that 
course of proceeding which is essential to the prevention of future misunder- 
standing. Her Majesty's Government have relinquished it with regret, in 
consequence of your Lordship’s subsequent communications, and have agreed to 
the mode of proceeding insisted upon by Count Buol, feeling, as did the French 
Government, that to refuse to enter upon negotiations, and to risk a rupture 
with Austria upon a point of form, however important, would not have been 
justifiable, Tt is right, I should add, that the objections to complying with 
Count Buol's demand were diminished by the entire reliance of Her Majesty's 
Government upon the firmness with which your Lordship will resist any 
attempts to impair the substance of those conditions upon which we are bound 
to insist. 

Her Majesty's Government consider it indispensable that no doubt should 
exist with respect to all Protectorate over the Principalities being abandoned by 
Russia; and that the suggestion for the revival of so much of the ancient 
Treaties between Russia and ‘Turkey as may not be inconsistent with the new 
Treaty, should be resisted. 

Those ancient ‘Treaties are objectionable in form as well as in substance, 
and are so many records of Russian aggression and of ‘Turkish humiliation and 
defeat. 

We should insist, rather, that as all former Treaties have been abrogated 
by the war, one new ‘Treaty should contain every stipulution wecessary for 
regulating the relations between Russia and Turkey. 

Her Majesty's Government strongly object to the proposal of Count Buol 
that the Conference should be divided into Committees. Such a course might 
have been useful at the Congress of Vienna, where there were a greater number 
of Plenipotentiaries, and where a vast amount of business was to be transacted, 
and questions distinct in their character were to be discussed; hut in the 
present instance, the business, if conducted In a proper spirit by the Russian 
Plenipotentiaries, should lie in a comparatively small compass; the questions at 
issue all hinge upon each other; their discussion by Committees would be 
unsatistactory to those members of the Conference who did not form part of 
such Committees; they would necessarily be reidiscussed: and a loss, instead of 
an economy of time, would be the result. 

The Principalitics should unquestionably be defended by frontier fortresses, 
but there can be no good reason why those fortresses should be oceupied by 
mixed Austrian and ‘Turkish garrisons. Such a proposal can only mean to 

repare the way for Austrian domination in the Principalities, which would not 
e preferable to that of Russia, Indeed the conduct of the Austrian troops in 
the Principalities, and their harsh and arbitrary treatment of the people, have 
rendered their occupation more hateful than the Russian; aud a system of 
mixed garrisons could not fuil to produce the most unfriendly relations between 
Austria and the Porte. 

Her Majesty's Government coneur with Count Buol that Russia should be 
required to surrender her territorial jurisdiction on the ieft bank of the Danube, 
This should be secured by binding provisions: and it is not only desirable, but 


422 


necessary, that there should be an English and a French member of the 
Syndicate for regulating the navigation of the Danube. 

Her Majesty's Government entirely approve the language held by your 
Lordship with respeet to the third basis. So long as [Russia maintains an 
imposing force at Sebastopol, with the means of transporting that force wherever 
she pleases, the Ottoman Empire is menaced by a standing danger, and the 
peace and the equilibrium of Europe are insecure. 

Count Buol’s reply to your Lordship can hardly have been sincere, for his 
Excellency must well know that long before the Sultan could call his allies to 
his aid, a Russian army might be in possession of Constantinople. 

Her Majesty's Government will be prepared to consider any proposition 
that Count Buol may desire to bring forward on this subject ; but it is proper 
that his Excellency should be warned that they do not sce the probability of 
assenting to any scheme that failed to secure the effectual limitation of the 
Russian naval furce in the Black Sca, because it appears impossible in any other 
way to provide for the safety of the Ottoman Empire, which is the object of the 
war, and must therefore be the condition of peace. 

‘Austria, has, no doubt, as your Lordship says, a real and deep interest im 
preventing Russian aggression on Turkey, but her established system is to 
temporize, She thinks the immediate danger to Turkey gone by, and balancing 
the evil to herself of future danger to Turkey from Russian aggression against 
the immediate evil to herself of the prolongation of a war into which she may 
be drawn as a party, she fears the present more than the future, and she would 
watch up matters any how for the present, and take her chance for the future, 
But the condition of England and Vranece is different; we have made war, 
we have made immense exertions and enormous sucrifices of all kinds, and we 
cannot consent to patch up the matter by an insufficient Treaty, as Count Buol 
appears to suppose, for such a course would be both dangerous and disgraceful. 
Russia, it 15 true, may say that we have not taken Sebastopol, nor destroyed 
her Black Sea fleet, and that we are therefore not entitled to demand a 
limitation of Russian naval power in the Black Sea, nor to stipulate with respect 
to the fortress of Sebastopol; but to that our reply must be, not that we will 
abandon conditions without which no peace can give future safety, but that we 
will withvall the resourees of England and France continue the war until we 
place ourselves in the position in whieh, according to the assumed Russian 
objection, we should be entitled to put forward those necessity demands, 

It is with great satisfaction, however, that Her Majesty's Government 
learn that Count Buel and his colleague are in your Lordship’s opinion earnestly 
desirous to ward off from Europe the dangers of Russian preponderance, and, 
indeed, it could hardly be otherwise, if those statesmen take a clear and compre- 
hensive view of the position of Austria, and admit that the gratification of 
Russian ambition in regard to ‘Turkey must be attended with consequences most 
disastrous to Austria; for the possession of Constantinople involves the iMie= 
diate possession of the Danubian Principalities and the kuropean provinces of 
‘Turkey, and at once brings Russia, in overwhelming and surrounding force and 
paes to the very threshold of the Austrian dominions, It was more fortunate 
on Austria than for any other Power, that the mine which Russia was preparing 
for Europe has been prematurely exploded, and that her vast designs of aggres- 
sion have been brought to light and frustrated. Most fortunate it is for Austria 
that this should not have occurred at a time when, according to the words of the 
Emycror Nicholas, Austria was bound to adopt the policy of Russia, but that it 
should have taken place at a moment when Austria ts alive to the reality and 
the imminence of her danger, and when she finds England and Franee, closely 
united in policy and in arms, ready to cooperate with her, and determined to 
maintain the independence of Europe, But most unfortunate it will be for 
Austria, if she fails to turn to her own account this favourable conjuncture of 
circumstances, Which may never return, i she adopts i temporizing policy, and 
contents herself with the minimum of security that she can ascertain that Russia 
will be disposed to grant, instead of wasuming an attitude betitting the magnitude 
of the oecusion, and preparing herself in curnest for a struggle, success in which 
will be worth all the saerifices it may entail, 

Her Majesty’s Government are deeply sensible of the value of the Austrian 
alliunee, not alone as an aid in the present war, but also as the most eflectual 
reaus of maintaining peace hereafter, and although in order to secure and cement 


423 


that alliance, they are prepared to sacrifice such preconceived opinions as may 
with safety be abandoned, yet, after all the exertions and all the sacrifices that 
this country has cheerfully made, and is still prepared to make, they cannot pive 
up any point on which the conscientiously believe that the future satety of 
Europe depends. Our national honour, and a due regard to the true interests 
of the country forbid us to agree to any inadequate arrangement, or to consent to 
any terms of peace that will not be ratified by public opinion in England, 

Your Lordship will have the goodness to communicate this despatch to 
Lord Westmorland. 

Lam 


» Ce 
(Signed) CLARENDON,

The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Cowley. 
(No. 280.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, March 15, 1855. 


| HAVE received your Excellency’s despatch No. 299 of the 12th instant, 
reporting the opinion of the French Government with regard to Count Buol's 
proposal as to the course to _be pursued in opening the Conferences at Vienna ; 
and I have to state to your Excellency in reply, that Her Majesty's Government 
think that Count Buol has departed from his engagement by endeavouring to 
substitute his own interpretation of the bases, whieh 16 in fact Prince Gortcha- 
kofl’s, for that of England and France, and that the English and French 
Plenipotentiaries would therefore have been entitled to refuse their assent to 
the proposal of the Austrian Plenipotentiary, and to suspend all further 
proceedings: but Her Majesty's Government concur with that of the Emperor 
of the French, that in the eyes of the world they would not have been justified 
in running the risk of a rupture with Austria, b declining to enter upon 
negotiations when a poimt of form alone, as it might he represented to have 
been, was in question, and it was upon this ground, aud in order that not the 
slightest doubt should attach to the sincerity of their intentions, that they have 
authorized the British Plenipotentiary to proceed im the manner proposed by

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received March 165; 


(No. 317. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, March 15, 1895. 


DURING an interview with which I was yesterday honoured by the 
Emperor, His Majesty informed me that the Austrian Government had at length 
made overtures for the signature of a Military Convention with France. ‘These 
overtures appear to have been addressed directly to the Emperor, as [ under- 
stood His Majesty to say that he had only yesterday morning apprized 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys of their import. I presume that they were made to His 
Majesty on Monday afternoon, when | know that M. de Hitbner had an audience 
of him. 

The Emperor stated to me, in general terms, the nature of the Austrian 
propositions, ‘They are based upon the supposition that to contend effectually 
with Russiu, the allies must bring 1,200,000 men inte the field, of which 800,000 
should form the first line of operations, and the remaining 400,00 the second. 
The Austrian caleulations for producing this force are twofold, namely, with 
and without the effective assistance of Prussia; but in both contingencies the 
cooperation of Sweden is reckoned upon. 

Supposing Prussia to enter the field against the aggressor, Austria requires 
of France 50,000 men in Galliciu, and 50,000 more to aid the Swedes in the 
north, besides the army engaged in the Crimea; and she calculates the forces of 
the allies as follows : 


Austria +e are ha 300,000 
Prussia ae a ise 150,000 
Germany 100,000 


Anglo-French army in the Crimea ... 150,000 
Franco-Swedish army in Baltic a 100,000 
French Contingent in Gallicia rs 50,000 


—. 


840,000 


The reserves of these armics, together with the Sardinian and Turkish 
contingents, would make up the amount required of 1,200,000 men. 

On the other hand, should Prussia persist in her present isolation, lrance 
would be required to make larger sacrifices, and to reais au effective force of 
300,000 men, exclusive of the army engaged in the Crimea, Austria would, 
under these circumstances, require 100,000 French soldiers in Galicia, and 
£0,000 more ready to mureh for the same destination at a moment's notice. 
She would also require the presence of a French army on the Rhine, to hold 
the Prussians in check. 


425 


After giving me these details, the Emperor said that of course he could 
have no difficulty in entering into the first of these combinations, and that he 
found, upon inquiry, he could take upon himself the engagements implied by 
the second; but -he should object, in any way, and under any circumstances, to 
sending troops to the Baltic, as he had no means of transporting them. The 
Swedish army, however, might be augmented, if Sweden was furnished with a 
subsidy, which might be easily arranged, His Majesty regretted, therefore, that 
he had not at once declared his readiness to enter into the obligations required 
of him; and upon His Majesty deigning to inquire of me whether T did not 
think that the Convention should be agreed to, I replied that the signature of 
any instrument which bound Austria more closely to the allied Powers would 
be a gain, and that this Convention, as having that effect, might, in ny humble 
opinion, be concluded with advantage. 

I have, however, since reflected, that this Convention would be concluded 
in virtue of the Seeret Article of the ‘Treaty of the 2nd of December ; and I 
thought it right, therefore, in informing M. Drouyn de Lhuys this morning of 
what the Emperor had confided to me, to remark that that Article provided for 
a common concert between the three Powers, and that although there was 
nothing which had passed at present between France and Austria, which could 
be objected to on the part of Her Majeaty’s Government, | deemed it my duty 
to eall his attention to the propriety of abiding strictly by the obligations 
contracted between the three Governments. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys said, that he should, of course, communicate imme- 
diately with Her Majesty’s Government upon the subject; that the overtures 
were as yet only of a confidential nature; that nothing had been settled; and 
that it was only yesterday morning that the Emperor had placed the Austrian 
statement in his hands, He would, however, send a copy of it to-night to 
Count Walewski, for your Lordship’s information. 

I should add, that the numbers and disposition of the troops, as mentioned 
generally to me by M. Drouyn de Lhuys, differed, though not very essentially, 
from those given to me by the Emperor. 

I have, &e. 


(Signed) COWLEY.

My Lord, Stuttgardt, March 12, 1855. 

THE Marquis de Ferriére le Vayer had lately an interview with the King, 
to take leave on his going to France for a few weeks, and he has informed me 
that His Majesty, in speaking of the Emperor Nicholas, demurred to his having 
been a great man, contending that he had given proof of his being neither a 
great general nora great politician, and that his chief claim to distinction was 
the energy and determination of his character. 

[may perhaps take the liberty of observing that this appreciation exactly 
coincides with the opinion I have always entertained of the Emperor Nicholas ; 
and it may possibly be suid of liim, as it has been of Louis XLV, that he was a 
vreat Sovercign but not a great man. 

The King criticized with some severity the late Emperor's conversations 
with Sir Hamilton Seymour. 5 

His Majesty insinuated that perhaps now the Western Powers might 
abandon the siege of Sebastopol, and that no reliance was to be pliced on the 
active cooperation of Austria; the replies to both of which observations were 
naturally more guarded than acquiescent, 

| may add, that disbelief in the possibility of Austrian hostilities against 
Russia seems rather prevalent here, 

In speaking of the Grand Duke Constantine, the King stated that he had 
reason to believe in His Imperial Hizhness's having lately adopted more 
moderate and peaceful views. 

His Majesty mentioned a report that Lord John Russell, while at Berlin, 


426 


had said that England wished for peace, but that France did not, 1 told 
M. de Ferridre that he might safely regard that report as a clumsy falsehood, in 
which he readily concurred. 1 added, that its origin might very possibly be the 
effete hope of sowing dissension between the two countries, in which he also 
concurred, 

The King expressed annoyance at the late vote of the Chamber of Deputies 
in favour of the policy of Austria. un ee 

Considering His Majesty's advanced age and high military reputation, it 
may be that much of his evident Austrian aversion springs from the youth and 
military tendencies of the Emperor Francis-Joseph. mites 

As to the King’s precise sentiments upon the Eastern question, if may 
perhaps be said, that neither success nor failure on either side would either elate 
or depress him, provided Russia were not to increase her former power, but that 
he would look. with pleasure on any event which might safely tend to expel the 
Turks from Europe. é 

His Majesty's remarks to the Marquis de Ferriere may possibly serve to 
show that Russian influence in Germany has been in great part the personal 
influence of the Emperor Nicholas. 

On the other hand, it is to be recollected that the recent debate in the 
Second Chamber, about putting the contingent on a war footing, during which 
Russia was frequently and virulently attacked, but never once defended, took 
place befcre the news of the Emperor's death. 

While considering that event, it seems natural to reflect how much depends 
on when a person dies. Had the Emperor Nicholas died two years ago, Europe 
might have deplored his loss, She now feels that loss to be a benefit. : 

Perhaps hardly more difference would have been made in the world’s 
opinion of Napoleon, had he died after the Pence of Tilsit. ; 

It may be no exaggeration to say, that the Emperor Nicholas has lost his 
life in sacrificing the best position for the worst—im exchanging the applause of 
Europe for her condemnation—in converting associated sympathy into confede- 
rated enmity. ee 

I feel that 1 may owe some apology to your Lordship for venturing on the 
above ohservations.

When he had finished reading, 1 remarke! on the omission of all reference 
to the ‘Treaties of Russia with Turkey, the non-renewal of which was put 
so prominently forward in the memorandum. ‘ 

Count Buol replied that the abolition of the protectorate of Russia over 
Wallachia and Moldavia, and of the right of protection over the Christian 
subjects of the Sultan, would necessarily lead to the non-renewal of those 
Treaties by which these protectorates were eanctioned, But these were not 
material points of the four points ; they were only consequences to be deduced 
from them. 

Baron Bourqueney said he was convineed Prince Gortchakoff would make 
no difficulty on this point; he had admitted these consequences is flowing 
necessarily from the first and fourth points of the memorandum. With respect 
te the second point the memorandum: states the alteration of the ‘Treaty of 
Adrianople as an alternative : and while it is declared that “im any case " there 
must be a syndicate to secure the free navigation of the Danube, it is only said 
to be desirable (‘il conviendrait) to alter the Hrd Article of the Treaty of 
Adrianople. It would be impossible, therefore, to bind Prince Gortchakolf to 
an alteration of Treaty, of the necessity of which the allies do not appear to be 
quite convinet. 

Count Buol had no objection to my stating to Prince Gortchakoff the 
non-renewal of the Treaties affecting the Protectorate of Wallachia and Moldavia, 
und of Christians generally, a8 a necessary consequence of the bases proposed. 

Baron Prokesch observed, that although the Treaties could not be wholly 
renewed, there might be some parts of them which were essential to the resto- 
ration of friendly relations between Russia and Turkey. I-said in such a case 
it would be better to insert those Articles in a new ‘Treaty, than to renew the 
old Treaties. 

I then raised the point of our ‘nstructions which prescribed positively the 
signature of a@ Protocol containing the memorandum delivered to Prince Gort- 
chakoff on the 28th of December. 

Count Buol said he could only have consented to the communication of 
that memorandum as a non-official document. He held it to be an agreement 
binding on Austria, France, and Great Britain, but not on Russia, 


Prince Gortchakoff had assented to it in principle, and therefore the three 
Powers had.declared themselves ready to enter into negotiations. That he was 
not prepared to require the renewed assent of Russia to the memorandum. 

Prince Gortchakof might fairly say, “I assented to your terms; you 
declared you were ready to negotiate ; 1 do not depart from what | have said; 
well, let us negotiate.” We know of no fair answer to such a statement, if 
made by Prinee Gortchakotf; and for his own part he was not ready, on the part 
of Austria, to require the signature of a Protocol containing the memorandum. 

Indeed he should protest strongly against it, and leave all the responsibility 
an the maritime Powers, who would be blamed by the public opinion of Europe 
for thus defeating the hopes of peace on ft point of form. Russia, since she 
accepted the four points, had been blameless, and if we now refused to negotiate, 
we should commit the fault of which she on former occasions had been guilty, 

It would not have been dificult to answer this reasonme of Count Buol; 
indeed it seems to me that the refusal to make the memorandum official, and 
yet to found upon Prince Gortchakoff’s acceptance of it-so solemn a proceeding 
as the opening of negotiations for peace, invelves a singular contradiction. 

The question was not, however, how to confute the logical positions of 
Count Buol, but how to obtain the objects of the war as declared in the four 
points. 

With this view the important matter to consider was, whether the statement 
to be made by Count Buol contained a sufficiently satisfactory statement of the 
four points as to justify ws in opening the negotiation; whether the bases so 
atated, with Austria on our side, would not be far better than an absolute refusal 


431 


to negotiate unless the memorandum were accepted by Prince Gortchakolf, at 
the risk, nay with the certainty, of a separation from Austria. 

When we placed before our eyes the colour which might be given to this 
transaction in Europe, and eanecially in Germany,—when we considered that the 
four points, so long insisted upon, might be said to be adopted by Austria with 
energy, and accepted by Russia without reserve, but rejected on a point of form 
by the very Powers who had first prepared them, we could not but feel 1t was 
right to request our Governments to sanction the opening of the Conference on 
the terms proposed by Austria. 

Indeed, my Lord, when I reflect on the long and vexatious discussions 
which took place last year between Petersburgh, Constantinople, and Vienna 
on the placing of parentheses and the collocation of adverbs,—when | consider 
that those discussions were merely the approaches of war, but that at the 
present moment all the horrors of war are raging, to the destruction of so many 
lives, and with the prospect of further bloodshed, I could not think we should 
be justified in refusing to commence negotiations for the sake of some phrases 
not so much omitted as left to be implied. 

Such was the view which presented itself to us in the contemplation of a 
possible peace, 

It is very probable, however, that in the course of the negotiations, perhaps 
very early, some question may arise upon which a rupture must ensue. But tn 
mater we shall break upon some security refused, or some material stipulation 
omitted, 

The cause would appear to all the world « valid ground of difference, and 
those most desirons of peace would at all events be convinced that no ght cause 
had led to the rupture of the negotiations. 

‘The Conferences would then have brought to light the real ground for the 
continuance of war. It is to be hoped that the point would be one which 
Austria would view in the same light with ourselves. In that case we should 
have an advantaze which in the present we should lose. It is my opinion, con- 
firmed by that of others, that if Russia refuses concessions which Austria, 
as well as Great Britain, think reasonable, Austria must hereafter take part in 
the war. She will of course be very wary in committing herself upon points 
on which Russia is likely to resist; but she will not refuse to concur in asking 
for guarantees, which, in her opinion, will form a sufficient barrier to Kussian 
ambition. 

It is in order to keep alive this hope that Ihave asked your Lordship to 
sanction the course which Lord Westmorland and I wish to take. Tt appeara 
to us to be consistent with the steps hitherto taken by the allies, clear and direct 
in itself, and calculated to reflect honour on the Powers which adopt it. 

I have, Xe. 
(Signed) J, RUSSELL.

(No. 17.) 
My Lord, Vienna, March 14, 1855, 


| RECEIVED this morning your Lordship's telegraphic despatch of 
esterday evening, and, after conferring with Lord Westmorland and Baron 
ourqueney, | waited upon Count Buol. 
At my request Count Buol read to me again his proposed address to the 
Conference, 

lu that address he proposes to state firmly that Austria adheres, and will 
adhere, to the course of policy she has adopted, and to her engagements to her 
allies, whatever snerifices it may cost her. 

He will declare that, the bases of pacification having been agreed upon 
between Austria, France, and Great Britain, have been communicated to the 
Russian Plenipotentiary, and were agreed to, principle, by him. 

He will then state the bases, as T have already enumerated them ta your 
Lordship, 


55 


a i -—~ 


443 


Upon listening to this enumeration, it appeared to me that the word 
“reconnus par les Sultans” applied as well to any improved Constitutions which 
the Sultans might confer upon the Principalities of Wallachia and Moldavia as 
upon their existing institutions. On my inquiry, Count Buol confirmed this 
interpretation. Indeed all our discussions have proceeded on the supposition 
that the present Constitution of the Principalities will he modified to the advan- 
tage of the inhabitants, as well as for the security of the Sovereign. 

I then proposed to Count Buol to insert words to the following effect in his 
address : 


«Nos Gouvernements se réservent, comme ils l'ont toujours fait, la faculte 

de poser elles: conditions particuliéres qui leur paraitraient exigées en sus des 

uatre garanties, par Vintéret gendral de l'Europe, pour prévenic le retour des 
dernitres complications.” 


Count Buol said he thought such words would come better from me as 
representing one of the belligerent Powers than from him; that if 1 would 
express my assent to the bases as laid down by him, and would conclude by 
making the reserve I proposed, he would not hesitate to give me his support. 

f said 1 would consult M. de Bourqueney, and endeavour with him to frame 
a suitable declaration. 

Lhave since heard that some doubts are entertained as to the propriety of 
making this reserve immediately after Count Buol’s address ; but it seems to 
me, | confess, both the right moment and that which is most in accordance with 
the instructions I have received. | 

T had afterwards a good deal of conversation with Count Buol with respect 
to the reserve made by Prince Gortchakoff on the third point, of the sovereign 
rights of his master. 

Count Buol observed very justly that if these rights were for the Sovereign 
to withhold, they were likewise his to concede. ‘Chat no one would doubt the 
right of the Sovereign Power to regulate duties of entry in the ports subject to 
it: but no one could doubt either that the Sovereign Power could make Treaties 
by which the duties of customs eould be fixed at a specified amount 

LT mentioned an argument 1 had heard from hich authority, that, although 
the right of the Emperor of Russia could not be questioned, yet the interest of 
Europe required a different arrangement, and Europe would be justified in 
making war on a point of European ‘terest. I added that it seemed to me 
that the interest of Europe would best be consulted by a diminution of the 
Rugsiun fleet, which was a perpetual menace to Turkey. 

Count Buol is quite prepared to. propose the reduction of the Russian fleet 
in the Black Sea as the best mode of carrying into effect the third basis; but 1 
cannot assert that: he will persist in urging the mode on the Plenipotentiary of 
Russia. 

I have, however, considered it a great advantage that the Foreign Minister 
of Austria should give his sanction to the proposal of France and Great Britain, 
ag the most expedient and most reasonable course. 

Should newotiations unhappily break off’ on this point, it will be impossible 
for him afterwards to allege that the bolligerents insisted on terms unreasonable 
‘1 themselves, and unnecessarily humiliating to Russia. 

What he may say is, that other securities might lave been found equally 
efficient, and less unpalateable to the Autocrat, whose pretensions have been 50 
lofty, and whose proclamations have so recently announced the continuance of 
the policy of Peter and of Catherine.

Lord John Russell to the Earl of Clarendon.— (Received March 18.) 


(No, 20.) 
My Lord, Fienna, March 15, 1855. 


1 HAVE the honour to inform your Lordship that the first Conference for 
the purpose of negotiating peace took place this day. 

The Conference began with the production of full powers on the part of the 
Representatives. . : 

As soon as this ceremony was over, Prince Gortchakoff took the oppor- 
tunity of saying that he only wished that every word uttered by members of the 

‘onference should be correctly taken down, ‘This abservation was apparently 
made on the appointment. of M. Meysenberg to draw up the Protocol of the 
Conference. . 

Count Buol then read his address to the members of the Conference. The: 
address was chiefly remarkable for the pointed and distinct manner in which 
Count Buol stated that Austria was prepared to encounter any sacrifices in order 
to fulfil her engagements; thereby clearly implying that Austria was ready to 
go to war, 

The four points were laid down as I have already stated them to your 

Lordship in a telegraphic despatch, and in my despatch No. 16 of the 12th 
instant. 
The Baron Bourqueney declared his agreement in the sentiments of Count 
Buol, and his adherence to the four points as laid down by him. He reserved 
the right of the belligerent Powers to add other stipulations over and above the 
four points, should the interests of Europe require it. 

I followed, and stated my agreement with Baron Bourqueney and the 
reserve nearly in the terms of the memorandum. Lord Westmorland agreed 
with me, 

Prince Gortchakolf then addressed the members of the Conference. He 
declared his adherence to the statement of the bases of peace laid down by the 
Minister of Foreign Affairs; put in a few words to show that he was bound not 
to the text, but to the principles of the memorandum inclosed in Lord Westmor- 
land’s despatch No. 501 of the 28th of December; declared his earnest desire 
for peace; but that, in the discussion of the Articles, he should object to any 
propose which would be injurious to the dignity of the Emperor of Russia. 

Je said he comprehended the reserve made by the belligerent Powers; but that 
as Austria was not a belligerent, she could not bea party to the reserve, 

Count Buol speedily undeceived him. He said that although he thought it 
unnecessary to make such a reserve on his. own part, he held himself at liberty 
to put forward or support any further propositions which the interests of Europe 
might seem to require. 

Baron Bourqueney wished the allusion to the dignity of the Emperor of 
Russia to be omitted in the remarks of Prince Gortchakoff, He thought the 
reserve unnecessary, and that it might give rise to misconstruction. 

L requested Prince Gortehakoff to repeat his declaration. 

He did so, but in a much wilder form, He expressed his wish to bring 
about agreement, and thought that was not to be done by disputing about 
words, but by considering in practical Articles how peace might be attained. 

There did not seem now any sufficient objection to the discussion of the 
Articles. 

The Turkish Ambassador made a reserve of the dignity of his Sovereign, 
and we then agreed that we might proceed to the discussion of the Articles, 

Your Lordship will observe that the four points in their integrity are thus 
accepted as a point of departure, The importance of this step is so great that 


439 


your Lordship will not fail to perceive its whole bearing. The right of protection 
assumed by Russia over the Christians inevery part of the Turkish Empire, is 
at once given up, and Russia, owning frankly the extent of her sacrifice, is 
prepared to.adopt the policy which Europe determines to establish. What may 
be the calculations of Russian statestnen as to the future Ido not attempt to 
divine ; but 1 think I see clearly that so long as Austrin, France, and Great 
Britain keep together, they will yield, Their hopes are founded not on their 
powers of resistance to the combined Powers, but on their hopes of disunion. 

A long discussion now took place on the first Article. 

Count Buol proposed that as soon as the stibstance of each Article should 
be agreed upon, the Article should be referred to a Commission chosen from 
amone the members of the Conference, for the purpose of collecting information, 
and bringing details into a manageable shape. To this there could be no 
objection, 

mi On the first Article Prinee Gortchakoff raised a discussion on the term 

Protectorate,” which he affirmed not to be contained in any of the Treaties 
between Russia and the Porte, It was in vain answered that many official 
documents contained the word “ Protectorate,” and that the thing which Europe 
wished to guard against was sulliciently expressed by that term. 

At length Baron Bourqueney suggested the word ‘‘ protection,” and it was 
agreed that no exclusive protection over the Principalities and Servia should 
hereafter be exercised. 

Baron Prokesch had prepared with great care, and with a knowledge of the 
constitution of the Principalities which experience had afforded him, several 
heads for the future government of those Provinees. 

These were discnissed one by one, and did not meet with much opposition ; 
but it was to be remarked that the Russian Plenipotentiary, when a defensive 
system for the Principalities was stated by Baron Prokesch as one of the 
securities. to be desired, evinced much anxiety for the contentment of the 
subjects of the Porte, and ealling the attention of the Turkish Ambassador to 
the danger of exciting disaffection, protested against the imposition of burden- 
some obligations on the Provinces, At the sume time he took care to put 
himself in the place of an advocate of the Principalities, and declared that of 
all the privilezes belonging to them none was more valuable or more appreciated 
than immunity from Turkish fortresses and Turkish garrisons. | 

It was obvious that, while apparently pleading the cause of Walluehia and 
Moldavia, the Russian Minister meant to leave them open to Russian invasion. 

But Baron Prokesch parried this thrust by proposing that native forces 
alone should garrison the proposed fortresses, and it was justly observed that the 
resources of two Provinces naturally so rich, would eusily enable them to 
maintain wl the troops necessary for their defence. ; 

After some further discussion it was resolved that the propositions of Baron 
Prokescl should be revised and brought before the Conference at a subsequent 
meeting, in order to be referred afterwards to a Commission, 

The Russian Plenipotentiary now suggested that, as time was precious, it 
would be advisable to proceed at our next meeting to the consideration of the 
second paint. The only remark made on this siigeestion wis, that Baron 
Prokesch’s proposals might be in such a state of forwardness as not to require 
much further time for their discussion, 

It was agreed to meet again on Saturday, the day after to-morrow.  Belore 
the Conference separated, however, another circumstance showed how little the 
Austriin Minister is disposed to yield to the influence of Russia, 

___ Prince Gortchakott proposed that the Ministers at the Conference should 
sien in a single column, according to the ranks of their respective countries, 
M. de Bourqueney observed, very justly, that it would not be desirable to mix 
poll-mell belligerents on opposite ‘sides, 

Prince Gortchakoff then suggested that there might be three columns, as 
Austria was not a belligerent, but Count Buol in the frankest manner declined 
this proposal. He said he was ready to adopt the suggestion of a single 
calunim; but if there were more than one, he must join his signature to that of 
the allies of the Emperor his muster. 

This is another proof of the fhirness w:th which the Austrian Government 
is disposed to carry into effect its engagements with France and Great Britain. 
Ni 


eee 


= 


— 


=: 


or 


436 


Upon the whole I submit to your Lordship that the results of this first 
Conference have been very satisfactory. Russia has openly, by a formal 
document, renounced pretensions which for a century have been sedulously 
nourished and pertinaciously advanced. It remains to be sec whether the 
allied Powers are able to raise barriers of sufficient solidity agaist renewed 
attempts to overpower and subdue Turkey. But the coneession of the four 
points, and especially the agreement to put an end to Russian preponderance 
inthe Black Sea, is an advantage which can hardly be exaggerated. To have 
obtnined such a concession at the end of a single year of war, 15 a success Upon 
which we could hardly have ventured to reckon. Even if negotiations were to 
break off, the moral cffect upon Russia, and upon Ente will be very great. 

ave, &c, 


(Signed) J. RUSSELL.

COUNT ESTERHAZY has this day communicated to Baron Manteuffel

ence at Vienna is announced as having been delayed in consequence of the 
necessity of new instructions and credentials being obtained from St. Petersburgh, 
but that they would now shortly commence, and that the Austriin Government 
deeply regrets that they will not be attended by a Prussian Plenipotentiary. 

After making this communication, Count Esterhazy read ta Baron Manteuttel 
a further circular to the German Courts, stating the object of the Vienna Confer- 
ences, the regret that Prussia should not be represented there, and conveying the 
expectation that the Plenipetentiarics appear animated with the best intentions, 
and that the Austrian Cabinet hopes the result of the Conferences will be an 
honourab.e and lasting peace, which will ensure the further happiness of 
Kurope.
