No. 475. 
The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Jolin Russell. 


(No. 18.) 
My Lord Foreign Office, March 20, 1855. 


| HAVE the satisfaction of conveying to you the approval of Her Majesty's 
Government of the language held by your Lordship at the Conference of the 
15th instant, and of the proceedings of yourself and Lord Westmorland, as 
reported in your despatch No. 20 of that date. 

Her Majesty’s Government concur with you in thinking that the result of 
the first Conference has been satisfactory, and that the moral effect of the con- 
cessions made by Russia will be considerable. It must, however, be borne in 
mind that they have only been made in principle; that they have not yet been 
realized. and that later, if Russia refuses to carry out these concessions to their 
legitimate consequences, and to adopt the interpretation of them that we think 
indispensable, we may find that this moderation has only been assumed at first 
for the purpose of disuniting the allies, and of depriving Austria of the support 
that she might reasonably expect from Germany if she declared war on finding 
that the maintenance of pretensions dangerous to Kurope was resolutely persisted 
in by Russia, 

With regard to the observations made at the Conference as to garrisoning 
the frontier fortresses of Moldavia, Her Majesty’s Government are of opinion 
that it would be desirable to garrison them with Turks, who would be much more 
to be depended upon than Moldavians for resisting & Russian attack. 

The subject of the protection to be given to the five Powers over the Prin- 
cipalities will require your Lordship's vigilant attention, because a right of 
protection given to the five might speedily degenerate into practical inter- 
ference by Austria and Russia in the internal affairs of the Principalities, and 
that interference would always tend to restrict their liberties and to detach them 
from the Porte. 

. Lam, &c. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

My Lord, Foreign Office, March 20, 1835. 

COUNT COLLOREDO his communicated to me a further circular 
addressed by Count Buol to the Austrian Ministers at the German Courts, dated 
Vienna, March 5, on the proceedings in the Diet. 

Count Buol observes that it was still doubtful, when he wrote the former 
circular (referred to in my despateh No. 98 of the 13th instant), whether the 
objections made verbally by the Prussian Plenipotentiary to. the Austrian com- 
munication to the Diet, on the Ind ultimo would be recorded in writing. 
M. de Bismark has, however, since made a declaration in writing, which has 
heen recorded im the Protocol of the sitting, 

Baron Prokesch immediately put in a rejoinder, which has been entirely 
approved by the Austrian Government ; and Count Rechberg has been instructed 
not to allow any doubt to exist, in the discussions of the Federal Committees, 
that, if the communication which has been thade of the * state’ of the Austrian 
army should be objected to in’ the sense of the Prussian declaration, or if in any 
other way practical effect should be given to that deelaration, the Austrian 
Government will be compelled to enter a protest against it, both as to its form 
and substance. 

Count Buol expresses bis hope that the reasons will be fully appreciated 
which have induced the Austrian Government to define, in the most unmis- 
takeable manner, the position of Austria as contradistinguished from that now 
assumed by Prussia, 

Copies of the Prussian declaration, and of the answer of Baron Prokeschi, 
are annexed to the despatch. 

The former is to the effeet that the declaration made by the Austrian 
Minister rests upon the supposition that the contingents, which are to be placed 
‘na state of preparation in accordance with the vesolutions of the 8th of 
February, are destined to defend the territories which have been placed under 
the common safeguard by the resolutions of the oath of July and the 9th of 
December last; that in the opinion of the Prussian Plenipotentiary this suppo- 
sition is not well founded ; and that if a further interpretation of the resolution 
of the Sth is necessary, and this interpretation ts sought in the motives which 
Jed to the adoption of the proposals of the Committee, it will be seen that the 
necessity for proceeding to the execution of the defensive obligations contracted 
hy the resolution of the Oth or December has not yet arisen; but that the 
present preparations are made by the Diet in order to meet the obligation 
imposed upon it by the second Article of the Federal Pact to provide for the 
external and internal security of Germany, and the independence and inviolability 
of the German States: lastly, that the Federal forces 50 prepared should be 
considered as available in every dinection, 

“Po this the Austrian Plenipotentiary replied, that the Austrian Govern- 
ment undoubtedly considered the resolution of the Sth of February as 4 further 
development of the resolutions of the oath of July and the $th of December. 
The Confederation must decide which is the correct view, the Austrian or 
Prussian, 

Baron Prokesch further observes that it is not the motives which led to the 
report of the Committee which are the mutter in debate, but the proposals made 
by that Committee ; and that acquiescence in the proposals themselves by no 
means implies acquiescence in the motives which led to them, Austria uccome 
panicd her acquiescence by the declaration that shein no manner accepted as

Lord John Russell to the Farl of Clarendon.—(Received March 21.) 


(NoL2))) 
My Lord, Vienna, March 16, 1855. 
THE ‘Turkish Ambassador called upon me the day before yesterday, and 

stated that he felt embarrassed by the absence of detailed instructions from his 
Court fer the guidance of his conduct in the discussions about to be: commenced, 
He said that he felt so more particularly in regard to the question of the Princi- 
palities, which stood first for consideration, and which was looked upon with 
especial interest by the Sultan's Government; and he seemed anxious to asecr 
tain my opinion how far he could take part in the discussions without compro- 
mising himself, or pledging his Government to the adoption of a course which 
might turn out to be at variance with their intentions and wishes. 

| explained to his Excellency that there could be no possible objection to 
his taking part in a conference on this point, as no final arrangement could be 
made in the first meeting ; that it would, of course, be open to him to contest 
any statements or suggestions made in the Conference, which, from his general 
knowledge of the policy of lis Government, he might consider likely to prove 
unpalateable to the Porte; and that he would, at all events, be free to reler to 
Constantinople for specific instructions on any points of a doubtful character. 

I recommended him, however, to lose no time in writing to his Government 
for such detailed information as to the views of the Sultan in regard to the 
several matters appoited to be brought under the consideration of the Conter- 
ence, as might enable him to take part +. the discussions with more contidence 
than he could do at present. ‘This he promised to do, by telegraphic message, 
without delay; and [have little doubt, from a communication which I have 
had with him to-day, that the progress which was made at the meeting of 
yesterday in the matter to whieh the ‘Turkish Ambassador's application to me 
more specifically referred, will not only ensure the exact fulfilment of his promise 
to apply immediately for fall instructions, but will also show the ‘Tuikish 
Government the necessity of bestirring thomselves if they wish to have a voice 
‘a the deliberations of the Conference before those deliberations have resulted inl 
a definite and tangible proposition, 

At all events, | think your Lordship should be aware of the possibility of 
embarrassment arriving hereafter from the remissness of the Porte to put the 
Sultan’s representative in the Conference in possession of its views and inten- 
tious. ‘The Porte might cndeed leave with safety to its allies to wateh over the 
sntercats of Turkey at this momentous crisis, for it should not doubt, after all 
that has passed, that the allies look upon those interests os identical with their 
own, But it appears to me that the Porte cannot be too 500m undeceived, if it 
entertaina and is prepared to act upon the opinion that it is at liberty to protract 
the negotiations at Vienna as nly est suit either its habitual indolence, or any 

ulterior abjects which if may have in view. 
I have, &e. 
(Signed) J. RUSSELL.

Lord John Russell to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received March 21.) 
(No. 23.) 


My Lord, Vienna, March 17, 1865. 

BEFORE the opening of the Conference, Prince Gortchakoff read to us a 
despatch which he had just received from St, Petersburgh, 

It contained assurances of the desire of the Emperor Alexander for peace, 
on terms compatible with the honour of Russia. At the same time, the Emperor 
declared his determination to carry on the war with the utmost vigour. There 
is nothing in this despatch which indicates any change of policy, 

Indeed it would be nearly tinpossible for the Emperor Alexander to depart at 
this moment from the line prescribed by his father. But if in the course of the 
negotiations a doubtful point should arise, it will be seen whether he has the 
courage to incline the balance towards peace, I cannot doubt that if he should 
do so, his power would be strengthened, and his hold over his vast Empire 
confirmed, The curb has heen held too tight, and a somewhat lighter hand will 
give a securer seat to the rider, as well as ease to the horse, Such at least is 
my conjecture. 

J have, &e. 
(Signed) J. RUSSELL.

My Lord, Constantinople, March 5, 1855. 


| HAVE the honour to forward to your Lordship by the present oppor- 
tunity a printed series of very important Turkish enactments, prepared for 
publication in the Porte’s official Gazette, of which T have heen courteously 
allowed by Aali Pasha to obtain an early copy, 

As T did not receive the paper in question till yesterday, it has been impos- 
sible for me to have it completely translated. But a translation, inclosed 
herewith, of the introductory paragraph, followed by an enumeration of several 
legislative acts, will acquaint your Lordship with the character and object of the 
whale communication. 

The Porte, as | am assured, intends to publish a full translation of the new 
judicial measures thus in course of promulgation, and to communicate it, when 
prepared, to the Diplomatic body residing here, 

That pertion of the new law which is direeted against venality and pecula- 
tion, was privately placed in my hands about four months ago, and, after carefully 
examining its contents with such professional assistance as happened to be 
within reach, T returned it to Aali Pasha, with the suggestion of certain amend. 
ments, which, asl was informed by him, were subsequently adopted, 

| have never indeed ceased to recommend the prompt completion, promul- 
gation and enforcement of all those reforms which have been so frequently 
promised by the Sultan and his Ministers. The language which | have held as 
well to lis Majesty as to the leading members of his Government, may be 
summed up, essentially, in very few words; Your present administrative system, 
| have said, is only leading you to destruction, Lt is anti-social; that of self, 
opposed to public interest, You eannot revert to (he period of energetic fanaticism. 
That fire, ina national sense, has burnt itself out. You must open other sources 
af prosperity and strength, and they are to he found in a system of administration 
which secures justice to all, removes inequality of civil rights, encourages know- 
ledge and industry, protects property, develops wealth, and extends the meine 
of defence. You nust also take measures to bring your revenue, ‘unpillaged, 
into the coffers of the State; to welcome seienee, capital and enterprize, from 
whatever quurters they come; and, above all, you must lay the axo without 
reserve.or compromise to the roots of that corruption which spreads its poison 
throughout the Empire, and casts a fatal shade on every germ of vegetation 
and every principle of lite, i 

Many veurs have passed during which | have never ceased to inculeate 
these ideas, and to urge the cuforcement of measures required to give them 
effect. 

Since the storm has burst over this Empire and shown to demonstration the 
consequences of neglecting such repeated admonitions, | have represented the 
importance of awakening, while there is yet tine, to asense of impending danger, 
and applying in carnest, even nt the eleventh hour, those principles of improve- 
ment which afford the only chance of escape. 

[venture to hope that the new enactments, herein communicated, may

pain and discredit of having the measures which it might have adopted spon- 


taneously, extorted from its Pleniporeuies by the united voice of Christendom.

Inclosure in No, 486. 
Substance of an Article in the Turkish Official “ Gazette” of March 3, 1855, 


(Translation. ) 

A HIGH Council of Reform having entered upon its functions for 
correcting, enforcing, and enacting new administrative laws and regulations, 
separate regulations have been drawn up respecting its duties and new internal 
organization, respecting the organization of the General Council for revising the 
work of the Council of Reform, and the manner of the discussions to be held 
therein. The Imperial Criminal Code is now under discussion, and that part of 
it respecting corruption is revised by the General Council, sanctioned by His 
Imperial Majesty, and hereby promulgated together with the other several 
regulations as follows ; 


1, Regulations on the duties of the Council of Reform. 

2. Regulations on the internal organization of the Council of Reform. 

3, Regulations on the organization and duties of the General Council. 

4, Regulation respecting the drawing up of all general regulations to be 
hereafter framed. 

5, Statement of the Penal Code against corruption.

Inclogure 2 in No. 489. 
Vice-Consul Rassam to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Moossul, January 29, 1855. 

1 HAVE the honour to inform your Excellency that since the date of my 
last despatch No. 1, news has reached this that Yezdasheer Bey has taken 
the town of Gharzan and committed fresh acts of barbarity at Sert; one of the 
persons who fell a victim to his rage is Haggi Mohammed Aga ibn Tahur A 
the Mutsellim of Buhtan, a man of much influence and wealth; he was pud- 
licly executed in Sert, and allhjs property confiscated. A Chaldean bishop 
named Mar Michael was put to the torture until he paid the sum of 25,000 
pinstres ; being very poor his commuity collected the amount and rescued their 
bishop from the hands of his tormentors. 

The rebel Yezdasheer Bey has also exacted the following sums from 
‘ndividuals by torture. From Mullah Mustapha, the Mufti of Sert, 25,000 
plastres 5 Yusseen Rassar, Mahommedan, 18,500 piastres ; Shemmus Tomu, a 
Christian, 25,000 piastres ; in fact, all respectable persons who will not join his 
cause are either executed or put to the torture until they consent to pay him 
large sums of money which he must have in order to pay his soldiers. 

When Yezdasheer Bey first grasped the reins of Government at Jezireh and 
Sort, he wrote to the Commander-in-chief at Kars that Osman Pasha and Hajji 
Suleiman Aga were the cause of his taking the course he had chosen; however 
he was still faithful to his Sultan, and hoped he would not be considered rebel- 
lious, as he intended to march early in the spring at the head of 8,000 men to 
fight the Russians. The Commander-in-chicf not suspecting his candour for a 
moment, sent a Camaicam to ert to asaist Yezdasheer Bey in raising troops; 
no sooner, however, did he arrive, than the Bey put him under arrest, of rather 
surrounded him with a guard, and would not allow him the least liberty, and 
finally sent him to Diaberkir under under a strong escort. | 

The rebels are busily engaged in repairing the castles formerly occupied by 
Bedr Khan Bey in the mountan fastnesses, and storing them with provisions, 
arms, and ammunition, that in ease of emergency they will shut themselves up 
there, and defy the Turkish arms. 

Maussoot Bey has gone among the Go-erye, a powerful Koordish tribe, to 
draw them over to their alliance. 

Yesterday Tahar Bey, with about 1,000 Nizam ‘and 400 Agail, entered 
Moossul from Bagdad ; ie Mohammed Pasha, a Commander of Artillery, with 
six cannon, On the 25th instant Helmy Pasha received a despatch from Hamel 
Pasha of Diabekir, informing him that Azmay Pasha of Aleppo had dispatohed 
one battalion of Nizam, with several pieces of Artillery. A detachment of 
Nizam had also left Kharpoot for Diarbekir, and when the whole foree arrived in 
that town they, with 300 Bushi-Bozouks, would march auinst the rebels. It is 
also reported that two battalions of Nizam has left Sulimainah on their way to 
join Tahar Bey's Division, and about 1,000 Bashi-Bozouks from Kerkook. 
With such a strong force I hope the rebels ere long will be subdued, and peace 
once more restored in the mountains of Bubtan, 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) Cc, A. RASSAM,

No. 491. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received March 22.) 


(No. 170.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, March 8, 1855. 

INCLOSED herewith in copy is the last despatch which I have received 
from Moossul respecting the progress of revolt in Koordistan. It may be hoped 
that the troops detached against Yezdasheer Bey by the Pasha of Bagdad will 
have better fortune than those which preceded them. Humanity and policy alike 
require a speedy suppression of the disorder, and I have repeatedly urged the 
Porte to adopt the necessary measures with promptitude and vigour. Whatever 
has been wanting in these respects ‘s not attributable to want of will, but of 
means. Had the Government and Empire been reduced to a state of less deplor- 
able weakness, the assistance of their allies would not have been required, and 
their independence might have been maintained, together with their internal 
tranquillity, at a less amount of sacrifice to Europe. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLILFE.

COUNT HATZFELDT stated to me yesterday that he had had the 
previous day an audience, with General Wedel, of the Emperor, during which

your Lordship has also been made acquainted by M. Usedom, eiving in general 
terms the propositions of the King of Prussia for necepting the Protocol of the 
sath of December, and signing an eventual ‘Treaty with the Western Powers. 
Count Hatafeldt added that the Emperor had Gon himself to be satisfied 
with this communication, and that His Majesty thought that an understanding 
might be arrived at on the bases therein indicated, 

I had the honour of dining yesterday at the Tuileries, and [ took an 
opportunity of ascertaming how far Count Hatzleldt’s appreciation of the 
Emperor's sentiments was correct. I certainly found His Majesty under the 
impression that there was now @ creater chance of coming to an understanding 
with Prussia than there had been. He seemed, however, to conceive, what does 
not appear to be the case, that the King of Prussia had offered to sign with the 
Western Powers a Treaty analogous to that sizned between those Powers and 
Austria; but the Emperor still maintained the opinion that until that Treaty was 
reduced to a shape acceptable to all parties, and that the word of the King of 
Prussia had been solemnly pledged to sign it, a Prussian Plenipotentiary could 
not be readmitted to the Vienna Conferences. In fuct, the only change that 1 
saw in the Emperor's language Wis, that whereas he had ABrTaSE made the 
sienature of a Treaty & sine qué non to Prussia’s taking a part in the Jonferences, 
His Majesty now seemed disposed to save the King of Prussia’s amour propre by 
inviting him to join the allies, provided the latter pledged his word to the 
signature of a Treaty, the tenour of which should be previously agreed to.

effort to conduct, with a proper character of moderation, the war in which the 
Russian Government are engaged with Great Britain, and which they would be 
happy, if met ina conciliatory spirit by Her Majesty’s Government, to be enabled 
to bring to an end. ; | 
As M. de Séniavine, however, has at the same time endeavoured to attri- 
bute the excesses of the Russian troops at Inkermann to the very improbable 
circumstance of British soldiers left as wounded in their rear by Russian 
advancing columns, having subsequently fired on them, and also to the death of 
a Russian non-commissioned officer alleged to have been treacherously shot by 
an English officer who had surrendered to him, I have thought it right to 
address a few lines to M. de Scheel, of which 1 inclose a copy herewith to your 
Lordship, in reply to his note, pointing out the improbability of the first state- 
ment, and stating that M. de Séniavine may be assured that the conduct 
complained of in the second, if it actually took place, will most certainly meet 
with the severe reprehension of Ficld-Marshal Lord Raglan and of Her Majesty s 
vernment.

Inclosure in No. 500, 
Circular addressed to the Prussian Representatives at the German Courts. 


(Translation.) Berlin, March 8, 1855. 

YOU will find inclosed a copy of a confidential despatch which I addressed 
to the Royal Minister at Paris on the 2nd instant. You will perceive that 1 have 
been induced to do so, in consequence of the conduct of the Royal Minister at 
a sitting in the Diet having been subjected to a criticism on the part of a foreign 
Government, which the Royal Government considers to be meompatible with 
the dignity and independence of Germany. For this very reason T have not 
entered into the matter itself with the French Government, and [ further believe 
that L can here likewise confine myself to a few remarks in defence of the point 
of view of the Royal Government against misrepresentations, which have been 
entered against us in several cases, 

The motives of the Decree of the Diet of the 8th of February are clear 
and distinct. If, therefore, it has been attempted later not to ignore them, but 
to convert them into the contrary: in other words, if a measure which had for 
its object the internal and external strengthening of Germany, without at the 
moment combining with it the smallest demonstration, was alterwards to be 
stamped as a demonstration against one side, the right of such an endeavour 
must be denied on principle. ‘This has been done by the Royal Minister at the 
ict. Is a demonstration against the other side therein vontained ? Not in 
the least. Germany would indeed’ be far gone, if the reference to the security 
and independence of the Germanic Confederation consequent on the menacing 
situation of Europe, was to be interpreted and taken amiss as & provocation 
towards a foreign country. We at least are of opinion that this reference is by 
far too much in consonance with the dignity of Germany to require a corrective 
at all, not to say one that originates in Treaties in which the Confederation had 
no part, and the practical range of which it does. not even clearly see at the 
present moment. We have reason to suppose that many of our German allies 
partake of this view; otherwise the motives for the Decree of the Sth of 
February would not lave been aecepted in the Committees, as well asin the 
assembly of the Dict, with a majority bordering on unanimity. Had not an 
interpretation been at a later period put upon these motives which was foreign 
to them, the Royal Envoy at the Diet would not have found himself obliged to 
re-establish them in their original and general form, which contains no demon- 
stration against any side; but as it was, the consequences of the principle had 
to be pointed out with precision and exaetness. 

It might have been hoped that this, chiefly a confidential exchange of 
ideas, would not have lost its original character by a premature and incorrect 
publicity, But also since this has unfortunately been done—an experience 
which Prussia is accustomed to by the pointed communications of the German 
as well as of the foreign press, by which, however, at the risk of being misunder- 
stood and suspected, she will not suffer herself to be misled—it would have 
been easy to separate the truth from the exaggeration. All sorts of proposals 
have been talked of, which Prussia had made or was going to make; as, for 
example, that the full Federal contingents should on all sides be placed in 
position on the territory of the Germanic Confederation ; that the Federal 
fortresses were to be armed, &c. We have indeed been surpriced at this activity 
developed in our name, We have particularly perceived from our diplomatic 
reports, that a series of Austrian circulars treats this matter, and as it were 
canvasses for votes against proposals which we were going to make to the Diet. 
Several German Governments: started with the decided supposition that these 
circulars had also been communicated tous; but this is not the case. IF the 
Cabinet of Vienna had mooted the matter with us, it would soon have been 
proved that the views attributed to us did not exist; the majority of those 


cireulars would thus have become without an object, and might perhaps lave 


been suppressed. 1 will not diseuss at present whether the true interests of 
Germany, who in this great European crisis longs for really independent unity 
and vigour, arising from a consciousness of her strength and the aims she has 


* 
| 
{ 
/ 
i

in view, but not for an attificial exertion of her energies, derived from foreign 
impulses, would have gained or lost by it, aie 

The position of the Royal Government towards the decree of the Diet 1s 
as simple as itis clear, As a Power of the Germanic Confederation they will 
stand by its * motives” as long #5 the Dict does not give them a more decided 
tendency by fresh decrees. Whether and in what sense the Diet will do this, 
is a question of futurity ‘which indeed stands on the threshold of the present. 
Prussia does not mistake the gravity of the moment, and will not desert the 
German fatherland. But exactly because she docs not mistake it, she will not 
permit her free sight to be veiled by interpretations forced upon her. With this 
view Prussia is however conscious that she is. free not only from every imtention 
of demonstration, but also from any hidden thoughts or irritated spirit against 


the Western Powers.

Lord Cowley to the Karl of Clarendon. —(Received March 23.) 


(No, 345. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Poris, March 22, 1Bo5. 
M. DROUYN DE LHUYS sends Count Walewski by to-night’s mail a 
memorandum on the possibility of terminating the question of Russian aupenincy 
in the Black Sea, by shutting that sea to ull vessels of war, Russian and Turkish 
included. It is not impossible that a scheme of this nature: might find greater 
favour with the Russian Plenipotentiaries than i plan of limitation which would 
admit of the presence of foreign pennants in the Black Sea. If the project 1s 
feasible, it would be the simplest of any, and would least interfere with the 


Treaty of 1841. 
{ thonghit it, however, right to remark to M, Drouyn de Lhuys that great 


precautions would be necessary in framing any Treaty on this basis, for unless 
. some security was taken against the assembling al large military forces on the 
f coasts of Russia, and against the construction of large steamn-transports, which 
might be easily and suddenly converted into ships of war, there could be no

M. Drouyn de Lhuys replied that he agreed in this opinion, and that he 
felt with me that if the system of “the neutrality of the Black Sea” (as he 
called it) was to prevail, as the basis upon which the third point should be 
discussed, considerable care would be required in framing the provisions which 
declared that neutrality. All he desired for the present was to submit the idea 
to your Lordship's consideration, He should send his memorindum on the 
subject at the same time to M. de Bourqueney, but with instructions not to 
make use of it unless the British Plenipotentiarics received orders to adopt the 
idea. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys argues that, if Russia admits the principle of the 
exclusion of all ships of war, it will follow as acorollary that none but commercial 
ports are wanted in the Black Sea, and that where there are commercial ports, 
there must be foreign Consuls. ‘Thus the three main objects of the notes 
exchanged between the English and French Governments, as those to be insisted 
on in discussing the third point, would find their solution: limitation, or rather 
disappearance of Russian vessels from the Black Sea; annihilation of military 
ports; introduction of Consular Agents. He observed further, that these regu- 
lations must of course be extended to the Sea of Azof. 

As I remarked before, the question is, Can this scheme be realized ? 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys said, that when he ientioned it to the Emperor, His 
Majesty was much taken by it. 

T think, on the whole, that M. Drouyn de Liuys’ language has been more 
firm those last twoor three days. He probably sees the impossibility of inducing 
the Emperor to agree to terms which would not effectually secure the objects 
for which the allies went to war. Nevertheless I cannot shut my eyes to the 
fact that his Excellency is not to be depended upon. The alliance with Austria 
having been one of the great objects of his policy, he would make peace, if it 
depended upon him, sooner than admit that he had failed in bringing Austria 
into the field, having always asserted that she would eventually joi the allies. 
Any danger, therefore, of the retraction of Austria, or any hope of preventing 
the Emperor going to the Crimea, would make him ready to aceept terms which 
I venture to think could not be agreed to by Her Majesty's Government,

No. S11. 
The Earl of Clarendon to Baron von Usedom. 


M. le Baron, Foreign Office, March 24, 1855. 

I HAVE the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your letter dated the 
Lith instant, together with its inclosures, 

Her Majesty's Government have carefully considered the project of declara- 
tion which, in the opinion of the King of Prussia, will serve to define the 
position of Prussia in the present conflict as well as in the negotiations for peace, 
and it is with sincere regret [ have to inform you, M_le Baron, that Her Majesty's 
Government, so fur from considering that the position of Prussia is defined by the 
proposed declaration, can discover in it nothing beyond a conditional neutrality. - 
Prussia agrees to sign the Treaty of 28th December, but implies that she does so, 
as it has already licen accepted by Russia, She will give an assurance not to take 
part with Tussia in the present conflict and will continue to consider herself 
placed on the side of the Western Powers, provided that their proceedings towards 
her do not assume a character that would wound her dignity or threaten her 
interests. 

Permitme to observe, M. le Baron, that the value of this assurance is greatly 
diminished by the vagueness of the condition on which it is made to depend. 
So long as England and France are in alliance with Prussia, it can never be their 
intention to wound her dignity or menace her interests; but it would seem that if 
any act of theirs should have that construction put upon it in the course of a war 
that may embrace the whole continent of Europe, they must then no longer reckon 
on Prussia considering herself as placed on their side, Prussia further declares 
her readiness eventually to take an active part ina western alliance having for 
its object to repel by foree of arms all future ageression on the part of Russia 
against the Ottoman Empire. Upon this Twillonly observe that such an alliance 
is not at present in contemplation; but should it hereafter be formed, the acces- 
sion to it by Prussia will be regarded by Her Majesty's Government as an event 
of great importance. 

You state, M. le Baron, that Prussia insists upon her right to take partin the 
Conferences before the official negotiation of the analogous Treaty is opened, and 
it is to be well understood that the project of, declaration is not to take effect if 
the invitation to the said Conferences is longer deferred, 

The rights of Prussia as a great European Power will always be readily 
acknowledged and faithfully observed by Her Majesty's Government, and if the 
position of Prussia as a great European Power had alone entitled her to take 
nat Inthe Conferences, the invitation to attend them would long since have 
wen conveyed to Berlin: but of the five Powers which take part in those 
Conferences four are actually belligerents, and the fifth is bound by a solemn 
engagement to become a belligerent, if certain conditions are not agreed to by 
Russia. 

Austria does not take part in the Conferences any as a great Kuropean 
Power, but in virtue of the engagement into which she has entered with England 
and Prince, The Treaty of December 2nd is the condition on which the Western 
Powers entered with Austria upon negotiations with Hussin. [1 that Treaty 
hail not been signed, Her Majesty's Government and that of the Emperor of the 
French would not have assented ta the Conference, and none would have been 
held at Vienna, 

It is clear, therefore, that in inviting Prussia to enter upon a similar engage- 
ment, England and France both recognised her position us a great European 
Power, und manifested their desire to plaice themselves on the same footing with 
her us with Austria, Prussia, however, has deelined to contract any engage- 
ment, immedinte or eventual, but still claims to aceupy a place in the Confer- 
ence, Which would be anomalous, undefined, and altogether distinct from that of 
the othor five Pawers, 

The dignity and the interests of Bogland and France forbid the admission 
of this clan; but no right of Prussia os a great European Power is thereby 
called in question or disregarded. Her Majesty’s Government deeply regrets that 
in this great crisis of European affairs, England and Prussia should not be found 
in close alliance together, They do not abandon the hope that a common interest

No. 516, 
Lord John Russell to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received March 24.) 


(No. 27.) 
My Lord, Vienna, March 20, 1855. 

IN considering the negotiations for peace, it is necessary to take into view 
our prospects should they be broken off. 

We blockade all the Russian ports in the Black Sea, and all the Russian 
ports in the Baltic during the time that sea is free from ice. 

Our policy with regard to neutrals, however, deprives us of one great means 
of crippling an enemy's trade, and Russian produce comes in large quantities 
into England, 

We have a considerable force of French and English in the Crimea. But 
the enemy, with an equal or superior foree, is strongly intrenched both in the 
town of Schastopol and outside its walls, 

Should the negotiation break off, leaving Austria neutral, the Russian army 
in the Crimea will be reinforced, and the Freneh and English troops, however 
superior in quality, can hardly be expected to advance: far beyond their present 
positions. Even if Sebastopol were to fall, however gratifying the triumph, this 
state of things would not be greatly altered. 

It seems therefore most desirable, in order to strike an effective blow at 
Russia, that Austria should come into the field. 

She might not only make a diversion to our attack on the Crimea, but she 
mizht invade and possess herself of Bessarabia, an ancient part of Moldavia, and 
perhaps make a suceessful attack on the Polish provinces of Russia. 

The present Emperor will hardly have that sway over his Generals and 
armies which his father exercised with such vigour and authority, 

It is therefore a great object to obtain the assistance of Austria. 

1 have, &e. 
(Signed) J. RUSSELL.

No. 518, 
Lord John Russell to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received March 24.) 


(Separate and Confidential.) 
My Lord, Vienna, March 21, 18595. 


DURING an interval of the sitting of the Conference on the 19th instant, 
and in the absence of the other members, I took an opportunity to say to 
Prince Gortchakof, that | hoped he would write to Count Nesselrode to be 
very cautious in his instructions on the third Article of the bases of negotiation. 

Prince Gortchakoff at once replied that his instructions never varied ; that 
they were such as, if a Russian, I should have given myself. Russia, he said, 
could not consent to limit the number of her ships: if she did so she would 
forfeit honours she would be no more Russia, 1 might ask, he continued, 
why she wanted a force in the Black Sea? He would tell me plainly, They 
did not want to possess ‘Turkey; they would be glad to maintain the Sultan, 
but they knew it was impossible; he must perish. They were resolved not to 
let any other Power have Constantinople. ‘They must not have that door to 
their dominions in the hands of a formidable European Power. 

Here, then, is an avewal on the part of Russia that she means not only to 
maintain a flect in the Black Sea, but a strong fleet. At any moment when a 
French ov English fleet might happen to be in the Levant, she might believe, or 
pretend to beheve, that we or the ferah were going to dethrone the Sultan, and 
try to get before us. 

This is a real danger to Europe, by Russia’s own showing. 

On the other hand, Count Buol is getting more and more uneasy. He sees 
how humiliating would be the position of Austria if, our proposals being 
reasonable, we were left at war, and Austria, after all her warlike preparations, 
were to yield to the policy of Prussia, Her position in Germany would be gone; 
her weight in Europe greatly diminished, 

I informed Count Buol, in a conversation I had with him yesterday, that 
Thad received a despateh from your Lordship (No. 14 of March 15), and that 
although Her Majesty's Government would be prepared to consider the measures 
he might propose on the second alternative, namely, that of establishing a 
counterpoise, instead of prescribing a limit to the Russian force in the Black 
Sea, they could not hold out hopes that sueh a plan would be found satisfactory, 

Count Buol was very anxious that we should keep together in our proposals. 
With this view he suggested that we might propose that Russia should not 
miaiitain a greater naval force m the Black Sea than she has ot the present 
time. Although this is short of what we proposed todemund, yet if Count Buol 
will stand by it, I strongly advise your Lordship and Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment to accept and support it. 

I do not believe Russia would agree to any limitation of her fleet, but her 
evident hope is to divide us from Austria, to give to Austria and to Germany 
all that Austria and Germany may be supposed to be anxious for, to insist on 
the euarantecs for the fourth point, and to refuse haughtily any limitation of her 
naval foree in the Black Sea, | 
The more | examine the plan of counterpoise as opposed to limitation, the 


493 


more | am convinced it would break down. Arsenals and ‘fleets in the hands 
of Turkey would be neglected and inefficient; constructed and maintained by 
France and England they would be found yery costly, and as soon as the 
danger was removed a little way off by time they would be reduced or abandoned. 

A Treaty of Alliance between Austria, France, Great Britain, and Prussia, 
for the defence of Turkey if attacked, would be a security, but it should be an 
additional security. 

My opinion is, therefore, that we should endeavour to combine with Count 
Buola joint plan of action before we discuss the third point in Conference. 
Baron Bourqueney is entirely of this opinion. 

Tt is said that the Russian Plenipotentiary was greatly disappointed at our 
union in the opening Conference, If we can maintain the same union on the 
third point, either Russia will yield, or Austria will join us in the war. 

or this purpose it is essential that our proposals should be as moderate as 
we can make them, consistently with the safety of Europe.

(No, 125.) 
My Lord, Vienna, March 20, 1855. 


| HAVE the honour of inelosing herewith to your Lordship a lithographed 
copy of the Protocol of the second Conference of the 17th, together with its three 
Annexes, which has been signed this day in the order settled at the first Contfer- 
ence; Count Buol signing as President in the centre, the Representatives of the 
allied Powers in the right column, which in the preceding Protocol was occupied 
hy the Representatives of Russia, and these latter in the left column, in which 
the allied Representatives had signed the last Protocol, 


498 


After this Protocol had been read and agreed to by the Conference, the 
diseussion of the first Article of the bases, which had been commenced at the 
previous Conference, was resumed. 

After due examination of the papers drawn up by Baron Prokesch and by 
the Russian Representatives, which | mentioned to your Lordship in my 
despatch No. 132 of the i7th instant, the general agreement come to with 
respect to the rights of the Principalities of Moldavia, Wallachia, and Servia, 
was, that all the privileges enjoyed by them up to the present time, from 
whatever source they emanated, were to. be maintained in full foree; that every 
improvement suggested by the Sultan or the allied Powers, which should be 
agreed to between them, should be carried out, and that no curtailment of the 
privileges nor of the territory of those Principalities should be tolerated. It 
was then determined that a record of what had passed on this subject should be 
attached to the Protocol in the form of annexes. 

Your Lordship will observe that these annexes are three in number. ‘Those 
marked A-and B are the papers drawn up by Prince Gortchakolf and M. de 
'Titoff in explanation of the privileges and prerogatives possessed by the Danubian 
Principalitices and by Servia, with snggestions for ameliorations im the Govern- 
ment of those Provinces to be submitted for the consideration of the Sultan 
and his allies, and to serve in developing. and arranging the ideas originally 
thrown out by Baron Prokesch, and enibodied in the Annex to the Protocol of 
the 14th of March. 

That marked C records the first general results arrived at after examination 
of the above-mentioned papers, and after a prolonged discussion, in which the 
several members of the Conference sugested alterations to be made in the 
proposils before them, and threw out fresh ideas for consideration, 

A lengthened debate took place respecting Article 4 (in the Annex C), which 
relates to the armed force of the country, respecting which the words as they 
now stand were substituted for those originally proposed by M. de ‘Titoff, and 
according to which that foree was to be developed “ dans la mesure des ressources 
du pays. * . 

In Article 5 several changes were made in ihe original proposals, with a 
view of regulating, in conjunction with the Porte, any discussions which might 
arise in the Principalities relative to hatti-sherits promulgated by the Sultan. 

In Article 6 it was established that no intervention whatever in the Princi- 
palities was to take place, “sans entente préalable et sans intervention égale au 
nom de P Evrope. ; 

Upon Article 7 Lord John Kussell and myself both objected to the engage- 
ment to be taken reciprocally by the Contracting Powers not to allow any 
attempt at creating disturbances in the Provinces by their own subjects, and we 
did so on the grounds that no case of such a nature was likely to occur, nor to 
he of any effect except from the countries bordering upon those Provinces, 
which by the previous Articles had been sufficiently guarded against, and we 
agrecd that this stipulation was therefore not required, It was then agreed 
that Article 7 should be altered in accordance with this suggestion, and [ 
beg therefore to point out to your Lordship that this Article does not appear in 
its final shape in the Annex C to the present Protocol: but it will appear in 
‘a corrected form, together with other changes which have been introduced into 
the paper, in the Annex to the lrotocol No. 3, which will be signed at the 
Conference to-morrow, and which will be forwarded to your Lordship as soon 
us it has been lithographed and distributed to the members of the Conference. 

| have thus given to your Lordship a sketch of some of the changes intro- 
duced into the development of the first point in the course of discussion ; and | 
doubt not that they will be detailed to your Lordship by Lord John Russell, in 
entire concurrence with whom I have acted upon this occasion, a8 Upon every 
other which has presented itself, 

I have, &e.

The Earl of Westmorland to the Rarl of Clarendon.—(Receied March 24.) 
(No. 131.) 
My Lord, Fienna, March 21, 1655. 


I HAVE the honour to forward herewith to your Lordship a despatch* 
which I have received under flying-seal from Her Majesty's Consul-General at 
Bucharest, respecting recent differences which have occurred between the 
Austrians and Wallachians at Krajova. 

On the receipt of this despatch T was most anxious to represent to General 
Hess the information it contained, and as 1 was myself very much engaged with 
the affairs of the Conference, | directed Mr. Fane to call on the General, and to 
bring the contents of the despatch before him in my name. 

From the report made to me by Mr. Fane of the conversation Which passed, 
it appears that Generai Hess had already been informed of the differences at 
Krajova by General Coronini, and although he had not yet received all the 
details, he was in possession of sufficient information to be sure that the death 
of the woman who had been killed in the unfortunate ‘‘rixe” which had taken 
place there, was in no manner attributable to any of the garrison. General Coro- 
nini, he said, had already ordered a fresh battalion to proceed to Krajova, and 
t was his iutention to cause the garrison to be immediately changed if it eould 
be proved that any part of it had in any way misconducted itself, 

With reference to Mr. Colquhoun's expression of regret that the conduct of 
the Austrian military authorities was not everywhere as satisfactory as at 
Bucharest, General Hess remarked that it was hig most earnest desire that the 
occupation of the country by the Imperial troops should everywhere proceed 
peacefully and with mutual satisiuction, and that the orders which he had issued 
to General Coronini respecting the differences at Krajova had been inspired by a 
desire to promote these objects, He was glad, he said, that Mr. Colquhoun had 
noticed and acknowledged the improved conduct of the Austrian troops about 
Bucharest, and it was his sincere wish that they should everywhere conduct 
theinselves as satisfactorily as they appeared to do there. 

General Hess concluded by saymg that he had sent orders to General 
Coronini to cause the strictest investigation to be instituted into the differences 
which had occurred at Krajova, and that it was his firm determination to visit 
with the greatest, severity any infractions of duty and of discipline, if they should 
be proved to have taken place. 

Ihave &e. _ 
(Signed) WESTMORLAND.

INTELLIGENCE reached me last evening of some unpleasant differences 
having arisen at Krajova, in Little Wallachia, between the Wallachians and the 
Austrians, 

The seeds of dislike were sown some weeks ago, when a “rixe ” occurred 
in which the life of a woman was sacrificed, and her husband severely 
wounded, | 

The Under-Secretary of State, describing the recent case, says * that, in

consequence of repeated differences between the inhabitants of Krajova and the

(No. 132. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, March 22, 1855, 


COUNT ESTERHAZY has had an audience of the King of Prussia for the 
purpose of delivering to His Majesty a letter from the Emperor of Austria 
announcins the accouchement of the Empress, and the birth of an Archduchess. 

The Austrian Minister has stated to me that he found the King most 
gracious and affable. He described His Majesty as ready to enter into conversa- 
tion on general topies, but desirous to avoid a political discussion. He, however, 
brought His Majesty to speak on the negotiations in London and Paris. He 
endeavoured to extract His Majesty's opinions as to the result to which they 
might lead, and informed me that the King did not express himself pointedly, 
but has left him the impression that though he would: willingly come to an 
understanding with Englund aad France as to the position to be occupied by 
Prussia in the present crisis, he is resolved to decline entering into any engage- 
ment which will involve him in war with Russia. | 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD,

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Recetved March 27.) 


(No, 360. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Parts; March 26, 1855, 

M. DROUYN DE LHUYS having been very unwell, [have hardly been 
able to see him upon business during the last two or three days. | found him, 
however, convalescent this morning, and had some conversation with him on the 
state of negotiations at Vienna. 1 found his Excellency exceedingly dissatistied 
with his last reports from that city, as also with a communication made to him 
yesterday by Baron Hiibner. | _ 

He said that the tone assumed by the Russian Plenipotentiaries at the 
second and third Conferences was most haughty; that they put themselves 
forward as defenders of the privileges of the Principalities and of Servia, as il 
these privileges had ever been mnenaved—quite forgetting that the object of the 
first point was to emancipate the Principalities from the protection of Russta, 
and to reinforee, though within proper limits, the authority of the Sultan. The 
abject of Russia was, no doubt, to put herselfin a good position, should the 
Conferences be broken off; but he had no intention that this should he offected 
at the expense of France, and he had, consequently, desired M. de Bourqueney, 
by telegraph, to profit by the first Conference to re-establish the true scope and 
meaning of the first point. He then observed that there were, in his opinion, 
some very objectionable points in Baron Prokesch’s memorandum, which 
appeared to have received the sanction of the Plenipotentiaries. He alluded in 


ee pee pe ee Serie 


‘ 


502 


particular to the possibility of foreign troops entering the Provinces subject only 
to au understanding upon the matter afterwards—a stipulation which, if agreed 
to, would place the Porte in a less favourable position than she had been in before 
the war, when she had at all events had an equal right of occupation in the 
Principalities with Russia. 

Passing to the communication which had been made to him yesterday by 
M. de Hitbner, and which related to the development of the third point, 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys did not conceal the vexation which the position taken up by 
Austria caused him. Your Lordship will have received a similar communication 
from Count Colloredo, and | need not, consequently, go into its details ; but I lose 
no time in informing your Lordship that M. Drouyn de Lhuys writes to-night 
to M. de Bourqueney, to express the astonishment and regret of the Emperor 
and his Government at the attitude assumed by Count Buol. M. Drouyn de 
Lhuys observes that there is not one of the three propositions submitted by 
Austria which is admissible. The direct limitation of the naval power of 
Russia in the way proposed by Austria would be of no value, because there 
would be no guarantee for its observance. Its indirect limitation by means of 
keeping an equivalent ‘Turkish foree in the same waters, with, perhaps, the 
addition of one or two foreign ships of war, would be risking a continual conflict 
to the advantage of Russia; while the third proposition, namely, that of permit- 
ting the Porte to call for the presence of the allied fleets whenever she thought 
herself menaced, was reverting to the state of things before the war, with the 
further objection, either that the allied fleets might be constantly called upon 
to act on needless alarms or apprehensions, or that if there was really occasion 
for their presence, they would probably arrive when they could no longer prevent 
the attack to ward off which they had been summoned. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys says, that he shall appeal to the loyalty of M. de 
Buol to answer whether, when the Austrian Government themselves admit that 
the real check to Russia in the Black Sea will be a limitation of her fleet, they 
are fiirly acting up to the engagements which they have contracted with 
England and France, in refusing to make the non-acceptance of that limitation 
by Russia a easus belli for Austria, He will remark (an argument which I have 
often endeavoured to prevail on him to employ towards Count Buol) that 
Austria forgets that England and France have actually effected that which they 
are determined to huve recognised by Russia if they make peace, namely, the 
ecssation of Russian preponderance in the Black Sea, Austria should remember 
that this state of things can be continued whether the armies are, or are not, 
successful in the Crimea, and, if these armies are brought away, at a compara- 
tively small expense. Austria, moreover, must be aware that the consent of 
Tussia is not required to any arrangement which the allies may make with the 
Porte, for the better defence of the territory of the latter; nor can Russia now 
prevent the signature ofa Treaty between the maritime Powers and the Porte, 
if they are so disposed, giving Franee and England the right of passing the 
Straits of the Dardanelles and the Bosphorus, to the exclusion of the ships of 
Russia hereafter, The best that Austria offers isa bad peace now, with the 
constant chance of war hereafter. 

Such is the tenour of the nstructions which M. Drouyn de Lhuys proposes 
sending to M. de Bourqueney. A copy will be transmitted to Count Walewski 
for your Lordship’s information. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys still hopes that the plan for neutralising the Black 
Sea, which could only have aatied Vienna lust night, may tind favour with the 
Conference; und, failing that, he seemed disposed to think that some arrange- 
ment might be made on the basis of an indireet limitation of Russian power in 
the Black Sea, with the opening of the Dardanelles whenever Turkey thought 
herself menaced, | have ventured to express my conviction that the two Govern- 
nents have but one chance—simall as that is in my humble opinion—of obtaining 
the military cooperation of Austria ; and that is, agreeing on the ultimatum they 
intend to adopt in regard to the third point, and telling Austria it is their firm 
determination to continue the war until they obtain it, As long as Austria sees 
wavering and uncertain counsels in the camp of the allies, so long will she waver 
and remuin inactive herself. Whether greater decision in that camp will produce 
better results at Vienna is a problem at all events worth while solving. 

[ have, &c, 
(Signed) COWLEY,

I shall nevertheless think it my duty to renew the proposition in the 
Conference. ‘ 

The diseussion on the third point was of more importance. 

Count Buol read to us his despatch to Count Colloredo. I have already 
stated that I think the proposal to limit the Emperor of Russia's flect in the 
Black Sea to the number he may have at the time of signing the preliminaries, 
is & good proposition, in so far as it would effectually restrain the maritime 
force of Russia in the Black Sea, without the humiliation of dismantling ships 
at present fit for sea. 

Beyond this 1 cannot concur in Count Buol’s despatch. 

The counterpoise proposed consists in: Ist. A small vessel-of-war to 
eruize at the mouth of the Danube. 2nd. The right of the Sultan to call up 
the fleet of his allies in case of menace, and to consider the augmentation of 
the Russian fleet in the Black Sea beyond twelve as such menace. rd. A 
general guarantee of the integrity of Turkey. . 

It is needless that | should point out to your Lordship the imperfections 
of this plan. . 

Count Buol holds cheap the danger of a coup de main on Constantinople, 
and maintains that it would only be formidable if supported by a large land 
army, marching by the Balkans. 

Austria, he maintains, would stop the march of such an army; she did 
not, however, take up arms last year to oppose the passage of the Danube. 

Imperfect ns this system of counterpoise as laid down by Count Buol 
manifestly is, the Austrian Minister has never sad that if we would lower our 
demands to his standard, and these demands were refused by Russia, Austria 
would consider such refusal equivalent to a declaration of war. 

Austria has always reserved a certain liberty of action upon this point. 
Count Buol’s language to Lord Westmorland was very positive. Ido not blame 
her for this reserve; she may properly wait to hear the language and the propo- 
sitions of Russia, But her silence in this respect adds considerably to the 
difficulty of our situation. 

I conceive there are only two possible solutions. Ist. The limitation of 
the Russian fleet in the Black Sea, 2nd. The complete abrogation of the 
Treaty of 1841, and the admission into the Black Sea of vessels of war of all 
nations not having possessions or establishments in the Black Sea, 

Lord Westmorland and I ean only speak on Monday, the day of our next 
Conference, so fav as we are authorized by our present instructions, 

The final determination of a matter so weighty, and so pregnant with 
consequences, must be reserved for the Governments of Great Britain and 
France. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) J. RUSSELL.

(No. 31.) 
My Lord, Fienna, March 23, 1855. 

ANOTHER ineeting of the Conference was held to-day. 

The Protocol of the last Conference was read and approved. 

The general features of Baron Prokesch’s plan for the freedom of navigation 
of the Danube consist in a declaration that the Lower Danube shall be subject 
to the general stipulations of the Treaty of Vienna in respect to the navigation 
of rivers: and the formation of two Commissions, the one to be appointed by 
ull the Contracting Powers, to make general regulations; the other to be 
appointed by the river-bordering Powers, Austria, Russia, and Turkey, to carry 
these general regulations into effect. 

Upon this subject I remarked that if the first Commission were of short 
duration, all that they regulated and preseribed might be neglected or thwarted 
by the Executive Commission, in whom the permanent power was to be placed, 
I therefore proposed that the Contracting Powers should also name the Executive

Poloszk, Rostof, Jaroslof, Belosersk, Udersk, Obdorsk, Coudinsk, Wityrpsk, 
Mstislawsk, and Sovereign of all the northern coasts, Lady of the Twersky 
country, of the Carthalinian and Grauzinian Czars, of the country of Carbadinia ; 
of the Princes of Circassia, and those of the mountains, and of the other 
countries, Heiress Lady, and Sovereign Ruler. 

Our endeavours to increase the trade of our own subjects, and of the other 
nations throughout the Black Sea and the Mediterranean, have met with the 
wished-for success; the Treaty of Commerce which we concluded with the 
Ottoman Porte on the 10th of June, 1783, having finally removed those impedi. 
ments and difficulties which, from the particular constitution of the Turkish 
Government, had obstructed the said trade in every step of its progress: which 
can only be guarded against by the institution of proper laws for the protection 
of commerce, and by granting it that entire freedom which its various specula- 
tions and turns so indispensably require. The principles of this unlimited 
freedom we have adopted, and followed from the carliest period of our govern- 
ment, as 18 manifest from the several edicts and regulations which have been 
issued from our throne; and we now extend these edicts and regulations in their 
utmost latitude to the trade of the Black Sea, The security and convenience 
of that commerce are now fully provided for by the annexation of the Province 
of Tauriea, and the neighbouring territories, to our other dominions; we have 
opened therein divers seaports for the use of all persons who will carry awny 
from thence the produce of Russia, and bring thither the produce and manufie- 
tures of other countries. 

It is well known that the last Turkish war (a war which, during the six 
years that it lasted, was signalized by so many victories to our arms) was no 
sooner concluded than we erected within the government of Catherinestaw, 
upon the River Dnieper, and at a short distance, the eity of Cherson; it having 
appeared to us that that situation was vrticularly commedious, as well for 
exporting the produce of Russia as for importing from other countries such 
things as might be useful to us; and we secured the trade thereof by the most 
effectual means of defence, encouraging it, moreover, by such helps as were best 
suited to it, and were not inconsistent with the general principles of commerce, 

This town, as also Sebastopolis (formerly called Acht-air) and ‘Theodosia 
(formerly called Kutta, both which latter are situated in the Province of Taurica, 
and are provided with excellent seaports, we have, on account of the commo- 
diousness of their situation, crdered to be opened to all nations living in amity 
with our Empire, for the purposes of their commercial intercourse with our 
faithful subjects. Accordingly we most solemnly declare, by these presents, 
that all such nations are at liberty to come to the said ports, either in their own 
or hired vessels, and under their own colours, as also to repair thither by land 
and they are likewise free to depart from thence at their pleasure, paying the 
duties of importation and exportation agreeable to the tariffs established in the 
respective custom-houses. Moreover, all persons, of what nations and countries 
socver, may remain in these towns as long as their business or inclinations may 
lead them, and enjoy the free exercise of their religion, agreeably to those laude 
able institutions which have been banded down to us. from our ancestors, 
Sovereigns of Russia, and which we ourselves have confirmed and iugmented, 
permitting all strangers residing in Russia to worship the Almighty agreeably to 
the religion of their forefathers, offering prayers to him, together with our own 
subjects, that he will increase the welfare and strengthen the power of our 
Empire. We give leave to all and every one to carry on their trade with abso- 
lute freedom, either singly or in companies, promising by our Imperial word, 
that all foreigners shall enjoy the same privileges in those three towns as they 
enjoy in our Imperial eity of St, Petersburgh, and in our provincial town of 
Archangel; and in case of a war, every one shall be secured by the principles of 
that neutral system which we have erected, and which, on our part, shall be 
kept sacred and inviolable, Finally, if any foreigners shall wish to settle in 
these or any other towns or places of our Empire, and to become our subjects, 
we will receive thom most graciously under our dominion, promising that they 
shall not only be allowed the free exercise of their religion (as mentioned above), 
but the full enjoyment of all such privileges and exemptions with regard to trade 
and navigation as have been granted to our other subjects; as also to erect 
fabrics and manutaetories, paying only such taxes as shall be paid by our other 


subjects of the same condition with themselves, All persons who shall thus 


o09 


become our subjects shall be at liberty, they and their descendants, to remain 
under our government as long as may be agreeable to them, or as their interest 
may require ; and in case they should afterwards choose to withdraw from the 
same, they shall be freely permitted so to do, on paying the taxes that had been 
laid upon them for three years to come, The perticulay privileges which wall be 
granted to the above-mentioned towns will be set forth in their respective 
charters, which are speedily to be published, 


Given at St. Petersburgh, the 29nd of February, 1784, and in the 22nd 
year of our reign,

Inclosure in No. 537. 


Abstract of two Despatches addressed by Count Buol to the Austrian Ministers 
at the German Courts. 


THE first despatch of Count Buol of the 28th of February, states that the 
Imperial Minister, President of the Diet, is instructed to communicate to the 
Diet an account of the whole Imperial army which stands on a war footing under 
the command of General Hess, in order to prove that Austria's preparations for 
war exceed the requirements of the decision of the Diet. 

The Imperial Cabinet felt it necessary to remark upon the circumstance 
that the Prussian Plenipotentiary had proposed that the preparation of the 
contingents should take place within the territory of the Confederation, "This 
proposition had found no favour among the members of the Confederation, and 
was not accepted as a resolution of the Diet; consequently the Imperial Cabinet 
remarked that the action of the Confederation in this matter did not depend onl 
on the Federal Treaties, but also on the Agreement of the 20th of April (24th 
July) and the decisions of the 9th of September of Jast year, and that therefore 
the Confederation was bound not only to defend its own territory, but also to 
enforce the carrying out of the four points, and to defend the Austrian Monarehy 
and the Austrian troops in the Principalitics against every attack ; but that the 
proposition of the Prussian Military Plenipotentiary completely sets aside all 
agreement between the Federal decision of the 8th, and the former position of 
the Diet. 

M. de Prokesch now informs us (the Imperial Cabinet) that when he, at 
the Federal meeting of the 89nd, laid before the Assembly the aceount of the 
Austrian army of operation, the Prussian Minister distinetly denied that the 
decision of the 8th depended on the decisions of the 24th of July and the 9th of 
December. : 

M. de Bismark wished to set aside entirely the case of the common defence 
of the Austrian Monarchy or of the Danubian Principalities, and to consider the 
decision of the Diet of the 8th of February as reposing on a new basis, namely, 
that of the necessity of making military preparations, to be employed in every 
direction, in consequence of the threatening aspect of European affairs. 

A further proceeding in this direction, on the part of the Prussian Minister, 
was made onthe question of the garrison of Rastadt, when Prussia proposed full 
war qarrisons for Rastadt, Landau, Mayence, and Luxembourg, because this 
measure must necessarily follow as a preparation for defence in all directions. 

How Prussia reconciles these Nectnrations with her explanations of the 
object of her missions to London and Paris, we seck in vain to understand, 

But we feel it our duty, in our care for the safety of Germany, to express our 
conviction that the German Confederation will involve itself in the most serious 
dificultics if it should give to its preparations for war any other object than the 
eventual fullilment of the obligations incurred by the decisions of the 24th of 
July and the 9th of December, 1854. The obligations which the German Con- 
federation have incurred, the nature of the task which we all those who 
recognise our policy as a truly German one, have to: fulfil, speak so plainly 
that no explanation is necessary as to the military measures taken by the 
Confederation. 

But the position would be quite different, if Germany, which is now jre- 

wired to arm itself, and when a short space of time must show whether the 
sya will sueceed in giving back peace to Europe, should in its further 


511 


declarations and measures follow a neutrality free from particular obligations. 
We should then feel it our duty to declare ourselves decidedly against such 
measures, and to refuse all responsibility for their possible consequences. 

We might especially declare the proposition that our contingent should be 
withdrawn on to German territory as only an indirect abandonment of the 
responsibilities incurred in the common interest of Germany, and regard the 
proposal of removing the garrisons to the fortresses on the French frontier as an 
uncalled-for provocation, 

The Imperial Minister President has received instructions to show, in the 
debates of the Committee, the gravity of the above considerations. We hope 
that he will find the same conclusions among the other Plenipotentiaries, and 
that the German Confederation will leave no room for doubt as to the object of 
the armaments. 

You will express to the Government of the importance we attach 
to the recognition of the above-mentioned views, and to the despatch of corre- 
sponding instructions to the Plenipotentiaries at the Dict, 


The second despatch of Count Buol, dated the Sth of March, states, that 
when the despatch of the 28th was written, in which mention was made of the 
objections raised by the Prussian Plenipotentiary at the meeting of the Diet of 
the 22nd to the Prone aee made on the part of Austria in fulfilment of the 
Federal decision of the 8th, a doubt still existed whether these verbal objections 
would be entered in the proceedings of the Dict. , 

_ ‘The Imperial Minister President of the Diet has sent us the declaration, 
which follows in copy, subsequently entered by M. de Bismark in the Protocol 
of that meeting, ; 

M. de Prokesch then made the declaration, which likewise follows in copy. 

We are consequently in 1 position to put in practice the views expressed in 
the despatch of the 28th, and we have consequently not only entirely approved 
the declaration of the Imperial Minister President, but have instructed Count 
Reechberg, that in case the communication of the state of the Austrian army 
should be objected to by the Diet in the Prussian sense, or in case in any other 
way a practical fulfilment of the Prussian declaration should ensue, he must 
make a protest in strict comformity with it. 

The Government to which you will communicate this despatch, as com- 
pleting that of the 28th, will, we hope, appreciate the importance of the reasons 
which make it our duty to point out, in the most decided terms, our position, in 
eontmi-declaration to that view which, to our regret the Prussian Cabinet considers 
reconcileable with the decision of the Diet of the 8th of February.

expense and inconvenience of maintaining fleets in the Black Sea for the 
purpose of keeping in check the naval force of Russia, | have to observe that 
that object has already been secured, for the greater part of the Russian fleet has 
been destroyed by the hands of the Russians themselves, and the flag of Russia 
has disappeared from the Black Sea, Wussia cannot expect that this advantage 
will be gratuitously surrendered, or that England and France will withdraw their 
fleets in order to restore Russia to a position which she cannot occupy with 
safety to Murope, 

The allied armies have suffered no reverse in the Crimea; but on the 
contrary their marked superiority over the Russians in the field has been on 
thiree occasions proved ; they have not, however, obtained the complete suceess 
that was expected. Sebastopol has not fallen; itis stronger than it was some 
months ago, and it may require still greater efforts for its reduction; large rein- 
forcements may be sent into the Crimea; the finances and trade of Russian may 
hitherto have suffered less than was expeeted, though well-founded information 
shows that they have already suffered greatly and extensively ; the national 
spirit may still be unbroken, and the Muscovite party imay still, to a certain 
degree, maintain itself in spite of the growing discontent excited in Russia hy 
the pressure of the war. Nevertheless, Her Majesty’s Government cannot, in 
the state of things, whether present or prospective, discover any justifiable 
ground for consenting to make peace on terms that would neither be hon surable 
for the allies nor safe for Europe, 

England and France have stood forth os the champions of Hurope; they 
have proclaimed the conditions which they think indispensable for securing 
Europe from a renewal of the present complications; and if they were now to 
abinnOn those conditions, and to sheathe their swords without obtaining the 
guarantees they have demanded, they would accomplish the object announced 
in the Mmperor Alexander's recent manifesto, of raising Wussia to the highest 
pitch of glory and power, they would lay the seeds of future and not distant 
war, their own position throughout the world would le destroyed, anid the 
alliance between England and France, associated as it would be with reminis- 
cences of failure and discredit, wonld soon come to an untimely end. If these 
considerations are presented to the Austrian Government, and pressed with all 
that weight of argument that your Lordship will well know how to employ, 
Her Majesty's Government cannot but entertain a hope that decided action will 
replace the now wavering policy of that Government. [t can hardly be doubted 


bei. 


518 


that the readiness with which Russia volunteered the acceptance of the four 
bases, and the haste with which Prince Gortchakoff presses on the discussion 1n 
the Conference, have no other object than to break up the alliance of Austria 
with the Western Powers; the Russian Plenipotentiary displays the utmost 
willingness to make concessions on the first and second bases in order to make 
a ease for Germany, and to lessen the power and the desire of Austria to stand 
firm on the third basis ; and if Austria should be so ill-advised as to fall into 
this unconcealed trap, your Lordship will remind Count Buol that no settlement 
af the first or second basis will be binding on the Western Powers, and that, if 
the whole of the buses are not unequivocably adopted by Russia, all negotiations 
must be at an end, . . 

This result would be regarded by Her Majesty's Government as a severe mis- 
fortune, but itis aeontingency that must have been contemplated by the Austrian 
Government, and Her Majesty's Government, therefore, are unwilling to doubt 
that Austria will faithfully adhere to her engagements with the Western Powers, 
and that, for her own interest as well as for her own honour, she will not neglect 
an opportunity that may never again recur effectually to restrain the ambition of 
Russia. 

The energy displayed by Austria in her preparations for war, the frankness 
with which she has professed to declare her policy to the Dict, and the just 
severity with which she has treated the vacillations of Prussia, have placed 
Austria in a position from which she cannot without discredit recede. 

If Austria were now to abandon the allies, she assuredly would not thereby 
restore peace to Europe; if by not taking a decided part with them she failed to 
obtain the guarantees of which she stands in need, the day may not be distant 
when single-handed she miy hive to contend for her moat vital interests, and it 
ig for Austria, but not for Her Majesty's Government, to estimate what would be 
her loss of position in Germany, and what amount of fresh powers she would give 
to Prussia, who might then, indeed, triumphantly declare that events had proved 
the wisdom of her own policy, and had verified her constant predictions of the 
course that Austria would ultimately pursue. 


In conclusion, | beg to assure your Lordship that Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment are fully alive to the great difficulties and to the eritical position in which 
vou are placed, and as they desire to share your responsibility they hope that 
Your Lordship will not hesitate to consult them on all questions respecting which 
iloubts may arise in your mind,

WITH reference to that passage in your despatch No. 27 of the 20th 
instant, in which your Lordship expresses an opinion, that even if Sebastopol 
were to fall, the state of things as regards Russia would not be greatly altered, 
[ may observe, that if the allied armies could take Sebastopol and occupy it, it

drive them from such a stronghold. Having the command of the sea, if the 
allies had possession of the northern and southern banks of the harbour af 
Sebastopol, their position could be maintained against all attack. 

Her Majesty's Government entirely concur with your Lordship, that if the 
war goes on, the cooperation of Austria will be most valuable and important, 
as a means of obtaining conditions of peace which would secure us against 
future dangers from the aggression of Russia against Turkey; but it is to be 
borne in mind, that if, in order to secure the alliance and cooperation of 
Austria we give up those conditions, we shall sacrifice the end to obtain the 
means, and shall thus defeat our own purpose.
