No. 542. 


The Earl of Clarendon to Lord John Russell, 


{No, 31.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, March 28, 1555. 
ALTHOUGH it appears from your Lordship’s telegraphic despatch of the 
97th instant, that the Annex © to Protocol No. 2 is the work of M. ‘Titoff, and 
probably therefore embodies the views and denotes the policy of Russia with 
respect to the future constitution and government of the Principalities, yet as 
there is no reason to doubt that those views and that policy would readily be 
adopted by Austria, Her Majesty's Government think it desirable to place on 
record their opinion respecting this project and the digastrous arrangements to 
which it would lead. 


Article 1 seems free from objection. 


Article 2 states that “all the clauses in former “hattis”” which have for their 
objects the prosperity of the Provinces are to be maintained.” 

This if fairly carried out is a nght stipulation, but who is to judge what is 
good for the prosperity of the Provinces, Russia and Austria would probably 
think the greatest amount of foreign interference and of internal despotism would 
most conduce to that prospenty. 


Article 8. The manner in which the guarantee contemplated in the 
last line is to be given would require great consideration. It is proposed 
that it shall only he given after mature cousideration by each Power. Is it 
likely that the Five Powers would take the same view, and how far would 
such guarantee give right of interference? Would it not be the first 
instance of a foreign guarantee for the internal organization of a part of the 
dominions of an independent Sovereign? Would not sufficient security for the 
maintenance of the rights granted to the Prineipalities by the Sultan, found 
in those rights themselves, in a solemn act of sanction on the part of the Sultan, 
and in the formal communication of those acts by him to the other Powers of 
Europe. ‘The great object to be kept in view in regard to the Principalitics, 15 
to exclude foreign interference, because that interference would be exercised 
necessarily and constantly by Russia and Austria; and the distinguishing character 
of the whole of the proposed arrangement is, that it would sanction and increase 
foreign interference in regard to Moldavia and Wallachia, and would for the 
first time apply that interference to Servia, which has hitherto been exempt 
‘from. it. 


Article 4. This proposed Article seems wholly inadmissible both in wording 
and in substance, .The result of it would be to place the military and armed 
force of Moldavia, Wallachia, and Servia under the direct control of Austria and 
Russia. In the first place it says, that the armed force is to be maintained in the 
interest of Europe,—a new service for the armed force of an independent State ; 
and then, that there may be no mistake, it goes on to Bay, that its augmentation 
is to be determined, in case of necessity, by an agreement between ‘Turkey on 
the one hand, and Austria and Russia on the other, and the result of such agrec- 
ment isto be communicated to the other Contracting Parties, who are to have 
no voice in the arrangement, 

The whole of this Article ought to be struck out, There is no stipulation in 
former ‘Treaties between Russia and ‘Turkey limiting in any way the armed force 
of Servia, and it would be most objectionable to introduce new restrictions and 
new rights of foreign interference us the results of a war undertaken for the 
purpose of maintaining the independence of the Sultan und the integrity of his 
dominions. 


Article 5, This erects the Four Powers, and of course Austria and Russia 
more especially, into 4 standing court of appeal and arbitration between the 
Sultan and the Governments of the three Provinces, and authorizes a direct and 
constant official communication with the Provincial Governments upon all 
mattera of internal administration in regard to which any pretence could be 
founded that a doubt had arisen as to the interpretation of the Constitution 
granted by the Sultan. This would be entirely new as to Servia, and ought not 


et Se 
ere | . ‘ 


52 


to exist for any of the three. If the Four Powers had reason to think, from 
information given them by their local agents, that the Constitution of any of the 
Provinces was violated by the Porte, they would naturally, and without any 
such stipulations, make friendly representations at Constantinople; but. it 
would be objectionable to establish, as proposed, a divided allegiance for the 
Principalities. 


Article 6. This Article is a perpetuation of the Treaty or Agreement of 
Balta Liman in regard to Moldavia and Wallachia, and its extension to Servia, 
to which Balta Liman did not apply. It conseerates, by the sanction of England 
and France, one of the principles of the Holy Alliance, namely, that the likeli 100d 
or existence of dangerous internal distaurbance in one State are to be judged of 
by neighbouring States, and that such neighbouring States are to be allowed, 
according to their discretion, to march an armed force in, either to prevent or 
to put down what they may please to assume to be popular or insurrectionary 
movements in such State threatening danger to their own interests. Such an 
Article never could be sanctioned by England and France. 


Article 7. This Article embodies another principle of the Holy Alliance, and 
applies it to all three Principalitics, to none of which it has hitherto been appli- 
cable, By this Article no agent ofany of the four Powers could give protection 
within either of the three Principalities to any person whatever, fellow-subject or 
other, whom Austria and Russia might desire to have expelled; and the Sultan 
would, for the first time, take a formal engagement to expel from his dominions 
any foreigner, of whatsoever nation he might be, whose expulsion Austria or 
Russia might demand. If this Article were agreed to by England and France, 
English and French subjects resident in the three Provinces would, by the 


consent of Fingland and France, be liable to be expelled at the demand of Austria 
or Russia. 


It is evident that these Articles have been drawn up by Prince Gortchakoff 
and M. de ‘Titoff, as an inducement to Austria to abandon England and France 
on the questions concerning the Black Sea and the real securities for Turkey. 
A Treaty concluded on such conditions would rivet on Turkey the yoke of 
foreign ascendancy and dominion in all three Principaiities, and would leave us 
without any security for Constantinople against a naval and military attack trom 
Russian ports in the Black Sea. 

Her Majesty's Government are of opinion that Servia wants and needs no 
new protection, and should be left untouched as she is, and that hereditary 
Princes in Moldavia and Wallachia would place those Provinces in & greater 
state of separation from the Porte. The evil has not been encroachments and 
uaurpations by the Sultan over the Provinces, but usurpations and encroachments 
by Russia, 

fam, &c. 
(Signed) CLARENDON,

No. 554. 
The Eurl of Clarendon to Lord John Russell. 


(No, 33.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, March 28, 1855. 

| HAVE to state to your Lordship, with reference to your despatch No. 31 
of the 24th instant, in which you give an account of the proceedings of the 
Conference on the 23rd instant on the second point, that Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment apprehend that, although the first Commission will have great power in 
framing regulations, it will not have similar power to secure those regulations 
being carried into effect, and it would therefore appear highly important that an 
English and French Commissioner should belong to the Executive Commission 
charged with keeping the mouths and channels of the Danube. Her Majesty's 
Government can well understand why Russia, who has always prevented the 
removal of obstructions to the free navigation of the Danube, should object to 
English and French Commissioners who would carefully watch her proceedings, 
but the ground on which Austria joins in and supports the objections of Hussia 
is not intelligible. 

Her Majesty's Government doubt whether the right to station a small 
English ship of war in or at the mouth of the Danube would be useful unless 
we have rights which that ship of war might enforce, and in time of peace it 
could enforce them only by representations. 

The evils complained of are not acts of violence which the presence of a 
ship of war could prevent, but acts of wilful omission which a member of the 
Executive Commission could watch and demand to have remedied.

My Lord, Constantinople, March 12, 1855, 


UT results from a conversation which I held with Aali Pasha this morning, 
that virtually, though not yet formally, the Porte has decided on sending a second 
Plenipotentiary to Vienna; that should the intention be realized, his Highness 
will be the person appointed, and that his departure will probably take place in 
ten days or a fortnight. 

Superior in standing and ability to Aarif Effendi, the Pasha will, no doubt, 
be left to exercise a wider diseretion in the negotiations; but T apprehend that, 
although he will be instructed to take his place generally on the same ground 
with his colleagues from London and Paris, he will hardly be empowered to 
commit the Sultan’s Government without reserve on those important and 
perhaps unforeseen particulars, which the application of admitted principles or 
the progress of military operations may eventually bring into question, 

There are certain points, such, for instance, as the future state of things in 
the Danubian Principalities, the interference of the Christian Powers in matters 
of social or administrative reform in Turkey, and the regulation of the several 
forces destined to have access hereafter to the Black Sea, which the Porte 
habitually regards as matters of vital interest to her Empire. For the final 
settlement of such essential questions it may be foreseen that she will always 
strive to retain, if possible, a preponderating, but at all events an independent, 
opinion.

No. 565. 
Lord Join Russell to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Reeeived March 30.) 
(No. 39.) 


My Lord, Mienna, March 26, 1855. 

BARON BOURQUENEY received yesterday evening the despatches to 
which your Lordship’s telegraphic message referred. 

As we had already made some progress in obtaining the concurrence of 
Count Buol to the limitation of the Hussian fleet, and Count Buol, on his side, 
had produced some effect on the mind of Prince Gortchakoff, the new proposi- 
tions arrived at an unfortunate time. 

Count Buol, whom we saw this morning scarcely half-an-hour before the 
Conference was to begin, seemed very unwilling to entertain the plan of 
neutrality, which he had had no time to consider. 

He accordingly opened the Conference upon the third point, by declaring 
that the preponderance of Russia in the Black Sea was a just cause of alarm to 
Europe, and that one of the prominent objects of the allies was to put an end to 
that preponderance. He thought it desirable, however, that the Russian and 
Turkish Plenipotentiaries should in the first place declare their views on a 
matter which concerned them both as Sovereigns on the coast of the Black Sea, 
and which concerned Turkey as holder of the gates of the Dardanelles and the 
Bosphorus, 

Baron Bourqueney, Lord Westmorland, and 1, having declared our wish to 
see a means found of attaining an object of Kuropean policy compatible with the 
honour of Russia, Prince Gortchakoff announced that he was prepared to discuss 
any pigposiciaee that might be made, but he was not prepared to make any 
himself. 

Hereupon, Count Buel expressed a desire that he would refer to his Court, 
which he declared himself willing to do. 

The Turkish Ambassador declared himsclf te be without instructions, 

It appeared to me at this moment that if we continned to discuss in the 
Conference the various propositions for carrying the third point into effect, we 
should dispel the hope of peace which had just appeared on the horizon; | 
therefore proposed that the regular Conference should be suspended, and that 
we should only mention in conversation various projects for the information of 
the Russian Plenipotentiary. 

This being agreed to, Baron Bourqueney threw out the idea of a neutral 
character to be given to the Black Sea, Prince Gortchakotf at once pointed out 
that such a plan would leave Russia disurmed in the presence of Turkey armed, 
and with no material defence against the fleets of France and England. Count 
Buol took no part in this discussion. 

I mentioned, on my side, the objections to a counterpoise; the constant 
rivalry it would foster; the weakness of Turkey it would display: und the logs 
of her independence which would follow. It was impossible, I argued, for 
Turkey to be calling her allies to her aid upon every diflerence that might arise, 
without shaking the belief in her means of resistance, and destroying her 
character ofan independent Power, 

These propositions being thus enunciated without any formal action of the 


530 


Conference, the whole question is kept. open for the day of regular discussion 
and final decision. 

‘As far as I can learn, the prospects for that day are nearly as follows :—- 

1. The project of a counterpoise in permanent action 1s not seriously 
entertained, Russia would only be willing to adopt it as a plan which would be 
found impracticable, and would leave her mistress of the field. 

2. ‘The proposal of limiting the Russian marine toa fixed number will be 
considered by Russia as inadmissible, ; 

3. ‘The Emperor of Russia, left to take his own line, and bound in honour 
to keep his engagement, as consigned in the Protocol on the third point, will, it 
is possible, declare to Turkey in the Conference, that he is willing to remove al 
cause of alarm to her, and of jealousy to Europe, by not increasing the number 
of ships of war he may have available in the Black Sea at the time of signing the 
preliminaries of peace. 


It has been my object, and that of Lord Westmorland, to keep for mature 
decision on the part of France and England, as well as Russia, the issue of these 
negotiations: 

~ Should they be broken off, no one can say under what circumstances 
they may be resumed, or what fields may be stained with blood, before peace 
ean be attained. 
, dew Conventions must be signed; the position of Austria must be advanced; 
that of Prussia must be detined. 

It has seemed to me well worthy of the foresight, the wisdom, and the 
benevolence of Her Majesty, as well as of her illustrious ally the Emperor of the 
French, to give a little time to reflection upon the first and second points of 
guarantee ulready urranged, and upon the prospects of Europe thus improved, 
before the gates of pence are finally closed, 

No Englishman would sce with satisfaction a peace which was not honour- 
able for his country and safe for Europe; which did not make amends for the 
éaevifices made, and remove to a distance a danger which hangs heavily upon 
the prospects of the world. But if the Emperor of Russia is willing to show his 
deference for the wishes of the alhed Powers, the extent of the concession he 
will make may be deliberately considered, and a grave question gravely 
determined. 

The next meeting of the Conference is on Thursday, and will commence 
on the fourth point. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) J. RUSSELL.

The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received March 30.) 
(No. 141.) 
My Lord, Fienna, March 26, 1855. 
YOU will learn from the report addressed to your Lordship by Lord John 
Russell that Count Buol and Baron Bourqueney met Lord John and myself by 
agreement yesterday, when Count Buol detailed to us the confidential conversa- 
tion which be had held on the previous day with Prince Gortehakoif, ae 
___ He reported that in this conversation he had mentioned his belief that the 
instructions of the English and French Ministers were of a nature to require the 
entire adoption by Russia of the engagement to which she had herself become a 
party by her adhesion to the third basis of the conditions of peace, by which he 
Wis bound to “ mettre fin Ala prépondérance de la Russie dans la Mer Noire.” 
; Count Buol called upon Prince Gortchakolf to conform himself in fall to 
this requirement, which he thought he might carry out more effectually and 
more to the satisfaction of his Government if he was to. take the initiative and 
himself’ make proposal by which this object might be attained; and he had 
suggested to him that by proposing to limit the naval force of Hussia to what at 
present remained of her fleet, and by engaging alter the war not to incrense it 
it might be taken into consideration, and might become the ground upon which 
some transaction might be come to. “ount Buol said that he cited many 
instances in which the riverains of an inland sea had come to iFemnseinacts 
amongst themselves according to which they bound themselves not to maintain 
u force on either side which might be considered as a menace to the other; und 
6U a 


532 


in arguing this point he had mentioned the case of the lakes in Italy, the shores 
of which were occupied by different Powers, as well as the lakes of Canada, 
where the British possessions and those of the United States were placed on 
opposite shores, 

Count Buol stated that in carrying out the stipulations of the third basis the 
question of right might be maintained, but there was also the principle of “ conve- 
nance ;” and between two Powers who were putting an end to astate of war with a 
sincere desire of re-establishing a durable peace, it was befitting that each party 
should remove, without injury to its own interests, in a state of peace such as it 
was entering upon, whatever might reasonably be considered as a cause of alarm 
or menace to the opposing Power. Count Buol added that Prince Gortchakoff 
must be aware that the peace of Europe had been broken by the acts of Russia, 
which by her preponderance in the Black Sea she had been able to carry out 
against ‘Turkey, and therefore that the allied Powers had felt it their duty to 
stipulate amongst themselves that this state of things must be put an end to, 
and as Russia had herself agreed to the fulfilment of this stipulation, he felt 
that he was only calling upon the Russian Government te carry out this engage- 
ment by assuming an initiative with regard to it in the manner the most 
appropriate to their own satisfaction and consideration. 

Count Buol stated that Prince Gortchakoff had replied to this reasoning 
by the assurance that he acknowledged the courtesy which had dictated the 
proposition; that he admitted the propriety of its being duly considered; and 
that he had no instructions to take such an initiative as had been proposed ; 
but that if he was allowed to refer it to his Government, he would faithfully 
report it, and would as speedily as possible inform us of the decision he might 
receive, 

Count Buol said that he had thought it his duty to acquaint us with what 
had thus taken place; and he left it with us to decide whether we would agree 
to allow him to bring this proposition forward in the Conference of this day, and 
whether, in ease Prince Gortchakoff proposed the reference to his Government, 
as above stated, we should feel ourselves authorised to agree to it, and he 
(Count Buol) strongly recommended we should do so. 

Just before our meeting with Count Buol took place yesterday, Lord John 
Russell and myself had received your Lordship’s telegraphic message of the 
94th instant, directing us to support a proposition for neutralizing the Black 
Sea, which hud been transmitted by the French Government to Baron Bour- 
queney, but that Minister had not received this communication ; it was, there- 

ore, impossible to enter upon any discussion with regard to it, ‘The message 
was, however, submitted to Count Buol, who conceived that the line of conduct 
he had recommended would, notwithstanding any other proposition, be the most 
advantageous to adopt; and both Lord John Russell and Baron Bourqueney, as 
well as myself, after considerable discussion, agreed to adopt the views of Count 
Buol for the opening of the Conference of this day. 

Ata late hour last night, Baron Bourquency received the communication 
from his Government which had been announced, and he this morning brought 
it to Lord John Russell and myself, and after consulting with regard to it, we 
took it to Count Buol. He said that it was so entirely new a proposal, that it 
was impossible, at the moment the Conference was ubout to take place, that he 
should give any opinion with regard to it; but it appeared to him to be wanting 
in any seautity to Russia; that if she entirely disarmed her fleets in the Black 
Sea, she might ut any time, upon the breaking out of any future hostilities, 
be at once overwhelmed by the fleets of Turkey, and possibly of her allies, who 
would enter that sea by the Bosphorus from Constantinople, or from any part 
of the world, without her being able to introduce into that sea a single ship for 
her defence. Count Buol also remarked that the whole plan was made subser- 
vient to the approval of the Government of the Sultan (whose acquiescence in 
it he very much doubted), before it could be officially proposed to the Russian 
Ministers, 

Count Buol stated, that under these circumstances, he strongly recommended 
an adherence to the plan which had yesterday been agreed to, although he 
admitted that if Baron Bourqueney thought it right to mention this fresh plan 
to the Conference, and if Lord John Russell and myself agreed to support the 
proposition, be did not see any inconvenience in our doing 80, 

Immediately after this discussion, the Conference assembled, and your 


bod 


Lordship will learn its result from the telegraphic message transmit: 
this day by Lord John Russell and myself. eee etait 
_ The very lengthened discussion which took place in that Conference will 
be fully reported to your Lordship by Lord John Russell, who in the ablest 
manner advocated your Lordship's views, to which I gave my anxious support. 
The decision taken appears to possess the advantage of proving, that while in 
the course of this important discussion we maintained every principle which we 
had been instructed to support, we at the same time displayed moderation in 
putting forward those principles, and in our endeavour to carry them out—a 
course which appeared to us the best calculated to ensure their adoption.

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received March 30.) 


(No. 143.) 

My Lord, Berlin, March 28, 1855. 
YOUR Lordship will have probably heard from Paris, that the French 

Government are of opinion that it would still be desirable to obtain the acces 

sion of Prussia to the Vienna Protocol of the 28th December, containing the 

four bases of negotiation with Russia. 

_M. de Moustier has been in communication with Baron Manteuftel on the 
subject, and it appears that the Prussian Government are now desirous to take 
this step in the following manner. ‘The Governments of France and England 
should communicate copies of the Protocol, vither here or in London and Paris, 
and the Prussian Government would then reply to the communication by a note 
accepting the engagements contained in this document. 

5 Baron Manteuffel would further propose the same course to the Cabinet of 
jenna, 

__ When his Excellency spoke to me this evening, and gave me this informa- 
tion, L asked his Excellency if the King intended this as a prelude to a Treaty. 
He replied that His Majesty had by no means changed his mind on this point, 
and that he had no intention of purchasing his admission to the Conferences by 
any such engagement, and that though he accepted the Protocol, he would not 
bind himself eventually to make war against Russia—a Power which certainly 
might have acted wrongfully at one time, but which had now given proof of a 
desire to make peace and to accept terms which the King thought ought to be 
satisfactory to the Western Powers, 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

Lord John Russell to the Earl af Clarendon.—(Received April | ) 
(No. 41. Confidential.) 


My Lord, Vienna, March 28, 1855, 

IN the instructions which I had the honour to receive from your Lordship, 
the object of my mission to this capital is very clearly defined to be, either to 
obtain guarantees against Russian aggression, or, in case of the continuance’ of 
the war, to have Austria asa belligerent on our side, 

There, are, however, other objects of great importance, which a deliberate 
examination of the four points will make apparent to any fair observer. 

France and Great Britain have expressly renounced any special advantages 
to themselves from the great sacrifices which, in entering upon this war, they 
were about to make. But when they were called upon to enumerate the con- 
ditions upon which they would consent to peace, they showed very clearly in 
their reniton: that while they were indifferent to advantages for themselves, they 
were not forgetful ofthe cause of civilization, or of the privileges and the happiness 
of those nations upon whose behalf they were about to stipulate, and upon 
whose fate they might be ealled upon to decide. I propose in this despatch to 
review the present negotiations in this triple view of security against Russia, 
friendship with Austria, and the welfare of the inhabitants of the territories 
subject to the sway of the Sultan. 

| have, for my own part, kept steadily in view these three objects, 


1. To check the aggressive spirit of Russia: 
2. To carry Austria with us in the negotiations, and, if peace should not be 
attained, in the further prosecution of the war. 


3. ‘To provide for the welfare and improvement of the Christian nations 
under Ottoman rule. 


With respect to the first of these objects, I have taken for granted it was 
generally, if not completely provided for in the four points. ‘The surrender of 
the exclusive protection of the inhabitants of Wallachia and Moldavia, which, in 
the course of eighty years, had been wearly converted from protection into 
dominion ; the admission of the free navigation of the Danube, to be secured by 
effectual means; the limitation of the naval power of Russia in the Black Sea, 
and the relinquishment of her menacing attitude, and, finally, the conversion of 
the official protection of the Christians of the Greek rite by Russia, into a peneral 
encourngement to the Sultan to persevere in his benevolent reforms: these 
changes, short of a diminution of territory which the state of the war did not 
allow us to ask, appeared to the Western Powers the best securities that could 
be obtained for the arrest of the ambitious designs of Kussia in the East. 

The concurrence of Austria, as your Lordship knows better than any one, 
has only been obtained by long and laborious negotiation. The position of 
Austria at the commencement of these differences was indeed one of extreme dilli- 
culty, Herarmy hid been reduced ; her tinances were embarrassed ; the fire of the 
insurrections of Hungary aud Lombardy still smouldered under the ashes. Had 
Austria at once taken part with Russia, Ttaly and Hungary would probably have 
burst into.a flame. Had she deelared for the Western Powers, a Hussian army 
might in six weeks have been at the gates of Vienna,

In these circumstances Austria has prepared her armaments gradually, made 
engagements cautiously, and without declaring open war has checked the advance 
of Russia. In this slow and passionless manner she has obtamed for herself the 
occupation of the Principalities, forbidden the advance of the Russian armies 
by the Balkan, and obtamed. in conjunction with the Western Powers, from a 
proud Sovereign the concession of guarantees which in August last he had 
haughtily refused. é Bee: 

I have conceived it to be my duty to tread in the path which Her Majesty s 
Government bad hitherto followed, and to attach a high value to the 
cooperation of Austria, whether in negotiation or in war, tage 

With respect to the third object, I need only refer to the despatches ot 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe for the last twelve years. It has appeared to us to 
be our manifest duty, while checking the arrogant and selfish pretensions of 
Russia, to take care that the condition of 11,000,000 of people, subjects of the 
Porte, should be improved and not rendered worse by our interference. 

‘The partial success of England and France in procuring fair treatment, for 
the Christians in Turkey might, | conceived, by tuking advantage ot this oppor- 
tunity, be converted into complete equality and permanent justice. The two 
sources of Ottoman misgovernment have been degradation by law in the first 
instance, outrage and plunder by abuse of power in the second. The law 
amended, and the administration purified, the Christians would have nothing to 
desire. Nor has the Sultan any wish to oppress or injure any class of his 
subjects. He is neither a tyrant by nature, nor a bigot by prejudice, and would 
willinely indulge his own benevolent disposition. ae 

Leaving these general considerations, I come to the four points in the order 
in which they have been placed. It will be observed that the first and third 
tend direetly to lessen Russian power ; the second promotes European commerce, 
and indirectly counteracts Russian monopoly ; the fourth provides for the welfare 
of the Christian inhabitants of Turkey, by means which will counterbalance 
Russian aggrandizcment, 

ist. The Priucipalities of Wallachia and Moldavia have, since the year 1829, 
been subject to the direct influence of Russiu. The despatch of Lord Aberdeen 
in reference to the Treaty of Adrianople points out the control over the Princt- 
palities which Rugsia was sure to derive from the Treaty of Adrianople. “The 
fact I believe to be, that while Russia has interfered in the daily government of 
the Principalities, the demands of the Sultan have been confined to the payment 
of the regular moderate tribute, and haye not embarrassed in any way the internal 
administration of the Hospodars. 

At the present moment three Powers might be expected to contend for 
control in the Principalities. |, Russia, while nominally yielding, might seek 
to retain, hy an ostentatious patronage, an influence with the inhabitants. 
2. ‘Turkey might seek to restore the direct means of government which she held 
before the later Treaties with Russia. 3. Austria might seek, by keeping up 
a permanent Conference, to regulate from Vienna the provinctal didmimistration, 

Lord Westmorland and 1 have not favoured any of these plans. By stipu- 
lating for a national administration with a collective guarantee of present and 
future privileges, und by denouncing and abolishing exelusive protection, we 

bar the claims of Russia. By not restoring the old powers of the Sultan, we 
shut out the evil of Turkish misgovernment. By refusing to erect a permanent 
Conference, we refuse to recognize a perpetual superintendence of the five 
Powers, which would end in the substitution of an Austrian for a Russian 
Protectorate. 

Tam aware it may be argued that the best mode of making the Princi- 
palities a barrier against Russia, would be to give the Turks a greater hold over 
the Principalities. But when I recollect the disorders which afflicted Thessaly 
and Albunia last year fiom the conflict of Christians and Mussulmans, [ cannot 
desire to expose the fertile and populous provinces of Wallachia and Moldavia 
to such a scourge. ee 

The only resouree, therefore, seems to be to strengthen the national institu 
tions of these Provinces, to influence the Porte to muke a good organic statute, 

and to leave the country to develop its natural resources, 

Many questions arise upon this subject, upon which we have not taken 
upon ourselves to pronounce, ‘ Sune 

For instance, should the Provinces be united? Should the Executive 


904 


nower be vested in the hands of an hereditary Prince, ora Prince appointed for 
life, or chosen for seven years? Should a representation be given extending to 
the people at large? Should any part of the military defence be entrusted to the 
Turks? Should Mussulmans be allowed, without taking part in the administra- 
tion, to settle in the Provinces ¢ 

These and other questions it appeared to us would be resolved far better 
in the presence of an Ambassador acquainted with the latest views of the 
Ottoman Government, or at Constantinople itself, than they could be by us, 
impressed as we were with the urgency of the business we had before us, and the 
scantiness of our information with regard to the exact state of the Principalities, 

There are some views, however, which it will be well to keep in mind. 

It would be desirable, certainly, to place the Executive power in the hands 
ofa Prince of enlightened views, and intent upon reforming the abuses which the 
corrupt rivalry of the Boyars has engendered in such loathsome profusion. 

There is to be objected however, in the first place, the difficulty of choice, 
and secondly, the consequences which would ensue. 

With respect to the difficulty of choice, the state of Belgium, as compared 
with that of Greece, shows the importance of the selection of a wise and prudent 
Prince. 

With respect to the second point, it may be enough to suggest that an 
hereditary Prince establishing himself by wise laws and conciliatory conduct would 
scarcely remain long a vassal of the Porte. ‘The Pasha of Egypt has the tie of 
religion to bind him to the Caliph ; but a Christian Prince, though he might call 
the Sultan his Suzerain, would be for all practical purposes independent. 

On the other hand, the election for seven years, and the power of removal 
by the Porte, keeps up a mischievous rivalry among the Boyars, and tends to 
perpetuate the rule of intrigue and corruption. 

With regard to free institutions, it must be remarked that the Sovereigns of 
Austria and Russia would never tolerate in the neighbourhood of Poland and 
Hungary promoters of disturbance and rebellion among their subjects, 

Freedom of discussion and liberty of the press would scarcely be suffered 
to proceed to any large extent unmolested; disturbance would be alleged, 
insurrection fenced ind armed intervention contemplated, Lt is questionable 
whether in such circumstances Great Britain could mterfere in behalf of these 
weak provinces with any citect. 

It is therefore worthy of consideration how far we should promote insti- 
tutions which we should not afterwards be able to protect. 

The removal of foreigners alleged to be engaged in plots: was sure to be 
insisted upon, und Lord Westmorland and I could only obtain a modification of 
the Article on this subject. At all events Wallachia and Moldavia might be 
expected to do for Austria and Russia what Belgium and Switzerland feel 
themselves bound to do for France, 

Kither at Constantinople or here the future condition of the Principalities 
must be carefully weighed, and the various questions | have glanced at be 
maturely considered, 

Should these questions be happily sulved, Russia will be effectually checked, 
Austria will be satisfied with the removal of a great rival from her immediate 
neighbourhood, and the welfare of 4,000,000 of people be permanently promated, 

2nily, The second point relates to the navigation of the Danube, 

The Russian Envoys have always alleged that the impediments to the free 
navigation of the Danube at its mouth have been owing to naturel obstacles, 
which the skill hitherto employed was not able to overeome. They have 
professed their willingness to lend their aid to any measures which might secure 
the freedom of navigation for the focure, 

The most important point in our discussions upon this subject, had 
reference to Article IL] of the Treaty of Adrianople. 

[ confess it did not appear to me, if the territory of Russia was not to 
suffer diminution, that we could give such proof of bad faith on thie part of 
Russia, as to justify ws in insisting upon the neutrality of the islands at the 
mouth of the Danube, As this proposal was strongly resisted by Russia, it was 
not pressed. 

‘The appointment of an European Commission in which a French and an 
English Commissioner will sit, will give the means of appointing men of practical 
scicnee to pont out how the existing obstacles may be removed, and new

I have thus gone over, I fear at tedious length, the discussious which have 
laken place upon two of the four points. | st} 

Whether the negotiations proceed happily, or break off suddenly, Her 
Majesty's Government are entitled to know the views upon which I have acted, 
and which seem to me to be in conformity both with the course hitherto 
sanctioned by Her Majesty, and with the instructions T have received. 

Your Lordship will have seen with regret that the Conference has not had

The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received April 2.) 


(No. 146.) 
My Lord, Vienna, March 30, 1855. 


L HAVE the honour of transmitting to your Lordship herewith the Protocol 
No. 6 of the Conference of the 26th of March, which was siencd this day, as 
well as its Annex, 

This Annex is the paper relative to the development of the first point, 
which has been drawn up by the French Government, and which Baron Bour- 
queney brought betore the Conference with a request that it might be attached 
to the Protocol, in order to serve as. a record of certain principles which, in the 
opinion of the French Government, should be taken into consideration when the 
Gnal settlement of the first guarantee was arrived at. It was not, however, his 
intention to open any fresh discussion upon the first point until it was known 
whether the Porte approved the views which the French Government had 
embodied in this paper. | 

Lord John Russell and I explained that the reason why we had abstained 
from bringing before the Conference any special suggestions relative to the future 
organisation of the Principalities, was founded on the conviction we entertained 
that it would not be expedient to do so until we should be enabled to know the 
precise views of the Ottoman Government respecting the principles on which the 
constitution of those Principalities should be remodelled. 

Count Buol said that he agreed entirely in the propriety of Baron Bour- 
queney bringing this document before the Conference, but expressed also his 
opinion that the views which it contained would most properly be brought 
forward by the Government of the Sultan ; and Prince Gortchakoff in concurring 
with Count Buol, said that he could not consider that any points respecting the 
first basis had been arranged, except those contained in the “ paraphe” Annexes 
to the former Protocols. 

he Turkish Ambassador, in giving his general adhesion to what had been 
said, reserved to his own Government the right of taking the initiative in 
carrying out the views embodied in the paper now presented to the Contorence 
by Baron Bourqueney. 

After this conversation, the discussion of the third article of the bases was 
commenced, the general tenow’ of which I have already reported to your Lord- 


553 


ship in my despatch No. 141 of the 96th instant, end which has been more 
amply detailed to your Lordship by Lord John Hussell. 

‘At the close of the Conference a proposal, made by Count Buol, to enter 
upon a preparatory consideration of the fourth basis at the next Conference, 
fixed for the 29th, gave rise to a statement on the part of Baron Bourqueney, as 
well as of Lord John Russell and myself, that before giving our consent to this 
proposal, we must refer to our respective Governments to learn their opinion 
upon it. This reference was accordingly made to your Lordship by Lord John 
Russell and myself in our telegraphic despatch of yesterday, which is also 
referred to in my despateh No. 145 of this day. 

I have, &c.

Mr. Bligh to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received April 2.) 


(No. 63.) 
My Lord, Hanover, March 31, 1855, 

I HAVE the honour of thanking your Lordship for your despatches 
marked Confidential, Nos, 82 and 33 of the 22nd instant, with their 
interesting inclosures, which enabled me, in conversation with M. de Lenthe and 
others, without betraying any confidence, to manifest that I have the full 
conviction of the vigorous support which Austria has been giving to the Plenipo- 
tentiaries of the Western Powers in their Conferences with those of Russia at 
Vienna; and of the firm determination which she has been showing in her 
official communications respecting Russian agency at the Dict, not to allow that 
agency to nullify the decisions of that body respecting the warlike preparations 
of Germany, | 

For thus I am assisted in strengthening the determination of this Govern- 
ment to continue to side with the Cabinet of Vienna, as being the most likely 
means of inducing Russia to go on so far in the path of concession, an which she 
has happily entered, as will authorise the conclusion of such a peace as the 
belligerents desire, and as will alone prevent the breaking out of that peneral 
war which the neutral and the wavering so much deprecate. 

General Budberg, cousin of the Russian Minister at Berlin, has heen here 
for two days, for the purpose of presenting letters, notifying to the King the 
accession of the Emperor Alexander. | 

He dined both days at Court, and received as his reward the Grand Cross 
of the Guelphic Order, having been decorated in a similar manner at the Courts 
of Darmstadt, Brussels, and the Hague, where he had previously been on the 
same errand, From hence he goes this day te Oldenburg, where, of course, a 
similar honour awaits him, As, if he had represented his Sovereign at each of 
these Courts for as any years as he will have employed days in this itinerary of 
temporary missions, he could not have been more highly favoured in this way,

The Earl of Clarendon to Lord John Russell. 
(No 35.) he est : 
My Lord, Foreign Office, April 3, 1855. 
~ COUNT COLLOREDO has read to mea despatch from Count Buol on the 
subject of the third point, which forms the greatest difficulty in the negotiations, 
and which is about to be taken into consideration by the Conference. 

Count Buol observes that Russia, having admitted the principle that her pre- 
ponderance in the Black Sea is to be put an end to, there can be no doubt that. 
apparently the simplest and most direct mode of attaming the end which the 
allies have in view would be by the limitation of the naval forces of Russia in 
that sea, ‘his result might be obtained by Russia engaging either to reduce 
her fleet to a fixed number of vessels, or not to increase their actual number: 
and the latter alternative, whilst it would make the sacrifice more easy, 
would come to nearly the same result, as half the fleet gt Sebastopol has already 
been sunk by the Russians themselves. 

But Count Buol thinks that there may be reason to apprehend that Russia 
may oppose this solution of the question, on the ground of its affecting her 
dignity and national honour, which the Emperor Alexander will have to consult 
as much, or perhaps even more, than his predecessor. tah 

He argues, therefore, that it will be necessary to provide for the case of 
Russia refusing categorically to enter into any positive engagement to reduce 
her naval forees. In such an event, and supposing that a complete agreement 


had been come to on the three other points, would the belligerent Powers, Count) 


Buol asks, consider it indispensable to continue the war on that account? But 
he adds, that whatever their decision might be, Austria, for her part, not being 
at present engaged in hostilities, would have no sufficient motive to declare war 
aginst Russia, if the sole obstacle to peace were the refusal of that I ower to 
consent to the direct limitation of the Russian naval forces in the Black Sea, 

In order then to arrive at a practical solution of the question, Count Buol 
js of opinion that recourse must be had to the system of cotunterpoise. For 
this purpose, he says that several possible combinations present themselves. 


Russia and ‘Turkey might enter into reciprocal engagements not to maintain - 


in the Black Sea more than an equal number of ships of war. A 

In this case the only other point to be considered would be the revision of 
the ‘Treaty of 1841, so far as to concede to the other Powers the right of main- 
taining a limited number of ships of war in the Black Sea, with the special object 
of watching over the due execution of the arrangements for keeping clear the 
Havigation of the Danube at its mouths. 


If, however, Count Buol adds, the naval forces of Turkey and Russia in - 


5a5 


the Euxine could not be placed in this manner on a footing of equality, the 
Porte might, whilst maintaining the principle of the closing of the Straits as 
a general rule, reserve to herself the right of calling into the Black Sea, as an 
exceptional measure, even in time of peace, as many ships of war of friendly 
Powers, as she might consider necessary whenever she found herself menaced. 

If Russia persisted in maintaining in the Black Sea a fleet larger than could 
be required for purposes of defence, and refused to consent to any kind of limita- 
tion of them, it would be impossible to contest the right of Europe to consider 
the maintenance of such force ag a permanent danger to Turkey: in this case the 
exception would become the rule, and the Porte would have continually reasons 
for giving firmans to the ships of war of friendly Powers to pass the Straits. 
Such astate of things would, Count Buol thinks, be little agreeable to Russia ; 
and it is by strongly supporting this argument, that it may be possible to con- 
vince Russia that it is more for her own interest to prefer either a direct or 
indirect system of limitation, 

I told Count Colloredo that I had listened to Count Buol’s despatch with 
equal surprise as concern, as it was nothing short of an announcement that 
Austria would not adhere to the Treaty of December 2, if the Western Powers 
persisted in carrying the third basis into effect, for Count Buol must be aware 
that his proposed system of counterpoise was both inadequate and impracticable. 
A reciprocal engagement between Russia and Turkey to maintain an equal 
number of ships in the Black Sea would secure the preponderance of Russia, 
whose ships would always be better manned, better armed, and in a better con- 
dition than those of Turkey; but Count Buol proposed, that at the same time 
other Powers should maintain a limited number of ships of war in the Black 
Sea, for the special object of keeping clear the navigation of the Danube, and 
upon that | begged to observe, that the special object might or might not be 
the real one, and Count Buol might be sure that England and France would not 
profess one thing while they intended another. If Count Buol’s proposals were 
really ta be adopted, I could only say that. ships of war would be utterly useless 
at the mouths of the Danube to watch over the fulfilment of stipulations that 
a Commission was appointed to carry out; that if these ships moved away from 
the mouths of the Danube, Russia would have just ground for complaint, and 
that if England and France were suddenly to be at war with Russia, this limited 
force might at once be overpowered by the foree that Russin would be suffered 
to retain. But if England and France, under pretext of watching the Danube, 
were to send a foree into the Black Sea to protect Turkey and keep Russia in 
check, then we should simply be continuing the present system, which effectually 
secures both these objects, but which system we are on every account desirous 
to put an end to. 

Count Buol's next proposal, that Turkey should call in as many foreign 
ships of war as she thought necessary, whenever she found herself menaced, 
appeared tome, I said, even more objectionable; for it would impose upon the 
Western Powers the duties of perpetual police, while 1 would relieve ‘Turkey 
from the care of providing for her own protection, as she would consider that she 
had acquired a right by Treaty to call upon England and France for aid when- 
ever she thought herself in danger, without reference to the cost and inconveni- 
ence to them orto the distance at which their fleets might happen to be stationed, 
As Count Buol, however, abandoned the notion of limiting the naval force of 
Russia, und consequently of preventing its indefinite augmentation, Turkey would 
always be in danger, and consequently would always consider hersell menaced. 

But what was the meaning, Lasked, of this right to cull upon foreign Powers ? 
Surely it could not be intended to uphold the independence of the Ottoman 
Empire by a stipulation which made its existence dependent upon forcign ussist- 
ance? And what were England and France to do in the event of their obeying 
these calls, which might constantly be repeated? Why, they would have to send 
into the Black Sea on cach occasion armaments as powerful as they now muain- 
tain there in order to be on a footing of equality with Russia, and they must 
always be expecting and be prepared to go to war with Russia, 

But Russia will be mistress of her own policy and her own actions, and will 
know how best to carry out her own designs at the right moment. 

So far from menacing Tass she might establish the most friendly relations 
with her, she might lull her into false security, and within three days after she had 
picked a quarrel with Turkey, a Russian army might be in possession of (on-

THE Baron de Bourqueney’s despatches having led the lrench Govern- 
ment to doubt whether it was the intention of Russia to accept the third basis 
in the sense in which it has always been understood by England and France, it 
occurred ta M. Drouyn de Lhuys that the object in view might he effectually 
attained, and that the dignity of Russia might be better consulted, by excluding 
all ships of war from the Black Sea. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys accordingly prepared a memorandum upon the means 
of giving effect ta the * neutralization’ of the Black Sea, and he proposed that 
with the concurrence of Her Majesty's Government this project should be sub- 
mitted to the Conference as a proof of the desire entertained by England and 
France to meet any reasonable objections on the part of Russia, and of the 
eincerity with which they labour to bring the negotiations to a peaceful conclu- 
ION. wie 

A copy of this memorandum 1s herewith inclosed for the information ot 

your Lordship and Lord Westmorland, 
"1 acquainted your Lordship by telegraph on the 24th ultimo, that Her 
Majesty's Government acceded to the project of the Prench Government with a 
reaerve which, on consideration of the memorandum of M, Drouym de Lhuys, it 
appeared prudent to make, “e oe | | 

The Baron de Bourqueney informed his Government that the project had 
not been favourably received at Vienna, and M. Drouyn de Lhays, alter taking 
the orders of the Emperor, determined to proeved himself to Vienna for the 
purpose of explaining and supporting hs views, but to come in the first instanee 
to Louden in order to estublish a complete understanding between the two 
Governments as to the course that itwould be expedient to pursue. M. Drouyn 

de Lhuys accordingly lett Paris on the 26th ultimo, and on the following day a 
mecting was held bere, at which were present t he French Ambassador, 
M. Drouyn de Lhuvs, Lord Palmerston, Lord Lansdowne, and myself, 

The questions of the neutralizution of the Black Sea, and that of the 
limitation of the Russian naval force in that sen, were fully discussed. 

With respect to the first (ncutralization), it was agreed to propose ; 


let. That Russia and Turkey should have no ships of warin the Black Sea, nor 


o07 


in the Sea of Azoff, excepting some few small vessels for the purposes of sea police 
to prevent piracy; and that as regarded the Sea of Marmora and the Bosphorus, 
an understanding should be come to with the Porte, with a view to ascertain 
whether the Porte would not be willing to include those waters in the arrange- 
ment if it should be necessary to do so, in order to obtain the consent of Russia 
to the application of the principle of neutrality to the Black Sea and to the Sea 
of Azoff. 

2nd. That the ports of the two Powers in the Black Sea and the Sea of 
Azoff should be solely commercial ports. 

3rd. That foreign Powers should be allowed to have Consuls in those ports. 

4th. That there should be no menacing assemblage of troops by cither 
Pewer on the shores of the Black Sea, 

Sth. ‘That the allied Powers (England, France, and Austria), should have 
the right to send their naval forces into the Black Sea if the provisions of the 
Treaty should be violated, 

th. That the two Powers (Russia and Turkey) should have the right to 
maintain a fixed number of light vessels for the police of the Black Sea, and 
unarmed transports exclusively adapted for the conveyance of troaps. 


With respect to the second question, viz. the limitation of the naval force of 
Russia, it was agreed to propose : 


Ist. That Russia and Turkey should each of them maintain in the Black 
Sea, and in the Sea of Azoff, no more than four sail of the line and four frigates, 
with a proportionate number of light vessels for the police of those seas, and of 
unarmed transports exclusively adapted for the conveyance of troops, and that 
this same limitation should apply to the naval foree which Turkey should 
maintain in the Bosphoras and in the Sea of Marmora. 

8ndly. That England, France, and Austria should each be permitted to 
maintain half that number of ships in the Black Sea, that is to say, two sail of 
the line, and two frigates, and some smaller vessels for each of the three Powers 
if they should think fit so to station them, Russian ships of war not to be 
allowed to enter the Bosphorus, nor to pass through the Straits into the 
Mediterranean. 

Srd. That, in case of danger to Turkey, and on the demand of the Porte, 
all the naval forees of England, France, and Austria, should be allowed to enter 
the Black Sea to assist in defending the Turkish Empire. 

4th. That the Contracting Powers should be allowed to have Consuls at 
all the Russian and ‘Turkish ports in the Black Sea and in the Sea of Azoff. 


It was then agreed : 


Ist; That the two systems, namely, that of the neutralization of the Black 
Sea, and that of the limitation of the naval forces of Russia and Turkey in the 
Black Sea, should be explained to Austria, and that she should be asked 
whether she would adopt either the one or the other, so as to cooperate with 
France and England in proposing it to Russia, undertaking further to cooperate 
in war with France and England if the plan so proposed should be rejected by 
Russia. 

Ond. That it should be understood that France and England would prefer 
the system of neutralization if Austria should leave the choice to England and 
France, 

Srd. That if Austria should refuse to bind herself to cooperate in war with 
France and England, in the event of Russia rejecting that one of the two pro- 
posals which Austria might coneur with France and England in proposing, then 
France and Englund should propose the plan of neutralization, and uf it ts 
rejected by Russia, the negotiation must be broken off. 


I have only further te add, that [ler Majesty's Government rely with 
confidence upon the best elforts af your Lordship and of Lord Westmorland 
being used for carrying into effect the agreement nt 
the Government of the Euiparor of the French.

My Lord, Foreign Office, April 3, 1855, 
THE Protocol No. 4, with its Annex, inclosed in your Lordship’s despatch 
No. 36 of the 26th ultimo, have been attentively considered by Her Majesty's 
Government, who are of opinion that if the navigation of the Danube is to be 
regulated in accordance with the Treaty of Vienna, the Commission should 
sonsist of a Bavarian, an Austrian, a Russian, and a Turk; and the regulations 
should apply to the whole course of the Danube, from the sea upto the point 
where it first becomes navigable; and such an arrangement would require no 
further guarantee. If, on the other hand, there 18 to be a special arrangement 
to which Bavaria is not to be a party, and which is to apply only to that part of 
the river from the sea upwards to the point where it ceases to divide Austrian 
and Turkish territory, that is, to the point where both banks are Austrian, then 
the ‘Treaty of Vienna is no longer the rule, and the Commission to be appointed 
ought to contain an English and a French member, because England and Franee 
are deeply interested in having the channels of the river kept tree and open, 

Your Lordship is well aware how often, in reply to our remonstrances, we 
have received from the Russian Government precisely the same assurances fs 
the Russian Plenipotentiaries have now given, that every means would be taken 
to keep the ehannel clear; those promises were never fulfilled, and Her Majesty's 
Government have now certain information that the English engineer em loyed 
in the steam-dredge to clear the Sulina Mouth was absolutely prohibited by the 
Russian authorities from working the steam-dredge in an effectual manner, 

‘Austria was. more interested in this question than Englund and France, but 
her trade has been checked and her remonstrances have met with no attention 
from Russia. 5. 

The same motives will again be in operation, and the utmost vigilance 
will be required to provent a renewal of the same obstacles. ; 

The opposition of Austria to the appomtment of an English and French 
member of the Commission is, therefore, unintelligible to Her Majesty’s 
Government. Count Buol pleads as a reason, the necessity of adhering to the 
Treaty of Vienna, but the proposed plan, a5 1 have shown, 1s a departure [rom 
that ‘Treaty; and even if it were not, there ean be no sullicient cause for adhering 
closely to the Treaty if an arrangement can be made by which important 
interests will be better protected. | 

Lam, &e.

The Earl of Clarendon to Lord John Russell.

My Lord, Foreiqn Office, April 3, 1855. 


WITH reference to your Lordship’s despatch No. 38 of the 26th ultimo, I 
beg to inform you that Her Majesty’s Government learn with much satisfaction 
that in your Lordship’s opiuion Count Buol has behaved with great fidelity to 
the spirit of the engagements which his Government had contracted ; and they 
concur in the observation of his Excellency to Prince Gortehakoff, that if it was 
true that Russia might keep up the forceshe pleased within her own limits, it was 
also true that other Powers hada right to require explanations, and upon their not 
being satisfactory to declare war. But the naval force maintained by Russia within 
her own limits gives her the preponderance in the Black Sea; and Austria, 
together with England and Irance, have declared that that preponderance must 
cease, The third basis is the form in which explanations are required of Russia, 
or in other words, the form in which Russia is invited to put an end to the 
uneasiness felt by other Powers at her vast means of aggression ; and if these 
explanations are not satisfactory, and if Russia will not remove the causes of 
apprehension, it is to be hoped that Count Buol will admit that a easus belli 
then arises for Austria, and that England and France cannot make peace with 
Thussia.

| HAVE the satisfaction to inform your Lordship that Her Majesty's 
Government entirely approve the course pursued by your Lordship and Lord

anxious that no door which affords an opening for the restoration of peace 
should be permanently closed, and it was quite right, therefore, that the Hussian 
Plenipotentiary should be permitted to refer to his Government the terms by 
which it was proposed to give effect to the third basis; but Her Majesty's 
Government have learned with much surprise Prince Gortehakoll’s announce- 
ment that he was prepared to discuss any propositions that might be made, 
but that he was not prepared to make any himself. 

Russia, however, having accepted the principle of the third basis, must 
have determined in what manner she would consent to its practical application ; 
and the refusal of the Russian Plenipotentiary to make any communication on the 
subject that most interested the belligerent Powers, is in singulur contrast with 
the readiness he exhibited in making proposals upon the first two bases, which 
more immediately affected Austria. Her Majesty’s Government are unwilling 
to assume, that by drawing this distinction between the three Powers, Prince 
Gortchakoff meant it to be understood that lie was there to listen to the terms 
on which England and France asked for peace; but if such should be your Lord- 
ship’s opinion, or should the same course again be pursued, Her Majesty's 
Goverument do not doubt that the error of Prince G cain kolf will be effectually 
corrected by your Lordship. Her Majesty's Government entirely concur in your 
Lordship's views respecting the inadequate and impracticable system of counter- 
poise; but a simple decluration on the part of the Emperor of Russia, that he 
would not increase the number of ships of war he may have in the Black Sea 
at the time of signing the preliminaries of peace, would be hardly less inadequate 
for removing the alarm of Turkey and the jealousy of Europe.

amount of limitation of the Russian flect that we require; but if the Emperor

My Lord, Frankfort, March 30, 1855. 

THE incidents of the sitting of the Diet of the 22nd of February, have lost 
most of their political importance by the disavowal of the Prussian Cabinet of any 
intention of holding out a menace or doing aught in on unfriendly spirit towards 
the Western Powers, and especially to France, 

M. de Bismark’s language on the occasion referred to, could not, however, 
but be so interpreted ; as whether he did or did not openly announce an intended 
motion for arming the fortresses on the French frontier, the pointed way in which 
he directed attention to the motives of the Federal resolution for military pre- 
paration, became, in its attempted ambiguity and the studied research with which 
it was sought to avoid the semblance of a menace to Russia, a clear declaration 
against lrance, 

In that sense the French Government were fully justified in regarding it, 
and in acting accordingly, as they did, by remonstrating at Berlin. 

The spirit in which those remonstrauces were received, was not apparently of 
a friendly nature, and a circular of M, de Manteuffel to the Representatives of 
Prussia at the German Courts, complaining that M. Drouyn de Lhuys should 
make what passed in the Dict a subject of remark or ground of interierence, is, 
as your Lordship bas no doubt remarked, drawn up in rather sharp terms, 

M. de Tallenay lias just shown me adespatel: which he reevived yesterday 
from his Government, and which he was directed to communicate to M. de 
Rechberg, which informs Mode Tallenay that the French Government do not 
admit M, de Muanteuffel's reasoning. ‘That in all matters concerning purely 
German interests, France would scrupulously abstain from anything of the 
sort, but when a foreign Governnient obtained a knowledge, as they had done, 
of anatters having passed in that assembly which intimately concerned them, 
they had both the right and the duty to point cut the dangers which the course 
indicated might bring on,

Lord Jokn Russell to the Earl of Clarendon —( Received April 4.) 


(No, 48.) 
My Lord, Vienna, March 31, 1859. 

1 HAD understood from your Lordship that as late ns the 20th of the present 
month, your Lordship and your colleagues were all of opinion that it was 
impossible to recede from our demand of limitation of Russian naval foree in the 
Black Sea. 

I had also understood that your Lordship was of opinion that the demand 
need certainly not be made in an offensive shape, and that it was possible that if 
Russia were allowed to view it as an arrangement required for the security and 
satisfaction of Europe, and as a proof of her non-aggressive intentions, mstead 
of a condition imposed upon her by England and France, Prince Gortchakoff 
might be instrocted to suggest restrictions on Russia that he would reject if 
proposed Lo him, 

This course would, if L understood your Lordship rightly, be sound policy 
for the Emperor Alexander himeell, who would thus begin his reign with the 
sympathies of Europe in his favour. 

Acting upon similar views, Count Buol had suggested to Prince Gortchakoff 
that it would be better to propose limitations on the Russian naval power in the 
Black Sea on the part of his Court, than to aceept such limitations when pro- 
posed hy the belligerent Powers. Prince Gortehakoff had proposed himself 
ready to scek for further instructions from his-Court, and the French Minister 
and we had fallen in with the iroposition of Count Buol, 

In. so doing, | aneelved 1 was acting entirely in accordance with your 
Lordship’s views. 

[ was therefore a good deal surprised when, within forty-eight hours of the 
meeting of the Conference upon the third point, L received a notice of a plan 
of neutralization of the Black Sea, which I was instructed to support. 

Baron Bourqueney received his despatches developing this plan late on the 
evening of the 25th, and it was not till 12 o'clock of the 26th that we and the 
Austrian Minister of Foreign Affairs were apprized of the contents of these 
despatches, 

Count Buol was unprepared to support, or even to examine, so novel a plan ; 
and in the Conference, as your Lordship is already informed, he pursued the 
course he had already, though imperfectly, communicated to us, 

{t may have been possible that the Governments of France and Great 
Britain had conceived the plan of neutralization to be more impartial and cone 
eiliatory than the plin of limitation. The French Minister, however, was soon 
made aware that it would not be so considered, 

It appears by your Lordship's telegraphic despatch of last night that the 
issue of the negotiation is to be made to turn on the acceptance of this plan, and 
not on that of the limitation of the Russian naval force in the Black Sen. 

It ia my duty to point out to your Lordship the consequences which may 
be expected to follow from this course. 

The Plenipotentiary of Russia will consider that he has heen induced by the 
representations of Austria, Great Britain, and Franee, to ask his Court to make 
concessions which, even if made, would not be considered satisiactory. 


otis 


_ ‘The Austrian Minister will find in this new proposition an easy way out of 
his promises to observe all the engagements he has made. 

Finally, the Western Powers, having so long dwelt on limitation, and 
changing their proposals at the last moment, may be liable to imputations 
which they have hitherto cast on Russia—of insincerity in the negotiations. 

These consequenees are so grave, that I have thought it my duty to lay them 
before your Lordship; and I trust they will be duly considered by Her Majesty's 
Government. 

[ have, &e.

My Lord, Vienna, April |, Leas:

and France those practices against which we have always protested, and which 
have rested up to this time only on the interpretation which Russia has pul upon 
her own ‘Treaties with the Porte” ; eu |

‘the former and the present Administration,

orders, delivered to Count Buol a note which lie was iistructed to declare 
resulted from “confidential communications which have taken place between 
the Courts of Vienna, Paris, and London.” eee 

In this note it was solemnly announced “ that the three Powers are equally 
of opinion that the relations of the Sublime Porte with the Imperial Court of 
Russia, cannot be re-established on solid and durable bases: cen

over the Principalities of Wallachia, Moldavia, and Servia be not discontinued 
for the future, and if the privileges necorded by the Sultans to those | pane

The provision which was declared necessary 1 the beginning of August 5

maintained at the end of December. In the memorandum delivered to Prince

“Que leurs Gouvernements, en jugeant de commun accord qu'il était

In like manner, at the first meeting of the Conference on the 15th of 
March, Count Buol declared in the name of the Austrian Government: “1. The 
Protectorate exercised by Russia over Moldavia and Wallachia shall cease, and 
the privileges acknowledged by the Sultan to belong to these Principualities, as 
well as to Servia, shall for the future be placed under the collective guarantee 
of the Contracting Powers.” | 

The despatch containing a report of what passed in this Conference was 
acknowledged by your Lordship in your despateh Ko. 18 of the 20th ultimo. 

___ | presume that your Lordship must have often reflected on the gravity and 
Inportance of the engagement to which Great Britain was to be pledged by this 
guarantee. 

It is a matter of no slight importance to guarantee a territory. But the 
object is at all events a simple one. So long as that territory is not invaded, or 
the independence of its Sovercign threatened, the guarantee is dormant. 

Not so with the guarantee of the privileges of a Province under the 
suzeraineté of another Power. No one can say how often or on how many 
points the privileges of the inhabitants of the Principalities might be violated by 
the Sultan, direetly or indirectly, 

The Ministers of the Porte might corruptly influence the nomination of a 
Hospodar, who, in his turn, might ask for Turkish troops to defend his violation 
of Wallachian or Moldavian privileges. In short, many cases may be con- 
ceived requiring representations to the Sultan, on the part of the guaranteeing 
Powers. 

The state of Bulgaria during the occupation of the British army list year, 
afforded lamentable instances of the excesses of the Turkish soldiery, “But 
neither will it have escaped your Lordship, for many months thinking and 
writing upon these subjects, that Austria and Russia, being neighbouring Powers, 
ave likely to lave a greater part in any interference than France and Great 
Britain can properly exercise, 

Tim far from saying that such an obligation is not onerous and inconvenient, 
but in my present position Tam not called upon to defend the collective 
Puaraintec, 

All 1 contend for is, that having embraced the principle, your Lordship, 
Her Majesty's Ministers, and 1, must bear the consequences, 

Vere is another point on which some explanation may be required. 

Lord Westmorland and I were careful to limit our sanction to the removal 
of disturbers of the peace, who might be foreigners, to disapprobation, and a 
refusal of protection. So much we have always admitted in respect to British 
subjects ibroad, andso much, if 1 am not mistaken, your Lordship and the 
Cabinet claimed from the United States in respect to their citizens engaged in 
fomenting disturbances in Ireland, 

For such an Article as is now inserted I have all along been prepared. 

I never expeeted that Austria and Russia would allow Hungary and Poland 
to be disturbed by the intrigues of forcigners in the Principalities. 

They are too jealous of their power to allow such dangers to exist in their 
neighbourhood. )

No. 604. 


The Earl of Clarendon to Lord John Russell. 
(No. 40.) ap 
My Lord, Foreign Office, April 5, 1855, 
WITH reference to your Lordship’s despatch No, 46 of the 30th ultimo, 
in which you state that the Austrian Government maintain that Constantinople 
eannot he taken by a coup de main, that the only formidable attack on Turkey 
must be made by the Balkan, and that Austria would employ all her forces to 
prevent the suceess of such an attack, | have to observe that if the Austrian 
Government, upon due reflection, entertain these opinions, they are quite 
justified in asserting them, but Her Majesty's Government are equally entitled 
to maintain their own opinions, which are in direct opposition to those of the 
Austrian Government. 

It appears unquestionable, that if Russia is permitted not only to retain, 
but indefinitely to increase, her nayal forces in the Black Sea, Constantinople 
must always be in imminent danger of a sudden attack, unless the Sultan were 
to keep up and hold in constant readiness a land and sea force sufficient to 
repel such an attack ; but even if the finances of Turkey permitted of sucha 
continuous exertion, it would create an armed and insecure truce, and not the 
state of peace that we are all desirous of restoring. There is no reason, however, 
why a combined movement should not be made by sea and laud, ey that a 
Russian army should not enter Turkey from Bessarabia, at the same time that 
a Russian fleet attacked Constantinople, and then, whatever might be the 
activity and goodwill of Austria, she would find it impossible to prevent the 
success of the operation. 

Her Majesty’s Government entirely concur with your Lordship, that: if 
Austria were to he thoroughly engaged with the Western Powers, and ready to 
take part with them in the war, her action would be seriously impeded by 
the policy of Prussia, but Her Majesty's Government would not think it expe- 
dient, at the present moment. to call upon Prussia to give the securities for har 
friendly neutrality that your Lordship has suggested for their consideration, 

A demand that two fortresses and a sea-port of Prussia should be placed 
in the hands of Austria, France, and England, would not only rouse the national 
spirit of the Prussians against the allies, but might induce the whole of Germany 
to adopt the cause of Prussia, and the King, thus supported and urged on, 
might then take part with Russia more openly than he has hitherto ventured 
to do. 

But whenever Austria declires war against Russia, Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment will be prepared at once to coneert with her as to the most effectual 
means of guarding against the designs of Prussia, if there should then be reason 
to consider thei hostile. 

Tam, &e. 
(Signed) CLARENDON,

nevertheless been the cause of uneasiness and alarm to Sweden ; while the 
extraordinary secrecy observed by Russia on the subject, and the great extent to 
which, as we now know, the fortifications were to be carried, prove that Russia 
had designs which she was deeply interested in concealing from Europe. 

In fact, there ean be little doubt: that Russia aimed equally at extending her 
dominion in the north and in the east, and that by the possession of the Sound 
as well as of the Bosphorus, she meditated a deadly blow at the independence 
of Europe: 


The fortress of Bomarsund is now laid in ruins, and it must not be recon- 


structed, We huve discovered the danger that threatened us, and it would be 
most unwise it we exposed ourselves to ‘ts recurrence; and Her Majesty's 
Government have therefore to request that your Lordship and Lord Westmorland 
will communicate with the Plenipotentiaries of France upon this important 
subject, amd that with their concurrence, you will bring it to the notice of the 
Russian Plenipotentiaries 

Whatever may be the opinion of Her Majesty's Government upon the 
Treaty of 1809, by which Sweden was compelled ta cede Finland to Russia, they 
do not, in the present state of the war, desire to disturl the existing arrangement ; 
but they have a fight to demand that under cover of that Treaty the security of 
other countries shall not be endangered, and that Bomarsund shall not be to the 
north of Europe the standing menace that Sebastopol is to Turkey. 

Her Majesty's Government would therefore propose that 4 Convention 
should be signed between England, France, and Russia, providing that no 
fortification of any kind shall heneclorward exist in the Aland Islands. 

It is to be hoped that this proposed measure of security will not be 
considered by Russia as offensive to her dignity, as historical precedents abound 
of great Powers consenting by sinilar guarantees to Temove the uneasiness that 
other Powers were justified in feeling ; and Her Majesty’s Government trust that 
the refusal of Russia may not Impose upon them the duty of considering in 
what way Her Majesty's naval forces in the Baltie may be rude instrumental 
towards an object that they desire to uttain by peacctul means. 

| inclose a copy of the ‘Treaties between Russia and Sweden, which it may 
be useful to your Lordship to possess. 

Tam, &e.

My Lord, Moossul, February 26, [Sac 

1 HAVE the honour to inform: your Excellency that on the: 24th instant, 
his Excellency Helmy Pasha received the following intelligence from. his Kahya, 
who left this for Semail about a month ago. That he had dispatched Hussein 
Bey. the Emir of Yeaidees, with his 2,000 followers, to attack the outposts of 
Vexdasheer Bey near Duraboona, That Hussem Bey had repulsed the Kurds 
with a loss of ane man killed, and several wounded : the enemy, however, Jost. 
several men, and were driven to Phashapoor. Hussein Bey pursued them, and 
the enemy not being able to keep their ground fled towards Jezerch in the greatest 
confusion ; he then directed his oh to Zukho, but the Kurdish garrison there, 
hearing of the defeat of their brethren, fled to the mountains with their Com- 
mander Adel Bey, leaving Hussein Bey in possession of the town, and he, the 
Kahva, had just received a letter informing him that he had taken the town in 
the name of His Majesty the Sultan. ; 

Mohammed Pasha, who left this with his army on the 10th instant, are 
still encamped at Chil-Agha, only twenty-five hours from Moossul. ‘There: 13, 
however, a report current here that Yezdasheer Bey surprised the camp on the 
night of the H98nd with 10,000 men, and was repulsed by the Nizam, with a 
severe loss of 3,000 killed, and 800 taken prisoners. This report requires 
confirmation, as since the army left this no official intelligence has been received 
from Mohammed Pasha.

Extract of a Letter from Aleppo. 


March 6, 1855. 

HIS Excellency Suliman Pasha left this for Antioch on the following day, 
Saturday the 8rd instant, accompanied with the same ceremonies, to a short 
distance from the city, by-all the abovementioned officers, but not, in full dress. 
His Excellency, who leaves universally regretted, visited in person, and took 
leave of all the Patriarchs and Bishops, as well as all the Consuls. 

The two French mail messengers who left this on the 28th, to meet the 
steamers or the Ist and 2nd at Alexandrettay were robbed between Kan Dinrbe- 
kerli and Beylan by twelve men, everything taken from them, and one of them 
wounded In eight places. 

It is currently reported ‘here that these men are the followers of Latiee 
Agha, in connection with Ahmet Bey, Mersaloglu, and that they hope by this 
step to compel the Government to replace that Chief in command of the 
Amk,! his rival. Izzet Bey being exceedingly unpopular. His Exeellency 
Ismail Pasha has-sent persons to investigate amd take measures to prevent any 
recurrence of such acts, ts
