(No, 228. Confidential.) 


My Lord, Constantinople, March 25, 1855. 

The Grand Vizier called upon me this morning, and entered into conversa 
tion on the subject of the negotiations by this time opened at Vienna, 

It ig evident from his Highness’s language that the Porte has strong 
opinions of its own on some of the points which are to be debated there. j 

An Austrian protectorate in the Prineipalites, however limited, would never 
meet with its cordial assent. ‘The consolidation of the two provinces under it 
single chief would also fail to receive its support. There is every disposition, | 
conceive, to improve the condition of the country, to secure its administrative 
independence, and to render the relations between the Boyards anid the inbiali- 
tants in general less onerous to the latter, The Porte, 1 believe, is not insensible 
to *he importance of calming the jealousy of Austria with respect to democratic 
institutions, and the advantages to which she looks for, herself, are less those of 
uses than of inereased revenue and of surer defence against Russia. The 
‘rinces, J apprehend, will remain to be chosen among the native aristocracy, 
and, if the Porte has its way, the tribute will be reasonably augmented, and the 
destroyed fortresses will be revived for the reception of Turkish garrisons. 

With. respect to the Danube and its freedom of navigation, the Porte, | 
doubt not, will enter willingly into any measures adopted in common for the 
attainment of that important object, The Grand Vizier would be delighted to 


exclude the Russians from contact with the river, but he would not consent to 
eede the Dobrudscha ta Wallachia,

(No.  .) 


My Lord, Constantinople, March 25, 1855. 

I WENT over to Constantinople this morning at an curly hour, and saw 
Reshid Pasha at a friend's house, where he had slept for two or three hours 
after passing the greater part of the night in Council, 1 found his Highness in 
cheerful spirits, notwithstanding the fatigue whieh he had undergone, and he 
told me, with every appearance of satistietion, that he had at length obtained the 
consent of his colleagues to the principal leads of that svstem of social reform 
and administrative iuprovement whieh he had contemplated for many years with 
soo much anxicty. 

According to Ins confidential statement, the harateh is finally condemned, 
a tax being to be substituted in its place under the denomination of a succour 
or subsidy for wir, Christians are to be received into the army, and to he made 
eapuble of holding rank as Colonels. In the administrative serviee, they are to 
be made cligible for employment in all the five classes of civil rank. This 
limitation would have them exeluded from high offices of State and chief pro- 
vincial commands, THe stated, that with respect to the haratel, clear trans 
gression of the Koran was undisguisedly adopted, but that the Slicik-ul-[slam 
had consented to the innovation, not indéed in’ lis spiritual capacity, but as 
Minister of State, Tle added, that the construction of anew code of law was 
in prowess; that he hoped the measures now adopted would open the wily ba 
other more complete reforms; that so great a change could not be effoeted at 
once; and that in his belief the Gavernment was now fairly launched Upon tb 
career of improvement which would lead in time to the happiest results, 

In expressing the pleasure which | derived from his communication, | was 
careful not to make too lane an admission, or to allow him to lose sight of the 
defective execution which has hitherto attended every principle and measure of 
reform promulgated by the Sultan, 1 reminded him of the practical abuses and 
idministrative crimes which pervaded the empire; of the fatal consequences 
which they entailed, and the necessity of foreign support and foreign superin- 
tendenee to secure the enforcement of sulutary laws. IL repeated what L had so 
olten urged before us to the dangerous condition of the Empire, and the slender 
prospect of its renovation, unless the system of ‘Tartar exchisiveness were 
ciscanded, aod the Eimpire not only internally imipraved in pomt of adminis- 
tration, justior, apd hutanity, but thrown open with littl: reserve to the capital, 
the mdustry, und the science of western eiviltzation. 

I should weary your Lordship if | were to recon the whole series of argu- 
ments which | pressed on the Vivier's attention: but | must do his Hichness 
the Justice fo sav that, inn making excuses for binsell and: his collouzues, he 
almitted the truth of my remarks: and expressed a sanauine hope that my

My Lord, Mienna, April 5, 1855, 


THE eighth Conference was held on Monday, April 2nd, when the Protocol 
of the former Conference was read and agreed to. 

Upon the declaration made by the French Minister, Lord Westmorland, 
and me, that our Governments did not agree to the discussion of the fourth 
point before the third was settled, Prince Gortehakoff took another opportunity 
of vaunting the sympathy of his Sovereign with the Christian subjects of the 
Porte, 

Baron Bourqueney and 1 refuted this pretension. I took occasion to refer 
to the exertions made by Lord Stratford de Redeliffe, and applauded the humanity 
of the Sultan and his ready compliance with our desires. 

When the Conference was over, Riza Bey thanked me for what I had said.

which I had heard complaints of the oppressive conduct, of the Austrian military 
in the Principalities had not ceased,

department which was responsible for the conduct of the Austrian army. In

my despatch on this subject.

expensive and troublesome; but Austria could not bear disturbance so near her

The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received April 8.) 


(No. 147.) 


My Lord, Fienna, April 4, 1855. 

REFERRING to my despatch to your Lordship No. 103 of the 10th of 
Mareh, in which I explained an error which had escaped me in my despatch 
No, 10 of the 8th of January, and referring also to my confidential communication 
to your Lordship upon the same subject of the 18th of March, 1 beg to state 
with greater precision the mode in which that error had arisen, 

I beg, in the first place, to remark that in the sixth paragraph of my 
despatch No, 10, I stated that Prince Gortchakolf “ then withdrew the unofhicil 
document he had read as merely a memorandum for his own guidance,” and in 
a confidential communication to your Lordship of the 9th of January, I reported 
that “this document was stated by Count Buol to be the one which Prince 
Gortchakoff had submitted to him the day after the first mecting on the 28th of 
December. 

I had also stated in my despatch No. 53 af the 8lst of January, in reply to 
an observation in your Lordship's despateh to me No. 24 of the vond of 
January, that “1 beg to declare distinctly that it (the document produced by 
Prince Gortchakoff) was not stated to be the embodiment of instructions received 
by him from his Government.” 

Under these circumstances 1 was very greatly surprised at finding, in your 
Lordship’s instruction to Lord John Russell and to myself, No. 4, which is dated 
the 22nd of February, that you should allude to the document read by Prince 
Gortehakot! on the 7th of January, “as purporting to be the substance of the 
instructions which he had received from his court,” more particularly as. this 
statement was in-such direct contradiction to the various despatches | have above 
cited up to the 8ist of January. 1 consequently turned to my original despateh 
of the 7th of January, when to my great annoyance T found that the insertion al 
the words “which he had embodied in an unoflicial document whieh he read,” 
and which words hud been transmitted by telegraph two days after my despatch 
had been sent to the Foreign Office, had cased the misunderstanding which had 
taken place. 1 must explain the manner in which the error was cominitted, 

On the second day after my despatch No. 10 had been transmitted to the 
Foreign Office, one of the gentlemen of the mission came to me to make the 
remark, that although I had stated in the sixth paragraph that Prince Gortehakolt 
then withdrew the unofficial document which he had read, yet | had made no 
mention in the beginning of the despatch of his having produced any such 
document, and that he thought I might have intended to have done so, 1 said 
that it certainly was an omission, und that I would write to explain it; he 
remarked it would be very casy to have it inserted in the first paragraph, and 
stated how. and | agreed to his suggestion without taking sufficient notice of the 
manner in which it was done, and till my attention was drawn to the statement 
in your Lordship’s despatch No. 5, above alluded to, I had never remurked that 
the terms in which the explanation was conveyed entirely altered the character 
of the transaction of which the original despateh, without the insertion of this 
addition, gave a correct account, 

1 bes your Lordship will excuse this error in consideration of the cireum- 
stances under which it was committed; L regret that the many contrdictions of 
this mistake which [ have recapitulated up to the Sist of January, did not 


Thesis eS Pepa ew, WES Pat ees Ae fe hse PD. 


ya 


prevent the insertion of the statement made in your Lordship's despatch of the 
22nd of February; but I feel that it was my original error which occasioned it, 


for which I beg again (as I have already done in my despatch of the 10th of 


March) to apologise to you, and to express my regret that it should have taken 
place. 
I have, &c. 


(Signed) © WESTMORLAND.

My Lord, Fienna, April 5, 1855, 

I HAVE the honour of transmitting herewith to your Lordship the aceom- 
manying despatches*® which I have received under flying-seal from Her Majesty's 
ronsulat Bucharest. [took oceasion, on the receipt of these despatches, to make 

a further representation with reference to their contents to General Hess, and | 


* Now. Ol and G49, 


oso 


urged upon him the expediency of rendering the military oeeupation of the 
Principalities as light as posite to the inhabitants. 

General Hess replied that not only was it his wish that it should prove so, 
but also the express desire of the Emperor, who had watched with anxious 
interest the inquiry into the late disturbances at Krajova. His Majesty, he said, 
had ordered that the garrison of that place should be changed, and these orders 
were now being carried into execution by General Coronini; and it was his 
sincere hope that this measure would put an end to all further dissension between 
the inhabitants and the Imperial troops. A vigorous inquiry, he said, was. still 
proceeding into the conduct of the late garrison, and the severest punishment 
should be dealt to any individual who might be found guilty of any offence, 
He believed, however, that part of the responsibility of whut had passed at 
Krajova lay with the Préfet and the authorities of the Principality, who had now 
been superseded by M, Rosetti, General Hess concluded by saying that he was 
happy to state that Krajova was the only place from which he had recently 
received complaints, and that all his accounts from other parts of the Prinei- 
palities were perfectly satisfactory.

(No. 160.) 
My Lord, Vienna, April 4, 1855. 

| HAVE the henour of submitting to your Lordship the inclosed copy of 
the Protocol of the Conference held on the 2nd instant, whieh has not yet been 
signed, but has been sent round to the different Representatives, metubers of the 
Conference, and approved by them, This Protocal will be signed at the 
Conference which is appointed to be heldon Monday next, the 9th instant, 

Your Lordship will receive the details of the discussion which took place at 
this Conference from Lord John Russell, in which his Lordship and myself 
communicated the instructions with which we had been furnished by the 
telegraphic message of the 30th March from your Lordship, not to enter upon 
any discussion or explanation as to the points contained in the fourth Article of 
the basis, until the question relating to the third basis had been decided upon. 

The early arrival of the French Minister of Foreign Affairs, M, Drouyn de 
Lhuys, was aunounced by Baron Bourquency, and that of Aalt Pasha, the 
Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Sultan, by the Turkish Ambassador, and it 
was consequently proposed by Count Buol, and ussented to by the wnembers of 
the Conterence, that the further meeting of the Representatives should he 
postponed to Monday. mt : 

The declaration made by the Russian Plenipotentiaries, that with regard to 
the engagements of the fourth basis, they abandoned all questions of political 
advantages, looking only with anxiety to securing the privileges which had been 
accorded by the Sultan to his Christian subjects, called forth from Lord John 
Russell and myself the declaration that our Governments had certainly never 
been behindhand in endeavouring, by the constant solicitude of Hor Majesty's 
Ambassador at Constantinople, to profit by the generous intentions of the 
Sultan to obtain every effectual guarantee which could be desired for the sceurity 
and well-being of the Christian population of the Turkish Empire. 

Baron de Bourqueney, on the part of his Government, made a similar 
declaration.

My Lord, Berlin, April 6, 1855, 

1 HAVE had the honour of reeciving your Lordship’s despatch No. 113 of 
the 27th ultimo, instructing me to seck of Baron Manteuffel an explanation of 
the contradiction between the statement made in an article in the “ Preussische 
Correspondenz,”’ and that made by his Excellency to myself, relative to M. de 
Bismark’s proceedings at Frankfort. . 

The day after your Lordship’s above-mentioned despatch was written, you 
will probably have received my No. 186 of the 25th ultimo, in which [ reported 
the varue and unsatisfactory explanations 1 had obtained irom Baron Manteuttel 
on the subject; and 1 trust that your Lordship, under the circumstances of my 
having already been told by the Prussian Minister for Foreign Affairs all that he 
is likely to suy on this affair, will approve of my not having renewed the 
discussion. 

| was the more inelined to let the matter drop, as the Marquis de Moustier 
Had received an instruction from his Government, which he told me he should 
read to Baron Manteuffel. It is an answer to his Excellency’s despatch to 
Count Hatzfeldt of the 2nd ultimo, copy of which was forwarded in my No. 135, 
maintaining the right of foreign Powers to notice questions brought under 
deliberation of the Diet, and finally alluding to the late reprehensible conduct of 
M. de Bismark, and to the disavowal of the same by Baron Manteuffél. 

M. de Moustier hud ulso previously requested an explanation from Baron 
Manteuffel, and received answers similar to those which | have reported; and he 
therefore felt convinced of the inutility of going again into details, and raising 
a discussion. Accordingly, he sought an interview of Baron Manteutlel, who it 
appears after listening to a few words, stopped M, de Moustier, and told him 
that the despatch appeared to be a long one, and that he should like to read it 
at his leisure, and begged him to leave it with him. ‘The French Minister pro- 
tested that he was not instructed even to read it to him; but on being pressed, 
M. de Moustier thought it was the best way of making Baron Manteuttel 
acquainted with the contents of the paper, and be left it with him. 

Two days afterwards, M, de Moustier culled on Baron Manteuttel, when his 
Excellency returned it to him without making a single observation on its con- 
tents; and the French Minister is therefore hound to consider that his Excel- 
leney accepts all that this despatch contaims, 

1 inclose a copy of this French despatch, for the confidential information 
of Her Majesty's Government, } 

L have, &e. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD,

My Lord, Berlin, April 6, 1855. 

GENERAL WEDEL arrived here a few days ago from Paris, and was the 
hearer of a private letter from the Emperor of the French to the King of Prussia, 
which I understand is full of friendly expresstons, and the desire of cultivating 
eood relations, but does not enter into any particulars as to the late fruitless 
negotiations with this Government. ‘The Emperor has, however, addressed a 
“lettre de Cabinet” to the King, in which His Imperial Majesty expresses his 
eratification at learning that the Prussian Government is ready to accede to the 
Protocol of the 28th December, adding, that he bears this resolution in mind. 
Nothing is as yet settled as to General Wedel’s return to Paris; but itis believed 
that he will be sent back next week with some fresh instructions and proposals. 

In the meantime the Prossian Government are annoyed at M. Drouyn de 
Liuy's not having passed through Berlin on his way to Vienna; and itis considered 
a bad return for the special mission to Paris. On the other hand this want of 
attention is producing a good effect on the public, who are beginning to feel 
some degree of dissatisfaction with the Government for having lowered the 
position of the country as an European Power; they have no Wish for an 
alliance with Russia, and hence the Government are desirous to have it believed 
thut serious negotiations for a better understanding with the Western Powers 
ave being earried on, and the continued stay of Baron d'Usedom in London, and 
the return of Geucral Wedel, are ineant to keep up this delusion. 

With Austria the same coldness exists; and the communications between 
the two Governments continue to be of an unsatisfactory nature; but Dam not 
informed that any fresh cause of estrangement has lately occurred. On the 
contrary, the Austrian Minister at this Court assures me that. his Government 
would willingly sce a better state of things established ; and he attributes the 
continuance of much of the ill-feeling to the influence of M, de Bismark, and to 
the jealousy of Austria at the Diet of Frankfort, 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD,

My Lord, Berlin, April 6, 1855. 

1 THINK it my duty to report to your Lordship that for some time back 
the most active vigilance and stringent measures have heen resorted to, both 
here and in other parts of Prussia, to repress the free political opinions of the 
2 » Phe ‘'Times" of the 14th March was confiscated for a leading article 
directed against Prussia, and the “ Indépendance Belge” of the 15th was likewise 
seized for reproducing this article. Both newspapers have been condemned by 
the tribunal of Cologne, and it is now in the power of the Minister of the 
Interior to prohibit at any time the entry of these journals into Prussia. | 

The editors of the journals here are entirely under the command of the 


587 


police authorities, who not only interfere for the purpose of prevention, but like- 
wise prescribe the political tone which they wish the press to adopt. 

There is, likewise, a central press bureau at Berlin, under the immediate 
control and guidance of the Prussian Foreign Office, which daily receives such 
information and political news as the Government are desirous of making public 
through the journals, in order to lead and direct public opinion, 

An instance of the influence exercised by the Government over the press, 
has lately been shown in the forced retirement of Dr. Briiggeman, the editor 
of the “‘ Cologne Gazette,” a journal noted for its. liberal views and its oppo- 
sition to the present Ministry. After repeated confiscation, and threats of 
further repressive steps, Dr. Briiggeman has heen at length ordered, under a 
threat of suppressing the journal altogether, to withdraw from the editorship ; 
and the journal has only received permission to be carried on, provided that it 
assumes 2 more moderate tone, and does not oppose the measures of the Govern- 
ment with such acrimony.

Mr, Buchanan to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received April 5.) 


(No, 56. Confidential.) 


My Lord, Copenhagen, March 30, 1855. 

ACCORDING to accounts received here last month from St. Petersburgh, 
| am assured that the Russian Government manufactories were expected to 
deliver 80,000 Minié rifles in the course of the spring, and great hopes were 
entertained that the use of that weapon would place the Russian soldier on terms 
of equality with the troops of the Western Powers. Large reinforcements were 
also suid to be on their march to the Crimea, and that not less than 40,000 men 
were forwarded to the army there in the month of February. In St. Peters- 
hurgh, therefore, it was generally believed that the allied expedition had no 
chance of success. 

Great exertions were making to improve the defences of Cronstadt, and 
thousands of men and horses were employed near Oranienbaum, and opposite to 
the coast of Finland, in the transport of materials for closing the passages to the 
harbour, which were left open last year. | 

I presume the passages referred to must be the shallow water between the 
shore and the fairway, by which gunboats and vessels of that description 
might attack the batteries advantageously, or by turning them angen the 
larbour. 

Preparations for a vigorous defence of Helsingfors and Sweaborg had also 
been made. The works of the fortress had been strengthened, and many 
batteries thrown up hurriedly last year, and in the efficiency of which the 
garrison had very little confidence, have now been converted into properly 
constructed and substantial works: ‘ 

While the organization of a national militia was carried on with activity, 
differences of opinion were said to exist among the people as to the expediency 
of prosecuting the war. ‘The language of the higher classes was, amevae 
cenenilly warlike ; and several anonymous letters of an insulting or threatening 
character were said to have been received by Count Nesselrode, who is looked 
upon as the leader of the peace party.

(Signed) ANDREW BUCHANAN,

A CONSIDERABLE diversity of opinion exists among the naval men of 
this country respecting the merits of the gunboat flotilla, or, 38 it is calle 
here, the @Skirgard fleet.” “The officers of the larger shi stationed at 
Carlscrona decry its usefulness, and extol that of their own ships ; while the 
wun-boat officers depreciate the use of ships of war for Swedish purposes, which 
may be summarily described as defending their own coasts oF attacking those 
of Russia, and vaunt the merits of their own peculiar armament. It is not 
improbable that there is some exaggeration on both sides, and 1 have endea- 
voured to obtain from the best and most experienced sources information 
respecting the gunboat flotilla, as ihe armament the least known in England, 
and the most likely to be brought into useful cooperation, should this country 
hereafter take a part in the war against Tussia. 

The result of these inquiries, though all tending to elucidate the same point, 
is divided into three parts, coming from different sources ; and whatever their 
practical merit may be in the ilies of professional persons in England, | can, | 
helieve, with entire trath add, that their ‘nformation is obtained from the best 
Swedish gunboat officers of the day, one of whom has had more practical 
experience in gunboat warfare than probably any man living, and others, who 
have cither written on the subject or etudied it theoretically. Under these 
circumstances, L am not without hopes that this information may, at the present 
moment, prove useful to Her Majesty’s Government,

appt as or landing troops on that coast, and contains the pith of the

fect, of gunboats, proving their advantage by reference to the poval campaigas

suffered, either in battle or from shipwreck, since their introduction.

Inclosure 2 in No. 628. 
Memorandum on the advantages of Gun-sloops and Yauels. 


THE advantages of the gun-sloops and yawls, and their ability to withstand 
fire, were proved incontestably in the war with Russia, 1789-90. In the battle 
of Svensksund in 1789, which lasted 15} hours, of the larger Skigard vessels 6 
out of 17 were lost, but only 1 out of 23 sloops. In the battle at the same place 
in 1790, which lasted 124 hours, the Russians lost 4 ships of war out of 5, 42 
larger Skiigurd vessels out of 66, but only 3 out of 80 gun-boat sloops; on the 
Swedish side, 44 of the guns (nearly half 12-pounders) were on Skigard: frigates 
and similar vessels, and 15 on galleys, but above three-fifths of the whole amount 
of cannon, being that part which especially contributed to the victory, were on 
board the gun-sloops and yawls, whose powerful fire principally contributed to 
the sinking of the Russian man-of-war “ Nicholas.” 

The general result of the whole war was, that out of 398, only 17, or about 
4 in 100, gun-sloops were sunk or blown up during sea-fights which lasted, on an 
average, 64 hours each. 

The sloops and yawls have each their peculiar advantages: the former are 
steacier in bad weather and have heavier cannon; they can land more men, and 
they keep their place in line better from their greater draught, and are more 
applicable to the open skigards and on the coasts : the latter ean, from their 
lesser draught, go into shallower places, and land troops on shallower shores ; 
they present a less surface to be shot at; they can fire quicker, as they can be 
swung round and given a certain direction with the oars quicker than the sloops; 
they require less men to work each gun, and are most useful in more: confined 
skiigards and waters. 

With the help of tug steamers, the transport of gunboats now becomes of 
course very ¢asy. 


Inclosure 3 in No. 625. 
History of Swedish Gunboats, and the small loss they have sustained, 


THE gun-sloops constructed by Chapman were introduced into the Swedish 
navy in the year 1785, and at the commencement of the war with Riissia in 
1788, there were at Stockholm 40, and at Sveaborg 40; but after the campaigns 
of 1788 and 1789 had proved their efficacy in the waters in which they had been 
used, the Swedish navy received during the winter of 1789-90, an augmentation 
of 150 small armed vessels, principally cun-sloops. 

In the month of May, the whole of the Stockholm squadron left that place, 
at the same time that 12 gun-sloops and 12 gun-yawls left Pomerania, and 16 
un-sloops Gothenburg, and the whole arrived without any loss at the Hussian 
frontier, in the Gulf of Finland. 

At the retreat from Wiborg, 6 gun-sloops and 7 yawls were taken by the 
enemy, out of a number of 127 of the former and 87 of the latter, but not a 
single one was lost by stress of weather, although they had to pass the open sea 
in a strong breeze, 

During the year 1808, when the war was vigorously carried on against 
Russia, only 2 sloops were lost by stress of weather, when returning late in the 
autumn to Stockholm, 

In 1809, 34 gun-sloops went from the Sound to Stockholm, and the whole of 
the Gothenburg squadron to Malmo in the Sound without any loss, 

In August 1504, on the undertaking of the expedition to Rathan, 45 gun- 
sloops went from Stockholm to Hernésand, and were towed by sailing vessels 
132 English miles in 36 hours, with 100 men of the army on board cach, and 


=~ hee a = io + ee ee 
ieee! otha ble yh ls © lag, te oe Oe ed ee 


093 


lastly returned to Stockholm by themselves, making in one day a passage of 76 
miles, with the loss of one sloop wrecked, but crew saved. 

In 1810, in the month of October, 12 gun-sloops left Malm for Gothenburg, 
under the command of an officer whose education had been made wholly in sail- 
ing vessels of larger dimensions; 4 sloops were lost. 

In 1811, 16 gun-sloops were stationed on different parts of the coast between 
Gothenburg and Carlshamn, the only open part of the coast of Sweden, and no 
loss ensued. 

In 1813, 16 sloops left Stockholm for the coast of Pomerania, and arrived in 
safety, although having had to encounter & hard gale of wind in the south part 
of the Baltic. 

During that year, 85 gun-sloops were in activity on the coasts of Sweden 
and Germany, without the loss of a single one. 

1814, 47 gun-sloops and 3 gun-yawls were employed on the coasts of 
Sweden and Norway, in the war against the latter, and all returned safely to 
their different stations. 


It ought to be remembered that gun-sloops in those days were very little 
unlike large ship launches, except in the heavier scantling necessary for carrying 
a heavier armament, whereas now they are decked, with openings for the men’s 
legs when stationed at the oars, to be covered at a moment’s warning with 
hatches, sufficiently to exclude any fear of foundering by getting water on deck. 


Gustavus III, a King, whom nobody ever yet suspected of want of judg- 
ment, after a war of two years with Russia, and in which Sweden, from particular 
reasons, thatis, the subsidies of France, brought out a fleet stronger, both actually 
and comparatively with the Russian fleet, than any man in his senses will 
suppose ever can be the case for the future, says to the Secret Committee of the 
States: “The experience of a former campaign has proved to me the greatest 
necessity, not only of restoring the navy of the narrow seas, (i.e. the gun-boat 
flotilla), but also of augmenting it as far as possible, and to have it ready as carly 
as possible, particularly as the operations of the war might be antic on, even 
when the navy of the line of battle ships had not arrived in the Gulf of Finland.” 

The victory of Svensksund, which was gained afew months later by this 
navy, and which undoubtedly must be considered as one of the principal corner- 
stones upon which the favourable peace of 1790 was founded, proved the cor- 
rectness of his views, and thus history will furnish proofs hardly to be overturned 
by the differing opinions of men, no doubt full of energy and knowledge in their 
own business, but without experience in this particular branch of the naval 
service,

Mr. Magenis to the Eurl of Clarendon.—{ Received April 8.) 
(No, 24) 
My Lord, Stockholm, March 25, 1855, 

I CAN hardly hope that the information contained in the inclosed paper, 
as to the best means of attacking Cronstadt, will throw much additional light 
upon a subject which has doubtlessly received such attentive consideration in 
England, but they are the speculations of an old and experienced naval officer 
here, who knows the ground and has thought on the subject, and possibly may 
be worth a perusal. 

I happen to know that Admiral Heyden, who was sent here to announce 
the death of the late, and the accession of the present, Emperor of Russia, and 
who, 1 believe, is Chief of the Staff of the Baltic fleet, stated to a person in this 
country, who repeated it to me, that he looked on Cronstadt as “impregnable ;” 
not that he thought it was impossible for ships, at great risk and loss, to attack, 
and even to take it, if they could get sufficiently near, but because the Russian 
Government would render it impossible for such ships to approach the fortress, by 
sinking in the channel some of their old aioe as had been done at Sebastopol.

(Signed) ARTHUR C. MAGENIS.

Inclosure in No. 629, 
Plan for taking Cronstadt. 


IT would be useless attempting to land troops on the north side of the 
island, owing to the force the enemy would have drawn up against them, and 
beeavse the ground on that side was, during last summer and autumn, in antici 
pttion of an attack, scientifically undermined, thereby exposing the troops to 
being blown up, even if they succeeded in getting on shore. Phat shore, too, is 
treacherous, as in many places there are several slips of sandbanks lying along 
it, which, although covered with two or three feet of water, have passages 
between of a depth of twelve to fifteen feet, ad soldiers jumping out of the 
boats on to these banks, and proceeding towards the shore, would suddenly fall 
into these deep passages. 

The plan suggested for attacking Cronstadt is the following : . 

By submarine sawing, mining, or other engineering means, to make a suffi- 
cient passage for the gun-boats, floating batteries, and steamers of light draught 
to pass throygh the barricade of poles, wrecks, and blocks of granite, &c., resting 
on a sandy bottom, which has been constructed between the north-eastern corner 
of the town and the mainland. The above vessels should then pass through the 
barricade, and, after repelling the Russian gun-boats and vessels which: might

INCLOSED is an extract from an article published in the columns of the 
« Augsburg Gazette,” by the author of several other articles which Rave ie 
time to time appeared on the present European crisis, and who, alt ah 16 
thinks proper to conceal his name, I run no great chance of contrac me 
stating to be a person employed in the Fore Department, and enjoying Ms 
confidence of the King. He has always wntten in a tone far more ae 
towards Russia than towards the Western Powers and their allies, al is 
present production nerdy forms an exception to the course he seems to have 

ke for himself. er 
marke aitidle now under our notice, commences by stating that Russia has 
remained true to the assurances given by her sinee the 29th of November of last 
rear, and that the question of the faith to be put in Russian promises, raised in 
the French notes, has been practically answered by the understanding come to 
at the Conference at Vienna on the first and second points of the guarantees, 
which the writer assumes to be definitively arranged, 

Thus the two points which principally interest Austria and Germany, may, 
he says, be considered as settled; and beth Austnia and the Western Powers 
have good ground for presuming the free navigation of the Danube and the 
future position of the Principalities to be assored : this, however, has not been 
attained without great sacrifices on the part of Russia. She had, as must be 
admitted, even supposing her to have acted for the extension of her own 
interests, and on the conviction of the breaking up of the Turkish Empire alone— 
for no other Christian State has any share in this merit—procured for the 
Christian population of those countries the privileges they enjoy, and if she has 
now abandoned her exclusive right of protection, she has thereby given a proof 
that she is determined to refute by a fact, at least from this moment, the 
reprouches and suspicions of other Powers that she took advantage of that pro- 
tection as a step towards ternitorial aggrandizement, or for the exercise of an 
improper influence. She has further done justice to German and European 
interests, in the matter of the free navigation of the Danube, by a comphance 
with the demands of the Powers opposed to her, These concessions the article 
asserts to have been made on so liberal a scale, that. the question at once ‘arose 
in Austria, and in the Austrian Cabinet, whether in the presence ot the 
assurances previously given to Russia in regard to the third point, there any 


599 


longer remained the possibility of war on the part of Germany. At any tate 
Austria now appears in the character of a mediator, having a double object in 
view,—to restrain the Western Powers from making such exeessive demands as 
shall be inconsistent with Russian honour, but principally to prevent the nature 
of the concessions from being such as might eventually be turned to account by 
the Western Powers to establish on their part a permanent and exelusive pre- 
ponderance in Turkey and in the Black Sea. 

The writer then proceeds to argue, that if the Bosphorus and the 
Dardanelies were entirely thrown open to the ships of war of all nations, the 
inevitable consequence would be that England and France would become 
masters of Turkey ; and he affirms that Russia could never, under such circum- 
stances, consent to the limitation of her maritime force in the Black Seca, for she 
would then be unjustly exposed to the attacks of an adversary more powerful 
than herself at sea. en 

_ On the other hand, if these two straits remain closed to vessels of war, 
tussia might submit to the diminution of her fleet, upon the understanding that 
that of Turkey should never exceed the number of ships prescribed for her. 

The above is the general tone of the article, of the concluding paragraph of 
which the accompanying inclosure is a translation. It is not easy to say from 
whence the author, who is a Prussian, has received his ins irations ; but he is 
on terms so much the reverse of amicable with Baron von der Pfordten, that I 
cannot suspect the latter of having had anything to do with it.

GERMANY, as well as the Germanic Confederation, would at all events 
raise another question, namely, how has the fourth point of the guarantees 
been considered or brought to a decision at Vienna? 

The German Cabinets would in any ease expect, we say, that in the event 
of the third point, which France and England desire effectually to settle, should 
remain unsettled; they would, we say, expect notwithstanding that the fourth 
point should be proceeded with, in order to be able to ascertain from it whether 
it would be worth while for Germany to enter upon a war for maintaining the 
integrity of Turkey and the independence of the Sultan, or whether it would not 
be more advisable earnestly to direct her efforts, in conjunction with Russia, to 
obtain for the Bulgarian, Bosniak, and Greek Christians in Turkey, and for the 
different Christian natioris, at least a similar or equal position with that in which’ 
Wolebian and Servian Chiristians are placed in the Principalities and in 

rvia,

No, 635. 
Coneul-General Ward to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received April 8.) 


601 


always so interpreted the Treaties, and so exercised her dominion as to hamper 
the navigation ina legal way, and the other Powers have been consequently 
obliged to submit. New Treaties would be evaded in the same way, and even 
the proposed canal to avoid the Russian territory would be frustrated in its object 
by Russian tactics. The only sure means is to drive Russia from her position at 
the mouth of the Danube, which she was allowed to take in 1829, by the third 
Article of the Adrianople Treaty. 

In this view of Dr. Wurm there are a great many who concur, and who 
fear that, whatever stipulations may be contracted at Vienna, the navigation of 
the Danube will never be, in fact, free, either for Germany or any other nation, 
80 long as Russia holds the islands at the mouth, as a part of her dominions, 

Another grievance, which is much complained of as injurious to the 
commerce of the East of Europe, is the system of vexatious restrictions upon 
trade, which Russia has established in the Kingdom of Poland. 

The Treaty between Russia and Austria of the 3rd of May, 1818, 
Articles XXIV and XXVIII, and that between Russia and Prussia of the same 
date, Articles XXII and XXVIII, stipulated for the free navigation of the 
Polish rivers, and for freedom of commerce between all parts of the ancient 
Poland, as it existed before the year 1772, Russia has notoriously violated 
these stipulations, and neither Austria nor Prussia have ever been able to obtain 
redress as regards their subjects, 

The Western Powers are not, indeed, parties to the Treaties cited, and so 
far as German interests are concerned, the Cabinets of Vienna and Berlin are 
alone to blame that the commerce of Poland has not been kept entirely free, 

The subject of Poland has, of late, a good deal occupied the liberal journals, 
and micoolpaons are thrown out as to the probable occupation of that country 
by a French army, if the war should continue, The late Parliamentary debate 
on Mr, Phinn’s motion has naturally excited much interest. The general 
impression seems to be that an insurrection could not. take place in Russian 
Poland, without a similar movement in the Prussian Provinces of Posen and 
West Prussia, where the population is chiefly Polish; and the experience of the 
year 1848 makes in favour of such a conclusion, This is one reason why the 
Prussian Government so much dreads the continuance of the war. 

The official organ of M. de Manteuftel, the “ Prussian Correspondenz,” is 
more sanguine than ever of its hopes of peace, since the French journals have 
declared that Sebastopol was not considered a point of honour for France. In 
the Prussian view, the Crimean expedition has been a. brilliant episode, which 
was never likely to decide the issue of the war, and the fortress is neither the 
key to the interior of Russia, nor even commands the whole of the Black Sea. 
Consequently Prussia has the less reason to regret having persisted in a policy 
of expectancy and mediation; and she may now, if the negotiations eae 


prove abortive, throw her power, undiminished in weight, into the scale of 
decision.

The Earl of Clarendon to Lord John Russell. 
(No. 54, Secret.) 


My Lord, Foreign Office, April 10, 1854. 

IN reply to your Lordship’s despatch No. 59 of the Sth instant, marked 
Confidential, [ have to state that in the opinion of Her Majesty's Government 
it will be necessary to come to a thorough understanding with Prussia respecting 
her future policy, whenever a rupture between Austria and Russia takes place; 
but until that event occurs, your Lordship will probably agree with Her 
Majesty's Government that it would not be prudent to adopt any course that 
might entail a quarrel between Prussia and the Western Powers, 

Austria and Prussia are now animated by feelings of bitter hostility towards 
each other, and it is natural that Austria should desire to commit France and 
England against her rival, but it would be unwise on their part thus to commit 
themselves prematurely, 

If Austria were to declare war against Russia, it is probable that several of 
the German Powers would be compelled to adopt her policy, and there might 
then be no great difficulty in dealing with Prussia, who would not yentare to 
join Russia, and would be comparatively powerless in Germany. + 

But if Austria were unfortunately not to fulfil her engagements, and thereb 
should verify the constant predictions of Prussia, it is not impossible that the 
latter Power should then wish to draw closer to England and France, of, at all 
events, we might expect from her a policy more strictly neutral than ‘she has 
pursued up to this time. In adopting such a policy, she might with reason 
claim the support of Germany, and Germany in all likelihood would rally round 
Prussia rather than Austria, but the position of Austria would then be alike 
humiliating and dangerous. Prussia would have obtained the superiority over 
her in Germany, She would hove lost the moral and material support of 
England and France; and the consequences which that loss would entail might 
in many ways be most serious to her. She could not unite with Russia against 
herself; the state of her finances would not permit her much longer to keep a

No. 651, 


Lord John Russell to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received April 13.) 
(No, 66.) 


My Lord, Vienna, April 10, 1855. 
AFTER the Conference yesterday, M. Drouyn de Lhuys, Baron Bour- 
uency, Lord Westmorland and I, met Count Buol and Baron Prokesch in 
sount Buol's official apartment. 
Count Buol addressed us in a very formal manner, told us that he was about 
to explain to us fully (& fond) the policy of the Austrian Government on the 
third point. In the course of this and his subsequent discourses he frequently 


referred to the authority of the Emperor. He said that the plan of neutralization 
as developed by M. Drouyn de Lhuys appeared to him on reflection to come 
within the third point, and to attain its object very completely. That he should 
have no difficulty in saying that Austria would be glad to see it accepted. He 
had not, however, any hope that Russia would accept it, as she would thereby 
be disarmed in the Black Sea, while Turkey would be armed in the Bosphorus, 
or at all events in the Mediterranean, 


He should in like manner be lad to see Russia consent to limit her forces, 
ut looking at the concessions Russia had made on the first and second point, 
and the probability of her acquiescence in what might be settled on the fourth 
point, Austria was not prepared to go to war on account of the refusal of Russia 
to limit her naval foree in the Black Sea. That force had been already nearly 
destroyed; what remained was blocked up, and Russian would hereafter be 
afraid to give offence to France and England for fear of similar consequences. 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys answered these observations very ably. He laid it 
down as a principle that the value of a Treaty or agreement of any kind is that 
each Article, instead of being the cause of the separate members became the cause 
of the whole, That without any ‘Treaty, Austria might have defended the 
Principalities, and the maritime Powers have sought to put an end to Russian 
preponderance in the Black Sea. That the value of the Treaty consisted in the 
union of objects and of efforts, In this spirit France and England had defended 
the free navigation of the Danube, and had Austria been thwarted in her endea- 


vours on that subject, her allies would have been prepared to continue the war 
in her support, That he expected in like manner Austria would urge the 
adoption of the third point, chicks was very clear and positive in its terms. 
That unless she did so the alliance would lose all binding foree, and would soon 
crumble to pieces, He explained and defended the plan of neutralization, which 
he conceived to be beneficial to the whole world. He therefore asked Count 
Buol very pointedly what he would do in support of the third point, which was 
essential to the conclusion of a durable peace. 

Before Count Buol could answer, [ requested his attention to what I 
conceived to be the position of Austria, From the first moment of Prince 
Menchikoff's leaving Constantinople I had thought that, with the assistance of 
Austria, we might easily defeat the designs of Russia in the Hast; that, without 
Austria, we should have a long, though doubtless a victorious, contest. 1 
remarked that there were three roads by which Russia might reach her long- 
cherished object, the possession of Constantinople : one by Asia, the second by 
the Pane ities and Bessarabia, the third by the Black Sea. ‘That the Asiatic 
route might be put out of consideration for the present purpose; that the route 
by the Principalities was stopped by Austria and the allies; that the third route 
remained to be considered. 

Marshal Marmont had gone into this question as a militar 
shown how, by embarking 10,000 men with twenty-five sail of the line at 
Sebastopol, and a march of 60,000 men by Bessarabia, Constantinople might be 
seized by Russia, He argued, however, that ull depended on priority ; this time 
we had the priority, another time Russia might have it. I might be told that 
Austria would intercept the invasion by land; she had, however, not interrupted 
the passage of the Danube or the siege of Silistria, and she might be equally 
slow on another occasion,

The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received April 13.) 


(No. 164.) 


My Lord, Vienna, April 10, 1855. 

I HAVE the honour of inclosing the lithographed copy of the Protocol 
No. 8, which was signed at the Conference which took place yesterday, and of 
which I have mikeady transmitted to you an ined copy in my despatch, 
No. 160, of the 5th instant. 

At this last Conference the French Minister of Foreign Affairs, M. Drouyn 
de Lhuys, presented his full powers, and took his seat with the Representatives ; 
and Aali Pasha, the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Turkey, presented also his 
full powers, and took his seat as a member of the Conference. 

Count Buol introduced these two Representatives, with the expression of the 
satisfaction with which he hailed their mission to the Conference, and expressed 
his hope that their presence would contribute to the great object for which we 
were assembled, of restoring the peace of Europe. 

Count Buol then referred to the engagement taken at the Conference of the 
26th, at which the Russian Plenipotentiaries undertook to refer to their Govern- 
ment for instructions as to the third point of the accepted conditions of peace, 
and inquired of them whether they had received any reply; upon being informed 
that they had not, he urged them to call upon their Government to lose no time 
in transmitting their decision upon the important question which had been sub- 
mitted to them. 

Count Buol added, that being satisfied that until this decision was received, 
it was the general feeling of the Representatives that the Conference could 
enter upon no other business, he proposed that our meetings should be 
adjourned until the Russian Representatives had received the reply they were 
expecting from their Government. . 

The Conference consequently separated, without fixing any further day on 
which we were to assemble, ate 

After the Conference had separated, Count Buol requested Lord John 
Russell and myself, as well as M. Drouyn de Lhuys and Baron Bourqueney, to 
meet him and Baron Prokesch, for the purpose of discussing the conduct which 
should be pursued by the allied Ministers in the future course of the nezotiation 
in order that entire unanimity between them might be preserved. ; : 

Lord John Nussell, who took a very prominent part in the discussion 
which ensued at this mecting, after the declaration of the Austrian policy which 
wis made by Count Buol, will fully report to your Lordship what took place, 
I will, therefore, not enter into details. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys explained the policy which he was directed hy his 
Government to pursue, and which he stated to be entirely in accordance with 
that of Her Majesty's Government. 

___ At the termination of this discussion, it was proposed that M. Drouyn de 
Lhuys should eonfer with the Turkish Minister of Foreign Affairs as to the plan 
for the neutralization of the Black Sea, which he was instructed by his Govern- 
ment to bring forward; and it was arranged that we should meet aeain 
to-morrow, with Aali Pasha, to learn the result of M, Drouwyn de Lhuys’ aGine 
munication to him, aN 

re I have, &e. 
(Signed) WESTMORLAND.

No. 657. 
The Eurl of Clarendon to Consul Longworth. 


(No. 1. Confidential.) ; ' 
My Lord, Foreign Office, April 15, 1855. 
JER Maiestv’s Government being desirous of obtaining accurate informa- 
tion ve tha eoeent state of affairs in Circassia, and as to the extent to which 
they might count on the cooperation of the various tribes inhabiting that 
country, if circumstances should render it advisable to call them into action, I 
have to instruct you to proceed at once to such place on the Circassian coast, as 
may appear to afford He nec ee On aan for communicating with the most 
influential Chiefs of the different tribes. oe 
eee ATive already resided in the country, you will have less difficulty in form- 
ing an opinion aa to the quarters to which you should address yourself eee it 
may be convenient to you to have in your possession a brief summary which has 


* No. 657. 


619 


recently been placed in my hands of the present state of the different tribes 
inhabiting the country on the eastern coast of the Black Sea. 

You will be careful not to give a political character to your visit to the 
country, 60 as to raise expectations which may not be realized, or to cause 
claims to be advanced, or promises exacted, which it might be difficult to evade, 
and still more so to make and keep. 

The ostensible object of your visit should be to inquire-as to the amount of 
Cavalry which the Circassian tribes could place at the disposal of the British 
Government, upon the ground that it is troublesome to send out horses from 
England, and that the Lritish Government place great reliance on the native 
horsemen. 3 | 

Atrangements will be made for enabling you to obtain at Constantinople a 
supply of lead and gunpowder, which are probably the most acceptable presents 
of which you could be the bearer; and there would be no difficulty in adding 
a supply of rifles and mountain guns, if the Circassians should stand in need of 
them, and which could be sent irom this country if the army stores at Constan- 
tinople cannot furnish them. 

You will endeavour to place yourself in communication with Schamyl, and 
learn what is his position with reference to the other tribes, wliat are his 
intentions and plans with regard to carrying on hostilities; and what are his 
means of doing so, 

As regards the Caucasian tribes in general, you will endeavour to ascertain 

the state and resources for active warfare of the country which they inhabit; 
whether the feuds among the different tribes would prevent their united action 
even against a common enemy; what prospect there would be of their future 
consolidation, and under what form of government; what sort of assistance they 
would desire or accept from the allies, against Russia; and what guarantees for 
their protection hereafter against that Power they would look for in return for 
their more active assistance during the war, 
You will, however, be particularly careful to abstain from pledging Her 
Majesty’s Government to anything beyond present assistance in carrying on 
the war. You may state, in general terms, that Her Majesty’s Government 
have taken a great interest in the struggle which the Caucasian tribes have 
s0 long prosecuted against Russia, and would see with pleasure that struggle 
terminated to the advantage of the several tribes ; and you may point out that 
at all events the cooperation of the tribes in the hostilities now in progress 
cannot place them in a worse position than that which they now cecupy, while 
by assisting the allies in their endeavours to cireumscribe the power of Russia, 
they will take the surest means of securing for themselves that independence 
Which they have so long and so successfully striven 1o maintain. 

Her Mujesty’s Ambassador at Constantinople will give you such further 
instructions as may seem necessary for the more effectual execution of the duties 
entrusted to you, and you will forward under flying-seal, through his Excellency, 
the reports that you may from time to time have the means of addressing 
to me, : 

You will continue to draw your full salary as Consul at Monastir, and 
Her Majesty's Ambassador will supply you with such funds as you may require 
to enable you to meet the expenses of your mission. 

Lam, &e. 


(Signed) CLARENDON,

Inclosure | in No. 660. 
Lord John Russell to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord Vienna, Marek 17, 1855, 


TAKE advantage of a courier whom the Turkish Ambassador is sending 
to Cog SROAL: to Hose your Excellency that the first Conference took place 
oe Ee ere represented as follows : 

The seve were were represente as 

Aste Gy Count Buol and Baron Prokeseh, France by Baron Houuaney, 
England by the Earl of Westmorland and myself, Russia by Prince Gortchakotf 
and M, de 'Titoff, and Turkey by Aurif Effendi. , ress 

Count Buol opened the Conference by reading an address, which was chiefly 


621 


remarkable for the pointed manner in which he stated that Austria was prepared 
to encounter any sacrifice to fulfil her engagements, and he concluded by 
reeapitulating the four points in the terms set forth in the document which I 
inclose, 

The French and English Plenipotentiaries severally declared their agreement 
in the sentiments expressed by Count Buol, and their adherence to the four 
points as laid down by his Excellency, but they reserved the right of the belli- 
gerent Powers to add other stipulations over and above the four points, should 
the interests of Europe require it. 

Prinee Gortchakofl' declared his adherence to the statement of the bases of 
peace as recited by Count Buol, and his-earnest desire for peace, but he added 
that he should object to any proposition which would be injurious to the honour of 
the Emperor of Russia. The Turkish Ambassador made a reserve in favour of 
the dignity of his Sovereign. 

he four points in their integrity being thus accepted by all parties asa 
point of departure, the Plenipotentiaries proceeded to the discussion of the first 
article, relating to the Principalities and to Servia; and after some discussion as to 
whether the word “ protectorate” correctly represented the relations heretofore 
existing between Russia and the provinces, it was suggested by the French 
Plenipotentiary that the term “ protection” might be substituted for it, and it 
was acconlingly agreed by the Plenipotentiaries that no exclusive protectorate 
over the Principalities should hereafter be exercised. 

Baron Prokesch then brought forward a paper which he had drawn up con- 
taining several heads for the future government of the Principalities, and after 
some discussion it was resolved that the paper should be revised, and brought 
before the Conference at a subsequent meeting, in order to be referred eventually 
to a Commission selected from the Plenipotentiaries, who should be charged to 
examine into the details of the question with the view of bringing them into a 
manageable shape. 

The Conference shortly after this separated with the understanding that the 
second mecting should take place to-day, when the Protocol of the previous 
mecting would be ready for signature. 

I fear [shall not be able to furnish your Excellency with a copy of that 
document by the present opportunity, but 1 will forward it to you as 500m as 
possible after I can obtain it from the Austrian Chancery. 

Prince Gortchakoff remarked before the meeting broke up, that as time 
was precious, it might be desirable to enter to-day on the consideration of the 
second Article, relating to the Danube, but no fixed determination was taken on 
his proposition. 

I may state to your Excellency, that the general impression which I derived 
from what passed on the first Conference, incidents which occurred,” I venture to 
draw the conclusion that the Austrian Government is disposed fairly to carry 
into effect its engagements with England and France; and it cannot be questioned 
that the formal renunciation by Russia of pretensions which for a century have 
been sedulously nourished and pertinaciously advanced, the concession of the 
four points, and especially the agreement to put an end to Russian preponderance 
in the Black Sea, are advantages which can Earp be exaggerated. 

I think it right, in conclusion, to state to your Excellency that, as you will 
see by the inclosed copy of a despatch which I have addressed to the Earl of 
Clarendon, the Turkish Ambassador expresses himself to be considerably embar- 
rassed by the want of definite instructions from the Porte. Your Excellency 
will, I am sure, perceive the importance of preventing any such omission on the 
pare of the Turkish Government from impeding the progress of the negotiations. 
‘he delay and difficulties which must result from the necessity of continual 
reference to Constantinople might otherwise lead to most serious consequences 
which it is not too much to say would fall more heavily on the Porte than on 
the allies of the Sultan, 

Your Excellency will, I conceive, do well to make the Turkish Government 
understand that if it will not do its utmost to facilitate the progress of the nego. 
tations, it may possibly happen that the allies may have to proceed without 
waiting for the result of the tardy deliberations of the Divan. 

Tam, &e. 
(Signed) J, RUSSELL,

The want of detailed instructions on the part of the Turkish Ambassador 
may be referred in part to his Excellency’s unwillingness to sanction an unshared

As your Lordship has done me the honour, but little deserved I fear, of

cannot but regret the circumstances which have delayed their transmission to

tunity, But the form alone is wanting. Whatever I have to offer substantially

despatches of this date, and I have to request that the communication may 
be viewed with indulgence.

Inclosure 4 in No. 660, 
Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to Lord John Russell, 


My Lord, Constantinople, March 81, 1855. 

IT was not till yesterday afternoon that I received a copy of the official 
instructions prepared for Aali Pashi Although they were immediately consigned 
for translation to the Oriental Secretary of Her Majesty's Embassy, 1 had no 
opportunity of perusing them till this morning. They were translated with 
clearness and rapidity by Mr. Alison, but their unwarrantable length precluded 
an entire completion of the task, 

A copy of the translation is inclosed herewith for your Lordship's particular 
information. The memorandum annexed to it is still in the translator's lands, 
and [ must therefore reserve the transmission of it to Vienna for another oppor- 
tunity. Iam not yet acquainted with its purport myself, 

I am just returned from Constantinople, where have been to tuke leave of 
his Highness the Pasha, who had previously taken leave of the Sultan. ‘The 
visit was necessarily too brief to admit of my entering at any length upon the 
subject matter of the instructions, [ availed myself of the opportunity, how- 
ever, to recommend that he should put full confidence in your Lordship, and 
never hesitate to refer to you for advice on any incidental question of doubt or 
difficulty. He assured me that such was his intention, [also enjoined him to 
consult the Porte’s interest by not insisting with too much perseverance on any 
special view opposed or unsupported by the allies. 1 admitted the perfect justice 
of the Sultan's claim to an indemnity from Russia for the expenses of the war, 
hut submitted the difficulty of realising such a claim, and advised a temperate 
course of proceeding in concert with your Lordship. ! did not take my leave of

foreign superintendence in the matter of Christian privileges, and I did not 
hesitate to add my opinion that without some auxiliary motives for enforeing the 
proposed measures the Sultan’s best intentions would be exposed to the hazard

To the 6th: 


The 705,000 piastres, representing a sum of 5,000/., and aid by the 
Treasury to the Department of the Mint for value of coals furnished by the 
latter to our ships, goes in deduction of 90,0001. odd required by M. Musurus itt 
London for contracts for ammunition, the amount of which will have to be 
defrayed by the fund of the loan. 

The said amount was first put down at from 80,0001. to 90,000/., and 
latterly, at from 125,000! to 130,0001, including the shipping expenses on the 
articles contracted. 


To the 7th: 


From the sum of 41,903,325 piastres, voted to the Mallich for payments 
made by that department for the extraordinary expenses of the war previous to 
the installation of the Commission on the loan, 18,055,164 piastres were subse- 
quently voted at the urgent demand of the Mallieh for some extraordinary 
application for the war, on condition of its being refunded by that department 
out of the first recoveries of the general revenue. 


To the 8th: 


The balance in hand of so many piastres (18,405,5894) was merely caleu- 
lated at about 140,0001., bringing out an exchange of something over 131 piastres, 
in order to equalize the amount in sterling. But the approximate actual balance 
in piastres, in which money the whole produce of the loan was converted, is that 
stated in my said statement. 


To the Sth : 


The average rate of exchange at which the bills drawn on account of the 
loan were cashed, is 1312 piastres per 1/, sterling, which was the current rate 
at the time of the issuing of the drafts (from the 7th September to the 14th 
December last), But the portion of the loan brought out in specie yields a 
more favourable result in piastres, the Treasury having kept it in its coffers much 
longer, and thereby benefited by the subsequent rise in the exchange and the 
monies. The average yield of the sovereigns thus received | calculate at about 
1364 piastres a-piece. 

To the 10th :; 


Although the schims have been issued on the recommendation of the Loan 
Commission, and for the specific object of paying off the debts contracted for 
the war previous to the installation of the said Commission, we have not been 
apprised yet either of the amount issued, or of their intended application. 

This had better, I believe, be inquired direct from the Porte, or rather from 
the Grand Vizier, I will also inquire myself from the Mallich and report, 


To the 11th and last : 


The war debts contracted with merchants previous to the nomination of the 
Loan Commission, were to be gradually liquidated out of the said additional 
fund of sehims, to which we would have added a portion out of the fund of the 
Commission, in order to facilitate the liquidation of the old war debts, but on 
condition of its coming under our control, the same as with the fund of the 
loan, in order to secure ifs regular and faithful application. 

Galata, March 17, 1855.

629 


defence of Moldavia and Wallachia is surely a matter of European interest, and 
as such, Her Majesty’s Government have treated it in their directions to me, to 
propose Turkish garrisons in Galatz, Ibraila, and Giurgevo. 

4, Ifa guarantee is given, and there is a question whether the Constitu- 
tional Act has been observed, it is not unreasonable that the guaranteeing 
Powers should endeavour to bring the Sultan and the Provinces to an under. 
standing. 

The provision for a perpetual tribunal of appeal has been struck out. 

6. The object of this Article is, I conceive, to prevent such an armed 
intervention on the part of Russia as took place in 1848. It provides, in such a 
case, for the presence of France and England to prevent or to disapprove, if they 
think fit, such intervention. This Article is perhaps unnecessary. 

7. The same may be said of the 7th Article. J doubt whether these 
Articles are necessary in a Treaty of Peace, and I conceive, if the negotiation 
continues, the presence of Aali Pasha will enable the Conference to introduce 
other Articles providing for the life tenure of the Princes of Moldavia and 
Wallachia, and the institution of a more popular representative assembly than 
that which now exists. The Organic Statute of Moldavia published at New 
York, shows the present Assembly to have a very narrow basis. 

The power to remove strangers who may be engaged in plots against the 
tranquillity of the Provinces, or against neighbouring States, has been provided 
for in this Article. I have already said I do not conceive it to form a necessary 
part of a Treaty of Peace. But it is not, as your Lordship supposes, provided 
that ““no agent of any of the four Powers could give protection within either 
of the three Principalities to any person whatever, fellow subject or other, whom 
Austria and Russia might desire to have expelled.” As the Article now stands, 
the Consular Agent of Great Britain would only be bound, in the case of a 
British subject, to take into serious consideration the complaints made eurainst 
his conduct. This, I conceive, he would be bound to do without a Treaty, In 
the case of a foreigner, the British Consul would be bound not to give protec: 
tion toa person engaged in plots which might be injurious to the peace of the 
Province or neighbouring States, But he must be satisfied of the truth of the 
charge. These Articles, | conceive, might well be omitted. But whether 
omitted or not, it is not to be expected that Austria will see with indifference an 
insurrection in Hungary or Poland organized in Bucharest or Jassy. ‘The 
Sultan, as a neighbouring Sovereign, would be expected to expel the organizers 
of such disturbance, and in fact is, as Aali Pasha informs me, bound to do so. 

Tam quite as much averse as your Lordship can be to the principles of the 
Holy Alliance, I should be very glad to think that Austria and Russia could be 
bound never to interfere vexatiously either with the internal government of the 
Principalities, or with the conduct of individuals, 

In discussing this subject in the Conference, I stated that a revolt in the 
Principalities might be justified by the oppressions and violences of a Hospodar ; 
that the cure for such revolt was to be found not in an armed intervention, but 
in the remedy of grievances at the same time as the suppression of disturbance. 
It is to be feared that the admission of a Turkish army into the Prineipalities 
would prove to be a remedy worse than the disease, | 

I have now before me a report of Mr, Vice-Consul Cunningham on the 
state of Bulgaria. In this report he says, “ Whenever I have asked a peasant or 
a Bulgarian of a town what their grievances were, what they had to complain of, 
they have always answered, ‘Only let an end be put to the robberies and murders, 
that we may have some guarantee for our lives and the freedom. of movement, 
and all else is bearable and may be remedied in time?” 

Again, in speaking of the Bulgarian inhabitant, he says: “ Only stay the 
murdering band of the Turk, and you have a happy and contented man fit for 
any social duty,” 

We must take care not to restore in Wallachia and Moldavia such cruel 
oppression. Besides every motive of humanity, such a course would attach to 
Russia every Christian inhabitant of the Princi palities, and bring down eurses on 
our name, 

In respect to the general state of the Principalities and of Servia, it is 
difficult to form any system which is not open to objection. If we allow the 
Sultan to send his troops at any time to put doen sie fresh abuses will grow, 
and the old habits of outrage will be resorted to in their support,

~ eH Vienna, April 12, 1855. 
ANOTHER meeting was held yesterday at Count Buol’s, at which Aah 
Pasha and Arif Pasha were present. 
Count Buol read to us a paper which he had drawnup, Sy 
I afterwards asked him for a copy of this paper, but he declined to give it 
me, saying it had no official character, and had not been seen by the ape : 
The paper, however, contained the present resolution of the Cabinet, 1s 
resolution is to hear the propositions of the Court of St. Petersburgh before coms 
mitting themselves further. It may he that the answer ol the Russian Babar 
may be so unfavourable and 50 peremptory, that Austria will at once concer 
with her allies on the mode of breaking off the negotiations, and stating to 
Russia a casus belli, But it may be that the Russian answer will admit of 
further discussion in Conference, with a hope of a pacific settlement. ‘The 
‘Austrian Government declines, therefore, to give any further pledge at the 
50 joment, , 
Pe This resolution, natural enough in itself, was based Ben very unsound 
reasoning. Count Buol maintained, that in the first draft o the four pomts tt 
was stated that the Treaty of L841 was to be revised 1n the interest of the 
balance of power, but that the plan of reducing Russian power In the Black Sea 
was an after-thought, and had been adopted by the Austrian Government rather 
to please her allies than from any conviction of its necessity. ‘That while they 
were ready to support the proposal in Conference, they were not prepared » from 
personal regard to their allies, to go to war without @ case ot proved necessity. 
M, Drowyn de Lhuys and | combatted this reasoning, We stated that the 
views of the French and English Governments were no secret to Austria, or to 
the world, Speeches in Parliament on the part of the English Government, 
official notes published in the “ Moniteur "on the part of the French, had 
attested in the most public manner, six or cizht months ago, our apprehensions 
of the danger, and our estimate of the means of providing against tt. We 
appealed to Aali Pasha as to the reality of the danger of an attack on the 
Bosphorus by & Russian fleet and army, aad he fully confirmed our views by his 


ow iphatic statements. 
oe Baar Suol argued that it was not neeessary to. make Turkey equal to 
Russia, as in the system of the balance of power small States could preserve their 
independence in the neighbourhood of States far superior to them in the number 
of their armies, and the extent of their resources, 

But this was answered by pointing to the peculiar situation of the Black 
Sea, where Russia had kept up a great naval force without any commerce tio 
guard, in the presence of no rival power, and too evidently for purposes of 
aggression, 


631 


Count Buol told us be had not pressed the neutrality of the islands at the 
mouth of the Danube, as he was sure if he had done so the Russian Minister 
would have broken up the Conference. He said he could not propose war to 
the Diet at Frankfort for two ships more or less. 

T answered that, had Austria insisted on the neutrality of the islands at the 
mouth of the Danube, and a rupture of the Conference had taken place, I 
should not have argued in the British Parliament that this was a point which 
only concerned Austria, but I should have represented it as the cause of an 
ally, and Iwas sure three-fourths of both Houses would have supported Her 
Majesty's Government in such a quarrel, 

" M. Drouyn de Lhuye observed that our'Treaty of December 2 was not with 
the Dict of Frankfort, but with Austria. 

We both appealed to Austria to make the plan of neutralization or that of 
limitation a casus belli, and expressed our belief that if this was done, Russia 
would at once give way. 

Count Buol positively declined to accede to this proposal, and maintained 
his former reserves, 

While T consider this course as not unnatural.on the part of a Power whieh 
has hitherto kept out of the war, and is very averse to plunge into it, 1 con- 
ceive the policy of such reserve to be unwise in itself, and unjust to her allies, 
Unwise, because Russia, alter so many sacrifices of her pride and military 
position in the Principalities to please Austria, would nearly to a certainty give 
way, and thereby secure the peace so much desired; unjust to her allies, 
because, after the sacrifices they have made and are making, it is due to them 
that their armaments should not retire from the Black Sea without obtaining in 
the conditions of peace some special security against Russian preponderance 
in that Sea. The interests of Austria may be fairly supposed to outweigh in 
the Austrian Cabinet the general interests of Europe. There is, however, 
some chance thal, at the last moment, Austria may prove firm. It seems to me 
that Russia must either refuse to limit her naval force in the Black Sea on the 
eround of her dignity and her greatness, or she must consent to make her 
limitation effectual for its object. In either case Gur position is a good one. 
Our present business is to concert with the French and Turkish Plenipotentiaries 
the exact mode in which we shall act in the Conference, and leave it to Prince 
Gortchakoff to declare the purport of the instructions which he may receive 
from St. Peteraburgh, 

Should these be of a nature to meet our proposals half way, M. Drouyn de 
Lhuys and I intend to declare at once what we would accept, without any further 
discussion, If this is refused, we break off; if'a fresh refercnee to St, Petersburgh 
is asked, we intend to say, that we can only consent to such reference on condi- 
tion that the answer must be a decided yes or no, Vor such an answer 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys and I should not wait. 

If a rupture of the Conference takes place forthwith, we propose to write 
notes calling upon Count Buol to take the measures provided br by the Treaty 
of December 2. ? 

If he shall decline to do this, the spirit, and perhaps the letter, of the 
pea of December 2 will, in our opinion, be violated by the Government of 

ustria. 

[n relating what passed at the meeting, I have omitted to say, that Count 
Buol, in the paper which he read to us, declared that if Russia were to refuse to 
euarantee the integrity of Turkey, it would be a casus belli with Austria. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) J. RUSSELL.

No. G68. 


Lord John Russell to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received April 15.) 
(‘Telegraphic.) Vienna, April 14, 1855. 

I HAVE just had an important conversation with M, Drouyn de Lhuys. 
The French Minister for Foreign Affairs and I have agreed, first, that if the 
Russian Minister declares against any limitation, we break off the Conference : 
if he should merely say that he is ready to hear the proposals, we ask him 
whether he is ready to hear and discuss the proposals for limitation which we 
have ready; if not, we break off the Conference. Secondly, the French 
Minister for Foreign Affairs will declare to Austria he abandons neutralization, 
provided Austria goes with us for limitation even to the point of war. Third, 
if Conference is broken off, we propose to present notes to Austria, asking her 
to execute the Treaty of December 2nd. If limitation admitted as a principle, 
the terms agreed upon between us are these :— 

First. Russia and the Sublime Porte shall not have in the Black Sea more 
than four sail-ofthe-line, four frigates, with proportionate number of light 
vessels, and unarmed vessels exclusively adapted for the transport of troops. 

Second, The Powers who possess no establishment in the Black Sea may 
each have one half of the above-mentioned number of vessels. | 

Third, In ease of danger, all the maval forees of Austria, Franee, and 
Great Britain may, at the summons of the Porte, enter the Black Sea. 

Fourth. ‘The Contracting Powers may have Consuls in all the ports of the 
two States on the Black Sea and the Sea of Azof,
