No. 675. 
The Earl of Clarendon to Lord John Russell, 


(No. 60.) 


My Lord, Foreign Office, April 16, 1855. 

HER Majesty's Government concur in the opinion expressed in your 
Lordship’s despatch No. 64 of the 10th instant, and [ lost no time in informing 
your Lordship, by the telegraph, that if Russia refused to admit the principle of 
limitation, or, admitting the principle, would not agree to a satisfactory mode of 
carrying it into effect, the system of neutralization should then be proposed to 
the Russian Plenipotentiaries. Russia would then have the same option between 
the two projects as Austria, If both should be declined, the negotiation will 
be at an end. 

Her Majesty’s Government assume that this mode of proceeding will have 
the support of M. Drouyn de Lhuys. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) CLARENDON. 


No. 676, 
The Earl of Clarendon to Lord John Russell, 


(No. 61.) 


My Lord, Foreign Office, April 16, 1855, 

I HAVE the satisfaction to inform your Lordship that Her Majesty's 
Government entirely approve your language in reply to Count Buol, as reported 
in your despatch of the LOth instant. 

The opinions of Her Majesty's Government could not have been more 
faithfully represented, or more ably expressed, 

Count Buol must now be convinced that no attempt on the part of the 
Austrian Government to induce the Western Powers to relinquish their 
moderate proposals on the third point can be successful, and it. is to be hoped 
that no more such attempts will be made; but when Count Buol speaks of 
treating the third point like the two former, of coming to no previous resolution 
respecting war, and of not engaging in hostilities for two ships more or legs, he 
does not appear to bear in mind that the third point differs from the two former, 
masmuch as upon them Russia was prepared to make concessions, while she 
considers that the third, which is the only real check upon her designs, involves 
her honour and dignity, and she is therefore not likely to yield upon it, Count 
Buol may object to a previous resolution respecting war, but he must be aware 
that England and Franee cannot agree to an unsate and dishonourable peace, 
and that if Russia will agree to no other terms, the casus belli for Austria will 
arise. He may think it inexpedient to engage in hostilities for two ships more 
or less, but the question is, whether the naval force of Russia in the Black Sea 
shall be so limited as not to endanger the Ottoman Empire and the future peace 
of Europe, for that is the object of the war, 

In the event of the negotiations being broken off, Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment, if M, Drouyn de Lhoys concurs, ave of opinion that the English and

No. 679. 


Lord John Russell to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received April 17.) 


(Telegraphic.) Vienna, Avril 16, 1855, 

THE Russian messenger will arrive to-day ; Conference will probably take 
place to-morrow. The Austrian Minister wishes it to adjourn for further 
deliberation till next day. 

If other hope is lost, I wish to propose to the Conference the following 
plan. The French Minister is favourable to it. Austria will not support any 
demand for cession of territory. 

Ist. As the existence of an aggressive Russian fleet in the Black Sea would 
be in flagrant contradiction with the assurance so often given by Russia, that 
she sees not wish to impair the integrity of the Ottoman Empire, it is 
agreed : 

(1.) That with the exceptions stated in the following Articles, the rule of 
closing the Dardanelles and Bosphorus, recognised by the Treaty of 1841, 
shall be force so long as the Russian naval force in the Black Sea shall not 
exceed four sail of the line, four frigates, and six smaller vessels. 

0.) That while the said rule subsists, two sail of the line, two frigates, 
and three smaller vessels of any Power which has no establishment in the Black 
Sea, and which is in ae with the Sultan, may enter the Black Sea upon 
giving four days’ notice to the Ottoman Government. 

(d.) Upon any inerease of the Russian naval forces beyond the number 
specified in Article 1, or on the existence of a larger Russian force being ascer- 
tained, a larger number of ships of war of the allies of the Sultan may pass 
through the Straits into the Black Sea, in conformity with the desires of the Sultan 
and in the proportions to be regulated from time to time by agreement with the 
Ottoman Porte: such increase not to form, at any time, a legitimate subject of 
remonstrance on the part of Russia. | 

(4.) At no time shall any ships of foreign nations, beyond the small ships 
belonging to the Embassies admitted hitherto, anchor in the Golden Horn, nor 
shall any number of line-of-battle ships belonging to foreign Powers not having 
establishments in the Black Sea exceeding four pass at one time before the 
capital in their passage from the Dardanelles to the Black Sea, or from the 
Black Sea to the Dardanelles, whilst the Sultan is at peace. 

2nd, The cession to Turkey of the islands at the mouth of the Danube 
surrendered by the Treaty of Adrianople. 
ae onl The Asiatic frontier, on the side of Russia, to be newly laid down and 

efined, 

4th. An European guarantee of the territorial circumseription of the Ottoman 
Empire in Europe as defined in the 'l'reaty, 


oth. The forts on the Asiatic coust, now abandoned by Russia, not to be 
reoceupied.

Lord Stratford de Redelijffe to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Recetved April 17.) 
(No. 266,) 


My Lord, Constantinople, April 5, 1855. 

IN the hope of increasing the salutary, though perhaps imperfect, impres- 
sion previously made upon Reshid Pasha and his colleagues with respect to the 
reforms so greatly needed and so strenuously recommended in this country, I 
directed M, Pisant to read your Lordship’s instruction No. 237 of the 23rd 
ultimo, to the Grand Vizier and Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs. 

M. Pisani, in reporting the execution of my instruction, states that these 
two Ministers gave assurance to the following effect, namely, that the “measures 
contemplated in the Reform Council would be earried into effect, and that 
Europe would have reason to be satisfied with the sincerity of the Porte and with 
the nature of the reforms affecting the Christian population of Turkey.” 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

My Lord, Paris, April 17, 1855.

very late intelligence from Vienna, | thought your Lordship would not disa 
prove of my reading to him the substance of Lord John Russell's telegraphic 
despatches which reached me this day. 

When I had finished reading these documents, M. Thouvenel said, he con- 
sidered the proposals upon which alone Austria seemed disposed to atlach a 
citsus belli to be altogether unacceptable; the first part of the plan, however, 
which Lord John Russell, in a subsequent despatch, proposes, if other hope is 
lost, to pee to the Conference, met with his approbation, and he believed 
Count Buol would not be indisposed to join the allies in demanding the adop- 
tion of a scheme of limitation which he (M. Thouvenel) designated as ‘une 
limitation facultative.” 

I have, &e.

No. 687. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Ciarendon.—(Received April 19.) 


(No. 275. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, April 9, 1855. 


SEVERAL coinciding cireumstances, brought successively to my know- 
ledge, tend to show that the French Government directs a more than usual 
attention to the Island of Candia. I have reason to believe that the appointment 
of Veli Pasha, the Porte’s late Ambassador at Paris, to that government, 
originated in a desire to please the French Emperor. His recall was delayed 
from the same motive; and when it was finally decided upon, the disappointment 
both to himself and to his supporters at Paris, was softened by his nomination 
toa command which had been formerly exercised by his father during several 
years with much distinction. 

His father, who held the office of Grand Vizier during the early part of 
last year, and whose political connections estrange him from Reshid Pasha, has 
lately had a lawsuit with that Minister, which terminated in his own discomfiture. 
The point at issue was the validity of an agreement for selling to Mustapha 
Pasha a small piece of grouud detached from a property which has lately come 
into the possession of the present Prime Minister. As far as my information 
goes, I believe that the purchase had been virtually completed, even to the 
payment of the price, but that an essential form was wanting to render the 
transaction legal. Reshid, 1 conceive, would have done better to give way, as 
it seems that the land in question was of more importance to his antagonist than 
to himself: but his friends allege that the purchaser acted with so much offensive 
CIRCE, as to warrant an appeal to the strict requirements of the law, 

The French Chargé d'Aflaires thought proper to interfere on behall of the 
former Governor of Candia, and even went so far as to have recourse in person 
to the Sultan at a private audience. He gained nothing by this intrigue, which 
was made known to Reshid by the Sultan himself; but he has, nevertheless, 
continued to annoy the Grand Vizier with renewed applications on the same 
subject, and an undisguised protection of his opponent, putting forward the 
Emperor's name. 

[ learn from the same authentic source whence this information has reached 
me, that an incident likely to create further alienation between the French 
Government and the present ‘Turkish Ministry has occurred recently in Egypt. 
It appears that M. de Lesseps, on returning to that country, obtained from Said 
Pasha the communication of a private and confidential letter which had been 
addressed to him by Kiamil Pasha, the President of the Council here, with the 
view of producing a postponement of the scheme for opening a canal through 
the Isthmus of Suez. Kiamil Pasha is married to a relative of the Viceroy, and 
formerly resided in Egypt. 

This indiseretion, or act of treachery, on the part of Said Pasha, has excited 
the more indignation here, as the letter has been sent to Paris by M. de 
Lesseps. 

_ ‘These circumstances are worthy of your Lordship’s consideration, as 
indicative of tendencies which in their progress may be productive of much 
serious inconvenience, and perhaps eventually of consequences more easily 
lamented than remedied. 

I have, &c. 


(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE,

The articles printed in the “ Moniteur” of the 11th of this month, are 
generally regarded here as having been written with the view of insuring a 
complete liberty of action for the Emperor Louis Napoleon, and of leaving him 
more free on the question of peace, by proving to the world that his original 
instructions had been disregarded, and that all the present difficulties originated 
in the having landed at Eupatoria instead of Theodosia. The tactics of those 
opposed to England and France are to try to excite suspicion of the sincerity of 
Austria. They say constantly that the liberty of commerce on the Danube 
being once established, she will leave us to finish the war as we can. Even His 
Saxon Majesty, when I had last the honour of seeing him, alluded to this, but 
added, “ England is sincere in her wish for peace, but the Emperor of the 
French is the real obstacle.” I answered that | believed an honourable peace, 
established on a lasting basis, was as much an object to the French as to the 
English Government, but experience had made us cautious in any dealings with 
Russia, whoever sat on the throne. The King merely smiled without further

WITH reference to your Execllency’s despatch No. 266 of the Sth instant,

the promises given to your Excellency by the Turkish Ministers, that the 
measures contemplated in Turkey would be carried into effect, and that Europe

refornis affecting the Christian population.

stantinople from the encroaching ambition of Russia. 

L await your Lordship’s answer, by the telegraph, to the present proposal

Inclosure in No. 695. 
Memorandum. 


AU moment ot les sujets non-Musulmans de Sa Majesté Impériale le 
Sultan fixent attention, il ne serait pas inutile de passer succinctement en 
revue quelles étaient leurs conditions avant les réformes si glorieusement 
entreprises par Sa Majesté le Sultan, et quel est le degré d’amélioration ov 
elles sont arrivées depuis quelques années. 

Pour démontrer l'importance du progrés qui s'est opéré, on n’aura besoin 
que d’énumérer seulement des faits, et en laisser le jugement 4 limpartialité du 
lecteur. 

La législation Musulinane, dans ses principes comme dans son esprit, 
préscrit et ordonne la tolérance la plus entiére pour toutes les communautcs 
religiouses soumises 4 la domination Ottomane, et en placant Vhonneur, la 
propri¢té, et Ja vie de tous les sujets non-Musulmans sous ln sauvegarde de la 
loi, elle établit pour ceux-ci une condition des plus avantageuses, et exempte de 
toutes les charges et obligations qu’impose le devoir de servir la patric. 

Dans aucune époque de histoire de Empire Ottoman on ne trouvera la 
moindre trace de ces persécutions religieuses qui ont ensanglante toute l'Europe 
durant la longue période du moyen Age. 

(est an moment of Constantinople venait d’tre conquise par la force des 
armées Ottomanes, que Sultan Mohammed I] a accordé spontanément au 
Patriarche Gree de cette capitale ces priviléges religieuses dont il est question 
aujourd'hui. Les successeurs de ce grand Monarque ont respecté et développé 
ces priviléges, sans qu’ils y fussent contraints pur aucune pression étrangere, 

Ainsi les priviléges religieux, loin d’étre violés ou limités, ont requ des 
développements considérables, et qui ont été, malgré les efforts de ceux qui 
veulent sc servir de la Turquie comme d'un instrument de persécution contre 
les autres communautés Chrétiennes, généralisés & |'égard de toutes ces commu- 
nautés. 

Cette assertion est tellement vraie que toutes les demandes qui ont amené 
l'état actuel des choses, ont eu pour origine et pour motif reel, quoique non 
avoué, la tendance de la Turquie de traiter tous ses sujets sur le pied de la plus 


parfaite we 
_ La Turquie a cependant eu son moyen jige aussi. Mais les priviléges 
religieux ont traversé cette période sans aucune atteinte. | | 

Pendant plus d'un sitele, tous les sujets de Empire, Musulmans et 
Chrétiens, ont souffert des abus administratifs et des vexations arbitraires des 
autorités subalternes, La vie, Vhonneur, et le bien des sujets se sont trouves 
sans garantie; les Chrétiens ont eu des distinctions humiliantes, une sorte d’inca- 
tolls ae emplois, des difficultés pour la construction ou la répuration de leurs 
églises, &c, 

La pensée de la réforme, en embrassant toutes les populations de |’Empire, 
a porté i cet état de choses un coup décisif. 

A peine commencée, elle donna d’heureux résultats pour ce qui concerne 
surtout les populations non-Musulmanes—reésultats qui doivent surprendre ceux 
qui comprennent la puissance du temps si lent et st paresseux d’ordinaire pour 


venir i Taide du réformateur, En peu d'années, le progrés fut grand et les sujets

non-Musulmans se trouvérent tout d'un coup dans une position, sous quelques

Nous parlerons d'abord de Ja capitation, 

Cet impét personnel était une simple redevance obligatoire pour tous les 
sujets non-Musulmans des pays conquis, mais qui en retour leur-accordait le 
libre exercice de leur culte, eb par sutte Vexemption du service militaire et la 


protection de la loi pour leur vie et leurs biens. 


Peu a peu, Vobligation de payer cette capitation devint une marque de 
distinction dégradante, une source de mépris et un moyen de vexation entre les 
mains des employés subalternes. 

Sa Majesté Impériale le Sultan vient dabolir cette redevance, malgré la 
puissance des préjugés populaires, ct le principe qui avait établi, 1 déclara 
par ce fait seul quil ne reconnaissait plus de distinction entre peuple conquérant 
et peuple conquis. 

Les sujets non-Musulmans portaient des costumes différents adaptés a leurs

No. 697. 
Lord John Russell to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received April 21.) 


(No. 83.) 
My Lord, Fienna, April 18, 1855. 


YESTERDAY after the Conference the Plenipotentiaries of France, Great 
Britain, and Turkey, met in Count Bual’s apartment. 

There had been an anxious fecling at the result of our former meeting. 
The position on both sides appeared to be uneasy, though much more on the 
side of Austria than onours. We should, indeed, have a greal war to conduct 
at an immense expense without any obvious termination. 

It would, indeed, in all probability have continued to be a struggle glorious 
to England and to France, and caleulated to maintain the reputation of those 
two great Powers, But the waste of life and money would be enormous. 

On the other hand, the fact of Austria’s declining to join in the war 
would have roused a very angry feeling ‘n France and in Great Britain. With 
the Western Powers alienated, Prussia triumphing over her in Germany, an 
Russia bent on her humiliation, her situation would have been almost intolerable. 
The state of her finances would hardly have allowed her to maintain during the 
whole period of the war her vast army, and yet ‘f che had diminished it she 
would have been forced to retire from the Principalities in breach of her 
engagements, 

These considerations on both sides led to the prevalence of a conciliatory 
spirit in the meeting of yesterday. After much discussion, which was conducted 
with great temper on all sides, and in which the judgment and tact of Aali Pasha 
were of material assistance, Count Buol proposed to the belligerent Powers 
general understanding to the following effect : 

1. That the plan of limitation of numbers agreed to in London should be 
first proposed, and be supported by Count Buol. 

>, That it should be proposed that Russia and Turkey, by mutual agree- 
ment, should maintain reciprocally a foree no larger than that which shall 
remain to Russia at the end of the war. A list to be drawn up, and the Conven- 
tion referred to in the Treaty to have the same force as if it formed part of the 
Treaty. Ships of war of the allies to be admitted into the Black Sea in limited 
numbers, not exceeding for each half the Russian force. | 

4 In case of the failure of both these propositions, he thought that bases 
of peace might be found in the following conditions : | 

A general engagement to respect the integrity of the Turkish Empire, on 
behalf of each of the Powers, and against any one of them which should violate 
this engagement. 

A provision that the closing of the Dardanelles and Bosphorus should con- 
tinue to be the rule, with the exception that Powers which have not establish- 
ments in the Black Sea may be admitted by the Sultan to the extent of half the 
number maintained by Russia for each Power. 

Consuls in the Russian ports. 

A ‘Treaty with Austria that if Russia shall inerense her naval foree in the 
Black Sea beyond the number maintained by her in 1853, it shall be a casus belli 
for the Contracting Powers. 

It was agreed that the guarantee of the integrity of Turkey should be 

roposed before any of these pling, the questions being taken in the order of 
ee euarantee ; 2nd, closing of Straits and limitation. 

{ reserved my opinion for further consideration. 

Sueh was the general result of this important meeting. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys called upon me in the evening, and we drew up 
together a rough outline of the proposals to be made. 

It will be seen, that supposing the second proposition to be rejected as well 
as the first, the value of the third depends on three things : 

|. Guarantee by all the Contracting Powers of the territory of Turkey. 

9. A system of counterpoise in the Black Sea, . 

3. 'The limitation of the Russian force in the Black Sea to the number of 
ships maintained before the war, under pain of war with the allies,

No. 701. 


The Karl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received April 21.) 


(No. 180 ) 


My Lord, Vienna, April 13, 1855, 

WITH reference to my telegraphic despatch of yesterday, I have to report 
to your Lordship, that at the meeting of the Representatives of the alhed 
Governments which took place after the Conference had been adjourned, Count 
Buel brought forward for discussion the general plan for the attainment of the 
engagement taken by the Protocol reservé of the 28th of December last, namely, 
‘(de faire cesser la prépondérance Russe dans la Mer Noire.” The plan which 
was developed by Count Buol consisted of the following propositions, which 
were successively to be offered to the Plenipotentiaries : 

First, The plan of the limitation of the Russian and Turkish ships of the 
line with a fixed number of frigates which was not to be exceeded. This 
stipulation was to be accompanied by the recognition of the principle of the 
closing of the Straits of the Dardanelles to all foreign ships of war, with the 
exception of two steam-frigates of each nation—England, France, and Austria— 
which, upon a firman of the Sultan, were to be admitted to the Black Sea, for 
the purpose of observing the strict execution of the Treaty for securing the 
freedom of the navigation of the Danube. 

Secondly. The Russian and Ottoman Governments might agree among 
themselves as to the number of vessels of war which each should employ or 
possess in the Black Sea, agreeing to announce to each other the “état” or 
amount of that number, and stipulating that without agreement among them- 
selves, they would not augment them. 

The stipulation for foreign vessels for the protection of the navigation of 
the Danube would remain the same ag stated in the first proposition, and the 
Governments of England and France would cach be empowered, upon the 
consent of the Sultan, to introduce into the Black Sea one half the number of 
vessels maintained by Russia. 

Thirdly. In case Russia refused both these proposals, the allied Govern- 
ments would propose that the Treaty of 1841 should be modified in the 
following manner ; 

That as Russia objected to any limitation of the number of her floating 
ships of war at present existing in the Black Sea, the Governments of England 
and France should each be empowered, upon the congent of the Sultan, to place 
a number of ships of war equal to half the mumber of Russian vessels in that 
sea; and if the Government of Russia increased their number of ships, for 
every two they added to their fleet, England and France would each have the 
power of adding one, until the amount of the Russian fleet reached the number 
of ships that Government possessed in 1853, before the commencement of the 
war: but if Russia exceeded that number, it would be announced to her that 
the Governments of England, Austria, and France, had engaged themselves by 
Treaty to consider it a casue belli, which Treaty would be published at the same 
time with the general Treaty of Peace. In case Russia engaged to agree to the 
above proposed limitation of her naval force, the ‘Treaty would still be signed by 
the three Powers; its existence would be notitied to Russia, but it would be 
considered as “ reservé,” and would not be published except by common consent 
anongst the Contracting Parties, . 

In addition to these stipulations, the presence of Consuls from each 
Government would be required to be received in the Russian ports, 

‘The regulation us to foreign ships passing to and from the Black Sea, with 
the firmans of the Sultan to that effeet, would be regulated according to the 
system hitherto established, or by agreement with the Porte,

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received April 21.) 


(No. 174.) 
My Lord, Berlin, April 19, 1855. 

I HAVE had some conversation this evening with Baron Manteuffel on 
the news from Vienna. His Excellency said that he had not much to commu- 
nicate on the subject, and all that he had heard was, that Prince Gortchakoff 
has informed the Conference that he was ready to discuss the third point, but 
he had no. propesitions to make. His Excellency did not seem to believe that 
there was likely to be an immediate termination of the Conferences, though he 
was unable to form any opinion as to the turn the affairs were likely to take. 
[ replied that it was strange that the Russian Plenipotentiary should have 
required so long a time to get 50 vague An answer from St, Petersburgh, and 
that 1 thought this unnecessary delay was only a further proof the desire of 
Ttussin to protract the discussions with a view to foster the existing state of 
indecision in Germany, and to keep Austria from entering Into new engare- 
ments with the Western Powers. 1 usked what he considered would be the 
course that Austria was likely to pursue? Tis Excellency replied that 
he believed that she might be induced to act with us; that means might 
be employed for this purpose; and threw out a hint that her pecuniary 
embarrassments were the main difficulty, and that if they were overcome 
there would be no objection left to her joining us. I then asked what we 
had to expect of Germany ? He answered that the influence of Austria was 
very great among the smaller States, that their general desire was for peace, a8 
wae the case in Prussia, and that we should meet with sympathies amongst 
them. Prussia then, I said, was our great difficulty and I feared her influence 
would he employed against us. ‘To this his Excellency observed that she was in 
io way engaged to Russia; that the King had certainly no intention at this 
moment of joing us, but that he would not ally himself with Russia as long as 
we respected his position, and did nothing to interfere with his independence, 
But | observed to his Excellency that His Majesty must see that in the interest 
of peace his feelings ought to be identical with ours, and that the war in which 
we were engaged could only be protracted by the ambiguous position of Prussia, 
whilst her neutrality could scarcely be maintained if the three other great Powers 
were united against Russia, 

Baron Manteutfel made no direct answer to this remark, but he endeavoured 
to convey the impression that Prussia would be ope to conviction, and that 
means might be found, even without serious ditfculty, of removing the difficul-

Another pretension of Russia, namely, that of making her Treaties with 
Turkey separate from the public law of Europe, is thus overthrown, 
pon the Articles in the project here annexed, which fix the numbers of 
Russian vessels in the Black Sea, being read, Prince Gortchakoff desired to hear 
the opinions of every member of the Conference. 

Count Buol, who spoke last, gave the plan proposed his hearty support. 

Prince Gortchakoff requested him to state how far he would carry the 
support of his Government ; but the Austrian Minister said, with great dignity 
and propriety, that the present object was to come to an understanding ; any 
ulterior purpose must be reserved for the time when it would be necessary to 
declare it. : 

Thus deserted on all sides and seeing nothing but a compact phalanx around 
him, Prince Gortchakoff asked the Conference to allow him forty-eight hours to 
prepare his reply. He left it quite uncevtain whether he meant to give a laboured 
negative to the proposal, or whether he would avail himself of a suggestion 
thrown out by us that he might make a convention with the Turkish Plenipo- 
tentiaries to he afterwards recorded in the Treaty; or finally, whether he meant 
to make proposals himself. 

But what was quite evident was, that since the 26th of March there has 
been a preat change in the hopes, whether of victory or disunion among the 
allies, which appeared to have animated the Russian Plenipotentinries at that 
time. ‘They complained that we seemed to be preparing for a rupture; they 
expressed sympathy with the Turks, and their fears of the power of France and 
England in the Mediterranean. 

Still there was no symptom of yielding so far as to fix the number of the 
Russian fleet to be kept up in the Black Sea by the Treaty of Peace. 

Lam, however, inclined to think that some proposition will be made to the 
allies on Saturday, intended to throw upon the allies the odium of exorbitant 
pretensions. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) J. RUSSELL

Lord John Russell to the Karl of Clarendon.—(Received April 22.) 


(No, 90,) 
My Lord, Vienna, April 19, 1855. 

[ AM much gratified to find that the language recorded in my despatch 
No. 66, has been approved by Her Majesty's Government. 

With respect to the transmission of a note to Austria, in case of the 
breaking off the Conference, calling upon her to execute the Treaty of December 2, 
I had some conversation with M. Drouyn de Lhuys, M. de Bourqueney, and 
Lord Westmorland, to-day. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys observed that such a note would produce a reply 
Justifying the conduct of Austria, and accusing the Western Powers of pressing 
their demands in an unwarrantable manner. He thought it would be unwise to 
irritate Austria, and rather wished to derive from the alliance such fruits as it 
might yet produce. 

Baron de Bourqueney and Lord Westmorland concurred in this view, which 
appeared to me to be just,

Gth. Austria will propose to Russia an engagement not to increase her

of war of all nations. 

Lord Westmorland asks these questions with me. I stay till Monday 
evening. In case my despatch No. 63 has not arrived, I add that I have 
expressed a hope that this proposition of Austria will not be rejected without 
my being present ; but seeing the urgeney I do not ask for this delay.

No, 714. 
The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland, 
(No. 164.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, April 24, 1855. 


THE memorandum by Aali Pasha, inclosed in Lord John Russell’s No, 81 
of the 18th instant, is dexterously drawn up, and has been read with interest by 
Her Majesty’s Government ; but I have to observe that it passes over some of 
the urgent wants of the Christian subjects of the Sultan. 

It is true that Christian evidence is admissible in criminal Courts, though 
in many places it is not admitted; but the judges in such eases are still exclu- 
sively Mahometans. The only mixed tribunals are the commercial Courts, 
Whose functions are very limited. Christian evidence is still inadmissible in 
civil cases ; and inasmuch as robbery is a more frequent crime than murder, civil 
injuries are oftener perpetrated against Christians than personal injuries, and the 
inadmissibility of Christian evidence in civil cases is a severe and daily-felt 
grievance. ‘There ought both in civil and criminal eases to be a Court composed 
of an equal number of Christian and Mahometan jadges, 

All the local authorities in the Provinces are still Mahometan, and this 
leads to endless oppression and injustice committed and connived at towards 
Christians. 

There ought to be some Christian officer of suitable rank attached to each 
Mussulman Governor, so that such Christian officer might be appealed to by 
injured Christians, and he should have the right of appealing to Constantinople 
in the event of his not being able to obtain justice from the local Governor. 

Christians ought to be allowed to rise to any rank in the military and civil 
services, and their advancement should not form an exception to the rule by 
which they are excluded from the higher ranks of their profession : the interests 
of the Sultan would unquestionably be promoted by enlarging the field of selec- 
tion, and taking into his service many able and intelligent men who have now 
ho access to tt. 

The description given in the memorandum of the Medical School at 
Constantinople, and of the kindly feelings which the youths of different creeds 
are taught to entertain towards each other, should encourage the Porte to 
proceed in a system which has been productive of such happy results, and 

rimary schools should be established in all the chief towns throughout the 
Purkish Empire, in which Christian and Mussulman children should receive 
elementary instruction together. 

Her Majesty's Government do full justice to the enlightened views and 
benevolent intentions of the Sultan, and they are convinced that if it depended 
solely on the will of His Majesty, justice would be impartially administered 
throughout his dominions, and the state of his Christian subjects would be 
prosperous and contented: but unfortunately the men on whom devolves the 
duty of giving effect to the Sultan's will are not animated by his spirit; and 
until rapacity, injustice, and corruption are systematically discountenanced and 
punished, the social system of ‘Turkey must continue to deteriorate, and the 
reforms and improvements upon which the prosperity and the independence of 
the Ottoman Empire depend will exist only in name, 

Your Lordship will communicate this despatch to Aali Pasha, and furnish 
him with a copy if he should desire it. 


Tam, &e. 
(Signed) CLARENDON,

No. 715. 
The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland. 


(No. 165.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, April 24, 1895, 

THE proposal No. 2 of Count Buol, contained in Lord John Russell's 
despatch No. 83 of the 18th instant, is that Russia and Turkey by mutual agree: 
ment should maintain reciprocally a foree no larger than that which shall 
remain to Russia at the end of the war; that a list should be drawn up and the 
Convention referred to in the Treaty to have the same foree as if it formed part 
of the Treaty. Ships of war of the allies to he admitted into the Black Sea in 
limited numbers, not exceeding, for each, half the Russian foree. 

This would leave the principle of the limitation of the Russian flect to stand 
upon a separate Conyention between Russia and Turkey, to which England and 
France would not be Contracting Parties ; and though such Convention would be 
referred to in the General Treaty, we know by experience that Russia has inva- 
riably attempted to escape from the obligations of such separate Conventions 
incorporated into the ‘Treaty of Vienna of 1815, alleging that, though so incor- 

porated, they concerned only the parties whe contracted them, that the incor- 
poration was only a registration, and did not mive the other parties who signed 
the General Treaty a right to require the execution of those separate Conventions, 
and this doctrine, which was repeatedly put forward in all questions relating to 
Poland, was equally maintained by Auatria and by Prussia, as well as by Russia. 

The proposal of Count Buol would also go much further than anything 
contemplated by England and France, because it would prevent ‘Turkey from 

haying anywhere, and not merely in the Black Sea, a naval foree greater than 
that which may remain to Russia in the Black Sea at the end of the war. 

In the event of the proposals being rejected by Russia, Count Buol, among 
other bases of peace, suggests a provision that the closing of the Dardanelles and 
Bosphorus should continue to he the rule, with the exception that Powers which 
have not establishments in the Black Sea may he admitted by the Sultan to the 
extent of half the number maintained b Russia for cach Power. 

This appears to allow an unlimite imerease of the Russian fleet in the 
Black Sea, while England and France should each have only half the Hussian 
sumber—a condition which, if Russia had a large tleet and England and France 
were not ready to-act jointly, would place that one af the two which happened 
to be ready in a condition of great inferiority to Russin. 

I have stated in my despatch of the 21st instant, the opinion of Her 
Majesty's Government with respect to the further proposal of Count Buol 
for a Treaty with Austria, that if Russia shall increase her naval foree in 
the Black Sea beyond the number maintained by her in 1843, it shall be a casus 
helli for the Contracting Powers. 

Tam, &c. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received April 25.) 


(No. 183.) 


My Lord, Frenna, April 22, 1855, 

THE Conference assembled yesterday for the purpose of receiving the 
answer of Prince Gortchakoff, to the proposals which had been made to him on 
the 19th instant, the substance of which has been reported to you in my 
despatch No. 181 of the same date. 

The Conference was first engaged in receiving the report of the Protocol of 
the Conference of Thursday, which, after some discussion was approved of, and 
has been signed this day, and which will be transmitted to your Lordship as soon 
as the lithographic copies are distributed from the Chancery of State. 

Prince Gortchakoff then read an elaborate reply to the proposals which had 
been submitted to him, and which he desired might be inserted in the Protocol. 

This reply was a total rejection of that part of the proposals which limited 
the number of ships of war which Russia was to possessin the Black Sea. 
Prince Gortchakoff stated that he conceived that by opening the navigation of 
the Black Sea to the ships of war of all nations, (but subject to the consent of 
the Porte) the Russian preponderance in the Black Sea would effectually be done 
away with, As the reply of Prince Gortchakoff is of considerable length, and 
as it will be transmitted to your Lordship with the Protocol, as soon as it is 
approved and signed, I will not enter into any details with regard to it, further 
than to state, that the mode in which the Russian Plenipotentiaries had thus 
responded to the proposals made to them, were considered hy all the Repre- 
sentatives of the allied Governments, as not fulfilling the expectations which had 
been formed from the general tenor of the language which Prince Gortchakolf 
and his colleague had hitherto been understood to ae employed, and this senti- 
ment was very strongly expressed during the remainder of the sitting, as will

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarentdon.—(Received April 25.) 
{No. 278.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, April 12, 1855, 

IN pusuance of your instructions, I have read, or rather caused to be read, 
to the Grand Vizier your Lordship’s despatch No. 293 of the 29th ultimo. 

Not having time to wait upon Reshid Pasha myself, 1 directed Mr. Odo 
Russell, attended by Mr. Stephen Pisani, to perform that duty. 

I have now the honour to inclose herewith, in copy, Mr. Russell's report of 
what passed on the occasion. 

Aali Pasha not being within reach himself, 1 know not from what better 
er other source I could hope to derive the information required by your 
Lordship. 

With respect to my own impressions, Tam not aware of having concealed 
any part of them from your Lordship, and without looking back into my previous 
correspondence, | have no hesitation in stating whatever occurs to my recollection 
upon the subject at this moment. 

It may be doubied whether the Turkish Ministers ever expected any 
advantage to result from the Conferences ut Vienna under existing cireum- 
stances, and it is not their habit to incur premature responsibility, Tt was also a 
question whether, on the meeting of the Plenipotentiaries, any approach to a 
pacific result could be obtained. They may therefore be presumed to have felt 
an unwillingness to take more part in the attempt to negotiate than what their 
ordinary diplomatic establishment allowed of. 

I was myself under an impression that expedition was of more consequence 
than the transmission of instructions wholly without reserve ; and finding, as it 
appeared, that my Frencl: colleague had no intention to press the appointment of 
a second or special Plenipotentiary, I urged the sending full powers with suitable 
‘nstructions to Aart Effendi, preferring that course to the loss of time insepar- 
able from the selection, preparation, and conveyance to Vienna of a more 
important personage, 

OF Arif Effendi | had never heard anything calculated to give me mean 
opinion of his capacity or fitness for negotiation. ‘The negotiitions of 1840-41 
were carried through by the late Chekib Effendi, an Ainbassador by no means 
remarkable for intellectual superiority, and unaequainted with any Christian 
language. Itiza Bey, who went out us Counsellor to the Turkish Ambassador 
at Vienna, was well able to supply his Excellency's deficiencies tn language and 
information af detail. 

When the Ambassador himself complained of responsibility, and eried out 
for help, £ ceased to acquiesce in the Porte's hesitations, and hastened the 
departure of Aali Pasha to the best of my power. L have no reason to doubt 
that M. Benedetti, who had mot differed from me in the outset, continued to 
pursue the same course with myself. 

[have only to observe in conclusion, that with all confidence in the friendly 
and enlightened regard entertained by Her Majesty's Government for the 
Sultan's interests, no powers of persuasion possessed by me could prevail on 
the Turkish Ministers to forego their own ideas on points to which they attach 
a vital, though perhaps an exaggerated importance, 

I have, &e, 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE,

Grand Vizier, and read to him the Earl of Clarendon’s despatch No, 253 of the 
20th ultiuno. 
His Highness desired me to express to you hoy much he regretted that 
any inconvenience should have been experienced at the first Conferences by the

Representatives of the allied Governments at Vienna in consequence of the 
absence of the second Ottoman Plenipotentiary. No doubt (certain reserves 
having been made) the Instructions sent to Aarit Effendi were limited, but not 
in such manner as to cause the Porte to apprehend that the progress of the 
negotiations could thereby suffer. 

On learning that Lord John Russell had undertaken a special mission to 
Vienna for the purpose of attending the Conferences, the Sultan had been 
deeply impressed with the necessity and importance of sending the ablest man 
to represent the interests of Turkey at those Conferences, and His Majesty had 
accordingly been pleased to make choice of His Minister for Foreign Affairs, 
whose abilities were well known, and whose conduct and policy had met with the 
approval of the allied Governments. Aati Pasha had been furnished with the 
necessary full powers ; but his Highness, having made himself acquainted with 
a large number of despatches and documents relating to the subjects under 
discussion in the Conferences, his departure had been necessarily delayed. The 
Grand Vizier ended ty repeating the expression of his deep regret that this 
anfortunate but unavoidable delay should have proved a source of annoyance to 


Her Majesty’s Government.

The French Charge d’Affaires, not contented with interfering between the 

Pasha and his adversary in a law suit, or obtaining privately from the Sultan a 
promise that Riza Pasha, the Ser askier, should not be removed from office, now 
fnsists on the dismissal of Kiamil Pasha, the President of the Council, for a 
private act, which implicates the Grand Vizier, and has a direct and sinister 
wearing, if not on British interests, at least on the views of Her Majesty's 
Government, 1 allude to a confidential letter addressed by Kiamil Pasha to the 
Viceroy of Egypt respecting M. de Lesseps and his projected canal. Tt was in 
right of family connection, and of a long tenure of office in the administration 
of Mchemet Ali, the Viceroy’s father, that Kiamil Pasha expressed his thoughts 
on that subject with the knowledge and private sanction of the Grand Vizier. 

This latter circumstance does not appear; but it is, no doubt, suspected by 
M. Benedetti, and I have reason to believe it true, though | knew nothing of 
the correspondence till long after it took place. 

The letter in question has been lately communicated to me in confidence, 
and I forward a translation of it herewith for your Lordship’s information. 

The Viceroy, in handing it over to M. de Lesseps, appears to have 
conunitted a flagrant breach of confidence, and I do not comprehend on what 
ground of publie right M. Benedetti can demand the punishment of its author, 
who docs not lie open to the charge of having given any just cause of offence, 
either by his expressions or by the objections which he urged against the imine- 
diate adaption of a scheme repudiated by the French Government as an object 
of their official support. 

Your Lordship knows how careful 1 have been to avoid giving umbrage by 
any kind of open or positive opposition to the proposed ent ‘prize. Crippled in 
thut respect by my unwillingness to compromise greater interests, I find the 
more reason to regret the advantage taken by M. Benedetti of my moderation, 
with the obvious purpose of not only forcing the acceptance af M. de ps 
project, but also of obtaining a signal triumph over Reshid Pasha to the complete

No. 73d. 
Lord John Russell to the Earl of Clarendon—(Received April 26.) 
(No. 99.) 
My Lord, Vienna, April 23, 1855. 


| HAD some further conversation with M, Bach, and subsequently with 
M. Cantono, the Sardinian Chargé d'Affaires, on the subject of the sequestra- 
tions. Afler some remarks on the ineorrectness of the list sent him, and the 
time required for a reference to Milan, M, Bach avowed that the chief difficulty 
in the way of granting a repeal of the sequestration order arose, from the open 
defiance of the Austrian Government by some of the persons affected, and tlie 
unwillingness of the Government to grant more liberal terms to others than 
those upon which Duke Litta and several more had claimed and received back 
their property. : 

used such arguments as occurred to me against the first of these objec 
tions. 1 quoted from M. Cantono the illustration that as the sequestration was 
said to be a measure of precaution, it resembled the precaution of a householder 
who has lost some property. He locks the door and stops all his servants from 
going out. But the search made for the guilty once over, he allows them all 
their liberty. Austria had been two years finding out the guilty, and ought to 
let those who were not guilty go free. 

The other objection I could not so well answer, What has been done by 
many proprietors, might, it seems to me, be done by the rest; [mean if it ts 
merely an assurance of quiet and peaceable conduct. 

I advised M. Cantono to get from M. Bach a copy of this assurance, and 
to send it to his Government. He will then take such steps as his Government 
may direct. 


I have, &c. 
(Signed) J. RUSSELL.

No, 735. 
The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received April 27.) 


(Telegraphic.) Vienna, April 26, 1855. 

COUNT BUOL called a Conference this day at the request of the Russian 
Representatives. I had a great objection to take part in it, but upon consulting 
with M. Drouyn de Lhuys, who determined to attend it, I did so upon the grounds 
explained in my despatch of this day, but declaring, in the words of Lord John 
at the last Conference, that my instructions were exhausted. 

The proposition of Prince Gortehakoff was, first, that the principle of 
closing the Straits should be maintained in time of peace. 

Secondly, that the Sultan should reserve to himself the right to accord a 

ce through the Straits to foreign ships of war at pleasure, or whenever he 
should think that his security was menaced. 

These propositions were not aceepted, either by Austria or the allies, as 
advancing the objects of the Conference.

No. 742. 
The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received April 29.) 


(No. 188.) 
My Lord, Vienna, April 24, 1855. 

M. DROUYN DE LHUYS called upon me this morning, to state that 
he had received an answer from his Government to the first proposition, which, 
in concert with Lord John Rusgell, and in accordance with the views expressed 
by Count Buol, he had transmitted to Paris, and that, to his great regret, this 
answer was not favourable. He said, that notwithstanding this first ‘ échee, 
he would not give up the hope of better success, ioularly as he believed the 
more detailed project he had since forwarded to the Emperor Napoleon, would 

roduce a more satisfactory result. He then expressed his anxious desire that 
Lord John Russell should be informed of the want of success of his first com- 
munication to Paria; and as he (Lord John Russell) was as convinced of the 
importance of the proposal as he was himself, that he should be requested to 
recommend it personally or by telegraph to your Lordship, in order that upon 
his arrival at Paris he might hope for the support of Her Majesty’s Government. 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys at the same time announced to me that he was going from 
my house to the Emperor, where he was to have his audience to take leave, 
and that he should leave Vienna the following morning, 

Under these circumstances, I decided upon transmitting to Lord John 
Russell the message of M. Drouyn de Lhuys by the messenger Haviland, who 
had remained in Vienna after Lord John Russell's departure, and I inclase for 

our Lordship’s information a copy of the private letter to Lord John, of which 
io was the bearer. 

In the course of the evening, and after the departure of the messenger, I 
again saw M. Drouyn de Lhuys, who informed me that since the morning he 
had reecived a more favourable communication from his Government; that they 
had consented to reconsider their first decision upon the project which had been 
transmitted to them, and consequently that he had determined not to leave 
Vienna in the morning as he had intended. , 

As soon as I received this intelligence, 1 sent a telegraphic message to 
Mr. Forbes (a copy of which I inclose}, requesting lim to announce to Lord 
John Russell the circumstances I have above stated. 


April 25. 

M, Drouyn de Lhuys has had an audience to take leave of the Emperor. 
His Imperial Majesty expressed to him, as he had done to Lord John Russell, 
his anxious hope that te project of alliance which had been discussed with 
Count Buol, might be accepted by the Governments of England and France. 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys assured me that he was so entirely convinced of the 
sincerity of this desire on the part of Wis Imperial Majesty and of his Govern.

The Earl of Westmorland to Lord John Russell. 


Dear Lord John, Pienna, April 24, 1855. 

M. DROUYN DE LHUYS has just been with me. He has received an 
answer from his Government to his telegraphic messages of the day before 
yesterday, which is against his project. He is now more convinced than he was 
before of the value of this project, and he consequently leaves Vienna to-morrow 
morning for Paris, that he may personally support it. He will try to see you on 
his journey; but he earnestly requests you will telegraph to London your own 
views, desiring that, if they make a fayourable impression on our own Govern- 
ment, a telegraph to that effect may be sent to the French Government so as to 
meet him (M. Drouyn de Lhuys) on his arrival at Paris, He is anxious that 
you should reach London as carly as possible in order to give your personal 
support to his project with your colleagues, 

I send the messenger Haviland with this letter to catch you at Leipsig, and 
he will then go straight on to London, so that you may send by him any 
communication which you wish should reach London before yourself. 

Believe me, &e. 
(Signe) WESTMORLAND.

Inclosure in No, 745. 
Extract from the “ Ost Deutsche Post" of April 2b, L855. 
(Translation.) 


THE “ Osterreichische Correspondenz” to-day declares the Conferences 
to be continuing, Lord Palmerston calls them adjourned, the public looks on 
them as closed. In these differences there is, however, no absolute contra- 
diction, The original organization of the Conferences, the powers entrusted to 
its members, the objects for which it was created, still exist; the deliberations 
have, however, for the moment been adjourned, ond one of its most important 
phases is certainly closed. A period which held the expectations of the whole 
world in breathless suspense is passed, without bringing us satisfaction, and 
we find ourselves at the termination of a moment of intense excitement, as far as 
regards the principal question, exactly where we were, months ago, Those who 
mistrusted Russia's peaceful prognostications and listened incredulously to the 
pon words of the last despatch of Nesselrode, have proved after all in the 
rigglit. 

— In the “Aide mémoire™ communicated by the three allied Powers to 
Prince Gortchakoff, in the preliminary meeting of December 28th, the third 
point was defined as follows: 

__“ The revision of the ‘Treaty of 1841 shall have for its object, to unite the 
existence of the Ottoman Empire more perfectly with the equilibrium of Europe, 
and to put an end to the preponderance of Russia in the Black Sea.” 

In the reply of Prince Gortchakoff to the four points in the Conference 
of January 7, the interpretation of the third point was given thus: 

“Revision of Treaty of 1841, to unite the existence of the Ottoman 
Empire more with the equilibrium of Europe. I do not refuse to come in 
formal conferences for peace to an understanding on the means which the three 
Courts will propose to put an end to what they call the preponderane of 
Russia inthe Black Sea, on condition that, in the means chosen, there shall be 
poring touching the rights of sovereignty of my august master within his own 
erritory. 

On this double programme the negotiations commenced, Each party 
knew what it must concede; Russia knew that the meaning of the third point 
was # restriction of her power in the Black Sea; the allies knew that this 
restriction must not comprise Russian territory. In accordance herewith, all 
restriction of Russian arms and defences on the shores of the Pontus was 
excluded from the demands of the allies, Now, that the secret which the 
members of the Conference had bound themselves to keep during their delibe- 
rations, has to a certain degree transpired, we learn gradually what was 
demanded, and what refused. ‘Two modifications were submitted to Russia for 
choice ; either to reduce her number of ships of war in the Black Sea‘ to a 
number which should make any future attempt against Constantinople impossible, 
or so to revise the Treaty of 1841, that it should be extended to the Pontus, so 
that in future ships of war of all nations sliould be excluded from the Darda- 
nelles ns well Hi he the Black Sen, If there iH hardly any restriction of ihe piglets 
of sovereignty of the Czar within his own territory, ta be found in the first 

8P 


696 


sition (for the sca is not Russian territory), still leas by far is there any in the 
second proposal which establishes reciprocity ; all exchange of obligations to be 
taken by all the Powers. 

But Russia refused also this proposition, and it became more and more 
evident that her object in the negotiations for peace, was solely to gain time 
against her enemies, to depress their warlike energies, and get more latitude for 
her own armaments, concentration of troops, fortifications, organisation of 
militia, &c. &e. Encouraged by the gradual approach of Prussian policy 
towards her, by the unsteady hesitation of some of the other German States, she 
thought heeae secure against a coalition of united Europe, and hoped to sepa- 
rate AGES from the Western Powers, and to. isolate her, if not to dmg her 
over in the wake of Prussia, to Russia’s own side. But the wreck of these hopes 
must now be evident to Russia. ‘The harmony between the Powers allied by 
the December ‘Treaty is the same that it was before the Conferences, Austria 
looks on the four pointsas one whole, and the supposed loss of a few concessions 
on the two first for the sake of loosening the unity regarding the third, hos not 
had the desired eflect. The alliance between Austria and the West is a 
principle; it is not the bubble of a day which bursts at the irst opportunity ; 
it is nota question of momentary expediency, but a programme: for the future, 
as far as human powers can foresce or control it. 

Those who hoped that Austria would not vindicate her honour, those who 
looked to see her-at the tail of Prussia, withdrawing her votes and propositions 
at Frankfurt, and bowing with a ery of“! peecavi,” before the statesmanship of 
Barons Manteuffel, Beust, and Van der I fordten, will not have long to wait 
before they are undeceived by substantial, material proofs of their error.

My Lord, Vienna, April 26, 1859. 

IN accordance with the decision communicated to you in my despatch of 
yesterday, No. 190, I attended’ at the Conference held this day, and I have 
already informed your Lordship, by telegraph, of the little importance which was 
attributed hy the Representatives of Austria and of the allied Governments to 
the propositions of Prince Gortchakoff, 

I have the honour of inclosing a copy of the document submitted to the 
Conference by that Minister, and 1 am satisfied it was rightly characterised by 
Count Buol, in the course of the discussion which followed its presentation, as 
being quite incapable of being of use towards enabling the Conference to bring 
to a settlement the important questions with which they were entrusted. 

Frevious to the presentation of this document, Prince Gortchakoff had 
entered into a lengthened discussion as to the extent to which his Government 
would agree to give their guarantee to the territorial integrity of the Turkish 
Empire, but as the discussion upon this point will be detailed in the Protocol, 
and as it led ta no real change in the nature of the propositions put forward by 
Prince Gortchakoff at the last Conference, 1 need not detain your Lordship in 
further reporting it. 

Immediately after the: statement had been made by Prince Gortchakoff 
of the objects for which he had requested the Conference to assemble, 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys made the declaration, that he could not "enter upow Any 
discussion of the proposals he (the Prince) had announced, and that his full 


yowers were “épuisés;’’ but he desired to reply to an insinuation which had

by France towards ‘Turkey with respect to the position of the Bey of ‘Tunis ;

of the last Conference the words which had been em sloyed by Lord John Russell, 
+ which he declared that his instructions were ex austed. I also repelled an 
‘nsinuation which Prince Gortchakoft had put forward, that England might 
menace sone of the possessions of ‘Turkey from ber establishment at Aden, and

an allusion. Prince Gortchakoff replied both to M. Drouyn de Lhuys and to me, 
by stating that what he had said was intended merely as alluding to the 
possibility of collisions which might arise from the possessions and positions of 
different Powers, but that he retracted any expression which might be construed 
as throwing any doubt upon the good faith of either of our Governments. 

Count Buol stated that he could only look upon the proposals of Prince 
Gortchakoff as an “‘esquisse,  oran © ébauche; he admitted that the principle

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received April 29.) 


(No. 183, Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, April 27, 1855. 

WHEN I was with Baron Manteuffel to-day T endeavoured to learn from 
his Excellency what news had reached him from Vienna, and he told me that 
lhe had received some account of a counter proposition which had been pe 
by the Russian Plenipotentianies, but he was either unaequainted with the details 
of this proposition, or he wished to avoid entering into any discussion on the 
subject, but he gave me to understand that the counter proposition had not 
heen well received, though he did not say it had been altogether rejected. He 
seemed, however, to believe that Austria was more inclined to act with the 
Western Powers than she had been. As to the position of Prussia, he said it 
was unchanged, » 

He replied to a question which I put to him as whether any fresh com: 
munication had been made to this Court from ot. Esser that matters were 
as before, but | have heard from a private source, on which place feliatice, that 
Baron Budberg had been making overtures to this Government to declare its 
neutrality and to set on foot a negotiation with the smaller German Powers to 
unite with Prussiain this sense, and to engage other States to join the coalition ; 
but Lam assured that this proposition was declined, and that the King has 

vositively declared that he will do nothing of the sort, but remain for the present 
independent of all engagements. My informant added, that though there 
existed much bitterness of feeling towards Austria the King would not hesitate 
to support her in the event of her being attacked by Russia, and that His 
Prussian Majesty had no intention whatever of entering into an alliance with 
Russia, that the King's feelings were always favourable to England, and that he 
was under the impression that he should hereafter be useful to her, and with 
this view he would keep himself free {o act as cireumstances might dictate. 

1 informed your Lordship in my Lada No, 179 of the 23rd instant, 
that Baron Budberg had accompanied the King to Brandenburgh last Monday, 
and I am assured that upon this occasion the Russian Minister sought to engage 
His Majesty to enter into conversation on the question of neutrality, and that 
he com realy failed in effecting his object, and that Baron Manteutfel was 
mainly instrumental in preventing any discussion on this point between his 
Royal Master and the Russian Minister. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD,

engagements with Great Britain and France, it is impossible not to admit, that

she runs risks calculated to cause deep anxiety, and not groundless hesitation. 

Her actual prospects with the Diet are anything but encouraging, and it is

accept; and, therefore, that her active support is to be obtained by an outlay on 
the part of Great Britain, which, knowing the unpalateableness of such a course, 
I should never have thought of recommending to your Lordship’s consideration, 


had I not looked upon it as the only certain means of securing so all-important 
a result.

The Karl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland. 
(No. 174.) 
My Lord, 


Foreign Office, May 1, 1855, 
YOUR despatches No, 190 of April 25, and No. 198 of April 26, have been 
received and laid before the Queen. 

have to acquaint your Lordship that Her Majesty's Government approve 
your having attended the Conference held on the 26th April, at the request of 
the Russian Plenipotentiaries. 

Her Majesty's Government concur with the allied Plenipotentiaries that 
the proposals made by Prince Gortchakoff at this Conference were entirely 
insufficient to satisly the expectation which had been raised, that the Russian 
Government was prepared to make such offers as were calculated to meet 
the views of the allies and to lead to the reestablishment of peace. 

With regard to your Lordship attending any future Conferences which may 
be called, Her Majesty's Government are of opinion that much inconvenience 
would arise irom the erroneous impressions which would be created by the 
meetings of the Conference on oceasions where there was no reasonable ground 
for expecting any useful result from such mectings, but that, on the other hand, 
it would be unidvisable to refuse a meeting, if there was any good ground for 
expecting that such meeting would lead to any satisfactory result, 

If, therefore, at any time Count Buol should express a wish for a meeting 
of the Conference for the purpose of considering any proposal to. be made, either 
by himself or by Prince Gortchakoff, your Lordship will request Count Buol to 
state and explain the nature of such proposal, in order that you may make it 
known to Her Majesty’s Government, who would then be enabled to judge 


whether it would be worth while or not that the Conference should assemble to 


discuss it. 


Tam, &c. 
(Signed) CLARENDON,

No, 758. 


Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received May 4.) 
(No. 503.) 


My Lord, Paris, May 3, 1855. 

DURING an interview which I had with M. Drouyn de Lhuys this morning, 
his Excellency stated that he had heard from Count Walewski that Her Majesty s 
Government had come to no decision on the modification proposed by the 
French Government to the Austrian propositions, but that they begged to be 
informed whether M. Drouyn de Lhuys considered Austria engaged to go to war 
immediately, if Russia refused the proposed ultimatum. His Excellency added, 
that he eet consulted the notes which he had brought with him from Vienna, 
and that he considered the declaration of Austria on this point to be unequivocal. 
He had so informed Count Walewski. 

I remarked to M. Drouyn de Lhuys that what he stated was in contradic- 
tion to what I had understood him to say the night before last; that he would 
recollect that I had put a similar question to him, and that he had replied that 
from the declaration which had been made to him by the Emperor and by Count 
Buol, he augured that Austria would take the the field immediately, but that in 
writing Count Buol had not committed himself so far, and had only engaged to 
recall the Austrian Minister from St. Petersburgh, and to concert further 
measures with the allies for attaining the object which they all three had in 
view. | said that I had so repeated Ins words to your Lordship. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys replied that I had correctly stated what had fallen 
from him. ‘The fact was that Count Buol had, at a meeting (held, I believe, 
on the L5th ultimo), to settle proceedings, read a paper which contained the 
assurance that if the ultimatum was refused, Austria would go to war immediately, 
but he had not given a copy of this paper; M. Drouyn de Lhuys however ais 
a note of it on the instant, and he thought Lord John Ruseell had done the 
same thing. 

I trouble your Lordship with this explanation, as there would otherwise 
appear to be a contradiction between my report to your Lordship and the 
statement of M. Drouyn de Lhuys made through Count Walewsk. 

L have, &c. 
(Signed) COWLEY,

No. 761, 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received May 4.) 
(No. 307.) 
My Lord, Consiantinople, April 20, 1855. 


THE work which have daily to go through personally in-doors from sun- 
rise to sunset, in reading correspondences, receiving visitors on business, giving 
instructions to the Dragomans, and writing official notes ‘and despatches, allows 
me but little time for going out, or even for seeing the Ottoman Ministers, who 
very rarcly pay visits themselves, or appear in Christian society. With Reshid 
Pasha, whose influence operates the most immediately on the progress of public 
lmusiness, by reason of his position, experience, ability, general good-will and 
admirable memory, my personal intercourse has found an additional cause of 
interruption in the distance at which he has lately resided from the eapital, A 
visit to his Highness requires, for any good purpose, the expenditure of half-a- 
day, to say nothing of inconvenience from weather and the wretched condition 
of the roads. ‘Ten days ago, when I went out to him by agreement, our conyer- 
sation had litthe more than begun when he was sent for by the Sultan; and after 
waiting more than two hours for his return, I received a note to inform me that 
a mecting of the Council ordered by His Majesty prolonged his detention, and 
[ was therefore obliged to go home, after the ee of a whole morning, to repeat 
the same operation a few days later. 

I trouble your Lordship with these particulars, in order to show how small 
would be the prospect of getting through business at all, if it were not for the 
nssistance derived from the interpreters, and occasionally also from the Oriental 
Secretary, | have, nevertheless, made a point of seeing the Grand Vizier at 
leisure within the lust few days, and of endeavouring to make a serious impression 
on his mind with respect to the dangers resulting from the dilatory, imperfect, 
ind sometimes deceptive manner in which the affairs of the Empire continue, 
with few exeeptions, to be conducted, It cannot be necessary for me to go in 
detail over ground already so well known to your Lordship. lt may suffice for 
me to state, that I placed without reserve belore his view my convictions as to 
the real nature and tendencies of the contest in which we are engaged. I con- 
jured hin to act with more systematic energy in the suppression of erime and 
disorder throughout the provinces; in the enforcement of the Sultan’s ordi- 
hinees apuinst corruption; in the selection of proper functionaries both here 
and elsewhere; in the conscientious fulfilment of the Porte'’s obligations towards 
her allies; and in the adoption and promulgation of those reforms which are 
become indispensable, as well for the satisfaction of Europe as for the admi- 
nistration of the Empire. IT did my best to.make hin comprehend. the conse- 
quences of any permanent failure on the part of the alliance against Russia, and 
the necessity of vigorous and sustained exertions, well combined and faithfully 
carried out, to prevent the occurrence of so dreadful a calamity, 1 asked hit 
whether, in the event of our conquering an honourable and secure peace from 
Russia, it wos to be expected that the Powers of Europe would look with 
indifference on a continuance of that shite of misgovernment and weakness which 
unhappily went so far to characterise the Porte’s administration at present, 
notwithstanding the many pledges of improvement which had, been given on 
the one side, and the many admonitions and opportunities afforded. on the 
other, 

| venture to hope that a salutary impression has been made on; Reshid 
Pasha by this language, though it has little novelty in my mouth, and incul- 


707 


cates only such truths as the most careless observer might perceive. It is the 
more essential that such should be the case, as the Grand Vizier, whatever 
defects or short-comings he may exhibit, is after all the most enlightened and 
efficient Minister in the Sultan's service, 1 cannot, indeed, conceal from myself 
that his overthrow, at a moment of such vital importance, not to Turkey alone, 
but to Europe at large, especially now that he 1s well seated in the Sultan’s 
confidence, and strengthened by the removal of his principal antagonist, would 
be a subject of the deepest regret. The circumstances which have come in aid 
of my exhortations, to reconcile him to the duty of remaining in office, not- 
withstanding the intrigues so perseveringly directed against him, and the more 
commanding efforts which may shortly be made to give them success, are well 
calculated to inerease his ascendancy, and to diminish that timidity whieh often 
restrains him from acting agreeably to his judgment and inclinations. If his 
firmness in conduct were equal to his discernment, to the liberality of his ideas 
and the generosity of his nature, he would be as great and os useful a man as 
the unpurified atmosphere of Constantinople permits to exist in ministerial 
power. I shall be more than ever disappointed if he does not now respond more 
truly and actively than heretofore to the requirements of this unparalleled 
juncture. The difficulties, however, engendered by weakness of every kind 
during a lapse of many years cannot be surmounted at once. An Empire so 
far gone in decay cannnt be galvanized into strength. The process of recovery, 
if to be realized at all, must necessarily be subject to frequent obstructions and 
occasional relapses. Your Lordship will be able to learn from my subsequent 
reports whether I have allowed myself to entertain too sanguine a hope, The 
conduct of the Porte in matters of pending interest will afford the best criterion 
in that respect, 
I have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE,

the project of a Treaty between Great Britain, France, and Austria, for 
uaranteeing the territorial intecrity of Turkey, to which it is understood that 
Austria will be prepared to assent. 

Count Walewski read to me a despatch from M. Drouyn de Lhuys, who 
expressed in it his opinion that the project would not only put an end to the 
preponderance of Russia in the Black Sea, but would establish there that of the 
allied Powers, and that the plan was upon the whole preferable to any other, 
with the exception perhaps of neutralization, that had yet been proposed for 
giving effect to the intentions of the allies. | 

i told Count Walewski, that the three Powers had pledged themselves to 
put an end to the preponderance of Russia in the Black Sea; and T much feared 
that that object would not be fulfilled by the plan of M. Drouyn de Lhuys, 
admitting though I did, that it was an improvement upon the Austrian 
proposal. 

Count 'Walewski, however, | said, well knew the dee anxiety of Her 
Majesty’s Government to put an end to the war by a justand honourable peace ; 
and it was unnecessary therefore, to say that any scheme by which the Govern- 
ment of the Emperor thought that that great abject might be achieved, was 
sure to meet with the favourable consideration of Her Majesty’s Government, I 
should accordingly lose no time in submitting the project to my colleagues, and 
informing them that Count Walewski had been instructed by M. Drouyn de 
Lhuys to recomend it to the adoption of Her Majesty's Government. 

I need not inform your Excellency that the projects reecived the most 
attentive and anxious consideration of Her Majesty's Government. It was 
impossible, however, to disguise trom ourselves that no limit being placed on the 
naval foree of Russia, and the naval forces of England, France, and Turkey 
being admitted without limit into the Black Sea, Russia would have a fair 
pretext for increasing her Black Sea fleet to the highest amount compatible 
‘vith her means: neither could we shut our eyes to the faet, that the prepon- 
derance of Russia in the Black Sea rests in the belief of her strength as much as 
in the display of that strength ; and that if with Sebastopol untaken, and the 
Russian army untouched, the armies and fleets of England and France were to 
retire without accomplishing the objects that they were to attain; and if the 
ships of Russia, which have now disappeared from the Black Sea, were per- 
mitted by Treaty to reassemble there in the number and force that we have 
repeatedly declared to be a standing menace and a danger to purkey, we shoul 
rive a moral and a military triumph to Russia that would raise and perpetuate 
her preponderance in the Black Sea, 

But notwithstanding the manifest objections to such an arrangement, Her 
Majesty's Government determined upon so grave a subject to come to no hasty 
decision, and the further consideration of it was adjourned to this day. 

Before the Cabinet met, however, to-day, Count Walewski informed me 
that he had received by telegraph a despatch from M. Drouyn de Lhuys, stating 
that after mature reflection, the Emperor preferred to adhered to the original 
project of limitation as it had been proposed at Vienna, instead of the last praject 
that had been sent to Count Walewski. 

Her Majesty's Government, for the reasons to which I have above alluded, 
have concurred in the opinion which M. Drouyn de Lhuys’ despatch conveys ; 
and it was agreed that with the concurrence of the French Government, Austria 
should be invited to concert with England and France the measures necessary 
for giving effect to the Treaty of December 2, accompanying that invitation by 
un assurance, that although there were parts of the proposal that she was pre- 
pared to make to Russia, with which it was impossible for us to agree, yet that 
we should gladly receive from her any further propositions for effectually 
attaining the object to which Austria stands pledged, together with England and 

France. 

Your Lordship is instructed to read this despatch to the French Minister 
for Foreign Affairs, 

Lam, &e. 
(Signed) CLARENDON,

Article 1. LE principe de la fermeture des Détroits du Bosphore et des 
Dardanelles en temps de paix, consacré par l’ancienne législation de la Sublime 
Porte et par le Traité du yy Juillet, 1841, reste en pleine vigueur.

iy Lord Berlin, May 8, 1855: 
BARON MANTEUFFEL stated to me to-day that he had been Heaiiee 
by the King to ‘iform me that His Majesty had seen with deep regret in mt 
«Kreuz Zeitung” an article containing allusions which were Chara rie 
disrespectful to the Queen, and that His Majesty had given orders that the edit 


717 


of the newspaper should in consequence be prosecuted, I told his Excellency 
that I learned this intelligence with satisfaction ; that I trusted this interference of 
the Government would have a beneficial effect in producing an improvement in the 
general tone of this journal ; that { had on former occasions frequently observed 
to his Excellency on the unfriendly allusions to England which pervaded the 
columns of the “ Kreuz Zeitung,” and that as the tone of it had undergone no 
change, I thought it useless to speak azain on the subject, but that I felt if the 
Government chose to put down this paper they might have established their 
influence over this in the same extent as they had now done over every other 
journal published in Berlin, as it was notorious that the power of the authorities 
over the press was amply sufficient to control it when they were so disposed. 
Instead of this being exercised in our favour, I said, the reverse appeared to be 
the case, However, | took the assurance his Excellency had just given me as 
one of goad omen for the future, and | hoped the success of the intended prose- 
cution would have beneficial results. 

Baron Manteuffel replied, that the press was less shackled than I appre- 
hended; and he gave me to understand that the “Kreuz Zeitung’ was a paper 
whose opinions were far too exaggerated to be agreeable to the Government, 
and that he bad not succeeded in establishing that control over it which he 
desired to have, 

I have the honour to inelose to your Lordship a translation of the article in 


question, and beg leave to add that a day rarely passes without some violent
