(Translation.) 


THE speech of Stall was held for Europe, We do not say that the orator 
took no account of the Prussian House of Lords, or left the relations of Prussia 
out of consideration. On the contrary, the subject. which the speaker proposed 
to himself, was to render the policy of Prussia clear on all sides, to declare 
openly why it was necessary to take up this position, and to maintain it. He 
has fulfilled it most successfully. But he has not only fulfilled itfor the Prussian 
House of Lords and for the people of Prussia,—all Europe can clearly and 
distinctly perceive from this beaut ul and lively picture, what are the wishes of 
all those in Prussia whose honour it is to preserve an independent position for 
their fatherland, and who prefer, not in vain pride, but in hopeful confidence, 
to be isolated with a good conscience rather than to be allied against, conscience. 

Such a neutrality does not stand at zero with a lukewarm heart between 
hot and cold, to rub their hands for their own gratification when losses occurred 
on the right or left; it has its force in the consciousness that a nature fulfils its 
duty by justice, and that he who prefers right to calculaticn, and honour to interest, 
will never come to shame. Clearly to know what one desires, and energeticall 
to desire what one knows, that is the stamp of a statesman. Half hearts and h 
cou load to half measnres, but never to a good goal. We wish, namely, 
that England may read and consider this Prussian s eech with attention ; 

erhaps, Lord Lyndhurst will then admit that one ean be conservative and a 
awyer without closing one’s cars in blind passion to the arguments of the 
adversary, Verily, Great Britain has other necessities than haughtily to get into 
a passion with those who will not walk in her path. It ia self-denial and a 
knowledge of herself that we desire for old England, above all at present, when 
she has done honour to the Ruler of the French by forgetting her own history ; 
or iw it desired to pursue this path further? The Waterloo Hall has already 
received a new name to please Napoleon IIT; is it perchance to be proposed that 
Her Majesty Queen Victoria should give up her own name, which she received 
in memory and in honour of the victory over the uncle? Shall she call herself 
hereafter “Francesea ;"’ for her second nume “ Alexandrina" would be also

No. 777. 
Sir J. Milbanke to the Earl of Clurendon.—{ Received May 5.) 


(No. 28.) 
My Lord, Munich, April 29, 1855. 

THE messenger Robbins arrived on the 27th instant, and delivered to me 
your Lordship’s despatches to No, 22 inclusive, with two marked Separate, 
leaving date the 14th and ord instant. 

The prospects of the Government here are in many respects the very 
revesse of satisfactory, and it really seems that at length the publie opimon of 
the country will succeed in producing some effect on the minds of those who 
are at this moment intrusted with the administration of affairs. ‘The circum- 
stances under which the recent dissolution of the Chambers took place, appear 
fo have aroused some misgivings as to the manner in which this ill-advised step 
inight be construed by the mass of the population, and the consequence Was that 
the King, who felt the necessity of clearing up all doubt upon this point, 
eummoned to the capital the Presidents of the different provinces into which the 
kingdom is divided, for the purpose of reporting to him confidentially the real 
state af public feeling in regard to the sudden dissolution of the Chamber, and 
the probable result of the new elections which must shortly commence. 

| understand, that with the single exception of the President of the Palati- 
nate, whose report excited so much surprise that he ts suspected of having 
misrepresented the sentiments of the BoE the whole of them stated, 
without the least disguise, that the sympathies of the provinces were decidedly 
adverse to the present foreign policy of the Government, and in favour of an 
immediate, close, and almost aneonditional alliance with Austria, into whose 
hands the entire country, with one voice, seems desirous of confiding the 
‘atercats of Germany during the actual European crisis, ‘This leaning towards 
Austria is so. strongly pronounced throughout the kingdom, that even the 
northern provinees, srhiel were generally supposed to entertain some lurking 
tendencies towards Prussia from religious and other motives of a more materi 
character, are now represented to be the most eager for the Austrian alliance. 

Upon all the details bearing upon these points, it is said the Presidents 
were very Closely questioned, and as their replies were by no means of a nature 
to reassure the Government, it is not unlikely that their visit to the capital 
may be so far beneficial as to Jead, for a time at least, to-a greater deference to 
public opinion than it has hitherto shown. 

‘That it has seriously compromised its own credit and popularity, by the 
undeniable incapacity whieh it has throughout distinguished its whole system of 

internal, and especially its financial, administration, is sufficiently manifest by the 
strange suspicions and accusations circulated, principally I believe by the 
organs of the ultramontane party, with the object evidently of exciting the 
popular feeling against Baron von der Pfordten, and again arousing apprehen- 
sion of the absolutist propensities of the Court, which he is said to do all he 
ean to encourage and strengthen. . 

The leaders of this party are highly incensed against Baron von der 


Hfordten, in consequence of his being either unable or unwilling to aid them in 


721 


carrying through the demards of the Episcopacy ; this has not only induced 
them to withdraw the SUPPat upon which he has mainly relied for the mainte- 
nance of his position in the country, but has conyerted them into open and 
Heelaven opbonente of himself personally, as well as of his policy, against whieh 
ie nee weight of their influence will be brought to bear in the approaching 
The adherents of Austria, of which the Pigh Church party | 
composed, found their hopes of getting rid of him ies the comairht < vty 
prospect of a more categorical declaration on the part of the Imperial Cabinet 
against the aggressive proceedings of Russian on the religious protectorate 
question, to foree on which all their efforts tend ; for they argue that it would be 
totally impossible for Baron von der Piordten to continue to occupy the post 
he now holds, if Austria could once be persuaded to cut short the intrigues and 
appeals of the minor German Governments, by quitting her present doubtful 
attitude, and placing herself frankly on the side of the Western Powers 
Whether this calculation be correct, is, | think, open to some doubt: but 
the chiefs of the ultramontane party are not easily discouraged or diverted 
from their objects, and in this country their power is so great as to be much 
dreaded by the Sovereign and his present advisers, who I am told make no 
secret of their expectation that the result of the next elections will, under the 
influence of the priesthood, be a Lower Chamber which will render all Govern- 
ment impossible, at least, according to their notions of constitutional rule. It is 
mols than probable that the consequences of the hasty course pursued by the 
porate may be such as are apprehended, but there must be other more 
eeply-seated influences at work, to foment the discontent which no one 
attempts to deny pervades all classes; for it can scarcely be su posed that the 
Protestant provinces of the north, which are reported to be to the full as anti- 
Prussian as the others, would allow their judgment to be swayed by a Catholic 
priesthood which they abhor, and with which they carry on a perpetual feud 
with a ee tolerance on either side. ; | 
rhe only plausible elucidation [ am able to offer for thi 
anomalous state of things is, that the anti-dynastic spirit of Freer sce! 
again abroad among the smaller German States even in a more intense, though 
perhaps less open, form than at that epoch. Instead of being confined to the 
lower, as was the case in that year of trouble, the conviction that the minute 
subdivision of Germany is an obstruction and hindrance to the welfare of the 
whole country, has now become deeply-rooted in the minds of the middle 
classes, which, although more cautious and less demonstrative, are’ not the legs 
determined to work out a change whenever a favourable and sate opportunity 
shall present itself I eannot eoubt the truth of the information which has 
reached me on this state of public feeling, for it has been more than once 
confirmed by the reluctant avowals of some of my German colleagues who are 
hest able to appreciate the effect produced by the recent senseless policy of their 
Governments on the Oriental question, The consciousness of the fermentation 
that is going on, and the appre rensions it inspires, are beyond question the real 
cause of the excessive devotion of all the small Potentates to Russia, whose 
power they are averse to sce weakened {rom considerations which, from their 
pout of view, there is no difficulty in comprehending. Baron von der Pfordten 
admits to every one that the sole aim and object of his policy is the preservation 
and advantage of this country, and that he is determined to resist ta the utmost 
all encroachment, however small, against its independence, and to oppose any 
participation in the present struggle until ‘the benefits which are to result froin 
it itre made porfectly clear to him. He is almost as averse to a closer union 
with Austria as with France and England, because, as he recently explained in a 
conversation with one of the leading members of the Chamber, which was 
subsequently repeated to me, he considers his Government to be embarked on 
the same liberal course which renders the other two so hateful to the would-be 
shells rulors of the minor States. What his notions of Royal authority may 
r¢, | will not tuke upon me to say; but if the actual system of government in 
France does not come up to them they must be somewhat exaggerated, nae 
I have, &e.

Inclosure 1 in No. 780. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to M. E, Pisani. 


Sir, British Embassy, April 22, 1855. 

YOU informed me yesterday, on the authority of the Grand Vizier, that 
the Council at which his Highness presided had come to a decision respecting 
the mode of furnishing the troops destined to be paid and officered by the 
British Government. I understand that 5,000 Regular Infantry are to be 
supplied from the army of the Danube, 2,500 from the garrison of Constanti- 
nople; that 7,500 Armenian conscripts are to be joined to them; and that 
Artillery and Cavalry are to be added, though it is not yet stated in what 
proportions, nor whence taken, except that a squadron or two of Cavalry may 
be obtained from here, and perhaps also the three battalions of Artillery reserved 
for Lord Raglan. 

I wish you to wait on Reshid Pasha this morning. You will express to 
him my satisfaction at the Council's decision to take recruits from among the 
Christians, and my persuasion that General Vivian will not object to receive a 
portion of them into the ranks of his corps. I presume, at the same time, that 
he will not approve of too large a number in the first instance; and on my part, 
T must add, that [ was not prepared to include Rayahs in the conscription at 
once. My notion has always been that the recruitment of Christians, or other 
Rayahs, for the Sultan's army, should be at first voluntary, and the more 60 a5 
their admission to the enjoyment of civil rights is at best limited, and has still 
to be declared and enforced. I feel convinced that Reshid Pasha will recognise 
the justness of my impressions, and comprehend, without difficulty, my objec- 
tion to receive any number of conseripta under the present circumstances. He 
may remember that I anticipated difficulty as to the Porte’s supplying the 
number of soldiers agreed upon without some recruitment; and his Highness, by 
allawing our officers to collect recruits themselves, will but enable me ta 
reconcile Her Majesty's Government to the deficiency of Regulars. 

You will read this instruction to the Grand Vizier; and you will also make 
inquiry as to the Artillery and Cavalry appointed to be placed under Lieutenant- 
General Vivian’s command, 

I cannot too strongly urge the importance of expedition. It is necessary 
at once to form a body of 10,000 men, of the three arms, duly proportioned 
and I conceive that the troops thus collected, en attendant the remainder, might 
be located near Hunkiar Skelessi. 

How is provision to be made for the conveyance of the troops from 
Bulgaria? 

Your, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

He had accordingly consulted the Plenipotentiaries of England and France, 
who, after taking into consideration the position of Austria, and the difficulties of 
various kinds that war would entail upon her, unless her motives for going to 
war were powerful and clearly established, had agreed to refer to their Govern- 
ments two propositions, that might, a5 a last resource, be presented to Russia as 
ultimatums, the rejection of which would lead (entrainerait) Austria to war. 

The first of these propositions was a guarantee by Treaty for the Ottoman 
Empire against Russia, by a system which, “without imposing any direct or 
explicit limitation upon Russia, would compel her nevertheless to impose a 
limit upon herself, as she would be under the weight of a graduated counter- 
poise, and a line would be traced which she could not pass without exposing 
herself immediately to war with the allied Powers.” 

The second proposition rested upon a limitation that was to be the result 
of an understanding between the Plenipotentiaries of Russia and Turkey. 

Count Buol concluded his despatch by saying, that. as Her Majesty's 
Government were informed of the details of the propositions, he had merely 
given the substance of them to Count Colloredo, 

I told Count Colloredo that the details alluded to by Count Buel had not 
reached Her Majesty's Government in a formal shape, and I could therefore 
offer no opinion upon the vague proposals in Count Buol’s despatch, or say more, 
at that time, than that Her Majesty’s Government were desirous to consider 
any proposal for a safe and just peace, that would give effect to the objects that 
Austria was pledged, in conjunction with England and France, to secure; but I 
ndded, as the Conferences were then suspended, and as Lord John Russell was 
to leave Vienna on the same day that Count Buol's despatch was dated, Her 
Majesty's Government had determined to take no further steps until his Lord- 
ship's arrival, and they had had the advantage of fiearing his advice and opinions ; 
the same course would, I believed, be pursued by the French Government, in 
waiting for the return of M. Drouyn de Lhuys. It is right I should here inform 
your Lordship that Her Majesty's Government are not at this moment, any more 
than at the time when Count Buol’s despatch was read to me by Count Collo- 
redo, in possession of any written document, containing in precise terms the 
proposal that Austria is willing to make to Russia. Such a document, however, 
was read on the 15th ultimo, by Count Buol to Lord Jobn Russell and 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys, but he declined to give them a copy; and when Count 
Buol was reminded of this by the English and French Plenipotentiaries before 
Lord John Russell's departure from Vienna, Count Buol stated that all the 
necessary information had been sent to Count Colloredo, by whom, however, as 
I learned yesterday, nothing further has been received than the despatch to which 
I have already alluded. 

But Lord John Russell and M. Drouyn de Lhuys rely upon the accuracy 
of the notes which they respectively took to assist their own recollection; and 
these have been the subject of anxious consideration on the part of Her Majesty's 
Government, Some delay has been caused in coming to a decision upon the 
subject, in consequence of a communication from the French Government, the 
nature and the result of which your Lordship will find detailed in my despatch 
to Her Majesty's Ambassador at Paris, a copy of which is inclosed. 

In consequence of the determination taken by Her Majesty's Government, 
which your Lordship will find announced in that despatch, and having ascer-

requested Count Colloredo to call upon me yesterday, and I read to him the 
following terms, which Lord John Russell had reported to Her Majesty's

I then proceeded to state that Her Majesty’s Government could not attach 
mich practical value to the engagement of Austria to make, at some future

or she had already declared that it was beneath her dignity to discuss numbers, 
and that she could not admit that the question of peace or war should turn 
upon eight or ten ships of the line; and if such were the case now, when 
circumstances would enable Austria to go to war with advantage, what prospect 
would there be of her doing so some years hence under circumstances likely to 
be far less favourable, for the very same cause, though in a lesser degree, that 
she would not now entertain. 

[reminded Count Colloredo that Austria was pledged to put an end to the 
areponderance of Russia in the Black Sea, and I asked how that pledge would 
be redeemed by the proposal that the allied armies and fleets should withdraw 
from the Crimea and the Black Sea, and that England, Franee, and Turkey should 
agree by Treaty that the naval forces of Russia should be re-established in that sea, 
the same in number and in power as before the war, which amount we had 
constantly declared, and Austria had agreed with us in declaring, was a menace 
to the Ottoman Empire, and to the peace and equilibrium of Europe. TI said

the opinion of Her Majesty’s Government upon this proposal, and it was hardly 
necessary to inform him that that opinion was unchanged. 

1 said, I was sure that Count Buol would admit that the Plenipotentiaries 
of England and France had faithfully adhered to the course of proceeding that 
he had himself suggested in a despatch communicated to me by Count 
Colloredo in November last, that England and France should not, in the 
course of the negotiations, bring forward demands of a nature calculated to 
insure their rejection; and the best proof of their having done so would be 
found in the fact, that the several proposals made by them to Russia had 
received the frank and cordial support of the Austrian Plenipotentiaries ; but as 
those proposals had been rejected by the Russian Plenipotentiaries, who had 
declared that no limitation of Russian forces would be listened to, and no inter- 
ference with the sovereign rights of Russia within her own territory would be 
allowed, and as, moreover, they would not even join in a real and bond fide 
guarantee of the territorial integrity of the Ottoman Empire, little doubt could 
exist that Russia had not abandoned her designs against Turkey; and that 
unless means were taken for curtailing her aggressive power, those designs 
would assuredly sooner or later be executed. 

The time was now therefore arrived for England and France to inyite

sary, 1 said, to inform Count Colloredo that Her Majesty s Government desired 

e, but they would prefer the continuation of the war to a peace that would 
not be honourable nor likely to last, and which would not effect the objects we

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received May 9.) 
(No, 514.) 
My Lord, Paris, May 7, 1855, 


M. DROUYN DE LHUYS has resigned the portfolio of Minister for 

Foreign Affairs. 
will endeavour, as far as I can, to make your Lordship acquainted with 
the causes that have led to this distinguished statesman s retreat. 

Your Lordship is aware, from my despatch No, 499 of the 2nd instant, as 
also from the more detailed commuications which have been made to you by 
Count Walewski, that M. Drouyn de Lhuys returned from Vienna, determined 
to give the weight of his support to the last propositious of Austria, that he 
found the Emperor unwilling to accept the sfatus quo of the Russian fleet 
in 1843, as the hinge on which future peace or war should tum, but that His 
Majesty proposed a modification to the Austrian plan, by which the state of the 
Russian fleet at the present moment should be taken as the basis of an arrange- 
ment. According to the Emperor’s modification, any augmentation of the 
Russian fleet beyond its actual numbers, so as to give it excessive proportions im 
the eyes of the Contracting Powers, would oblige those Powers tc unite for the 
defence of the Ottaman Empire. 

L should state that the object which the Emperor proposed to himself, and 
which His Majesty conceived had been attained by this modification, was, first, 
to limit the naval power of Russia to the number of ships actually afloat when- 
ever peace should be signed ; and, secondly, to meet the views of the Austrian 
Government by not making the addition of one or two ships to that number a 
cause of war. The casus belli would only arise when the iilies became con- 
vineed that the development of the Russian navy in the Black Sea must be 
intended for aggressive purposes. 

With these views, and uader the supposition that his modification attained 
them, His Majesty desired that it should Ne transmitted to London, in order to 
aseortain whether the idea was approved by Her Majesty’s Government. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys misunderstood the Emperor's intentions, and, instead 
of transmitting the proposition for the consideration of Her Government, appears 
to have instructed Count Walewski to bring it forward in the Emperor’s nanie, 
und to urge it on the acceptance of the Cabinet, 

The Emperor, in the mean time, alter further consideration of the terms, 
which he thought had only been sent confidentially to London, became con- 
vineed that there was no direct limitation imposed by them on Russia. He 
learned also that Her Majesty’s advisers, while desirous of meeting wishes which 
they supposed had been so unequivocally expressed by His Majesty, were yet 
anxious to know the motives which dictated them, and that they felt in fact 
that they were called upon to make an entire change in the conditions of peace 


. (such in reality not being His Majesty's intentions'. He found that the honour 


of his army would not, in the opinion of the highest military authorities, be 
satisfied by such a conclusion of the war as that proposed, and he determined in 
consequence to direct M. Drouyn de Lhuys to state to Her Majesty’s Govern- 
ment, through Count Wualewski, that, all things considered, His Majesty was of 
opinion that it would be better to reject the Austrian propositions in @ courteous 
manner, and maintain the plan of limitation brought forward by the maritime 
Powers and supported by Austria at the Vienna Conferences. 

This occurred on Friday last. On the evening of that day M. Drouyn de 
Lhuys wrote to the Emperor, and placed his resignation im Elis Majesty's hands 
‘The Emperor replied in the kindest tone, reminding M. Drouyn de Lhuys that 
if any one bad reason to complain, it was His Majestyhimself, since M. Drouyn 
de Lhuys had acted at Vienna in direct contradiction to his instructions, and ne 
reproach had been addressed to him. THis Majesty invited M. Drouyn de Lhuys 


Hi 
to come to him on the following day to talk the matter over. M. Drouyn de 
Lhuys declined the Emperor's invitation, and Count Walewski was then 
written to to undertake the business of the Foreign Department. 
| haye not succeeded in seeing M. Drouyn de Lhuys since these events 
oeeurred; but J understand that he defends his conduct, not on the ground that

Lord Cowley to the Kurl of Clarendon.—(Received May 9.) 


(No. 515. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, May 7, 1855. 

THERE are some details connected with the subject of my preceding 
despatch, which Iam desirous of submitting to your Lordship in a more con- 
fidentia! form; the more so, as my namie has, in some of the Parisian circles 
been brought forward in connection with M, Drouyn de Lhuys’ resignation. It 
is right, therefore, that your Lordship and Her Majesty’s Government should 
know what participation I have had in this event, : 

Before proceeding, however, to the enumeration of these details, it is 
lesen that I should call your Lordship's attention to matters of anterior 
date, 

Your Lordship will recollect, that from the commencement of the differences 
between the Western Powers and Russia, M. Drouyn de Lhuys was the most 
ardent promoter of hostilities. Russia had not a more bitter enemy, or more 
determined antagonist, The series of remarkable papers which have been 
published under his signature, expose in the most able and lucid manner the 
danger to be apprehended from the Northern Colossus, and the means to be 
employed to avert them. In fact, it was more necessary to calm than to excite 
the late Minister for Foreign Affairs. I freely confess that, in the outset, | 
thought this language and conduct to be the result of apprehensions for the fate 
of the Turkish Empire, and for the perils which would naturally ensue to the 
equilibrium of Europe should Turkey fall into the hands of Russia, Subse- 
quent events, however, convinee me that these apprehensions had but inferior 
influence over the policy of M. Drouyn de Lhuys; that the principal cause of 
his antipathy to Russia was the advantage which she had obtained in the question 
of the * Sacred Places,” and the refusal of the Czar to acknowledge the Emperor 
Napoleon as his brother. The aggression of Russia upon Turkey was rather the 
pretext for, than the actual reason of, M. Drouyn de Lhuys’ animosity. Accord- 
ingly, we find him gradually abandoning the ground which he had at first oceunied 
His object is changed. He imagines that the severest blow to Russia an the 
most brilliant achievement for himself, will be to detach Austria from Rursia 
and so to break up the Northern alliance, which had been conceived in hostility 
to France. For this purpose, he is willing to forget all his previous decent 
all his recorded engagements; for this purpose, whilst professing to me—Her 
Majesty's Representative—unbounded attachment to, and implicit confidence in 
England, to the Representatives of Austria, of Prussia, and of the Gavan 
States, he represents the necessity of an alliance with France, in order to kee 
the demands of Great Britain within bounds: for this purpose he would bats 
sacrificed the alliance of England, and have aecepted any terms of peace with 
Kussia that Austria might be inclined to support. — ; us 

Such were the feelings, Lam convinced, with which M. Drouyn de Lhuys 
proposed to the Emperor that he should be sent to Vienna ; and it was under 
this conviction that I pressed upon him the necessity of going in the first 
instance to London, in order that his plans might be fully discussed and under 
stood by Her Majesty's Government, and that there might be no mistake in 
future negotiations, [do not pretend that M. Drouyn de Lhuys did not intend 
to have carried the plans, so aceepted, into execution, if he could have won the 
consent of Austria, on whieh he counted; and | had even hoped thut, after the 
discussions which had taken place in London, he would have jaund it tn nog ble: 
to do more, 2 ; 

_ Such, however, has not been the case; and this brings me to the recital 
of those details respecting myself, which L would gladly have saved your Lord.

M. Drouyn de Lhuys returned to Paris on Monday, the 30th of April. On 
Tuesday, the Ist of May, he saw the Emperor, when the Austrian propositions 
were discussed, and the !’mperor'’s modification was sent to London. I had an 
interview with him on the evening of that day, the details of which I had the 
honour to report to your Lordship in my despatch No. 499 of the 2nd instant. 

I saw M. Drouyn de Lhuys again on the Thursday morning, when I 
informed him that no decision had been taken by Her Majesty’s Government 
with respect to the Emperor's modilication—that it was a grave matter, which 
required deliberation, &c, On the afternoon of that day I was honoured by a 
letter from the Emperor, at the end of which His Majesty inquired what I 
thought of the modification which he proposed to the Austrian propositions. 
Unwilling to give an opinion upon a matter which was under the discussion of 
Her Majesty's Government, 1 took the liberty of making no reply to His 
Majesty’s interrogation; and the following morning I was summoned to the 
Tuileries, when the Emperor put the same question to me. 

[told His Majesty I was embarrassed how to reply; that Her Majesty's 
Government had come to no decision, ke. He went on to show what, in his 
opinion, were the advantages of the scheme; and I soon found that His Majesty 
was under the idea that the notification which had been sent to London 
contained a direct limitation to be accepted by Russia of her naval force in the 
Black Sea. I showed him that this was not the case; and he then desired me 
to telegraph to your Lordship to state his impression that no arrangement could 
be made which did not place restrictions on Russia. On His Majesty stating 
that he would see M. Drouyn de Lhuys again on the matter, I honestly confess 
that, having no faith in the political honesty of that gentleman, I asked permis- 
sion to be present at the interview, and most heartily do [ rejoice that the 
plas granted it, though the fact may be taken as one of hostility to M. Drouyn 
de Lhuys. 

The Emperor thought proper to summon Marshal Vaillant to be present at 
the same time. 

During the meeting, the question of the tendency of the Emperor’s modifi- 
cation was first discussed, but the discussion naturally extended to the objects 
of the war, and how far they were realised by the Vienna propositions. The 
Emperor stated his desire to have been to find terms which, while they bound 
Russia, should yet be palateable to Austria; but he declared that if his modification 
did not impose some sort of limitation on Russia, he would abandon it at once. 

M. Drowyn de Lhuys was obliged to admit that the Vienna proposal 
contained no direct limitation of Russian power; but he argued long and ably, 
though, I think, inconclusively, on the advantages which that proposal oflered— 
ie es which he considered greater than those contained in the plan of the 
allies. 

Marshal Vaillant confined himself to stating that the army would not be 
satisfied with a peace on those terms. : 

I, on my part, said that I wished rather to establish facts than to give an 
opinion, for I did not doubt that at the moment I was speaking, Her Majesty's 
Government were discussing the merits of the proposal, It was agreed on all 
sides, | said, that neither the Austrian proposal nor the Emperor's modilication 
contained a limitation of Russian power. ‘The question, then, which the two 
Governments would have to consider, was whether, having declared that the 
objects for which they went to war, as far as the third point was concerned, 
were to destroy Sebastopol and prevent its reconstruction as a naval arsenal, to 
destroy the Russian forts in the Black Sea, to limit the naval power of Russia in 
those waters, and to appoint Consuls in order to exercise some supervision, 
whether, these being the objects which they had originally in view, they were 
now prepared to abandon, not one or two, but the whole of them; nay more, 
whether, having solemnly declared that their intention was to cause the prepon- 
derance of Russia in the Blick Sea to cease, they were prepared to reestablish 
that preponderance. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys denied that this was the case; but I aid that, if the 
two Governments permitted Russia to maintain her actual fleet, while they 
limited the allied squadron to four frigates, that preponderance was in the first

No, 794. 


Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received May 12.) 
(No, 528.) 


My Lord, Paris, May 10, 1855. 

COUNT WALEWSKI having assumed the direction of Foreign Affairs, | 
took an early opportunity of waiting upon him. 

His Excellency observed, that he had thought it right to establish at once, 
that nothing was changed in the policy of the French Government by his having 
assumed the direction of Foreign Affairs; that he had seen M. de Hiibner, and 
reassured him on this point. His Excellency went on to say, that before leaving 
London he hadcome to a distinct understanding with Her Majesty's Government, 
as to the line to be pursued in regard to Austria. He then read mea despatch 
which he had addressed to M. de Bourqueney, in which this policy was set forth. 
It will have been communicated to your Lordship by M. Baudin, and I need not 
enter into details. 

This morning Count Walewski informed me that Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment objected to the immediate signature of a tripartite Treaty with Austria. 
His Excellency said that he had never intended to make it the subject of a 
proposition to Austria, as your Lordship appeared to suppose; he had merely 
admitted the possibility of such a proceeding should Austria desire it: however, 
he had now telegraphed to M. de Bourqueney not to take the initiative in it, 

I am afraid, notwithstanding this precaution, that if the idea is palateable to 
Austria, difficulties may yet arise; as I have reason to think that before knowing 
your Lordship’s wishes, Count Walewski had told M, de Hiibner that France 
and England were not averse to the signature of a tripartite Treaty. 

Lhave, &e. 


(Signed) COW LEY.

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received May 12.) 
(No. 534.) 


My Lord, Paris, May 11, 1855. 

1 BEG to call your attention to the inclosed copy of an article from the 
“« Indépendance Belge,” giving an account of the reasons which led to M. Drouyn 
de Lhuys’ resignation. It is known to have been written under that gentleman's 
dictation, and was considered to be so offensive that the responsible correspon 
dent of the newspaper in question was sent for by the Minister of the Interior 
yesterday, and informed that he must not permit himself to be the channel for 
the publication of such articles in future. 

T'o the astonishment of every one, the article appeared this morning in the 
columns of the ‘ Moniteur,” which may be said to be tantamount to the recog- 
nition of its exactitude by the French Government. I found Count Walewski 
much disturbed over its appearance, and intending to speak to the Emperor upon 
the subject. | 

1 take this opportunity of mentioning that Count Walewski has addressed « 
circular despatch to the Agents of the French Government at the principal 
Courts of Europe, explaining the retirement of M. Drouyn de Lhuys as havin 
been occasioned by a misunderstanding of the Emperor's orders, which had plaeed 
him (M. Drouyn), as that gentleman thought, in a false position, Count 
Walewski gives assurance at the same time that the Emperor's policy has 
undergone no change. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) COWLEY.

No. 798. 
The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—({ Received May 14.) 


. (No. 223.) 


My Lord, Vienna, May 9, 1855, 

_ COUNT ARNIM waited upon Count Buol on Monday last, by order of 
his Government, to ask whether there was any truth in the report that your 
Lordship had made a statement in the House of Lords, that the European 
guarantee and Protectorate of the Principalities, which it was proposed to substi 
tute for the present Protectorate of Russia, would not include the guarantee of 
Prussia, as she was not a member of the Conference, and therefore would not be 
a signing party to the Treaty which might result from the Conferences now 
asssernbled. 

The reply of Count Buol was, that while Prussia remained, as at present, 
entirely aloof from the negotiations for peace, she could not naturally take part 
in any result which might proceed from them, and could not become one of the 
Contracting Parties; but whenever she chose to become so, her presence would 
be received with great satisfaction. 

T have, &e. 


(Signed) WESTMORLAND,

My Lord, Pera, May 2, 1855. 

| HAVE the honour to inform your Excellency, that in consequence of the 
recall of Mehemet Aali Pasha from banishment, and the constant attacks of 
M. Benedetti against Reshid Pasha, his Highness last night tendered his resigna- 
tion, which having been accepted by the Sultan, Aali Pasha has been selected 
hy His Majesty to succeed him, and until the latter arrives from Vienna, the 
Malié Naziri, Shefik Pasha, is to act as Caimakam, Fuad Effendi replaces 
Aali Pasha in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs with the rank and title of Pasha. 
Nutlar Bey, formerly Minister of Finance, has been called to fill that post again, 
with the rank and title of Pasha. 

Reshid Pasha is to go to Vienna as Plenipotentiary to the Conferences on 
the part of the Porte; Aali Pasha is to remain there until the former reaches 
that city. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) ET. PISANI,

No. 807. 
Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received May 19.) 


(No. 570, Confidential.) 


My Lord, Paris, May 18, 1855. 

COUNT WALEWSKI informed me last night, that if the telegraphic 
despatches received from M, de Bourqueney had been rightly understood, the 
intention of Austria, when the Conference was a in assembled, was to propose 
the adoption of the Annex B to the eleventh Protocol. He said, that if this 
was the case, no time should be lost, in the opinion of the Emperor and of him- 
self, in acceding to the proposition of Austria to meet again in Conference, 
Annex [ contained all for which the allies had contended,—a limitation of the 
Russian naval force in the Black Sea ; an equal number of allied ships to those 
9 D 


ra 


744 


which it would be permitted to Russia to keep; and consequently, a free passage 
of the Bosphorus for them, without reciprocity to Russia ; Consuls in the ports 
of the Black Sea, wherever it was judged expedient to establish them, 

Count Walewski observed, that ‘? Russia accepted these terms, the allies 
would hardly be justified in refusing them; but that to avoid future discussion, 
it would be necessary to appoint a Commission to verify the actual state of the 
Russian fleet. Admiral Bruat's opinion was, that there were but three ships of 
the line left. ° 

On the other hand, if Russia refused them, Austria would be forced to 
break off the Conferences, and would be more bound to the allies than would 
be the case if they refused to accede to her invitation to meet the Russian 
Plenipotentiaries again. 

i observed, that it was very difficult to diseuss a proposition the tenour of 
which was as yet but imperfectly known 5 but supposing it to be that which 
Count Walewski imagined, I asked whether he was prepared to adopt it without 
any engagement on the part af Austria to make its refusal by Russia a casus 
heli, His Exeellency replied, that he considered the rupture of the Conferences 
by Austrin herself’ to be worth purchasing by an appearance at a fresh Con- 
ference; that the rapture having taken place, it would be in the power of the 


‘allies to make what representations they pleased to Austria; that he had dis- 


cussed this point with the Emperor, and that their idea was, that if the allics 
obtained any success in the Crimea, Austria should be summoned to declare 
horself; that, in fact, the language to be used towards Austria must depend very 
much on the state of the warfare in the Crimea. 

TL then said that there was another point of view in which the question must 
be considered; namely, the probability of the acceptance by Russia of the 
Austrian proposals. Was I to understand that France was ready to make peace 
on the terms supposed to have been sent from Vienna? ‘ Yes,” replied Count 
Walewski, “ supposing always that we have obtained an advantage (un succes) 
over the Russians.” “But,” I rejoined, “ supposing # reverse—and a few days 
will probably give one or the other—what then?” “ Oh, then,” replied the 
Count, “it would be impossible to make peace on any terms, The honour of 
our arms would require to be avenged.” “* You would then,” ! replied, ‘be in 
this predicament ;—you would have accepted terms of peace, without a decided 
intention of abiding by them.” 1 did not think, I added, that such a position 
would be accepted by Her Majesty's Government, oF by the nation to whom Her 
Majesty’s Government was accountable. 

Count Walewski observed, that after the regulation of the third point, the 
war would naturally continue until after the fourth point had been settled ; “et 
then in the opinion of both Governments there were many parts of the first .oint 
which required reconsideration ; that the two Governments had further reserved 
to themselves the right of adding other conditions to those contained in the four 
points; that they might ask indemnities, &c. To which I replied, that if the 
question of Russian supremacy in the Black Sea was once settled, no matter 
how, hostilities could not, in my humble opinion, be continued: that an arms 
tice would be the natural consequence ; that Commissioners. could not be sent to 
examine the effective state of the Russian fleet while the opposing armics were 
‘n active conflict ; and that I did not believe that either France or England 
would comprehend the continuation of warfare after the preponderance of Russia 
‘n the Black Sea had been declared by the two Governments to have been 
reduced to safe proportions. 

T mention these details of a conversation, purely confidential, in order that 
your Lordship may understand exactly how matters stand here, You will draw 

‘our own conclusions from them, as t have drawn mine, but | am bound to say, 
that the more L see of this Government, the less do I conceive that any reliance 
can be placed in the stability of their intentions, Everything 15 done to meet 
the expediency of the moment. Not a lesson has been learnt from the past; 
not a thought cast towards the future. It appears to me that Her Majesty's 
Government must make up their minds on the consideration of what their own 
honour and interests require, and having done so, maintain their opinions in 
face of any opposition here. The more we yield, the more we shall be expected 
to yield. Firmness, tempered by digeretion, will, I feel confident, do more for 
the alliance than concessions which we regret, in however friendly a spirit they 
may be made.

Before closing this despatch, | should add, that in speaking of Annex B, 
Count Walewski evidently intended the second of the three systems mentioned 
in Lord John Russell’s despatch No. 83 of the 18th ultimo. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) COWLEY.

No. 808. 
Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received May 19.) 


(No. 573. Confidential.) 


My Lord, Paris, May 18, 1800. 

_ COUNT WALEWSKI gave me this morning, in confidence, to read, a 
circular despatch addressed by the Fussian Government to its Agents abroad, 
giving the Russian version of what has taken place at the Conference at Vienna. 
This document 1s evidently intended for publication. Itisof considerable length, 
and is of course written to display to Europe the magnanimity of the Czar upon 
the first, second, and fourth points of negotiation, and the return with which that 
magnanimity has been met by the imperious bearing of the wllies on the third 
point, As usual, nothing has been neglected to make Russia appear to be the 
real advocate and protector of the privileges of the Principalities and of the 
Christian subjects of the Porte. | 

Count Walewski ts occupied in drawing up an answer, to be published 
whenever this despatch sees the light. 
___ As his Excellency has obtained possession of this copy from a secret source, 
it is possible that your Lordship may not yet have seen it. I have requested 
him, therefore, to send a copy to M. Baudin, for your Lordship’s information, 
which he has promised me to do. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) COWLEY,

the honour to inclose,

No. 811. 


The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received May 19.) 


(No. 2382.) 
My Lord. Vienna, May 16, 1855. 


THREE days ago | received a message from General Hess, stating that he 
had only that day received from the Austrian officer in command in the Prinei- 
pality of Wallachia, a report as to the issue of an order which is entitled 
“ Standrecht,” and which is applicable to the Austrian army, and to all persons 
who should be guilty of secking to seduce them from their ranks by desertion, 
or in any other way, from their allegiance. ; 

General Hess stated that this order had been issued in consequence of 
repeated attempts of that nature which had taken place in the Principalities, 
and, in some cases, to the detriment of military discipline. He liad, however, 
heen in total ignorance up to that day of the issue of that order, and he had 
called for explanations upon the subject. ; 

I canieniataly applied to Count Buol upon the subject, requesting that he 

would explain to me the cause and the intention of this proceeding, which had 
heen reported to Baron Bourqueney 8s well as to myself, and also to Aali 
ashi. 
Conn Buol stated that the measure had not been reported to the military 
authorities in Vienna till after it had been taken; that he had immediately sent 
directions that it should in no way be made applicable to any foreign residents 
in the Principalities, and that im case any complaints. of the nature contem- 
plated by the order were made against any foreigners, they should be addressed 
to the Consuls or Agents of the countries to which they belonged. 

Count Buol stated the same to the Turkish Ambassador, who has reported 
the same to his Government. 

L have, &e, 
(Signed) WESTMORLAND.

ofthe Sth instant. But I pressed upon Count Buol the great importance of 
that despatch, and my anxious desire to receive from him a satisfactory answer 
us to the decision he intended to take upon it.

in that despatch as strongly as I could repreren it to him, and that he was

No. 813. 
The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received May 19.) 


(No. 204.) 
My Lord, Vienna, May 16, 1855, 

THE proposition of Count Buol, a sketch of which was sent to your Lord- 
ship in my telegraphic despatch of this day, is annexed to this despatch, 

Count Buol has felt that since the publication of the Protocols of the Con- 
ferences by Her Majesty's Government, the position of Austria in the eyes of the 
public would be rendered extraordinary if she did not take any measure to fulfil the 
words which he had himself used at the last Conferences, namely, that Austria 
would still zeck the means of bringing about an understanding between the 
Great Powers of Europe. Having in view, therefore, the fulfilment of this 
engagement on the part of Austria, which had now been made public, and having 
as as cond object to give to the final closing of the Conferences (if, indeed, they 
were to be closed) the dignity of an official form, Count Buol had drawn up the 
proposition now submitted to your Lordship, which he thought had the great 
advantage of not betraying that that perfect unity of ideas between Austria and 
the Western Powers which had been so manifest during the whole course of the 
negotiations had in any manner been disturbed. 

Count Buol, therefore, making use of the right to convoke the Conference 
which appertains to each of its members so long as it 1s not formally dissolved, 
proposes to state to the assembled Plenipotentiarics that, in accordance with the 
language he had held at the twelth and thirteenth Conferences, he had invited 
them to ussemble in order to submit to them the proposition which accompanies 
this despatch, all the stipulations of which had originally been suggested by the 
British and French Plenipotentiaries. 

Count Buol believes that the proposition will be supported by the Repre- 
sentatives of England and France, and that it will be rejected by the Russian 
Representatives, as it has already in part been rejected by them. Count Buol 
would then declare, on the refusal of the Russian Plenipotentiaries to entertain 
this project, that it appeared to him that there was no further object for the 
meeting of the Conference, which he would then formaily close. 

In communicating this plan to Baron Bourqueney and myself, Count Buol 
begged that our Governments should be solicited to consider its communication 
as of the most confidential character, With regard to the proposition itself, he 
pointed out to us that it was entirely based upon ideas which had emanated from 
the British and French Plenipotentiaries, to which he had added some modifica- 
tions of his own. Tle stated distinctly that the proposition, such as it was, was 
one which must be cither accepted or rejected by Russia, and that he would 
not bring it forward as one capable of bearing discussion and modification, 

Count Buol then stated that as he still considered that the project 
which had recently been submitted (as Austria’s ultimatum to Russia) to the 
British and French Governments and rejected by them, fulfilled the engagements 
which Austria had taken with regard to the third basis, he would not consider that 
the rejection of the present proposition by the Russian Plenipotentiaries in Con- 
ference would ectail upon Austria the giving effeet to the extreme obligations of 
the Trenty of the 2nd of December. 

Count Buol then said, that while he recognised the right of the British and 
French Governments to abstain from the Conference which he intended to 
convoke, he must remark to us that such abstention would constitute the 
rupture of the negotiations by our Governments, and would thus render patent 
bie dissidence of opinion which prevailed between them and the Government of 

Ustria,

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe ta the Earl of Clarendon.—(Reveived May 20.) 
(No. 335.) 


My Lord, Constantinople, May 7, 1856. 

INCLOSED herewith, for your Lordship’s information, is a translated 
copy of the instruction addressed by the Porte to the Roumeli Valessi, or 
Governor-General of Roumelia, for the relief of certain Christian villages in 
Albania, recommended to my consideration by Mr. Longworth, and to that of 
the Turkish Government hy me.

THE Ministerial changes which have recently taken place here are already 
announced bo your Lordship. Subsequent inquiries show that the resignation 
of Reshid Pasha was brought on by the intrigues of the French Chargé d' Affaires, 
and there is some reason tO believe that M. Benedetti was not unconcerned in the 
steps which preceded the recall of Mehmet Aalt Pasha. 

1 regret the success of his manceuvres, not only on account of their total 
want of foundation in 4 diplomatic sense, and the discredit which they entail 
on the Sultan and his Government, but also in consideration of their injurious 
jolitical consequences, and bearing on the position and character of Her 
fajesty’s Embassy.

Ministerial changes; iuder critical circumstances, their colleagues, who have to

According to di lomatic usage, M. Benedetti is not entitled to approach

of confusion and weakness.

769 


that the cotton-mills and other manufactories are almost at a stand-still for 
want of material to work with: and that the shortness of the supply of foreign 
produce is becoming generally and seriously felt. 

It is therefore with a view to increase the distress already existing that I 
have suggested the adoption of measures which shall restrict still further the 
trade of Russia. Iam, however, by no means prepared to say that the Prussian 
Government would agree to a demand that we might address to them on this 
subject, but 1 believe that they would hesitate in their answer if they were made 
aware that our demand would be enforced by coercive measures, and that in the 
end they would yield to the necessities of the case, rather than expose their 
merchants to complete ruin, 

If, however, Her Majesty's Government is not wepared to support the 
demand by coercion, it had better not be made, for russia will not willingly 
resign the advantages of her present position, and will hold to her independence 
as long as she can do so without exposing herself to material injury. 

On the other hand it may be observed that the effect of coercion on Prussia 
might work an advantageous change in our political relations. Prussian trade 
has, up to the present moment, derived benefit from the war; the Government 
desire the continuance of the existing state of things, but it might become a 
question whether the employment of coercive measures fo put down a trade 
chiefly advantageous to our enemy might nof cause ao reaction against the 
Government, 

It is certainly a doubtful experiment, but as the system of conciliation which 
we have adopted towards Prussia during the last fifteen months, has not been 
productive of good results, might not an opposite course be more advantageous ? 

Our forbearance is not valued as it should be; it may be considered a proof 
of goodwill towards Germany, but it has not called forth any corresponding 
sentiment on their part. - 

I have, &c.

M. Drouyn de Lhuys’ presence, it had been understood that the last word had

admitted that he was not so satisfied; still, on the whole, he thought the 
advantages of going into Conference were greater than the disadvantage of staying 
away. We could not prevent Austria making her propositions, and we had 
better show confidence in her by supporting them, After the late circular of 
Count Nesselrode, he felt certain that Russia could not accept the terms offered, 
and in that case she must break with Austria, 

I remarked, that I differed from him in opinion, and that 1 felt convinced 
that Austria would propose nothing, cf the acceptance of which by Russia she 
was not previously sure; and I asked the Count whether he authorized me to 
state to your Lordship that France was prepared to make peace on the terms 
now proposed by Austria ? . 

Count Walewski evaded an answer to this question. He said that all he 
wished to do at present was to consult Her Majesty’s Government ; that, as he 
had already stated, the Emperor and himself thought the proposed terms 
acceptable ; but that if Her Majesty's Government still insisted on a larger 
number of allied ships being admitted into the Black Sea, and if they wished for 
the establishment of Consuls, the French Government would then propose that 
we should state confidentially to Austria, that we would go into Conference to 
support her propositions as far as they went; but that, if they were accepted 
by Russia, we should afterwards put forward our own propositions for an 
augmented squadron and for the establishment of Consuls, 

As | was obliged to leave Count Walewski in order to. make some presen- 
tations to the Emperor, T had but little conversation with him, His manner, 
however, showed how little he was at his case in recommending the course of 
action | have had the honour thus rapidly to place before your Lordship, 

The Emperor detained me atter the presentations, | told His Majesty, after 
some conversation on other subjects, what had passed between myself and Count, 
Walewski; and [ begged him to inform me (in the strictest confidence, if he 
would) whether his own opinions were changed, and whether he really was will- 
ing to make peace on the terms proffered by Austria. His Majesty replied, in the 
most decided language possible, that nothing would induce him ever ta accept 
such terms; that he had thought M. Drouyn de Lhuys’ best plans had enough, 
but that these were far worse: but that what he wanted was to prevent Austria 
having any excuse for joining Russia; that, therefore, inasmuch as Count Buol 
had supported our propositions in Conference, reserving to himself the right of 
proposing others, if ours were not accepted by Russia, so, he thought, we might 
turn the tables and aecede to the propositions of Austria, ns far as they went, 
reserving to ourselves the right of asking for whatever additions the two Govern- 
ments night think advisable. Thus Austria would have no cause to complain, 
and no excuse to join Russia, ‘ For," His Majesty added, “ I must fairly own, 
France is not strong enough to carry on a war in the East, and at the same time a 

contest with all Germany.” His Majesty asked what J thought. 

I replied nearly us follows: That the reserve made by Austria towards us, 
was very different to the reserve France proposed to make towards her. ‘That 
Austria might fairly say, “if your propositions are not accepted, I reserve to 
myself the right of proposing less ;” but that we could hardly say in return, ‘if 

our propositions are uceepted, we reserve to ourselves the right of usking more.” 
Chat I must, moreover, express the conviction, that public opinion in England 
would not brook this sort of double dealing; if peace was to be made, the nation 
would insist upon its being made at once without erriere pensée, and, if upon bad, 
at all events upon comprehensible, terms. But that no Government could stand 
before Parliament having accepted conditions of peace, with the intention of con- 
unuing the war, That the intentions of Austria were clear: she intended, with 
or without us, to make propositions which she thought or knew could be accept- 
able by Russia; Russia would accept them, and would then wiih right say to 
Austria, “ 1 have aceepted what you think fair proposals, and you cannot declare 
acuinst me now.” Lut this came would be layed whether we went into Con- 
ference or not, and it seemed to me safer and better to refuse the Conference, 
than to establish points of difference between ourselves and Austria in the 

presence of the Russian Plenipotentaries,

arrangements have been made for the pay and provisioning of the Contingent; 
preparations have been made for the organisation of the force; and its 
Commander and several officers of high rank have long since arrived at Constan- 
tinople, But not a single man has been prepared by the Turkish Government ; 
and out of the Contingent of 20,000 men, which the Porte engaged to furnish, 
not a company nor a section is forthcoming. 

Her Majesty's Government had reason to believe, several weeks ago, from 
authentic sources, that Onier Pasha would not spare a man for service in this 
Contingent ; and this information should have been furnished by the Porte when 
your Excellency first called upon it to provide the stipulated amount of men, in 
which case you micht have succeeded in inducing the Turkish Government to 
look at once to other quarters for the troops, instead of continuing to rely upon 
a source of supply which it knew would fail; and your Excelleney would not

No. 828. 
Mr. Hudson to the Earl of Clarencon.—(Received May 21.) 


(No. 79.) 
My Lord, Turin, May 15, 1856. 


HAVING oceasion to see Count Cavour on business this morning, at the 
close of our conversation he said that he thought he had some cause to take 
exception to the mode in which the Sardinian Government had been treated at 
the Vienna Conferences. 

No communication with regard to what had taken place at those Con- 
ferences had yet been made to the Sardinian Government, who thought that the 
interests of the King, as one of the allies, had been treated lightly by the 10th 
Article of Annex B to Protocol No. 11, which Article runs as follows : Sa 
Majesté le Roi de Sardaigne est comprise dang la présente paix. Les 
relations commerciales et autres sont retablis, &e." 

M. de Cavour thought that considering the mode in which Sardinia had 
been treated by Russia, who withdrew her Minister from Turin on account of 
the reforms in the Sardinian Administration, who had never renewed amicable 
relations with this Court, and considering that m such cases us that of the 

present war, Articles such as the 10th generally contain a declaration as to the 
renewal of amicable and diplomatic relations, he thought, he sad, that the 
Article in question passed lightly over the position of Sardinia, and especially 
because, if the last part of the 10th Article was ever carried out, ‘le pied on 
les relations ¢ctaient avant la déclaration de guerre * would be a state of non- 
intercourse, as far as diplomatic and amicable relations were concerned, between 
Russia and Sardinia. 

M. de Cavour said he desired not to complain, hut to point these things 
out to me, and he added that he was eertain my Government would appreciate 
the conduct of the Sardinian Cabinet in the matter of the sequestrations of 
Picdmontese property in Lombardy ; that he had never pressed for an answer, 
that he had desired to give every time and opportunity to the good offices of the 
Ministers of the allies at Vienna to take effect ; that this question had heen put off 
from day to day by the Austrian Cabinet + but still, knowing the great interests 
at stake, he had not urged the settlement of this great cause of complaint to 

Sardinia, lest he might injure the progress of nevotiations and the hope of a 
general peace. 

| told M. de Cavour that T would report to your Lordship what he now suid § 
that I had last night received from your Lordship a copy of the papers relating to 
the negotiations at Vienna, but that us Thad searcely had time to open them, he 
could not expect me to discuss with him the merits of the 10th Article of the 

lth Protocol: and that I was quite willing to bear testimony to his desire not 
to embarrass the negotiations in question by bringing forward matters whieli 
solely affected Sardinia. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) JAMES HUDSON,

THERE is some discrepancy between the statement made to me, and 
alluded to in my confidential despatch No, a74 of the 18th instant, respecting 
the inquiries made by Prussia at Vienna with regard to her admission as a party 
to the Protectorate of the Danubian Provinces, and the report made to your 
Lordship by Lord Westmorland in his despatch No.223 of the 9th instant on 
the same subject. 

It would appear by the latter that the answer of Austria had been precise: 
and final, whereas my informant gave me to understand that a second communi- 
cation, more favourable to Prussia, had been made lately. 

On further inquiry, 1 find that this second communication had been made 
verbally at Berlin by Count Ksterhazy, and that it admitted the right of Prussia 
to be included in the Protectorate,

No. 833, 
Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon. —( Received May 22.) 


(No. 690. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, May 21, 1890. 

| HAVE have had-a farther interview with Count Walewski this morning. 

1 found his language somewhat changed from yesterday. 

He said that he had not yet sent the despatch which he had informed me 
he was about to address to M. Baudin, but that it would go to-day, 

If 1 understand his Ixcellency correctly, what he “now proposes to Her 
Majesty's Government is, that Great Britain and France should state to Austria 
that they approve her propositions if the force of the combined squadron to be 
forthe future in the Black Sea is increased to that of the Russian, and if the mari- 


PAG tapers sie So 


779 
time Powers are to have Consuls in that sea. If Austria refuses to accept these 
amendments, Count Walewski is still of opinion that the Plenipotentiaries of 
Great Britain and France should assist at the Conference convoked by Austria, 
but that they should declare, should the Russian Plenipotentiaries accept the 
propositions of Austria, which he considered unlikely, that they could not be 
satisfied with less than has been stated ubove. 

T observed to Count Walewski that his plan appeared to me far more caleu- 
lated to deteriorate than to improve our position with Austrian, What would 
infallibly happen in a Conference 50 conducted would be this: Austria would 
propose her plan: the Russian Plenipotentiaries would naturally ask whether it 
met with the approval of the allies, and we could not refuse to answer, We 
should be obliged to state our amendments and our objections; Austria would 
not support them, and the moment that this was ascertained by the Russians 
they would close with the Austrian propositions, and call upon Austria to separate 
from us. This was, probably, what Austria wanted. | thought a far better 
plan would be to state to Austria, in temperate language, what our position was, 
and how impossible it must be for us to subseribe to terms such as she proposed ; 
and to add that, if she persisted in convoking # fresh Conference, for which there 
was no real necessity, it could only be tor the purpose of showing the disagree: 
ments which existed between her and the maritime Powers, with a view of 
disengaging herself from the alliance which she had, partially at least, contracted 
with them. ‘There might be a hope in preventing the convocation of a fresh 
Conference, and that should be the object to have in view. 

Count Walewski admitted that, if Her Majesty’s Government objected to 
the course which he proposed, some such measure as that which | had suggested

My Lord, Paris, May 23, 1855. 

ON calling this morning on Count Walewski I found that le was in pos- 
session of the decision taken by the Cabinet yesterday, that the late proposals of 
Austria should be courteously declined. 

Count Walewski said that he was about to submit by to-night’s mail a fresh 
proposition to your Lordship, that. it had been considered by the Council, and 
had received the approbation of the Emperor and the French Ministers. This 
proposition, the Count observed, had at all events the merit of being short, 
simple, and easily understood, It would place the whole question 1nan intelligible 
manner before Europe, and he trusted would be acceptable to Her Majesty's 
sovernment. 

He proposed to state to the Austrian Government that if Count Buol, on 
summoning the Conterence, would agree to ask the Russian Plenipatentiaries 
purely and simply (purement et simplement) whether they adopted the principle 
of limitation, and would declare the Conferences broken off it @ reply was givet 
in the negative, that the belligerent Powers on their part would consent to 
continue the negotiations if the answer was given In the affirmative. 

Count Walewski remarked that if, as he believed would be the ease, the 
Russian Plenipotentiaries refused to acknowledge the principle of limitation, the 
rupture of the Conferences would fall upon them. Lf on the other hand, they 
accepted the principle, the Conferences would continue, and he should be quite 
willing to see further negatiations conducted ou the basis laid down between 
Her Majesty's Government and M. Drouyn de Lhuys during the short visit 
which the latter paid to London, His Excellency then read me ® telegraphic 
despatch containing instructions in the sense ‘dicated above, which he proposed 
addressing to M. de Bourqueney, if it met with the approbation of Her 
Majesty’s Government, Lasked for a copy of it for your Lordship's informa- 
tion; but the Count informed me that the Emperor had not yet seen it, that he 
should submit it to His ajesty later in the day, and that he would then 
transmit me a copy of that or whatever else it might be proposed to send in the 
place of it. II veoeive it in time it will be annexed to this despatch. 

Lasked Count Walewski, after he had developed his plan, whether | was 
to understand that he was willing to make peace upon it, observing, as I had 
done befure, that Her Majesty's Government would, 1 was convineed, be no 
parties to 0 proceeding ‘retituted either to gain time or to cajole Austria; that 
they would consider his proposition, and farm their opinion of it, upon its 
‘ntrinsic merits only, and with reference to an immediate peace, or to & cone 
Hnuation of the war. Count Walewski's answer was less precise thun I could 
have wished; but I gathered from it that much would depend upon the state of 
affairs in the Crimea, 

I then inquired, supposing Austria to refuse the proposition which his 
Excellency now suggested, what he proposed doing. le had evidently not 
taken this alternative into his consideration. Ile replied at first that the belli- 

erent Powers might themselves ask the question of Russia ; and at a later period 
of the conversation, he said Mhat he would be willing to leave to Her Majesty's 
Government the decision of going into Conference, should Austria persist 1p 
insisting on the acceptance of her original plan.

want usto take anch an imswer ‘yto consideration. Count Walewski's reply

receive inatructions by telearaph.

No, 841. 
Lord Stratford de Redclijfe to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received May 24.) 


(No. 343.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, May 14, 1855. 


IN pursuance of your instructions 1 have given to Licutenant-General 
Vivian, since his arrival here, all the assistance in my power towards the callec- 
tion and assignment to him of the Ottoman troops destined by the terms of the 
Convention to serve under his command. ‘The operation, like every other In 
this country, is subject to difficulty and delay. I cannot say that any apparent 
attempt has been made by the ‘Turkish authorities to evade the execution of the 
Treaty, and they always maintain that in some way oF other the troops are 
forthcoming; but it 15, nevertheless, true that the preparations for assembling 
the numbers agreed upon are still only in progress, and much remains to be done 
hefore the expected corps can be dul adapted to the principles of its formation 
and rendered fit to take the field with confidence. ‘The Porte, however, is not 
unprovided with plausible excuses, for the delsy: The transfer of so large @ 
portion of Omer Pasha’s army to the Crimea has ereated an unexpected diffi- 
culty, and the heavy demands wpon the steam-transport service for the convey- 
anee of French and Sardinian troops, to say nothing of our own wants, Increase 
the causes of delay. Before General Vivian's arrival, when 1 repeatedly urged 
the ‘Turkish Ministers to allow us to recruit, by means of our own officers, in 
the event of any demur, | was assured in the most positive terms that the Porte 
would fulfil her engagements to the letter, and that, if there should he a defi- 
ciency, whieh was mot expected, in the number of Regulars and Rediffs, the 
Porte would supply the recruits which might be wanted to complete the corps. 

As the matter now stands, the Seraskier proposes to furnish 15,750 
Infantry, 3,200 Cavalry, and 950 Artillerymen, with 4? guns, making in all the 
complement of 20,000 men. 

He proposes to take 4.937 men from the army of the Crimea, 826 Cavalry, 
637 Artillery, and similar amounts from the army of Roumelia, making together 
10,000 men. From Constantinople he offers 1,968 Infantry, 414 Cavalry, and 
118 Artillery, making 2,000 men. ‘These principally, if not entirely, are to come 
from Thessaly. 

The remainder, amounting to 7,500, he proposes to take from the new 
conseription of Christians, which, under present circumstances, 1 conceive to be 
an objectionable arrangement, and have therefore withheld my consent. The 
Seraskier has undertaken to attend to my representations, and I hope, with 
General Vivian's concurrence, to limit the number of Christians in the first 
‘nstance to 2,000 at most. 

The result of a further communication with the Seraskier this morning 18; 
that five days hence 5,000 troops will be ready for embarkation at Varna, and 
8 500 at Volos. 

Lam under a strong impression that Omer Pasha will not detach any part 
of his army from the Crimea, and that he will be countenanced by the opinion 
of Lord Raglan and General Canrobert. The Seraskier, in reply to my remarks 
on that hand, asserts that the Pasha will be obliged to submit to the orders of 
lis Government. 

It is thought adviseble to make arrangements for the reception of the 
troops in this neighbourhood in preference to any more distant locality. 

For means of transport, we are up to this moment quite at a loss. The 
Porte las no steamers at its immediate disposal, but consents to defray the 
expense of hiring them. In hopes of saving time, Lhave addressed myself to 
Admiral Grey, and a copy of my letter to him is inclosed herewith for your 
Lordship’s information. 

[ have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

WE will not object to. some roposal being made to Count Buol, but we 
earnestly desire that there should no question of the principle of limitation ; 
the principle alone is utterly valueless, and it would be fatal if the principle 
were admitted by Russia, and that we were to be entangled in discussions about

military success.

My Lord, Berlin, May 25, 1855. 

I UNDERSTAND that CountEsterhazy, the Austrian Minister at this 
Court, has lately communicated three circulars to the Prussian Government. 
The first, transmitting copies of the Protocols of the Vienna Conferences, 
Russia having done so likewise. The second contains regrets at M. Drouyn de 
Lhuys’ resignation, expresses confidence in his successor, and states that Austria 
holds to her engagements of the 2nd of December. The third contains the 
opinions of the Austrian Government on the despatch addressed to M. de 
Glinka, copy of which was forwarded to your Lordship in my despatch No, 200 
of the 18th instant. In this despatch Jam told that Count Buol invites his 
confederates in Germany to take no step in consequence of this Russian com-

A MIXED Commission empowered to superintend the application of funds 


appropriated to the prosecution of the war against Russia, being formed of 
members appointed on one side by the Porte, and by the Embassies of England 
and France on the other, the course at proceeding is proposed to be as follaws: 
|. The Porte au receiving # requisition trom any departinent would refer it 
to the Mixed Commission, 
9. ‘The Commission would make inquiry as to the object of the proposed 
appropriation, and vive or withhold its sanction according to the result. 


S01 


3. In the former case when contracts are to be made for the supply of the 
armies, the prices and qualities of the articles to be furnished would have to be 
brought under the notice of the Commission, which, on this account, must have 
power to examine the agents and merchants concerned, 

4, When issues are to be made for paying the forees, taking up transports, 
or, in general, giving course to any operat ‘on of war, the Commission must, 11 
like manner, have power to take commmzance of and to audit the expenses. ji 

5, ‘To insure the prompt transmission of supplies according to their desti- 
nation, and the due employment of the same, the Military Commissioners at 
the head-quarters of the Turkish armies should be authorised to correspond 
with the Mixed Commission through their respective Embassies at Constanti- 
nople. It would be their duty to report any delays, deficiencies, or abuses 
connected therewith, 

6. The Mixed Commission would, moreover, have power to inquire into the 
time and manner of effecting the several payments, with a view to economy and 
the Porte’s credit.
