Either we are prepared to give up the conditions which, with the concur- 
rence of Austria, we have hitherto demanded as the means of carrying out that 
object of the third point which consists in making the preponderance of Russia 
inthe Black Sea cease, or we are not prepared todo so. If we had brought 
our minds to despair of success in war, and were ready therefore to make peace 
on any terms which will at once put an end to hostilities, then the pro posal 
which Austria offers to make on our behalf to Russia would be inexpedient, 
beeause it contains the principle of limitation to which Russia has already 
objceted, and her objections to which she has now publicly announced in her 
circular of May 10; and if such were the hopeless state of our altairs, it would be 
necessary to make some proposal that Russia would be likely to aceept, mstead 
of one which, in the opinion of Count Buol, Russia is almost certam to 
reject. 

But if on the other hand, we still think the future prospects of the war 
sufficiently favourable to entitle us to persevere in demanding the conditions 
which we have put forward as affording a foundation for future security, then 
the proposal of Austria is open to serious objections ; because, though it con- 
tains the principle of u limitation of the naval forces of Russia in the: Bluck Sea, 
the principle is not applied ina manner that would be effectual for its purpose, 
and it does not contain the principle of Consular upon and supervision, 
which is the best security that the limit which may be agreed upon might not be 
exceeded without the knowledge of the Sultan and his allies, ' 

| must also observe, that the stipulation for a general amnesty 1s alto- 
wether omitted in the proposition of Count Buol, and no allusion is made to 
Surdinia, who is new in active cooperation with England anid France, and for 
whose dignity and interests they are especinily hound to provide, and who by her 
active cooperation in the wat is entitled to become a Contracting Party to any 
Treaty of Peace, | ; 

But what are the inducements held out by Austria to persuade us to 
empower her to make such offers on our behalf to Russia ? | 

There are, indeed, two inducements which might he held out to us as a 
temptation to make renewed proposals of peace to Russia. oe 

Nhe one would be, that the proposals intended to be made, being in their 
nature such as would be satisfactory to us, would on all probability be accepted 
by Russia, and that thus peace might be obtained on terms alike honourable to 
both parties and affording security against arenewal of war, fi 

The second inducement would he, that the proposal being always mits 
nature such as would be satisfactory to us, Austria would engage that in the 
event of its being rejected by Russia, she would forthwith take part with the 
Western Powers in the war, and would assist them in compelling Russia to 
accept the conditions so proposed, Citas 

But in the present case no such inducements are held out; the conditions 
are not in themselves such as would be satistactory ta us. 

We arc told that Ruesin would in all probability refuse them, and Count 

Buol informed your Lordship that this rejection by Russia would not lead 
Austria to give full effect to the obligations of the Treaty of the 2nd Deoember, 
by uniting her arms to ours, ‘The only consequence. then of the course of pro- 
ceeding which Count Buol proposes thit we should adopt, would be a formu) 
declaration by Austria that the Conferences were at an end, and, it is to be pre- 
sumed, a subsequent announcement that she had determined to mamtam her 
neutral position, aud to tike no part with England and Pranee in the war 

Undoubtedly, in the present state of things, Her Majesty's Crovernment ave 
no udyantuge in the eoutinnunce of the Conferences, and are prepared to concur 
in their being closed ; but an announcement hy Austria that she meant to take 


803 


no part in the war, would be most injurious to the cause which Austria has 
morally and politically espoused, and would on that account be deeply regretted 
by Her Majesty's Government. 

The value which Her Majesty's Government attach to the Austrian alliance 
is too well known to Count Buol to need any fresh assurances on this occasion. 
His Excellency must be equally well aware of the desire of Her Majesty's 
Government to put a stop to the effusion of blood and to the calamities that 
are inseparable from a state of war, and his Excelleney will not therefore doubt 
that his proposition has been anxiously considered by Her Majesty’s Govern- 
ment, and that it is with extreme reluctance they have arrived at the conclusion 
that it does not accomplish the objects of the war, and consequently does not 
afford the prospect ofa safe and honourable peace. 

It only remains for ne to express the regret of Her Majesty's Government 
that Count Buol should be of opinion, that by making a proposal which England 
ant Franee are unable to agree to, Austria has complicd with the engagements 
she contracted by the Treaty of the 2nd of December, 1854; but Her Majesty’s 
Government think that, upon reflection, his Excellency will scarcely adhere ta 
that opinion; the engagement contracted by that Treaty was, that if peace should 
not by a given time be assured on the basis of the four points, Austria would 
enter into concert with England and Vrance for the purpose of devising the 
means of attaining the objects of the alliance. 

The time has gone by, and peace has not been so assured. The failure has 
arisen from the refusal of Russia to agree to terms which Austria thought just 
and reasonable, and which, as such, she supported in the Conference; and the 
true execution of the Treaty of the 2nd of December would surely be, that Austria 
should enter into concert with England and France as to the best means of com- 
pelling Russia to accept the conditions so proposed to her, and of thus obtaining 
the great objects of the alliance. 3 

Your Lordship is instructed to read this despateh to Count Buel, and te 
furnish him with a copy of it, should his Execllency desire to have one.

Coronini has found it necessary to establish martial law. 

The proclamation is undoubtedly caleulated to disturb the minds of the 
people, to whom it was particularly addressed, and the Austrian General is of 
course bound to adopt all necessary measures for maintaining the discipline of 
his army. | i id 

But the Austrians occupy the Prineipalities as friends and defenders. They 
are there to maintain the rights, and liberties, and laws of the inhabitants. They 
are not there as conquerors, and they can lave no right to supersede the esta- 
blished law of the land hy the martial law of the Austrian uri. Tf the soldiers 
af the Austrian army are guilty of indiscipline, let them be punished by the 
Military Code of Austria; but there is no ground of right or justice by which 
that Militury Code can be applied to the people of the Principalities, 

Such a state of things as lias been established must necessarily lead to 
the greatest abuses; and when it is considered that the Austrian troops have 
already committed acts of violence and oppression in the Principalities, Her 
Majesty’s Government may justly request the Austrian Government to instruct 
its General to rescind, without delay, a decree which was established without any

No. 864. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.— (Recetwerd May 30.) 


(No. 372.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, May 21, 1859. 


IT js not my attention only, or that of Her Majesty’s Consuls in this 
country, but your Lordship's attention also, that has been called to several 
afficting instances of sanguinary violence and oppressive cruelty which have 
unhappily occurred in some of the Turkish provinces within the last ten or 
twelve months. 

None of these atrocities have been overlooked ; and measures, which ought 
to have answered the ends of justice, have, in most of the cases, been obtained, 
and put into course of execution, 

The enforcement of the remedial measures thus adopted by the Porte, has, 
however, been so imperfect, and so little security is still afforded against the 
eecurrenee of crimes which are no less discreditable to the Government than 
revolting to humanity, that I have thought it necessary to carry out your Lord- 
ship’s views more completely by bringing the whole question in a formal and 
impressive manner under the consideration of the Turkish Council, and, if need 
be, of the Sovereign himself. 

I might have performed this duty at an earlier period had I not thought 
that so unpalateable an appeal would meet with a better reception, and be carried 
through with more effect, if T allowed ample time for testing the Porte’s sincerity, 
and evinced a reluctance to embrace conclusions unfavourable to its character, 

The official note which I have recently addressed to Fuad Pasha contains a 
proposal to which I haope his seroe CY will accede, insomuch as it is calculated 
to bring into clearer light the particulars of criminality on the one side, and of 
remissness on the other; while, at the same time, it may help to realize more 
completely such further measures as may be needed for the vindication of 
justice, and the security of those who are exposed to administrative oppression 
or fanatical violence. } 

A copy of the note is inclosed herewith, and I shall take an early oppor- 
tunity of making your Lordship acquainted with the results of its presentation. 
| took oceasion some time ago to prepare the Sultan for the step which | had in 
contemplation, 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to Muad Pasha. 


British Embassy, Pera, May 14, 1855. 

IN times anterior to the present war, long habits of friendly intercourse 
between Great Britain and ‘Turkey, the confidence inspired by acts of mutual 
advantage and interest common to both parties induced the British Govern- 
ment on many occasions to point out dangers which threatened the Ottoman 
Empire, and to suggest improvements calculated to renovate its internal strength. 
Such counsels, offered with sincerity and not unfrequently pressed with earnest- 
ness, never failed to be received as proofs of cordial sympathy, and were some- 
times productive of salutary though imperfect results. In proportion as the 
progress of events brought out into fuller relief the adininistrative embarassments 
and political complications with which the Porte was destined to contend, the 
admonitions of Great Britain assumed a graver tone, and expectations warranted 
by assistance given with success in moments of need, were frankly and impres- 
sively declared, 

What was then little more than an effect of hearty goodwill, stimulated ly 
missing occurrences and ¢lirected to objects of future importance, is now an 
indispensable obligution admitting of no compromise and calling imperatively 
fur an immediate and eflicient conviction of evils not only discreditable and

or safety. The Sultan and his allies are engaged in common resistance to a 
Power whose pretensions have been rejected on a clear understanding that His 
Majesty's Christian, or rather non-Mussulman, subjects should be relieved by 
their Sovercign himself from all just causes of complaint and practices of 
oppression, 

The continued disappointment of an expectation thus seated in justice and 
good faith, nor less recommended by wisdom and humanity, must necessarily 
east a shade over the fairest prospects of the alliance, and ultimately involve the 
Ottoman Empire in complications of a most embarrassing and perilous 
description.

No. 865, 


Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received May 30.) 
(No. 476.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, May 21, 1855. 

L REPEAT what [ had the honour of stating in one of my previous 
numbers, that I do not feel myself justified in accusing the Porte of any 
unwillingness to fulfil the conditions of ler Military Convention with us, Some 
causes of difficulty and delay have been already conveyed to your Lordship’s 
knowledge. L must be allowed to add, that I had no instructions for collecting 
the troops before General Vivian’s arrival; that I had no definitive answer 
to my applicution to Lord Raglan for his Lordship’s opinion, or that of Omer 
Pasha; and finally, that no steps had been taken for carrying out the Vth Article 
of the Convention, which was of course to be done by persons of the military 
profession, 

[have now the honour to forward herewith a correspondence which has 
recently passed between General Vivian and myself. Your Lordship will find 
in its contents a full account of what relates to the Contingent under present 
circumstances. 

Lalso inclose herewith an extract or copy of a despatch received within 
the last few days by Fuad Pasha, from the ‘Turkish Envoy in London, 

Your Lordship will easily comprehend that the execution of the terms of 
the Convention is not facilitated by notices of a conflicting character, which 
reach the Forte from different quarters—irom the Mmbassy on one side, from 
Eupatoria on the other, and again, unknown to me except by accident, from 
London, 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

Major-General Shirley, who is to command the whole of the Cavalry of the 
Contingent, bas just returned from Eupatoria. Your Lordship will, [am con- 
fident, participate in the regret. I feel at learning from this officer that his 
Highness Omer Pasha has received an order from the Porte to detach from his 
army in the Crimea 5,000 men, to form a portion of my division. Ido not 
suppose that a measure so exceedingly inexpedient is at all likely to be carried 
into effect ; but 1 very much fear that the reception ofthis order by his Highness 
may indispose him to render that friendly and powerful assistance which he had 
proposed, for I will not disguise from your Lordship that L[ attach the highest 
importance to securing his Highness’s influence on our behalf, and feel contident 
that his selection of officers and troops would tend greatly to insure success to 
our undertaking. 

It occurs to me that your Excellency would probably desire to see Major- 
General Shirley; and in such case, I will desire him to wait on your Lordship 
at about 5 p.m., when, I presume, the mails will have been dispatched.

Inclosure 3 in No. S65. 


Lord Stratford de Redelijfe to Lieutenant-General Vivian. 
Sir, Constantinople, May 21, 1855, 
[ HAVE before me your letters of the 18th and 21st instants. | 
A messenger is just come in from England; another is going out. In con 


sideration, however, of your anxiety to have an carly answer, | set aside every 
other affair to aeet your wishes, But I cannot be expected to make this 
sacrifice often, 


The first point for decision concerns the number of troops to be obtained 
for your corps from Bulgaria, and the best place for assembling them, 

Lam under an impression that we had come to-an agreement in this respect 
during our conversation, in presence of General Mitchel, and that you enter- 
tained the intention of receiving that portion of the Contingent which is ta be 
provided here, and then proceeding, either in person or by deputing some of 
your officers, to take charge of that other and larger portion of it assembled at 
Varna. 

I am still of opinion that the fulfilment or this intention is the course 
best calculated to promote the object in view; and | am officially informed that 
the Seraskicr Pasha is prepared to offer to your inspection, and to place at your 
disposal, the day after to-morrow, 1,525 Infantry, two batteries of Horse 
Artillery, with 320 men, aud Cavalry to the amount of 170. 

[am authorized to add that a steam-vessel leaves this evening for Volos, 
where three battalions of Infantry and a regiment of Cavalry are ready for 
Seabartietion, amounting, if complete, to about 3,000 men, with nearly S800 
lores, 


The portion of the Contingent at Varna is stated to be composed of 3,930 
Infantry, 830 Cavalry, and 237 Artillery. 


It remains for me to notice that part of your correspondence which relates 
to Omer Pashia, 

Lagree with you in regretting that he should have been ordered to detach 
any part of his army from the Crimea, and in presuming that the order will not 
be carried into effect, 

I hope that he will he instructed to point out such additional troops as may 
be taken from the army in Bulguria, and placed at your disposal, together with 
the 6,000 already at Varna, 

In this sense | propose, with your concurrence, to advise the Porte, and to 
write through Colonel Simmons to the Otteman Generalissimo. 

Jam sorry to conelude, by stating. on the authority of Rear-Admiral Grey,

Baron Manteuffel to Count Arnim. 


(Translation.) Berlin, May 23, 1855. 

MY despatch of the 19th instant addressed to your Excellency, was 
already on its way to Vienna, when Count Esterhazy was good enough to com- 

munieate to me the annexed circular of the L7th instant, together with the 
despatch of the same date, likewise herewith inclosed, addressed to him. Your 
Excellency will therefore have been already enabled to give Count Buol the 
certain assurance that the Russian despatch communicated by M. de Glinka to 
the members of the Assembly of the Diet does not appear to us to give any 
cause, for the moment, for proposals or explanations in the midst of that 
Assembly ; and that we are also willing and ready to allow this document, 
always relating so closely to German interests, to be taken tito consideration 
likewise, in combination with the more explicit communications of which the 
[mperial Austrian Cabinet has repeatedly held out the expectation. 

But precisely because we reserve to ourselves for a while our judgment of 
the Russian explanations, conformably with the wishes of the Imperial Austrian 
Cabinet and in regard of the negotiations still pending at this moment, we cannot 
consider it as beneficial, nor even is there any foundation to view it wholly in 
the light and deseribe it in the way which has been done by Count Buol. 1 
confess my conviction does not enable me to follow the argument which liys 
down that Russia aimed at the disunion of Germuiny, when she gives in the face 
of all Germany an explanation which, as is said in the Austrian circular, fills 
even the Imperial Austrian Government with satisfaction; and when she holds 
firm to results, for the recommendation and attainment of which Austria claims 
a merit which I am far from wishing to diminish; although it would be casy to 
prove that Prussia’s constant endeavours also at St. Petersburgh to induce 
Russia to yield on the four points have been at least cooperative. 

That the St. Petersburgh Cabinet was desirous to assure itself prematurely 
of the decisions of the German Courts by the communication of M, de Glinka, I 
am inclined to doubt: as, in so faras I know, and as the terms of the despatch 
confirm, no counter-declaration of assent of any sort was provoked—nay, even 
expected, 

When, in former phases of the negotiations, the sincerity of the intentions 
of the Western Powers was, from the beginning, denied on the part of Russia, 
Prussia openly declared herself at St. Petersburgh against such procedure. She 
has done so also on similar oceasions in London and Paris, unmoved by the 
eurrent of public opinion, and she would consider it as opposed to the friunkness 
which she owes to her German allies, if she did not also in the present instance 
denote at least an impartial and unprejudiced appreciation required by the 
honour and interests of Germany of the step in question of the Petersburgh 
Cabinet. 

We are ready, as we have said, in the meantime to settle a fixed reso- 
lution, as to the part which it may, perhaps, behove us to take, as revards this 
especial point on a joint examination of the European position and of the 
obligations arising therefrom for Germany ; and then after a more precise know- 
ledue of the communications promised by Austrin, to take it into closer 
consideration [| will not here examine whether that degree of seeresy at least 
aimed at towards us, even in & greater measure than towards other German 
Governments, with which Austria has surrounded her negotiations with the 
Western Powers, corresponds with that confidence which she, on her part, 
continually claims fram us. On the contrary, | have expressly to observe that 
the Government of His Majesty the King, in full acknowledgment of the difficult 
position of Austria and of the endeavours muking to overcome them, has no 
intention to press the Imperial Government in any way for further com- 
munications. 

But, on the other band, the latter herself will certainly always bear in mind 
that if we, out of regard for Austria, suspend our reflections and decisions, we do 
hot yet thereby renounce the unimpaired right of the freest and fullest cxamina- 
tion in regard to the question itself, 

We stand, and with us Germany, on the basis of the April Convention and 
its Additional Article, |

Whatever has been negotiated, concerted, or stipulated beyond this pale 
without the knowledge and participation of the Contracting Parties—for imstance, 
we count among them the ‘Treaty of December Hd; the Protocols of the late 
Vienna Conferences; and those agreements which the Vienna Cabinet may 
possibly have taken on the basis of her late confidential exchange of notes with 
the Western Powers—are facts which on fixing our decision we should certainly 
have to take into the most serious consideration ; but which rightly ean have 
no species of reactive force on the sphere of our obligations, nor, 1m our opinion, 
on the obligations of Germany. 

We shall sincerely rejoice if that which Austria has to communicate to us 
coincides with our repeatedly expressed point ol view. 6 be 

We shall indeed, | need scarcely repeat, strive on examination of the matter 
to prove by wish, opinion, ane resolution that Prussia, both as an Eurepean and 
a German Power, is necustomed ta consider herself as theally of Austria But 
we claim this examination with unfettered and equal right for us and Germany. 
And if Austria reserves to herself to judge what, in her opinion, the mterests 
of Europe und of Germany demand, so likewise shall we have to judge at the 
proper time _that is, when our own interests and thase of Germany and of Europe 
appear to us U0 require it—how fat the Austrian Views; anc whatever the 
Imperial Cabinet my have concerted on that basis without asking our opinion, 
may be brought ta harmonize with our convictions, and are, therefore, of a 
nature to pave the wity for that active community of Germany and of her two 
Great Powers by which not only the endeavours of the German Govern- 
ments, but also the wishes and hopes of the nation, will assuredly find their 
realization. 

Your Excellency will express yourself to Count Buol in the sense of the 
foregone observations, leaving with him a copy of this. despatch ; and we con- 
fidently hope that he will find our words of candour 1m conformity with the 
seriousness of the moment, and will acknowledge there a renewed proot of 
our lively desire for a real and sincere understanding, and for a community of 


action founded thereon. 
I have, &e.

The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received June 2.) 


(Telegraphic.) Vienna, June 1, 1855. 

HAVING received your Lordship’s telegraphic message, T went to Count 
Bae to-day, with M. de Bourqueney, who had received his messenger from 

Pla. 

Count Buol will call the Conference for Monday. He feels himself pledged 
to bring forward his proposals; he has no doubt they will be refused by 
the Russian Plenipotentiaries, but in every case his creat desire is to remain 
united with Baron Bourqueney and myself, in the execution of our instructions, 
I read to him the telegraphic despatch { had received. He has little doubt the 
Conference will be closed by the refusal of the Russian Menipotentianes: to 
accept his proposal, At any rate ‘t will be for Baron Bourqueney and 
myself to close it by the statement that we can entertain no new proposal, 
since the declaration of M. Drouyn de Lhuys that Russia had refused the 
principle of limitation in every shape. 


No, 872, 
The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland. 


(‘Telegraphic.} Foreign Office, June 2, 1899. 

IT appears by your despatch of yesterday, that for some reason unexplained 
to us, Count Buol persists im bringing forward at the Conference proposals of 
which we disapprove. Vou will inform Count Buol that we object to this course, 
and your Lordship will take no part in any discussion beyond stating that 
nothing having been proposed of a nature that we ean accept, your Government 
considers that negotiations are at an end, and that the Conference is finally 
closed. 

You will not attend any fresh Conference, if one should be called, 

If you let me know directly after the Conference that it is closed, the news 
might arrive before the division in the House of Commons, on Monday night, 
and it will be most important to have it.

My Lord, Foreign Office, June 2, 1855. 

| HEREWITH transmit the copy of a despatch® from Count Buol to 
Count Colloredo, with its inclosures, which have been placed in my hands by 
Count Colloredo. 

L have told the Austrian Minister that, after an attentive perusal of these 
documents, 1 could only iain express my regret that proposals to which it wis 
impossible for Her Majesty's Government to agree, should have been renewed 
by the Austrian Government; but that the sincerity of our regret could not be 
doubted by Count Bual atter the many proats that [ler Majesty's Government 
had given of the importance they attach to the coaperntion af Austria i a Cause 
which concerns her more directly even thin ‘++ does the Western Powers, aun 
from which Her Majesty’s Government could not believe that her support 
would now be withdrawn, | 

| told Count. Collorede that 1 lad already discussed with him one of the 
propositions transmitted hy Count Buol, ane that the opinion of Her Majesty's 
Government upon it had been conveyed to your Lordship in my despatch of the

8th of May, and communicated to Count Buol; and that the other proposition 
having been forwarded by your Lordship, | would read to him the answer which 
was about to be sent to you. . ) 

After reading to Count Colloredo my despatch No. 205 of May 25 to your 
Lordshi », 1 said I wished to avoid all discussion that might be irritating, and 
which, from the tone of Count Buol’s despatches, | was led to think would be 
useless; but that there were some statements in those despatches to Count 
Colloredo and M. de Hitbner upon whicli 1 should take the liberty of offering a 
few remarks, : 

In the despatch to M. de Hubner, Count Buol states that Austria provides 
a progressive support of much weight and value fo ‘Turkey, by stipulating that, 
for each new ship that Russia may construct, the allics shall be permitted to 
make a proportionate addition to their naval stations in the Black Sea; and that, 
‘n the event of the Porte thinking itself menaced, it may call the allied fleets 
to its aid, 

Upon this 1 begged to observe that the real object of the third basis 
appeared to be lost sight of, and that, so far from causing the preponderance of 
Russia to cease, the proposed conditions would go te establish a competition for 
eA a between the allies and Russia. Such a state of things would not 

e peace, but a constant preparation for war, and a constant source nf uneasiness 
to Europe. | 

The Porte, { said, required no permission from any other Power to call 
upon its allics for assistance when threatened with danger. The Sultan might 


at any time do so of his own free will and pleasure; and if the proposal of 


Austria were adopted, and no effectual limitation were placed on the Russian 
fleet, that fleet would be a standing menace to Turkey, und the Sultan would be 
continually justified in asking for the aid of his allies, who would be in lonour 
hound to afford it. If the danger was imminent, the allied fleets night arrive 
ton late to save Turkey; but whether the danger Was imminent or prospective, 
the naval forces of England and France could only be summoned to the Black 
Sea for the purpose of repelling Russian ageression, and on every such occasion 
Europe would have to fear, and England and France would have to be prepared 
for, the renewal of hostilities, 

Count Buol in the same despatch says that the common efforts of the allies 
should be directed to limiting the political power of Russia, so as to render it, if 
not impossible, at least eminently difficult for her to abuse her matertal 
resourees, but that the cessation of Russian preponderance in the Black Sea 
would only be one of the means towards that end, as the diminution, or even 
the total destruction of that fleet would not alone he sufficient to deprive 
Russia of the advantages over ‘Turkey which she derives from her geographical 
position. 

ie 1 expressed my entire coneurrence with Count Buol as to the desirublencss 
of limiting the political power of Russia, but instead of entering upon anew 
at the practical solution of which was not even alluded to by Count Buol 

thought it would be more prudent for the allies to confine themselves. to the 
question at isauc, Which was how to give effect to the third basis, and to put an 
end to the preponderance of Russia im the Black Sea, and os yet no way 50 
simple or so effectual had been discovered as such a limitation of her naval 


forces in that sea as should render ther amount consistent with the safety of 


Turkey, 

Tn his despatch to Count Collorede, Count Buol expresses his firm 
conviction that the proposal of Austria for giving effect. to the third basis 
would be effectual, complete, and in conformity with the interest of Europe ; 
and his Excellency adds that its rejection by the Western Powers docs not 
permit Austria to cast exclusively upon Russia the responsibility of the failure 
of the negotiations. 

Upon this I remarked that England and France being at war with Russia, 
and having made vast sacrifices, must be allowed to judge for themselves on 
what terms they could make peace consistently with their honour, anil with the 
objects. for which such sacrifices had been made, and that the necessity under 
which they felt themselves of declining the proposals of Austria, proved “that in 
their judgment those proposals were neither effectual nor complete, nor likely 
to be for the advantage of Europe, But Russia, L said, had rejected terms that 
Austria thought reasonable in themselves, und necessary for the peace of Europe, 


819 


and that were not inconsistent with the dignity of Russia ; and because she had 
so rejected them, and because the Western Powers could not agree to conditions 
that Austria has since proposed, and which are altogether different and ineffectual 
for their object, it is surely unjust to Say that England and France oppose 
obstacles to peace, and that Russia is no longer exclusively to blame for the 
failure of the negotiations. 

I must also, I said, express my regret that Count Buol should now be of 
opinion that the proposal to limit the naval forces of Russia could only be 
considered as one of the conditions which the bellierents had expressly 
reserved to themselves the night of imposing beyond the four soints, and which 
the continuation of hostilities might render necessary ; for his Excellency, +o 
the best of my belief, had not regarded the proposal in that light, even when 
discussing it with the Plenipotentiaries of England and France, and he had 
supported it in the Conference, and had recommended it to the acceptance of 
the Russian Plenipotentiaries, as. the hest means for giving effect to the third 
basis. 

The object of the third basis is to put an end to the preponderance of 
Russia in the Black Sea; the limitation of the Russian fect in that sea comes 
then strictly within that object, and is not a distinct and separate proposal apart 
fom the four bases, and such as the allies veserved to themselves the right to 
bring forward, according a8 the events of the war might make it necessary. 

I requested Count Colloredo to assure Count Buol that we did not, as he 
supposed, exclude by anticipation any other project that would be equally 
efficacious ; but that we declined, and must continue to decline, all such means as 
are manifestly ineffectual for the objects we have in view, 

Count Colloredo observed that some sacrifice should be made to secure the 
alliance of Austria. 

[ said 1 entirely agreed with him, and that we had shown all possible 
deference to Austria, It-was solely out of deference to her that England and 
France had agreed to the four bases, and had consented to enter upon negotin- 
tions for peace; it was to mect the views, and to secure the egoperation of 
Austria in a eause which might be considered essentially her own, that England 
and France adopted a course which they would not otherwise have pursued 
until the events of war had more distinctly defined the relative position of the 
belligerent Powers. 

Count Colloredo then adverted to the great interests which Austria had at 
stake, and the risk she would incur by going to war with Russia without 
being able to reekon upon the material support of the Western Powers, while 
she would have to tear the ill-will, if not the hostility, of Prussia and of some of 
the German States. 

T anid that so far from questioning these considerations, Her Majesty's 
Government gave great weight ta them, and never failed to make allowance for 
the disadvantages under which Austria thought herself labouring. It was for 
Austria to decide between the considerations alluded to by Count Colloredo, and 
the engagements slic had entered into with the Western Powers; but whatever 
her decision might be, and whatever view Austrian might take of her own 
interests and obligations, no effort on the part of [Her Majesty's Government 
would be wanting to maintain unimpaired the friendly relations that now existed 
between the two countries. 

On the other hind, however, we must claim to be the best euarcliinns af our 
own honour and the best judges of our own ‘nterests, and Austria would have 
no just cause for complaint ‘ave declined to accept conditions which we might 
regard as inconsistent with our honour and ineffectual for the objects that England 
and France had pledged themselves to secure. 

Lam, &e. 
(Signed) CLARENDON, 


P.S.—Your Lordship is instructed to read this despatch to Count Buol, 
and to give him a copy of it should his Excellency desire to have one.

No. 877: 
The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Cowley. 


(Telegraphic.) Foreign Office, June 2, 1855. 

AS Count Buol persists, for reasons which he docs not explain, in bringing 
forward at (he Conference proposals to which we object, we think our Ministers 
should take no part in any discussion, beyond declaring that nothing having 
been proposed of a nature that we can accept, their Governments consider that 
negotiations are at an end, and that the Conference is finally closed, and 
that the Ministers should not attend any fresh Conference if one should be 
called. 

We hope that instructions to that effect will be sent to M, de Bourqueney, 


or we shall certainly be entangled in fresh negotiations, that can lead to no 
useful end.

Circular addressed to the Austrian Ministers al the German Courts. 


(Translation.) 
Your ; Vienna, May 14, 1855. 

THE resolution of the Government of Her Britannic Majesty to lay the 
Protocols of the Vienna Conferences before Parliament, makes the negotiations 
for peace carried on hitherto, public at @ moment when they cannot be looked 
upon as terminated. 

In the close of the Protocol at the twelfth Conference, Austria declares 
that she does not look upon the means of bringing about a solution of the 
negotiations relative to the third point as exhausted, and that she would regard 
it as her peculiar task to occupy herself with bringing about an understanding 
by examining the “ modalités.”” ‘The Plenipotentiaries of England and France 
declared that their instructions were exhausted, but not that the negotiations 
were closed, and when, subsequently, in the 13th Protocol, the refusal uf @ 
proposal of Russia's had been recorded, Austria determined to recommend 
conhidentially some new proposals to the serious consideration of the Courts of 
Parig and London, in which proposals she believes a loyal and entire fultilment 
of the guarantee of the third point may be found, and whieh His Majesty the 
Emperor, our Imperial Master, considers adapted to be laid as an ultimatum 
before the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh. 

The last Protocols of the Conferences have therefore left the negotiations 
still pending, and the Austrian Government for their part would have hesitated 
at this moment to emerge from the due reserve which in the interest of an 
object equally important to all, they had imposed on themaclves. 

Our jutention always was to inform our German allies, as soon a5 we should 
be at liberty to do so, of the entire course of the negotiations for peace, and 
we should have looked upon ib as incompatible with our sentiments as a member 
of the German Confederation, to have delayed fulfilling, this intention a moment 
longer than appeared to us necessary, out of consideraton for the uninterrupted 
course of the pending negotiations. The announcement, in the English Parlia- 
ment, of the production of the Protocols, made it therefore appear necessary to 
us to cause these documents to be printed, for communication to the Govern- 
ments of Germany, and you are herewith desired to forward the inclosed official 
documents, with a copy of this despatch, to the Government of : 

As we make this communication before the result of the negotiations 
(which are mot yet terminated) is determined, we attach to it no other object 
than the fulfilment of a due consideration towards our German allies. We do 
not at present combine with it any opinion on the present state of things, but 
shortly we may be in situation to lay clearly before the Governments of the 
German Confederation our views, whieh cannot be uninfluenced hy the answer 
from the Cabinets of Paris and London to our above-mentioned proposals. 

Believe me, &c. 


(Signed) BUOL.

No. 886, 


The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon. —(Recewed June 5, 7°30 a.m.) 


(Telegraphic.) Vienna, June 4, 1855. 

1 AM just come from the Conference, which has closed its sittings. 

After the opening speech of Count Buol, in bringing forward his project, | 
stated, after M. de Bourqueney, that I came to the Conference only at the 
- witation of Count Buol, and that I had no proposal to make. The Russian 
Plenipotentiaries desired to refer Count Buol’s proposal to their Government, 
and the inquiry was addressed to Baron Bourquency and myself if our 
‘astructions enabled us to agree to this. M. de Bourqueney replied that his 
Government considered the last refusal by Russia of any limitation of her fleet 
as final, and the Conference therefore as elused. I concurred with Baron 
Bourgueney’s declaration, and stated that my Government saw no advantage to 
be derived from the continuance of the Conferences, and that they therefore 
considered the negotiations at an end, and the Conferences finally closed. 

Count Buol concluded by stating that under these circumstances he 


considered the pledge he had given as fulfilled, and the Conference separated,

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received June 9.) 


CNo. 658.) | 
My Lord, Poris, June 3, 1855. 

| CALLED this morning at an early hour upon Count Walewski for the pur- 
pose of communictaing to him the purport of your Lordship’ second tulegraphic 
despatch of yesterday's date, which reached me in the night. Upon my request 
ing him to send instructions by telegraph for M. de Bourqueney's guidance 10, 
the Conference to be held to-morrow, analogous to those which your Lordship 
informed me that you had addressed to the Karl of Westmorland, Count 
Walewski observed that there was no aeeasion for his 80 doing, ag the written 
instructions with which M, de Bourqueney was already furnished coincided com- 
pletely with the views of Her Majesty's Government. 1 found, however, upon 
inquiry that, although those mstructions prescribed to M. de Bourqueneys S 
case Count Buol persisted in bis intentions to make the propositions which h ‘ 
been objected to by the belligerent Powers, to declare the Conferences closed, 
there was this difference in the manner of doing it: Her Majesty's Government 


desire Lord Westmorland to declare “that nothing having been proposed of 


a nature that they can aceept, they consider that negotiations are at an end, and 


a3 


that the Conference is closed ;7’ whereas M. de Bourqueney is instructed to say, 
“that since the principle of limitation has not been accepted by the Russian 
Plenipotentiaries, the French Government consider, &e."” 1 remarked that it was 
this very principle of limitation that Her Majesty's Government were anxious 
should not be put forward, because they feared that it might be seized upon both 
by Austria and Russia as a handle for further negotiation. 

Count Walewski answered, that in mentioning the word “ limitation ’’ he 
had taken it from your Lordship’s telegraphic despateh of the 25th ultimo. 

I replied that your Lordship's proposal in which the word “limitation” was 
to be found applied to very different circumstances. Her Majesty’s Government 
might be willing to join in a declaration with Austria to close the Conferences, 
‘‘hecause Russia had rejected limitation in every form,” but the matter assumed 
a different aspect when the Plenipotentiaries of the maritime Powers were called 
upon to make a declaration in opposition to proposals made by Austria. 

I will not weary your Lordship with the details of a conversation which 
showed, as I have had the honour to remark before, a fixed intention on the 
part of Count Walewski, whatever may be his reasons, to bring the word ‘* limi- 
tation” again before the Russian Plenipotentiaries. It was in vain that he 
attempted to persuade me that whether “limitation” was mentioned by us or 
not, it came to the same thing, since if Russia really meant to give way in this 
point, we could not prevent her taking steps of her own accord to show this 
intention. Iremarked upon the difference between proposals emanating from 
Russia, and hints—not to call them offers—proceeding from ourselves, and I was 
forced at last to observe to him that the instructions sent to Lord Westmorland 
were precise, and could not be changed in the present state of public opinion in 
England, whoever might be Her Majesty’s advisers, and it was for his Excel- 
lency therefore to consider whether he was prepared to show the Austrian and 
Russian Plenipotentiaries at Vienna that a difference of opinion, slight as it 
might be, prevailed between the Governments of the belligerent Powers. What 
wag M. de Bourqueney to reply, if he was taken at his word, and the Russian 
Plenipotentiaries offered to continue negotiations on the principle of limitation, 
while Lord Westmorland maintained that none of Count Buol’s proposals were 
satisfactory ? Having said this, | added, | had done my duty, and should press 
the matter no further. 

The conversation then turned on other subjects, but later Count Walewski 
reverted to this, and said—as if it had been a port already decided between us— 
that if he had the Emperor’s sanction, he should write to M. de Bourqueney 
to say, that he had seen your Lordship's instructions of yesterday to Lord 
Westmorland, and that he concurred in them. 

I must in justice to Count Walewski add, that throughout this conversation 
his Fxcellency was most anxious to make it appear that the French Govern- 
ment was ag desirous as could be that of Her Majesty to close the Conferences. 
He reiterated that the only difference of opinion between them was, respecting 
the manner in whieh this should be done, so as to prevent Austria having an 
excuse to retire from the alliance and to adopt the policy of Prussia. 

He wasalso careful to state, and he requested me to repeat it to your 
Lordship, that negotiations once broken off, the French Government would 
consider themselves unbound by anything that had passed during the Confer- 
ences, and free to act in any future negotiations in such a manner as, alter 
preliminary consultation with Her Majesty’s Government, might be deemed best 
for the interests of the two countries. 

I have, &e. 


(Signed) COWLEY.

No. 896. 
The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon —(Received June 9.) 


(No. 253.) 
My Lord, Vienna, June 5, 1855. 

IMMEDIATELY upon the receipt of your Lordship’s despatch No. 205 of 
the 29th ultimo,* 1 waited upon Count Buol, and, in pursuance of his desire, 
[furnished him with a copy of it in accordance with your instruction, 

Count Buol, after expressing his ‘satisfaction at the courteous expressions 
which your Lordship had employed in this despateb, announced his mtention of 
replying to it through Count Celloredo; but he remarked upon some points, in 
which he thought his intentions in making his proposal to the Conference had 
not been correctly understood, 

He stated that his object was, in fulfiling the pledge he had given as 
recorded in the last Protocol of the Conference, to nake a proposition not in 
any way in behalf of the Governments of England and France, but cntively 
independent of them, and at the same time go much in unison with the views 
they had put forward in the course of the late negotiations, that it was entirely 
framed in accordance with the project M. Drouyn de Lhuys had drawn up, and 
had mentioned in the twellth Conterence. 


* No. G0. 


837 


In preparing his own proposal, Count Buol saidl that he had not men- 
tioned the details, such as the nomination of Consuls in the Russian harbours, 
because he considered that this point was included in the agreement proposed to 
be settled between the Russian and Turkish Plenipotentiaries, and atterwards to 
be sanctioned by the general Conference ; and he considered it to be sufficiently 
alluded to in the wording of the 2nd Article of Ins Project, which stated that 
‘“seront Ggalement insérés les moyens dont les memes Plénipotentiaires seront 
convenus 4 l’effet de contrdler lexacte et constante observation des dispositions 
du présent Traité.” 

With respect to the stipulation of a general amnesty, and to the necessary 
mention of the position and interests of Sardinia, he considered these points as 
belonging to the general terms required for the completion of any Treaty of 
Peace, and it therefore was with no intention of excluding them that he thought 
it unnecessary to record them in his project. | 

_, Count Buol said that in drawing up his proposal, he had no intention of 
giving up any of the conditions which the Governments of England and France 
had demanded for carrying out the object of putting an end to the preponderance 
of Russia in the Black Sea, for his project was based upon the proposals of 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys. for the accuracy of which statement he could confidently 
appeal to all the Representatives of the Four Powers who had taken part in the 
discussion which had taken place on the day previous to the assembling of the 
twelfth Conference. 

With regard to the closing part of your Lordship’s despatch, which refers. 
to the fulfilment of the obligations contracted by Austria by the Treaty of the 
2nd of December, Count Buol said that this was asubject which was more 
immediately connected with the ultimatum which Austria had proposed to 
address to the Russian Government, in which was involved the question of an 
“mmediate declaration of war, and which he had submitted to your Lordship, but 
which it appeared you had declined, althougli he had not as yet received your 
decision upon the last communication he had made upon the subject through 
Count Colloredo, nor any acknowledgment of the receipt of the documents 
which accompanied it. He would therefore reserve himself until he received the 
answer he expected, before replying to your Lordship upon that part of your 
despateh. | :

follow until the Plenipotentiaries of the belligerent Powers had spoken. 

M. de Bourquency then declared that, since Russia had refused the 
of limitation proposed by the allics at a former Conference, he must consi

ment.

No, 902. 
Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received June 9.) 


(No. 685. Confidential.) 


My Lord, Paris, June 8, 1895. 

_M. DE BOURQUENEY has written to Count Walewski to state that the 
position of the belligerent Powers at Vienna is becoming one of extreme gravity, 
and that great care and delicacy will be necessary in order to prevent the 
Austrian Government from declaring their neutrality. Every effort will 
naturally be mare by the Russian Plenipotentiaries to obtain this concession, 
and Count Buol is evidently prepared to throw upon France and England a part 
at all events of the blame of the rupture of the Conferences. 

_ Count \Walewski wishes Her Majesty’s Government to take this state of 
things into their earnest consideration. Every effort should be made, he thinks, 
to prevent Austria taking the step apprehended by M. de Bourqueney. His 
Excellency has desired the latter to endeavour to ascertain what the intentions 
of the Austrian Government really are, and to caution Count Buol, if necessary, 


as to the consequences which a complete separation from the allies may have 
for Austria. 

_ The first question which will present ‘tself will be the occupation of the 
Principalities. It will, ‘1 Count Walewski’s opinion, be impossible to leave 
Austria in the possession of them, How could a neutral Power occupy a part 
of the territory of one of the belligerents ; 

Then it was to be apprehended that from neutrality Austria would wish to 
advance to mediation, Count Walewski wished your Lordship to reflect 
seriously on this position of affairs, and to concert with him the attitude which 
the two Governments should assume at Vienna. 

1 said that nothing could have been more cautious than the tone of your 
Lordship’s last despatches to Vienna, and that there was not @ word in them 
which could give Austria any pretext for separating from the Western Powers. 
I observed that, perhaps, one of the best methods to prevent the defaleation of 
Austria would be to hint that asa neutral she could not be left in possession of 
the Principalitics. 

Count Walewski seid that he was of this opinion also, but that the hint 
must be given with courtesy and delicacy. 

With regard to Austria taking the part of a mediator, I observed that 
luckily for the Western Powers there were declarations of Austria on reeord 
which showed that, openly at least, she utterly abjured any such pretension. 
Count Walewski replied that he had not forgotten this, and that during a con- 
veraation which M. de Bourqueney had lately held with Count Buol, in which 
the former liad declared, under instructions, that the French Government could 
never permnit that of Austria to assume such a position, Count Buol had repeated 
his former declarations. 

Count Walewski is of opinion that it would not be prudent at the present 
moment to press Austria to fulfil the obligations which she contracted by the 
Treaty of the 2nd December, She might find in such @ proceeding @ pretext 
for declaring herself absolved from them.

(Signed) COWLEY.

849 


tion, recognized the four points taken together as the only proper basis of a 
peace ; consequently it would be highly inconsistent, if not impossible, for any 
German State to make a separate arrangement with Russia founded upon two 
points only ; and that, as the matter now stands, the assurances of Russia are of 
ittle value; for in the circular note referred to, Russia plainly declared, that in 
order to give effect and binding force to the arrangements respecting the Prinei- 
palities and the River Danube, they must be reduced to the form of a Treaty ; 
and this is obviously impracticable, now that the Conferences are at an end. 

It appears, from the tenour of the Austrian circular despatch of the 17th 
of May last, that the mew Russian overtures respecting the first and second 
points, were addressed not to the Dict, but to the States separately. No doubt, 
more than one of the German Courts would be disposed, if they could, to 
accept such overtures; but itis highly improbable they would venture to take 
auch a step in the face of a positive resolution of the Federal Dict. The Federal 
Resolution of the 9th of December, was to this effect : 

1. That the Germanic Confederation, as an European Power, recognizes 
the well-known four points in substance as a proper basis for bringing about a 
state of legal and peaceful security in Europe, but especially adopts and holds 
to the first and second point in the point of view of German interests also. 

2, That the conditions of peace are to be followed up accordingly with 
energy upon the basis above-mentioned. 

So long, therefore, as the above resolution stands unrescinded in the records 
of the Dict, it is impossible to believe that the Russian intrigues will succeed in 
inducing any Germanie State to enter into a separate compact of a dilferent 
nature, 

It is reported that Austria intends shortly to renew her motion in the Diet 
for setting the Federal army in marching order, and that Prussia, Buvaria, and 
Saxony will oppose it, as well on the ground formerly taken,—that they are no 
parties to the engagements entered into by Austria with the Western Powers,— 
as forthe additional reason that Russia is willing to concede all that German 
interests require, in the manner above explained. The motion of Austria will 

robably fail in the Diet, and this will serve her as an excuse to the Western 
‘owers for not acting up to the spirit of the Treaty of the 2nd of December 
last. 

The mischievous effects of the Russian influence over the German Courts 
is here very manifest; they are indeed precluded from treating separately with 
Russia; but they are able to hamper the action of Austria, and even to neutralize 
the effect of the resolutions which the Federal Diet has actually passed for getting 
the troops in readiness, and for settling the basis of peace in accordance with the 
views of the Western Powers. 

T have, &c. 


(Signed) J. WARD. 


P.S.—In observing that the German States are able to hamper the action 
of Austria, 1 do not, of course, suppose that Austria has any serious intention 
of taking the offensive, but that she will find, in the strong desire for peace 
entertained by her German Federal allies, a pretext for not proceeding further 
in the spirit of the Treaty of the 2nd December. 

J. W.

Sir A, Malet to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received June 12.) 
(No. 69. Confidential.) 


My Lard, Frankfert, June 9, 1855. 

M. DE GLINKA, the Russian Chargé d’Affaires, has returned to the 
charge with the note holding out the observance of the first two of the four 
points to Germany, but this time as the price of their actual attitude, instead of 
the absolute neutrality demanded in the former note. 

The course now followed is, as lam informed, quite different. M.deGlinka 
has communicated with the President of the Diet before sounding the several 
members of the Diet; indeed, I do not think that more than one or two of those 
gentlemen, beyond the Prussian Plenipotentiary, have any knowledge of what is 
intended. 

Unless, however, I am altozcther misinformed, this second measure in the 
same sense has, as was the case with its precursor, been contrived at Berlin, 
between M. de Budberg and M. de Manteuffel, insomuch that I feel authorized 
to state that M.de Glinka has not received his orders from St. Petersburgh 
direct, but from M. de Budberg, and that the assent of his Government to the 
measure, in the form it now bears, has been obtained by telegraph, and at the 
earnest personal instance of the King of Prussia, 

The step is intended as a countermove to that which was projected by 
Austria, viz., to endeavour to bind the Diet to her policy by a declaration which, 
as Tam told, would be couched in a sense still holding out the expectation that in 
certain contingencies Austria might enter on a position of actual hostility to 
Russia. 

I think | may venture to assure your Lordship that no discussion will be 
entered into on the Mussian communication, which, in the form in which it is 
now tendered, the President will have to lay before the Diet, and probably in the 
Ritting of next week. Tt will then be entered on the Protocol, and the Prussian 
Minister will most probably endeavour to insert some phrase which may be 
specially agreeable to the Petersburgh Cubinet in the acknowledgment. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) A. MATET.

The Burl of Clarendon to Lord Cowley, 
(No. 583.) 
My Lord, Fareiqn Office, June 18, 1855 

LT HAVE to state to your Excellency, with reference to your confidential 
despatch No, G84 of the 8th instant, that Her Mojesty’s Government entirely 
concur with Count Walewski that great care should be used, and that no: etforts 
should be omitted, to prevent the Austrian Government from declaring their 
neutrality, 

If vour Exeelleney has not already done so, you will read to Count 
Walewski uy despatches to the Earl of Westmorland Nos, 205 and 211 of the 
29th ultime and 2nd instant, by which his Excelleney will learn that Her 
Majesty's Government have pointed out the great injury that would be inflieted 
bya declaration of neutrality upon the cause to which Austria lias hitherto given her 
moral and politicul support, and likewise the reasons why, in the Opinion of Her 
Majesty’s Government, it would be unjust to affirm that England and France 
were apposed to reasonable terms of peace, or that Russia was not exclusively 
Peneaatble for the rupture af the negotiations. , ; wee 

With respect to the eccupation of the Principalities and to the impossibility 
of leaving Austria in possession of them, asa neutral cannot occupy a part of 
the territory of one of the belligerents, Her Majesty's Government would desire 
to remind Count Walewski that it is in virtue of a Treaty with the Porte, and 
without declaring war against Russia, that Austria has hitherto cecupied the 
Principalitics, and there appears to be no sufficient reason for her not continuing so 
to occupy them. ; 

Austria has bound herself by that Treaty to prevent by force the return of 
the Russians to the Principulities ; and if she were now to evacuate them, either 
in compliance with the wishes of England and Franee, or in disregard ol her 
obligations to the Porte, there can he little doubt that the Russiens would 
return, that the line of the Danube would be menaced, and that the Sultan tor 


B55 


the defence of his territory might then think it necessary to recall the 
greater part of Omer Pasha’s army from the Crimea. 

Her Majesty’s Government are of opinion with Count Walewski that, in 
dealing with Austria at this moment, great courtesy and delicacy should be 
used; and they are accordingly disposed to think that a discussion upon the 
occupation of the Principalities should for the present be avoided; for no ques- 
tion 1s more likely to cause irritation to the Austrian Government, whose 
greatest fear is the occupation of Wallachia and Moldavia by a Russian army, 

It must, however, be borne in mind, that even if England and France 
possessed the means of enforcing their demand for the withdrawal of the Austrian 
army from the Prineipalities, Austria would be justified in resisting the demand, 
and in pleading her engagement with the Porte to defend the Principalities, 
which engagements were taken by her as a neutral Power and with the full 
sanction of England and France. 

It is possible, as Count Walewski apprelends, that from neutrality Austria 
might wish to advance toarmed mediation; but if is hardly probable that she 
would resort to means which would not advance the cause of peace, but which 
would stamp her policy with bad faith, and would entail a rupture with England 
and France. 

If, however, any ground for suspecting such an intention should exist, Her 
Majesty's Government are of opinion that Count Buol should be at once 
reminded of the repeated declarations he had made on the subject ; and at the 
same time he should be informed that England and France are now unfettered 
by engagements; that they are the sole judges of the terms on which they will 
make peace; and that they will resist any attempt, come from what quarter it 
may, to control the free exercise of their judgement upon matters which affect 
their honour ane their interests. 

Her Majesty's Government think that the attitude of the two Governments 
at Vienna should undergo as little change as possible. Their communications 
with the Cabmet of Vienna will, doubtless, not be of the same unreserved and 
cordial character as heretofore; but the ohjeet should be to maintain lriendly 
relations with Austria; and it should still be assumed that her interests in the 
successful prosecution of the war ure identical with those of the Western 
Powers. It may be prudent, for the reason assigned by Count Walewski, not 
to press Austria at the present moment to fullil the obligations which she 
contracted by the Treaty of December 2; but neither, on the other hand, would 
it be prudent to allow the assertion, that she has fulfilled those obligations, to 
pass uncontradicted. 

Her Majesty’s Government would strongly recommend that the language 
of menace should not be used towards Austria; butif Austria were to adopt that 
tone towards Englund and Vranee, she might be reminded that England and 
Franec entered into the warfor reasons of the deepest importance; that the same 
paramount reasons will compel them to carry an the war until the objects for 
Which it was undertaken are obtained; and that they are fully contident in their 
own strength for that purpose. 

Lam, &¢, 
(Signed) CLARENDON,

opinion that the interests af Savdinia should be represented by a Menipotentiary 
at any future Conference, 

The alucrity with which Sardinia responded to the appeal of England and 
France, the good faith with whieh she fulfils her engagements, and the suorificves 
she is-now making and is further prepared to moke, constitute a claim which it 
would be unjust not to recognize. It must, moreover, be borne in mind, that 
Sardinia has aeceded to the Treaty of the 0th April, 1854; and Her Majesty's

Government conceive that England and France have, by the third Article, con- 
tracted an engagement with Sardinian not to entertain any overture or any 
proposition having for its ubject the cessation of hostilities, nor to enter into any 
arrangement with the Imperial Court of Russia, without having frst deliberated 
thereupon in common. 

Her Majesty's Government concur with Count Walewski that it would be 
prudent to conform on the present occasion to the precedents established at the 
Congress of Vienna of is14-1815+ but in the Conferences there held the 
minor Powers who had actually taken port in the war, appeur to have had

Peace. 

Her Majesty’s Government would therefore propose to the Government

Russia; and that he shall be empowered to sign the General Treaty of Pence.

which the King and people of Sardinia naturally feel upon ths important ques-

things in Europe.

Although, as regards the last point, it might be observed that a guarantee 
to be enforced by five Powers might be attended with less embarrassment to the

(No. 724. Conlidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, June 14, 1859. 
YESTERDAY M. de Hiibner again pressed Count Walewski for an answer 

to the late communication from Vienna. | 

Count. Walewski replied: that until he had heard the opinions of Her 
Majesty's Government he could state nothing officially beyond this,—that if the 
Austrian Government desired to maintain the ground of ‘the @nd of December, 
the French Government would expect two things at least: that Austria should 
neither change her military nor her diplomiutic position towards Russia. What 
he meant by that was, that the Austrian army should not be diminished, nor its 


862 


cantonments changed; in short, that its threatening (** comminatoire’’) attitude 
should be preserved, 50 with regard to the diplomatic language of Austria, the 
French Government would expect that in the declaration which Count Buol was 
ahout to address to Germany, he should make as much light as possible of the 
slight difference of opinion. whieh had manifested itself at the last Conference 
between Austria and the Maritime Powers, and should declare that the under- 
standing between the three Powers remained unbroken. If Austria refused to 
do this, she would prove that the estrangement between herself and the Western 
Powers, which would be the natural consequence, proceeded from her. 

M, de Bourqueney writes word from Vienna that the late successes of the 
allies in the Crimea have had a perceptible effect on the public mind, and if 
continued, must materially influence the decisions of the Austrian Government.

Inclosure 2 in No. 937. 


Lieutenant-General Vivian to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Constantinople, June 4, 1855. 


DR. SARELL will have communicated to your Excellency the result of 
the examination of the Kilia ground, which took place yesterday morning. 
Staff-Surgeon Campbell was associated with Dr, Sarell, and Major-General 
Michel accompanied these gentlemen, 

Good encamping ground was found, quite equal to that which had been 
prev surveyed (if not superior to it) at some distance from Kilia, nearer to 

uyukdére, 

As this new grofind is free from all presumed injurious influences, 1 
propose that my eamp shall be pitched in the vicinity of the villages named in 
the inclosed memorandum. . 

I proceeded this morning with my Chief of the Staff and Deputy Quarter- 
termuster-General, to the ground proposed, and find it well adapted for our 
purpose; and as it has been pronounced unobjectionable a the medical gentle- 
men who inspected it yesterday, I request that your Lordship will be so kind as 
to cause the necessary application being made to enable me to occupy it 
forthwith, as 1 consider there can be no possible objection to the measure. 

| propose at once haying the road placed in a proper state of repair; and I 
beg to report to your Lordship that, within three days from the time when your 
Excellency may convey to me the necessary sanction for taking possession of the 
ground, 1 shull be prepared to receive the Turkish troops which I inspected 
last week. 

I require three 
troops. 
| beg further to solicit that the Turkish authorities may be required to 
pitch tents, without loss of time, for the troops about to be handed over from 
the garrison of Constantinople, and for such others as-may be expected from 
Volos aud elsewhere, , 

I shall be happy to send officers to aid in pointing out the exact spots 
where the tents should be pitched; and my officers will be ready at any moment 
to accompany any Turkish authorities sent to meet them. 

1 have, &e. 
(Signed) R. J. H. VIVIAN.

Inelosure 4 in No. 937. 


Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to Lieutenant-General Vivian. 


Sir, British Embassy, Pera, June 6, 1895. 


1 HAVE received your despatch dated yesterday, confirming, in substance, 
Dr. Sarell’s report as to the cround proposed for your encampment, and 
requesting that I will apply to the Porte for whatever may be necessary to 
enable you to occupy the situations named in a memorandum accompanying 
your despatch. 

I shall do myself the honour of transmitting your suggestions at an early 
hour to the Seraskier Pasha; and it may be hoped that nothing further will 
occur to impede the progress of your very important duties. 

[ learn, from M. Pisani’s report of his interview with Fuad Pasha and the 
Seraskier, that the Turkish Ministers are themselves desirous of fixing at once 
the ground for your encampment, in order to be prepared for the troops expected 
from Volos, which, on their arrival, will find no other place for their accommo- 
dation. [have to state, on the same authority, that the number of troops to be 
placed under your command here, in the first instanee, amounts, with the 
proportion of Cavalry and Artillery, to 5,000 men. ‘The five battalions comprised 
in the number are computed at 3,740 in all. 

In reply to my inquiries respecting the 10,000 of 11,000 men to be drawn 
from the army in Bulgaria, in order to make up, with those at Varna, Bourgas, 
and here, a total of 20,000, the Turkish Mt inisters express their readiness to 
consign the required number of troops to you, provided they ave not to be 
removed from their present station. 

It is unnecessary for me to enter into the merits of their motive for this 
condition, as they propose to meet you at Conshintinople to-night, with the 
view of discussing the whole matter, and expect from me, what T hope you will 
enable me to give, an acceptance of the mvitution. . 

[ have, &e. 


(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE,

informed that they were ready to hand over that number, provided they were 
not removed from their present stations. 

Your Excellency is acquainted with the reasons assigned for ther inability 
to withdraw further troops from that part ot the country. It Wks stated thit in 
the present aspect of affairs, and considering the large body of troops that had 
already been withdrawn thence for the Crimea, under his Highness Omer Pasha, 
it would be impossible to remove more men from that quarter; nevertheless, if 
the point were pressed, they would submit the subject to Field-Marshal Lord 
Raglan and his Highness Omer Pasha, and that they were prepared to be eruiced 
by their decision. 

[ think your Lordship will remember that, in the earlier discussion on this 
subject, when his Highness Omer Pasha recommended the withdrawal of these 
men for the Contingent, he proposed that their places should he partially 
supplied by troops from Bosnia. ‘Thus even his Highness Omer Pasha did not 
contemplate their removal, unless relieved to a certain extent ; and | gathered 
from Ministers last night that they had no means of affording this relief. 1 
certainly did not feel myself ina position to press the subject. Your Lordship 
will be better able to judge whether the reasons assigned be valid or other- 
Wise. i 

L consider that my aceeptance of the troops on the terms offered would: be 
altogether inexpedient and object ‘onable: it would, in fact, be simply bringing 
such troops on British pay, without securing their services to the British Contin- 
gent, since the troops would have to retain at their present stains. 

lt is possible that, if the point had been pressed, an agreement might have 
been entered into to collect these 10,000 or | 1.000 men-at seme given spot; but 
still the objection would have remained in full foree, that the troops must have 
continued in Bulgaria, and that they could not be removed without the consent 
of the Turkish authorities, 

My great desire is to have the force collected. “This is most necessary, for 
the purpose of the practice of manceuvring a large hody—a sysber in which 
‘Turkish troaps are defective. It is, aeait, most requisite that, at starting, f 
should be near my depéts, which must be formed on the Bosphorus or al-some 
seaport. 

If 1am to he removed inland, Pshall have to incur the greater expense 
of inland carriage, and to encounter at every (rh the difficulties presented by a 
want of transports for the conveyance of my stares, —felt already to such an 
extent in the mere conveyance of a portion of my troops from Varn and 
Volos. 

‘Thon, again, in the present condition of my Pay and Commissariat Depart: 
ment | have not offieers sufficient to detach for the encrows duties devolying on 
them: and lastly, L deen it of the highest importance tat at the commencement 
af the undertaking | should have the power of easy communication with the 
authorities ab Constantinople, aud part icularly that | should not be far removed 
from the benefit of your Lordships influence, which | am confident your Excel- 
lency must feel to be of the greatest Hpartinee to me. 

On the first formation of the Contingent, constant reference to the Turkish 
authorities will be necessary, and without your Lordship’s assistance Tam well 
aware that my difficulties will be largely added to. 

1 have endeavoured to submit a plain and eandid statement of my views on 
the subject; and having done so, | will only add that in your Excelleney's 
opinion there be 10 other wity of forming the Contingent, [will of course in that

My Lord, Vienna, June 13, 1859. 

WITH reference to my despateh to, your Lordship No. 261 of the 7th 
instant, I have the honour to report that His Majesty the Emperor left Vienna 
Jast night on his tour of inspection of the army at present assembled in Gallicia 
and the Bukowina. The news of His Majesty's arrival at Cracow has already 
been telezraphed to Her Majesty the Empress. 

His Majesty, who is accompanied only by @ gmall portion of his staff, 
‘ntends to complete this inspection of his troops as 7 vdly as possible and with 
the hope of returning to Vienna within a month. He will proceed as far as 
Czernowits, on the borders of Moldavia.

(No, 273.) 
My Lord, Vienna, June 13, 1859. 
A GENERAL report having circulated in Vienna, that the Austrian army at 


present assembled on the frontiers of Russia was about to be reduced, T inquired 
of Count Buol whether there was any foundation for this report. [He replied 
that no such measure as the reduction of the army was at present contemplated, 
but owing to the great amount of epidemic diseases, which had oceasioned a 
large mortality amongst the fron ‘t would be necessary to change the localities 
of some of the corps, and to allow a part of the reserves to return home on 
furlough, but subject to be recalled to their regiments whenever they were 
required.

No. 945. 
The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.— (Received June 18.) 


(No. 274.) 
My Lord, Vienna, June 13, 1855. 
IN obedience to your Lordship’s instructions f brought before Count Buol 
your despatch No, 2t1 of the 2nd of June, and I left with him a copy of it. 
Count Buol was gratified by the language in which your Lordship speaks, in 
this despateh, of your desire to maintain unimpaired the friendly relations that 
now exist between England and Austria, and he desired me to state that he 
would return his answer to it ina despatch addressed to Count Colloredo, which 
would be submitted to your Lordship. Count Buol, in reading this despatch, 
remarked upon the expression, in the first paragraph, of regret that the proposals 
to which it was impossible Her Majesty's Government could agree, should have 
been renewed by the Austrian Government; he said, he did not consider he had 
renewed these proposals, for they had originally been entrusted to M. Drouyn de 
Lhuys and to Lord John raeall who lad undertaken to bring them before their 
Governments; and it was only when the Austrian Government became aware hy 
your Lordships despatch No. 180 of the Sth ultimo, that Her Majesty's Govern- 
‘ent were not in possession of any written document containing in precise 
terms the proposal that Austria was willing to make, and that these Ministers 
had only supplied (by notes they be shvamnse: es taken in Vienna, to assist

their own recollection) the gencral basis of the propositions they had agreed to, 
that he (Count Buol) thought it necessary to forward to your Lordship the whole 
of the documents relating to his proposal, together with the explanations they 
required, 

With respect to the progressive support which the Austrian Pee 
provides tor Turkey by the gradual atdition to the naval forces o the allied 
Powers in the Black Sea upon the inerease of the Russian fleet, and ta which 
your Lordship objects as tending to establish a competition for preponderance 
Fetween the allies and Russia, Count Buol remarked that the present Russian 
fleet being only six sail of the line afloat, with a corresponding number of frigates, 
+ ould be no menace to “Turkey. To heeame one, new ships must be built, 
for vessels of war could not be brought into the Black Sea but by the Bosphorus 
and with the permission of the Sultan: this process must be radual, it would 
be watched, and a counter-force would be provided, $0 that no danger could 
arise to Turkey on & sudden, and Count Buol said he had hoped that these 
arrangements would have avoided, as long as the Treaty which had been proposed 
between the three allied Powers existed, any cause of uneasiness to Europe from 
any preponderance on the part of Russia. 

With respect to your Lordship’s remark that England and France must be 
allowed to judge for themselves on what terms they could make peace, Count 
Buol gave his entire adhesion to it, and stated that in so doing he was perfectly 
convinced that your Lordship would concede to Austria the same rights and 
latitude: but he wished to assure your Lordship that according to his belief the 
conditions which Austria had proposed would be quite as efficient for the ultimate 
object entertained by the allies as the one proposed by your Lordship and which 
he had notwithstanding supported +, Conference, although he had not agreed to 
make it an ultimatum, or its rejection a cists belli. 

Count Buol stated that with respect to the consent of Her Majesty's 
Government to enter into negotiations, and whieh he was convinced was done by 
all parties in the desire of attaining the object for which they were undertaken, 
he could only regret. that those negotiations had not led to a more satisfactory 
conclusion, but he said that Austria had not been influenced in the part she had 
taken in these negotiations by considerations of her own position, but by the 
views entertained of the best manner of bringing about a enfe and durable 
arrangement for the peace of Burope, and he said that your Lordship might rely 
upon it that 10 effart would be wanting on his part to maintain unimpaired the 
friendly relations at present existing with the British Government and the engage- 
ments by whieh those relations were secured, 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) WESTMORLAND.
