No. 944. 
Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recerwed June 18.) 


(No. 240.) 
My Lord, Berlin, June 16, 1855. 

COUNT ESTERHAZY eommunicated to Baron Manteuffel, at the end 
of last week, a copy of the closing Protocol of the Vienna Conferences ; and he 
has since delivered to lis Excellency, contidentially, copies of the last Austrian 
despatcties addressed to London and Paris. Baron ¥ anteuftel mentioned this 
to me yesterday, observing that, Count Buol invited the Prusstan Government 
to express an approval of the proceedings of Austria at the Conferences, main- 
taining that the policy af Austria had been dictated ly just and sound motives, 
and im accordance with the true interests of Germany, and he hoped, therefore, 
would be duly appreciated at Berlin. 

Buron Manteuffel said, further, that he apprehended the abject of the 
‘Austrian Government in this communication was to engage Prussia to support 
her at Frankfort, with a view ta obtain her concurrence in an appeal to be 
hereafter addressed to the Diet, to contribute towards defraying the military 


r . . L! n a ™ age 
expenses incurred by Austria, that twas put forwant in a spirit of conciliation, 


877 


and im order to discover the future intentions of Prussia, and frame her next 
communication to the German Diet accordingly. His Excellency did not give 
me to understand that the King had yet given any order respecting the answer 
to be returned to Vienna, and, to judge from his tone and manner in speaking 
of Austria, the feelings of the Prussian Government are not improved. At the 
same time, it would es that Count Buol desires to place the relations of the 
two countries on a better footing; and notwithstanding the bitterness against 
Austria which exists at the present moment, a change may come over the 
King’s mind at no distant period, for His Majesty is most desirous to get out of 
his present awkward position, and will gladly avail himself of the first favourable 
opportunity of doing so. ; 

(ndecd, Baron Manteuflel hinted the same to me to-day, in the course of a 
a short conversation which I have had with him, and said that he had just sent 
to Paris and London despatches which he hoped would be well received there, 

Prussia is clearly beginning to feel her loss of position amongst the Great 
Powers; her opinions may also be influenced by our late successes in the 
Crimea and the Sea of Azoff; and whilst she pretends to consider that her 
conduct entitles her to as much goodwill from the Western Powers as that of 
Austria has done, she is seeking to reestablish herself in the European concert. 
She takes advantage of the moment when Austria is apparently receding from 
her alliance with us, and loses no time in addressing a communication to London 
and Paris, with a view of reestablishing more cordial relations with the Govern- 
ments of England and France, but not, T fear, with any other purpose for there 
is no appearance of a change in her policy on the Eastern question, 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD,

No. $47. 
The Karl of Clarendon to the Bart of Westmorland. 


(No. 202. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, Sune 19, 1855. 


IF the Austrian Government eoneurs with the English and French Govern- 
ments in desiring that the alliance established by the Treaty of December 2 
should still be rnaintained 4 and if Austria 18 determined, notwithstanding 
certain recent differences ot opinion, to cooperate with England and France in 
bringing the war to a cuceessiul termination, Her Majesty's Government comtl- 
dently expect that the attitude of Austria towards Uussia will undergo mo 
change. 

Her Majesty's Government. trust that the Austrian army will not be 
materially reduced, ad that the troops, if moved trom their present canton- 
ments, may not he placed in such positions a8 would by their nature be incien- 
tions of a change of policy, 8 it i of great importance, with respect both to the 
conduct of Russia and the military operations af the allies, that Russia should 
not consider herself relieved from apprehension as to the course which Austria 
may hereafter pursue. 

The policy of Germany, and the support or discouragement which Russia 
may derive from that policy, will much depend upon the language held to the 
Diet by the Cabinet of Vienna; and Her Majesty's Government accordingly 
hope that in any communication which may be addressed to: that body, Count 
Buol will declare that the policy of Austria 1s unchanged, and that with respect 
to the objects of the war no difference of opinion exists between the three Powers. 

Your Lordship is instructed to bring these matters under the consideration 
of Count Buol. You will do so in the manner you may think most expedient, 
and in terms which will leave no doubt on the mind of his Excellency a> to the 
desire of Her Majesty's Government to maintain the most friendly relations with 
Austria; but it unfortunately Count Buol should decline to adopt the course 
which 1 have indicated in this despatch, your Lordship will not conceal from him 
that in the opinion of Ler Majesty's Government the estrangement between 
Austria and the Western Powers, and the responsibility of the consequences that 
may follow from that estrangement, will rest upon Austria alone, 

Lam, &¢ 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

No. 949. 


Circular Despatch addressed to Her Majesty's Representatives at Foreign Courts. 


Sir, . Foreign Office, June 19, 1854. 

ON the dth instant a Conference was summoned at Vienna by Count Buol 
the proceedings at which are recorded in the Protocol of which | inclose copy.t 

. This Protocol, together with the Protocols of the Conferences held at 
Vienna between the rth of March and the 26th of April, of which copies have 
been transmitted to you, will place you in possession of the details of the nego- 
tiations in which Her Majesty, in conjunction with her allics, has recently been 
engaged, and which, to Her Majesty's great regret, have not resulted im the 
conclusion of a peace with the imperor of Russia, 
ad consider that the present will be a fitting opportunity to state for your 
information and guidance the views of Her Majesty’s Government upon the 
negotiations which have thus been brought to a close. | 
ee The stipulations for which, while. reserving. to themselves the right of 
insisting Upon ather special and additional conditions, Her Majesty and her 
allies considered it more particularly incumbent on them to provide, were as 
follows : ele 

__ 1, That the exclusive right to interfere to certain extent in the internal 
affairs of provinees belonging to the ‘Turkish Eurpire, which Russia had in former 
times wrung from the necessities of the Porte, should no longer be exercised 
by that Power. ; 

2. "That the channel of the Lower Danube, and more especially the outlets 
of that river into the Black Sea, should no longer be subject to the exclusive 
control of Russia, but should, on the contrary, be confided ta the superintendence 
of delegates appoimted by other Powers as well as by Russia, and who should 
take measures for freeing and Keeping free [rom obstructions the great water 
communication of Central Germany with the rest of the world. 

_8, That the Turkish Empire should become part of the system of European 
equilibrium, and that meats should be taken to put an end to the preponderance 
of Russia in the Black Sea. | | 

wos That the pretensions of Russia officially to protect the Christian subjects 
of the Porte should be renounced, und that the Powers should use their 
‘afluence to obtain from the Sultan, by an act of his own sovereign authority 
the confirmation and observance of the religious privileges ol his Christian 
subjects. | 

A communication to this effect was made to, the Court of Russia at the 
close of last year, and wis accepted by that Power as the busis on which 
negotiations might he entered into. ; 

Le Negotiations were accordingly commenced at Vienna, bot unfortunately 
it is only on the first and second points that anything approaching to me 
agrecment Wis arrived at; for the refusal of the Russian P enipotentiaries tay

Hussia has asserted thata regard for her dignity precludes her from acceding 
ta the terms proposed by the allies on the third point. But the dignity of 
Russia cannot require that she should keep up in time of peace, and on she 
immediate threshold of her weeker neighbour, a foree: wholly unnecessary for 
purposes of self-defence, but enabling her at the shortest notice ta subvert the 
independence of that neighbour, and to change the territorial distribution ol 
Europe. Yet such is the position which Russia has maintained in the Black 
Sea, and which she has even now publicly avowed her determination not to 
renounce. 

It is necdless to dwell on the absence of any motive of scli-preservation to 
justify this determination on the part of Russia. Tt would be a mockery to 
pretend that she has anything to fear from the hostility of Turkey ; and while 
Turkey is at peace and free from threatened attack hy Russia, and while the 
Straits between the Mediterrnean and the Black ea are closed except to a 
‘emall and limited number of ships of war of the Western Powers, Russia has 
nothing to fear from the naval forces of England and France; while, on the 
other hand, the present state of things in the Black Sea demonstrates that when 
war exists between Russia and Turkey, and when the Straits are consequently 
open to all the naval forees of the Sultan's allies, Fngland and France, if suflicient 


time be afforded them, can collect in the Iuxine a naval armament strong 


enough to sweep from the waters of that sea every ship bearing the flag of 
Russia. 


Ttussia has indeed alleged that the preponderance which she wishes to 
maintain in the Black Sea is essential for the security of the Turkish Empire 
acaiist (he aggressions of other Powers: but it is not from the hostility of the 
Western Powers, but fram the traditionnl, and itis not too much tocsay avowel, 
policy of Russia, that the Takish Eampire has danger to apprehend. “The 
present war has been undert aken to provide securities against thease ambitious 
designs of Russin whieh menace the safety ob Turkey and the future repose at 
Europe, and in-short, to quote the words of a recent Russian Proclamat ion, to 
prevent, as fir as Turkey is conectned, the accomplishment. of the wishes and 
the views of Peter, of Catherine, of Alexander, and of Nicholas. 

The Western Powers, in conjunction with Austria, have considered that this 
object would mest effectually he secured by restricting within rensonaule bounds 
the power of Russia in the Black sea. They would have preferred as the most 
certain means to this end that Russia and the Porte should both renounce the 
right to maintain in the Black Sea any naval force beyond whit might be 
required for the mere purposes of police; but the Western Powers were willing 
to iequiesce in the maintenance by Russia of a limited and specified amount of 
naval force in the Black Sea, reserving te themselves the right of maintaining 1 
the aggregate, on their own purt, ‘i that sea a corresponding amount of foree ; 
requiring also, however, #5 ceeurity for the observance of such a stipulation, 
the further right to establish Consuls inall the Russian ports to the eustward of 
the Straits. But the Western Powers, who now hold exelusive possession ol 
the Black Sea, where the Russian flag dares not show itsel’, had no intention of 
proposing to Russia conditions derogatory to her dignity; and they never 
pretended to assert that ussin should be hound to aceept as Consul every 


individual whom they might think proper to appoint us such, and that she 
should be precluded from exercising the usual diserction as to withholding the 
exequatur trom any pe 


ron Hgainst whom well-founded abjection could be raised, 
Russia, however, has refused to subseribe to these reasonuble 
and in ther place she has otfered two echemes of modification of the Treaty of 
1841, the practical effect of which would be, that whichever of the two schemes 
the Western Powers might accept, those Powers would be obliged to keep up 
perpetually in the vieinity of the Dardanelles a large naval farce prepared to act 
in any contingeney which might occur. For according ta one scheme Kusera 
proposed that the Straits between the Mediterrancan and the Black Sea should 


at all times be open to the ships of war of all nations, ind therefore, of course, to 
her own Black Sea and Baltic fleets.

The effect of this scheme would have been, that Constantinople would at 
all times have been exposed to all the dangers which might have arisen from the 
sudden appearance before that city of an overwhelming Russian armament ; 
while the tranquillity of the Mediterranean, and all the great interests in that 
sea, would have been liable to disturbance by the action of a powerful Russian 
fleet, sallying forth at any moment from the Euxine. 

‘To guard against this double danger, the Governments of England and of 
France would have been compelled to maintain in the Mediterranean war- 
establishments in time of peace, and permanently to station their armaments at 
a great distance from their arsenals and resources; 80 that a peace concluded on 
such conditions would have been nothing more than an armed truce divested of 
the security which ts the essence of peace, and unaccompanied by that cessation 
of expenditure which ought to follow the termination of & war. 

According to the other plan proposed by Russia, by which the Straits were 
to be closed, while Russia was to remain at liberty to maintain an unlimited 
naval force in the Black Sea, theré might at all times have been in that sea a 
Russian foree equipped for war, and available fora sudden descent on the capital 
of the Turkish Empire, keeping alive the apprehensions of the Porte, and giving 
constant anxiety to Burope. This scheme would have equally imposed upon the 
Western Powers the necessity of maintaining in the Mediterranean a foree 
sufficient at all times to hasten to the protection of the Turkish Empire, at any 
moment when the Porte might require its assistance. 

Her Majesty's Government would appeal to what passed in the twelfth 
Conference, as recorded in the Protocals, ‘is evidence to show how well-founded 
was the determimation of the Western Powers ta insist.on the cessation of the 
preponderance of Tarssia in the Black Sea, as alone offering any real security 
for ‘Vurkey and for Europe against any ulterior designs on the part of that 
aevressive’ Power, For in that Conlerence the Plenipotentiaries of Russia 
insisted on substituting on the part of Russia a merely moral for a material 
ruarantes of the territorial interrity and independence of the Turkish Empire, 
and they refused to be parties to an engagement which the other Powers were 
prepared to contract, not only that they should themselves respect but also that 
they should cause, and, in case of need, by force compel, that independence and 
that territorial integrity to be respected by others. 

‘The refusal of the Russian Plenipotentiaries to acquiesce in any arrange- 
ment by which the objects contemplated by the third point could be effectually 
secured necessarily interrupted the Conterences, and accordingly the fourth point 
did not come formally. under diseussion. ‘The interest which Bngland and France 
have uniformly taken in the welfare of the Christian sulijects of the Sultan 1s, 
however, 4 sufficient guarantee as to the spirit in whieh the two Powers would 
have entered upon the discussion of the fourth point; and though cireumstaunces 
hevond the coutral of those Powers closed the door against that discussion, it 1s 
with no small satisfietion they have seen that sinee the commencement of the 
war, and since the ‘interference of Russia in"lurkish affairs has been made to 
cease, the Sultan lias eontinucd to ceive elleet to his benevolent intentions in 
favour of his Christian subjects, whose condition has of late been materially 
improved: by the wise and spontancous action of their own sovercivn, 

L cannot, however, wholly pass over an observation which fell from the 
Russian Plenipotentiary, and which is recorded in the Protocol of the cighth 
Conferenee, that the question involved in the fourth poiut wak one of conscience, 
and not of poliey. 

it would, indeed, have been fortunate for Europe if this plea of conscience 
had not been used as an instrument for destroying the political independence of 
Turkey. . 

By the Treaty of Kainardji it is provided, that the Sultan shall protect the 
Christian religion and its churches; and ib was wpon a complete misinterpreta- 
fan of this Treaty, but without even an allegation that ita stipulations had been 
violated, that Russia eluiined a right of interference between the Sultan and 
10,000,000 0f the Sultan's Christian subjects. HL the claim had been yielded 
to, and if a great wrong hol thus been perpetrated, the authority of the Sultan 
within his own dominions would, ine great deerce, have been transferred to a 
forvizn Power, and an inportint step would have been taken towartls the over- 
throw of the Turkish Empire, and the catablishinent of Russian supremacy on 
ike Pub SS, 


885 


Rurope, then, is indebted to the timely and energetic interference of the 
Western Powers for its preservation from the disastrous consequences with which 
such a catastrophe must inevitably have been followed. 

The Conferences of Vienna are now closed, under circumstances which 
preclude all speculation as to the period at which negotiations for peace may 
with any prospect of success be renewed. But when that period shall happily 
arrive, Her Majesty's Government will steadily keep im view the principles 
which have guided them throughout the past negotiations ; and while seeking to 
provide for the security, the welfare, and the happiness of the people of 
Wallachia, Moldavia, and Servia, and to insure the removal of the obstructions 
which have rendered the navigation of the Danube difficult and precarious, they 
will neglect no means of obtaining for the Turkish Empire, and for Europe at 
large, sufficient guarantees against the recurrence of the danger which it is the 
object of the present war to avert. 

In the meanwhile, Her Majesty’s Government have reason to expect that 
the Sultan will make liberal and effectual provisions for the privileges and 
interests of all his Christian subjects, 

You are authorized to read this despatch to the Minister for Foreign Affairs 
of the Court te which you are accredited,

No. 950, 
The Burl of Clarendon to the Margins df Azegiio. 


Sir, Foreign Office, June 19, 1855. 

| HAVE the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 15th 
instant, claiming on behall of your Government that Sardinian should be 
admitted to take part in any future Conferences having for then object the 
reestablishment of peace between the allies and Russia. 

Her Majesty’s Government entirely appreciate the motives which induce 
the Sardinian Government to desire that a Sardinian Representative should take 
part in any such Conferences; and they are happy to find, on communication with 
the Government of France, that the Emperor shares with them the satisfaction 
which they feel at having this opportunity of proving to the Sardinian Government 
the high value which they attach to the cordial cooperation of Sardinia in the 
present war; and that His Imperial Majesty recognizes with then the claim of 
Sardinia to take part in any future Conferences. 

1 have accordingly the honour to state to you that Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment, in accordance with that of France, conceive that a Sardinian Plenipo- 
tentiary should take a direct and personal share in all discussions in which 
questions affecting the special interests of Sardinia might be involved; that he 
should be kept fully informed by the Representatives of England and France, 
in regard to all overtures or projects of general interest which might be brought 
forward or discussed in the Conferences to which he might not be summoned ; 
and that, finally, the Sardinian Plenipotentiary should sign the General Treaty 
by which the conditions of peace are settled. 

In requesting you to convey this answer to the knowledge of your Govern- 
ment, I have only to add that Her Majesty's Government do not doubt that the 
Cabinet of ‘Turin will look upon it as a fresh proof of the friendly feelings of the 
Queen towards Sardinia, and of the value which Her Majesty attaches to the 
alliance with that country, : 

Dam, &e. 
(Signed) CLARENDON,

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received June 20.) 
(No. 756.) 


My Lord, Paris, June 19, 1855, 

AT an interview which M. de Hiibner had yesterday with Count Walewski, 
he communicated to his Excellency, in virtue, as Count Buol desired him ta 
state, of the engagement taken by Austria not to make any overture to Russia 
without apprizing the belligerent Powers, the copy of a despatch which the 
Austrian Minister for Foreign Affairs had addressed to the Austrian Envoy 
at St. Petersburgh, after the elose of the Vienna Conferences. This despatch, 
Count Walewski said. while declaring that Austria did not separate herselt from 
the Western Powers, was equally explicit in stating her determination not to go 
to war with Russia under present circumstances. 

Although the tone of this despatch, Count Walewski observed. was on the 
whole uneatisfactory, yet there was nothing init to which he could positively 
object, but he had at once protested against the construction put by Count Buol 
upon the obligations which Austria had contracted towards the allies. He main- 
tained that Austria had done more than engage herself to communicate any 
overtures which she might make to Russia. She had, if the Treaty of the 2nd of 
December was of auy value, bound herself not to enter ito any arrangement 
with the Russian Government without a previous deliberation with Great Britain 
and France. 

M. de Hiibner then read to Count Walewski adespatch addressed by Count 
Buol to the Internuncio at Constantinople. This despatch, while recognizing 
the obligations imposed on Austria by the Treaty of the of June, not to 
interfere, during her occupation of the Principalities, with any military operations 
undertaken cither by the Porte or its allies, expressed a hope that the Sultan, in 
consideration of the difficult position of Austria, would engage not to pursue 
hostilities against Russia upon the Danube, Count Buol added, that as this 
engagement, if known to Russia, might prove of disadvantage to the belligerent 
Powers, the utmost secresy should be observed about it, . 

Count Waleswki assured ine that he had at once taken exception to this 
demand on the part of Austria. ‘The utmost, ie said, that Count Buol could do 
would be to express a wish (un veen) upon the subject, and that if the demand 
was made, the French Government would be obliged to protest agamst it, 

After these communications had been made, Count Waleweki observed to 
M. de Hibner, giving him however to understand that there was nothing official 
in his remarks, that he could not conceal his regret at what he had heard; that 
the French Government was sinecrely anxious to maintain the Treaty of the 
Ind of December, but that they could not permit that it should be unilateral, 
that is, that it should bind the belligerent Powers while it left Austria free: the 
least, in his opinion, which Austria could do. would be to propose a prolongation 
of the term at which her obligations as a belligerent Tail commence, grounding 
her proposal on the fact, that the settlement of the third pomt had been 
admitted by all parties to depend on the events of the war, [Hf Austria was 
disposed, which seemed probable, to let the Treaty of the 2nd of December 
beeome a dead letter, and if the allied arms were blessed with victory, Count 
Buol must not deceive himself with the idea that negotiations could be resumed 
where they had broken off, nor indeed would Count Walewski answer that 
peace would not be concluded between the beiligerents alone, Ue should be 
sorry to sec Austria excluded from & participation in future negotiations, as 
Prussia had been in those now broken off; but he could not conecal from 
M. de Hiibner-that such might be the result of her conduct. M. de Hiibner 
exclaimed that Austria might also make her arrangements with Russia, but 
Count Walewski reminded the Austrian Enyoy that there were no ariugements 
to make, because Austrian was still at peace with Russia, .

My Lord, Constantinople, June 10, 1855. 

| BEG leave to remark, with respect to the first paragraph of your 
Lordship’s instructions No. 401 of the 26th ultimo, that on learning the late 
Seraskier's intention to require Omer Pasha to detach 5,000 men from his army 
in the Crimea to make up the number of General Vivian’s corps, | expressed 
my opinion that the measure was injudicious, and 1 intended to make a deter- 
mined pesistance to its adoption as soon as I should learn that the Turkish 
Comimander-in-chief had submitted his objections. 

in the second paragraph of the same despatch your Lordship observes, that 
I have given no reasons for my opinion that a large admission of Christian 
reeruits into General Vivian's army would be objectionable, I beg to reply 
that, in my humble judgment, the reasons are obvious, The formation of the 
Turkish Contingent is an experiment. ‘The Mussulman soldiers of this country 
are required for the first. time to act under the command of British officers 
unused to their habits, and ignorant, forthe most part, of their language, These 
incongruities endanger the success of the plan, though not, I trust, to an insur- 
mountable degree, and although they are well encountered in prospect of the 
ultimate advantages, they require to be steadily kept in view, and to be managed 
with address and firmness. The Christian enlistment is also on innovation of 
doubtful issue; the more hazardous on account of its being first adopted m time 
of war, and in-a manner ill caleulated to remove all feelings of mistrust and 
anxiety from the minds of the eonseripts, To mix up these raw and suspicious 
recruits with the Turkish regiments, commanded for the first time by British 
oflicers, would, | conceive, be to introduce into General Viviaw’s corps a fresh 
element of difficulty and an additional hazard of failure, 

When the conscription is completed, and the reeruits have received the 
first rudiments of military discipline, they may be more fitly united with the 
Turkish Contingent, itself by that time habituated to the new organization, and 
then indeed, it seems to me, and I believe General Vivian agrees in the opinion, 
that much mutual advantage muy accrue from the junction of Christians with 
Mussulmans under British command, 

An earlier attempt might end in failure at drill, or in disaster before the 
enemy. 

I have, &e. 


(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFPE,

Inclosure in No. 966. 
Memorandum upon Military Schools. 


(Translation.) 
‘ETE, establishments for military education 10 general are classed under 
three different heads, viz. :— 

1. Those intended for the education of non-commissioned officers: Ist, the 
Junior Military School; Znd, the Senior Military School; 3rd, the School for 
Companies. 

9. ‘Those intended for the education of pupils as officers; the institutions 
for Cadets; the Military Academics: 

4 ‘Those intended purtly for i special course of education, and partly for 
completing aud perfecting the previous education of officers: lst, the Military 
Teachers’ School; 2nd, that for the high course of Artillery and Engineering 
S.d, the School for Military ‘Tactics: 

Fach of the two first “nentioned class of schools, though forming inde- 

endent catublishments, are “1 Tuutnal connection 5 thie poe af the Junior 
Kchool being admitted, when they have distinguished t iemselves, Into the 
institution for Cadets, and in the same manner the best pupils of the ‘Technical 
Company 5 Schoals—that 16 tO Ay, af the Artillery, Engineers, Pioneers, 
Flotilla, and Naval Schools,—are transferred to the Academy, after which they 
huye a claim to be appointed inte the service as SUpertor officers. On the other 
hand, those pupils whose progress lus not been satisfactory are gent bick from 
the Cadet Institution and the Academy to the Senior Educational Schools and 
the School for Compunics. 

The students in the military educational establishments are either on the 
foundation, oF paying-students. 'The former are from ihe military in general, 
and students from military departments. 

In general it is & rule that the children of superior officers are left. under 
parental charge till the age of eleven years, while those of privates come under 
the charge of the Stute on reaching their eighth year. 

On payment every Austrian subject, with the requisite conditions, has @ 
claim to adinisssion. The appombtment ta be placed on the foundation of any 
af the military establishments rests with the * Army-ober-command. The 
presentation 10 the institution of Cudets and the Academies 1s reserved to His 
Majesty the imnperor. | 

A pupil once removed from one of these military establishments, for what- 
ever cause ib may be, 18 under na pretest to receive an officer's commission

COUNT COLLOREDO has placed in my hands a copy of a despatch 
from Count Buol, of which a copy is herewith inclosed, 

I told Count Colloredo that [ wished to avoid all irritating discussion ; and 
that, although I did not doubt that Count Buol considered that Austria had 
fulfilled the engagements of the Treaty of December 2, yet 1 must be permitted 
to adhere to the opinion which | had already expressed upon the subject; and I 
begged to remind Count Colloredo that Austria had only intended to make a 
casus belli of What was called'an “ ultimatum’ to Russia, but which was wholly 
unacceptable to England and France: and that with respect to the latter 


proposal, Count Buol had distinctly declared that its rejection by Russia would 
id that her position with respect to 


not constitute a casus felli tor Austria, i 
Russia would not undergo any change in consequence of such rejection.
